items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that the 'carrying out' on Shabbat involves two categories that are four inside and two that are four outside. It then illustrates with cases of a poor person and a householder, detailing who is liable and who is exempt in various scenarios of reaching and transferring objects.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating the general rule: the 'carrying out' on Shabbat involves two categories that are four inside and two that are four outside.
The mishnah asks 'How so?' to introduce the illustrative cases.
The mishnah presents the first scenario: the poor person reaches inside and gives to or takes from the householder — the poor person is liable (חייב) and the householder is exempt (פטור).
The mishnah presents the second scenario: the householder reaches outside and gives to or takes from the poor person — the householder is liable (חייב) and the poor person is exempt (פטור).
The mishnah presents the third scenario: the poor person reaches inside and the householder takes from or gives into his hand — both are exempt (פטורין).
The mishnah presents the fourth scenario: the householder reaches outside and the poor person takes from or gives into his hand — both are exempt (פטורין).

items.text: פתיחת הגמרא: השוואה לשבועות
items.text_en: Gemara's opening reference
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel mishnah from Tractate Shevuot that uses a similar formulation: 'Shevuot, two that are four.' This begins the Gemara's analysis of the mishnah's structure.
items.desc: הגמרא פותחת בציטוט משנה ממסכת שבועות, האומרת 'שבועות שתים שהן ארבע', ומתחילה להשוות בין המשניות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a parallel mishnah from Tractate Shevuot that uses the same structural formulation 'two that are four', beginning its analysis of the mishnah's pattern.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בציטוט המשנה ממסכת שבועות ומתחילה להשוות בין המשניות.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three sets of laws: knowledge of impurity (two that are four), appearances of plagues (two that are four), and the 'hotza'ot' of Shabbat (two that are four). This sets up the Gemara's question about the differing formulations.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing three sets of laws: knowledge of impurity (two that are four), appearances of plagues (two that are four), and the Shabbat hotza'ot (two that are four).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's formulation
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's formulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah on Shabbat only says 'two that are four' without specifying 'inside' and 'outside' as in the other Mishnayot, while the other Mishnayot do specify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah on Shabbat only says 'two that are four' without specifying 'inside' and 'outside' as in the other Mishnayot.

items.text: First answer: Shabbat is primary, so it includes both avot and toladot
items.text_en: First answer: Shabbat is primary, so it includes both avot and toladot
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that since Shabbat is the main topic, the Mishnah lists both primary categories (avot) and subcategories (toladot), whereas the other Mishnayot are not primary and only list avot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that since Shabbat is the main topic, the Mishnah lists both primary categories (אבות) and subcategories (תולדות), whereas the other Mishnayot are not primary and only list אבות.

items.text: Objection: Avot are only two, not four
items.text_en: Objection: Avot are only two, not four
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the primary categories (avot) are only two (hotza'ot), not four, so the Mishnah's 'two that are four' cannot refer to avot and toladot. It then suggests that perhaps some are for liability and some for exemption, but rejects this because the parallel to plagues (all for liability) shows all must be for liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the primary categories (אבות) are only two (יציאות), not four, so the Mishnah's 'two that are four' cannot refer to avot and toladot.
The Gemara suggests that perhaps some are for liability and some for exemption, but rejects this because the parallel to plagues (all for liability) shows all must be for liability.

items.text: Rav Pappa's answer: liability and exemption
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer: liability and exemption
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that since Shabbat is primary, the Mishnah lists both liable and exempt cases, whereas the other Mishnayot only list liable cases. The two categories are the two for taking out and two for bringing in.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that since Shabbat is the primary subject, the Mishnah teaches both liable and exempt cases, whereas elsewhere it teaches only liable cases.
The Gemara questions what the liable cases are, noting that 'יציאות' (takings out) are only two, not four.
Rav Pappa clarifies that the four cases consist of two for taking out and two for bringing in.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof: 'hotza'ah' includes bringing in
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof: 'hotza'ah' includes bringing in
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Tanna calls bringing in also 'hotza'ah', as proven from a Mishnah where 'hamotzi' includes bringing in from public to private domain. The reason is that any removal of an object from its place is called 'hotza'ah'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that the Tanna also calls bringing in 'hotza'ah', citing a Mishnah where 'hamotzi' includes bringing from public to private domain.
The Gemara proves Rav Ashi's claim from the Mishnah that says 'hamotzi' is liable, which includes bringing in from public to private domain, and still calls it 'hotza'ah'.
The Gemara explains the reason: any removal of an object from its place is called 'hotza'ah' by the Tanna.

items.text: Ravina's support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Ravina's support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Ravina notes that the Mishnah itself supports this, as it says 'hotza'ot' and immediately explains bringing in. This is conclusive.

sub.desc_en: Ravina argues that the Mishnah itself supports the interpretation, because it lists 'יציאות' (carrying out) and immediately explains bringing in, proving the point conclusively.

items.text: Rava's alternative: 'reshuyot' and the counting objection
items.text_en: Rava's alternative: 'reshuyot' and the counting objection
items.desc_en: Rava says the Mishnah actually says 'reshuyot' (domains), not 'hotza'ot'. Rav Matna objects that there are eight domains, not two, and Abaye counters that by that logic there would be sixteen. The Gemara begins to resolve this, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah actually teaches 'reshuyot' (domains) rather than 'hotza'ot', i.e. 'the domains of Shabbat are two'.
Rav Matna objects to Abaye: according to the system of domains, there should be eight domains of Shabbat, not two; moreover by the logical extension there would be twelve domains.
Abaye retorts: according to your (Rav Matna's) own reasoning, that would yield sixteen domains, not twelve.
Abaye begins to resolve the counting objection, saying 'this is not difficult — for...', but the text is cut off at this point.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah's omission
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah's omission
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's first clause (Bava d'Reisha) does not include the category 'exempt and permitted', but the second clause (Bava d'Siefa) presents a difficulty because it states 'exempt but forbidden'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's first clause (Bava d'Reisha) does not include the category 'exempt and permitted', but the second clause (Bava d'Siefa) presents a difficulty because it states 'exempt but forbidden'.

items.text: Shmuel's statement on exemptions
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement on exemptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's rule that all Shabbat exemptions are 'exempt but forbidden' except for three specific cases: trapping a deer, trapping a snake, and lancing a boil, which are 'exempt and permitted'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is any case of 'exempt and permitted' on Shabbat, citing Shmuel's statement that all exemptions on Shabbat are 'exempt but forbidden' except for three specific cases.
Shmuel answers: All Shabbat exemptions are 'exempt but forbidden' except three: trapping a deer, trapping a snake, and lancing a boil — these are 'exempt and permitted'.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of Shmuel's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of Shmuel's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel's statement was only necessary regarding exemptions that involve an action (ma'aseh), but there are many exemptions without an action that are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel's statement only referred to exemptions involving an action (מעשה), while exemptions without an action are numerous.

items.text: Counting the exemptions
items.text_en: Counting the exemptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that there are thirteen exemptions in the Mishnah, and explains that the count includes only those that could lead to a sin-offering, excluding those that cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's list still totals only twelve, and resolves that it counts only exemptions that could lead to a sin-offering (חטאת), not those that cannot.
The Gemara answers that the count includes only exemptions that could lead to a sin-offering (חיוב חטאת), excluding those that cannot.

items.text: Principle of joint liability for Shabbat labor
items.text_en: Principle of joint liability for Shabbat labor
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the case where two people perform a forbidden labor together and are exempt, citing Rabbi's derivation from the verse 'ba'asotah' and a supporting statement from Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the case of 'both are exempt' when a forbidden labor was performed between them, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives from the verse 'מעם הארץ בעשותה' that one who performs the entire act is liable, but two who perform it are exempt.
Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda similarly taught that the verse 'בעשותה' indicates that an individual who performs the act is liable, but two who perform it are exempt.

Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda adds that the same principle was stated by a group of scholars: the verse 'בעשותה' (in its doing) teaches that an individual who performs it is liable, but two who perform it are exempt.

items.text: Rav's inquiry about carrying via one's body
items.text_en: Rav's inquiry about carrying via one's body
items.desc_en: Rav asks Rabbi whether causing a friend to carry food outside by moving one's body is considered a direct act of carrying, and Rabbi responds that one is liable because the body rests (is at rest) while the hand does not.

sub.desc_en: Rav asked Rabbi: If one's friend loaded him with food and drink and he carried them outside, is he liable because moving his body is like moving the object, or not?
Rabbi answered that he is liable, and it is not comparable to his hand, because his body rests (is at rest) while his hand does not rest.

items.text: אזהרת רבי חייא לרב ותשובת רבי יהודה הנשיא
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's rebuke and the supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya rebukes Rav for asking Rabbi about a different tractate, but then notes that Rabbi's answer was correct. He cites a baraita: if one was carrying food before Shabbat and took it out after dark, he is liable because it is unlike his hand.
items.desc: רבי חייא מזהיר את רב שלא ישאל את רבי יהודה הנשיא שאלה ממסכת אחרת כשהוא עסוק במסכת הנוכחית, כדי לא לביישו. עם זאת, הוא מציין שהתשובה שנתן רבי יהודה הנשיא הייתה טובה, ומביא ברייתא המבחינה בין הוצאת אוכלין ומשקין שהיו טעונים מבעוד יום לבין הוצאת ידו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya rebukes Rav for asking Rabbi about a different tractate, warning that without Rabbi's greatness he would have given a false answer.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya's citation of a baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's citation of a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya notes that Rabbi's answer was correct and cites a baraita: one who carries food out before Shabbat and takes it out after dark is liable because it is unlike his hand.

items.text: Abaye's certainty about the hand's status
items.text_en: Abaye's certainty about the hand's status
items.desc_en: Abaye states it is obvious that a person's hand is neither like a public domain nor like a private domain, as it differs from the hand of a poor person and the hand of a homeowner.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states it is obvious that a person's hand is neither like a public domain nor like a private domain, as it differs from the hand of a poor person and the hand of a homeowner.

items.text: Abaye's question: Is the hand like a karmelit?
items.text_en: Abaye's question: Is the hand like a karmelit?
items.desc_en: Abaye asks whether the hand is considered a karmelit, and whether the Sages penalize one to prevent returning the hand to its owner.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks whether the hand is considered a karmelit (כרמלית), and whether the Sages penalize one to prevent returning the hand to its owner.

items.text: Attempt to resolve from a tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from a tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a tannaitic dispute: one baraita forbids returning a hand full of fruit taken out, another permits it. He suggests they argue whether the hand is like a karmelit.

sub.desc_en: Abaye brings a tannaitic dispute between two baraitot — one forbids and one permits returning fruit taken out in the hand — and suggests they argue whether the hand is considered like a karmelit (כרמלית).

items.text: First answer: Distinction by height
items.text_en: First answer: Distinction by height
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, saying both agree the hand is like a karmelit, but the dispute is about whether the hand is below or above ten handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that both opinions agree the hand is like a karmelit (כרמלית), but the dispute is about whether the hand is below or above ten handbreadths.

items.text: Second answer: Distinction by time
items.text_en: Second answer: Distinction by time
items.desc_en: Alternatively, both agree the hand is not like a karmelit, but the dispute is about before or after dark: before dark no penalty, after dark penalty applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative resolution: both baraitot refer to below ten handbreadths, but the dispute is about time — before dark no penalty, after dark the rabbis penalize.

items.text: Objection to the second answer
items.text_en: Objection to the second answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: logically, before dark one should be penalized to prevent inadvertent sin, while after dark one should not be penalized since discarding would cause a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the opposite reasoning is more logical: before dark, when discarding would not lead to a sin-offering, the rabbis should penalize; after dark, when discarding would lead to a sin-offering, they should not penalize.

items.text: קשר לבעיית רב ביבי בר אביי
items.text_en: Resolution of Rav Bibi's question
items.desc_en: Since the Gemara did not answer as the objection suggests, it resolves Rav Bibi bar Abaye's question: one who stuck bread in the oven is not permitted to remove it before coming to liability for a sin-offering.
items.desc: הגמרא מציינת שמכך שלא תירצנו כתירוץ ההפוך, ניתן לפשוט את בעיית רב ביבי בר אביי: האם מותר לרדות פת מהתנור קודם שיבוא לידי חיוב חטאת? התשובה היא שלא התירו, שכן לא חששו שיבוא לידי חיוב חטאת. הגמרא דוחה את הקושי שזה סותר את אי-הכרעת הבעיה הקודמת, וקובעת שאפשר לפשוט.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the fact that the previous objection was not answered that Rav Bibi bar Abaye's question is resolved: one who stuck bread in the oven is not permitted to remove it before coming to liability for a sin-offering.
The Gemara concludes definitively that the answer is that they did not permit removing the bread before liability.

items.text: Third answer: Distinction by intent
items.text_en: Third answer: Distinction by intent
items.desc_en: Alternatively, the dispute is about an unintentional versus intentional act: no penalty for unintentional, penalty for intentional.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a third answer: the dispute is about an unintentional (שוגג) versus intentional (מזיד) act — no penalty for unintentional, penalty for intentional.

items.text: Fourth answer: Penalizing the unintentional to deter the intentional
items.text_en: Fourth answer: Penalizing the unintentional to deter the intentional
items.desc_en: Alternatively, both cases are unintentional, and the dispute is whether the Sages penalize the unintentional to deter the intentional.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that both cases involve unintentional acts, and the dispute is whether the Sages penalize the unintentional to deter the intentional.

items.text: תירוץ רביעי: הבדל בין אותה חצר לחצר אחרת
items.text_en: Fifth answer: Distinction by courtyard
items.desc_en: Alternatively, there is no penalty at all, and the dispute is about a different courtyard.
items.desc: הגמרא מציעה תירוץ אחרון: לעולם לא קנסו, והברייתא המתירה עוסקת בהחזרת היד לאותה חצר (מותר), ואילו הברייתא האוסרת עוסקת בחצר אחרת (אסור). הקטע נקטע באמצע.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a fifth answer: the rabbis never imposed a penalty (קנסו) at all, and the dispute in the baraita is about a different courtyard (חצר), not about the hand's status.

items.text: Rava's question about returning fruit to a different courtyard
items.text_en: Rava's question about returning fruit to a different courtyard
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether one may return a hand full of fruit to the same courtyard or a different courtyard after taking it out. Rav Nachman permits returning to the same courtyard but prohibits returning to a different one, explaining that in the latter case the person's intention has been fulfilled.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether one may return fruit to the same courtyard or a different courtyard after taking it out; Rav Nachman permits the former and prohibits the latter.
The Gemara objects: what is the difference between the two cases?

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Nachman's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Nachman's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the same courtyard the person's intention has not been fulfilled, but in a different courtyard it has been fulfilled.

items.text: Rav Bibi bar Abaye's question about rescuing bread from an oven
items.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye's question about rescuing bread from an oven
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye asks whether one is permitted to remove bread from an oven before incurring liability for a sin-offering. Rav Acha bar Abaye questions the scenario, and after analysis, Rav Sheila suggests it refers to a case where others may remove it for him. Rav Sheshet objects that one cannot sin for another's benefit, so Rav Ashi concludes it must be about avoiding the death penalty, and Rav Acha bar Rava explicitly states the question is about rescuing before incurring the prohibition of stoning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye raises a dilemma: for one who stuck bread in an oven on Shabbat, did the Sages permit him to remove it before he incurs liability for a sin-offering, or not?

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Abaye to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Abaye to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Abaye questions the scenario: if the person acted unwittingly and never remembered, to whom did the Sages permit removal?
Rav Acha bar Abaye argues that if the person later remembered, he would not be liable for a sin-offering, citing the rule that liability requires unwittingness from start to finish.
Rav Acha bar Abaye objects that if the person acted intentionally, the dilemma should refer to avoiding the stoning penalty, not a sin-offering.
Rav Sheila answers that the case is indeed unwitting, and the dilemma concerns whether others are permitted to remove the bread for him.
Rav Sheshet objects strongly: does one tell a person to sin so that another may benefit?
Rav Ashi resolves that the case is intentional, and the text should read 'before he incurs the prohibition of stoning'; Rav Acha bar Rava explicitly teaches this version.

items.text: The poor person's hand and the requirement of a four-by-four space
items.text_en: The poor person's hand and the requirement of a four-by-four space
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the poor person is liable for taking produce from the homeowner's hand, given that carrying requires lifting and placing on a four-by-four handbreadth area. Rabba explains that this follows Rabbi Akiva's view, who does not require a four-by-four space, as he holds that 'absorption is considered as placement.' The Gemara then notes that Rabba assumes this principle is straightforward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the poor person is liable for taking produce from the homeowner's hand, given that carrying requires lifting and placing on a four-by-four handbreadth area, and a hand is not that size.

Rabba answers that the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva, who does not require a four-by-four handbreadth area, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva deems one liable for throwing through the public domain while the Sages exempt.
The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Akiva holds that 'absorption is considered as placement,' while the Sages do not.
The Gemara notes that Rabba assumes the principle that 'absorption is considered as placement' is straightforward.

items.text: Resolution of Rava's dilemma
items.text_en: Resolution of Rava's dilemma
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava's question about whether the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages is below ten handbreadths or above ten handbreadths is resolved: after asking, it became clear to him that Rabbi Akiva holds that an object caught in midair is considered as having been placed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages is within ten handbreadths, and presents Rava's dilemma: below ten handbreadths they disagree about the principle of קלוטה (an object caught in midair) being considered as placed, while above ten handbreadths all agree one is exempt.
The Gemara resolves that after Rava asked the question, it became clear to him that Rabbi Akiva holds the principle of קלוטה (an object caught in midair) is considered as having been placed.

items.text: Challenge: Does Rabbi Akiva require lifting?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does Rabbi Akiva require lifting?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: perhaps Rabbi Akiva only exempts the need for placing, but still requires lifting? This raises a new difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps Rabbi Akiva only exempts the need for a proper placement (הנחה), but still requires a proper lifting (עקירה) from a domain.

items.text: Rav Yosef's identification: the Mishnah is Rabbi's
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's identification: the Mishnah is Rabbi's
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that the anonymous Mishnah is actually the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, not Rabbi Akiva, shifting the discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the Mishnah in question follows the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (Rabbi).

items.text: First attempt: Rabbi's ruling on a ledge
items.text_en: First attempt: Rabbi's ruling on a ledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a baraita where Rabbi holds one liable for throwing an object onto a small ledge, but the Sages exempt. Abaye explains the case involves a tree extending from private to public domain, and the dispute is whether we follow the branch after the root.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Rabbi is meant, first suggesting the baraita where Rabbi holds liable for throwing onto a small ledge (זיז) and the Sages exempt.
Abaye explains that the case involves a tree standing in private domain with its branch extending into public domain, and the object was thrown and landed on the branch.
Abaye resolves the dispute: Rabbi applies the principle of 'cast the branch after its root' (שדי נופו בתר עיקרו), treating the branch as part of the private domain, while the Sages do not.

items.text: Second attempt: Rabbi's ruling on throwing across domains
items.text_en: Second attempt: Rabbi's ruling on throwing across domains
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita where Rabbi holds one liable for throwing from public to public domain with private domain in between, and Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says Rabbi would hold him liable for two sins, showing Rabbi does not require lifting or placing on a four-by-four handbreadth area. The Gemara notes that Rav and Shmuel both said this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi holds one liable for throwing from public domain to public domain with a private domain in between, while the Sages exempt.

Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains that Rabbi would hold the thrower liable for two sins — one for הוצאה (taking out) and one for הכנסה (bringing in) — showing Rabbi does not require lifting or placing on a four-by-four handbreadth area.
The Gemara notes that both Rav and Shmuel said this ruling.

items.text: Initial assumption: Rabbi's ruling applies only to a covered private domain
items.text_en: Initial assumption: Rabbi's ruling applies only to a covered private domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that Rabbi's ruling (from the Mishnah) applies only to a covered private domain, because an uncovered domain is not considered a proper 'house'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that Rabbi's ruling applies only to a covered private domain, because an uncovered domain is not considered a proper 'house'.

items.text: Objection: Covered public domain is exempt
items.text_en: Objection: Covered public domain is exempt
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's case is a covered private domain, then a covered public domain would also be liable, but Rav's ruling exempts one who carries in a covered public domain, as it is unlike the wilderness camp.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's case is a covered private domain, then a covered public domain would also be liable, but Rav's ruling exempts one who carries in a covered public domain, as it is unlike the wilderness camp.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's resolution: The Mishnah follows Acheirim
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's resolution: The Mishnah follows Acheirim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves that the Mishnah follows the opinion of Acheirim, who hold that if one stood in place and received an object, he is liable, implying that a four-by-four handbreadth domain is not required for placement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves that the Mishnah follows Acheirim, who hold that if one stood in place and received an object, he is liable, implying that a four-by-four handbreadth domain is not required for placement.

items.text: Challenge: Perhaps only placement is not required, but uprooting is
items.text_en: Challenge: Perhaps only placement is not required, but uprooting is
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that perhaps Acheirim only exempt placement from requiring a four-by-four domain, but still require uprooting; alternatively, perhaps the recipient spread his garment to receive it, constituting a valid placement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that perhaps Acheirim only exempt placement from requiring a four-by-four domain, but still require uprooting; alternatively, perhaps the recipient spread his garment to receive it, constituting a valid placement.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's explanation: Received with a basket
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's explanation: Received with a basket
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba explains the Mishnah as a case where the recipient received the object with a basket and placed it on another basket, so there is a valid placement; he emends the text to 'basket in his hand'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba explains the Mishnah as a case where the recipient received the object with a basket and placed it on another basket, so there is a valid placement; he emends the text to 'basket in his hand'.

items.text: Objection: A basket in the public domain is a private domain
items.text_en: Objection: A basket in the public domain is a private domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the basket is in the public domain, it itself is a private domain, so the case is not analogous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the basket is in the public domain, it itself is a private domain, so the case is not analogous.

items.text: Discussion of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: Discussion of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the Mishnah aligns with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that a cane stuck in the public domain with a basket on top is a valid domain. It then distinguishes between above and below ten handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah does not align with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, citing his opinion that throwing an object onto a basket atop a cane in the public domain is liable.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, the owner's act of placing into the poor man's hand would be from private to private domain, not liable.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, the distinction is that there the basket is above ten handbreadths, while here it is below ten.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's explanation: Lowered hand below three handbreadths
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's explanation: Lowered hand below three handbreadths
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that the Mishnah refers to one who lowered his hand below three handbreadths and received the object, and addresses the objection about 'standing' by suggesting he was stooping, in a pit, or a dwarf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rabbi Abbahu's earlier explanation, noting that the Mishnah explicitly says 'his hand' and not 'a basket in his hand'.
Rabbi Abbahu explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where the poor person lowered his hand below three handbreadths and received the object, making his hand a significant place.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says the poor person is standing, so how can his hand be below three handbreadths? Rabbi Abbahu answers that he is stooping.
Alternatively, the Gemara suggests the poor person was standing in a pit, or that he was a dwarf, so his hand could be within three handbreadths of the ground.

items.text: Rava's principle: A person's hand is like a four-by-four domain
items.text_en: Rava's principle: A person's hand is like a four-by-four domain
items.desc_en: Rava states that a person's hand is considered like a four-by-four handbreadth domain, and Rabbi Yochanan agrees, resolving the Mishnah's difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects the forced explanations and establishes the principle that a person's hand is considered like a four-by-four handbreadth domain.
Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan stated the same principle, confirming Rava's resolution.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's statement: Throwing into a friend's hand is liable
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's statement: Throwing into a friend's hand is liable
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that throwing an object that lands in a friend's hand is liable, teaching that the hand is considered a domain even if the recipient did not designate it.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that throwing an object into a friend's hand is liable, and the Gemara clarifies that this teaches that a person's hand is considered a significant domain even without the recipient's prior designation.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: Stood in place vs. uprooted
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: Stood in place vs. uprooted
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one stood in place and received, he is liable; if he uprooted from his place and received, he is exempt, and this is supported by a baraita of Acheirim.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Ilai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Ilai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one stood in place and received, the thrower is liable; if he uprooted and received, the thrower is exempt.
A baraita of Acheirim supports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, stating the same distinction between standing and uprooting.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's dilemma: Two forces in one person
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's dilemma: Two forces in one person
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan raises a dilemma about one who throws an object and then uproots himself to catch it, questioning whether two forces in one person are considered one person (liable) or two (exempt), left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan raises a dilemma: if one throws an object and then uproots himself from his place and catches it, what is the law?
Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that the dilemma concerns whether two forces in one person are considered like one person (liable) or like two people (exempt).
The Gemara presents the two sides of the dilemma and concludes with תיקו (let it stand unresolved).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on receiving rainwater and Rabbi Zeira's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on receiving rainwater and Rabbi Zeira's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who inserts his hand into a friend's courtyard to catch rainwater and then removes it is liable. Rabbi Zeira objects that there is no uprooting, and Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Huna explains it was from a sloping wall.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who inserts his hand into a friend's courtyard, catches rainwater, and removes it is liable.
Rabbi Zeira objects that there is no difference between being loaded by a friend or by Heaven; the person did not perform an act of lifting (עקירה).
The Gemara answers that the case is not one of passively receiving (קיבל) but actively gathering (קלט) the rainwater.
The Gemara questions how one can be liable for lifting without lifting from a place of four by four handbreadths.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Huna explains that the case is where he gathered the rainwater from atop the wall, which is a significant place.
The Gemara objects that the rainwater did not rest on the wall, so it is not considered lifting from a place.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves an inclined wall (כותל משופע), as Rava stated elsewhere, so the water rests momentarily.
The Gemara asks where Rava's statement was said, and introduces the next mishnah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes a case where a scroll falls from one's hand while reading on a doorstep or roof, and the Gemara questions why one must turn it over on its writing when it reaches within ten handbreadths, since it has not yet come to rest.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a scroll rolling from one's hand on a doorstep or roof, and the rule that once it reaches within ten handbreadths, one may only turn it over on its writing.
The Gemara questions why one must turn the scroll over on its writing, since it has not yet come to rest in the public domain.

items.text: Rava's first answer and objection
items.text_en: Rava's first answer and objection
items.desc_en: Rava initially explains the Mishnah refers to a sloping wall, but the Gemara objects that while a scroll might rest on a slope, water would not, so this cannot apply to the case of water.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the case involves a sloping wall, where the scroll can rest.
The Gemara objects that while a scroll might rest on a slope, water would not, so this cannot apply to the case of water.

items.text: Rava's second answer about a pit
items.text_en: Rava's second answer about a pit
items.desc_en: Rava revises his answer, explaining the case involves water that was caught in a pit, which is a clear case of resting. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but Rava's statement teaches that water on water is considered resting.

sub.desc_en: Rava revises his answer, explaining the case involves water that was caught in a pit, which is a clear case of resting. The Gemara notes this is obvious, but Rava's statement teaches that water on water is considered resting.

items.text: Rava's principle and unresolved question
items.text_en: Rava's principle and unresolved question
items.desc_en: Rava establishes that water on water is considered resting, but a nut on water is not. He then raises an unresolved question about a nut in a floating vessel: whether we follow the nut (which rests) or the vessel (which moves). The question remains undecided (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava's earlier ruling aligns with his principle that water on water is considered a placement, while a nut on water is not.
Rava raises an unresolved dilemma: if a nut is in a vessel floating on water, do we follow the nut (which rests) or the vessel (which moves)?
The dilemma remains unresolved and is left standing as תיקו (let it stand).

items.text: Dispute about oil floating on wine
items.text_en: Dispute about oil floating on wine
items.desc_en: A Mishnah is cited about oil floating on wine: if a טבול יום touches only the oil, Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri holds both are connected, while the Sages say only the oil is affected. This illustrates the principle of floating substances.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the dispute between Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and the Rabbis regarding oil floating on wine.
Cites the Mishnah: if a טבול יום touches only the oil, the Sages rule only the oil is disqualified.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri holds that oil and wine are considered connected, so both are disqualified.

items.text: Rabbi Yohanan's ruling on carrying without stopping
items.text_en: Rabbi Yohanan's ruling on carrying without stopping
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yohanan rules that if one carries food and drink while entering and exiting all day without stopping, he is not liable until he actually stands still, establishing the need for a resting (הנחה) for liability.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who carries food and drink while entering and exiting all day is exempt until he stands still, establishing the need for a resting (הנחה) for liability.

items.text: Abaye's clarification about standing to rest
items.text_en: Abaye's clarification about standing to rest
items.desc_en: Abaye specifies that the standing must be for the purpose of resting (לפוש), not for readjusting the load (לכתף). He cites a distinction: within four cubits, standing to rest is exempt, but to adjust is liable; outside four cubits, the opposite applies.

sub.desc_en: Abaye clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's exemption applies only when one stops to rest (לפוש), not when stopping to adjust the burden (לכתף), citing the distinction within and beyond four cubits.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about redundancy
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Abaye's statement is needed, since Rabbi Yohanan already taught a similar principle about the initial intention (עקירה משעה ראשונה). The answer is that the two statements are from different Amora'im, each using a different formulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what principle Abaye's statement teaches, suggesting it is the principle that there was no initial lifting for that purpose.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan already stated this principle once, citing the tradition of Rav Safra in the name of Rabbi Ami.

sub.text: Rav Safra citing Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Safra citing Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Safra transmits in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one who transfers objects from corner to corner and changes his mind to take them out is exempt, because the initial lifting was not for that purpose.
The Gemara resolves that the two statements are from different Amora'im, each transmitting the same principle in a different formulation.

items.text: Baraita on carrying through a portico
items.text_en: Baraita on carrying through a portico
items.desc_en: A Baraita states that one who carries from a shop to a public domain via a portico (סטיו) is liable, but Ben Azzai exempts him. This introduces a dispute about whether walking is considered standing.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that one who carries from a shop to a public domain via a portico is liable.
Ben Azzai exempts the carrier, introducing a dispute about whether walking is considered standing.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ben Azzai holds that a walker is considered as standing (מהלך כעומד דמי), so the object never rests in the portico. The Sages disagree, but the Gemara questions how they can find liability in such a case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ben Azzai's opinion is understandable because he holds that a walker is considered as standing (מהלך כעומד דמי), so the object never rests in the portico.
The Gemara questions how the Rabbis, who hold that walking is not like standing, can find liability in this case, since there is no direct transfer from domain to domain.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer (unfinished)
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer (unfinished)
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite Rabbi Yochanan's answer via Rabbi Safra and Rabbi Ami, but the text cuts off, leaving the resolution incomplete.

sub.text: Rav Safra citing Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Safra citing Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite Rabbi Yochanan's answer via Rabbi Safra and Rabbi Ami, but the text cuts off, leaving the resolution incomplete.

items.text: First attempted comparison: carrying an object in the public domain
items.text_en: First attempted comparison: carrying an object in the public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to compare the case of carrying from a private domain to a public domain via a side area (סטיו) to the case of carrying an object within the public domain. In that case, even though one is exempt while moving, one becomes liable upon placing the object down. The Gemara suggests the same should apply here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a comparison: just as one who carries an object in the public domain is exempt while moving but liable upon placing it down, so too here one should be liable when placing the object in the side area (סטיו).

items.text: Rejection of the first comparison
items.text_en: Rejection of the first comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the comparison: in the public domain, wherever one places the object is a place of liability, but here, if one places it in the side area (סטיו), it is a place of exemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the comparison: in the public domain, any place where one places the object is a place of liability, but here the side area (סטיו) is a place of exemption.

items.text: Second attempted comparison: carrying within four cubits
items.text_en: Second attempted comparison: carrying within four cubits
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries another comparison: carrying an object from the beginning of four cubits to the end of four cubits. In that case, even though one is exempt if placing within four cubits, one is liable when placing at the end of four cubits. The Gemara suggests the same should apply here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara tries a different comparison: one who carries an object within four cubits in the public domain is exempt if he places it within four cubits but liable if he places it at the end of four cubits, so here too it should be no different.

items.text: Rejection of the second comparison
items.text_en: Rejection of the second comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this comparison as well: in the case of four cubits, the place is exempt only for this particular person, but for everyone else it is a place of liability. Here, the side area (סטיו) is a place of exemption for everyone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects: there, the place is exempt only relative to this particular person but is a place of liability for everyone else, whereas here the side area is a place of exemption for everyone.

items.text: Third attempted comparison: carrying from private to public via the sides
items.text_en: Third attempted comparison: carrying from private to public via the sides
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries a third comparison: carrying from a private domain to a public domain via the sides of the public domain. In that case, even though one is exempt if placing on the sides, one is liable when placing in the public domain itself. The Gemara suggests the same should apply here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a third comparison: one who carries from a private domain to a public domain via the sides of the public domain is exempt if he places it on the sides but liable if he places it in the public domain itself, so here too it should be no different.

Rav Pappa objects that the comparison only works for the Rabbis who hold that the sides of a public domain are not like the public domain itself, but for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who holds they are like the public domain, what can be said?

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika answers that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov only holds the sides are like the public domain where there are no partitions (חיפופי), but here there are partitions, so the comparison stands.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge based on Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge based on Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges the third comparison: it works only according to the Sages who say that the sides of the public domain are not like the public domain. But according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who says the sides are like the public domain, what can be said?

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: this comparison works only for the Rabbis who hold that the sides of the public domain are not like the public domain, but for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who holds they are like the public domain, what can be said?

items.text: Rav Acha's resolution: distinction of חפופי
items.text_en: Rav Acha's resolution: distinction of חפופי
items.desc_en: Rav Acha, son of Rav Ika, answers Rav Pappa: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov only says the sides are like the public domain where there are no חפופי (overhanging branches or obstructions). But where there are חפופי, he does not say that. Therefore, the case of the side area (סטיו) is like that.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika answers: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling applies only where there are no overhanging roofs (חיפופי), but where there are overhanging roofs, even he would agree, so the comparison stands.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and a baraita on Ben Azzai's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and a baraita on Ben Azzai's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that Ben Azzai concedes in the case of throwing. A baraita supports this: one who carries from a store to a plaza via a side area is liable. Ben Azzai says that carrying and bringing in are exempt, but throwing and passing are liable.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and supporting baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and supporting baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Ben Azzai agrees in the case of throwing, and a baraita supports this: one who carries from a store to a plaza via a side area is liable, and Ben Azzai distinguishes between carrying (exempt) and throwing or passing (liable).
A baraita is cited supporting the general rule: one who carries from a store to a plaza via a side area (סטיו) is liable, and this applies to all modes of transfer.
Ben Azzai distinguishes: carrying out (מוציא) and bringing in (מכניס) are exempt, but passing (מושיט) and throwing (זורק) are liable.

items.text: Tannaitic list of four domains for Shabbat
items.text_en: Tannaitic list of four domains for Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Tannaim teach that there are four domains for Shabbat: private domain, public domain, כרמלית, and place of exemption. The baraita defines each: a private domain is a trench or fence ten handbreadths high and four wide; a public domain is a highway, large plaza, and open alleyways. It also discusses the laws of carrying between domains, the status of a כרמלית, courtyards, and the threshold (איסקופה).

sub.desc_en: The Tannaim open by listing the four domains for Shabbat: private domain, public domain, כרמלית, and place of exemption.
The baraita defines a private domain as a trench or fence ten handbreadths high and four wide.
The baraita defines a public domain as a highway, large plaza, and open alleyways, and states the penalties for carrying between them.
The baraita defines a כרמלית as a domain that is neither private nor public, and states that carrying within it or between it and other domains is exempt from punishment.
The baraita rules that courtyards and non-open alleyways are permitted if an עירוב (merging of domains) is made, otherwise forbidden.

The baraita states that a person standing on the threshold may take from the homeowner or the poor person and give to the other, but not directly transfer between them; if they do, all three are exempt.
Others argue that the threshold serves two domains: when the door is open it is like inside, when closed like outside; if it is ten handbreadths high and four wide, it is its own domain.

items.text: Interpretation of 'this is the private domain' to exclude Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'this is the private domain' to exclude Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the phrase 'this is the private domain' in the baraita comes to exclude the view of Rabbi Yehuda, who says that one who has two houses on opposite sides of a public domain may...

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the baraita says 'this is the private domain' — what does it exclude? It answers: it excludes the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says that one who has two houses on opposite sides of the public domain may make a certain arrangement (the text is cut off).

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes a case of two side-posts or beams with a space in between, and the Sages reject this as a valid eruv for reshut harabim.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes a case of two side-posts or beams with a space in between, and the Sages reject this as a valid eruv for reshut harabim.

items.text: Gemara's question about the term 'gemura'
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the term 'gemura'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this case is called 'gemura' (complete), and explains that it teaches that even for throwing, the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this case is called 'gemura' (complete).
The Gemara explains that the term 'gemura' teaches that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Yehuda even regarding throwing, not just carrying.

items.text: Clarifying 'this is reshut harabim' and the term 'gemura'
items.text_en: Clarifying 'this is reshut harabim' and the term 'gemura'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'this is reshut harabim' excludes Rabbi Yehuda's case of a public road dividing a courtyard. It then explains that the term 'gemura' in the latter clause is used because it was used in the former clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the emphasis 'this is reshut harabim' comes to exclude.
The Gemara answers that it excludes Rabbi Yehuda's case of a public road dividing a courtyard, citing the mishna where Rabbi Yehuda requires diverting the road and the Sages disagree.
The Gemara asks why the latter clause uses the term 'gemura'.
The Gemara answers that the term 'gemura' is used in the latter clause for uniformity, because it was used in the former clause.

items.text: Question about the desert as reshut harabim
items.text_en: Question about the desert as reshut harabim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the desert is not listed as reshut harabim, and Abaye resolves that the baraita refers to the time when Israel was in the desert, while the Mishnah refers to the present time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the desert is not listed among the places considered a public domain, citing a baraita that includes the desert.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the time when Israel dwelt in the desert, when it was frequented by multitudes, and the present time, when it is not.

items.text: Liability for Shabbat violation
items.text_en: Liability for Shabbat violation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's statement about liability for unintentional and intentional violation is obvious, but the part about intentional violation (karet and stoning) is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states the liability for carrying out or in on Shabbat: unwittingly brings a sin-offering, intentionally is liable to karet and stoning.
The Gemara asks: that unwittingly one is liable to a sin-offering is obvious.
The Gemara answers: it was necessary to teach the case of intentional violation, that it entails karet and stoning, and the unwitting case was included for completeness.

items.text: Rav's teaching about the number of labors
items.text_en: Rav's teaching about the number of labors
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement teaches like Rav, who found a scroll stating that Isi ben Yehuda says one is only liable for one of the 39 labors. The Gemara resolves a contradiction with Rabbi Yochanan's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tosefta needed to state the obvious case of intentional violation, and suggests it comes to teach like Rav.
Rav reports finding a hidden scroll in Rabbi Ḥiyya's house stating that Isi ben Yehuda says one is liable only for one of the 39 labors.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah lists 39 labors and Rabbi Yochanan explains the count teaches liability for each labor separately, contradicting Isi's statement.
The Gemara resolves that Isi means one of the 39 labors is not liable for stoning, and the Tosefta teaches that carrying out is among the certain ones.

items.text: Status of a valley as karmelit
items.text_en: Status of a valley as karmelit
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a valley is not considered reshut hayachid or reshut harabim, citing a Mishnah that in summer it is reshut hayachid for Shabbat. Ulla explains it is always karmelit, and Rav Ashi adds a further point.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that a sea, valley, colonnade, and karmelit are neither like a private domain nor like a public domain.
The Gemara questions whether a valley is indeed not like a private domain, citing a Mishnah that treats it as a private domain for Shabbat in summer.
The Mishnah states that in summer the valley is a private domain for Shabbat and like a public domain for impurity, while in winter it is a private domain for both.
Ulla resolves that the valley is always a karmelit, and the Mishnah calls it a private domain only to emphasize that it is not a public domain.
Rav Ashi begins to offer an alternative explanation, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Ulla's statement about a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim
items.text_en: Ulla's statement about a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim
items.desc_en: Ulla quotes Rabbi Yochanan: a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim that was not enclosed for dwelling, even if it is a kor or two kor, one who throws into it is liable because its partitions are valid but lack residents.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishna's valley refers to one with partitions, citing Ulla's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim not enclosed for dwelling is still a private domain by Torah law, since its partitions are valid but lack residents.

items.text: Gemara's question about Ulla and Rav Ashi's disagreement
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Ulla and Rav Ashi's disagreement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Ulla did not follow his own earlier statement, and explains that Ulla would say that if it has partitions it is called a 'bik'ah' not a 'karpaf', while Rav Ashi calls it a 'reshut hayachid'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Ulla did not follow his own earlier statement, given that Rav Ashi's explanation is understandable.
The Gemara explains that Ulla would argue that if the area has partitions, it would be called an enclosure (קרפף), not a valley (בקעה).
The Gemara adds that Rav Ashi, however, notes that the mishna explicitly teaches 'private domain' (רשות היחיד), supporting his interpretation.

items.text: קרן זווית הסמוכה לרשות הרבים
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a corner near public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists karmelit separately, and Rav Dimi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: it is needed only for a corner near public domain, which is considered karmelit because its use is not comfortable even though people sometimes enter it.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע המשנה מוסיפה 'כרמלית' אם כל המקומות כבר כרמלית, ומביאה את דברי רב דימי בשם רבי יוחנן שמדובר בקרן זווית הסמוכה לרשות הרבים, שאף על פי שהרבים דוחקים ונכנסים לשם, מכיוון שאין נוח להשתמש בה, היא נחשבת כרמלית.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tosefta lists karmelit separately, since all the other places listed are also karmelit.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כל המקומות שנמנו במשנה הם כרמלית, מה באה להוסיף המילה 'כרמלית'?

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan's answer: the extra karmelit refers to a corner adjacent to the public domain, which is considered karmelit because its use is inconvenient even though people sometimes enter it.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כל המקומות שנמנו במשנה הם כרמלית, מה באה להוסיף המילה 'כרמלית'?

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on spaces between pillars and Rabbi Zeira's addition
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on spaces between pillars and Rabbi Zeira's addition
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: the space between pillars is judged as karmelit because even though people tread there, they do not walk comfortably. Rabbi Zeira adds that the bench in front of pillars is also karmelit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the space between pillars is judged as karmelit because although people tread there, they cannot walk directly.
Rabbi Zeira adds that the bench in front of the pillars is also judged as karmelit.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the two rulings
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the two rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to the one who said 'between pillars', the bench is certainly included; but according to the one who said 'bench', only the bench is karmelit because its use is not comfortable, while between pillars is comfortable. A second version says that between pillars is sometimes trodden by the public and thus considered public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that according to the one who said 'between the pillars', the bench is certainly included as a karmelit.
The Gemara explains that according to the one who said 'bench', only the bench is karmelit because its use is not comfortable, but between the pillars, whose use is comfortable, is not karmelit.
The Gemara presents an alternative version: between the pillars, since the public sometimes strides there, it is considered like the public domain.

items.text: לבנה זקופה ברשות הרבים
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on an upright brick and subsequent qualifications
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Sheila quotes Rav Chisda: if one throws at an upright brick in public domain and it lands on its side, he is liable; if on top, exempt. Abaye and Rava qualify that this applies only if the brick is three handbreadths high so the public does not tread on it, but thorns and thistles are exempt even if less than three. Chiyya bar Rav adds even thorns and thistles, but not dung; Rav Ashi adds even dung.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את דברי רבה בר שילא בשם רב חסדא שלגבי לבנה זקופה ברשות הרבים, אם זרק וטח בפניה חייב, אבל על גבה פטור. אביי ורבא מוסיפים שזה דווקא אם היא גבוהה שלושה טפחים, אבל אם יש קוצים או צואה, יש דעות שונות אם הם נחשבים חלק מרשות הרבים.

sub.text: רבה בר שילא בשם רב חסדא
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Sheila citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Sheila cites Rav Chisda's ruling: throwing at an upright brick in the public domain and hitting its side makes one liable, but landing on top makes one exempt.
sub.desc: רבה בר שילא בשם רב חסדא פוסק שלגבי לבנה זקופה ברשות הרבים, הזורק וטח בפניה חייב, אבל אם נח על גבה פטור.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava qualify that the ruling applies only when the brick is three handbreadths high, so the public does not tread on it; but thorns and shrubs are exempt even if less than three.
sub.desc: אביי ורבא מגבילים את דברי רב חסדא ללבנה גבוהה שלושה טפחים, אבל קוצים ושיחים נחשבים חלק מרשות הרבים אף שאינם גבוהים שלושה.

sub.desc_en: Chiyya bar Rav adds that even thorns and shrubs are exempt, but not dung.
sub.desc: אביי ורבא מגבילים את דברי רב חסדא ללבנה גבוהה שלושה טפחים, אבל קוצים ושיחים נחשבים חלק מרשות הרבים אף שאינם גבוהים שלושה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi extends the exemption even to a place with dung, as people rushing to work will step on it.
sub.desc: אביי ורבא מגבילים את דברי רב חסדא ללבנה גבוהה שלושה טפחים, אבל קוצים ושיחים נחשבים חלק מרשות הרבים אף שאינם גבוהים שלושה.

items.text: גובה הכרמלית
items.text_en: Dimensions of karmelit: minimum four, maximum ten
items.desc_en: Rabbah of Bei Rav Sheila quotes Rav Dimi quoting Rabbi Yochanan: a karmelit is no less than four handbreadths. Rav Sheshet adds that it holds up to ten. The Gemara clarifies that this means up to ten handbreadths it is karmelit, but above ten it is not, citing Shmuel's instruction to Rav Yehuda not to be involved in Shabbat matters above ten, and explaining that this does not refer to reshut hayachid which extends to the sky.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את דברי רב דימי בשם רבי יוחנן שאין כרמלית פחותה מארבעה טפחים, ורב ששת מוסיף שהיא תופסת עד עשרה. יש דיון מה פירוש 'עד עשרה', ומביאים את דברי שמואל שאין לעסוק בדיני שבת למעלה מעשרה, אך דוחים זאת מפני שרשות היחיד עולה עד לרקיע.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah of Bei Rav Sheila cites Rav Dimi quoting Rabbi Yochanan that a karmelit is no less than four handbreadths.
sub.desc: רבא מבית רב שיילא מביא בשם רב דימי בשם רבי יוחנן שאין כרמלית פחותה מארבעה טפחים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet adds that a karmelit extends up to ten handbreadths.
sub.desc: רבא מבית רב שיילא מביא בשם רב דימי בשם רבי יוחנן שאין כרמלית פחותה מארבעה טפחים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rav Sheshet means by 'extends up to ten'.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש 'ותופסת עד עשרה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the interpretation that a karmelit requires a partition of ten handbreadths, citing Rav's ruling about a house with walls less than ten handbreadths that is still considered a karmelit inside.
sub.desc: רבא מבית רב שיילא מביא בשם רב דימי בשם רבי יוחנן שאין כרמלית פחותה מארבעה טפחים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that 'extends up to ten' means that up to ten handbreadths is karmelit, but above ten is not.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש 'ותופסת עד עשרה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's instruction to Rav Yehuda not to be involved in Shabbat matters above ten handbreadths as support.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש 'ותופסת עד עשרה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what halakha is derived from Shmuel's statement.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש 'ותופסת עד עשרה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that Shmuel meant there is no private domain above ten, citing Rav Chisda's ruling that a private domain extends to the sky.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש 'ותופסת עד עשרה'.

items.text: Clarification of the principle that there is no public domain above ten handbreadths and its application to karmelit
items.text_en: Clarification of the principle that there is no public domain above ten handbreadths and its application to karmelit
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the statement that there is no public domain above ten handbreadths is already a Mishnah. It then explains that the same applies to karmelit: above ten handbreadths it is not a karmelit, and the Sages were lenient with it, combining leniencies of private domain and public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's statement by noting that the principle that there is no public domain above ten handbreadths is already an explicit Mishnah.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah about throwing an object at a wall, which distinguishes between above and below ten handbreadths, to prove the principle.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that Shmuel's statement applies to karmelit, not public domain, and elaborates the leniencies applied to karmelit.

items.text: Rav Giddel's statement about a house less than ten handbreadths high with a roof completing it
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's statement about a house less than ten handbreadths high with a roof completing it
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav Chiyya bar Yosef quoting Rav: In a house whose interior is less than ten handbreadths high but whose roof completes it to ten, one may carry on its roof entirely, but inside one may only carry four cubits.

sub.text: Rav Giddel quoting Rav Chiyya bar Yosef quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Giddel quoting Rav Chiyya bar Yosef quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel transmits Rav's ruling: in a house whose interior is less than ten handbreadths high but whose roof completes it to ten, one may carry on the entire roof, but inside one may only carry four cubits.

items.text: Abaye's addition: if he dug four by four and completed it to ten, it is permitted
items.text_en: Abaye's addition: if he dug four by four and completed it to ten, it is permitted
items.desc_en: Abaye adds that if one dug a hole of four by four handbreadths in the floor, completing the interior to ten handbreadths, one may carry throughout the entire house. The reason is that the hole is considered a 'hole of a private domain', and holes of a private domain are like the private domain itself. The Gemara then cites a dispute about holes of a public domain: Abaye says they are like the public domain, while Rava says they are not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that if one dug a four-by-four handbreadth hole in the floor, completing the interior height to ten handbreadths, one may carry throughout the entire house.
Abaye explains the reason: the dug-out area is a hole of a private domain, and holes of a private domain are considered like the private domain itself.
The Gemara cites the dispute about holes of a public domain: Abaye holds they are like the public domain, while Rava holds they are not.

items.text: Rava's challenge to Abaye from Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a corner near the public domain
items.text_en: Rava's challenge to Abaye from Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a corner near the public domain
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye: according to your view that holes of the public domain are like the public domain, why is a corner near the public domain not considered like a hole of the public domain? The Gemara answers that there the use is not convenient, but here the use is convenient.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye: according to your view that holes of the public domain are like the public domain, why is a corner near the public domain not considered like a hole of the public domain?
The Gemara answers that there the use is not convenient, but here the use is convenient.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah about throwing four cubits into a wall and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah about throwing four cubits into a wall and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah: throwing four cubits into a wall above ten handbreadths is like throwing into the air, below ten is like throwing onto the ground. It questions what 'like throwing onto the ground' means, since it did not rest. Rabbi Yochanan answers that they taught this regarding a fig cake. The Gemara then challenges: if holes of the public domain are like the public domain, why not explain it with a pebble that rests in a hole?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about throwing four cubits into a wall and questions what 'like throwing onto the ground' means, since the object did not rest.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Mishnah was taught regarding a juicy fig cake that sticks to the wall.
The Gemara challenges: if holes of the public domain are like the public domain, why not explain the Mishnah with a pebble that rests in a hole?

items.text: Two answers to the challenge and proof that the wall has no hole
items.text_en: Two answers to the challenge and proof that the wall has no hole
items.desc_en: The Gemara gives two answers: sometimes it is explained that a pebble might bounce back, and sometimes that the wall has no hole. It proves from the first clause that the wall has no hole, because if it had a hole, throwing above ten would also be like throwing onto the ground. It then addresses a potential objection about a hole less than four by four, citing a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis about whether we consider the hole as if it were completed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara gives one answer: a stone or object is different because it might bounce back and not rest in the hole.
The Gemara gives another answer: the mishna refers to a wall that has no hole.
The Gemara proves from the first clause that the wall has no hole, because if it had a hole, throwing above ten would also be like throwing onto the ground.
The Gemara raises a potential objection: perhaps the mishna refers to a hole less than four by four, citing the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis.
Rabbi Yehuda cites Rabbi Chiyya that throwing into a hole of any size brings us to the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis about whether we consider the hole as if it were completed.
The Gemara concludes that the mishna indeed refers to a wall with no hole.

items.text: Rav Chisda's statement about a cane in a private domain and its connection to Rabbi's view
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's statement about a cane in a private domain and its connection to Rabbi's view
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: If one stuck a cane in a private domain and threw an object that rested on top of it, even if it is a hundred cubits high, he is liable, because the private domain extends to the sky. The Gemara suggests this aligns with Rabbi's view, who holds that a ledge of any size is considered a place, unlike the Sages who require four by four.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that if one stuck a cane in a private domain and an object rested on top of it, even at a height of a hundred cubits, he is liable because the private domain extends to the sky.
The Gemara suggests that Rav Chisda's ruling aligns with Rabbi's opinion, which does not require a four-by-four area for a place.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi deems one liable for throwing an object onto a projection of any size, while the Sages exempt, proving that Rabbi does not require a four-by-four area.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on a tree in the public domain
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on a tree in the public domain
items.desc_en: Abaye clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis is about a tree whose trunk is in a private domain but whose branches extend into the public domain. Rabbi considers the branches as following the trunk, while the Rabbis do not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis concerns a tree standing in a private domain with branches extending into the public domain, where Rabbi applies the principle of 'שְׁדִי נוֹפוֹ בָּתַר עִיקָּרוֹ' (the branches follow the trunk) and the Rabbis do not.

items.text: Dispute about a beehive in the public domain
items.text_en: Dispute about a beehive in the public domain
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that a beehive ten handbreadths high but less than six wide in the public domain renders one liable for throwing, but if it is six wide, one is exempt. Rava disagrees, saying even if less than six wide, one is exempt because the cane tips rise above ten. If the hive is turned over, Abaye says seven and a bit renders liable, seven and a half exempt; Rav Ashi says even seven and a half is liable because the partitions are made for the interior.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states the law: throwing a beehive into the public domain — if it is ten handbreadths high but less than six wide, one is liable; if it is six wide, one is exempt.
Rava objects, arguing that even if the beehive is less than six wide, one is exempt because the cane tips inevitably rise above ten handbreadths.
Abaye rules that if the beehive is turned over on its opening, a height of seven and a bit renders one liable, but seven and a half renders one exempt.
Rav Ashi objects, arguing that even seven and a half renders one liable because the partitions are made for the interior of the hive.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on a column in the public domain
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on a column in the public domain
items.desc_en: Ulla states that if a column nine handbreadths high stands in the public domain and people commonly shoulder burdens on it, throwing and landing on it makes one liable. The reasoning is that less than three handbreadths is trodden by the public, from three to nine is neither trodden nor shouldered, and nine is certainly shouldered.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules that a pillar nine handbreadths high in the public domain, which the public shoulders against, makes one liable for throwing and landing on it, because below three handbreadths the public treads on it, from three to nine they neither tread nor shoulder, and at nine they definitely shoulder.

Ulla rules that one who throws and lands on it is liable, explaining the reasoning: below three handbreadths is trodden, three to nine is neither trodden nor shouldered, and nine is certainly shouldered.

items.text: Dispute about a pit in the public domain
items.text_en: Dispute about a pit in the public domain
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef about a pit, and Rav Yosef says the same rule applies. Rava disagrees, arguing that use by pressure is not considered use. Rav Adda bar Matna challenges Rava with a baraita about a basket in the public domain, and the Gemara clarifies that the baraita's conclusion refers to the first clause, not the second.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef about the status of a pit (גוּמָּא) in the public domain, and Rav Yosef responds that the same rule applies as for a basket.
Rava disagrees, arguing that use of a pit is by pressure (תַּשְׁמִישׁ עַל יְדֵי הַדְּחָק) and is not considered valid use.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Matna's challenge with a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Matna's challenge with a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Matna challenges Rava by citing a baraita about a basket in the public domain that concludes 'וכן בגומא' (and similarly for a pit), implying the pit is treated like the basket.

The Gemara clarifies that the baraita's conclusion 'וכן בגומא' refers to the first clause (the case of a basket ten handbreadths high and four wide), not the second clause (the case of a smaller basket), thus not supporting Rava's position.

items.text: Further challenge to Rava
items.text_en: Further challenge to Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another challenge to Rava's position, beginning with 'אֵיתִיבֵיהּ' (he challenged him), though the content is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The gemara begins another objection, but the text is incomplete.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one intends to rest in the public domain and places his eruv in a pit above ten handbreadths, it is valid; below ten, it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one intends to rest in the public domain and places his eruv in a pit above ten handbreadths, it is valid; below ten, it is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's question and first resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and first resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's scenario: if the pit is ten handbreadths deep, the eruv's placement above or below ten makes no difference as the person and eruv are in different domains. It concludes the pit must be less than ten, proving that use by pressure (תשמיש על ידי הדחק) is considered valid use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's scenario: if the pit is ten handbreadths deep, the eruv's placement above or below ten makes no difference as the person and eruv are in different domains.
The Gemara concludes the pit must be less than ten, proving that use by pressure (תשמיש על ידי הדחק) is considered valid use.

items.text: Alternative explanations: Carmelit or Rabbi's view
items.text_en: Alternative explanations: Carmelit or Rabbi's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative explanations: either the pit is a carmelit and called 'public domain' only because it is not a private domain, or it follows Rabbi's view that rabbinic prohibitions are not decreed during twilight.

sub.desc_en: Rava's first alternative: both he and his eiruv are in a carmelit, and the baraita calls it 'public domain' only because it is not a private domain.
Rava's second alternative: he is in the public domain and his eiruv is in a carmelit, and the baraita follows Rabbi's view that rabbinic prohibitions were not decreed during twilight.

items.text: Proof from a Mishnah about a water puddle
items.text_en: Proof from a Mishnah about a water puddle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asserts its first explanation is definitive, citing a Mishnah about a water puddle less than ten handbreadths where walking is considered walking, but use by pressure is not considered use. This supports the distinction between walking and use.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that his earlier answers are not evasive but accurate, introducing the Mishnah as proof.
Cites the Mishnah about a water puddle less than ten handbreadths where throwing four cubits is liable, establishing the puddle as part of the public domain.
Explains the repetition of 'swamp' in the Mishnah: one case for summer, one for rainy season, each needed to teach that the puddle is part of the public domain in both seasons.
Concludes from the repetition of 'the public domain passes through it' that walking under duress is considered walking, but use under duress is not considered use, supporting the distinction.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement about a reed
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement about a reed
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says that one who repeatedly throws and erects a reed is not liable until he uproots it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one who repeatedly throws and erects a reed is not liable until he uproots it.
