items.text: Analysis of the threshold (איסקופה)
items.text_en: Analysis of the threshold (איסקופה)
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's ruling about a person standing on a threshold, questioning its domain. It rejects public, private, and carmelit possibilities, concluding it is a place of exemption (מקום פטור) less than four by four handbreadths, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Tosefta's ruling about a person standing on a threshold and asks what type of threshold is being discussed.
The Gemara considers the possibility that the threshold is part of the public domain, but objects that taking from the homeowner would be carrying out from private to public domain.
The Gemara considers the possibility that the threshold is part of the private domain, but objects that taking from the poor person would be carrying in from public to private domain.
The Gemara considers the possibility that the threshold is a karmelit, but objects that even if it is not a full domain, there is still a rabbinic prohibition.

The Gemara concludes that the threshold is a place of exemption (מקום פטור) with less than four by four handbreadths, and cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that such a place may be used for adjusting burdens as long as no exchange occurs.

items.text: Challenge to Rava's view
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's continuation that all three are exempt, and challenges Rava's statement that one who carries an object from beginning to end of four cubits in the public domain is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's continuation that all three are exempt, and challenges Rava's statement that one who carries an object from beginning to end of four cubits in the public domain is liable.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the previous Mishnah's ruling that one who throws an object onto a threshold is liable, arguing that there the object did not rest, but here it rests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's ruling about a threshold is inconsistent: there the object did not rest, but here it rests.

items.text: Acherim's statement about the threshold
items.text_en: Acherim's statement about the threshold
items.desc_en: Acherim state that a threshold serves two domains: when the door is open it is like inside, when closed it is like outside.

sub.desc_en: Acherim answer that a threshold serves two domains: when the door is open it is like inside, when closed like outside.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Acherim
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Acherim
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Acherim's view by citing Rav Chama bar Gurya's statement that the inside of a doorway requires another side-post to permit it, even if it lacks four by four handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the view of Aḥerim (אחרים) by asking whether the threshold is considered like the inside even without a side-post (לחי).

sub.text: Rav Ḥama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Ḥama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Ḥama bar Gurya cites Rav that the inside of a doorway requires another side-post to permit carrying there.
The Gemara raises a possible objection: perhaps the threshold lacks an area of four by four handbreadths, which would exempt it from needing a side-post.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing Rav Ḥama bar Gurya's statement that even without four by four handbreadths, a side-post is still required.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's resolution: threshold of an alleyway
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's resolution: threshold of an alleyway
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav resolves that the case involves the threshold of an alleyway (אסקופת מבוי) that is half roofed and half not, with the roofing facing inward, so the status depends on the door.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav resolves that the case involves the threshold of an alleyway (אסקופת מבוי) that is half roofed and half not, with the roofing facing inward, so the status depends on the door.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution: threshold of a house
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution: threshold of a house
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case involves a house threshold roofed with two beams each less than four handbreadths wide and less than three apart, with a door in the middle, so the threshold's status follows the door.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that we are dealing with a house threshold roofed with two beams each less than four handbreadths wide and less than three handbreadths apart, with a door in the middle.

items.text: Ruling on a large threshold and support for Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi
items.text_en: Ruling on a large threshold and support for Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi
items.desc_en: If the threshold is ten handbreadths high and four wide, it is a domain unto itself, supporting Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi who cited Rabbi Meir that a pillar in a private domain of those dimensions is forbidden to carry upon, as a decree due to a mound in the public domain.

sub.text: Supporting baraita and Rabbi Meir's ruling
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita and Rabbi Meir's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that if the threshold is ten handbreadths high and four wide, it is its own domain, supporting Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi's citation of Rabbi Meir that any place with two domains that are one domain, like a pillar in a private domain, is forbidden to carry on due to a decree because of a mound in the public domain.
The gemara states that this ruling supports Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi citing Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi citing Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi cites Rabbi Meir that any place where two domains meet but are effectively one, such as a pillar in a private domain ten handbreadths high and four wide, is forbidden to carry upon as a decree due to a mound in the public domain.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists activities one may not begin close to mincha time until after praying, but if one has already started, they need not interrupt except for Shema; for the Amidah they do interrupt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists activities one may not begin close to mincha time until after praying, but if one has already started, they need not interrupt except for Shema; for the Amidah they do interrupt.

items.text: Gemara's question: Which mincha?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Which mincha?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which mincha is meant: the large mincha (early afternoon) or the small mincha (late afternoon). It concludes it must be the small mincha, as there is plenty of time left in the day for the large one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which mincha is meant — the large mincha (midday) or the small mincha (late afternoon) — and concludes it must be the small one, because the large one leaves too much time.
The Gemara concludes that the mishnah refers to the small mincha (late afternoon).

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling that one need not interrupt an activity that began before mincha contradicts Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who says that once mincha time arrives, one may not taste anything before praying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from the Mishnah's rule that one need not interrupt activities, against Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that once mincha time arrives, one may not taste anything before praying.

items.text: First resolution: Large mincha with specific cases
items.text_en: First resolution: Large mincha with specific cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to the large mincha, but only when the activity is a major one: a haircut by Ben El'ashah, a full bath, a large tannery, a large meal, or the beginning of a court case. This avoids the contradiction with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by reinterpreting the Mishnah's restrictions as applying to specific large-scale activities, not ordinary ones.

items.text: Second resolution: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's explanation
items.text_en: Second resolution: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the Mishnah refers to ordinary activities, but the prohibition is only ab initio due to various concerns: the scissors might break, one might faint, see a loss in business, be drawn to continue eating, or find a reason to overturn a verdict.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah refers to ordinary activities, but the prohibition is a גזירה (decree) due to various concerns like breaking scissors, fainting, distraction, or prolonging the activity.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the prohibition is a decree (גזירה) lest the scissors break, and similarly for the bathhouse, lest one faint.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the tannery prohibition is a decree lest one see a loss in business and become distracted.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the eating prohibition applies to a small meal, lest one be drawn to continue eating.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that the judgment prohibition applies to the conclusion of the case, lest one find a reason to overturn the verdict.

items.text: Definitions of when each activity begins
items.text_en: Definitions of when each activity begins
items.desc_en: Rav Avin defines when each activity is considered to have begun: for haircutting, when the barber's cloth is placed on the knees; for bathing, when one removes his garment; for tanning, when one ties the hide between his shoulders; for eating, Rav says when one washes hands, Rabbi Chanina says when one unties his belt. The Gemara notes these are not contradictory but apply to different groups (Babylonians vs. others).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From when is the beginning of haircutting (so that one must stop for prayer)?
Rav Avin answers: From when he places the barber's cloth on his knees.
The Gemara asks: From when is the beginning of bathing?
Rav Avin answers: From when he removes his garment.
The Gemara asks: From when is the beginning of tanning?
The Gemara answers: From when he ties the hide between his shoulders.
The Gemara asks: From when is the beginning of eating?
Rav answers: From when he washes his hands.
Rabbi Chanina answers: From when he unties his belt.
The Gemara resolves: They do not disagree; Rav's definition applies to us (Babylonians) and Rabbi Chanina's to them (others).

items.text: Abaye's challenge from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the view that one who holds evening prayer is optional does not trouble him to retie his belt, citing the Mishnah that for mincha, which is obligatory, one does not interrupt an activity that began, even though Rabbi Chanina said the beginning of a meal is when one unties his belt.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects: if for the evening prayer (ערבית), which is optional (רשות), we do not trouble one who has loosened his belt, then for mincha, which is obligatory (חובה), we should certainly trouble him — yet the Mishnah says one need not interrupt.
Abaye cites the mishnah's rule that one does not interrupt, and Rabbi Chanina's definition of the beginning of a meal, to highlight the contradiction.

Abaye objects: mincha (מנחה) is obligatory for everyone, yet the Mishnah rules that if one began a meal, he does not interrupt, and Rabbi Chanina defined the beginning of a meal as when one unties his belt.

items.text: Preparation for prayer: dressing appropriately
items.text_en: Preparation for prayer: dressing appropriately
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why one must prepare for prayer, citing the verse 'Prepare to meet your God, O Israel.' It then recounts how Rava bar Rav Huna and Rava would dress or remove their cloaks when praying, depending on circumstances, and Rav Ashi describes Rav Kahana's practice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference between the afternoon and evening prayers: drunkenness is uncommon in the afternoon, and the fixed time of the afternoon prayer makes one anxious, preventing negligence, whereas the evening prayer's all-night window leads to negligence.
Rav Sheshet objects: is tying one's belt a burden? If so, one could stand without a belt and pray.
The Gemara resolves that one must wear a belt while praying, citing the verse 'Prepare to greet your God, Israel' (Amos 4:12), requiring preparation and adornment before God.
Rava bar Rav Huna would don expensive socks and pray, citing the verse 'Prepare to greet your God, Israel' as support for adorning oneself before prayer.
Rava would remove his cloak and clasp his hands in prayer, acting as a slave before his master.

Rav Ashi describes Rav Kahana's practice: in times of suffering, he would remove his cloak and clasp his hands like a slave before his master; in times of peace, he would dress and wrap himself, citing the verse 'Prepare to greet your God, Israel.'

items.text: Balancing prayer and Torah study
items.text_en: Balancing prayer and Torah study
items.desc_en: Rava criticizes Rav Hamnuna for prolonging his prayer at the expense of Torah study, but Rav Hamnuna holds that prayer and Torah have separate times. Rabbi Zeira rebukes Rabbi Yirmeya for rushing through Torah to pray, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rava criticizes Rav Hamnuna for prolonging his prayer, saying he abandons eternal life (Torah) for temporal life (prayer).
The Gemara explains that Rav Hamnuna held that the time for prayer is distinct from the time for Torah study, so prolonging prayer does not detract from Torah.
Rabbi Zeira rebukes Rabbi Yirmeya for hurrying through Torah study to pray, citing the verse that one who turns his ear from Torah has his prayer abominated.

items.text: When does the court session begin?
items.text_en: When does the court session begin?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Yonah debate whether the court session begins when the judges wrap themselves in their cloaks or when the litigants begin their arguments. They conclude both are correct depending on whether the litigants are already engaged in the case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from when the beginning of a trial is considered.
One opinion (attributed to Rabbi Yirmeya) holds that the trial begins when the judges wrap themselves in their cloaks.
The other opinion (attributed to Rabbi Yonah) holds that the trial begins when the litigants begin their arguments.
The Gemara resolves that the two opinions do not disagree: one refers to a case where they were already engaged in a previous trial, and the other to a case where they were not.

items.text: Judges and the ideal duration of court
items.text_en: Judges and the ideal duration of court
items.desc_en: Rav Ami and Rav Asi would sit between pillars and invite litigants. Rav Chisda and Rava bar Rav Huna would judge all day until their hearts grew weak. Rav Chiya bar Rav Midifti teaches that a judge who judges truthfully even for one hour is considered a partner with God in creation, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ami and Rav Asi would sit between the pillars studying and periodically knock on the door bolt, inviting anyone with a case to come in for judgment.
Rav Chisda and Rava bar Rav Huna would sit in judgment all day until their hearts grew weak from hunger.

Rav Chiya bar Rav Midifti taught them a baraita: Moses did not judge all day, but any judge who judges a true judgment even for one hour is credited as a partner with God in creation, as derived from the verses about Moses and the creation account.

items.text: The proper time for the meal and court adjournment
items.text_en: The proper time for the meal and court adjournment
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet says court sits until mealtime. Rav Chama cites a verse about kings eating at the proper time. A baraisa lists meal times for different classes, and Rav Pappa adjusts the schedule. Abaye adds that this applies only if one hasn't eaten in the morning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks until when judges may sit in judgment, and Rav Sheshet answers until mealtime.
Rav Sheshet rules that the court sits until mealtime.
Rav Chama cites a verse from Ecclesiastes to support that ministers eat at the proper time, interpreting 'in strength' as the strength of Torah.
A baraita lists the meal times for different classes: first hour for Ludim, second for robbers, third for heirs, fourth for workers, fifth for all people.
The Gemara objects that Rav Pappa said the fourth hour is mealtime for all people, contradicting the baraita.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by emending the baraita: fourth hour for all people, fifth for workers, sixth for Torah scholars, and eating later is like throwing a stone into a barrel.
Abaye qualifies that the rule about eating late applies only if one has not tasted anything in the morning; if he has, it is fine.

items.text: Praying in a bathhouse
items.text_en: Praying in a bathhouse
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava permits praying in a bathhouse. The Gemara objects with a baraisa detailing restrictions in bathhouses based on nudity. Rav Adda's statement is reinterpreted as referring to a new bathhouse with no people, but a question about designation for a bathhouse remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava states that one may pray in a bathhouse.
The Gemara raises a baraisa that details restrictions on prayer, Torah reading, and tefillin in different areas of a bathhouse based on nudity, contradicting Rav Adda's blanket permission.
The Gemara answers that Rav Adda referred to an empty bathhouse with no people.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's statement is cited to object that even an empty bathhouse is prohibited for prayer, just as a bathroom is prohibited even without feces.
The Gemara answers that Rav Adda referred to a new bathhouse that had not yet been used.
The Gemara raises Ravina's unresolved dilemma about whether designation as a bathroom is halakhically significant, and asks if the same applies to a bathhouse.
The Gemara rejects the comparison, suggesting that the bathhouse case may differ, leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Prohibition of saying 'Shalom' in a bathroom
items.text_en: Prohibition of saying 'Shalom' in a bathroom
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the prohibition against saying 'Shalom' in a bathroom is because 'Shalom' is a name of God. It distinguishes this from saying 'Heimanutah' (faith), which is permitted because it is not a direct name of God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the bathroom is different because it is disgusting, distinguishing it from the bathhouse.

sub.text: Tosefta and Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla
sub.text_en: Tosefta and Rav Hamnuna in the name of Ulla
sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states that there is no greeting in the bathhouse, supporting Ulla's ruling that it is forbidden to say 'Shalom' there because it is a name of God.
The Gemara questions whether the word 'Heimanutah' (faith) should also be forbidden in the bathroom, citing the verse 'the faithful God', and notes Rav's ruling that it is permitted.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that 'Heimanutah' is not a name of God itself, but 'Shalom' is, as the verse calls God 'Shalom'.

items.text: Gift-giving requires informing the recipient
items.text_en: Gift-giving requires informing the recipient
items.desc_en: Rav teaches that one who gives a gift must inform the recipient, citing the verse about Shabbat. A baraita supports this with the analogy of God telling Moses to inform Israel about Shabbat. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applies this to giving bread to a child, and Abaye and Rav Pappa discuss practical measures.

sub.text: Rava bar Meḥasseya in the name of Rav Ḥama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rava bar Meḥasseya in the name of Rav Ḥama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav states that one who gives a gift must inform the recipient, citing the verse 'לָדַעַת כִּי אֲנִי ה׳ מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם' (to know that I am God who sanctifies you).
A baraita supports Rav's ruling: God told Moses to inform Israel about the gift of Shabbat, as it says 'לָדַעַת כִּי אֲנִי ה׳ מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם'.
From this, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel derives that one who gives bread to a child must inform the child's mother.
The Gemara asks what one should do to the child so that the mother will know a gift was given.
Abaye answers that one should smear the child with oil or apply eye shadow so the mother notices.
The Gemara asks what should be done now that we are concerned about witchcraft from using oil or eye shadow.
Rav Pappa answers that one should smear the child with the same type of food that was given to him.

items.text: Reconciling conflicting views on informing the recipient
items.text_en: Reconciling conflicting views on informing the recipient
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction with Rav Chama bar Chanina's statement that one need not inform the recipient, citing Moses. It resolves that the requirement applies to matters that will not become known, whereas Shabbat's reward is not known.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the requirement to inform the recipient by citing Rav Chama bar Chanina's view that one need not inform, based on Moses not knowing his face shone.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between matters that will become known (no need to inform) and those that will not (must inform), and explains that Shabbat's reward is not known.

items.text: Rav Chisda's reward for a novel teaching
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's reward for a novel teaching
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda offers a gift for a new teaching from Rav. Rava bar Machseya cites Rav's teaching about informing the recipient, receives the gift, and they discuss the value of Rav's teachings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda holds two priestly gifts and offers them to anyone who brings a new teaching in Rav's name.
Rava bar Machseya cites Rav's teaching that one who gives a gift must inform the recipient, citing the verse about Shabbat.
Rav Chisda gives the gift to Rava bar Machseya.
Rav Chisda asks Rava bar Machseya if Rav's teachings are so beloved to him.
Rava bar Machseya affirms that Rav's teachings are indeed beloved to him.
Rava bar Machseya quotes Rav's aphorism that fine wool is precious to those who wear it, implying that only one who appreciates Rav's teachings values them.
Rav Chisda expresses surprise that Rav said this, and declares that this latter teaching is even more precious to him than the first, and he would give another gift if he had one.

items.text: Do not favor one child over others
items.text_en: Do not favor one child over others
items.desc_en: Rav teaches that one should never favor one child over others, as Jacob's favoritism toward Joseph led to the brothers' jealousy and the descent to Egypt.

sub.text: Rava bar Meḥasseya in the name of Rav Ḥama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rava bar Meḥasseya in the name of Rav Ḥama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav teaches that one should never favor one child over others, citing Jacob's gift to Joseph as the cause of the brothers' jealousy and the descent to Egypt.

items.text: Choose a city with a recent settlement
items.text_en: Choose a city with a recent settlement
items.desc_en: Rav advises living in a city that was settled recently, as its sins are fewer. Rabbi Avin supports this with a gematria from Lot's plea to flee to Zoar.

sub.text: Rava bar Meḥasseya in the name of Rav Ḥama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rava bar Meḥasseya in the name of Rav Ḥama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav advises that a person should always seek to dwell in a city whose settlement is recent, because its sins are few.
Rav cites the verse where Lot describes Zoar as 'close' and 'small' to support the advice.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'close' in the verse, suggesting it might mean close in distance and small, but notes that the angels could see it.
The Gemara explains that 'close' means its settlement was recent, and therefore its sins are few.
Rabbi Avin supports the interpretation with a gematria: the word 'na' has the numerical value of 51, while Sodom was 52 years old, indicating Zoar was newer.

items.text: Opening biblical verse
items.text_en: Opening biblical verse
items.desc_en: The daf opens with a verse from Genesis about the years of servitude to Chedorlaomer, setting the stage for the following aggadic statements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Genesis to support the calculation of twenty-six years of tranquility.

items.text: Rav's statement: high roofs cause destruction
items.text_en: Rav's statement: high roofs cause destruction
items.desc_en: Rav, via Rava bar Machseya and Rav Chama bar Gurya, states that any city whose roofs are higher than the synagogue will ultimately be destroyed, citing a verse. Rav Ashi comments that he ensured his city did not suffer this fate.

sub.text: Rav via Rava bar Machseya and Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.text_en: Rav via Rava bar Machseya and Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.desc_en: Rav states that any city whose roofs are higher than the synagogue will ultimately be destroyed.
Rav cites the verse 'לְרוֹמֵם אֶת בֵּית אֱלֹהֵינוּ וּלְהַעֲמִיד אֶת חׇרְבוֹתָיו' as proof that the synagogue must be elevated.
The Gemara clarifies that the rule applies only to the houses themselves, not to poles and towers extending from them.
Rav Ashi says he ensured the city of Mata Meḥasseya was not destroyed by building the synagogue higher.
The Gemara objects that Mata Meḥasseya was indeed destroyed.
The Gemara resolves that the city was destroyed due to other sins, not because of the synagogue's height.

items.text: Rav's hierarchy of neighbors
items.text_en: Rav's hierarchy of neighbors
items.desc_en: Rav presents a hierarchy of preferable neighbors: under an Ishmaelite rather than a gentile, under a gentile rather than a haber, under a haber rather than a Torah scholar, and under a Torah scholar rather than an orphan or widow.

sub.desc_en: Rav presents a hierarchy of preferable neighbors: under an Ishmaelite rather than a gentile, under a gentile rather than a haber, under a haber rather than a Torah scholar, and under a Torah scholar rather than an orphan or widow.

items.text: Rav's list of worst afflictions
items.text_en: Rav's list of worst afflictions
items.desc_en: Rav lists the worst types of suffering: any illness except intestinal illness, any pain except heartache, any ache except headache, any evil except a bad wife.

sub.desc_en: Rav lists the worst types of suffering: any illness except intestinal illness, any pain except heartache, any ache except headache, any evil except a bad wife.

items.text: Rav's hyperbole on the depth of authority
items.text_en: Rav's hyperbole on the depth of authority
items.desc_en: Rav declares that even if all days were ink, reeds pens, heavens parchment, and all people scribes, they could not write the depth of authority (reshut). Rav Mesharsheya cites a verse from Proverbs.

sub.desc_en: Rav declares that even if all seas were ink, reeds pens, heavens parchment, and all people scribes, they could not write the depth of authority (רשות).
Rav Mesharsheya cites the verse from Proverbs (25:3) to support Rav's statement about the unsearchable depth of kings' hearts.

items.text: Rav's statement on fasting for a dream
items.text_en: Rav's statement on fasting for a dream
items.desc_en: Rav states that fasting for a dream is as effective as fire for flax. Rav Chisda adds that it must be on the same day, and Rav Yosef says even on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that a fast is as effective for a bad dream as fire is for chaff.
Rav Ḥisda adds that the fast must be on the same day as the dream.
Rav Yosef adds that one may fast even on Shabbat for a bad dream.

items.text: Story of Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi and fasting for a dream
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi and fasting for a dream
items.desc_en: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi visits Rav Ashi, who offers him a calf. He declines, saying he is fasting. They cite Rav Yehuda's principle that one may borrow a fast and repay it, but he explains it is a dream fast, repeating Rav's statement and the opinions of Rav Chisda and Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehoshua ben Rav Idi arrives at Rav Ashi's house, and they prepare a third-born calf for him.
They invite him to taste the food.
He declines, explaining that he is fasting.
They challenge him, citing Rav Yehuda's principle that one may borrow a fast and repay it later.
He explains that this is a fast for a dream, which cannot be postponed.
Rav's statement is cited: a fast is effective for a dream like fire burns chaff.
Rav Chisda adds that the fast must be on the same day as the dream.
Rav Yosef adds that one may fast even on Shabbat for a bad dream.

items.text: Interrupting Torah study for Shema and prayer
items.text_en: Interrupting Torah study for Shema and prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita about friends studying Torah: they interrupt for Shema but not for prayer. Rabbi Yochanan limits this to those whose Torah is their occupation, but for people like us, we interrupt for both. A contradiction is raised and resolved by distinguishing the case of intercalating the year, where they do not interrupt at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishna repeats that they do not interrupt, since the first clause already stated this.
The Gemara explains that the latter clause refers to Torah study, citing a baraita that friends studying Torah interrupt for Shema but not for prayer.
Rabbi Yochanan limits the baraita to those whose Torah is their occupation, but for people like us, we interrupt for both Shema and prayer.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says just as they do not interrupt for prayer, they also do not interrupt for Shema.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to those engaged in intercalating the year, citing Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok that they did not interrupt for either Shema or prayer.

items.text: Mishnah: not going out with a needle near dark, and Gemara's discussion
items.text_en: Mishnah: not going out with a needle near dark, and Gemara's discussion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits a tailor from going out with a needle near dark lest he forget and carry it, and similarly a scribe with his quill. It also prohibits picking garments or reading by lamp light. The Gemara cites a related Tosefta about not standing in a private domain and drinking in a public domain, with an exception if one inserts his head and most of his body.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions near dark on Shabbat eve: a tailor may not go out with his needle, a scribe with his quill, one may not pick garments or read by lamp light; the attendant may see where children read but not read himself; similarly a zav may not eat with a zava.

The Gemara cites a related mishna: one may not stand in a private domain and drink from a public domain or vice versa, but if he inserts his head and most of his body into the place where he drinks, it is permitted.

items.text: Opening statement about the winepress
items.text_en: Opening statement about the winepress
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that the same rule applies to a winepress (גת). This sets up the discussion about whether a winepress is considered a karmelit.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that the same rule applies to a winepress (גת), setting up the discussion about its domain classification.

items.text: Dispute about the status of a karmelit
items.text_en: Dispute about the status of a karmelit
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate whether a karmelit is considered a distinct domain. Abaye argues it is the same as a winepress, while Rava says it is a decree and we do not add a decree to a decree. They bring support from the mishnah and a baraita about tithes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: what is the status of a karmelit (a domain that is neither public nor private)?
Abaye asserts that a karmelit is the same as a winepress (a distinct domain).
Rava argues that the karmelit itself is a decree, and we cannot add a decree to a decree.
Abaye supports his position by citing the mishnah's phrase 'וכן בגת' (and similarly in the winepress), arguing that the winepress must be a karmelit, not a private or public domain.
Rava and Rav Sheishet reinterpret the mishnah's phrase 'וכן בגת' as referring to tithes, not Shabbat domains, citing a baraita about drinking at the winepress.

items.text: Discussion about a tailor's needle on Shabbat eve
items.text_en: Discussion about a tailor's needle on Shabbat eve
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a mishnah about a tailor not going out with his needle near dark. It clarifies whether the needle is stuck in his garment or held in his hand, and cites a baraita with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's opinions on an artisan's liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah about a tailor not going out with his needle near dark, and asks whether the needle is stuck in his garment or held in his hand.
The Gemara initially suggests the needle is stuck in his garment, then rejects this and says it is held in his hand.
The Gemara brings a baraita that explicitly says the needle is stuck in his garment, but then clarifies that the baraita refers to Shabbat itself, not Shabbat eve.
The Gemara cites another baraita that explicitly mentions Shabbat eve, and resolves that it follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that an artisan going out in his professional manner is liable.

sub.text: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing various artisans and their tools, where Rabbi Meir says one is פטור אבל אסור (exempt but forbidden) and Rabbi Yehuda says an artisan going out in his professional manner is חייב (liable).

items.text: Contradiction about a zav's bag
items.text_en: Contradiction about a zav's bag
items.desc_en: Two baraitot contradict each other regarding a zav going out with his bag: one says he is exempt but prohibited, the other says he is liable for a sin-offering. Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing them to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a zav (one with a seminal emission) may not go out with his bag, and if he does, he is exempt from a sin-offering but it is prohibited.
Another baraita contradicts the first, ruling that if a zav goes out with his bag, he is liable to bring a sin-offering.

Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Meir (who holds that an artisan is exempt but prohibited) and the second to Rabbi Yehuda (who holds an artisan is liable).

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rav Yosef's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rav Yosef's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's attribution, arguing that Rabbi Meir only exempts when the item is not one's typical way of carrying, but for a zav's bag which is his typical way, Rabbi Meir would also hold him liable.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbi Meir's leniency applies only to items not part of one's normal way, but for a zav whose bag is essential, Rabbi Meir might still hold him liable.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a zav with two sightings (who needs examination) and one with three sightings (who needs counting). The Gemara questions this and Rabbi Zeira explains that the tanna does not consider preventing soiling as significant.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction regarding 'כי יותן'
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction regarding 'כי יותן'
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between two sources about the status of liquids that fall on a wall or into a trough. Abaye and Rava explain that the first source follows Rabbi Yehuda and the second follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the first source: if the wall is not intended to absorb the liquid, why is it not subject to the rule of 'כי יותן' (the condition for liquids to render food susceptible to impurity)? It distinguishes: there the liquids are not wanted at all, but here the pouch is wanted to receive discharge.

The Gemara reframes the problem: the first source is actually comparable to the second case in the baraita — a trough where dripping water collects — where the water that splashes out is not subject to 'כי יותן' but the water inside is.
Abaye and Rava resolve the contradiction: the first source follows Rabbi Yehuda (who holds that intention matters) and the second follows Rabbi Shimon (who holds that intention does not matter).

items.text: The obligation to feel one's phylacteries on Shabbat eve
items.text_en: The obligation to feel one's phylacteries on Shabbat eve
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one may go out with phylacteries on Shabbat eve at dusk, because one must constantly feel them, as derived from the frontplate. Rabbi Yosef calls this a great halakha for Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael states that one may go out with phylacteries (תפילין) on Shabbat eve at dusk.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this ruling.
Rabba bar Rav Huna explains that one must constantly feel the phylacteries (תפילין), derived via a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the frontplate (ציץ) of the High Priest.
The Gemara concludes that one will therefore remember the phylacteries (תפילין) and not violate Shabbat.
A baraita adds that Chananya says one must feel one's garment on Shabbat eve at dusk.
Rabbi Yosef declares this a great halakha (הלכה) for Shabbat.

items.text: The reason for the prohibition of picking lice and reading by candlelight
items.text_en: The reason for the prohibition of picking lice and reading by candlelight
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether the prohibition of picking clothes and reading by candlelight is due to the concern of killing (lice) or tilting the lamp. A baraita from the upper chamber of Chananya ben Chizkiya ben Garon proves that both are due to the concern of tilting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: is the prohibition of picking lice from clothes by candlelight due to the concern of killing (lice), as per Rabbi Eliezer, or is it due to the concern of tilting the lamp, like reading?
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states 'one may not pick lice nor read by candlelight,' questioning whether this baraita is stronger than the Mishnah.
The Gemara brings a second baraita from the upper chamber of Chananya ben Chizkiya ben Garon, which lists both prohibitions together, proving that both are due to the concern of tilting the lamp.

items.text: Distinguishing one's own garment from his wife's
items.text_en: Distinguishing one's own garment from his wife's
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says one may not even distinguish his garment from his wife's by candlelight. Rava limits this to residents of Mehoza, and only regarding old women's garments.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that one may not even distinguish his own garment from his wife's by candlelight.
Rava limits the prohibition to residents of Mehoza (מחוזא) and only regarding old women's garments, since others can easily distinguish.

items.text: Picking lice in the public domain and methods of removal
items.text_en: Picking lice in the public domain and methods of removal
items.desc_en: A baraita prohibits picking lice in the public domain due to dignity. Another baraita allows rubbing and throwing, but Abba Shaul says one may take and throw without rubbing. Rav Huna rules like the first, and various Amoraim demonstrate their practice.

sub.desc_en: A baraita prohibits picking lice in the public domain due to dignity.

sub.text: Baraita with Rav Yehuda or Rabbi Nechemya
sub.text_en: Baraita with Rav Yehuda or Rabbi Nechemya
sub.desc_en: A parallel baraita prohibits making an apiktovizin (a type of medical treatment) in the public domain for the sake of dignity.
A baraita permits rubbing and throwing lice from one's garment, provided one does not kill them.
Abba Shaul says one may take and throw without rubbing.
Rav Huna rules like the first baraita: one rubs and throws, and this is dignified even on a weekday.

Various Amoraim demonstrate their practice: Rabba and Rav Sheshet cut them off, Rava throws them into a water jug, and Rav Nachman instructs his daughters to kill them so he can hear the sound of his sandals.

items.text: Killing a louse on Shabbat: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Killing a louse on Shabbat: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports that Beit Shammai prohibit killing a louse on Shabbat, while Beit Hillel permit it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states: Beit Shammai prohibit killing a louse (מאכולת) on Shabbat, while Beit Hillel permit it.

items.text: Prohibitions of arranging marriages, teaching, comforting, and visiting on Shabbat
items.text_en: Prohibitions of arranging marriages, teaching, comforting, and visiting on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that Beit Shammai prohibit arranging marriages, teaching children, comforting mourners, and visiting the sick on Shabbat, while Beit Hillel permit.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that Beit Shammai prohibit arranging marriages, teaching children, comforting mourners, and visiting the sick on Shabbat, while Beit Hillel permit.

items.text: What to say when visiting the sick on Shabbat
items.text_en: What to say when visiting the sick on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who visits a sick person on Shabbat says 'Shabbat is for refraining from crying, and healing is near to come.' Rabbi Meir says one says 'It (Shabbat) is capable of having mercy.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the formula for visiting the sick on Shabbat: 'Shabbat is for refraining from crying, and healing is near to come.'
Rabbi Meir offers an alternative formula: 'It (Shabbat) is capable of having mercy.'

items.text: Formulations for visiting the sick on Shabbat
items.text_en: Formulations for visiting the sick on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei debate the correct blessing for a sick person on Shabbat. Shebna of Jerusalem's practice is cited, and Rabbi Chanina's ruling is aligned with Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states the blessing for a sick person on Shabbat: 'May the Omnipresent have mercy on you and on the sick of Israel.'
Rabbi Yosei gives an alternative formulation: 'May the Omnipresent have mercy on you among the sick of Israel.'
Shebna of Jerusalem's practice is cited: upon entering he says 'Peace,' and upon leaving he says a longer blessing that includes 'Shabbat is from crying out.'
The gemara aligns Rabbi Chanina's ruling that one should include the sick person among the sick of Israel with Rabbi Yosei's formulation.

items.text: Permission to console mourners and visit the sick on Shabbat
items.text_en: Permission to console mourners and visit the sick on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that consoling mourners and visiting the sick on Shabbat was permitted with difficulty. Rabba bar bar Chana describes Rabbi Elazar's practice of using Aramaic, which seems to contradict the rule against asking needs in Aramaic. The Gemara resolves that a sick person is different because the Divine Presence is with him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that consoling mourners and visiting the sick on Shabbat was permitted with difficulty.
Rabba bar bar Chana describes Rabbi Elazar's practice of using both Hebrew and Aramaic when visiting the sick on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar's use of Aramaic contradicts the rule that one should never ask needs in Aramaic, as angels do not understand it.
The Gemara resolves that a sick person is different because the Divine Presence (שכינה) is with him, so no angelic intermediary is needed.

items.text: Proof that God supports the sick
items.text_en: Proof that God supports the sick
items.desc_en: Rav Anan citing Rav derives from a verse that God supports the sick. A baraita adds that one visiting the sick should sit with reverence because the Divine Presence is above the sick person's head. Rava citing Ravin also derives that God sustains the sick from the same verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan in the name of Rav asks from where we know that God supports the sick, and answers with the verse 'ה׳ יִסְעָדֶנּוּ עַל עֶרֶשׂ דְּוָי' (God will support him on the bed of suffering).
A baraita is cited that supports the same verse, teaching that one visiting the sick must sit with reverence because the Divine Presence (שכינה) is above the sick person's head.
Rava in the name of Ravin also derives from the same verse that God sustains the sick.

items.text: Prohibition of reading by candlelight and exceptions
items.text_en: Prohibition of reading by candlelight and exceptions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states one may not read by candlelight. Rabba extends this even to a high lamp. A contradiction is raised from a baraita that forbids even two people. Rabbi Elazar resolves: one topic is forbidden, two topics are permitted. Rav Huna adds that by a bonfire, even ten people are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of reading by candlelight on Shabbat.
Rabba extends the prohibition to any height, even a lamp ten houses high.
The Gemara infers from Rabba's statement that two people reading is permitted, but a baraita forbids even two.
A baraita is cited that forbids reading by candlelight for both one and two people.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction: one topic is forbidden, two topics are permitted.
Rav Huna adds that by a bonfire (מדורה), even ten people are forbidden.

items.text: An important person may read by candlelight
items.text_en: An important person may read by candlelight
items.desc_en: Rava rules that an important person may read by candlelight. An objection is raised from Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, who tried to read and almost tilted the lamp, and Rabbi Nathan who records that he did tilt it. Rabbi Abba distinguishes Rabbi Yishmael because he considered himself an ignoramus regarding Torah matters.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that an important person may read by candlelight on Shabbat.

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha tried to read and almost tilted the lamp, and Rabbi Nathan records that he did tilt it, showing that even an important person is not exempt.
Rabbi Abba resolves the objection by distinguishing Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, who considered himself an ignoramus regarding Torah matters, thus not qualifying as an important person.

items.text: Contradiction regarding a shamash checking vessels by candlelight
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding a shamash checking vessels by candlelight
items.desc_en: Two baraitot contradict each other: one permits a shamash to check cups and bowls by candlelight, the other forbids it. The Gemara resolves: one refers to a permanent shamash, the other to a non-permanent one. Alternatively, both are permanent but one involves oil and the other naphtha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two contradictory baraitot: one permits a shamash to check cups and bowls by candlelight, the other forbids it.
The Gemara resolves: one baraita refers to a permanent shamash, the other to a non-permanent one.
Alternatively, both baraitot refer to a permanent shamash, but one involves oil and the other naphtha.

items.text: Inquiry about a non-permanent shamash with oil
items.text_en: Inquiry about a non-permanent shamash with oil
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: what about a non-permanent shamash with oil? Rav rules it is halacha but not to be taught publicly. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says it is halacha and may be taught. A story illustrates that Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's practice followed his own ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: what is the ruling for a non-permanent shamash (attendant) using oil (שמן) to check vessels by lamp light?
Rav rules that it is the הלכה (binding law) but one should not teach it publicly.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba rules that it is the הלכה (binding law) and one may teach it publicly.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates that Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's practice followed his own ruling, as he checked a lamp by oil light at Rabbi Assi's house, and his wife's objection was dismissed because he followed his teacher's view.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement about the chazzan
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement about the chazzan
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'the chazzan sees where the children read.' It clarifies that this does not mean he reads, but rather he arranges the chapter headings. Rabba bar Shmuel confirms that one may arrange chapter headings but not the entire portion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'the chazzan sees where the children read,' asking whether this implies he actually reads along.
The Gemara answers that the chazzan does not read but merely arranges the chapter headings.
Rabba bar Shmuel confirms that one may arrange chapter headings but not the entire portion.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about children reading by candlelight
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about children reading by candlelight
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says children would arrange and read portions by candlelight. The Gemara offers two answers: either they read only the headings, or children are different because fear of their teacher prevents them from adjusting the lamp.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says children would arrange and read portions by candlelight.
The Gemara offers the first answer: the children read only the headings of the portions.
The Gemara offers the second answer: children are different because fear of their teacher prevents them from adjusting the lamp.

items.text: Baraita about a zav not eating with a zavah and its analysis
items.text_en: Baraita about a zav not eating with a zavah and its analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a zav should not eat with a zavah due to habit of sin. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar praises Israel's purity. A similar ruling: a zav perush (separate) should not eat with a zav am ha'aretz. The Gemara questions the reason, and Abaye and Rava offer explanations about feeding him untithed or impure foods.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a zav should not eat with a zavah due to habit of sin.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar praises Israel's purity, noting the baraita's restriction is only due to habit of sin.
A similar ruling is cited: a zav perush (separate) should not eat with a zav am ha'aretz, lest he habituate him.
The Gemara questions what harm comes from habituating him.
The Gemara rephrases: the concern is that he might feed him impure foods.
The Gemara objects: does the zav perush himself not eat impure foods?
Abaye explains: the concern is that he might feed him untithed foods (דברים שאינן מתוקנין).
Rava explains: most amei ha'aretz tithe properly, but the concern is that he might become habituated and feed him impure foods during his days of purity.

items.text: Inquiry about a niddah sleeping with her husband in separate garments
items.text_en: Inquiry about a niddah sleeping with her husband in separate garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a niddah may sleep with her husband, each in their own garment. Rav Yosef attempts to bring proof from the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about a bird and cheese on the table, but the Gemara distinguishes because there is no 'dei'ot' (distinct tastes). The Gemara then supports this distinction from a ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel about two guests, as explained by Rav Chanin bar Ami quoting Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a niddah may sleep with her husband, each in their own garment.
Rav Yosef attempts to bring proof from the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about a bird and cheese on the table, where the bird is not eaten but may be on the table.
The Gemara rejects the proof because there, with the bird and cheese, there are no distinct tastes (דֵּיעוֹת) to cause concern, unlike the case of a husband and wife.

sub.text: Gemara's support from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Gemara's support from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the distinction by citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling about two guests eating on one table, and Rav Chanin bar Ami quoting Shmuel that the leniency applies only when they do not recognize each other, while here the husband and wife recognize each other, yet the case is different because there are both distinct tastes (דֵּיעוֹת) and a change (שִׁנּוּי) in garments.

items.text: Alternative version of the proof from guests
items.text_en: Alternative version of the proof from guests
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the proof is presented: from the ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel about two guests, with Shmuel's distinction. The Gemara again rejects the proof because there is a change (shinui) here, unlike there.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version cites the same baraita about two guests eating at one table.
Shmuel's ruling is repeated: the leniency applies only when they do not know each other.
The Gemara objects: here too, they know each other.
The Gemara answers: there, intimacy exists but no change; here, both intimacy and change exist.

items.text: Proof from the zav and zavah baraita
items.text_en: Proof from the zav and zavah baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove the matter from the baraita that a zav should not eat with a zavah. The Gemara rejects this because there is no change (shinui) there, unlike here where there is both change and distinct tastes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from the baraita: a זב (zav) may not eat with a זבה (zavah) due to habitual sin.
The Gemara answers: here too, intimacy exists but no change of garments.

items.text: Proof from a verse about a niddah
items.text_en: Proof from a verse about a niddah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a verse that juxtaposes a niddah to another man's wife: just as with another man's wife, each in their own garment is forbidden, so too with a niddah. The Gemara concludes: learn from this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a verse: Ezekiel did not approach a נִדָּה (menstruant).
The Gemara deduces: just as with a married woman, he in his garment and she in hers is forbidden, so too with his נִדָּה (menstruant) wife.
The Gemara concludes: learn from this that it is forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Pedat and Ulla about closeness to a niddah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Pedat and Ulla about closeness to a niddah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pedat argues that the Torah only forbids actual closeness for forbidden relations, citing a verse. Ulla, however, would kiss his sisters on their hands, and he holds that even any closeness is forbidden, based on the principle 'go around, do not approach the vineyard'. This contradicts the previous proof.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute with Rabbi Pedat, who holds that the Torah only forbids closeness (קורבה) for forbidden relations, citing the verse 'אל כל שאר בשרו לא תקרבו לגלות ערוה'.
The gemara reports that Ulla, when returning from the study hall, would kiss his sisters on their hands (or chest), showing a lenient practice regarding closeness to a niddah.
The gemara notes that Ulla's own statement contradicts his practice, as he said that even any closeness (קורבה) is forbidden, based on the principle 'go around, do not approach the vineyard'.

items.text: Story of a scholar who died young
items.text_en: Story of a scholar who died young
items.desc_en: A story is told from the school of Elijah about a student who studied much, read much, and served many sages, yet died in the prime of his life. His wife would take his tefillin and go around synagogues and study halls, citing the verse 'for it is your life and the length of your days'.

sub.desc_en: A story is told from the academy of Eliyahu about a student who studied much and died in the middle of his life.
His wife would take his tefillin and circulate them in synagogues and study halls, citing the verse 'for it is your life and length of days.'

items.text: Story of the pious man and the menstruant
items.text_en: Story of the pious man and the menstruant
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story about a pious man who served many Torah scholars but died young. His wife recounts that during her menstrual period he never touched her, but during her white days he would eat, drink, and sleep with her in close bodily contact without improper thoughts. The narrator concludes that the man was justly killed for not honoring the Torah's command not to approach a menstruating woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story about a pious man who served many Torah scholars but died young, and no one could explain why.

The wife recounts that during her menstrual period (ימי נדות) he never touched her, but during her white days (ימי ליבוניך) he ate, drank, and slept with her in close bodily contact without improper thoughts.
The narrator concludes that the man was justly killed for not honoring the Torah's command not to approach a menstruating woman (ואל אשה בנדת טומאתה לא תקרב).
Rabbi Dimi adds that they shared a single bed.
In the West they say that Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef stated that a belt (סינר) separated between them.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The eighteen decrees
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The eighteen decrees
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists that these are among the halakhot stated in the upper chamber of Chananiah ben Chizkiyah ben Garon, where Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel and eighteen decrees were issued that day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists that these are among the halachot (הלכות) stated in the upper chamber of Chananya ben Chizkiya ben Garon, where Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel and decreed eighteen matters on that day.

items.text: Gemara's question: 'Eilu' or 'Ve'eilu'?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: 'Eilu' or 'Ve'eilu'?
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the Mishnah reads 'Eilu' (these are) or 'Ve'eilu' (and these are). He brings a proof from a baraita that lists 'Einu polin l'or haner' and then says 'Ve'eilu min hahalakhot', concluding that the Mishnah reads 'Ve'eilu'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the Mishnah reads 'אלו' (these) or 'ואלו' (and these), questioning if it introduces new items or continues a previous list.
The Gemara brings a proof from the Mishnah's own wording 'אין פולין לאור הנר ואין קורין לאור הנר, ואלו מן ההלכות' — concluding that it reads 'ואלו' (and these).

items.text: Who wrote Megillat Ta'anit?
items.text_en: Who wrote Megillat Ta'anit?
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that Chananiah ben Chizkiyah and his group wrote Megillat Ta'anit because they cherished troubles. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that they too cherish troubles but cannot write them all due to lack of time.

sub.desc_en: The baraita asks who wrote Megillat Ta'anit and answers that Chananiah ben Chizkiyah and his group wrote it because they cherished troubles.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that they too cherish troubles but cannot write them all due to lack of time.

items.text: Two 'Davar Acher' statements and a clarification
items.text_en: Two 'Davar Acher' statements and a clarification
items.desc_en: Two additional statements are introduced: 'A fool is not afflicted' and 'The flesh of a dead person does not feel the scalpel'. The Gemara questions the latter from Rav Yitzchak's statement that worms are as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh, and resolves that it means the flesh of a dead person that is still attached to a living person does not feel the scalpel.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the first Davar Acher statement: 'A fool is not afflicted.'
Introduces the second Davar Acher statement: 'The flesh of a dead person does not feel the scalpel.'
Objects to the second statement by citing Rav Yitzchak's teaching that worms are as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh.
Resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the statement to mean that flesh of a dead person still attached to a living person does not feel the scalpel.

items.text: Praise for Chananiah ben Chizkiyah
items.text_en: Praise for Chananiah ben Chizkiyah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah says in the name of Rav that Chananiah ben Chizkiyah is remembered for good, for had it not been for him, the Book of Ezekiel would have been hidden because its words contradicted the Torah. He brought up 300 jugs of oil, sat in an upper chamber, and reconciled the contradictions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav says: That man is remembered for good, Chananya ben Chizkiya, for if not for him, the book of Ezekiel would have been hidden because its words contradicted the Torah.
What did he do? They brought him three hundred jugs of oil, and he sat in an upper chamber and resolved them.

items.text: The eighteen decrees listed and questioned
items.text_en: The eighteen decrees listed and questioned
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the eighteen decrees are and cites a Mishnah listing those who disqualify terumah: one who eats a first-degree food, one who eats a second-degree food, one who drinks impure liquids, one whose head and most of his body enter drawn water, a pure person upon whose head and most of his body three log of drawn water fall, a book, hands, a tevul yom, and foods and vessels that became impure through liquids. The Gemara then asks who taught that eating first- and second-degree foods disqualify but do not render impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the eighteen decrees are.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah listing those who disqualify תרומה (priestly portion): one who eats a first-degree food, one who eats a second-degree food, one who drinks impure liquids, one whose head and most of his body enter drawn water, a pure person upon whose head and most of his body three log of drawn water fall, a book, hands, a טבול יום (one who immersed that day), and foods and vessels that became impure through liquids.
The Gemara asks who taught that eating first- and second-degree foods disqualify but do not render impure.

items.text: Identification of the Tanna behind the decree
items.text_en: Identification of the Tanna behind the decree
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah identifies that the decree regarding one who eats second-degree foods is according to Rabbi Yehoshua, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute the status of one who eats foods of varying impurity levels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Do they not transmit impurity?
Rabbah bar bar Chanah answers that the decree follows Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute the impurity status of one who eats foods of varying impurity levels, with Rabbi Yehoshua ruling that there is no second-degree impurity for תרומה (priestly portion) in חולין (non-sacred food) prepared with the purity of תרומה.

items.text: Reason for the decree on one who eats second-degree foods and drinks impure liquids
items.text_en: Reason for the decree on one who eats second-degree foods and drinks impure liquids
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the rationale for the decrees: one who eats impure foods might then eat terumah foods, and one who drinks impure liquids might then drink terumah liquids. It clarifies that both decrees are necessary despite their similarity, as one might think the latter is less common.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages decreed impurity on one who eats a second-degree food, explaining the concern that he might then eat terumah foods.
The Gemara asks why the Sages decreed impurity on one who drinks impure liquids, explaining the concern that he might then drink terumah liquids.
The Gemara objects that the two decrees seem identical.
The Gemara resolves that both decrees are necessary, lest one think the second is less common and thus not decreed.

items.text: Reason for the decree on one who immerses with drawn water
items.text_en: Reason for the decree on one who immerses with drawn water
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi explains that initially people used cave water for immersion, which was stagnant and foul, so they added drawn water. When they began to treat the drawn water as primary, the Sages decreed impurity on such a person. Abaye and Rava debate the precise nature of the 'fixing' that triggered the decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages decreed impurity on one who immerses his head and most of his body in drawn water.

sub.text: Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi explains that initially people used cave water for immersion, which was stagnant and foul, so they added drawn water; when they began to treat the drawn water as primary, the Sages decreed impurity.
The Gemara asks what exactly constituted the 'fixing' (קבע) that triggered the decree.
Abaye explains that people said 'not these (drawn water) purify, but both these and those (cave water) purify,' treating drawn water as equally effective.
Rava objects that if they still immerse in the cave water, what difference does their statement make?
Rava explains that people said 'not these (cave water) purify, but these (drawn water) purify,' treating drawn water as the sole purifying agent.

items.text: Reason for the decree on a pure person who receives drawn water
items.text_en: Reason for the decree on a pure person who receives drawn water
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the decree on a pure person upon whom three log of drawn water fall is necessary to support the previous decree regarding one who immerses with drawn water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages decreed impurity on a pure person upon whom three log of drawn water fall.
The Gemara answers that this decree is necessary to support the previous decree regarding one who immerses with drawn water, as without this one, that one would not stand.

items.text: Reason for the decree on a Torah scroll
items.text_en: Reason for the decree on a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya explains that initially people stored terumah foods near a Torah scroll, reasoning that both are holy. When this led to damage (mice eating the scroll), the Sages decreed impurity on the scroll to prevent such storage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages decreed impurity on a Torah scroll.

Rav Mesharshiya explains that initially people stored terumah foods near a Torah scroll, reasoning that both are holy, but when this led to damage (mice eating the scroll), the Sages decreed impurity on the scroll to prevent such storage.

items.text: Reason for the decree on hands and the connection to the Torah scroll
items.text_en: Reason for the decree on hands and the connection to the Torah scroll
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that hands are decreed impure because they are busy. A baraita adds that hands that come from handling a scroll also disqualify terumah, citing Rabbi Parnach's statement that one who holds a Torah scroll naked is buried naked, which is explained as without that mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that hands are decreed impure because they are busy (עסְקָנִיּוֹת).
A baraita adds that hands that come from handling a Torah scroll also disqualify תרומה (the priestly portion).
Rabbi Parnach cites Rabbi Yochanan that one who holds a Torah scroll naked is buried naked.
The Gemara objects: can it enter your mind that he is literally buried naked?
Rabbi Zeira resolves: 'naked' means without מצות (commandments).
The Gemara objects: can it enter your mind that he is buried without any commandments at all?
The Gemara concludes: 'naked' means without that specific מצוה (the mitzvah of handling the Torah scroll).

items.text: Question about the chronological order of the decrees
items.text_en: Question about the chronological order of the decrees
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to question which of these decrees was enacted first, starting with the possibility that the decree on hands was first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which of the decrees was enacted first, proposing that the decree on hands might have been first.

items.text: Gemara's question on the sequence of decrees
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the sequence of decrees
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the decree on hands was already enacted first, why was another decree needed later? It answers that the first decree was on hands alone, and the second on all hands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the first decree was already enacted, why was a second one needed?
The Gemara answers: the first decree was on hands alone, and the second was on all hands.

items.text: Challenge regarding a tevul yom
items.text_en: Challenge regarding a tevul yom
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that a tevul yom is biblically impure, as it is written 'and when the sun sets he shall be pure', so why is it listed among Rabbinic decrees? It dismisses this by noting that tevul yom is derived from here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that a טבול יום (one who immersed but awaits sunset) is biblically impure, citing the verse 'וּבָא הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְטָהֵר' (and when the sun sets he shall be pure), so why is it listed among Rabbinic decrees?
The Gemara dismisses the challenge by noting that the impurity of a טבול יום is derived from here (the verse), meaning it is a Rabbinic extension based on a biblical hint.

items.text: Challenge regarding foods impured by liquids
items.text_en: Challenge regarding foods impured by liquids
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: foods impured by liquids—what liquids? If from a sheretz, it is biblical; rather, it is from liquids that come from hands, a decree due to liquids from a sheretz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: regarding foods impured by liquids, what liquids are the source of the impurity? If from liquids that come from a sheretz, that is biblical.
The Gemara answers: rather, the decree applies to liquids that come from hands, a rabbinic decree due to liquids that come from a sheretz.

items.text: Challenge regarding vessels impured by liquids
items.text_en: Challenge regarding vessels impured by liquids
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: vessels impured by liquids—what liquids? If from a zav, it is biblical; rather, it is from liquids that come from a sheretz, a decree due to liquids from a zav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: vessels impured by liquids—what liquids? If from a zav, it is biblical.
The Gemara answers: rather, it is a decree regarding liquids from a sheretz, due to liquids from a zav.

items.text: Challenge: Did Shammai and Hillel decree on hands?
items.text_en: Challenge: Did Shammai and Hillel decree on hands?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Shammai and Hillel decreed impurity on hands, citing a baraita that lists earlier decrees by Yosei ben Yoezer and others, and then states that Shammai and Hillel decreed impurity on hands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Shammai and Hillel themselves decreed impurity on hands, given the baraita listing their decree.
The Gemara cites a baraita listing decrees by earlier sages, concluding that Shammai and Hillel decreed impurity on hands.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction about Shammai and Hillel
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction about Shammai and Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Shammai and Hillel themselves decreed but it was not accepted, while their students decreed and it was accepted, citing Rav Yehuda and Ilfa to support that the decree was initially for burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if Shammai and Hillel themselves decreed impurity for hands, why does the Mishnah attribute the decree to their students?
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel states that the eighteen decrees were disputed, but Shammai and Hillel themselves only disagreed in three places, implying they did not decree about hands.
The Gemara proposes an alternative: perhaps Shammai and Hillel decreed only for תלויה (suspension) and their students for burning, but Ilfa's statement contradicts this.
Ilfa states that the initial decree about hands was for burning (שרפה), not suspension.
The Gemara resolves: Shammai and Hillel decreed but it was not accepted, while their students decreed and it was accepted.

items.text: Challenge: Did Solomon decree hand washing?
items.text_en: Challenge: Did Solomon decree hand washing?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Solomon decreed hand washing, citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that when Solomon instituted eiruvin and hand washing, a bat kol praised him. The daf breaks off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Solomon decreed hand washing, citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that when Solomon instituted eiruvin and hand washing, a bat kol praised him.

items.text: The eighteen decrees and their resolution
items.text_en: The eighteen decrees and their resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that eighteen decrees were enacted, and initially there was a dispute about them, but later they were agreed upon. It cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that eighteen decrees were made and in eighteen matters they disagreed, but a baraita states they were unified; the resolution is that they disagreed on the same day and agreed the next.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Solomon decreed regarding consecrated items, and the later sages added a decree regarding תרומה (the priestly portion).
The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that eighteen decrees were enacted and in eighteen matters they disagreed.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states they were unified, not divided.
The Gemara resolves that they disagreed on the same day and agreed the next day.

items.text: Three disputes between Shammai and Hillel
items.text_en: Three disputes between Shammai and Hillel
items.desc_en: Rav Huna lists three places where Shammai and Hillel disagreed: the measure of dough liable for challah, the measure of drawn water that invalidates a mikveh, and the status of a woman's menstrual impurity. In each case, the Sages rejected both opinions and established a third view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna introduces three disputes between Shammai and Hillel, beginning with the first: the measure of dough liable for challah.
Shammai holds that a dough of one kav is liable for challah.
Hillel holds that a dough of two kav is liable for challah.
The Sages reject both opinions and rule that a dough of one and a half kav is liable for challah.
After the measures were enlarged, the Sages ruled that five quarters of flour are liable for challah, with Rabbi Yosei adding a nuance.
Rabbi Yosei specifies that five quarters are exempt but five and a fraction are liable.
The gemara transitions to the second dispute: Hillel's position on drawn water invalidating a mikveh.
Shammai holds that nine kav of drawn water invalidate the mikveh.
The Sages reject both opinions until two launderers testified from Shmaya and Avtalyon that three log of drawn water invalidate the mikveh.
The Sages upheld the testimony of three log as the standard.
The gemara transitions to the third dispute: Shammai's position that a woman's menstrual impurity is retroactive only to the time of examination.
Hillel holds that impurity is retroactive from the last examination, even many days earlier.
The Sages compromise: a woman's impurity is retroactive from examination to examination, but a 24-hour period reduces the examination-to-examination span, and vice versa.

items.text: Exclusion of other disputes
items.text_en: Exclusion of other disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there are additional disputes between Shammai and Hillel, such as the issue of leaning on a sacrifice and the case of one who harvests grapes for the winepress. It explains that Rav Huna only listed cases where there was no involvement of earlier authorities, and that in the grape-harvesting case Hillel remained silent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there are additional disputes between Shammai and Hillel, citing the case of leaning on a sacrifice (סמיכה).
The Gemara explains that Rav Huna only listed cases where there was no involvement of earlier authorities, and in the grape-harvesting case Hillel remained silent.

items.text: Chronology of decrees on impurity
items.text_en: Chronology of decrees on impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the decrees of Yosei ben Yoezer and Yosei ben Yochanan regarding impurity of the land of the nations and glass vessels. It cites Rav Kahana's tradition from Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei that these decrees were made eighty years before the destruction of the Temple, and addresses a chronological difficulty by noting that these earlier sages preceded Hillel and his descendants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Yosei ben Yoezer and Yosei ben Yochanan decreed impurity on the land of the nations and on glass vessels.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's tradition from Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's tradition from Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei, on his sickbed, transmitted that eighty years before the Temple's destruction the decree of impurity on the land of the nations and glass vessels was enacted, and that forty years before the destruction the Sanhedrin went into exile, ceasing to adjudicate capital cases.

The Gemara objects that the decree cannot be attributed to Yosei ben Yoezer and Yosei ben Yochanan, because a baraita shows that Hillel and his descendants held the presidency for one hundred years before the destruction, whereas Yosei ben Yoezer and Yosei ben Yochanan lived much earlier, so the eighty-year timeline does not match them.

items.text: First proposal: decree on solid contact for burning, on airspace for nothing
items.text_en: First proposal: decree on solid contact for burning, on airspace for nothing
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the early Sages decreed that uncertainty about solid contact (gusha) requires burning, while uncertainty about airspace (avir) requires nothing. Then the later Sages of the eighty years decreed that uncertainty about airspace requires suspending.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the early Sages decreed burning for uncertainty about solid contact (גושּׁא) and nothing for airspace (אווירא), while the later Sages of the eighty years decreed suspension for airspace.
