items.desc_en: Ulla reports that two Western amoraim dispute: one says Beit Shammai corresponds to the days that will enter (future days) and Beit Hillel to days that have passed; the other says Beit Shammai corresponds to the bulls of Sukkot (decreasing), and Beit Hillel follows the principle of ascending in holiness. Rabbah bar bar Chanah adds that two elders in Tzaidan each gave one of these reasons.

sub.desc_en: עולא (Ulla) reports that two Western amoraim, רבי יוסי בר אבין (Rabbi Yosei bar Avin) and רבי יוסי בר זבידא (Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida), dispute the reasoning behind the opinions of בית שמאי (Beit Shammai) and בית הלל (Beit Hillel).

sub.text: First Amora (Rabbi Yosei bar Avin or Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida)
sub.text_en: First Amora (Rabbi Yosei bar Avin or Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida)
sub.desc_en: One amora explains that בית שמאי (Beit Shammai) lights according to the days that will enter (future days), and בית הלל (Beit Hillel) according to the days that have passed (outgoing days).

sub.text: Second Amora (Rabbi Yosei bar Avin or Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida)
sub.text_en: Second Amora (Rabbi Yosei bar Avin or Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida)
sub.desc_en: The other amora explains that בית שמאי (Beit Shammai) corresponds to the bulls of the festival of סוכות (Sukkot), which decrease, and בית הלל (Beit Hillel) follows the principle of ascending in holiness (מעלין בקודש ואין מורידין).

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רבה בר בר חנה (Rabbah bar bar Chanah) in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) adds a supporting story: two elders in צידן (Tzaidan) each acted according to one of the opinions, one giving the reason of the bulls of the festival and the other the principle of ascending in holiness.

items.text: Placement of the Chanukah lamp and use of its light
items.text_en: Placement of the Chanukah lamp and use of its light
items.desc_en: A baraita taught that the Chanukah lamp is placed at the entrance outside (or at a window adjacent to the public domain), and during times of danger on the table suffices. Rava adds that one needs an additional lamp to use its light, unless there is a fire; but an important person needs an extra lamp even with a fire.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the basic placement of the Chanukah lamp: at the entrance outside, or at a window adjacent to the public domain for an upstairs dweller, and during danger on the table suffices.
Rava adds that one needs an additional lamp to use its light, unless there is a fire; but an important person needs an extra lamp even with a fire.

items.text: The story of the Chanukah miracle
items.text_en: The story of the Chanukah miracle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the origin of Chanukah: when the Greeks entered the Temple they defiled all the oils, but the Hasmoneans found one sealed cruse of oil with enough for one day, and a miracle allowed it to burn for eight days. The next year these days were established as a holiday with Hallel and thanksgiving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks 'What is Chanukah?' and cites a baraita recounting the miracle of the single cruse of oil that burned for eight days, leading to the establishment of the festival with Hallel and thanksgiving.

items.text: Liability for fire from Chanukah lamp: height and exemption
items.text_en: Liability for fire from Chanukah lamp: height and exemption
items.desc_en: A Mishnah states that if a camel carrying flax catches fire from a storekeeper's lamp, the camel owner is liable unless the storekeeper placed his lamp outside, in which case the storekeeper is liable. R. Yehuda exempts in the case of a Chanukah lamp. Ravina cites Rabbah that this implies the Chanukah lamp must be placed within ten handbreadths, otherwise one could argue that he should have placed it higher and out of reach; but perhaps too much burden would deter one from the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Mishnah from elsewhere about liability for fire caused by a blacksmith's spark or a camel's flax.
Rabbi Yehuda (רבי יהודה) rules that in the case of a Chanukah lamp, the storekeeper is exempt.

sub.text: Ravina citing Rabbah, with Gemara's objection
sub.text_en: Ravina citing Rabbah, with Gemara's objection
sub.desc_en: Ravina (רבינא) cites Rabbah (רבה) that this implies the Chanukah lamp must be placed within ten handbreadths; otherwise the camel owner could argue the storekeeper should have placed it higher, but the Gemara rejects that because excessive burden would deter one from the mitzvah (מצוה).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Derashah on the Pit
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Derashah on the Pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Chanukah lamp placed above twenty cubits is invalid, like a sukkah or an alleyway. Rav Kahana then cites a derashah from Rav Nathan bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Tanchum on the verse 'And the pit was empty, there was no water in it,' explaining that the extra phrase teaches that while there was no water, there were snakes and scorpions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a Chanukah lamp placed above twenty cubits is invalid, analogous to a sukkah or an alleyway.

sub.text: Rav Kahana citing Rav Nathan bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Tanchum
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana citing Rav Nathan bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Tanchum
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana cites a derashah on the verse 'והבור רק אין בו מים' (the pit was empty, there was no water in it), explaining that the extra phrase teaches that while there was no water, there were snakes and scorpions.

items.text: Placement of the Chanukah Lamp
items.text_en: Placement of the Chanukah Lamp
items.desc_en: Rabbah states that the mitzvah is to place the Chanukah lamp within a handbreadth of the entrance. There is a dispute between Rav Acha bar Rava and Rav Shmuel bar Difti about whether to place it on the right or left side, and the halakhah is on the left so that the Chanukah lamp is on the left and the mezuzah on the right.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that the mitzvah is to place the Chanukah lamp within a handbreadth of the entrance.
The Gemara asks where one should place the lamp.
Rav Acha bar Rava says to place it on the right side.
Rav Shmuel bar Difti says to place it on the left side.
The halakhah is on the left, so that the Chanukah lamp is on the left and the mezuzah on the right.

items.text: Prohibition Against Using the Chanukah Lamp for Mundane Purposes
items.text_en: Prohibition Against Using the Chanukah Lamp for Mundane Purposes
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav Asi in the name of Rav states that it is forbidden to count money opposite a Chanukah lamp. Shmuel questions whether the lamp has inherent sanctity, but Rav Yosef counters by citing a baraita about covering blood, which teaches that one must not degrade mitzvot by using the blood itself for covering; similarly, one must not degrade the Chanukah lamp by using its light for mundane purposes.

sub.text: Rav Yehudah citing Rav Asi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav Asi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav Asi in the name of Rav states that it is forbidden to count money opposite a Chanukah lamp.
Shmuel questions whether the lamp has inherent sanctity, implying the prohibition is not obvious.
Rav Yosef counters by analogy: just as blood used for covering has no inherent sanctity yet must not be degraded, so too the Chanukah lamp.
A baraita teaches that one must cover blood with what was spilled, not with the foot, so that mitzvot are not degraded; the same principle applies to the Chanukah lamp.

items.text: Using Sukkah Decorations During the Festival
items.text_en: Using Sukkah Decorations During the Festival
items.desc_en: The students asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi whether one may benefit from sukkah decorations during the seven days of Sukkot. He replied by citing the prohibition against using the Chanukah lamp for mundane purposes. Rav Yosef objects, noting that the sukkah case is explicitly taught in a baraita (which forbids using decorations until after the festival unless one stipulated), while the Chanukah case is not. He concludes that the source for all such prohibitions is the law of covering blood.

sub.text: Students' question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Students' question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi whether one may benefit from sukkah decorations during the seven days of Sukkot.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers by citing the prohibition against using the Chanukah lamp for mundane purposes, implying a similar rule for sukkah decorations.
Rav Yosef objects that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is linking a case that is explicitly taught in a baraita (sukkah) to one that is not (Chanukah).
A baraita is cited that explicitly forbids using sukkah decorations until after the festival unless one stipulated otherwise.

Rav Yosef concludes that the source for all such prohibitions (sukkah, Chanukah, and covering blood) is the law of covering blood, which teaches that מצוות (commandments) should not be treated with contempt.

items.text: Disputes Between Rav and Shmuel on Transferring Mitzvah Objects
items.text_en: Disputes Between Rav and Shmuel on Transferring Mitzvah Objects
items.desc_en: Three disputes between Rav and Shmuel are recorded: Rav forbids lighting one Chanukah lamp from another, while Shmuel permits it; Rav forbids transferring tzitzit from one garment to another, while Shmuel permits it; Rav rules that the halakhah does not follow Rabbi Shimon regarding dragging, while Shmuel rules that it does.

sub.desc_en: The gemara records the first dispute: Rav forbids lighting one Chanukah lamp from another, while Shmuel permits it.
The gemara records the second dispute: Rav forbids transferring tzitzit from one garment to another, while Shmuel permits it.
The gemara records the third dispute: Rav rules that the halakhah does not follow Rabbi Shimon regarding dragging, while Shmuel rules that it does.

items.text: Abaye's Ruling: Mar Follows Shmuel in Three Cases
items.text_en: Abaye's Ruling: Mar Follows Shmuel in Three Cases
items.desc_en: Abaye states that Mar (the master) generally follows Rav except in these three cases where he follows Shmuel: lighting from lamp to lamp, transferring tzitzit, and the halakhah following Rabbi Shimon regarding dragging. A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon permits dragging a bed, chair, or bench as long as one does not intend to make a furrow.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that Mar (the master) follows Rav in all matters except three, where he follows Shmuel: lighting from lamp to lamp, transferring tzitzit, and the halakhah following Rabbi Shimon regarding dragging.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon permits dragging a bed, chair, or bench as long as one does not intend to make a furrow.

items.text: Reason for Rav's Prohibition: Degradation vs. Diminishment
items.text_en: Reason for Rav's Prohibition: Degradation vs. Diminishment
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi stated before Rav Adda bar Ahavah that Rav's reason for forbidding lighting from lamp to lamp is due to degradation of the mitzvah. Rav Adda bar Ahavah corrects him, saying the reason is that it diminishes the mitzvah (by reducing the oil). The practical difference between them is whether lighting from one lamp to another is permitted: according to the degradation reason, it is permitted; according to the diminishment reason, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi sits before Rav Adda bar Ahavah and states that Rav's reason for forbidding lighting from lamp to lamp is due to degradation of the mitzvah.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah corrects the rabbi, telling the listeners not to heed him, because Rav's reason is that it diminishes the mitzvah (by reducing the oil).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two reasons.
The Gemara explains the difference: according to the degradation reason, lighting from one lamp to another is permitted; according to the diminishment reason, it is forbidden.

items.text: Objection from the Law of the Shekel of the Sanctuary
items.text_en: Objection from the Law of the Shekel of the Sanctuary
items.desc_en: Rav Avya raises an objection from a baraita about the shekel of the Sanctuary, which seems to contradict the previous discussion. The segment is cut off, but it begins a new argument.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya raises an objection from a baraita about the shekel of the Sanctuary, which seems to contradict the previous discussion.

items.text: Gemara's objection to Rav and Shmuel's positions
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rav and Shmuel's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav and Shmuel's views on lighting one lamp from another, arguing that if Shmuel permits even using a wick, the objection stands. Rabba explains the prohibition as a decree lest one not measure precisely and thereby desecrate the lamp.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav and Shmuel's positions on lighting one lamp from another, arguing that if Shmuel permits even using a wick, the objection stands, and Rabba explains the prohibition as a decree lest one not measure precisely and thereby desecrate the lamp.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection from the Menorah
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection from the Menorah
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects from the Menorah in the Temple, where the western lamp was lit from another lamp, showing that lighting one lamp from another is permitted. The Gemara notes that this contradicts both opinions (bizuy mitzvah and achshuy mitzvah).

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges the positions by citing the Menorah's western lamp, which was lit from itself and served as testimony, showing that lighting from one lamp to another is permitted, posing a difficulty for both reasons of ביזוי מצוה (disrespect of the commandment) and אכחושי מצוה (diminishing the commandment).
The Gemara asks what the testimony is, and Rav answers that it is the western lamp which was lit from another lamp and in which the lighting was completed.

The Gemara objects that since the lamps are fixed, one must take oil and light from another lamp, which contradicts both the opinion that it is due to bizuy mitzvah and the opinion that it is due to achshuy mitzvah.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution with long wicks
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution with long wicks
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the Menorah case involved long wicks, so there was no diminishment. However, the objection remains for the opinion that forbids due to achshuyei mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the objection by explaining that the case involved long wicks, but the difficulty remains for the view that the prohibition is due to אכחושי מצוה (diminishing the commandment).
The Gemara objects that for the opinion which forbids due to achshuyei mitzvah (diminishing the mitzvah), the difficulty remains unresolved.
The Gemara concedes that the objection stands unresolved.

items.text: The dispute: lighting vs. placing as the mitzvah
items.text_en: The dispute: lighting vs. placing as the mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua observes that the permissibility of lighting one lamp from another depends on whether the mitzvah is fulfilled by lighting or by placing. The Gemara then states that this was an unresolved question.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the halakhic conclusion is regarding lighting from lamp to lamp.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua states that the permissibility of lighting from lamp to lamp depends on whether the mitzvah is fulfilled by lighting or by placing.
The Gemara notes that this was an unresolved question: whether lighting or placing accomplishes the mitzvah.

items.text: Proof from Rava: holding the lamp does nothing
items.text_en: Proof from Rava: holding the lamp does nothing
items.desc_en: Rava states that if one holds a Chanukah lamp while standing, he has done nothing. This seems to prove that placing is the mitzvah, but the Gemara deflects: an onlooker might think he holds it for his own use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a proof from Rava's statement that holding a Chanukah lamp while standing accomplishes nothing, implying that placing (הנחה) is the essential act of the mitzvah.
The Gemara rejects the proof: the reason is that an onlooker might think he holds the lamp for his own needs, not for the mitzvah.

items.text: Proof from Rava: lighting inside and taking out
items.text_en: Proof from Rava: lighting inside and taking out
items.desc_en: Rava says that if one lights the lamp indoors and then takes it outside, he has done nothing. This supports the view that lighting is the mitzvah (since it must be done in place), but the Gemara deflects again: an onlooker might think he lit it for his own use.

sub.desc_en: Rava's statement that lighting indoors and then taking it out accomplishes nothing is brought as evidence that lighting (הדלקה) fulfills the commandment, but the Gemara again deflects due to concern about an observer's perception.
The Gemara explains that this supports the view that lighting (הדלקה) is the mitzvah, since lighting must be done in the proper place.
The Gemara objects: if placing (הנחה) is the mitzvah, why would moving the lamp after lighting invalidate it?
The Gemara deflects: an onlooker might think he lit it for his own use, so the case is inconclusive.

items.text: Another proof from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Another proof from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another statement from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi to resolve the question, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another statement from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi as further evidence on the question.

items.text: Proof that lighting constitutes the mitzvah
items.text_en: Proof that lighting constitutes the mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues from the Mishnah's case of a lamp that burned all day: if lighting is the mitzvah, extinguishing and relighting is proper; if placement were the mitzvah, one would need to lift and place it. Additionally, the blessing 'to light the Chanukah candle' proves lighting is the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves from the Mishnah's case of a lamp that burned all day, and from the blessing formula, that lighting (הדלקה) constitutes the mitzvah of Chanukah, not placement.

items.text: Who may light and women's obligation
items.text_en: Who may light and women's obligation
items.desc_en: Since lighting is the mitzvah, a deaf-mute, insane person, or minor cannot fulfill it. A woman certainly may light, as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says women are obligated because they were part of the miracle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor who lights fulfills nothing, but a woman certainly lights, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that women are obligated because they were also part of the miracle.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that women are certainly obligated in the Chanukah light because they were part of the miracle.

items.text: Guest's obligation in Chanukah candles
items.text_en: Guest's obligation in Chanukah candles
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet says a guest is obligated in Chanukah candles. Rabbi Zeira relates that when he was at the Rav's house, he would share in the cost with the host; after marrying, he no longer needed to, as his wife lit for him at home.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet rules that a guest is obligated in Chanukah lighting, and Rabbi Zeira relates his own practice: as a student he shared in the cost, but after marriage he relied on his wife lighting at home.
Rabbi Zeira relates his own practice: initially he shared the cost with the host, but after marrying he relied on his wife's lighting at home.

items.text: Best oils for Chanukah candles
items.text_en: Best oils for Chanukah candles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says all oils are good for the lamp, but olive oil is best. Abaye relates that his master initially sought sesame oil for its long-lasting flame, but after hearing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, he sought olive oil for its clearer light.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that all oils are suitable for the Chanukah lamp but olive oil is best; Abaye relates that he initially sought sesame oil for its long-lasting light, but after hearing this, he sought olive oil for its clearer light.
Abaye relates that his master initially preferred sesame oil for its longer-lasting flame, but after hearing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement, he switched to olive oil for its clearer light.

items.text: Best oils for ink and related debate
items.text_en: Best oils for ink and related debate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says all oils are good for ink, but olive oil is best. A question arises whether this refers to mixing or smoking. Rav Shmuel bar Zutra teaches it applies to both. Another version says all smokes are good, and Rav Huna says all resins are good, with resin of balsam best.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says all oils are good for ink, with olive oil being best; the Gemara asks whether this refers to mixing the ink or to smoking the parchment.
Rav Shmuel bar Zutra's baraita clarifies that the statement applies both to mixing and smoking; additional versions from Rav Shmuel bar Zutra and Rav Huna discuss the best smoke and resin for ink.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rav Shmuel bar Zutra
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rav Shmuel bar Zutra
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rav Shmuel bar Zutra that explicitly states the rule applies both to mixing and to smoking, resolving the question.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Shmuel bar Zutra
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Shmuel bar Zutra
sub.desc_en: An alternative version of Rav Shmuel bar Zutra's teaching is presented: all smokes are good for ink, with olive oil smoke being the best.
Rav Huna adds that all resins are good for ink, and resin of balsam (קט

items.text: Blessings for lighting and seeing Chanukah candles
items.text_en: Blessings for lighting and seeing Chanukah candles
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi says in Rav's name that one who lights must bless. Rav Yirmeya says one who sees must bless. Rav Yehuda details: on the first day, the one who sees blesses two, the one who lights blesses three; thereafter, the lighter blesses two, the seer blesses one. The Gemara explains that the omitted blessing is 'time' (shehecheyanu), not 'miracle', since the miracle persists all days.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that one who lights the Chanukah lamp must recite a blessing; Rav Yirmeya adds that one who sees it must also bless; Rav Yehuda details the blessings: on the first day the viewer says two and the lighter says three, thereafter the lighter says two and the viewer says one, omitting the blessing of time (שהחיינו) because the miracle is present every day.
Rav Yirmeya adds that one who sees the Chanukah candle must also recite a blessing.
Rav Yehuda resolves the dispute by detailing the number of blessings: on the first day the seer recites two and the lighter three; thereafter the lighter recites two and the seer one.
The Gemara asks which blessing is omitted after the first day, suggesting it could be the blessing for the miracle (נֵס) rather than the blessing for the time (זְמַן).
The Gemara answers that the miracle (נֵס) persists all days, so the omitted blessing is the blessing for the time (שֶׁהֶחֱיָנוּ), not the miracle.

items.text: Source for the blessing on Chanukah candles
items.text_en: Source for the blessing on Chanukah candles
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what blessing is recited and where the commandment is derived. Rav Avya says from 'Do not turn aside' (Deut. 17:11), and Rav Nechemya says from 'Ask your father and he will tell you' (Deut. 32:7).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what blessing is recited, and cites the formula 'אשר קדשנו במצותיו וצונו להדליק נר של חנוכה'; Rav Avya and Rav Nechemya debate the scriptural source for this rabbinic commandment, citing 'לא תסור' and 'שאל אביך ויגדך' respectively.

The Gemara asks where the commandment is derived, and cites two opinions: Rav Avya says from 'Do not turn aside' (Deut. 17:11), and Rav Nechemya says from 'Ask your father and he will tell you' (Deut. 32:7).
Rav Avya answers that the commandment is derived from the verse 'Do not turn aside' (Deut. 17:11), which obligates obedience to rabbinic enactments.

Rav Nechemya answers that the commandment is derived from the verse 'Ask your father and he will tell you, your elders and they will say to you' (Deut. 32:7), which implies that one must follow the traditions of the elders.

items.text: Challenge from demai and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from demai and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Amram challenges: if all rabbinic commandments require a blessing, how can one separate demai (doubtfully tithed produce) when naked? Abaye answers that certain rabbinic commandments require a blessing, but doubtful ones do not. The Gemara objects that the second day of Yom Tov is a doubtful rabbinic matter yet requires a blessing; the answer is to prevent disrespect. Rava offers an alternative: most amei ha'aretz do tithe.

sub.desc_en: Rav Amram challenges: if all rabbinic commandments require a blessing, how can one separate demai (doubtfully tithed produce) when naked, violating the requirement of a holy camp?
Abaye answers that certain rabbinic commandments require a blessing, but doubtful ones do not.
The Gemara objects that the second day of Yom Tov is a doubtful rabbinic matter yet requires a blessing.
The Gemara answers that the blessing on the second day of Yom Tov is to prevent disrespect (זלזול).
Rava offers an alternative resolution: most amei ha'aretz (common people) do tithe, so demai is not a doubtful matter.

items.text: Multiple candles for a courtyard with two entrances
items.text_en: Multiple candles for a courtyard with two entrances
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says a courtyard with two entrances requires two Chanukah candles. Rava qualifies this only if the entrances are on different sides; if on the same side, one suffices. The reason is suspicion: people might think the resident didn't light at all. A proof is brought from Rabbi Shimon's teaching about leaving pe'ah at the end of the field to avoid suspicion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a courtyard with two entrances requires two Chanukah candles.
Rava qualifies that this applies only if the entrances are on different sides; if on the same side, one candle suffices.
The Gemara questions the reason, suggesting that if it is due to suspicion, even a single side should require two candles.
The Gemara objects that if the suspicion is from townspeople, even two sides should not require two candles.
The Gemara resolves that the suspicion is from townspeople who might pass by only one entrance and assume the resident did not light at all.
The Gemara brings a supporting baraita from Rabbi Shimon, who lists suspicion as one of the reasons for leaving pe'ah at the end of the field.

items.text: Reason for the Mishnah's ruling about pe'ah
items.text_en: Reason for the Mishnah's ruling about pe'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about giving pe'ah is due to preventing the poor from wasting time, suspicion, and the prohibition of 'bal t'chaleh'. Rava adds that it is also to prevent deceivers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara gives three reasons for the Mishnah's ruling: preventing the poor from wasting time, avoiding suspicion, and the prohibition of 'בל תכלה' (do not destroy).
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'בל תכלה' as a separate reason, since all the reasons are essentially about preventing waste.
Rava answers that the Mishnah's ruling is also to prevent deceivers (רמאים) who might exploit the system.

items.text: Lamp with two wicks and a bowl of oil
items.text_en: Lamp with two wicks and a bowl of oil
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Redifa quotes Rav Huna that a lamp with two wicks counts for two people. Rava adds that if one fills a bowl with oil and surrounds it with wicks, covering it makes it count for many, but if uncovered it is like a bonfire and not even for one.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Redifa citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Redifa citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a lamp with two wicks (שני פיות) fulfills the obligation for two people.
Rava adds that if one fills a bowl with oil and surrounds it with wicks, covering it with a vessel, it fulfills the obligation for many people.
Rava qualifies that if the bowl is not covered, it becomes like a bonfire (מדורה) and does not fulfill the obligation even for one person.

items.text: Priority between Shabbat lamp, Chanukah lamp, and Kiddush
items.text_en: Priority between Shabbat lamp, Chanukah lamp, and Kiddush
items.desc_en: Rava states that the Shabbat lamp takes precedence over the Chanukah lamp and Kiddush due to domestic peace. He then questions whether Chanukah lamp or Kiddush is more important, concluding that Chanukah lamp is preferred because of publicizing the miracle.

sub.desc_en: Rava states two settled rulings: the Shabbat lamp (נר ביתו) takes priority over the Chanukah lamp and over Kiddush of the day, because of domestic peace (שלום ביתו).
Rava raises a question: between the Chanukah lamp and Kiddush of the day, which takes priority — Kiddush because it is frequent (תדיר), or Chanukah because of publicizing the miracle (פרסומי ניסא)?
Rava resolves his own question: the Chanukah lamp takes priority because of publicizing the miracle (פרסומי ניסא).

items.text: Rewards for being careful with mitzvot and stories of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Rewards for being careful with mitzvot and stories of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: Rav Huna lists rewards for being careful with lamp, mezuzah, tzitzit, and Kiddush. Stories are told of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda predicting great scholars would emerge from homes where lamps were plentiful, and their predictions came true.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna teaches that one who is diligent in lighting the Shabbat lamp (נר) will have sons who are Torah scholars, and similarly for mezuzah, tzitzit, and Kiddush.

sub.text: Story about Rav Huna and Rabbi Avin the carpenter
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Huna and Rabbi Avin the carpenter
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates Rav Huna's teaching: he saw that Rabbi Avin the carpenter was diligent in lighting lamps, and predicted that two great men would come from him, which was fulfilled by his sons Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Chiyya bar Avin.

sub.text: Story about Rav Chisda and Rav Sheizvi
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Chisda and Rav Sheizvi
sub.desc_en: Another story: Rav Chisda saw that the household of Rav Sheizvi was diligent in lighting lamps, and predicted a great man would come from there, which was fulfilled by Rav Sheizvi himself.

items.text: Story of Rav Yosef's wife and the timing of lighting
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yosef's wife and the timing of lighting
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef's wife was late in lighting the lamp. Rav Yosef cited a verse about the pillar of cloud and fire complementing each other, implying she should light earlier. An elder corrected him, saying one should neither light early nor late.

sub.text: Story about Rav Yosef and his wife
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Yosef and his wife
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef's wife was late in lighting the Shabbat lamp, and Rav Yosef cited a verse about the pillar of cloud and fire to teach that the lamp can be lit later, so she thought to light it early.
An elder corrected Rav Yosef's wife, citing a tradition that one may neither light too early nor too late (בלבד שלא יקדים ושלא יאחר).
The elder corrects Rav Yosef, stating that one should neither light early nor late.

items.text: Rewards for honoring rabbis
items.text_en: Rewards for honoring rabbis
items.desc_en: Rava states that one who loves rabbis will have sons who are rabbis, one who honors rabbis will have sons-in-law who are rabbis, and one who fears rabbis will himself become a scholar, or at least his words will be heard like a scholar's.

sub.desc_en: Rava teaches that one who loves Torah scholars will have sons who are scholars, one who honors them will have scholarly sons-in-law, and one who fears them will himself become a scholar or at least his words will be heard as a scholar's.

items.text: Discussion of 'shemen s'reifah' and the prohibition on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.text_en: Discussion of 'shemen s'reifah' and the prohibition on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'shemen s'reifah' is oil from terumah that became impure, destined for burning. It is prohibited on Shabbat due to a decree lest one tilt the lamp. Abaye questions why it is also prohibited on Yom Tov, and the answer is a decree lest one come to violate Shabbat. Rav Chisda offers an alternative explanation that the case is Yom Tov that falls on Friday, and the reason is that one cannot burn sacred items on Yom Tov. Rav Chanina from Sura clarifies that the Mishnah is stating the reason for the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'shemen s'reifah' (oil of burning) refers to.
Rabbah explains that it is oil from terumah (תרומה, priestly portion) that became impure and is designated for burning.
The Gemara explains that on Shabbat it is prohibited due to a decree lest one tilt the lamp to improve the flame.
Abaye objects that if the reason is the decree of tilting, then on Yom Tov (יום טוב, festival) it should be permitted, yet the Mishnah prohibits it.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition on Yom Tov is a decree lest one come to violate Shabbat.
Rav Chisda offers an alternative explanation: the case is Yom Tov that falls on Friday, and the reason is that one cannot burn sacred items on Yom Tov.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's first clause (about Shabbat) does not mention Yom Tov, implying the second clause is a separate case, not a continuation.

Rav Chanina mi'Sura resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah is stating the reason for the prohibition: 'What is the reason that one may not light with shemen s'reifah on Yom Tov? Because one does not burn sacred items on Yom Tov.'

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Chisda's view that oils prohibited for Shabbat lamps are permitted on Yom Tov, except for shemen serayfah because sacred items are not burned on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Chisda's ruling that all oils prohibited for Shabbat lamps are permitted on Yom Tov, except for shemen serayfah (oil of burning sacred items), because sacred items are not burned on Yom Tov.

items.text: Inquiry about Hanukkah in Birkat HaMazon
items.text_en: Inquiry about Hanukkah in Birkat HaMazon
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Hanukkah is mentioned in Birkat HaMazon, given its rabbinic status. Rava cites Rav Huna that one does not mention it, but if one wishes, they do so in the Thanksgiving blessing. Rav Sheishet rules similarly, comparing it to the Amidah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one mentions Hanukkah in Birkat HaMazon, given its rabbinic status, weighing the possibility that it is omitted or included due to publicizing the miracle.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Sechorah citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Sechorah citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rava reports in the name of Rav Huna that one does not mention Hanukkah in Birkat HaMazon, but if one wishes to do so, they mention it in the Thanksgiving blessing (הוֹדָאָה).

Rav Sheishet rules that Birkat HaMazon follows the pattern of the Amidah: just as Hanukkah is mentioned in the Thanksgiving blessing of the Amidah, so too in Birkat HaMazon it is mentioned in the Thanksgiving blessing.

items.text: Inquiry about Rosh Chodesh in Birkat HaMazon
items.text_en: Inquiry about Rosh Chodesh in Birkat HaMazon
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rosh Chodesh, a biblical institution, is mentioned in Birkat HaMazon. Rav says yes, Rabbi Chanina says no. Rav Zerika rules like Rav, supported by Rabbi Oshaya's baraita distinguishing days with and without a musaf offering regarding mention in Birkat HaMazon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rosh Chodesh, a biblical institution, is mentioned in Birkat HaMazon, considering that it does not prohibit work.
Rav rules that one does mention Rosh Chodesh, while Rabbi Chanina rules that one does not.
Rav Zerika rules like Rav, citing Rabbi Oshaya's baraita that supports Rav's position.
Rabbi Oshaya's baraita distinguishes days with a musaf offering, like Rosh Chodesh, which require mention in Birkat HaMazon, from days without a musaf offering, which do not.

items.text: Inquiry about Hanukkah in Musaf prayer
items.text_en: Inquiry about Hanukkah in Musaf prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Hanukkah is mentioned in the Musaf prayer, given there is no Musaf for Hanukkah itself. Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda say no, while Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan say yes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one mentions Hanukkah in the Musaf prayer, given that Hanukkah itself has no musaf offering, but it is a day requiring four prayers.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda vs. Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda vs. Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda rule that one does not mention Hanukkah in Musaf, while Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan rule that one does mention it.
Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan both rule that one does mention Hanukkah in Musaf.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef by citing Rav Giddel's ruling that on Shabbat Rosh Chodesh, the haftarah does not mention Rosh Chodesh. The Gemara distinguishes this case because there is no haftarah on Rosh Chodesh alone. Instead, it compares to Rav Achadvoi's ruling about Yom Tov on Shabbat, where the haftarah does not mention Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef by citing Rav Giddel's ruling that on Shabbat Rosh Chodesh, the haftarah does not mention Rosh Chodesh, because without Shabbat there is no haftarah on Rosh Chodesh.

The Gemara distinguishes Abaye's case, noting that Rosh Chodesh has no haftarah at all, and instead compares it to Rav Achadvoi's ruling about Yom Tov on Shabbat, where the haftarah does not mention Yom Tov.

items.text: Ruling on Ne'ilah when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat
items.text_en: Ruling on Ne'ilah when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who requires mentioning Shabbat in the Ne'ilah prayer on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat, because it is a day obligated in four prayers. This contradicts the earlier ruling of Rava about Yom Tov falling on Shabbat, but the Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that the cases are different: on Yom Tov, the evening prayer is not normally said, while on Yom Kippur it is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who requires mentioning Shabbat in the Ne'ilah prayer on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat, because the day is obligated in four prayers.

The Gemara raises a contradiction: the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, yet it also holds like Rava, who ruled that on a Festival falling on Shabbat, the prayer leader need not mention the Festival in the evening prayer, since without Shabbat there would be no evening prayer on a Festival.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: in Rava's case, the evening repetition was instituted only due to danger, not from the day's obligation, whereas on Yom Kippur the day itself is obligated in four prayers, so Shabbat must be mentioned.

items.text: Transition to Mishnah about oils
items.text_en: Transition to Mishnah about oils
items.desc_en: A brief note about a disagreement between the Tanna Kamma and the Sages regarding the law of aliyah (the tail), with a reference to Rav Berona citing Rav, but the matter is not concluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Isn't the opinion of the Sages identical to the first tanna (תנא קמא) regarding the prohibition of lighting with the tail?
The Gemara answers: The practical difference between them is with regard to the ruling of רב ברונא (Rav Beruna) citing רב (Rav) about lighting with cooked fat to which oil was added.
The Gemara notes that the matter is not concluded — it is unclear which tanna accepts or rejects that ruling.

items.text: Mishnah: Oils for Shabbat lights
items.text_en: Mishnah: Oils for Shabbat lights
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not light with burnt oil on Yom Tov. Rabbi Yishmael prohibits using עִטְרָן (a type of oil) due to the honor of Shabbat, while the Sages permit all oils, including sesame, nut, radish, fish, gourd, עִטְרָן, and naphtha. Rabbi Tarfon permits only olive oil.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not light with burnt-offering oil on Yom Tov; Rabbi Yishmael forbids עִטְרָן (a type of oil) due to Shabbat honor; the Sages permit all oils; Rabbi Tarfon permits only olive oil.
Rabbi Yishmael prohibits lighting with עִטְרָן (a type of oil) due to the honor of Shabbat.
The Sages permit all oils, including sesame, nut, radish, fish, gourd, עִטְרָן, and naphtha.
Rabbi Tarfon permits only olive oil for lighting.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from Hezekiah
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from Hezekiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why burnt oil is prohibited on Yom Tov and answers that sacred offerings are not burned on Yom Tov. Hezekiah derives this from the verse about the paschal lamb, which gives a second morning for its burning, implying that burning is not done on Yom Tov itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the reason for the Mishnah's prohibition of lighting with burnt-offering oil on Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers: because one may not burn consecrated items on Yom Tov.

Chizkiyah and the Tanna of the school of Chizkiyah derive from the verse 'וְלֹא תוֹתִירוּ מִמֶּנּוּ עַד בֹּקֶר' that the leftover must be burned on the second morning, implying that burning consecrated items is deferred and not permitted on Yom Tov.

items.text: Abaye's derivation
items.text_en: Abaye's derivation
items.desc_en: Abaye derives the prohibition from the verse 'עוֹלַת שַׁבָּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ', which teaches that only the Shabbat offering is brought on Shabbat, not a weekday offering, and similarly not a weekday offering on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: Abaye derives from the verse 'עוֹלַת שַׁבָּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ' that only the Shabbat burnt-offering is offered on Shabbat, not a weekday burnt-offering on Shabbat or Yom Tov.

items.text: Rava's derivation
items.text_en: Rava's derivation
items.desc_en: Rava derives the prohibition from the verse 'הוּא לְבַדּוֹ יֵעָשֶׂה לָכֶם', which excludes preparations (מכשירין) and also excludes circumcision not at its proper time, via a kal vachomer argument.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse 'הוּא לְבַדּוֹ יֵעָשֶׂה לָכֶם' that only the holiday offering itself is permitted, not its preparatory acts (מכשירין), and not a circumcision that is not at its proper time, which is derived by a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.
Rava derives from 'הוּא' that preparations (מכשירין) are excluded from the permission to perform work on Yom Tov.
Rava derives from 'לְבַדּוֹ' that circumcision not at its proper time (מילה שלא בזמנה) is also excluded, via a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) argument.

items.text: Rav Ashi's derivation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi begins a derivation from the word 'שַׁבָּתוֹן', but the text is cut off, indicating an incomplete argument.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi begins a derivation from the word 'שַׁבָּתוֹן' (a rest day), but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening question about Yom Tov and the prohibition
items.text_en: Opening question about Yom Tov and the prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that on Yom Tov, burning impure terumah is forbidden because it involves both a positive and negative commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a negative one. This implies that on a weekday it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that on Yom Tov, burning impure terumah is forbidden because it involves both a positive and negative commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a negative one.

items.text: Rav's derivation from the verse about two terumot
items.text_en: Rav's derivation from the verse about two terumot
items.desc_en: Rav states that just as it is a mitzvah to burn impure sacred items, so too it is a mitzvah to burn impure terumah. The Torah indicates that at the time of disposal, one may benefit from it, as derived from Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha: the verse 'And I have given you the charge of My terumot' refers to both pure and impure terumah, and 'to you' means it is yours to use for heating your food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that on a weekday it is permitted to burn impure terumah, and asks for the reason.
Rav answers that just as it is a מצוה (commandment) to burn impure sacred items, so too it is a מצוה to burn impure terumah.
Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha cites a verse to show that the Torah permits benefiting from terumah at the time of its disposal, specifically for fuel under one's cooking.

items.text: Alternative derivation from Rabbi Avahu and the kal vachomer challenge
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from Rabbi Avahu and the kal vachomer challenge
items.desc_en: An alternative source is presented: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse 'I have not removed from it in impurity' that one may burn impure terumah oil. The Gemara questions why this does not also permit burning impure sacred oil, and answers that a kal vachomer from maaser would forbid it. The Gemara then asks why terumah itself is not forbidden by a kal vachomer, and answers that the word 'from it' excludes terumah from the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative derivation: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'ולא בערתי ממנו בטמא' (I have not removed from it in impurity) to permit burning impure terumah oil.
The Gemara challenges: why not also permit burning impure sacred oil (קודש) from the same verse?
The Gemara answers that a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from maaser (מעשר) would forbid burning sacred oil, since maaser is less stringent yet the verse prohibits burning it when impure.
The Gemara objects: if so, the same קל וחומר should also forbid burning impure terumah, undermining the original derivation.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'ממנו' (from it) in the verse excludes terumah from the קל וחומר, allowing its burning.

items.text: Justification for excluding sacred items over terumah
items.text_en: Justification for excluding sacred items over terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one would exclude sacred items rather than terumah from the permission. It answers with a mnemonic: sacred items have piggul, notar, korban, me'ilah, and karet, and are forbidden to an onen, so they are more stringent. The Gemara begins to counter that terumah also has stringencies (death penalty and one-fifth), but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one would exclude sacred items (קודש) rather than תרומה (terumah) from the permission to benefit from burning.
The Gemara answers with a mnemonic (פנ״ק עכ״ס): sacred items have piggul, notar, korban, me'ilah, and karet, and are forbidden to an onen, making them more stringent than terumah.
The Gemara counters that one could equally exclude terumah, since it has stringencies of death penalty (מיתה) and one-fifth (חומש), but the argument is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's list
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's list
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's list of forbidden oils is extensive, and questions why additional oils are mentioned if they are already included in the general category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists additional forbidden oils when they are already included in the general category of forbidden oils.

items.text: First answer: קודש חמור
items.text_en: First answer: קודש חמור
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the oil is from קודש (sacred property) which is more stringent because it carries the penalty of כרת. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives from the verse that the oil is given to the priest for his own use, not for burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the additional oils are mentioned because they are קֹדֶשׁ (sacred) and carry the penalty of כרת (excision).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives from the verse 'תִּתֵּן לוֹ' (you shall give it to him) that the oil is given to the priest, not for lighting, implying it is oil suitable for lighting.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's reason and the obligation of Shabbat candles
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's reason and the obligation of Shabbat candles
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Yishmael's reason for forbidding certain oils: because their smell is bad, one might leave the candle and go out. Abaye objects, and Rava responds that lighting Shabbat candles is an obligation, citing Rav Nachman bar Rav Zavda (or Rav Nachman bar Rava) quoting Rav that lighting is a חובה, while washing hands and feet in hot water on Friday evening is a רשות, but Rava considers it a מצוה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Yishmael's opinion regarding forbidden oils.
Rava explains that the oil is forbidden because its bad smell might cause one to leave the lamp and go out, violating Shabbat.
Abaye objects: why would one leave the lamp just because of a bad smell?
Rava responds that lighting the Shabbat lamp is a חוֹבָה (obligation), so one might leave to avoid the bad smell and thus neglect the mitzvah.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Zavda / Rav Nachman bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Zavda / Rav Nachman bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Zavda (or Rav Nachman bar Rava) cites Rav that lighting the Shabbat lamp is a חוֹבָה (obligation), while washing hands and feet in hot water on Friday evening is optional, though the speaker considers it a מִצְוָה (commandment).

items.text: The practice of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai and the dispute about ציצית on a סדין
items.text_en: The practice of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai and the dispute about ציצית on a סדין
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the מצוה of washing: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai would bathe his face, hands, and feet in hot water on Friday evening and sit in fringed linen garments, resembling an angel. His students would hide the corners of their garments, and he rebuked them, citing the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding a linen garment with ציצית, ruling like Beit Hillel who obligate ציצית, while the students feared a decree due to night garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the nature of the מִצְוָה (commandment) regarding washing hands and feet.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav describes the custom of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai, who would wash his face, hands, and feet in hot water on Friday evening and dress in fine linen, resembling an angel of God.
The students would fold the corners of their garments to avoid the appearance of wearing ציצית (ritual fringes) on a garment that might be exempt.

Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai rebukes his students, citing the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding a linen garment with ציצית (ritual fringes), ruling that the הלכה (binding law) follows Beit Hillel who obligate fringes.
The students thought that a night garment is exempt from ציצית (ritual fringes) due to a גזירה (decree) against wearing it during the day.

items.text: Exegetical interpretations of the verse from Lamentations
items.text_en: Exegetical interpretations of the verse from Lamentations
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'ותזנח משלום נפשי נשיתי טובה' as referring to various comforts lost in exile: Rabbi Avahu says it refers to Shabbat candle lighting, Rabbi Yirmeya to the bathhouse, Rabbi Yochanan to washing hands and feet in hot water, Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha to a nice bed and fine vessels, and Rabbi Abba to a made bed and a decorated wife for Torah scholars.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Lamentations: 'וַתִּזְנַח מִשָּׁלוֹם נַפְשִׁי נָשִׁיתִי טוֹבָה' (You have removed my soul from peace, I have forgotten goodness).
Rabbi Avahu interprets 'וַתִּזְנַח מִשָּׁלוֹם נַפְשִׁי' as referring to the lighting of the Shabbat lamp.
Rabbi Yirmeya interprets 'נָשִׁיתִי טוֹבָה' as referring to the bathhouse.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'נָשִׁיתִי טוֹבָה' as referring to washing hands and feet in hot water.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha interprets 'נָשִׁיתִי טוֹבָה' as referring to a beautiful bed and beautiful vessels on it.
Rabbi Abba interprets 'נָשִׁיתִי טוֹבָה' as referring to a made bed and a decorated wife for Torah scholars.

items.text: Definitions of wealth
items.text_en: Definitions of wealth
items.desc_en: A Tosefta lists definitions of wealth: Rabbi Meir says one who is content with his wealth (with the mnemonic מטק״ס), Rabbi Tarfon says one who has 100 vineyards, fields, and slaves, Rabbi Akiva says one who has a wife of good deeds, and Rabbi Yose says one who has a toilet near his table.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states: Who is rich? — Anyone who has satisfaction from his wealth, the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Tarfon defines a rich person as one who has a hundred vineyards, a hundred fields, and a hundred slaves working them.
Rabbi Akiva defines a rich person as one who has a wife beautiful in deeds.
Rabbi Yosei defines a rich person as one who has a toilet near his table.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's prohibition of צרי
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's prohibition of צרי
items.desc_en: A Tosefta states that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids lighting with צרי (balsam oil). Rabbah explains the reason: because its fragrance spreads, one might use it for other purposes. Abaye questions this reasoning.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: One may not light with צרי (balsam oil).
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling.
Rabbah explains that because its fragrance spreads, there is a גזירה (decree) lest one use it for personal benefit.
Abaye begins to raise an objection against Rabbah's explanation.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's reason
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement about balsam oil (צרי) includes two reasons: first, because it is volatile (עף), and second, a decree lest one become uncertain about its use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement about balsam oil (צרי) includes two reasons: first, because it is volatile (עף), and second, a decree lest one become uncertain about its use.

items.text: Story about balsam oil and a verse about perfume collectors
items.text_en: Story about balsam oil and a verse about perfume collectors
items.desc_en: A story is told of a mother-in-law who told her daughter-in-law to anoint herself with balsam oil and then light a lamp, which caused a fire. Then a verse is cited about perfume collectors and snail hunters, linking to the balsam oil trade.

sub.desc_en: A story is told of a mother-in-law who hated her daughter-in-law, told her to anoint with balsam oil and then light a lamp, causing a fire that consumed her.

A verse is cited about perfume collectors and snail hunters, and Rav Yosef interprets them as referring to balsam oil collectors from Ein Gedi to Ramta and snail hunters from the ladders of Tyre to Haifa.

items.text: Baraita: Prohibition of lighting with impure tevel and white naphtha
items.text_en: Baraita: Prohibition of lighting with impure tevel and white naphtha
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may not light with impure tevel (untithed produce) even on a weekday, and certainly not on Shabbat. Similarly, white naphtha is prohibited because it is volatile. The Gemara asks why impure tevel is prohibited, and answers with a verse about two types of terumah, teaching that both pure and impure terumah are only permitted from the time of separation onward.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one may not light with impure tevel (untithed produce) on a weekday, and certainly not on Shabbat.
The baraita adds a parallel ruling: similarly, one may not light with white naphtha on a weekday, and certainly not on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks: granted, white naphtha is prohibited because it is volatile (עף), but what is the reason for prohibiting impure tevel?

The Gemara answers by citing a verse (במדבר יח:ח) that speaks of 'two terumot' (תרומותי), teaching that both pure and impure terumah are only permitted from the time of separation onward, so impure tevel (which has not been separated) is forbidden for lighting.

items.text: Tannaitic opinions on prohibited oils
items.text_en: Tannaitic opinions on prohibited oils
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita with various opinions: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar prohibits balsam oil (צרי) and defines it as resin from the balsam tree; Rabbi Yishmael prohibits all tree exudates; Rabbi Yishmael ben Beroka permits only fruit oils; Rabbi Tarfon permits only olive oil.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's opinion that one may not light Shabbat lamps with balsam oil (צרי), defining it as resin from the balsam tree.
Rabbi Yishmael states that all tree exudates are prohibited for lighting.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Beroka permits only oils that come from fruit.
Rabbi Tarfon restricts lighting to olive oil alone.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's objection and conclusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's objection and conclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects to the restrictive opinions, asking what people in various regions who have only specific oils (e.g., sesame oil, nut oil, radish oil, naphtha) will do. He concludes that one may only use what the Sages explicitly permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objects by asking what people in various regions who have only specific oils (sesame, nut, radish, naphtha) will do.
He concludes that one may only use what the Sages explicitly permitted for lighting.

items.text: Permitted oils and a dispute about fish oil
items.text_en: Permitted oils and a dispute about fish oil
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits fish oil and tar. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds gourd oil and naphtha. Somkhos says no animal-derived oil except fish oil. The Gemara notes that Somkhos seems to repeat the first Tanna, and mentions a dispute about a statement of Rav Berona quoting Rav that is not concluded.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permitted oils for Shabbat lights: fish oil, tar, and according to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, gourd oil and naphtha.
Somkhos rules that no animal-derived oil may be used for Shabbat lights except fish oil.
The Gemara asks: does Somkhos merely repeat the first Tanna's ruling about fish oil?
The Gemara notes that there is a practical difference between them based on a statement of Rav Berona quoting Rav, but the matter is not resolved.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on tree exudates for sukkah covering
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on tree exudates for sukkah covering
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says all tree exudates are not subject to the three-by-three handbreadth rule for impurity and may be used for sukkah covering, except flax. Abaye begins to comment.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling that all tree exudates are exempt from the three-by-three handbreadth impurity rule and may be used for sukkah covering, except flax.
Abaye begins to comment on the baraita, setting up the next discussion.

items.text: Identifying the parallel positions
items.text_en: Identifying the parallel positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael said the same thing regarding the impurity of garments. It then explains the Tanna's derivation: since the Torah mentions 'garments' generally and specifies wool and linen in one place, all garments are only wool and linen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael said the same thing.
The Gemara asks what the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael's position is.
The Gemara cites a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: since 'garments' is stated generally in the Torah and specified as wool and linen in one place, all garments are only wool and linen.

items.text: Rava's distinction between them
items.text_en: Rava's distinction between them
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael concerns a three-by-three fingerbreadth patch in non-wool/linen garments: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds it is susceptible to impurity, while the Tanna holds it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the dispute: the difference between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael is whether a three-by-three fingerbreadth patch in non-wool/linen garments is susceptible to impurity.

items.text: Source for three-by-three in wool and linen for negaim
items.text_en: Source for three-by-three in wool and linen for negaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the impurity of a three-by-three fingerbreadth patch in wool and linen for negaim. It cites a baraita that derives it from the word 'וְהַבֶּגֶד', and then discusses why it cannot be derived by a kal vachomer from the impurity of threads. It concludes that a three-by-three patch, which is useful for both rich and poor, could have been derived by kal vachomer, but a three-by-three patch, which is only useful for the poor, cannot; thus a verse is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For all opinions, a three-by-three fingerbreadth patch in wool and linen is impure for negaim — what is the source?
A baraita is cited: The verse 'בֶּגֶד' (garment) alone would include only a full garment; the extra 'וְהַבֶּגֶד' (and the garment) teaches that a three-by-three patch is also included.
The Gemara objects: Why not derive the three-by-three patch by a kal vachomer (a fortiori) from threads (שתי וערב), which are smaller yet become impure?

The Gemara resolves: A three-by-three patch, useful for both rich and poor, could be derived by kal vachomer; but a three-by-three patch, useful only for the poor, cannot be derived by kal vachomer, so a verse is necessary.

items.text: Excluding non-wool/linen from three-by-three
items.text_en: Excluding non-wool/linen from three-by-three
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse should not include a three-by-three patch in non-wool/linen garments. It answers that the verse says 'בֶּגֶד צֶמֶר וּפִשְׁתִּים', implying only wool and linen. It then asks why it should not exclude only patches smaller than three-by-three, but include three-by-three. It answers that two exclusions are written: one for less than three-by-three, and one for three-by-three.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse should not include a three-by-three patch in non-wool/linen garments.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'בֶּגֶד צֶמֶר וּפִשְׁתִּים', implying only wool and linen.
The Gemara asks why the verse should not exclude only patches smaller than three-by-three, but include three-by-three.
The Gemara answers that two exclusions are written: one for less than three-by-three, and one for three-by-three.

items.text: Clarifying Rava's position
items.text_en: Clarifying Rava's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara reiterates Rava's position that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael concerns a three-by-three patch in non-wool/linen garments, with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holding it is impure and the Tanna holding it is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reiterates Rava's position that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael concerns a three-by-three patch in non-wool/linen garments, with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holding it is impure and the Tanna holding it is not.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where does one derive the law? It cites a baraitha that the word "or a garment" (או בגד) includes a three-by-three handbreadth piece from other fabrics.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where the law is derived, and cites a baraitha that the word 'או בגד' (or a garment) includes a three-by-three handbreadth piece from other fabrics.

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate the derivation
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate the derivation
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the word "or a garment" is needed to include a three-by-three piece of wool or linen for impurity from creeping things. Rava counters that the Torah revealed the law regarding negaim (leprosy) and it applies equally to creeping things. Abaye objects that negaim are stricter because they apply to warp and woof. The Gemara continues with further objections and responses.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks what the word 'אוֹ בֶגֶד' (or a garment) comes to teach, and answers that it includes a three-by-three handbreadth piece of wool or linen for impurity from creeping things.
Rava counters that the Torah revealed the law regarding negaim (leprosy) and it applies equally to creeping things.
Abaye objects that negaim are stricter because they apply to warp and woof.
The Gemara responds that if negaim were stricter, the Torah would have written the law regarding creeping things and derived negaim from them.
The Gemara further responds that negaim cannot be derived from creeping things because creeping things are stricter in that they impart impurity at the size of a lentil.

items.text: Abaye cites a contradiction in the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Abaye cites a contradiction in the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives a different law from "or a garment" — to include various types of fabrics like camel wool, rabbit wool, and silk — contradicting the earlier derivation.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by noting that one Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives a different inclusion from 'או בגד' (or a garment) than another Tanna of the same school.

items.text: Rava's resolution and retraction
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and retraction
items.desc_en: Rava initially says that the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael does not have the law for other fabrics in general, but does have the law for a three-by-three piece. The Gemara objects that Rava himself said the three-by-three law applies only to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, not to the school of Rabbi Yishmael. Rava then retracts, or alternatively, Rav Pappa said it.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael does not have the law of a three-by-three patch for other fabrics in general, but does have it for a three-by-three patch specifically.
The Gemara objects that Rava himself previously said the three-by-three law applies only to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, not to the school of Rabbi Yishmael.
Rava retracts from that earlier statement.
Alternatively, the Gemara suggests that Rav Pappa, not Rava, originally said the statement about the three-by-three patch.

items.text: Rav Pappa's explanation and rejection
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation and rejection
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says that "or a garment" comes to include kilayim (mixed fabrics). The Gemara objects that kilayim is explicitly written, but Rav Pappa thought it might only apply to wearing, not to mere lifting. The Gemara then argues with a kal vachomer that if wearing is prohibited only with wool and linen, then lifting is certainly prohibited only with those. The Gemara concludes that Rav Pappa's statement is a fabrication.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that 'or a garment' comes to include kilayim (mixed fabrics), because one might have thought the prohibition of wearing kilayim applies only to wearing, not to mere lifting.

The Gemara objects with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if wearing kilayim, which benefits the whole body, is prohibited only with wool and linen, then lifting, which is less severe, should certainly be limited to those materials.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Pappa's statement is a fabrication (בדותא), because the kal vachomer refutes it.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says that "or a garment" comes to include something else, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers another interpretation of the word 'או בגד' (or a garment).

items.text: Gemara's question on tzitzit and sha'atnez
items.text_en: Gemara's question on tzitzit and sha'atnez
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse about tzitzit is needed to include wool and linen, since sha'atnez already mentions them. It suggests that Rava's resolution is being taught, where the verse 'the corner' implies any type, but 'wool and linen together' limits it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse about tzitzit (ציצית) is needed to include wool and linen, since the prohibition of sha'atnez (שעטנז) already mentions them.

The Gemara explains that the verse is needed because one might have thought like Rava's resolution: the verse 'the corner' (הכנף) implies any type, but 'wool and linen together' (צמר ופשתים יחדו) limits it, so the tzitzit verse teaches that wool and linen are permitted for tzitzit even together.

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge and resolution regarding other garments
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge and resolution regarding other garments
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi why the tanna of Rabbi Yishmael's school doesn't include other garments from the phrase 'which you cover yourself with'. The Gemara answers that this phrase comes to include a blind person's garment, excluding night garments, as derived from a baraita.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi why the tanna of Rabbi Yishmael's school, who includes other garments for impurity from 'אוֹ בֶגֶד', does not similarly include other garments for tzitzit from 'אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ'.

sub.text: Gemara's answer (via Rav Ashi or stam)
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer (via Rav Ashi or stam)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the phrase 'אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ' comes to include a blind person's garment, as derived from a baraita that contrasts 'וּרְאִיתֶם אוֹתוֹ' (excluding night garments) with 'אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ' (including a blind person's garment).

The baraita explains the logic: a blind person's garment is included because it is subject to visibility by others, while a night garment is excluded because it is not subject to visibility by others.

The Gemara objects: why not say the phrase includes other garments (not just a blind person's garment)? The answer is that since the verse is dealing with wool and linen, it would be illogical to include other materials.

items.text: Abaye's statement linking Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Somkhos
items.text_en: Abaye's statement linking Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Somkhos
items.desc_en: Abaye says that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Somkhos said the same thing. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view is the one already mentioned, and Somkhos's view is from a baraita about sukkah roofing made of spun flax being invalid because it is susceptible to impurity.

items.text: Mishnah: Only flax is permitted for wicks and tent-impurity
items.text_en: Mishnah: Only flax is permitted for wicks and tent-impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything that comes from a tree may not be used for lighting (Shabbat lamps) except flax, and anything that comes from a tree is not susceptible to tent-impurity except flax.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states: anything that comes from wood may not be used for lighting (on Shabbat) except flax; and anything that comes from wood is not susceptible to impurity from tents (טומאת אהלים) except flax.

items.text: Gemara's derivation that flax is called 'tree' and the source for tent-impurity
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation that flax is called 'tree' and the source for tent-impurity
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra proves that flax is called 'tree' from the verse about Rahab hiding the spies in 'flax of the tree'. Rabbi Elazar derives the rule about tent-impurity from a verbal analogy of 'tent' from the Tabernacle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that flax is called 'tree'?
Mar Zutra answers by citing the verse about Rahab hiding the spies in 'flax of the tree'.

items.text: Deriving that only linen is called 'tent'
items.text_en: Deriving that only linen is called 'tent'
items.desc_en: The Gemara uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the tent of the Tabernacle and the tent of impurity to establish that only linen is called 'tent'. It then questions whether this analogy also requires the threads to be twisted and sixfold, and answers that the repetition of 'אוהל' excludes that requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the tent of impurity and the Tabernacle tent to prove that only linen is called 'אוהל' (tent).
The Gemara questions whether the analogy also requires the threads to be twisted and sixfold like the Tabernacle curtains.
The Gemara answers that the repetition of 'אוהל' (tent) excludes the requirement of twisted and sixfold threads, but then questions what remains of the verbal analogy.

items.text: Rejecting planks and introducing Rabbi Elazar's question
items.text_en: Rejecting planks and introducing Rabbi Elazar's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects a suggestion that planks (קרשים) are also called 'משכן', and then addresses a difficulty: if the outer covering is not called 'tent', how can Rabbi Elazar ask about the hide of an unclean animal? It resolves by noting that the verse juxtaposes the upper and lower coverings, so the upper is also called 'tent'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the analogy might require planks (קרשים) as well, since the Tabernacle had planks.
The Gemara answers that the verse calls the Tabernacle 'משכן' (Tabernacle), not 'קרשים' (planks), so planks are not called 'משכן'.
The Gemara objects that by the same logic, the covering (מכסה) of the tent would not be called 'אוהל' (tent), yet it is.

sub.text: Gemara's digression to Rabbi Elazar's question
sub.text_en: Gemara's digression to Rabbi Elazar's question
sub.desc_en: The Gemara digresses to cite Rabbi Elazar's question about whether the skin of an unclean animal can become impure through tent impurity, and challenges it.
The Gemara answers that the covering is called 'אוהל' (tent) because the verse juxtaposes the upper covering to the lower tent, equating them.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question and Rav Yosef's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question and Rav Yosef's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether the hide of an unclean animal can contract tent impurity. Rav Adda bar Ahava suggests he is asking about the tachash (a kosher or non-kosher animal). Rav Yosef objects, citing a baraita that only the hide of a clean animal is fit for heavenly work.

sub.text: Gemara's introduction of Rabbi Elazar's question
sub.text_en: Gemara's introduction of Rabbi Elazar's question
sub.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rabbi Elazar's question about whether the skin of an unclean animal can contract tent impurity.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Elazar's question is about, and Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that he is asking about the תחשׁ (tachash) from Moses' time — whether it was clean or unclean.
Rav Yosef objects that the question is unnecessary, citing a baraita that only the skin of a clean animal is fit for heavenly work.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's objection from the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's objection from the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba raises an objection from a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya about the coverings of the Tabernacle. Rabbi Nechemya says one covering was like a 'tela ilan' (a multicolored animal), which is impure, but the Gemara clarifies it only resembles it, and is actually pure. Rav Yosef notes this is why it is called 'sasgona' (rejoicing in many colors).

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's citation of a dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's citation of a dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba cites a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya about whether there were two coverings or one covering for the Tabernacle.
The Gemara questions that if the covering was like a תְּלָא אִילָן (a type of unclean animal), it would be unclean, contradicting the assumption.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Nechemya meant it was like a תְּלָא אִילָן in having many colors, but it was actually a clean animal.
Rav Yosef concludes that this explains why the Targum translates 'תחש' as 'ססגונא' (sasgona), meaning it rejoices in many colors.
Rav Yosef notes that this explains why the tachash is called 'sasgona' (rejoicing in many colors).

items.text: Rava's first proof from leprosy
items.text_en: Rava's first proof from leprosy
items.desc_en: Rava attempts to prove that the hide of an unclean animal is susceptible to tent impurity from a baraita on leprosy (נגעים) that includes 'or' and 'be'or' to include unclean hide. However, the Gemara refutes this because leprosy also applies to warp and woof, unlike a corpse.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives that the skin of an unclean animal can contract tent impurity from the repetition of 'עור' (skin) in the context of leprosy.
Rava further derives from 'אוֹ בְּכׇל מְלֶאכֶת עוֹר' (or in any work of skin) that even a patchwork of various skins is included.
The Gemara objects that the derivation from leprosy is flawed because leprosy also applies to warp and woof, which tent impurity does not.

items.text: Derivation from creeping things and the common element
items.text_en: Derivation from creeping things and the common element
items.desc_en: The Gemara instead derives from creeping things (שרצים) that 'or' includes unclean hide. It then builds a common element (צד השווה) from leprosy and creeping things: both have impurity for hide and treat unclean hide like clean hide. This is applied to tent impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara instead derives from creeping things (שרצים) that the skin of an unclean animal is included, using the word 'אוֹ עוֹר' (or skin).
The Gemara objects that creeping things are different because they impart impurity in the size of a lentil, unlike a corpse.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via a בנין אב (common element)
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via a בנין אב (common element)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves by constructing a בנין אב (common element) from leprosy and creeping things, concluding that the skin of an unclean animal is treated like that of a clean animal for tent impurity.
