The Gemara constructs a common element (צד השווה) from leprosy and creeping things: both have impurity for hide and treat unclean hide like clean hide.
The Gemara applies this common element to tent impurity (אוהל המת), concluding that unclean hide is treated like clean hide in that context.

items.text: Rava mi-Barnish's refutation
items.text_en: Rava mi-Barnish's refutation
items.desc_en: Rava mi-Barnish refutes the common element: leprosy and creeping things are impure in less than an olive's bulk, whereas a corpse is only impure in an olive's bulk. Thus the analogy fails.

sub.desc_en: Rava of Barnish objects to Rav Ashi that the common element is flawed because leprosy and creeping things impart impurity in less than an olive's bulk, unlike a corpse.

items.text: Rava mi-Barnish's alternative answer (incomplete)
items.text_en: Rava mi-Barnish's alternative answer (incomplete)
items.desc_en: Rava mi-Barnish begins to offer an alternative derivation, but the text cuts off at the end of the amud.

sub.desc_en: Rava of Barnish begins to offer an alternative derivation, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Attempted a fortiori argument for impure animal hide
items.text_en: Attempted a fortiori argument for impure animal hide
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive that the hide of an impure animal is susceptible to tent-impurity from the hide of a goat, which is not susceptible to leprosy but is susceptible to tent-impurity. The argument is rejected implicitly by the following discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if goat hair, which is not susceptible to leprosy, is susceptible to tent-impurity, then the hide of an impure animal, which is susceptible to leprosy, should certainly be susceptible to tent-impurity.

items.text: Clarifying the halakha of pure animal hide for heavenly work
items.text_en: Clarifying the halakha of pure animal hide for heavenly work
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of Rav Yosef's teaching that only pure animal hide is fit for heavenly work. It suggests tefillin, but that is rejected because tefillin require an animal permitted in the mouth. The Gemara then considers the hide for the tefillin boxes, the hair for binding, the sinews for sewing, and the straps, each time encountering a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai that already covers the requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what halakhic purpose is Rav Yosef's teaching that only pure animal hide is fit for heavenly work?
The Gemara suggests the hide is for tefillin, but rejects this because tefillin require an animal permitted in the mouth.
The Gemara suggests the hide is for the tefillin boxes, but Abaye objects that the boxes are a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.
The Gemara suggests the hide is for wrapping and sewing tefillin, but this too is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.
The Gemara suggests the hide is for straps, but Rabbi Yitzchak notes that black straps are a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai, though the requirement for pure hide is not.

items.text: The nature of the tachash in Moses' time
items.text_en: The nature of the tachash in Moses' time
items.desc_en: Rabbi Il'a in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish quotes Rabbi Meir that the tachash was a unique creature with one horn, and the Sages were uncertain whether it was a domesticated or undomesticated animal. The Gemara proves from the single horn that it was pure, citing a verse about Adam's ox, but cannot determine its species because the keresh also has one horn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the nature of the tachash that existed in Moses' time.

sub.text: Rabbi Il'a citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish citing Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Il'a citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish citing Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that the tachash was a unique creature with one horn on its forehead, and the Sages were uncertain whether it was a domesticated or undomesticated animal; it was temporarily available to Moses for the Tabernacle and then hidden.

sub.text: Gemara's inference from the single horn
sub.text_en: Gemara's inference from the single horn
sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the single horn that the tachash was pure (טהור), citing Rav Yehuda's statement that Adam's ox had one horn, as derived from the verse 'וְתִיטַב לַה׳ מִשּׁוֹר פָּר מַקְרִין מַפְרִיס'.
The Gemara objects that the word 'מַקְרִין' could imply two horns, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that it is written 'מַקְרָן' (with a kamatz, meaning one horn).
The Gemara asks whether we can resolve from the single horn that the tachash was a domesticated animal (בהמה).
The Gemara resolves that since the keresh (a wild animal) also has only one horn, the tachash could be a wild animal, so no definitive conclusion can be drawn.

items.text: Mishnah: Folded wick that was not singed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Folded wick that was not singed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says a folded wick that was not singed is impure and may not be used for lighting, while Rabbi Akiva says it is pure and may be used.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: regarding a wick of cloth that was folded but not singed, Rabbi Eliezer says it is impure and may not be lit, while Rabbi Akiva says it is pure and may be lit.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the dispute regarding impurity and lighting
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the dispute regarding impurity and lighting
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute regarding impurity: Rabbi Eliezer holds that folding does not nullify the cloth's status, while Rabbi Akiva holds it does. Regarding lighting, Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav Oshaya and Rav Adda bar Ahava explain that the case involves a three-by-three handbreadth cloth on a Festival that falls on Shabbat eve. Both agree with Rabbi Yehuda that one may burn vessels but not broken vessels, and with Ulla that one must light from the majority protruding. Rabbi Eliezer holds folding does not help, so the remaining part is a broken vessel; Rabbi Akiva holds folding nullifies the vessel status, so it is just wood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that regarding impurity, the dispute is clear: Rabbi Eliezer holds folding does not nullify the cloth's status, while Rabbi Akiva holds it does.
The Gemara asks: regarding lighting, what is the basis of their dispute?

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav Oshaya and Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rav Oshaya and Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: They explain the dispute: the case involves a three-by-three handbreadth cloth on a Festival that falls on Shabbat eve, both agree with Rabbi Yehuda that one may burn vessels but not broken vessels, and with Ulla that one must light from the majority protruding; Rabbi Eliezer holds folding does not help, so the remaining part is a broken vessel, while Rabbi Akiva holds folding nullifies the vessel status, so it is just wood.

items.text: Rav Yosef's clarification and a question on Rav Adda bar Ahava's view
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's clarification and a question on Rav Adda bar Ahava's view
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef notes that this explains the Mishnah's phrase 'exactly three by three' which he did not understand. The Gemara then infers that Rav Adda bar Ahava holds like Rabbi Yehuda, but questions this based on another statement of Rav Adda bar Ahava.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef notes that the Mishnah's phrase 'שלוש על שלוש מצומצמות' (exactly three by three) now makes sense, as he previously did not know its halachic purpose.
The Gemara infers that Rav Adda bar Ahava holds like Rabbi Yehuda, but then questions this based on another statement of Rav Adda bar Ahava that seems to contradict this alignment.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a Jew may use a pit dug by a gentile on Yom Tov, asking why it is not considered a nolad (newly created item). It explains that the Mishnah is stated according to the views of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva, but the Tanna himself does not hold that view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a pit dug by a gentile on Yom Tov is permitted for a Jew, since it appears to be a nolad (newly created item).
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's ruling is stated according to the views of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva, but the Tanna himself does not hold that view.

items.text: Rava's explanation and the baraita of three-by-three
items.text_en: Rava's explanation and the baraita of three-by-three
items.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: one may not light with an uncharred wick or uncharred rags. The Gemara then asks about the purpose of Rav Yosef's baraita regarding 'three-by-three exact', concluding it refers to the laws of impurity, citing a Mishnah about the minimum size for a cloth to be susceptible to impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: one may not light with an uncharred wick or uncharred rags.
The Gemara asks what halachic purpose is served by the baraita of Rav Yosef regarding three-by-three exact measures.
The Gemara answers that the baraita pertains to the laws of ritual impurity (טומאה), citing the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages about the exact size of a three-by-three cloth.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on fuel and the necessity of three cases
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on fuel and the necessity of three cases
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav's ruling: one may burn vessels but not broken vessels, dates but not their pits, nuts but not their shells, according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Shimon permits all. The Gemara explains why all three cases are necessary to teach the principle of nolad and the distinctions between them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Rav's ruling that one may burn vessels but not broken vessels, dates but not their pits, and nuts but not their shells according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Shimon permits all.

The Gemara explains why all three cases are necessary: each case teaches a distinct aspect of the principle of נולד (nolad, a new entity created on the festival), and without all three, one might mistakenly permit one of the cases.

items.text: The incident with Rav and the dispute over acceptance
items.text_en: The incident with Rav and the dispute over acceptance
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav's ruling was not stated explicitly but inferred from an incident where Rav ate dates and threw the pits into a basket. Rabbi Chiyya rebuked him, saying it is forbidden on Yom Tov. The Gemara debates whether Rav accepted this ruling, and concludes that the incident in Babylonia involved Aramaean pits which are usable with their mother, so no rejection occurred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav's ruling was not stated explicitly but inferred from an incident where Rav ate dates and threw the pits into a basket, and Rabbi Chiyya rebuked him, saying it is forbidden on Yom Tov; the Gemara then questions whether Rav accepted this ruling.
The Gemara brings a supporting incident: when Rav came to Babylonia, he ate dates and threw the pits to the animals, suggesting he did not accept Rabbi Chiyya's ruling.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the incident in Babylonia involved Aramaean pits which are usable with their mother, so no rejection of Rabbi Chiyya's ruling occurred.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chana's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chana's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chana asks Rav Yosef: according to Rabbi Yehuda, once a vessel is partially burned it becomes broken vessels, so how can one stoke the fire? The Gemara answers that one acts like Rav Mattana, who said one may add prepared wood to the fire, thus the broken pieces are considered prepared.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chanah's question
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chanah's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chanah asks Rav Yosef: according to Rabbi Yehuda, once a vessel is partially burned, it becomes broken vessel fragments, so how can one turn it over on Yom Tov without violating the prohibition?
Rav Yosef answers that one acts according to the method of Rav Mattanah, who said that if wood fell from a palm tree into an oven on Yom Tov, one adds prepared wood and burns them together.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's alternative explanation and the Mishnah of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's alternative explanation and the Mishnah of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna explains that the case involves cloth less than three-by-three, and the leniencies of מטלניות (rags) are taught here. The Gemara then notes that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva follow their own views, citing a Mishnah about the status of a small cloth prepared for various uses, and Ulla's statement that all agree if thrown into the trash it is pure.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna explains that the case involves cloth less than three-by-three, and the leniencies of מטלניות (rags) are taught here.

The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva follow their own views, citing a Mishnah about the status of a small cloth prepared for various uses, and Ulla's statement that all agree if thrown into the trash it is pure.

items.text: Dispute about the status of a key placed in a box or behind a door
items.text_en: Dispute about the status of a key placed in a box or behind a door
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding a key placed in a box or behind a door, and how Rabbi Akiva initially sides with each in different cases but later retracts.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Akiva retracted to Rabbi Yehoshua's view
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Akiva retracted to Rabbi Yehoshua's view
items.desc_en: Rava proves that Rabbi Akiva retracted to Rabbi Yehoshua's view based on the wording 'פתילת הבגד' in the Mishnah, indicating the cloth is still considered a garment.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition of placing an eggshell on a lamp
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition of placing an eggshell on a lamp
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits placing an eggshell or clay shard on a lamp to catch dripping oil, but Rabbi Yehuda permits it. If the potter attached it initially, it is permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Need for both cases in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Need for both cases in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to teach both the case of an eggshell and a clay shard, and also the case of a bowl placed next to the lamp, to clarify the positions of the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Clarification of 'if the potter attached it'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'if the potter attached it'
items.desc_en: A beraita teaches that if one attached the shard with lime or clay it is permitted, and the Gemara explains that the Mishnah's term 'potter' means 'like a potter'.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's anecdote and refutation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's anecdote and refutation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda recounts that he and others did this in the attic of Beit Nitzah in Lod, and the Sages did not object. The Sages respond that Beit Nitzah is different because they are diligent.

items.text: Story of Avin from Tzippora and the decree
items.text_en: Story of Avin from Tzippora and the decree
items.desc_en: Avin from Tzippora dragged a bench in the upper story of Shisha, and Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar warned him that silence like that granted to Rabbi Yehuda could lead to destruction, decreeing a gezeirah.

items.text: Dispute about dragging furniture on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about dragging furniture on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The head of the synagogue in Botzra dragged a bench before Rabbi Yirmeya the Great, who questioned whether he followed Rabbi Shimon's leniency. Ulla states the dispute is only about small items, but for large items all permit.

items.text: Objection from a beraita about dragging a bed
items.text_en: Objection from a beraita about dragging a bed
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef raises an objection from a beraita where Rabbi Shimon permits dragging a bed, chair, or bench, provided one does not intend to make a groove. The beraita mentions both large and small items, challenging both views.

items.text: Resolutions by Ulla and Rabbi Yirmeya the Great
items.text_en: Resolutions by Ulla and Rabbi Yirmeya the Great
items.desc_en: Ulla and Rabbi Yirmeya the Great each resolve the objection according to their own view: Ulla says the bed is like a chair (small), while Rabbi Yirmeya says the chair is like a bed (large).

items.text: Refutation of Rabbi Yirmeya the Great's view
items.text_en: Refutation of Rabbi Yirmeya the Great's view
items.desc_en: Rabba raises an objection from a beraita about cloak sellers, where even though one could act like the modest ones (small items), Rabbi Shimon permits it ab initio if there is no intent. This refutes Rabbi Yirmeya the Great's view.

items.text: Mishnah: Extinguishing a lamp for various reasons
items.text_en: Mishnah: Extinguishing a lamp for various reasons
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who extinguishes a lamp out of fear of gentiles, bandits, an evil spirit, or to let a sick person sleep is exempt. But if one is sparing the lamp, oil, or wick, he is liable. Rabbi Yosi exempts in all cases except the wick, because he makes it into charcoal.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's use of 'exempt' for a life-threatening patient, arguing it should say 'permitted'. It resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, and the language is due to the structure of the Mishnah. A baraita from Rabbi Oshaya is cited and explained as referring to a non-life-threatening patient and following Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's use of 'exempt' for a life-threatening patient, arguing it should say 'permitted', and for a non-life-threatening patient it should say 'liable for a sin-offering'.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah always refers to a life-threatening patient, but uses 'exempt' because the structure of the Mishnah requires matching the 'liable' in the latter clause.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita of Rabbi Oshaya that says one who extinguishes a lamp for a patient is exempt but forbidden, contradicting the Mishnah's 'exempt'.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a non-life-threatening patient and follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an act performed without intent for a prohibited purpose is exempt but forbidden.

items.text: Question about extinguishing a lamp for a Persian noble
items.text_en: Question about extinguishing a lamp for a Persian noble
items.desc_en: A question is raised before Rabbi Tanchum from Noy: may one extinguish a lamp on Shabbat for a Persian noble? He responds by rebuking Solomon, pointing out contradictions between Solomon's words and his father David's, and between Solomon's own statements.

sub.text: Questioner before Rabbi Tanchum from Noy
sub.text_en: Questioner before Rabbi Tanchum from Noy
sub.desc_en: A question is raised before Rabbi Tanchum from Noy: may one extinguish a lamp on Shabbat for a Persian noble?
Rabbi Tanchum rebukes Solomon, pointing out contradictions between Solomon's words and his father David's, and between Solomon's own statements.

items.text: First resolution: David's verse about the dead not praising God
items.text_en: First resolution: David's verse about the dead not praising God
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the first contradiction: David's statement 'The dead do not praise God' means that one should engage in Torah and mitzvot before death, as after death one is free from them. Rabbi Yochanan explains the verse 'Among the dead, free' similarly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that David's verse 'The dead do not praise God' means one should engage in Torah and mitzvot before death, as after death one is free from them.
Rabbi Yochanan supports the resolution by interpreting the verse 'Among the dead, free' to mean that upon death one becomes free from Torah and mitzvot.

items.text: Second resolution: Solomon's praise of the dead
items.text_en: Second resolution: Solomon's praise of the dead
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Solomon's statement 'I praise the dead who have already died' in two ways: first, that when Israel sinned in the desert, Moses' prayers were only answered when he invoked the patriarchs; second, that unlike mortal kings whose decrees are not observed after death, Moses' decrees endure forever.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Solomon praised the dead because when Israel sinned in the desert, Moses' prayers were only answered when he invoked the patriarchs.
The Gemara offers a second explanation: unlike mortal kings whose decrees are not observed after death, Moses' decrees endure forever, so the dead are praiseworthy.

items.text: Third resolution: Solomon's praise of the dead, with the story of David's sin
items.text_en: Third resolution: Solomon's praise of the dead, with the story of David's sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another explanation: Solomon's praise of the dead refers to David. David asked God to forgive his sin and give a sign in his lifetime. God said He would not reveal it in David's life but in Solomon's. When Solomon built the Temple, the gates would not open until he invoked David's merit, proving God had forgiven David. This is why Solomon praised the dead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another explanation of Solomon's praise of the dead, citing a tradition from Rav Yehuda said by Rav.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that David asked God to forgive his sin and give a sign in his lifetime, but God said He would reveal the forgiveness only in Solomon's lifetime.
The narrative recounts that when Solomon built the Temple, the gates would not open until he invoked David's merit, proving God had forgiven David, thus justifying Solomon's praise of the dead.

The Gemara interprets the verse about the eighth day of the Temple dedication, showing that the people's joy included the knowledge that God had forgiven David's sin and also atoned for Israel's sin of Yom Kippur.

items.text: Fourth resolution: Solomon's statement 'a living dog is better than a dead lion'
items.text_en: Fourth resolution: Solomon's statement 'a living dog is better than a dead lion'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Solomon's statement 'a living dog is better than a dead lion' through a story about David. David asked God to know his end, but God refused. He was told he would die on Shabbat. When he asked if he could die on Friday, God said one day of Torah study is better than a thousand offerings Solomon would bring.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Solomon's statement 'a living dog is better than a dead lion' and attributes its explanation to Rav Yehuda citing Rav.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav introduces the verse where David asks God to know his end.
God refuses to reveal David's end or the measure of his days, stating it is a decree not to inform humans.
God tells David he will die on Shabbat and explains that he cannot die on Sunday because Solomon's kingship has already begun and one kingdom does not overlap with another.

When David asks to die on Friday, God responds that one day of Torah study is better than a thousand offerings Solomon will bring, explaining why a living dog (David alive) is better than a dead lion (Solomon's offerings).

items.text: David's death and Solomon's query
items.text_en: David's death and Solomon's query
items.desc_en: The Angel of Death tricks David into stopping his Torah study, causing his death. Solomon asks the Beit Midrash what to do with David's body and the hungry dogs; they reply with halakhic instructions and a homiletic message about the superiority of the soul's 'lamp' over the body's.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes how David studied Torah every Shabbat, and the Angel of Death tricked him into stopping, causing his death.

sub.text: Solomon's query to the Beit Midrash
sub.text_en: Solomon's query to the Beit Midrash
sub.desc_en: Solomon asks the Beit Midrash what to do with David's body exposed to the sun and the hungry dogs.
The Beit Midrash instructs Solomon to cut the carcass for the dogs and to move David's body using a loaf or a child.

The Beit Midrash adds a homiletic message citing Solomon's verse and explaining that the soul's 'lamp' (נר) is superior to the body's, so it is better to let the body be moved for the sake of the divine lamp.

items.text: Why Kohelet was not hidden
items.text_en: Why Kohelet was not hidden
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that the Sages sought to hide Kohelet due to its internal contradictions, but refrained because its beginning and end contain words of Torah. The beginning implies reward for Torah study, and the end commands fear of God.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that the Sages sought to hide Kohelet due to its contradictions, but refrained.
The reason they did not hide it is that its beginning and end contain words of Torah, with interpretations from Bei Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Abba bar Kahana, and Shimon ben Azzai.

items.text: Resolving contradictions in Kohelet
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions in Kohelet
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies two contradictions in Kohelet: between 'anger is better than laughter' and 'I said of laughter, it is mad', and between 'I praised joy' and 'what does joy accomplish'. It resolves them by distinguishing contexts: divine anger at the righteous in this world vs. divine laughter with the righteous in the next, and joy of a mitzvah vs. joy not of a mitzvah. The Shekhinah rests only through joy of a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the internal contradictions in Kohelet are, citing two pairs of verses: 'anger is better than laughter' vs. 'I said of laughter, it is mad', and 'I praised joy' vs. 'what does joy accomplish'.

The Gemara resolves the first contradiction by distinguishing contexts: divine anger at the righteous in this world is better than divine laughter with the wicked in this world, while 'I said of laughter, it is mad' refers to divine laughter with the righteous in the world to come.

The Gemara resolves the second contradiction by distinguishing joy of a mitzvah from joy not of a mitzvah, and teaches that the Shekhinah rests only through joy of a mitzvah, citing a verse and adding that this applies also to halachic discourse and good dreams.

items.text: Joy before Torah study
items.text_en: Joy before Torah study
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: Rav Giddel says a student's lips should drip bitterness, implying seriousness, but the previous teaching required joy. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between before and after the rabbi begins his lecture, citing Raba's practice of opening with a lighthearted remark.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rav Giddel citing Rav said a student's lips should drip bitterness (מר), implying seriousness, but the previous teaching required joy.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the rabbi and the student, or alternatively between before and after the rabbi begins his lecture, citing Raba's practice of opening with a lighthearted remark.

items.text: Contradictions in Mishlei and their resolution
items.text_en: Contradictions in Mishlei and their resolution
items.desc_en: The Sages also sought to hide Mishlei due to contradictions, but reasoned that since they found a resolution for Kohelet, they should examine Mishlei too. The contradiction between 'do not answer a fool according to his folly' and 'answer a fool according to his folly' is resolved: the former applies to worldly matters, the latter to words of Torah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that the Sages also sought to hide the book of Mishlei due to internal contradictions, but decided to examine it as they did with Kohelet.
The gemara asks what the contradiction is, citing the verses 'do not answer a fool according to his folly' and 'answer a fool according to his folly'.
The gemara resolves the contradiction: the first verse applies to worldly matters, the second to words of Torah.

items.text: Examples of answering a fool in worldly matters
items.text_en: Examples of answering a fool in worldly matters
items.desc_en: Two incidents illustrate answering a fool according to his folly: a man claiming Rabbi's wife is his wife and children are his, and another claiming Rabbi Chiyya's mother is his wife. Both are given wine and die. Rabbi Chiyya notes that Rabbi's prayer to be saved from insolent people prevented the man from becoming a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi claiming Rabbi's wife is his and his children are his; Rabbi offers him wine, he drinks and dies.
Another man comes before Rabbi Chiyya claiming his mother is his wife and he is his son; Rabbi Chiyya offers him wine, he drinks and dies.
Rabbi Chiyya explains that Rabbi's prayer to be saved from insolent people prevented the man from becoming a mamzer.

items.text: Examples of answering a fool in matters of Torah
items.text_en: Examples of answering a fool in matters of Torah
items.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel teaches three future miracles: women giving birth daily, trees producing fruit daily, and the land of Israel producing baked goods and silk garments. A student mocks each with 'there is nothing new under the sun'. Rabban Gamliel shows him real-world parallels: a hen, a caper bush, and mushrooms/truffles and a type of silk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for an example of answering a fool in matters of Torah.

sub.text: Story of Rabban Gamliel and the student
sub.text_en: Story of Rabban Gamliel and the student
sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel teaches that women will give birth daily; a student mocks with 'there is nothing new under the sun', and Rabban Gamliel shows him a hen as a real-world parallel.

sub.text: Second story of Rabban Gamliel and the student
sub.text_en: Second story of Rabban Gamliel and the student
sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel teaches that trees will produce fruit daily; the student mocks again, and Rabban Gamliel shows him a caper bush as a parallel.

sub.text: Third story of Rabban Gamliel and the student
sub.text_en: Third story of Rabban Gamliel and the student
sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel teaches that the land of Israel will produce baked goods and silk garments; the student mocks, and Rabban Gamliel shows him mushrooms/truffles and a type of silk as parallels.

items.text: Be humble like Hillel
items.text_en: Be humble like Hillel
items.desc_en: The daf begins a teaching that one should always be humble like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai, introducing a story about two men.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma opens with a teaching that one should always be humble like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai, introducing a story about two men.

items.text: The story of the man who tried to anger Hillel
items.text_en: The story of the man who tried to anger Hillel
items.desc_en: A man bets 400 zuz that he can anger Hillel. He repeatedly interrupts Hillel's preparations for Shabbat with frivolous questions about the physical features of various peoples. Hillel patiently answers each question, and when the man reveals his scheme, Hillel responds that it is worth losing money to maintain his calm.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a story: people made a bet that whoever could anger Hillel would receive 400 zuz, and one man took the challenge on a Friday evening while Hillel was washing his hair.
The man rudely calls Hillel by name and asks why Babylonians have round heads.
Hillel patiently answers that Babylonians have round heads because they lack skilled midwives.
After waiting an hour, the man returns and asks why the eyes of Tadmorites are bleary.
Hillel answers that Tadmorites have bleary eyes because they live among sand dunes.
After another hour, the man asks why Africans have wide feet.
Hillel answers that Africans have wide feet because they live in swamps.
The man expresses fear of angering Hillel, then asks if Hillel is the Nasi of Israel.
Hillel confirms his identity, and when the man laments losing 400 zuz, Hillel replies that it is worth losing even more money to maintain his calm.

items.text: First convert: the gentile who doubted the Oral Torah
items.text_en: First convert: the gentile who doubted the Oral Torah
items.desc_en: A gentile approaches Shammai, asking to be converted on condition that he only learn the Written Torah. Shammai rebukes him. He then goes to Hillel, who converts him and teaches him the alphabet, then reverses the letters the next day, demonstrating that one must rely on oral tradition.

sub.desc_en: A baraita introduces a story: a gentile came before Shammai asking how many Torahs there are.

The gentile asks Shammai how many Torahs there are, and upon hearing there are two (Written and Oral), he says he only believes the Written and asks to be converted on condition of learning only the Written Torah.
Shammai rebukes the gentile and drives him away; the gentile then comes before Hillel.

Hillel converts the gentile and teaches him the alphabet, then reverses the letters the next day, demonstrating that the gentile must rely on Hillel's oral tradition, thereby proving the necessity of the Oral Torah.

items.text: Second convert: the gentile who wanted the entire Torah on one foot
items.text_en: Second convert: the gentile who wanted the entire Torah on one foot
items.desc_en: A gentile asks Shammai to convert him while teaching him the entire Torah while standing on one foot. Shammai pushes him away. He goes to Hillel, who converts him and teaches the golden rule: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. The rest is commentary.

sub.desc_en: Another baraita introduces a second gentile who came before Shammai.
The gentile asks to be converted on condition that Shammai teach him the entire Torah while standing on one foot; Shammai pushes him away with a builder's measuring rod.
Hillel converts the gentile and teaches him the golden rule: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow' — this is the entire Torah; the rest is commentary — go and learn it.

items.text: Third convert: the gentile who wanted to be High Priest
items.text_en: Third convert: the gentile who wanted to be High Priest
items.desc_en: A gentile hears about the priestly garments and decides to convert in order to become High Priest. Shammai rejects him, but Hillel converts him and teaches him that even a king cannot approach the sanctuary. The convert realizes his error, praises Hillel, and the three converts later acknowledge that Shammai's harshness would have driven them away, while Hillel's humility brought them under the wings of the Shekhinah.

sub.desc_en: A gentile hears about the priestly garments and decides to convert to become High Priest; Shammai rejects him, but Hillel converts him.
Hillel teaches the convert that even a king cannot approach the sanctuary, and the convert infers from a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that he, as a convert, certainly cannot become High Priest.

The convert acknowledges his error, praises Hillel, and the three converts together declare that Shammai's harshness would have driven them away while Hillel's humility brought them under the wings of the Shekhinah.

items.text: Resh Lakish's interpretation of a verse about the six orders of Mishnah
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's interpretation of a verse about the six orders of Mishnah
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'And the faith of your times shall be a stronghold of salvations, wisdom and knowledge' as referring to the six orders of the Mishnah: Zeraim, Moed, Nashim, Nezikin, Kodashim, and Taharot. He concludes that despite all this, fear of God is the true treasure.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'And the faith of your times shall be a stronghold of salvations, wisdom and knowledge' as referring to the six orders of the Mishnah, concluding that fear of God is the treasury.

items.text: Rava's teaching on the questions asked in the heavenly court
items.text_en: Rava's teaching on the questions asked in the heavenly court
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that when a person is brought to judgment, they are asked about their honesty, setting fixed times for Torah study, engaging in procreation, hoping for salvation, debating wisdom, and understanding one thing from another. Yet all this is only valid if they have fear of God, which is the essential treasure. A parable illustrates that without the 'kav of chomton' (fear of Heaven), the entire load of wheat (Torah) is worthless.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that when a person is brought to judgment, they are asked a series of questions: whether they conducted business faithfully, fixed times for Torah study, engaged in procreation, hoped for salvation, debated wisdom, and understood one thing from another.

Rava concludes that even with all these, if one has fear of God it is a treasure, but if not, nothing avails, illustrated by a parable of a person who brought a kor (measure) of wheat to the attic but forgot to mix in a kav of חומטון (a preservative), making the wheat worthless.
Rava illustrates with a parable: a person who sends wheat up to the attic without a קַב חוֹמְטוֹן (a preservative measure) is told it would have been better not to bring it up at all.

items.text: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael on mixing chomton
items.text_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael on mixing chomton
items.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael states that one may mix a kav of chomton into a kor of grain without concern, implying that a small amount of fear of Heaven suffices to preserve the whole.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that one may mix a kav of חומטון (a preservative) into a kor of grain without concern, supporting the parable's point that a small amount of fear of God preserves all Torah study.

items.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna on Torah without fear of Heaven
items.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna on Torah without fear of Heaven
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna states that anyone who has Torah but lacks fear of Heaven is like a treasurer who has the inner keys but not the outer keys, and thus cannot enter. This underscores that fear of Heaven is the prerequisite for accessing Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna begins a statement about a person who has Torah but lacks something else, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Fear of heaven as the key to inner wisdom
items.text_en: Fear of heaven as the key to inner wisdom
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares one who has fear of heaven but lacks Torah study to a treasurer who has inner keys but not outer keys—he cannot enter. Rabbi Yannai laments such a person, and Rav Yehuda states that God created the world only for fear of Him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara compares one who has יראת שמים (fear of heaven) but lacks Torah study to a treasurer who has inner keys but not outer keys—he cannot enter.
Rabbi Yannai laments such a person, saying woe to one who has no courtyard yet makes a gate for it.
Rav Yehuda states that God created the world only for יראה (fear) of Him, citing a verse.

items.text: Debate: Fear of heaven vs. Torah scholarship
items.text_en: Debate: Fear of heaven vs. Torah scholarship
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simon and Rabbi Elazar debate whether to rise for Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha because he is a God-fearing man or a Torah scholar. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar prioritized fear of heaven, citing Rabbi Yochanan in his name that God desires only fear of heaven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simon and Rabbi Elazar are sitting; Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha passes by, and one suggests rising for him as a God-fearing man, the other as a Torah scholar.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar was the one who prioritized fear of heaven, citing Rabbi Yochanan in his name that God desires only יראת שמים (fear of heaven).

items.text: The paradox of 'do not be overly wicked'
items.text_en: The paradox of 'do not be overly wicked'
items.desc_en: Rav Ulla interprets the verse 'do not be overly wicked' to mean that one should not be wicked to a great extent, but a little wickedness is acceptable? He answers with a parable: one who ate garlic and smells should not eat more garlic to worsen the smell.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ulla raises a question on the verse 'אל תרשע הרבה' (do not be overly wicked): does it imply that a little wickedness is permitted?
Rav Ulla answers with a parable: one who ate garlic and smells should not eat more garlic to worsen the smell, meaning one should not add sin to sin.

items.text: The wicked are not troubled by death
items.text_en: The wicked are not troubled by death
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Ulla and Rabbah explain verses showing that the wicked are not distressed by death, their hearts are healthy, and they know their path leads to death but have fat on their loins (i.e., they are complacent).

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Ulla interprets the verse 'כי אין חרצובות למותם ובריא אולם' to mean that God laments that the wicked are not distressed by death and their hearts are healthy like a hall.
Rabbah adds that the wicked know their path leads to death but have fat on their loins (complacency), and the verse 'ואחריהם בפיהם ירצו סלה' shows it is not forgetfulness.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's view on extinguishing a lamp on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's view on extinguishing a lamp on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yose's ruling in the Mishnah that one is liable for extinguishing a lamp but not for cutting a wick. Ulla explains that Rabbi Yose follows Rabbi Yehuda and considers 'destroying in order to build' only when building in the same place. Rabbah objects from the Tabernacle, and Ulla distinguishes because the camp moved by God's word. Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Yose follows Rabbi Shimon, and the case involves a wick that needs to be charred, which even Rabbi Shimon admits is a constructive act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna Rabbi Yose follows, noting that if he follows Rabbi Yehuda he should be liable for cutting the wick too, and if he follows Rabbi Shimon he should be exempt for extinguishing the lamp.
Ulla answers that Rabbi Yose follows Rabbi Yehuda but holds that only destroying in order to build in the same place is considered a constructive act, not destroying to build elsewhere.
Rabbah objects that all prohibited labors are derived from the Tabernacle, where the camp dismantled and rebuilt elsewhere, which is destroying to build not in the same place.
Ulla rejects the objection, arguing that since the camp moved by God's word, it is considered as if they were building in the same place.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that Rabbi Yose follows Rabbi Shimon, and the case involves a wick that needs to be charred, which even Rabbi Shimon admits is a constructive act of fixing a vessel.
Rava provides supporting evidence from the Mishnah's wording that the wick is actively made into charcoal, not merely becoming charcoal, confirming Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation.

items.text: Mishnah: Three sins for which women die in childbirth
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three sins for which women die in childbirth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that women die in childbirth for neglecting niddah, challah, and lighting the Shabbat lamp. The Gemara explains that for niddah, since she sinned with her womb, she is punished there. For challah and lighting, a Galilean expounded that God gave a quarter-log of blood and warned about blood (menstruation and challah).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that women die in childbirth for three transgressions: neglect of niddah, challah, and lighting the Shabbat lamp.
The Gemara asks why niddah is singled out as a cause of death in childbirth.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that since she sinned with the chambers of her womb (by neglecting niddah), she is punished in those same chambers.
The Gemara asks what explanation applies to challah and lighting the lamp, which are not bodily sins.

The Galilean preacher, citing Rav Chisda, explains that God gave a quarter-log of blood (the menstrual blood and the challah dough) and warned about blood, so neglecting challah and the lamp (which involves blood-like oil) brings punishment.

items.text: Opening homily on the verse 'Reishit'
items.text_en: Opening homily on the verse 'Reishit'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a homily interpreting the verse 'Reishit' (first) as referring to the first of the harvest (terumah) and the soul as a 'ner' (candle), warning that if one does not observe these, God will take their soul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a homily interpreting the verse 'Reishit' (first) as referring to the first of the harvest (terumah) and the soul as a 'ner' (candle), warning that if one does not observe these, God will take their soul.

items.text: Proverbs on why women die in childbirth
items.text_en: Proverbs on why women die in childbirth
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why women die specifically in childbirth, and various Amoraim offer proverbs: Rava says 'the ox falls, sharpen the knife'; Abaye says 'catch the wild ass with one stick'; Rav Chisda says 'leave the drunkard, he will fall on his own'; Mar Ukva says 'the shepherd is lame and the goats run, at the door of the stick is a word, and at the door of the load is a calculation'; Rav Pappa says 'at the door of the shops there are many brothers and friends, at the door of disgrace there are no brothers or friends'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why women die specifically in childbirth.
Rava offers a proverb: 'the ox falls, sharpen the knife' — implying that when a woman is vulnerable in childbirth, punishment is prepared.
Abaye offers a proverb: 'catch the wild ass with one stick' — meaning that a single sin can bring punishment at a vulnerable time.
Rav Chisda offers a proverb: 'leave the drunkard, he will fall on his own' — implying that the woman's own sins cause her death.

Mar Ukva offers a proverb: 'the shepherd is lame and the goats run, at the door of the stick is a word, and at the door of the load is a calculation' — meaning that when a woman is in childbirth, her sins are scrutinized.

Rav Pappa offers a proverb: 'at the door of the shops there are many brothers and friends, at the door of disgrace there are no brothers or friends' — meaning that in childbirth, a woman faces judgment alone.

items.text: Where men are examined and the bridge
items.text_en: Where men are examined and the bridge
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where men are examined (for punishment), and Resh Lakish answers 'at the time they cross the bridge'. The Gemara clarifies 'a bridge and no more? Rather, say something like a bridge.' It then relates that Rav would not cross a bridge where a gentile sat, lest judgment be decreed on the gentile and Rav be caught with him, while Shmuel would only cross a bridge with a gentile, saying Satan does not rule over two nations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: where are men examined (for punishment)?
Resh Lakish answers: at the time they cross the bridge.
The Gemara objects: a bridge and no more? (i.e., only at a literal bridge?)
The Gemara resolves: rather, say 'something like a bridge' (any dangerous crossing).
Rav would not cross a bridge where a gentile sat, lest judgment be decreed on the gentile and Rav be caught with him.
Shmuel would only cross a bridge with a gentile, saying Satan does not rule over two nations.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's practice and the danger of relying on miracles
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's practice and the danger of relying on miracles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai would check and cross (the bridge), consistent with his view that one should never stand in a dangerous place expecting a miracle, for perhaps a miracle won't happen, and if it does, it deducts from one's merits. Rabbi Chanin cites the verse 'I am unworthy of all the kindnesses and all the truth'. Rabbi Zeira would not go out between palm trees on a hot day.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Yannai would check the bridge before crossing, and notes that this aligns with his own view.
Rabbi Yannai states that one should never stand in a dangerous place expecting a miracle, for perhaps a miracle won't happen, and if it does, it deducts from one's merits.

Rabbi Chanin cites the verse 'קָטֹנְתִּי מִכֹּל הַחֲסָדִים וּמִכׇּל הָאֱמֶת' (I am unworthy of all the kindnesses and all the truth) as a scriptural support for the principle that miracles deduct from merit.
Rabbi Zeira would not go out between palm trees on a hot day, illustrating avoidance of danger.

items.text: Prayer to avoid illness and the verse 'ki yipol hanofel'
items.text_en: Prayer to avoid illness and the verse 'ki yipol hanofel'
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda says one should always pray not to become ill, for if one becomes ill, they are told 'bring merit and be acquitted'. Mar Ukva cites the verse 'ki yipol hanofel mimenu' (when the fallen falls from him) — from him to bring proof. The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that this person was destined to fall from the six days of Creation, but since he didn't fall, the verse calls him 'fallen' — rather, merit is brought about through a worthy person and guilt through a guilty one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda states that one should always pray not to become ill, because if one falls ill, they are told to bring merit and be acquitted.
Mar Ukva cites the verse 'כי יפול הנופל ממנו' (when the fallen falls from him) — from him to bring proof, supporting the idea that illness brings judgment.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the person was destined to fall from the six days of Creation, yet since he did not fall, the verse calls him 'fallen' — rather, merit is brought about through a worthy person and guilt through a guilty one.

items.text: Confession and advocates for a person
items.text_en: Confession and advocates for a person
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: One who is ill and near death is told to confess, as all those executed confess. A person going to market should consider themselves as handed over to a sergeant; if they have a headache, as if put in a collar; if they go to bed and fall, as if brought to the scaffold to be judged. The advocates for a person are repentance and good deeds. Even if 999 angels accuse and one defends, they are saved, as per the verse 'If there is an advocate angel, one out of a thousand, to declare a person's uprightness, then He will be gracious to him and say,

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a person near death is told to confess, and compares stages of life to stages of judgment, concluding that one needs advocates to be saved.
The baraita specifies that repentance and good deeds are a person's advocates, and even a single advocate outweighs 999 accusers, citing the verse about an advocate angel.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili adds that even if 999 of the same angel's aspects accuse and one defends, the person is saved, citing the same verse.

items.text: Three sins for which women die in childbirth
items.text_en: Three sins for which women die in childbirth
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: For three transgressions women die in childbirth. Rabbi Elazar says women die in childbirth (for negligence regarding niddah, challah, and lighting the Shabbat candle). Rabbi Acha says for the sin of washing their children's excrement on Shabbat. And some say for calling the Holy Ark 'Arana'. A baraisa adds that Rabbi Yishmael ben Elazar says amei ha'aretz die for two things: calling the Ark 'Arana' and calling the synagogue 'Beit Am'. Rabbi Yose says three 'devekei mitah' (things that cling to death) were created in woman: niddah, challah, and lighting the candle.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that women die in childbirth for three transgressions.
Rabbi Elazar states that women die in childbirth (for negligence regarding niddah, challah, and lighting the Shabbat candle).
Rabbi Acha adds that women die for washing their children's excrement on Shabbat.
Some say women die for calling the Holy Ark 'Arana'.
A baraisa adds that Rabbi Yishmael ben Elazar says amei ha'aretz die for two things: calling the Ark 'Arana' and calling the synagogue 'Beit Am'.
Rabbi Yose says three 'devekei mitah' (things that cling to death) were created in woman: niddah, challah, and lighting the candle, aligning one with Rabbi Elazar and one with the Sages.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on the essentials of Torah
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on the essentials of Torah
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that the laws of consecrated items, terumot, and ma'asrot are the very body of the Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel declares that the laws of consecrated items, terumot, and ma'asrot are the very body of the Torah.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Nathan and Rabbi on the sin of vows causing death of wife or children
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Nathan and Rabbi on the sin of vows causing death of wife or children
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nathan states that the sin of vows causes a man's wife to die, citing a verse. Rabbi says that the sin of vows causes young children to die, citing a different verse and explaining that 'the work of your hands' refers to children.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nathan states that the sin of vows causes a man's wife to die, citing the verse 'If you have nothing to pay, why should he take your bed from under you?'
Rabbi counters that the sin of vows causes young children to die, citing a different verse and explaining that 'the work of your hands' refers to a man's sons and daughters.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on the sin causing children's death
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on the sin causing children's death
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says children die due to the sin of vows; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says due to neglect of Torah. The Gemara questions the proof for neglect of Torah and offers a verse. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that the verse for vows also implies 'vain matters'. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi heard the opinion from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and retracted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says children die due to the sin of vows; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says due to neglect of Torah.
The Gemara questions: for the opinion of vows, the verse is as stated; but for the opinion of neglect of Torah, what is the scriptural proof?
The Gemara provides the verse: 'In vain I struck your children; they accepted no discipline.'
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that even for the opinion of vows, the same verse implies 'vain matters' (שוא).
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is the same as Rabbi (who earlier said vows cause children's death); how can he now say neglect of Torah?
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi heard the opinion about neglect of Torah from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and retracted his earlier view.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yosei: sin of mezuzah vs. neglect of Torah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yosei: sin of mezuzah vs. neglect of Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yosei disagree: one says children die due to the sin of mezuzah, the other due to neglect of Torah. The Gemara explains that the one who says mezuzah interprets a verse 'before it' but not 'before its face', while the other interprets 'before it and before its face'.

sub.text: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yosei: one says children die due to the sin of mezuzah, the other says due to neglect of Torah.
The Gemara explains the scriptural derivation: for the mezuzah opinion, the verse is interpreted only by what precedes it; for the Torah opinion, by both what precedes and follows.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda: sin of mezuzah vs. sin of tzitzit
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda: sin of mezuzah vs. sin of tzitzit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree: one says children die due to the sin of mezuzah, the other due to the sin of tzitzit. The Gemara provides scriptural support for each view, including a verse from Jeremiah for tzitzit and an alternative interpretation for mezuzah by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak.

sub.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda: one says children die due to the sin of mezuzah, the other says due to the sin of tzitzit.
The Gemara explains the mezuzah opinion: the verse 'write them on the doorposts of your house' is followed by 'so that your days and your children's days may be multiplied.'
The Gemara asks: what is the scriptural basis for the opinion that children die due to the sin of tzitzit?
Rav Kahana (or alternatively Sheila Mari) cites the verse: 'Also in your wings (כנפיך) is found the blood of innocent poor souls.'
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that even for the mezuzah opinion, the same verse implies they made their doorways like a thief's tunnel.

items.text: Reish Lakish's statement on the reward for being careful with tzitzit
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's statement on the reward for being careful with tzitzit
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says that one who is careful with tzitzit merits being served by 2,800 servants, citing a verse from Zechariah about ten men from all languages holding onto the corner of a Jewish man.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that one who is careful with tzitzit merits 2,800 servants, citing the verse about ten men holding the wing (כנף) of a Jewish man.

items.text: Rabbi Nechemya and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yehuda on sins of baseless hatred and challah
items.text_en: Rabbi Nechemya and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yehuda on sins of baseless hatred and challah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemya says that the sin of baseless hatred causes strife, miscarriages, and children's death. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yehuda says that the sin of challah causes no blessing in storage, a curse at the gates, and others eating one's produce, but if they give challah they are blessed.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic lists the sins: hatred, challah, terumah, robbery, judgment, oath, spillage, uncovered wine, and carrion.
Rabbi Nechemya teaches: due to the sin of baseless hatred, strife increases in one's home, his wife miscarries, and his children die young.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yehuda says: due to the sin of challah, there is no blessing in stored grain, and a curse is sent; but if they give challah, they are blessed, as the verse states.

items.text: Sin of neglecting terumot and ma'asrot: heavens withhold rain, famine, and loss
items.text_en: Sin of neglecting terumot and ma'asrot: heavens withhold rain, famine, and loss
items.desc_en: The sin of neglecting terumot and ma'asrot causes the heavens to withhold dew and rain, leading to famine and loss. The Gemara cites a verse and explains it: for things commanded in summer not done, snow waters are taken in winter. If they give, they are blessed, with a verse about opening the heavens.

sub.desc_en: Due to the sin of neglecting terumot and maasrot, the heavens are withheld from bringing dew and rain, prices rise, wages are lost, and people run after sustenance without attaining it.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael explains the verse: because you did not observe the commandments given in summer, the snow waters will be taken from you in winter.
If they give the tithes, they are blessed, as the verse promises that God will open the heavens and pour out blessing until there is no lack.
Rami bar Chama quoting Rav explains 'עד בלי די' (until there is no lack) means until your lips wear out from saying 'enough'.
States that if they give terumot and ma'asrot, they are blessed, citing the verse about opening the heavens.
Asks the meaning of the phrase 'עַד בְּלִי דָי'.
Explains that 'עַד בְּלִי דָי' means until your lips are worn out from saying 'enough'.

items.text: Sin of robbery: the tax collector rises and famine leads to cannibalism
items.text_en: Sin of robbery: the tax collector rises and famine leads to cannibalism
items.desc_en: The sin of robbery causes the tax collector to rise and famine to occur, leading people to eat their own children. The Gemara cites a verse from Amos about cows of Bashan oppressing the poor. Rava comments on the women of Mechoza.

sub.desc_en: Due to the sin of robbery, the tax collector rises, famine occurs, and people eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, as the verse states.
Rava gives an example: like the women of Machoza who oppress the poor.
Rava applies the verse to the wealthy women of Mechoza who oppress the poor.

items.text: Opening: Punishment for eating without working
items.text_en: Opening: Punishment for eating without working
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses describing plagues and famine as punishment for those who eat but do not work, interpreting 'flesh of his arm' as 'flesh of his seed' (children).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing verses that describe plagues and famine as punishment for those who eat without working, interpreting 'flesh of his arm' as 'flesh of his seed' (children).

items.text: Punishment for perversion of justice and Torah neglect
items.text_en: Punishment for perversion of justice and Torah neglect
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists sword, plunder, plague, and famine as punishments for delaying justice, perverting justice, corrupting justice, and neglecting Torah, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists four sins—delaying justice, perverting justice, corrupting justice, and neglecting Torah—and their punishments: sword, plunder, plague, and famine, citing verses.

items.text: Punishment for false oaths and desecration
items.text_en: Punishment for false oaths and desecration
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that for vain oaths, false oaths, desecration of God's name, and desecration of Shabbat, wild beasts multiply, livestock perish, people diminish, and roads become desolate, linking verses through the word 'chillul'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for vain oaths, false oaths, desecration of God's name, and desecration of Shabbat, wild beasts multiply, livestock perish, people diminish, and roads become desolate.
The Gemara cites verses linking the punishment to oaths and desecration through the word 'chillul' (חילול).

items.text: Punishment for bloodshed
items.text_en: Punishment for bloodshed
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that for bloodshed, the Temple is destroyed and the Divine Presence departs from Israel, as derived from a verse about not defiling the land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for the sin of bloodshed, the Temple is destroyed and the Divine Presence departs from Israel, citing a verse about not defiling the land.

items.text: Punishment for forbidden relations, idolatry, and sabbatical years
items.text_en: Punishment for forbidden relations, idolatry, and sabbatical years
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that for forbidden relations, idolatry, and neglect of sabbatical and jubilee years, exile comes to the world, and others dwell in their place, citing verses for each sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for forbidden relations, idolatry, and neglect of sabbatical and jubilee years, exile comes to the world, and others dwell in their place.
The Gemara cites verses from Leviticus regarding punishment for idolatry, including scattering among the nations.
The Gemara cites verses from Leviticus regarding the land enjoying its sabbaths during exile for neglecting sabbatical and jubilee years.

items.text: Punishment for obscene speech
items.text_en: Punishment for obscene speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that for obscene speech, many troubles and harsh decrees arise, young enemies of Israel die, and orphans and widows cry out but are not answered, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for obscene speech (נבלות פה), many troubles and harsh decrees arise, young enemies of Israel die, and orphans and widows cry out but are not answered, citing a verse.

items.text: Gemara's elaboration on obscene speech
items.text_en: Gemara's elaboration on obscene speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'and still His hand is stretched out' with statements from Rabbi Chanan bar Rava, Rabbah bar Sheila quoting Rav Chisda, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, teaching that obscene speech reverses favorable decrees and deepens Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'and still His hand is stretched out' and cites Rabbi Chanan bar Rava's answer that obscene speech reverses favorable decrees to evil.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Sheila quoting Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Sheila quoting Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Sheila in the name of Rav Chisda teaches that one who speaks obscenely has Gehinnom deepened for him, citing the verse 'a deep pit is the mouth of strange women'.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that even one who hears obscene speech and remains silent is punished, citing the verse 'the wrath of God will fall there'.

items.text: Punishment for preparing for sin
items.text_en: Punishment for preparing for sin
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya states that one who prepares himself for sin will have wounds and sores, and is punished with hidrokan (dropsy), as per verses. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that hidrokan is a sign of sin.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya states that one who prepares himself for sin will have wounds and sores, as per the verse 'חבורות פצע תמרוק ברע'.
Rav Oshaya adds that such a person is also punished with hidrokan (dropsy), citing the verse 'ומכות חדרי בטן'.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that hidrokan is a sign of sin.

items.text: Three types of hidrokan
items.text_en: Three types of hidrokan
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that there are three types of hidrokan: one from sin (thick), one from hunger (swollen), and one from sorcery (thin).

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught a baraita introducing the topic of hidrokan (dropsy) and its three types.
The baraita specifies the three types: one from sin (thick), one from hunger (swollen), and one from sorcery (thin).

items.text: Stories of sages afflicted with hidrokan
items.text_en: Stories of sages afflicted with hidrokan
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Shmuel HaKatan, Abaye, and Rava were afflicted with hidrokan, with explanations for each case, including Rava's suffering due to being forced by the Sages to teach against his will.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by recounting that Shmuel HaKatan was afflicted with hidrokan, prayed to God, and was healed.
The Gemara reports that Abaye was afflicted, and Rava explains that Abaye's suffering was due to his self-affliction (asceticism).
The Gemara questions how Rava could be afflicted with hidrokan, given his own statement that more people die from overeating than from starvation.
The Gemara answers that Rava's case is different because the Sages forced him to teach against his will, causing him distress.

items.text: Four signs of sins
items.text_en: Four signs of sins
items.desc_en: The Sages taught four signs: hidrokan for sin, jaundice for baseless hatred, poverty for haughtiness, and askara for evil speech.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach four signs: hidrokan for sin, jaundice for baseless hatred, poverty for haughtiness, and askara for evil speech.

items.text: Introduction to askara
items.text_en: Introduction to askara
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that askara comes to the world, beginning a new discussion on this affliction.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught that askara (croup) comes to the world, introducing the topic of this affliction.

items.text: Opening dispute about the plague's cause
items.text_en: Opening dispute about the plague's cause
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Yosi says the plague comes for evil speech. Rava or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites a verse to support this.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Yosi states that the plague comes because of evil speech (לשון הרע).
Rava (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) cites a verse (Psalms 63:12) to support the connection between the plague and evil speech.

items.text: Clarifying Rabbi Elazar's intent
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabbi Elazar's intent
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether Rabbi Elazar meant the plague is specifically for evil speech or also for other sins. A story from Yavneh is brought where the sages discuss why the plague begins in the intestines and ends in the mouth. Rabbi Yehuda says it is because the mouth completes the speech, Rabbi Elazar says it is because people eat untithed foods, and Rabbi Shimon says it is for neglecting Torah study.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question whether Rabbi Elazar bar Yosi meant the plague is specifically for evil speech or also for other sins.
The Gemara brings a story from Yavneh where the sages discuss why the plague begins in the intestines and ends in the mouth.
Rabbi Yehuda says the plague begins in the intestines and ends in the mouth because the mouth completes the speech.
Rabbi Elazar bar Yosi says the plague is because people eat untithed foods (דברים שאינן מתוקנים).
Rabbi Shimon says the plague is for neglecting Torah study.

items.text: Objection to Rabbi Shimon's answer
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbi Shimon's answer
items.desc_en: The sages object to Rabbi Shimon's claim that the plague is for neglecting Torah study, arguing that women, gentiles, and children also neglect Torah but are not punished in the same way.

sub.desc_en: The sages object to Rabbi Shimon's claim that the plague is for neglecting Torah study, arguing that women, gentiles, and children also neglect Torah but are not punished in the same way.

items.text: Resolution: Children are punished for the generation
items.text_en: Resolution: Children are punished for the generation
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Guryon: when there are righteous people, they are punished for the generation; when there are no righteous, schoolchildren are punished. A verse is cited to support this. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar meant the plague is also for evil speech.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Guryon's principle that when there are righteous people, they are punished for the generation, and when there are none, schoolchildren are punished.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ze'iri citing a verse
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ze'iri citing a verse
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ze'iri cites a verse from Song of Songs to support the principle that children are taken as punishment for the generation.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei also includes evil speech as a cause of the plague.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the danger of speech
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the danger of speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rabbi Yehuda was called 'the chief speaker in every place.' A story is told where Rabbi Yehuda praised the Romans, Rabbi Yosi was silent, and Rabbi Shimon criticized them. Yehuda ben Gerim reported this to the authorities, leading to punishment: Rabbi Yehuda was elevated, Rabbi Yosi exiled, and Rabbi Shimon sentenced to death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda was called 'the chief speaker in every place,' setting up the story.
Rabbi Yehuda praises the Romans for their public works: markets, bridges, and bathhouses.
Rabbi Yosi remains silent, neither praising nor criticizing the Romans.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai objects, arguing that all Roman constructions serve selfish purposes: markets for prostitution, bathhouses for self-indulgence, bridges for tolls.
Yehuda ben Gerim reports the conversation to the Roman authorities.
The Roman authorities issue a decree: Rabbi Yehuda, who praised, is elevated; Rabbi Yosi, who was silent, is exiled to Tzippori; Rabbi Shimon, who criticized, is sentenced to death.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon and his son hide in the cave
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon and his son hide in the cave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon and his son hide in a study hall, then in a cave for twelve years, sustained by a carob tree and spring. They study Torah, and Elijah announces the Caesar's death, ending the decree.

sub.desc_en: The narrator recounts that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his son hid in a study hall, then in a cave for twelve years, sustained by a carob tree and spring, until Elijah announced the Caesar's death.

items.text: Leaving the cave and the lesson about anger
items.text_en: Leaving the cave and the lesson about anger
items.desc_en: Upon leaving, Rabbi Shimon and his son burn people engaged in worldly pursuits. A heavenly voice rebukes them, and they return for twelve months. After another voice permits them to leave, Rabbi Shimon heals his son's injuries, saying they are enough for the world.

sub.desc_en: Upon leaving the cave, Rabbi Shimon and his son see people plowing and sowing, and they burn them with their gaze for abandoning eternal life for temporal pursuits.
A heavenly voice rebukes them for destroying the world and orders them to return to the cave.
They return to the cave for twelve months, reasoning that the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom is twelve months.
A heavenly voice permits them to leave the cave.
Upon leaving, wherever Rabbi Elazar strikes, Rabbi Shimon heals, and Rabbi Shimon tells his son that they are enough for the world.

items.text: The old man with myrtle branches
items.text_en: The old man with myrtle branches
items.desc_en: On Friday evening, they see an old man running with two myrtle branches for Shabbat. He explains one is for 'remember' and one for 'observe.' Rabbi Shimon is comforted by the people's love for mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes that at twilight on Friday evening, Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar saw an old man running with two myrtle branches.
They ask the old man what the myrtle branches are for.
The old man answers that they are for the honor of Shabbat.
They ask why one branch would not suffice.
The old man explains that one branch corresponds to 'remember' and one to 'observe' (the two versions of the fourth commandment).
Rabbi Shimon tells his son to see how beloved the mitzvot are to Israel, and their minds were set at ease.

items.text: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's welcome and the miracle of healing
items.text_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's welcome and the miracle of healing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, Rabbi Shimon's son-in-law, sees his wounds and weeps. Rabbi Shimon explains that his suffering was necessary for his greatness, as he could now answer many questions. He then decides to rectify something.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, Rabbi Shimon's son-in-law, hears of his arrival and goes out to greet him.
Rabbi Pinchas brings Rabbi Shimon to the bathhouse, sees wounds on his body, and weeps over them.
Rabbi Shimon responds that seeing him in this state is fortunate, because without the suffering Rabbi Pinchas would not have found him so learned.

The narrative explains that initially Rabbi Shimon asked questions and Rabbi Pinchas gave twelve answers, but later Rabbi Pinchas asked questions and Rabbi Shimon gave twenty-four answers, showing his growth.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's plan to rectify a place of impurity
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's plan to rectify a place of impurity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon decides to go and rectify something, citing Jacob's arrival at Shechem and the sages' interpretations about establishing coinage, markets, and baths. He asks if there is a place needing rectification due to impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai declares his intention to go and rectify something, citing the miracle of his survival.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of verses and Amoraim
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of verses and Amoraim
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about Jacob's arrival at Shechem and the interpretations of Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan that Jacob established coinage, markets, and baths respectively.
Rabbi Shimon asks if there is a matter that needs rectification.
They tell him there is a place with a doubt of ritual impurity (ספק טומאה) that needs rectification.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the elder
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the elder
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai purifies a place of doubtful impurity, citing Ben Zakkai's precedent. When an elder mentions that Rabbi Shimon himself had purified a cemetery, Rabbi Shimon rebukes him for not objecting at the time and kills him with a glance, then kills Judah ben Gerim for a similar slight.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai purifies a place of doubtful impurity, following Ben Zakkai's precedent, marking firm ground as pure and loose ground as impure.
The elder objects that Rabbi Shimon himself had once purified a cemetery, implying inconsistency.
Rabbi Shimon rebukes the elder for not objecting at the time, kills him with a glance, and then kills Judah ben Gerim for a similar slight.

items.text: Mishnah: Three declarations on erev Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three declarations on erev Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person must say three things in his home on Friday at dusk: 'Have you tithed? Have you made an eruv? Light the lamp.' It then rules that during doubtful twilight one may not tithe definite produce, immerse vessels, or light lamps, but may tithe demai, make an eruv, and cover hot foods.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three things one must say at home on Friday evening at dusk: tithe, eiruv, and light the lamp, and distinguishes between definite and doubtful cases.
The Mishnah rules that during doubtful twilight one may not tithe definite produce, immerse vessels, or light lamps, but may tithe demai, make an eruv, and cover hot foods.

items.text: Gemara: Source and manner of the declarations
items.text_en: Gemara: Source and manner of the declarations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives the three declarations from a verse. Rabbah bar Rav Huna adds that they should be said gently so the household accepts them. Rav Ashi says he did not hear this tradition but inferred it logically.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the scriptural source for these three declarations.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites the verse 'וְיָדַעְתָּ כִּי שָׁלוֹם אָהֳלֶךָ' (and you shall know that your tent is at peace) as the source.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna adds that these three things must be said gently so that they are accepted.
Rav Ashi testifies that he had not heard Rabbah bar Rav Huna's statement but deduced it logically.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah resolved
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah resolved
