items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah first says the declarations are said 'with darkness' (exactly at dusk), implying not during doubtful twilight, but then permits eruv during doubtful twilight. Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav resolves this by distinguishing between eruv techumin (which requires certainty) and eruv chatzeirot (which is permitted during doubt).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: it first says the declarations are said 'with darkness' (exactly at dusk), implying not during doubtful twilight, but then permits eruv during doubtful twilight.
A mnemonic sign is inserted to aid memory of the discussion.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between עירובי תחומין (eruv techumin, which requires certainty) and עירובי חצרות (eruv chatzeirot, which is permitted during doubt).

items.text: Rava's case of two agents and twilight eruv
items.text_en: Rava's case of two agents and twilight eruv
items.desc_en: Rava presents a case where two people ask an agent to make an eruv for them: one before twilight, one during twilight. If the first's eruv is eaten during twilight and the second's after dark, both acquire the eruv. The Gemara questions this, but explains that twilight is a doubt and rabbinic doubts are lenient.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a case: two people ask an agent to make an eiruv for them, one before dusk and one at twilight; both eiruvin are valid.
The Gemara challenges: if twilight is day, only the later one should acquire; if night, only the earlier one should acquire.
The Gemara resolves: twilight is a doubt, and a doubt in rabbinic law is treated leniently, so both eiruvin are valid.

items.text: Rava on covering hot foods after dark
items.text_en: Rava on covering hot foods after dark
items.desc_en: Rava explains why one may not cover hot foods with something that does not add heat after dark: a decree lest one cause the pot to boil. Abaye objects that the same should apply during twilight, but Rava responds that pots are generally already boiling then.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks why the Sages forbade insulating food after dark with a material that does not add heat.
Rava answers: it is a decree lest one come to boil the food on Shabbat.
Abaye objects: if so, the decree should also apply at twilight.
Rava rejects the objection: at twilight, pots are typically still boiling, so there is no concern of reheating.

items.text: Beginning of Rava's next statement
items.text_en: Beginning of Rava's next statement
items.desc_en: The daf ends with the start of another statement by Rava, which is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new statement by Rava, continuing the discussion.

items.text: Reason for the prohibition on insulating with heat-adding materials
items.text_en: Reason for the prohibition on insulating with heat-adding materials
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why one may not insulate food even before twilight with materials that add heat: a decree lest one insulate in hot ashes containing a live coal, and then stoke the coals. Abaye questions this, and the Gemara answers that the decree is lest one stoke the coals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages prohibited insulating food even before twilight with a material that adds heat.
The Gemara answers that it is a decree lest one insulate in hot ashes that contain a live coal.
Abaye objects: why not allow insulating in such ashes, since one could simply not stoke the coals?
The Gemara resolves that the decree is lest one stoke the coals, which would be a Shabbat violation.

items.text: The baraita on twilight and its definitions
items.text_en: The baraita on twilight and its definitions
items.desc_en: A baraita states that twilight is a doubt whether it belongs to day or night, and is treated stringently for both days. It then gives three definitions of twilight: Rabbi Yehuda defines it by the reddening of the eastern sky, Rabbi Nechemya by the time to walk half a mil, and Rabbi Yosi as a blink of an eye.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited defining twilight (בין השמשות) as a doubtful period, with three opinions: Rabbi Yehuda defines it by the reddening of the eastern sky, Rabbi Nechemya by a half-mil walk, and Rabbi Yosi as the blink of an eye.
Rabbi Yehuda defines twilight as the period from sunset until the eastern sky reddens, with specific signs of darkening.
Rabbi Nechemya defines twilight as the time it takes to walk half a mil after sunset.
Rabbi Yosi defines twilight as the blink of an eye, when day and night exchange, and it is impossible to determine precisely.

items.text: Application of the stringency to purity laws
items.text_en: Application of the stringency to purity laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for what halakha the twilight is treated stringently for two days. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers: for impurity, as in the mishna about a zav who sees discharge during twilight, creating doubt about impurity and sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the practical application of the rule that twilight is treated stringently for two days.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua answers that the rule applies to matters of ritual impurity (טומאה), citing a Mishnah about a zav who sees discharges during twilight.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers that the stringency applies to impurity, citing the mishna about a zav who sees discharge during twilight, creating doubt about impurity and sacrifice.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in the baraita
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in the baraita: it first says twilight is from sunset while the east is red, implying that when the lower horizon darkens it is night, but then says that when the lower darkens it is twilight. Rava and Rav Yosef each offer a resolution: Rava rephrases the baraita to include both as twilight, while Rav Yosef rephrases it to distinguish day, twilight, and night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: the first definition implies that when the lower sky darkens it is night, but the second clause calls that same state twilight.

sub.text: Rabbah's resolution in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbah's resolution in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbah, citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, resolves the contradiction by rephrasing the baraita: the reddening period is twilight, the darkening of the lower sky is also twilight, and only when the upper sky matches the lower is it night.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's alternative resolution in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative resolution in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef, also citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, offers a different resolution: the reddening period is day, the darkening of the lower sky is twilight, and the equal darkening is night.

items.text: Dispute over the duration of twilight
items.text_en: Dispute over the duration of twilight
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rava and Rav Yosef follow their own views on the length of twilight: Rava (citing Shmuel) says three-quarters of a mil, while Rav Yosef (citing Shmuel) says two-thirds of a mil. The Gemara clarifies the fractions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the two Amoraim follow their respective positions regarding the duration of twilight.
The Gemara asks: what is the duration of twilight?

sub.text: Rabbah's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbah's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbah, citing Shmuel, states that twilight lasts three-quarters of a mil, clarifying that the phrase 'three parts of a mil' means three quarters.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef, citing Shmuel, states that twilight lasts two-quarters of a mil, i.e., half a mil.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef on the size of dough
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef on the size of dough
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the difference between two measures of a mil (two-thirds of a mil vs. half a mil) and then cites a dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef about the maximum size of a dough (חלתא) that may be moved on Shabbat. Rabbah permits moving a dough of two kor but forbids three, while Rav Yosef permits three and forbids four.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the difference between two-thirds of a mil and half a mil, and answers that the difference is half a danqa.
The Gemara shifts the discussion to the size of a dough (חלתא) that may be moved on Shabbat.
Rabbah rules that a dough of two kor may be moved on Shabbat, but one of three kor is forbidden.
Rav Yosef permits a dough of three kor but forbids one of four kor.

items.text: Abaye's inquiry and support from a baraita
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry and support from a baraita
items.desc_en: Abaye reports that he asked his master (Rabbah) and was not permitted even a two-kor dough, aligning with a Tanna who rules that a basket (כוורת) holding forty se'ah in liquid (two kor in dry) is ritually pure. Abaye deduces that the 'extra bulk' (גודשא) is one-third of the total.

sub.desc_en: Abaye reports that he asked his master (Rabbah) in practice, and even a two-kor dough was not permitted to him.
Abaye cites a baraita about a beehive of straw or reeds that holds forty se'ah (two kor) and is pure, implying that two kor is a significant measure.
Abaye concludes that the heaped measure (גודשא) adds one-third to the capacity.

items.text: Interpretation of 'eastern face' in twilight
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'eastern face' in twilight
items.desc_en: Abaye sees Rava looking westward and questions him based on a baraita that says twilight begins when the eastern face reddens. Rava explains that 'eastern face' does not mean the actual east but the face that reddens the east (i.e., the western sky). An alternative version has Rava seeing Abaye looking eastward and giving the same explanation, with the mnemonic 'כוותא' (a window).

sub.desc_en: Abaye sees Rava looking westward and asks him about the baraita that says 'as long as the eastern face reddens'.
Rava explains that 'eastern face' does not mean the actual eastern horizon, but the face that reddens the east (the western sky).
An alternative version reports that Rava saw Abaye looking eastward and gave the same explanation, with a mnemonic of a window (כוותא).

items.text: Rabbi Nehemya's measure of twilight
items.text_en: Rabbi Nehemya's measure of twilight
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nehemya defines twilight as the time it takes to walk half a mil after sunset. Rabbi Chanina illustrates this measure: one places the sun at the top of Mount Carmel, descends, immerses in the sea, and ascends — that is Rabbi Nehemya's measure.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nehemya says the time between sunset and nightfall is the time to walk half a mil.
Rabbi Chanina provides a practical demonstration: one places the sun at the top of Mount Carmel, descends, immerses in the sea, and ascends — that is Rabbi Nehemya's measure.

items.text: The well of Miriam and a moving spring
items.text_en: The well of Miriam and a moving spring
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya describes how to see the well of Miriam: ascend Mount Carmel and look, seeing something like a sieve in the sea. Rav adds that a moving spring (מעיין המטלטל) is pure, and that is the well of Miriam.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya says that one who wants to see Miriam's well should go to the top of Mount Carmel and see a sieve-like formation in the sea.
Rav adds that a portable spring is pure, and that is Miriam's well.

items.text: Twilight of Rabbi Yehuda for priests' immersion
items.text_en: Twilight of Rabbi Yehuda for priests' immersion
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that during the twilight period according to Rabbi Yehuda, priests may immerse (for purity). The Gemara clarifies that this applies to Rabbi Yosei's view, not Rabbi Yehuda's, because Rabbi Yehuda's twilight is a doubt. The Gemara then explains that the twilight of Rabbi Yosei does not overlap with that of Rabbi Yehuda; rather, Rabbi Yehuda's twilight ends before Rabbi Yosei's begins.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that during Rabbi Yehuda's twilight, priests may immerse for purity.
The Gemara asks: to whose view does this apply? If it is Rabbi Yehuda's own view, his twilight is a doubt, so immersion would be ineffective.
The Gemara answers: the statement refers to Rabbi Yehuda's twilight being used for immersion according to Rabbi Yosei's view.
The Gemara objects: this is obvious! It might have been thought that Rabbi Yosei's twilight overlaps with Rabbi Yehuda's, so the statement teaches that they do not overlap.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yehuda's twilight ends completely before Rabbi Yosei's twilight begins, so there is no overlap.

items.text: Halakhic ruling: Rabbi Yehuda for Shabbat, Rabbi Yosei for terumah
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling: Rabbi Yehuda for Shabbat, Rabbi Yosei for terumah
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda for Shabbat (stringently) and Rabbi Yosei for terumah. The Gemara questions the application for terumah: if it refers to immersion, it is a doubt, so the ruling is clarified.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda for Shabbat and Rabbi Yosei for terumah.
The Gemara accepts that following Rabbi Yehuda for Shabbat is a stringency.
The Gemara asks: but regarding terumah, what is the practical application?
The Gemara asks: if it is for immersion, it is a doubt (and immersion in doubt is not valid).

items.text: Clarification of twilight for terumah
items.text_en: Clarification of twilight for terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier discussion about bein hashemashot applies specifically to terumah consumption, since priests do not eat terumah until Rabbi Yosei's twilight period ends.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier discussion about bein hashemashot (twilight) applies specifically to the consumption of terumah (priestly portion), as priests do not eat terumah until Rabbi Yosei's twilight period ends.

items.text: Definition of twilight by stars
items.text_en: Definition of twilight by stars
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines bein hashemashot as the time when two medium stars appear, with one star indicating day and three indicating night. A baraita supports this, and Rabbi Yosei specifies that the stars are neither large (daytime) nor small (nighttime) but medium.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel a rule for determining twilight: one star visible means it is still day, two stars indicate bein hashemashot (twilight), and three stars mean night.
A baraita (תניא) is cited that supports Shmuel's rule with identical language: one star is day, two stars are twilight, three stars are night.
Rabbi Yosei qualifies the rule: the stars referred to are neither the large ones visible by day nor the tiny ones visible only at night, but intermediate-sized stars.

items.text: Practical ruling for twilight and cloudy days
items.text_en: Practical ruling for twilight and cloudy days
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida states that one who performs labor during two twilight periods is liable for a sin-offering. Rava instructs his servant to light the lamp when the sun is atop palm trees, and for cloudy days, to observe roosters in town or ravens in the field.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida states that one who performs labor during two twilight periods (Friday and Saturday) is liable to bring a חטאת (sin-offering) regardless of which period is actually Shabbat, invoking the principle of ממה נפשך (from whichever side you look).
Rava instructs his attendant, who is not precise in the rabbinic measure of twilight, to light the lamp when the sun is at the top of the palm trees.
The Gemara asks what to do on a cloudy day, and answers: in a settled area, observe the rooster; in the wilderness, observe the crows or ravens.

items.text: Six shofar blasts on Shabbat eve
items.text_en: Six shofar blasts on Shabbat eve
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that six blasts are sounded on Shabbat eve: the first to stop field work, the second to stop city and shop work, and the third for lighting the lamp (Rabbi Natan) or removing tefillin (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi). After a pause, the shofar is sounded with a tekiah, teruah, and tekiah, and then Shabbat begins.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught in a baraita that six blasts (תקיעות) are sounded on Shabbat eve: the first blast is to stop people from working in the fields.
The second blast is to stop work in the city and close shops; the third blast, according to Rabbi Natan, is for lighting the lamp.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says that the third blast is for removing tefillin (phylacteries), not for lighting the lamp.
After the third blast, one waits the time it takes to roast a small fish or to stick bread in the oven, then sounds a תקיעה, תרועה, and תקיעה (tekiah, teruah, tekiah) and then rests (enters Shabbat).

items.text: Critique of Babylonian practice
items.text_en: Critique of Babylonian practice
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel criticizes the Babylonians for sounding only a tekiah and teruah and then ceasing, which would total only five blasts. He explains that they actually sound a tekiah, repeat a tekiah, then a teruah, and cease during the teruah, but this is their ancestral custom.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel laments the practice of the Babylonians, who sound a תקיעה and תרועה and then rest immediately after the תרועה, without the final תקיעה.
The Gemara objects: if they sound a תקיעה and then a תרועה, that would only be five blasts (not six), so the description is inconsistent.
The Gemara corrects: rather, they sound a תקיעה, then repeat a תקיעה and a תרועה, and then rest after the תרועה, and this is their ancestral custom.

items.text: Dispute about the third blast's purpose
items.text_en: Dispute about the third blast's purpose
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches his son Rav Yitzchak that the second blast is for lighting the lamp, but the Gemara notes this aligns with neither Rabbi Natan nor Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. It corrects that the third blast is for lighting, consistent with Rabbi Natan.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching to his son
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching to his son
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda taught his son Rav Yitzchak that the second blast is for lighting the lamp.
The Gemara asks: whose opinion does this follow? It is neither Rabbi Natan's (who says the third blast is for lighting) nor Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's (who says the third blast is for removing tefillin).
The Gemara resolves: rather, Rav Yehuda taught that the third blast is for lighting the lamp, and this follows Rabbi Natan's opinion.

items.text: Detailed description of the blasts' effects
items.text_en: Detailed description of the blasts' effects
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael elaborates on the six blasts: the first stops field work, the second closes shops and removes shutters, the third prompts removal of pots and lighting lamps. After a pause, a final tekiah-teruah-tekiah is sounded, and Shabbat begins.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that six blasts are sounded on Shabbat eve; at the first blast, those in the fields stop plowing, digging, and all field work.
After the first blast, those near the city may not enter until those far away arrive, so that everyone enters together.
At the second blast, the shutters are removed and shops are locked, but hot food and pots remain on the stove.
At the third blast, one removes pots, insulates food, and lights the lamp; then waits the time to roast a small fish or stick bread in the oven, sounds a תקיעה, תרועה, and תקיעה, and then rests.
The third blast prompts removal of pots and lighting of lamps.
After a pause, a final tekiah-teruah-tekiah is sounded, and Shabbat begins.

items.text: Permissibility of lighting after blasts and handling shofar
items.text_en: Permissibility of lighting after blasts and handling shofar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina reports that one may light after the six blasts, as the Sages allowed time for the synagogue attendant to take his shofar home. When challenged that this sets a fixed time, he explains the attendant has a private place on the roof. A baraita states a shofar may be moved but not trumpets; Rav Yosef resolves this by distinguishing individual (usable for drinking water) from communal use.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina reports that one may light after the six blasts, because the Sages allowed time for the synagogue attendant to take his shofar home.
The Gemara objects that this would set a fixed time, which is problematic.
The Gemara answers that the attendant has a private place on the roof, so no fixed time is implied.
A baraita is cited stating that a shofar may be moved but trumpets may not.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between individual use (where a shofar is movable) and communal use (where trumpets are not).
Abaye questions what use an individual would have for a shofar.
The Gemara answers that a shofar is usable for drinking water, so it has a permitted use for an individual.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution regarding moving a shofar
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution regarding moving a shofar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita that allows moving trumpets like a shofar, and resolves the apparent contradiction by attributing the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda and the opposing view to Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Nechemya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita about moving trumpets, asking whether a poor child could use them for drinking.
The Gemara raises a second difficulty: a baraita explicitly permits moving trumpets like a shofar.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda and the opposing view to Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Nechemya.

items.text: Rav Chisda's principle: name swaps after the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's principle: name swaps after the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that three terms changed meaning after the Temple's destruction: 'trumpet' became 'shofar' and vice versa, with practical relevance for the Rosh Hashanah shofar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that after the Temple's destruction, the names 'trumpet' and 'shofar' were swapped, so the baraita's 'shofar' actually refers to trumpets.

items.text: Second swap: 'arava' and 'tzafzafa'
items.text_en: Second swap: 'arava' and 'tzafzafa'
items.desc_en: The second pair of swapped terms is 'arava' (willow) and 'tzafzafa' (a type of willow), with practical relevance for the lulav.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda gives a second example of name-swapping: 'ערבה (willow)' and 'צפצפה (poplar)' were exchanged, affecting the laws of the lulav.
The gemara asks what practical halachic difference this name swap makes.
The gemara answers that the difference matters for the laws of the lulav (the four species taken on Sukkot).

items.text: Third swap: 'patura' and 'paturta'
items.text_en: Third swap: 'patura' and 'paturta'
items.desc_en: The third pair is 'patura' (a type of vessel) and 'paturta' (a small vessel), with practical relevance for sales transactions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda gives a third example: 'פתורה (table)' and 'פתורתא (tray)' were swapped, affecting sales transactions.
The gemara explains that the practical halachic relevance of this name swap is for sales transactions (מקח וממכר).

items.text: Abaye's addition: 'hublila' and 'bei chasei'
items.text_en: Abaye's addition: 'hublila' and 'bei chasei'
items.desc_en: Abaye adds a fourth pair: 'hublila' (a type of cup) and 'bei chasei' (a cup holder), with practical relevance for a needle found in the thickness of a cup holder, determining kosher status.

sub.desc_en: Abaye adds a fourth example: 'הובלילא (a type of vessel)' and 'בי כסי (cup-holder)' were swapped, affecting the kosher status of a needle found in the thickness of a cup-holder.
Abaye explains the practical halachic relevance: a needle found in the thickness of a cup holder determines kosher status based on whether it penetrates from one side or both sides.

items.text: Rav Ashi's addition: 'Bavel' and 'Borsif'
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's addition: 'Bavel' and 'Borsif'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi adds a fifth pair: 'Bavel' (Babylon) and 'Borsif' (a city), though the practical implication is not stated here.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi adds a fifth example: 'בבל (Babylon)' and 'בורסיף (Borsif)' were swapped.

items.text: Transitional link to Gittin
items.text_en: Transitional link to Gittin
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly notes a practical implication of the previous discussion for divorce documents, then transitions to the new chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a practical implication of the previous discussion for divorce documents (גיטי נשים), then transitions to the new chapter.

items.text: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard formula 'hadran alach' marks the end of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך במה מדליקין' (we return to you, 'With what may we kindle').

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the laws of placing cooked food on a stove on Shabbat, distinguishing between fuels and the opinions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding hot water and cooked dishes, as well as taking off and returning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the law of placing cooked food on a stove on Shabbat, distinguishing between fuels and presenting the opinions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding hot water, cooked dishes, and the permissibility of returning pots.

items.text: Gemara's question on the meaning of 'lo yiten'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the meaning of 'lo yiten'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt: does the Mishnah's phrase 'lo yiten' prohibit returning a pot (but allow initial placement), or does it prohibit initial placement (and certainly returning)? It suggests that the first possibility aligns with Chananya's lenient view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does the Mishnah's phrase 'לֹא יִתֵּן' (he shall not place) refer to returning a pot (but placing it initially is permitted), or does it refer to initially placing (שיהוי) such that only with a cleared stove is it permitted, and certainly returning is forbidden?

The Gemara cites a baraita where Hananya rules that any food cooked to the level of בן דרוסאי (Ben Drusai's meal) may be placed on a stove even if it is not cleared of coals or covered with ash, supporting the interpretation that the Mishnah permits initial placement.
The Gemara raises the alternative: perhaps the Mishnah prohibits initial placement, and only allows it if the stove is raked or ash-covered, and certainly prohibits returning.

items.text: Resolution from the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Resolution from the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the doubt by analyzing the Mishnah's clauses: if 'lo yiten' meant returning, the Mishnah would have used consistent language for initial placement and returning. The redundant clauses prove that 'lo yiten' refers to initial placement, and the dispute about returning is separate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the doubt by showing that if 'lo yiten' meant returning, the Mishnah's structure would be redundant, proving it refers to initial placement.
The Gemara elaborates that if the Mishnah discusses leaving (שהייה), the two clauses about placement and returning are consistent and non-redundant.
The Gemara objects that if 'lo yiten' meant returning, the Mishnah's second clause about returning would be entirely redundant, proving the interpretation is wrong.

items.text: First resolution: the Mishnah is about returning, with a missing clause
items.text_en: First resolution: the Mishnah is about returning, with a missing clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah actually deals with returning (להחזיר) and is missing a clause. It reconstructs the Mishnah to include both returning and leaving, and notes that the dispute about returning is only between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah deals with returning (להחזיר) and is missing a clause, then reconstructs it.
The reconstructed Mishnah states that on a stove heated with straw or chaff one may return a dish, but with peat or wood one may not return until scraping or adding ash.
The reconstructed Mishnah adds that for leaving (לשהות) one may leave even without scraping or covering.
The reconstructed Mishnah records the dispute about what may be left: Beit Shammai say hot water but not a cooked dish, Beit Hillel say both.
The Gemara clarifies that the dispute about returning is only between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, not unanimous.

items.text: Proof from Rav's distinction between top and inside
items.text_en: Proof from Rav's distinction between top and inside
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a statement by Rav that the permission to return applies only to the top of the stove, not the inside. This supports the interpretation that the Mishnah is about returning, not leaving, because the distinction between top and inside is relevant only for returning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo quotes Rav that the leniency applies only on top of the stove, not inside it.
The Gemara argues that if the Mishnah deals with returning, the distinction between top and inside makes sense, but if it deals with leaving, the distinction is irrelevant.
The Gemara rejects the objection by explaining that Rabbi Chelbo's statement refers to the end of the Mishnah about returning, not the beginning about leaving.

items.text: Second proof: a baraita about two stoves
items.text_en: Second proof: a baraita about two stoves
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about two adjacent stoves, one cleared and one not, which discusses leaving (שהוי) and returning. The baraita includes a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about whether one may return a pot after removing it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited about two adjacent stoves, one scraped and covered and one not, stating that one may leave food only on the scraped and covered one.
The baraita records the dispute about what may be left: Beit Shammai say nothing, Beit Hillel say hot water but not a cooked dish.
The baraita records that if one removed food, all agree one may not return according to Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Yehuda reports the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about returning.

items.text: Analysis: which Tanna does the baraita follow?
items.text_en: Analysis: which Tanna does the baraita follow?
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita: if the Mishnah is about leaving, the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda; if about returning, it fits neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Meir, as it contradicts both in different ways.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah deals with leaving, it follows Rabbi Yehuda; if it deals with returning, it fits neither Rabbi Meir nor Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara asks: if the Mishnah is about returning (להחזיר), which Tanna does it follow? It fits neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Meir.

The Gemara objects: if it follows Rabbi Meir, it contradicts Beit Shammai in one point and Beit Hillel in two; if it follows Rabbi Yehuda, the issue of a swept and ash-covered stove (גרופה וקטומה) is problematic.

items.text: Second resolution: the Mishnah is about returning, and our Tanna partially agrees with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Second resolution: the Mishnah is about returning, and our Tanna partially agrees with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is about returning, and our Tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point (hot water and cooked food, and taking and returning) but disagrees on another (leaving even without clearing, whereas Rabbi Yehuda requires clearing).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah deals with returning, and our Tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point (hot water and cooked dish, taking and returning) and disagrees on another (leaving without scraping).
The Gemara presents the reconstructed Mishnah: a stove heated with straw or chaff allows returning cooked food, but with peat or wood one may not return until scraping or placing ash.
The Gemara adds that for leaving (לשהות), one may leave even without scraping or covering.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute about what may be left: Beit Shammai says hot water but not cooked food, Beit Hillel says both hot water and cooked food.
The Gemara clarifies that the returning rule is not unanimous but a dispute between Beit Shammai (take but do not return) and Beit Hillel (even return).

The Gemara resolves that our Tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on hot water and cooked food and on taking and returning, but disagrees on leaving: our Tanna permits leaving even without scraping, while Rabbi Yehuda requires scraping.

items.text: New inquiry: may one lean a pot against the stove?
items.text_en: New inquiry: may one lean a pot against the stove?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new question: is it permitted to lean a pot against the stove (but not on top or inside), or is it forbidden like placing it on top or inside?

sub.desc_en: A question is raised: is it permitted to lean a pot against the stove, or is it no different from placing it on top or inside?

items.text: Attempted proof from the baraita about two stoves
items.text_en: Attempted proof from the baraita about two stoves
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the baraita that leaning is permitted, since it allows leaving on a cleared stove even when heat rises from the uncleared one. But it rejects the proof, noting that the elevated stove is exposed to air, which mitigates the heat.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited about two adjacent stoves where one may lean on a scraped stove even though heat rises from the other, but the Gemara deflects that the case is different because the elevated stove is exposed to air.
The Gemara rejects the proof, arguing that the case is different because the elevated stove is exposed to air, which mitigates the heat.

items.text: Proof from Rav Safra's statement and its analysis
items.text_en: Proof from Rav Safra's statement and its analysis
items.desc_en: Rav Safra says that if a stove is covered with ash and the ash has cooled, one may lean a pot against it and keep it there, and also take and return. The Gemara initially tries to infer that leaning is only permitted when covered, but then reinterprets: the mention of 'taking' is for the sake of 'returning', and similarly 'leaning' is for the sake of 'keeping'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra cites Rav Chiyya that if a stove's ash has cooled, one may lean a pot against it and keep it there, and also take from it and return.
The Gemara infers that leaning is only permitted when the ash has cooled, not otherwise.
The Gemara objects that by the same logic, taking would also be limited to when ash has cooled, which is not the case.
The Gemara resolves that 'taking' is mentioned only for the sake of 'returning', and similarly 'leaning' is mentioned only for the sake of 'keeping'.
The Gemara objects that taking and returning are in one place, but leaning and keeping are in different places, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Final resolution: leaning is permitted even without clearing
items.text_en: Final resolution: leaning is permitted even without clearing
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states that one may lean a pot against a stove heated with gevet or wood, but may keep it there only if the stove is cleared or covered. Coals that have dimmed or are covered with fine flax waste are considered covered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the question by citing a baraita: one may lean on a stove heated with peat or wood, but may only keep food on it if scraped and covered; coals that have dimmed or been covered with fine flax waste are considered covered.

The Gemara brings a baraita: One may lean a pot against a stove heated with gevet or wood, but may keep it there only if the stove is cleared or covered; coals that have dimmed or are covered with fine flax waste are considered covered.

items.text: Additional ruling: leaving on a covered stove
items.text_en: Additional ruling: leaving on a covered stove
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani quotes Rav Oshaya: if a stove is covered with ash and the fire has been banked, one may leave on it hot water that has been fully heated and cooked food that has been fully cooked.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani quoting Rav Oshaya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani quoting Rav Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani quotes Rav Oshaya that if the stove is covered and the coals are burning, one may leave fully heated hot water and fully cooked food on it.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference and rejection
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from a previous statement that מצטמק ויפה לו is permitted, but rejects the proof because the case involved crushed coals (קטמה). It then explains that the statement was needed to teach about the removal of coals (הובערה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from a previous statement that a dish that shrinks and improves (מצטמק ויפה לו) is permitted to leave on the stove.
The Gemara rejects the inference, distinguishing the case because it involved crushed coals (קטמה).
The Gemara asks: if so, what novel point does the statement teach?
The Gemara explains that the statement was needed to teach about the removal of coals (הובערה), lest one think the original prohibition returns.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan permits leaving even fully cooked food on a stove with crushed coals, even with רותם coals. The Gemara again infers that מצטמק ויפה לו is permitted, but rejects the proof due to the crushed coals, and explains that the novelty is the allowance of רותם coals.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one may leave hot water and fully cooked food on a stove that has been crushed and cleared of coals, even with coals of broom-plant.
The Gemara again infers that מצטמק ויפה לו (a dish that shrinks and improves) is permitted.
The Gemara rejects the inference, again distinguishing because the stove was crushed (קטמה).
The Gemara asks: if so, what novel point does the statement teach?
The Gemara answers that the statement was needed to teach about the removal of coals (הובערה).
The Gemara objects: this is the same as the previous statement!
The Gemara resolves that the novel point is specifically about coals of broom-plant (גחלים של רותם).

items.text: Rav Sheshet's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet reports that Rabbi Yochanan permits leaving partially cooked food on a stove heated with gevet or wood, but forbids returning a pot unless the stove is swept or covered with ash. He holds that the Mishnah only forbids returning, not leaving (שהייה).

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that on a stove heated with oil-cake or wood, one may leave water that has not fully heated and food that has not fully cooked.
Rav Sheishet rules that if one removed a pot, one may not return it unless the stove is scraped or covered with ash.
Rav Sheishet explains that the Mishnah only prohibits returning (להחזיר), but leaving (לשהות) is permitted even without scraping or covering.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava argues that both laws (שהייה and החזרה) are already taught in the Mishnah: שהייה from the case of bread in the oven, and החזרה from Beit Hillel's ruling that requires a swept or covered stove. Rav Sheshet merely clarifies the Mishnah's implication.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that both rulings (leaving and returning) are already taught in the Mishnah.
Rava cites a Mishnah that one may not put bread in the oven at nightfall unless its face has formed a crust, implying that once it has crusted, leaving it is permitted.
Rava cites that Beit Hillel permit returning only to a scraped and covered stove, not otherwise.
Rava concludes that Rav Sheishet was merely teaching the precise inference from the Mishnah.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's ruling and the dispute with Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's ruling and the dispute with Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports that Rabbi Yochanan permits even מצטמק ויפה לו on a stove heated with gevet or wood. A rabbi objects, citing Rav and Shmuel who forbid it. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda clarifies he is only reporting Rabbi Yochanan's view. Rav Ukva from Meishan advises that those close to Rav and Shmuel should follow them, while others follow Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports that Rabbi Yochanan permits leaving even a dish that improves by simmering (מצטמק ויפה לו) on a stove heated with gevet or wood.
A certain rabbi objects, citing Rav and Shmuel who both forbid a dish that improves by simmering.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda clarifies that he is aware of Rav and Shmuel's prohibition but is only reporting Rabbi Yochanan's permissive view.

sub.text: Rav Ukva from Meishan to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Ukva from Meishan to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Ukva from Meishan advises Rav Ashi that those close to Rav and Shmuel should follow their stringency, while others may follow Rabbi Yochanan's leniency.

items.text: Abaye's inquiry and practical precedents
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry and practical precedents
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether leaving food is permitted. Rav Yosef cites Rav Yehuda's practice, but Abaye distinguishes Rav Yehuda's case due to danger. Rav Yosef then cites Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's practice in Sura. Rav Ashi recalls leaving a cup of הרסנא before Rav Huna, unsure if it was because מצטמק ויפה לו is permitted or because the dish has liquid and is מצטמק ורע לו.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef: what is the law regarding leaving a dish on the stove?
Rav Yosef answers that Rav Yehuda would leave such a dish and eat it.
Abaye objects that Rav Yehuda was ill and thus permitted even on Shabbat; what is the ruling for healthy people like Abaye and Rav Yosef?
Rav Yosef answers that in Sura they leave such dishes, citing Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak as a precedent.

Rav Ashi testifies that he stood before Rav Huna, who left a cup of הרסנא (a fish dish) and ate it, though Rav Ashi is unsure whether it was because מצטמק ויפה לו is permitted or because the dish had liquid and was מצטמק ורע לו (shrinks and worsens).

items.text: Rav Nachman's general rule and exceptions
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's general rule and exceptions
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that מצטמק ויפה לו is forbidden, and מצטמק ורע לו is permitted. He provides a rule: any dish with liquid is מצטמק ורע לו, except for a turnip dish which improves even with liquid. If the dish has meat, it is מצטמק ויפה לו unless guests are expected, in which case it is מצטמק ורע לו. Lentils, porridge, and dates are always מצטמק ורע להם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that a dish that shrinks and improves (מצטמק ויפה לו) is forbidden, while one that shrinks and worsens (מצטמק ורע לו) is permitted.
Rav Nachman states the general rule: any dish with liquid is מצטמק ורע לו (shrinks and worsens), except for a turnip dish (לפתא) which, even with liquid, is מצטמק ויפה לו (shrinks and improves).
Rav Nachman qualifies that this applies only if the dish contains meat; without meat, it is מצטמק ורע לו (shrinks and worsens).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's further qualification about guests
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's further qualification about guests
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman further qualifies that even with meat, if the dish is designated for guests, it is מצטמק ורע לו (shrinks and worsens).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on specific foods
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on specific foods
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that לפדא דייסא (a type of porridge) and dates are מצטמק ורע להם (shrinks and worsens).

items.text: Inquiry from Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
items.text_en: Inquiry from Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
items.desc_en: The Gemara records that a question was asked of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, but the content is not provided in this segment.

sub.text: The question to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: The question to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: A question was asked of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba (the content is not provided in this segment).

items.text: Opening question and initial ruling
items.text_en: Opening question and initial ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case: one forgot a pot on the stove and it cooked on Shabbat. The question is whether the food is permitted. The teacher remains silent, but the next day he rules that one who cooks intentionally may not eat, but one who cooks unintentionally may eat, and adds 'ולא שנא' (and it is no different).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the status of a pot forgotten on the stove that cooked on Shabbat.
The teacher initially remains silent, but the next day rules that one who cooks intentionally may not eat, but one who cooks unintentionally may eat, adding 'ולא שנא' (and it is no different).

items.text: Dispute over the meaning of 'ולא שנא'
items.text_en: Dispute over the meaning of 'ולא שנא'
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain 'ולא שנא' leniently: the intentional cook performed an action, so he may not eat, but the forgetful one did no action, so even if he intended to leave the pot, he may eat. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains it stringently: the intentional cook will not scheme, so he may eat if unintentional, but the forgetful one might scheme, so even if unintentional, he may not eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'ולא שנא' (and it is no different) means.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that 'ולא שנא' permits the food even when the forgetfulness was intentional, since no active cooking act was performed.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'ולא שנא' forbids the food even when the forgetfulness was unintentional, to prevent deliberate evasion.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's positions
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that distinguishes between fully cooked and undercooked foods: for undercooked food, unintentional is permitted, intentional is forbidden; for fully cooked food, both are permitted according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda adds that fully cooked hot water is permitted because further cooking harms it, but fully cooked food is forbidden because further cooking improves it, and he lists examples.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that distinguishes between undercooked and fully cooked foods: for undercooked, unintentional is permitted and intentional is forbidden; for fully cooked, both are permitted according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that fully cooked hot water is permitted because further cooking harms it, but fully cooked food is forbidden because further cooking improves it, listing examples.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita with the dispute
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita with the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita discusses undercooked food. For Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, there is no difficulty: the baraita is before the decree, and his ruling is after the decree. But for Rabbah and Rav Yosef, who are lenient, the baraita's distinction between intentional and unintentional is problematic: if before the decree, the intentional case contradicts them; if after the decree, the unintentional case contradicts them. It remains a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita mentions undercooked food, and questions how this fits with the positions of Rabbah and Rav Yosef versus Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, concluding that it is difficult.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution for Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution for Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: For Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, there is no difficulty: the baraita reflects the situation before the decree, while his ruling applies after the decree.

sub.text: Gemara's objection against Rabbah and Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection against Rabbah and Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: For Rabbah and Rav Yosef, who are lenient, the baraita is problematic: if it is before the decree, the intentional case contradicts them; if after the decree, the unintentional case contradicts them.
The difficulty remains unresolved (קשיא).

items.text: Explanation of the decree
items.text_en: Explanation of the decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the decree: initially, the rule was that an intentional cook may not eat, but a forgetful one may eat. However, when people began intentionally leaving food and claiming forgetfulness, the Sages penalized the forgetful person as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the decree: initially, one who forgot was treated like an unintentional cook, but after people deliberately delayed and claimed forgetfulness, the Sages penalized the forgetful person.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel citing Rabbi Abba citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel citing Rabbi Abba citing Rav Kahana citing Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the decree: initially, the rule was that an intentional cook may not eat, but a forgetful one may eat; however, when people began intentionally leaving food and claiming forgetfulness, the Sages penalized the forgetful person as well.

items.text: Resolving contradictions within Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions within Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes apparent contradictions between Rabbi Meir's statements and between Rabbi Yehuda's statements. It resolves: for Rabbi Meir, one statement is for initially leaving the pot (forbidden), the other is after the fact (permitted). For Rabbi Yehuda, one applies to a swept and covered stove (permitted), the other to an unswept and uncovered stove (forbidden).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an apparent contradiction between Rabbi Meir's statements and between Rabbi Yehuda's statements.

The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Meir's apparent contradiction is between לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and בדיעבד (after the fact); Rabbi Yehuda's is between a swept and covered stove versus one that is not.

items.text: Inquiry about one who transgressed and left food
items.text_en: Inquiry about one who transgressed and left food
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one violated the decree and left food, is it penalized? It brings a story: Rabbi Yosi went to Tzippori and found hot water left on the stove and did not forbid it, but found shriveled eggs and forbade them. The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition was for the following Shabbat, not that Shabbat. It then confirms that shriveled eggs are improved by further cooking, citing a story with Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one who transgressed the decree and left food on the stove is penalized.

sub.text: Shmuel bar Natan citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Shmuel bar Natan citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: A story is brought: Rabbi Yosi went to Tzippori and found hot water left on the stove and did not forbid it, but found shriveled eggs left on the stove and forbade them.
The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition was for the following Shabbat, not that Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Chama bar Chanina citing Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rav Chama bar Chanina citing Rabbi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara confirms that shriveled eggs improve with further cooking, citing a story where Rabbi and Rav Chama bar Chanina ate many such eggs.

items.text: Beginning of a new topic: Beit Hillel's ruling on returning a pot
items.text_en: Beginning of a new topic: Beit Hillel's ruling on returning a pot
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion with Beit Hillel's statement that one may even return a pot to the stove. Rav Sheshet comments on this.

sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel states that one may even return a pot to the stove.
Rav Sheshet begins a comment about the opinion of the one who says something, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Opening story: Rabbi Oshaya's precedent for returning a pot
items.text_en: Opening story: Rabbi Oshaya's precedent for returning a pot
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story where Rabbi Oshaya and others returned a pot to a stove on Shabbat in the presence of Rabbi Chiyya, who did not object, implying that returning a pot is permitted even on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story where Rabbi Oshaya and others returned a pot to a stove on Shabbat in the presence of Rabbi Chiyya, who did not object, implying that returning a pot is permitted even on Shabbat.

items.text: Dispute: returning a pot placed on the ground
items.text_en: Dispute: returning a pot placed on the ground
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika quotes Rabbi Abba quoting Rabbi Taddai that the leniency only applies if the pot is still in hand, but if placed on the ground it is forbidden. Rabbi Ammi rejects this, citing Rabbi Chiyya quoting Rabbi Yochanan that even if placed on the ground it is permitted.

sub.text: Rabbi Zerika's statement in the name of Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Taddai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zerika's statement in the name of Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Taddai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Taddai limits the leniency to when the pot is still in hand, but if placed on the ground it is forbidden.
Rabbi Ammi dismisses Rabbi Taddai's view as a personal stringency and cites Rabbi Chiyya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that even if placed on the ground it is permitted.

items.text: Further dispute and Hezekiah's qualification
items.text_en: Further dispute and Hezekiah's qualification
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi and Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda dispute in the name of Rabbi Elazar: one says only if still in hand, the other says even on the ground. Hezekiah quotes Abaye that the leniency for 'in hand' requires intent to return, implying that on the ground it is forbidden even with intent.

sub.text: Dispute between Rav Dimi and Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Dispute between Rav Dimi and Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Two amoraim dispute in the name of Rabbi Elazar: one says only while still in hand is permitted, on the ground forbidden; the other says even on the ground is permitted.

sub.text: Chizkiyah's resolution in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Chizkiyah's resolution in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah in the name of Abaye qualifies: while in hand is permitted only if he intends to return it, but if not, it is forbidden; on the ground is forbidden even if he intends to return it.

sub.text: Second position (Rav Dimi or Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda)
sub.text_en: Second position (Rav Dimi or Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda)
sub.desc_en: The other says: even if placed on the ground it is permitted.
Hezekiah quotes Abaye that the leniency for 'still in hand' applies only when one intends to return the pot, implying that on the ground it is forbidden even with intent.
The gemara infers that on the ground it is forbidden even with intent to return.

items.text: Alternative version of Hezekiah's statement and unresolved questions
items.text_en: Alternative version of Hezekiah's statement and unresolved questions
items.desc_en: An alternative version of Hezekiah's statement says the prohibition for placing on the ground only applies without intent to return, but with intent it is permitted, implying that in hand it is permitted even without intent. Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Ashi raise unresolved questions about hanging the pot on a stick or placing it on a bed, and about transferring from a hot to a warm place.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version: on the ground is forbidden only if he does not intend to return it, but if he intends to return it, it is permitted; while in hand is always permitted even without intention to return.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks about intermediate cases: if the pot is hung on a stick or placed on a bed, what is the law?
Rav Ashi asks about moving a pot from a hot place to a warm place, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah: rules for tanur and kupaḥ
items.text_en: Mishnah: rules for tanur and kupaḥ
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a tanur (oven) was heated with straw or stubble, one may not place food inside it or on top of it. For a kupaḥ (a small oven), if heated with straw or stubble it is like a kirah (stove), but if heated with geft (olive waste) or wood it is like a tanur.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a furnace (תנור) heated with straw or stubble, one may not place food inside or on top; for a stove (כופח) heated with straw or stubble it is like a range (כירה), but with oil-cake or wood it is like a furnace.

items.text: Gemara: Abaye's objection to Rav Yosef's interpretation
items.text_en: Gemara: Abaye's objection to Rav Yosef's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef thought the Mishnah only prohibits placing food inside or on top of the tanur, but leaning against it is permitted. Abaye objects from the Mishnah's ruling on kupaḥ: if heated with straw it is like a kirah (permitted), but if with wood it is like a tanur (forbidden). This implies that leaning against a tanur is also forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef thought that the Mishnah's prohibition applies only to placing inside or directly on top, but leaning against the furnace is permitted.

Abaye objects from the Mishnah's ruling on a stove (כופח): if heated with straw it is like a range (permitted to lean), but with wood it is like a furnace (forbidden to lean), proving that leaning is indeed prohibited for a furnace.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's resolution and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's resolution and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that the Mishnah deals with a kupaḥ that is swept or covered with ashes (garuf vekatum), and a tanur that is also garuf vekatum. The kupaḥ is like a kirah (permitted) when garuf vekatum, but the tanur is forbidden even when garuf vekatum. A baraita supports Abaye's view that leaning against a tanur is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah explains that the Mishnah deals with a stove that is swept and covered (גרוף וקטום), and the furnace is also swept and covered, yet leaning is forbidden for the furnace but permitted for the range.

A baraita supports Abaye: for a furnace heated with straw, one may not lean against it, and certainly not place on top or inside; for a stove heated with straw, one may lean but not place on top; with wood, one may not lean.

items.text: Rav Acha's question and Rav Ashi's answer about kupaḥ
items.text_en: Rav Acha's question and Rav Ashi's answer about kupaḥ
items.desc_en: Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi: if a kupaḥ is like a kirah, it should be permitted even with wood; if like a tanur, it should be forbidden even with straw. Rav Ashi answers that a kupaḥ has more heat than a kirah but less than a tanur, so its status depends on the fuel.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava questions the distinction: if a stove is like a range, even with wood it should be permitted; if like a furnace, even with straw it should be forbidden.
Rav Ashi answers that a stove's heat is greater than a range's but less than a furnace's, explaining the intermediate ruling.

items.text: Definition of kupaḥ and kirah
items.text_en: Definition of kupaḥ and kirah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina defines a kupaḥ as a place for one pot, a kirah for two pots. Abaye or Rabbi Yirmeya supports this from a Mishnah about impurity: a kirah divided lengthwise is pure, but widthwise is impure; a kupaḥ is pure in both cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definitions of a stove (כופח) and a range (כירה), and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers: a stove holds one pot, a range holds two pots.
Abaye (or Rabbi Yirmeya) supports this from a Mishnah: a range divided lengthwise is impure, widthwise pure; a stove is pure in both cases, confirming the size difference.

sub.text: Abaye or Rabbi Yirmeya's supporting evidence
sub.text_en: Abaye or Rabbi Yirmeya's supporting evidence
sub.desc_en: Abaye or Rabbi Yirmeya cites a Mishnah about impurity to support the definitions: a kirah divided lengthwise is impure, but widthwise is pure; a kupaḥ is pure in both cases.

items.text: Mishnah: prohibition of cooking an egg and heating water
items.text_en: Mishnah: prohibition of cooking an egg and heating water
items.desc_en: The Mishnah forbids placing an egg next to a hot water vessel to cook, or wrapping it in cloths to cook. Rabbi Yosei permits. It also forbids burying an egg in hot sand or dust. It then recounts the incident of the people of Tiberias who brought cold water into a hot spring, and the Sages ruled that on Shabbat it is forbidden for both washing and drinking, on Yom Tov forbidden for washing but permitted for drinking.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of placing an egg next to a hot water vessel or wrapping it in cloths to cook, with Rabbi Yosei permitting, and also forbids burying an egg in hot sand or dust.

The Mishnah recounts the incident of the people of Tiberias who brought cold water into a hot spring, and the Sages ruled that on Shabbat it is forbidden for both washing and drinking, on Yom Tov forbidden for washing but permitted for drinking.

items.text: Gemara: question about gilgel (rolling an egg)
items.text_en: Gemara: question about gilgel (rolling an egg)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one rolled an egg (gilgel) to cook it, what is the law? Rav Yosef says he is liable for a sin-offering. Mar bar Ravina supports this from the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the egg rolled and cooked on its own, what is the law? Rav Yosef answers that one is liable for a sin-offering.
Mar bar Ravina cites a Mishnah to support Rav Yosef's ruling, though the citation is cut off.
Mar bar Ravina supports Rav Yosef's ruling by citing a Mishnah that implies the same conclusion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything that was placed in hot water before Shabbat may be soaked in hot water on Shabbat, but items not pre-cooked may only be rinsed. Exception is old salted fish and Spanish colias, whose rinsing completes their preparation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that items pre-cooked in hot water before Shabbat may be soaked in hot water on Shabbat, while uncooked items may only be rinsed, except for old salted fish and Spanish colias whose rinsing completes their preparation.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rabbi Yosei or the Rabbis, citing a baraita about placing food in a pit or water in the sun, and suggests it might be Rabbi Yosei's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that one may not wrap an egg in a cloth to cook it reflects only Rabbi Yosei's lenient view, not the Sages' stricter position, citing a baraita about placing food in a pit.

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman clarifies that all agree heating directly from the sun is permitted, and from fire is forbidden. The dispute is about derivatives of the sun (e.g., water heated by the sun), where Rabbi Yosei permits and the Rabbis forbid due to a decree against derivatives of fire.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the question by distinguishing three categories: heating by direct sunlight is permitted by all, by fire-substitutes (תולדות האור) is forbidden by all, and the dispute is only about solar-substitutes (תולדות החמה), where Rabbi Yosei permits and the Sages forbid due to a decree.
Rav Nachman continues that all agree heating from derivatives of fire (תולדות האור) is forbidden.

Rav Nachman concludes that the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis is specifically about derivatives of the sun (תולדות החמה): one master (the Rabbis) decrees them forbidden due to a גזירה (decree) against derivatives of fire, while the other master (Rabbi Yosei) does not decree.

items.text: Debate on burying in sand
items.text_en: Debate on burying in sand
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yosei does not dispute the ruling against burying an egg in sand. Rabba says it is a decree lest one bury in hot ashes, while Rav Yosef says it is because one moves dirt from its place. The difference between them is loose dirt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yosei does not also dispute the Mishnah's prohibition of burying an egg in hot sand, and records two explanations: Rabbah says it is a decree lest one bury it in hot coals, and Rav Yosef says it is because one moves earth from its place.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations, and answers that the difference is loose, powdery earth which does not involve moving earth from its place.
Rav Yosef answers that the prohibition is because one moves dirt from its place (מזיז עפר ממקומו).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations.
The Gemara resolves that the difference between them is loose dirt (עפר תיחוח), which is not subject to the decree of moving dirt but might still be forbidden under Rabba's decree.

items.text: Challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits rolling an egg on a hot roof but not on hot lime. This challenges Rav Yosef's reason (moving dirt), since a roof has no dirt, but supports Rabba's reason (decree of hot ashes).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits rolling an egg on a hot roof but not on hot lime, and resolves that for the explanation of moving earth, a typical roof has no earth, so there is no decree.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita supports Rabba's reason (decree of hot ashes) since a typical roof has no dirt, so there is no concern of moving dirt.

items.text: Challenge from the Tiberias incident
items.text_en: Challenge from the Tiberias incident
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings the incident of the people of Tiberias who brought cold water through a channel of hot water, which the Sages forbade. This challenges Rav Yosef's reason, as it involves moving water, not dirt, but fits Rabba's reason of a decree against hot ashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from the incident of the people of Tiberias who brought cold water through a hot water channel, and questions how the explanation of moving earth applies to that case.

items.text: Resolution of the Tiberias incident
items.text_en: Resolution of the Tiberias incident
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tiberias incident relates to the first clause about wrapping in cloth, not the sand clause. The Rabbis argued it was a derivative of the sun, but Rabbi Yosei countered it was a derivative of fire, as the water passed by the entrance of Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Tiberias incident is not about the end of the Mishnah (burying in sand) but about the beginning (wrapping in cloth), and the Sages forbade it because the water was heated by fire-substitutes (תולדות האור), as it passed the entrance of Gehinnom.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis argued to Rabbi Yosei that the Tiberias incident involved a derivative of the sun (תולדות חמה) and was forbidden.
Rabbi Yosei countered that the Tiberias water was a derivative of fire (תולדות אור), as it passed by the entrance of Gehinnom.

items.text: Introduction of Rav Chisda's statement
items.text_en: Introduction of Rav Chisda's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda begins to speak, likely continuing the discussion, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda begins a new statement, which will be elaborated in the following segments.

items.text: Opening story and Ulla's ruling
items.text_en: Opening story and Ulla's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the incident of the people of Tiberias who heated water on Shabbat and were prohibited by the Sages, establishing that insulation with something that adds heat is forbidden even from before Shabbat. Ulla rules like the people of Tiberias, but Rav Nachman dismisses this, saying they have already broken their pipes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the incident of the people of Tiberias who heated water on Shabbat and were prohibited by the Sages, establishing that insulation with something that adds heat is forbidden even from before Shabbat.
Ulla rules like the people of Tiberias, that the prohibition applies.
Rav Nachman dismisses Ulla's ruling, saying the people of Tiberias have already broken their pipes (i.e., their practice is rejected).

items.text: Question about the nature of the bathing
items.text_en: Question about the nature of the bathing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what type of bathing the people of Tiberias did, suggesting it might be full-body bathing. It then notes that if the water was heated before Shabbat, it should be permitted, but a baraita states that one may only wash face, hands, and feet with such water, not the whole body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of bathing the people of Tiberias did, suggesting it might be full-body bathing.
The Gemara objects that if the water was heated before Shabbat, it should be permitted for full-body bathing.
A baraita is cited stating that with water heated before Shabbat, one may only wash face, hands, and feet, not the whole body.

items.text: Comparison with Yom Tov and Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Comparison with Yom Tov and Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the continuation of the baraita regarding Yom Tov, which states that water heated on Yom Tov is forbidden for bathing but permitted for drinking. This suggests the baraita follows Beit Shammai, who require water to be fit for drinking before heating for the feet, unlike Beit Hillel who permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points to the baraita's continuation about Yom Tov, which states that water heated on Yom Tov is forbidden for bathing but permitted for drinking.
The Gemara infers that the baraita must follow Beit Shammai, who require water to be fit for drinking before heating for the feet, unlike Beit Hillel who permit it.

items.text: Resolution: the case of pouring over the body
items.text_en: Resolution: the case of pouring over the body
items.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Chananya explains that the baraita deals with pouring water over the entire body (הִשְׁתַּטְּפוּת), not immersion. He cites a dispute between Rabbi Meir (who forbids), Rabbi Shimon (who permits), and Rabbi Yehuda (who forbids hot water but permits cold).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ika bar Chananya resolves the earlier difficulty by explaining that the baraita deals with pouring water over the entire body (הִשְׁתַּטְּפוּת), not immersion, and cites the dispute among Rabbi Meir (forbids both), Rabbi Shimon (permits both), and Rabbi Yehuda (forbids hot but permits cold).

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction and correction
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction and correction
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda initially states that the dispute applies only to a vessel, but in a spring (קרקע) all agree it is permitted. The Gemara objects that the Tiberias incident involved a spring and the Sages prohibited it. Rav Chisda then corrects himself, saying the dispute is about a spring, but in a vessel all agree it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yehuda applies only to a vessel (כלי), but regarding a spring (קרקע) all agree it is permitted.
The Gemara objects that the incident of the people of Tiberias involved a spring (קרקע), yet the Sages prohibited it, contradicting Rav Chisda's claim.
Rav Chisda corrects himself, stating that the dispute is actually about a spring (קרקע), but regarding a vessel (כלי) all agree it is forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the general principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the general principle
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled like Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Yosef asks whether this was heard explicitly or inferred from a general rule. The Gemara then cites a principle from Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Yannai: wherever there are two disputants and one who decides, the law follows the decider, except in the case of leniencies of matlaniot (a specific dispute).

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Yosef asks whether Rabbi Yochanan's ruling was heard explicitly (בפירוש) or inferred from a general rule (מכללא).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the general rule
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the general rule
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the general rule: wherever there are two disputants and one who decides (מכריע), the הלכה follows the decider, except in the leniencies of matlaniot (קולי מטלניות), where even though Rabbi Eliezer is stringent, Rabbi Yehoshua is lenient, and Rabbi Akiva decides, the law does not follow the decider because Rabbi Akiva is a student.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva retracts and clarifies his source
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva retracts and clarifies his source
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva retracts his position before Rabbi Yehoshua, who clarifies that his ruling was explicitly heard as a tradition, not derived from a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva retracts his position before Rabbi Yehoshua, who clarifies that his ruling was explicitly heard as a tradition, not derived from a mishnah.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on bathing in pre-heated water
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on bathing in pre-heated water
items.desc_en: Rav permits bathing the entire body limb by limb, while Shmuel restricts to face, hands, and feet. A baraita supports Shmuel, but Rav deflects by interpreting 'not all his body' as not at once, and 'face, hands, and feet' as similar to those limbs.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the dispute: Rav permits bathing the entire body limb by limb in water heated before Shabbat, while Shmuel restricts to face, hands, and feet.
The gemara cites a baraita that explicitly permits only face, hands, and feet, contradicting Rav's lenient position.
Rav deflects the objection by interpreting 'not all his body' in the baraita as meaning not all at once, but limb by limb is permitted.
The gemara objects that the baraita explicitly lists only face, hands, and feet, not the entire body limb by limb.
Rav answers that the baraita means bathing limbs similar in size to face, hands, and feet, not literally only those limbs.

items.text: Baraita supports Shmuel; Rabba's version of Rav's ruling is refuted
items.text_en: Baraita supports Shmuel; Rabba's version of Rav's ruling is refuted
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly supports Shmuel, prohibiting even limb-by-limb bathing. Rabba taught Rav's ruling in a different version (leaving one limb unwashed), but all refutations are brought against it, concluding it is refuted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Shmuel, explicitly forbidding bathing the whole body even limb by limb, and certainly water heated on Yom Tov.

Rabbah transmits Rav's ruling in a different version: one bathes the whole body but leaves one limb unwashed; the gemara notes that all the refutations apply to this version as well, concluding it is a refutation.
All the previous refutations are brought against Rabba's version, concluding that it is refuted.

items.text: Rav Yosef questions whether Rabba followed Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Yosef questions whether Rabba followed Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Abaye if Rabba acted according to Rav's ruling. Abaye reasons that since Rav's ruling was refuted, Rabba likely did not follow it, unless he was unaware of the refutation. Abaye notes that Mar (Rabba) generally followed Rav except in three leniencies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Abaye whether Rabba acted in accordance with Rav's ruling.
Abaye first says he does not know, then reasons that Rabba likely did not follow Rav because Rav's ruling was refuted.
Abaye raises the possibility that Rabba was unaware of the refutation, in which case he would have followed Rav.
Abaye cites the general rule that Mar (Rabba) followed Rav in all matters except three leniencies where he followed Shmuel, and that he followed Rav's stringencies but not his leniencies.

items.text: Bathhouse regulations for Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.text_en: Bathhouse regulations for Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that if a bathhouse's drains were sealed before Shabbat, one may bathe immediately after Shabbat; if sealed before Yom Tov, one may enter and sweat and then rinse in the outer room. A story about Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva illustrates this, with the sages permitting even without boards covering the hot water, until transgressors increased and restrictions were imposed.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that if a bathhouse's drains were sealed before Shabbat, one may bathe immediately after Shabbat; if sealed before Yom Tov, one may enter and sweat and then rinse in the outer room.

Rabbi Yehuda relates a story about Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva who acted in accordance with the baraita, and the sages initially permitted even without boards covering the hot water, until transgressors increased and restrictions were imposed.
The baraita adds that one may walk in the bathhouses of large cities without concern.

items.text: Historical account of decrees due to transgressors
items.text_en: Historical account of decrees due to transgressors
