items.text_en: Levi bar Shmuel's question about reassembling a Tarsian bed
items.desc_en: Levi bar Shmuel finds Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya at the entrance of Rav Huna's house and asks about reassembling a Tarsian bed on Shabbat. They say it is fine. He then brings the matter before Rav Yehuda, who says that Rav and Shmuel both rule that one who reassembles such a bed is liable for a sin-offering.

sub.text: Levi bar Shmuel's question to Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya
sub.text_en: Levi bar Shmuel's question to Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya
sub.desc_en: Levi bar Shmuel finds Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya at the entrance of Rav Huna's house and asks whether one may reassemble a bed of Tarsians on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya's answer
sub.desc_en: They answer that it is permissible (שפיר דמי).
Levi bar Shmuel brings the matter before Rav Yehuda, who objects that both Rav and Shmuel say that reassembling a bed of Tarsians on Shabbat incurs a sin-offering (חטאת).

items.text: Supporting baraitot and tannaitic opinions
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot and tannaitic opinions
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita: one who reassembles a candelabrum on Shabbat is liable; a plasterer's pole is forbidden but exempt; Rabbi Simai distinguishes between a round horn (liable) and a straight horn (exempt). The Gemara notes that these opinions align with a baraita about bed frames, legs, and boards of a bed, which are forbidden but exempt.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: reassembling a lamp stand incurs a sin-offering; a plasterer's rod is forbidden but exempt; Rabbi Simai distinguishes between a round horn (liable) and a straight horn (exempt).
The Gemara resolves that Rav and Shmuel's ruling aligns with the Tanna who says that bed frames, legs, and boards of a bed of Tarsians are forbidden to reassemble but exempt from a sin-offering.
Rabbi Simai distinguishes: a round horn is liable, a straight horn is exempt.
The Gemara notes that the earlier opinions align with a baraita about bed frames, legs, and boards, which are forbidden but exempt.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara on a movable bed
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara on a movable bed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not insert a wedge into a hole, but if one did, he is liable. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits if it is loose. The Gemara recounts an incident with a movable bed on a festival, where Rava follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient view.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition against inserting a wedge into a hole, with liability for doing so, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient position if the wedge is loose.
The Gemara recounts an incident with a movable bed on a festival, where a Sage questions Rava's leniency, and Rava justifies his position by citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling.

items.text: Mishnah: Placing a vessel under a lamp to catch sparks
items.text_en: Mishnah: Placing a vessel under a lamp to catch sparks
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits placing a vessel under a lamp to catch sparks on Shabbat, but forbids putting water in it because that would extinguish the sparks. The Gemara questions whether this nullifies the vessel's designated use, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers that sparks have no substance.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah permits placing a vessel under a lamp to catch sparks on Shabbat, but forbids putting water in it because that would extinguish the sparks.
The Gemara questions whether placing the vessel under the lamp nullifies its designated use (בטול כלי מהיכנו).
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers that sparks have no substance (ממש), so the vessel is not considered designated for them.

items.text: Gemara: The prohibition of adding water and Rabbi Yosei's view
items.text_en: Gemara: The prohibition of adding water and Rabbi Yosei's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rabbi Yosei, who forbids causing extinguishment. It then distinguishes between Shabbat and erev Shabbat, concluding with Rav Ashi's explanation that even the Rabbis would forbid because it hastens extinguishment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's anonymous ruling aligns with Rabbi Yosei, who forbids causing extinguishment (גורם לכיבוי).
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei's prohibition applies only on Shabbat itself, not on erev Shabbat.
A baraita is cited showing that the Mishnah's ruling about not adding water applies on erev Shabbat, not Shabbat, contradicting the assumption that it follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Ashi resolves that even the Rabbis would forbid adding water on erev Shabbat because it hastens the extinguishment (מקרב את כיבויו), distinguishing this case from general causation.

items.text: Mishnah: Materials for insulating food
items.text_en: Mishnah: Materials for insulating food
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists materials that may not be used for insulating food on Shabbat, such as gevet, manure, salt, lime, and sand, whether wet or dry. It also lists materials like straw, grape pits, wool, and grass that are forbidden when wet but permitted when dry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking what materials may be used for insulating food on Shabbat, and lists forbidden materials (gevet, manure, salt, lime, sand) whether wet or dry.
The Mishnah adds that straw, grape pits, wool, and grass are forbidden when wet but permitted when dry.

items.text: Gemara: Inquiry about the type of gevet
items.text_en: Gemara: Inquiry about the type of gevet
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's gevet refers to olive gevet (which is worse) or sesame gevet. Rabbi Zeira cites a tradition that a basket placed on olive gevet is forbidden, implying olive gevet is the subject. The Gemara then suggests that both types are forbidden for insulation, but the tradition specifically addresses placing a basket on it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's גֶּפֶת (olive waste) refers specifically to olive gevet (which is worse) or to sesame gevet (which is better), and whether the latter would be permitted.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing a Sage from the school of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing a Sage from the school of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a tradition that a basket placed on olive gevet is forbidden, implying that the Mishnah's gevet is specifically olive gevet.
The Gemara resolves that both types of gevet are forbidden for insulation, but the tradition specifically addresses placing a basket on it, not the general insulation rule.

items.text: Opening distinction between olive and sesame waste
items.text_en: Opening distinction between olive and sesame waste
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens by distinguishing between olive waste, which generates heat, and sesame waste, which does not, setting the stage for the discussion of insulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by distinguishing between olive waste, which generates heat (הבלא), and sesame waste, which does not, setting the stage for the discussion of insulation.

items.text: Stories of Rabba and Rabbi Zeira about heat generation
items.text_en: Stories of Rabba and Rabbi Zeira about heat generation
items.desc_en: Rabba and Rabbi Zeira visit the Exilarch's house. Rabba rebukes a servant for placing a water jug on a kettle, and later for placing a cloth over a pot with a bowl on top. Rabbi Zeira questions the rulings, and Rabba explains the distinctions between merely retaining heat and generating it, and between cases where one is particular about the cloth or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that Rabba and Rabbi Zeira visited the Exilarch's house; Rabba rebuked a servant for placing a water jug on a kettle.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabba why this case differs from the permitted case of placing a hot vessel on another hot vessel.
Rabba answers that there the vessel merely retains heat, while here the water jug generates new heat.
The Gemara narrates that Rabba again rebuked a servant for placing a cloth over a pot and a bowl on top.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabba why this action is prohibited.
Rabba tells Rabbi Zeira to wait and see; later the servant is seen wringing the cloth, showing it was used as a cover.
Rabbi Zeira asks why this case differs from the permitted case of a cloth used as a pot holder (פרונקא).
Rabba answers that there one is not particular about the cloth, but here one is particular, making it a vessel.

items.text: Question about moving מוכין used for insulation
items.text_en: Question about moving מוכין used for insulation
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Masna asks Abaye whether one may move wool (מוכין) that was used for insulation on Shabbat. Abaye responds with a rhetorical question, implying that if one has no straw, does that permit moving the wool?

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Masna asks Abaye whether one may move wool (מוכין) that was used for insulation on Shabbat.
Abaye responds with a rhetorical question, implying that if one has no straw, does that permit moving the wool?

items.text: Support and clarification from a baraita
items.text_en: Support and clarification from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that says one may insulate with wool but may not move it. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to wool that was not used for insulation; if it was used, it may be moved. The Gemara then explains that the baraita teaches that even though the wool could be used for sitting, it is still prohibited to move it if not designated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that permits insulating with wool fleeces and wool wads but prohibits moving them on Shabbat.
The Gemara rejects the support by clarifying that the baraita refers to wool that was not used for insulation; if it was used, it may be moved.
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that even though the wool could be used for sitting, it is still prohibited to move it if not designated for insulation.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling and objection regarding returning wool to a pillow
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling and objection regarding returning wool to a pillow
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda permitted returning wool to a pillow on Shabbat. Rav Chanan bar Chisda objected with a baraita that forbids placing wool into a pillow on Shabbat. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between new wool (which is forbidden) and old wool (which is permitted).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda permitted returning wool to a pillow on Shabbat.
Rav Chanan bar Chisda objected by citing a baraita that forbids placing wool into a pillow on Yom Tov and certainly on Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between new wool (forbidden) and old wool (permitted).

items.text: Supporting baraita for the distinction
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for the distinction
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly states that one may not place wool into a pillow on Yom Tov, and certainly not on Shabbat, but if the wool fell out, one may return it on Shabbat. This supports the distinction between new and old wool.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the distinction: One may not put wool-combings into a pillow on Yom Tov, and certainly not on Shabbat; but if they fell out, one may return them on Shabbat, and certainly on Yom Tov.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling and Rav Kahana's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling and Rav Kahana's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that one who opens a neck-hole (בית הצואר) on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering. Rav Kahana objects to this ruling, setting up a further discussion.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav that one who opens a neck-hole (בית הצואר) on Shabbat is liable to bring a sin-offering.
Rav Kahana objects to Rav Yehuda's ruling, setting up a further discussion.

items.text: Rava's distinction between a lid and a stopper
items.text_en: Rava's distinction between a lid and a stopper
items.desc_en: Rava explains the difference between a lid of a barrel (which is not a connection) and a stopper (which is a connection) based on the concept of חיבור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the difference between this (a lid) and a barrel stopper (מגופת חבית).
Rava answers that this (the stopper) is a connection (חיבור), and that (the lid) is not a connection.

items.text: Contradiction between two sources on חיבור
items.text_en: Contradiction between two sources on חיבור
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya raises a contradiction: one source says a washer's line and key chain are connected for impurity even when not in use, while another says a handle is only connected during work.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya raises a contradiction: a baraita states that a washer's line and key chain are connected for impurity even when not in use, implying חיבור (connection) applies outside work time.
Rabbi Yirmeya cites a contradictory source: a handle attached to an axe is connected for impurity only during work, not when not in use.

Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction: the axe handle is discarded when not in use, so it is not considered connected, but the washer's line and key chain are kept clean and thus remain connected even when not in use.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction: in the case of the handle, it is not connected when not in use because one might discard it, but the washer's line remains useful even when not in use to prevent soiling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the handle, which is discarded when not in use, from the washer's line, which remains useful to prevent soiling.

items.text: Question about the Tanna of the principle
items.text_en: Question about the Tanna of the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna behind the principle that anything attached to a vessel is considered like the vessel itself, citing different traditions from Sura and Pumbedita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna behind the principle that anything attached to a vessel is considered like the vessel itself, noting that the tradition is attributed to Rav Chisda in Sura and to Rav Kahana or Rava in Pumbedita.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Meir, citing a Mishnah about a stove's compartments that are susceptible to impurity by touch but not by air, according to Rabbi Meir.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Meir, citing a Mishnah about a stove's compartments that are susceptible to impurity by touch but not by air, according to Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Shimon declares them pure.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Meir's logic: if the compartments are like the stove, they should be impure by air; if not, they should be pure by touch. The answer is that the Sages made a distinction to prevent burning terumah and kodashim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Meir's logic: if the compartments are like the stove, they should be impure by air; if not, they should be pure even by touch.
The Gemara answers that the compartments are not like the stove, but the Sages decreed impurity by touch; the objection is raised that if they decreed, they should have decreed even by air.
The Gemara resolves that the Sages made a distinction (הכירא) so that one would not come to burn terumah and kodashim on them.

items.text: Baraita on scissors and scalpel
items.text_en: Baraita on scissors and scalpel
items.desc_en: A Baraita states that a barber's scissors and a surgeon's scalpel are connected for impurity but not for sprinkling. Rava explains that by Torah law, during work they are connected for both, but not during work they are connected for neither.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that a barber's scissors and a surgeon's scalpel are connected for impurity but not for sprinkling.
The gemara objects: if the tools are connected, they should be connected for sprinkling too; if not, they should not be connected for impurity either.
Rava resolves: by Torah law, during work they are connected for both impurity and sprinkling, but not during work they are connected for neither.

items.text: Gemara's question about 'moist' materials
items.text_en: Gemara's question about 'moist' materials
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the meaning of 'moist' in the context of insulating materials: does it mean moist from their own moisture or from an external source?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about whether 'moist' in the context of insulating materials means moist from their own moisture or from an external source.

The Gemara cites a baraita listing materials that are not used for insulation when moist, and argues that if 'moist' means from an external source, the list works, but if from their own moisture, one must explain how wool (מוכין) can be moist from itself—by sweat between the thighs.

The Gemara cites Rabbi Oshaya's baraita that one may insulate with dry clothing or dry fruit but not with moist ones, and again explains that moist clothing from its own moisture can only be found by sweat between the thighs.
The Mishnah is cited, stating that one may insulate with clothing, fruit, dove wings, sawdust, and fine flax waste, and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits the fine waste but permits the coarse.

items.text: Resolution from the Mishnah's list
items.text_en: Resolution from the Mishnah's list
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the question by citing the Mishnah's list of forbidden materials when moist. It argues that if 'moist from themselves' is meant, then 'moist wool-combings' would be impossible to find, so it must mean moist from an external source. The Gemara answers that wool-combings can be moist from themselves due to sweat from the armpits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's list of forbidden materials when moist and argues that if 'moist from themselves' is meant, moist wool-combings would be impossible to find.
The Gemara answers that wool-combings can be moist from themselves due to sweat from the armpits.

items.text: Support from Rabbi Oshaya's baraita
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Oshaya's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita of Rabbi Oshaya that forbids insulating with moist clothing or moist fruit, and asks how moist clothing can be found if not from an external source. The answer is again from sweat between the armpits.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Oshaya's baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Oshaya's baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Oshaya that permits insulating with dry clothing and dry fruit but forbids moist clothing and moist fruit.
The Gemara asks how one can find moist clothing that is moist from its own moisture, as opposed to external moisture.
The Gemara answers that the moistness comes from sweat between the armpits (מרטא דביני אטמי).

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted insulating materials
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted insulating materials
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permitted insulating materials: clothing, fruit, dove wings, wood shavings, and fine flax waste. Rabbi Yehuda forbids fine flax waste but permits coarse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing permitted insulating materials: clothing, fruit, dove wings, wood shavings, and fine flax waste.
Rabbi Yehuda forbids fine flax waste but permits coarse flax waste for insulation.

items.text: Gemara: The story of Elisha Ba'al Kenafayim
items.text_en: Gemara: The story of Elisha Ba'al Kenafayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara digresses to explain why dove wings are mentioned, citing Rabbi Yannai's statement that tefillin require a clean body like Elisha 'Ba'al Kenafayim'. Abaye and Rava explain what 'clean body' means. The Gemara then recounts the story of Elisha who risked his life to wear tefillin and miraculously they turned into dove wings, and explains the symbolism of the dove.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai states that tefillin require a clean body, like Elisha 'Ba'al Kenafayim'.
The Gemara asks what 'clean body' means.
Abaye answers that it means one should not pass gas while wearing them.
Rava answers that it means one should not sleep while wearing them.
The Gemara asks why Elisha was called 'Ba'al Kenafayim'.
The Gemara recounts the story of Elisha who risked his life to wear tefillin, and miraculously they turned into dove wings when a Roman official caught him.
The Gemara asks why specifically dove wings were mentioned, rather than wings of other birds.
The Gemara answers that the dove symbolizes the Jewish people, as its wings protect it, so too do the commandments protect Israel.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehuda's dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehuda's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's dispute in the Mishnah is about wood shavings or flax waste. It resolves from a baraita that Rabbi Yehuda specifically refers to fine flax waste as like dung.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's dispute in the Mishnah is about wood shavings (נסורת של חרשים) or about flax waste (נעורת של פשתן).
The Gemara resolves the question by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda explicitly says that fine flax waste (נעורת של פשתן דקה) is like dung, proving he refers to flax waste.

items.text: Mishnah: Insulating with hides and wool
items.text_en: Mishnah: Insulating with hides and wool
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses insulating with hides (which may be moved) and wool fleeces (which may not be moved). It describes how to remove the food, and records a dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and the Sages about whether one may replace the cover.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may insulate with hides and move them, but with wool fleeces one may not move them; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says to tip the basket on its side, while the Sages say one may take and return the cover.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says one should tilt the basket on its side and take the food, lest one take the cover and be unable to replace it.
The Sages disagree and permit one to take the cover and replace it.

items.text: Gemara's question about hides of a craftsman
items.text_en: Gemara's question about hides of a craftsman
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling about moving hides applies to householder's hides or craftsman's hides, since a craftsman is particular about them. Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar suggests it refers to householder's hides, and Rabbi Chanina bar Chama cites Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a question about whether the Mishnah's ruling on moving hides (שלוחין) refers to householder's hides or craftsman's hides, since a craftsman is particular about them.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar answers that the Mishnah refers to householder's hides, but a craftsman is particular about his hides and therefore they may not be moved.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina bar Chama citing Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Chama citing Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Chama supports the answer by citing a tradition from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Abaye's practice and challenge from planks
items.text_en: Abaye's practice and challenge from planks
items.desc_en: Abaye would sit on bundles of planks, implying they are permitted for sitting. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita that distinguishes between household planks (movable) and craftsman's planks (not movable), unless designated for guests. The Gemara deflects by saying planks are different because the owner is particular about them.

sub.desc_en: Abaye, a messenger, would ask for bundles of planks to sit on, implying they are permitted for sitting on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that distinguishes between household planks (movable) and craftsman's planks (not movable), unless designated for guests.
The Gemara deflects by saying planks are different because the owner is particular about them, so they are not considered designated for sitting.

items.text: Challenge from hides and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from hides and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that hides, whether tanned or not, may be moved on Shabbat, and the distinction of tanned is only for impurity. The Gemara initially assumes this applies to both household and craftsman hides, but then clarifies it only refers to household hides. The Gemara questions why the baraita didn't specify this distinction, and answers that the entire baraita deals with household hides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that permits moving hides on Shabbat regardless of tanning, and notes the tanning distinction applies only to impurity.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita applies equally to household hides and craftsman hides.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers only to household hides, not craftsman hides.
The Gemara objects that if the baraita only discusses household hides, it should have specified that distinction explicitly.
The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita deals exclusively with household hides, so no further specification is needed.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on hides
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on hides
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: the first Tanna says household hides may be moved but craftsman hides may not; Rabbi Yosei permits moving both.

sub.desc_en: The baraita records a dispute: the first Tanna permits moving household hides but not craftsman hides, while Rabbi Yosei permits moving both.

items.text: Question on the source of 39 labors
items.text_en: Question on the source of 39 labors
items.desc_en: The Sages sitting together ask: what do the 39 categories of labor correspond to? Rabbi Chanina bar Chama answers: corresponding to the labors of the Tabernacle. Rabbi Yonatan bar Elazar reports Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei ben Lakonya's answer: corresponding to the 39 instances of the word 'melacha' in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Sages sitting together ask: to what do the 39 categories of labor correspond?
Rabbi Chanina bar Chama answers: they correspond to the labors of the Tabernacle.

sub.text: Rabbi Yonatan bar Elazar reporting Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei ben Lakonya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan bar Elazar reporting Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei ben Lakonya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan bar Elazar reports Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei ben Lakonya's answer: they correspond to the 39 instances of the words 'melacha', 'melachto', and 'melechet' in the Torah.

items.text: Rav Yosef's query and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's query and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether the verse 'and he came home to do his work' is included in the count. Abaye suggests bringing a Torah scroll to count, citing a precedent. Rav Yosef explains his doubt: perhaps the verse refers to personal needs, or perhaps it is part of the count and the other verse 'the work was sufficient' means the work was completed. The Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (undecided).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether the verse 'וַיָּבֹא הַבַּיְתָה לַעֲשׂוֹת מְלַאכְתּוֹ' (and he came home to do his work) is included in the count of thirty-nine labors.
Abaye suggests bringing a Torah scroll to count the instances, citing a precedent from רבה בר בר חנה (Rabba bar bar Ḥana) in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan).

Rav Yosef explains that his doubt arises because of the verse 'וְהַמְּלָאכָה הָיְתָה דַיָּם' (and the work was sufficient), which might be included in the count, and then the Joseph verse would be interpreted as referring to personal needs.

The Gemara presents the alternative possibility that the Joseph verse is included in the count and the other verse means the work was completed, and concludes with 'תֵּיקוּ' (the matter stands unresolved).

items.text: Support for the Tabernacle view
items.text_en: Support for the Tabernacle view
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the view that the labors correspond to the Tabernacle: one is liable only for a labor similar to those performed in the Tabernacle. Examples are given: sowing, reaping, lifting planks, etc. The Gemara clarifies that moving from one private domain to another via a public domain is also included.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the view that the labors correspond to the Tabernacle, stating that one is liable only for a labor similar to those performed in the Tabernacle, with examples of sowing and reaping.
The baraita continues with examples of carrying planks from ground to wagon and from wagon to ground, corresponding to carrying from public to private domain and vice versa.
The Gemara asks what labor is involved in moving from one private domain to another private domain.

sub.text: Abaye and Rava (or Rav Adda bar Ahavah)
sub.text_en: Abaye and Rava (or Rav Adda bar Ahavah)
sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava (or Rav Adda bar Ahavah) answer that it refers to moving from one private domain to another via a public domain.

items.text: Rava on wool fleeces and a challenge
items.text_en: Rava on wool fleeces and a challenge
items.desc_en: Rava states that wool fleeces may be moved on Shabbat only if one has stored food in them; otherwise not. A young scholar challenges Rava with a baraita that says one may insulate with fleeces but not move them, and asks how to proceed.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that wool fleeces may be moved on Shabbat only if one has stored food in them, otherwise not.
A young scholar challenges Rava by citing a baraita that permits insulating with fleeces but prohibits moving them, and asks how one should proceed.

items.text: Rava's distinction: designation for insulation
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: designation for insulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies a previous statement by Rava: the prohibition against moving wool shears applies only if they were not designated for insulation; if they were designated, they may be moved. A supporting tradition from Rabbi Yaakov quoting Rabbi Asi ben Shaul quoting Rabbi is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishna's case: one lifts the cover and the wool fleece falls by itself, implying it is not moved directly.
Rava clarifies that the prohibition applies only when the wool was not designated for insulation; if designated, it may be moved.
A supporting tradition is cited: Rabbi Yaakov quoting Rabbi Asi ben Shaul quoting Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi confirms Rava's distinction.

items.text: Ravina's alternative: merchant's wool
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative: merchant's wool
items.desc_en: Ravina asserts that the ruling applies specifically to merchant's wool (shel hefteq), not to wool designated for home use. A baraita supports this: merchant's wool may not be moved unless the owner prepared it for use.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asserts that the mishna's ruling about wool fleece applies specifically to merchant's wool (של הפטק), not to wool designated for home use.
A baraita supports Ravina: merchant's wool may not be moved on שבת (Sabbath), but if the homeowner prepared it for use, it may be moved.

items.text: Dispute on palm branches: tying required?
items.text_en: Dispute on palm branches: tying required?
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana teaches before Rav: if one cuts palm branches for firewood and then decides to use them for seating, one must tie them. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees, saying tying is unnecessary. Rav rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.text: Tanna (Rabba bar bar Chana) before Rav
sub.text_en: Tanna (Rabba bar bar Chana) before Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana teaches before Rav that if one cuts palm branches for firewood and then decides to use them for seating, one must tie them.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees, stating that tying is unnecessary.
The Gemara reports that Rav himself taught the baraita and ruled in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Three opinions: tying, thinking, or sitting
items.text_en: Three opinions: tying, thinking, or sitting
items.desc_en: Rav requires tying, Shmuel requires mental designation (choshev), and Rav Asi permits sitting even without tying or thinking. The Gemara aligns Rav with the first tanna and Shmuel with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, then questions Rav Asi's source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports three opinions: Rav requires tying, Shmuel requires mental designation (חוֹשֵׁב), and Rav Asi permits sitting even without tying or thinking.
The Gemara aligns Rav with the first tanna and Shmuel with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, then questions which authority supports Rav Asi's lenient position.

items.text: Rav Asi's source and Rav Ashi's support
items.text_en: Rav Asi's source and Rav Ashi's support
items.desc_en: Rav Asi aligns with a baraita about dyed and wrapped wool: if worn for an hour before Shabbat, no further preparation is needed. Rav Ashi cites a mishna about straw on a bed: if food or bedding was placed on it before Shabbat, it may be moved, supporting the principle that prior use suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Asi's position aligns with a baraita about dyed and wrapped wool: if worn for an hour before Shabbat, no further preparation is needed.
Rav Ashi cites a mishna about straw on a bed: if food or bedding was placed on it before Shabbat, it may be moved, supporting the principle that prior use suffices.

items.text: Identifying the disputant: Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva
items.text_en: Identifying the disputant: Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva as the one who disputes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. A story is told: he found palm branches cut for wood and told his students to mentally designate them for sitting the next day. The Gemara infers that only in a busy context (wedding or mourning) is mental designation sufficient; otherwise, tying is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva as the one who disputes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.text: Story via Rav Dimi and Ze'iri
sub.text_en: Story via Rav Dimi and Ze'iri
sub.desc_en: A story is told: Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva found palm branches cut for wood and told his students to mentally designate them for sitting the next day, but the Gemara notes uncertainty whether it was a wedding or mourning context.
The Gemara infers that only in a busy context (wedding or mourning) is mental designation sufficient; otherwise, tying is required.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on earth and the dispute about ma'aseh
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on earth and the dispute about ma'aseh
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one may bring a basketful of earth into the house and use it for any need, provided one designates a corner for it. The Gemara debates whether this follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (no ma'aseh needed) or the Rabbis (ma'aseh required). Rav Pappa explains that the Rabbis require ma'aseh only for items that can undergo an action, not for earth.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one may bring a basketful of earth into the house and use it for any need.
Mar Zutra adds that this is only permitted if one designates a corner for the earth.
The Rabbis before Rav Pappa ask whether this ruling follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (no ma'aseh needed) or the Rabbis (ma'aseh required).
Rav Pappa explains that even according to the Rabbis, they require ma'aseh only for items that can undergo an action, not for earth.

items.text: Dispute about scouring agents: ma'aseh or not?
items.text_en: Dispute about scouring agents: ma'aseh or not?
items.desc_en: A tannaitic dispute is presented: one baraita permits scouring vessels with natron and sand (except silver vessels with a special compound), while another forbids natron and sand. The Gemara initially suggests the dispute is about requiring ma'aseh, but resolves that both agree ma'aseh is not needed; rather, the dispute is between Rabbi Yehuda (who forbids unintended consequences) and Rabbi Shimon (who permits them). The Gemara then questions this resolution by citing a mishna that forbids scouring hair, which would be problematic for Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute: one baraita permits scouring vessels with all agents except silver vessels with a special compound, implying natron and sand are permitted.
The Gemara cites a conflicting baraita that forbids natron and sand, and suggests the dispute is about whether a ma'aseh (deliberate act) is required to permit use.
The Gemara rejects the initial suggestion, stating that both baraitot agree ma'aseh is not required; rather, the dispute is between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding unintended consequences.
The Gemara explains that the first baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who permits an unintended consequence (דבר שאין מתכוין), while the second follows Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids it.

The Gemara objects: if the permissive baraita is attributed to Rabbi Shimon, its continuation forbids scouring hair, which would contradict Rabbi Shimon's lenient position, as a mishna is cited to challenge this.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a Mishnah about a nazirite who may rub and part his hair but not comb it, setting the stage for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that a nazirite may rub and part his hair but not comb it.

items.text: Reconciliation of tannaitic disputes
items.text_en: Reconciliation of tannaitic disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the conflicting rulings are both attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, but represent two different tannaitic traditions regarding whether combing removes hair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing both positions to Rabbi Yehuda, with two different Tannaim arguing in his name about whether combing causes hair removal (גריר).

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding face, hands, and feet
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding face, hands, and feet
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the ruling that one may wash face, hands, and feet, as this involves removing hair, and resolves by limiting the ruling to a minor, a woman, or a eunuch.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the ruling that one may wash face, hands, and feet, noting that this involves removing hair, which is forbidden.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by limiting the ruling to a minor, a woman, or a eunuch, who lack significant hair growth.

items.text: Permitted powders for cleaning
items.text_en: Permitted powders for cleaning
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda, Rav Yosef, Rava, and Rav Sheshet each permit specific powders (e.g., brick dust, jasmine powder, pepper dust, and barda). Rav Yosef defines barda as a mixture of one-third each of aloe, myrtle, and sage, and Rav Nechemya bar Yosef adds that it is fine if aloe is not the majority.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda permits brick dust for cleaning on Shabbat.
Rav Yosef permits jasmine powder for cleaning.
Rava permits pepper dust for cleaning.
Rav Sheshet permits barda (a specific powder mixture) for cleaning.
The Gemara asks what barda is.
Rav Yosef defines barda as a mixture of one-third each of aloe, myrtle, and sage.
Rav Nechemya bar Yosef adds that the mixture is fine as long as aloe is not the majority component.

items.text: Splitting olives on Shabbat
items.text_en: Splitting olives on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a question about splitting olives on Shabbat; Rav Sheshet responds that it is not even permitted on a weekday due to food waste. The Gemara considers a contradiction with Shmuel's ruling about bread, but resolves that bread does not become repulsive while olives do.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask Rav Sheshet whether it is permitted to split olives on Shabbat.
Rav Sheshet responds that splitting olives is not even permitted on a weekday, because it causes food waste (הפסד אוכלין).
The Gemara considers that Rav Sheshet's ruling might contradict Shmuel's ruling that one may do all one's needs with bread on Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves that bread does not become repulsive (מאיס) when handled, whereas split olives do become repulsive, so there is no contradiction.

items.text: Dispute about using barda on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about using barda on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi were served barda; Amemar and Rav Ashi rubbed it, but Mar Zutra did not. Rav Mordechai explains that Mar Zutra holds like a baraita that permits scraping for pain but not for beautification, while the others hold like another baraita that permits washing for honor of one's Maker.

sub.desc_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi were seated and served barda; Amemar and Rav Ashi rubbed it, but Mar Zutra did not.

sub.text: Amemar and Rav Ashi to Mar Zutra
sub.text_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi to Mar Zutra
sub.desc_en: They asked Mar Zutra: Does the Master not hold of what Rav Sheshet said, that barda is permitted?
Rav Mordechai replied: Mar Zutra does not even hold of that opinion on a weekday.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Mar Zutra's position
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Mar Zutra's position
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra holds like a baraita that permits scraping scabs for pain but forbids it for beautification.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Amemar and Rav Ashi's position
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Amemar and Rav Ashi's position
sub.desc_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi hold like another baraita that permits washing one's face, hands, and feet daily for the honor of one's Maker.

items.text: Dispute about a basket with a broken rim
items.text_en: Dispute about a basket with a broken rim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rules that one may tilt a basket on its side to take produce, but if the rim breaks, it is forbidden to replace it. The Gemara analyzes the dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and the Sages, concluding they disagree about whether we are concerned that the rim might break.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rules that one may tilt a basket on its side to take produce, but if the rim breaks, it is forbidden to replace it.

sub.text: Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav reports that all agree that if the rim broke, it is forbidden to replace it.
The Gemara cites the Sages' position that one may take and replace the rim, and asks: under what circumstances?
The Gemara reasons: if the rim did not break, the Sages' ruling is fine; therefore, the dispute must be about a case where the rim broke.
The Gemara rejects the previous assumption and resolves: the dispute is about a case where the rim did not break, but they disagree about whether we are concerned that it might break.

items.text: Rulings on cleaning knives and a challenge
items.text_en: Rulings on cleaning knives and a challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Shmuel rule that a knife may be cleaned by sticking it in and out of the ground repeatedly; Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi add that a reed knife is fine. Rav Mordechai reports a challenge from Rav Katina regarding the law of one who stores vegetables under a vine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a knife may be cleaned on Shabbat by repeatedly sticking it in and out of the ground, but not by scraping.
Shmuel gives a parallel ruling for a knife stuck between beams, also permitting cleaning by repeated insertion and removal.

sub.text: Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi's addition
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi's addition
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi adds that a reed knife is fine for cleaning in this manner.

sub.text: Rav Mordechai's challenge from Rav Katina
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai's challenge from Rav Katina
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai reports a challenge from Rav Katina citing a baraita about one who stores vegetables under a vine, which may contradict the lenient rulings.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the items mentioned in the previous Mishnah are not subject to the prohibitions of kilayim, shevi'it, or ma'aser, and may be moved on Shabbat. This is presented as a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the items in the previous Mishnah are not subject to kilayim, shevi'it, or ma'aser, and may be moved on Shabbat, presenting this as a refutation.

items.text: Mishnah: Insulating on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Insulating on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one did not cover a pot before Shabbat, they may not cover it after dark. If it was covered and then uncovered, it may be recovered. One may fill a pitcher and place it under a pillow or cushion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one did not cover a vessel before Shabbat, he may not cover it after dark; if it was covered and became uncovered, he may re-cover it; and one may fill a pitcher and place it under a pillow or cushion.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on insulating cold items
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on insulating cold items
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel permitting insulating cold items. Rav Yosef questions the novelty, as the Mishnah already allows placing a pitcher under a pillow. Abaye explains that the Mishnah might only permit items not typically insulated, but Shmuel teaches that even items typically insulated are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that it is permitted to insulate cold food on Shabbat.
Rav Yosef questions the novelty of Shmuel's statement, noting that the Mishnah already permits placing a jug under a pillow.
Abaye explains that Shmuel teaches a novel point: the Mishnah might only permit insulating items not typically insulated, but Shmuel permits even items typically insulated.

items.text: Rav's conflicting ruling and resolution
items.text_en: Rav's conflicting ruling and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna quotes Rav forbidding insulating cold items. A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitted it. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi initially permitted it, but after hearing from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei that his father (Rabbi Yosei) permitted it, he retracted and forbade it, saying 'A elder has already ruled.' Rav Papa comments on the mutual respect between the sages.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna quotes Rav forbidding insulating cold food on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitted insulating cold food.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi initially permitted it, but after hearing from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei that his father Rabbi Yosei permitted it, he retracted and forbade it, saying 'A elder has already ruled.'
Rav Papa comments on the mutual respect between the sages, noting that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi deferred to Rabbi Yosei's ruling despite his own stature.

items.text: Rav Nachman's practice and Rabbi Ami's reaction
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's practice and Rabbi Ami's reaction
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman instructs his servant to insulate cold items and bring him hot water from a certain innkeeper. Rabbi Ami hears and is upset. Rav Yosef explains that Rav Nachman acted in accordance with both Rav and Shmuel: one ruling permits insulating cold items, and the other permits eating food that is edible raw, thus no issue with cooking by a non-Jew. The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman considered himself an important person, for whom the rules might differ.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman instructs his servant Daru to insulate cold food and bring him water heated by a gentile innkeeper.
Rabbi Ammi hears of Rav Nachman's actions and becomes angry.
Rav Yosef questions why Rabbi Ammi was angry, noting that Rav Nachman acted according to his teachers.

Rav Yosef explains that Rav Nachman followed Shmuel's ruling permitting insulating cold food and Rav's ruling that food edible raw is not subject to the prohibition of בישולי גויים (food cooked by gentiles).
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Ammi was angry because he held that an important person like Rav Nachman should be stringent and avoid even the appearance of a prohibited act.

items.text: Additional rulings on insulation and covering
items.text_en: Additional rulings on insulation and covering
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that although one may not initially insulate after dark, one may add insulation. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains how to adjust coverings. He also rules that transferring a pot from one heater to another is permitted, though the Gemara questions this. The baraita then discusses cases where the covering material is movable or not on Shabbat, and when one may remove and replace the covering.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that although one may not initially insulate after dark, one may add insulation, and asks how this is done.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains that one may adjust the coverings by replacing sheets with cloaks or vice versa.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel further rules that transferring a pot from one heater to another is permitted.
The Gemara objects: now, cooling them would cool them further, but heating them would reheat them? (i.e., the transfer seems counterproductive).
The baraita resolves that if one insulated and covered with a movable item on Shabbat, or insulated with a non-movable item but covered with a movable one, one may remove and replace the covering.
The baraita concludes with the case where both insulation and covering are non-movable, stating that if part of the pot is exposed one may remove and replace, but otherwise not (the text is cut off).

items.text: Concluding Mishnah of 'Bameh Tominin'
items.text_en: Concluding Mishnah of 'Bameh Tominin'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions regarding insulation on Shabbat: one may not take and return a cover, Rabbi Yehuda considers fine flax tow as dung, and one may place a hot-water urn on another but not a pot on an urn. It also forbids insulating cold items and crushing snow or hail to melt them, though one may place them in a cup.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may not take and return a cover on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda states that fine flax tow is considered like dung (and thus permitted for insulation).

The Mishnah rules that one may place a hot-water urn on another urn or a pot on another pot, but not a pot on an urn or vice versa, and one may seal the mouth with dough only for preservation, not for heating.
The Mishnah states that just as one may not insulate hot items, one may not insulate cold items, but Rabbi permitted insulating cold items.
The Mishnah concludes that one may not crush snow or hail on Shabbat to melt them, but one may place them in a cup or bowl without concern.

items.text: Closing formula and new chapter heading
items.text_en: Closing formula and new chapter heading
items.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'Hadran alach' marks the end of the chapter, followed by the opening Mishnah of the new chapter 'Bameh Behemah Yotzah'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara closes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' and introduces the new chapter with the opening Mishnah heading 'במה בהמה יוצאה'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: What animals may go out with
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: What animals may go out with
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permitted and prohibited items for animals on Shabbat: a camel may go out with a bridle, a na'akah with a nose-ring, lubdakim with a prombya, and a horse with a chain. All chain-wearing animals may go out with a chain and be led by it, and one may sprinkle water on them and immerse them in place.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking which items an animal may wear when going out on Shabbat, and lists the first set of permitted items: a camel with a bridle, a na'akah with a nose-ring, lubdakim with a prombya, and a horse with a chain.
The Mishnah states a general rule: all animals that wear a chain may go out with it and be led by it.
The Mishnah adds that one may sprinkle water on these animals and immerse them in place on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of terms and an anecdote
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of terms and an anecdote
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the terms 'na'akah' and 'lubdakim': Rabba bar bar Chana explains na'akah as a white she-camel with an iron nose-ring, and Rav Huna explains lubdakim as a Luban donkey with iron fetters. An anecdote about Levi sending money to buy a Luban donkey illustrates that the donkey's fetters are made of hair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's term 'נאקה בחטם' (a she-camel with a nose-ring) means.
Rabba bar bar Chana explains that 'נאקה' refers to a white she-camel (נאקתא חיורתי) with an iron nose-ring (זממא דפרזלא).
Rav Huna explains that 'לובדקים בפרומביא' refers to a Luban donkey (חמרא לובא) with iron fetters (פגי דפרזלא).
An anecdote about Levi sending money to buy a Luban donkey illustrates that the donkey's fetters (ניגרי) are made of hair (שערי), not iron.

items.text: Debate: Exchanging items between animals and the status of a camel with a nose-ring
items.text_en: Debate: Exchanging items between animals and the status of a camel with a nose-ring
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel asks Rabbi about exchanging items between animals. The Gemara raises a question about a camel with a nose-ring: since a camel is already led by a bridle, is the nose-ring a burden or added security? Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei cites his father's tradition that four animals go out with a bridle, excluding a camel with a nose-ring.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel asked Rabbi about exchanging items between animals, specifically whether a camel can go out with a nose-ring (חטם) and a female camel with a bridle (אפסר).

The Gemara clarifies the question: a female camel with a bridle is obviously a burden since it is not led by it, but the doubt is about a camel with a nose-ring — since it is already led by a bridle, is the nose-ring a burden or added security?

Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei cites his father's tradition that four animals go out with a bridle (horse, mule, camel, donkey), excluding a female camel with a bridle, implying a camel with a nose-ring is permitted.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: Whether a wild animal may go out with a collar
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: Whether a wild animal may go out with a collar
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that lubdakim and a camel go out with a bridle. A dispute between the first Tanna and Chananya is presented: the first Tanna forbids a wild animal from going out with a collar, while Chananya permits it with any restraining device. The Gemara clarifies the dispute concerns a cat: the first Tanna considers a simple rope sufficient, making a collar a burden, while Chananya holds that extra security is not a burden. Rav Huna bar Chiya in the name of Shmuel rules like Chananya.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that lubdakim and a camel go out with a bridle (אפסר).
A dispute is cited: the first Tanna forbids a wild animal from going out with a collar (סוגר), while Chananya permits it with any restraining device.
The Gemara asks what type of wild animal is under dispute, rejecting both a large and a small wild animal as implausible.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute concerns a cat: the first Tanna holds that since a simple rope suffices, a collar is a burden; Chananya holds that extra security is not a burden.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chiya citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya in the name of Shmuel rules like Chananya.

items.text: Anecdote: Levi's donkey overtakes Rabba bar Rav Huna's
items.text_en: Anecdote: Levi's donkey overtakes Rabba bar Rav Huna's
items.desc_en: Levi's donkey overtook Rabba bar Rav Huna's on the road, causing Rabba bar Rav Huna distress. He considered saying something to Levi, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Levi's donkey overtook Rabba bar Rav Huna's on the road.
Rabba bar Rav Huna felt distressed and considered saying something to Levi, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Rav Yosef's question about a donkey with bad habits
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's question about a donkey with bad habits
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether a donkey with bad habits may go out with a muzzle on Shabbat. The reply is that the halakha follows Chananya.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether a donkey with bad habits may go out with a muzzle on Shabbat.
The interlocutor replies that the halakha follows Chananya, as Shmuel said.

items.text: The case of a goat with a strap between its horns
items.text_en: The case of a goat with a strap between its horns
items.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Menashe teaches that a goat with a strap between its horns may go out on Shabbat. Rav Yosef raises a question about a strap tied to its beard, and the Gemara concludes with 'teiku'.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Menashe
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Menashe
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Menashe teaches that a goat with a strap carved between its horns may go out with an אפסר (halter) on Shabbat.
Rav Yosef asks: if the strap is inserted into the goat's beard, what is the law?
The Gemara considers one side of the doubt: since removing the strap would cause pain, the owner will not come to remove it.
The Gemara raises the opposite concern: sometimes the strap might loosen and fall, leading the owner to carry it four cubits in the public domain.
The Gemara concludes with 'תֵּיקוּ' (let it stand unresolved).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the strap between horns
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the strap between horns
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an animal may not go out with a strap between its horns. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reports a dispute: one says both for adornment and for guarding are forbidden, the other says adornment is forbidden but guarding is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that an animal may not go out with a strap between its horns.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's report of a dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's report of a dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reports that Rav and Shmuel dispute the Mishnah's ruling.
One authority holds that both for adornment and for guarding, the strap is forbidden.
The other authority holds that for adornment it is forbidden, but for guarding it is permitted.

items.text: Rav Yosef's attempt to prove Shmuel's position
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's attempt to prove Shmuel's position
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that Shmuel holds adornment is forbidden and guarding is permitted, citing Rav Huna bar Chiyya who said Shmuel ruled like Chananya.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that Shmuel's position can be determined: adornment is forbidden, guarding is permitted.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Huna bar Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Huna bar Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef supports his claim by citing Rav Huna bar Chiyya, who reported that Shmuel ruled like Chananya.

items.text: Abaye's counter-proof from Shmuel's statement about mules
items.text_en: Abaye's counter-proof from Shmuel's statement about mules
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that Shmuel holds both adornment and guarding are forbidden, citing Rav Yehuda who said Shmuel reported that mules of Rabbi's household went out with a halter, implying only a halter is permitted, not a strap.

sub.desc_en: Abaye counters Rav Yosef's proof, arguing that Shmuel actually holds both adornment and guarding are forbidden, citing Rav Yehuda's report about mules of Rabbi's household going out with a halter.

items.text: Resolution of the dispute with explicit statements
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute with explicit statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by citing explicit statements: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi said Rav holds both are forbidden, and Rav Chiyya bar Avin said Shmuel holds adornment is forbidden and guarding is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Abaye prioritized one proof over the other.
The Gemara answers that the priority is justified because explicit statements resolve the dispute.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi reports that Rav holds both adornment and guarding are forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin reports that Shmuel holds adornment is forbidden and guarding is permitted.

items.text: Challenge from the law of the red heifer
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of the red heifer
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from the law of the red heifer: if a halter is considered a burden, the Torah says 'upon which no yoke has come'. Abaye, Rava, and Ravina offer different answers: leading from city to city, because its blood is expensive, or because it is a wild cow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the red heifer law: if a halter (מוסרה) is considered a burden (משאוי), then the Torah's phrase 'upon which no yoke has come' would be contradicted.
Abaye answers that the case involves leading the cow from city to city, not merely placing a halter.
Rava answers that the red heifer is different because its blood is expensive, so the halter is not considered a burden.
Ravina answers that the cow is a wild (מורדת) cow that cannot be led without a halter, so the halter is not a burden but a necessity.

items.text: Dispute about leading animals: wrapped or pulled
items.text_en: Dispute about leading animals: wrapped or pulled
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says horses go out with a halter and are led. Rav Huna says they may go out wrapped or pulled; Shmuel says they go out pulled but not wrapped. A baraita and Rav Yosef's observation support Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'go out' and 'are led'.
Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah permits both wrapping the halter around the animal's neck and leading it by the halter.
Shmuel restricts the Mishnah: animals may be led out by the halter but not with the halter wrapped around them.
A baraita explicitly states that animals go out with the halter wrapped around them in order to be led, supporting Rav Huna's position.
Rav Yosef testifies that he saw the calves of Rav Huna's household going out with their halters wrapped around them on Shabbat, providing practical evidence for Rav Huna's view.

items.text: The mules of Rabbi's household and the necessity of both reports
items.text_en: The mules of Rabbi's household and the necessity of both reports
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that the mules of Rabbi's household go out with halters on Shabbat. The Gemara questions whether wrapped or pulled. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda clarifies they go out wrapped. Rav Asi explains that both reports are necessary: one to show acceptance, the other to permit wrapping.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Chanina that the mules of Rabbi's household go out with their halters on Shabbat.
The Gemara raises a question: were the mules led out with the halter wrapped around their necks or pulled by hand?

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda clarifies in the name of Rabbi Chanina that the mules went out with the halter wrapped around their necks.

The rabbis before Rav Asi object that Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's report is unnecessary, since Rav Dimi's report already implies wrapping, and if it meant pulling, Rav Yehuda's report of Shmuel would suffice.

sub.text: Supporting citation of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Supporting citation of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda's report that Shmuel described how they would exchange halters before Rabbi, listing four animals that go out with a halter, implying that pulling is permitted.
Rav Asi responds that both reports are necessary: Rav Dimi's report shows that Rabbi accepted the ruling, which Rav Yehuda's report alone would not prove.
Rav Asi adds that Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's report is also necessary, because without it one might think Rav Dimi permitted only pulling, not wrapping.

items.text: Question about sprinkling and immersing rings in place
items.text_en: Question about sprinkling and immersing rings in place
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the rings of animals are susceptible to impurity, citing a Mishnah that a human's ring is impure but an animal's ring is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the rings of animals are susceptible to impurity, citing a Mishnah that a human's ring is impure but an animal's ring is pure.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that certain items are pure (טְהוֹרוֹת). This sets the stage for the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that certain items are pure (טְהוֹרוֹת), setting the stage for the Gemara's discussion.

items.text: Gemara's debate on the reason for purity
items.text_en: Gemara's debate on the reason for purity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha and Rav Yosef debate why these items are pure: one says because they transition from human ornament to animal ornament, the other because humans use them to lead animals. Rav Yosef supports his view with a baraita about a metal staff.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha states that these items are pure because they transition from human ornament to animal ornament.
Rav Yosef offers an alternative reason: these items are pure because humans use them to lead animals, and supports this with a baraita about a metal staff.

items.text: Question about immersion and Rabbi Ammi's answer
items.text_en: Question about immersion and Rabbi Ammi's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how these items can be immersed in place, given the problem of interposition (חציצה). Rabbi Ammi answers that they were softened (שריתּכן).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how these items can be immersed in place, given the problem of interposition (חציצה).
Rabbi Ammi answers that the items were softened (שריתּכן), removing the interposition.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Ammi's view
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Ammi's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Rabbi Ammi agrees with Rav Yosef, because if he agreed with Rabbi Yitzchak, softening would constitute an action that removes impurity, contradicting the principle that vessels only become pure through a change of action. It then proposes Rabbi Ammi follows Rabbi Yehuda, who says an action for improvement is not considered a change.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Ammi's view aligns with Rav Yosef, because if he agreed with Rabbi Yitzchak, the softening action would remove impurity, contradicting the principle that vessels only become pure through a change of action.
The Gemara cites a baraita that vessels become susceptible to טומאה (ritual impurity) through intention but only become pure through a change of action.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Ammi follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an action for improvement (תיקון) is not considered a change of action (שינוי מעשה) for purification purposes.

items.text: Alternative teaching in the Tosefta
items.text_en: Alternative teaching in the Tosefta
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that these items are considered 'profane' (מחוללין), i.e., they have lost their sanctity but are not yet pure.

sub.desc_en: A baraita in the Tosefta teaches that the items discussed are חולין (non-sacred), not subject to the laws of impurity.

items.text: Dialogue between a student and Rabbi Eliezer about rings and needles
items.text_en: Dialogue between a student and Rabbi Eliezer about rings and needles
items.desc_en: A student asks Rabbi Eliezer about distinctions between rings and needles. Rabbi Eliezer initially says the distinction applies only to Shabbat, not impurity. The Gemara then challenges this, citing various baraitot that show distinctions in impurity laws as well. Each time, Rabbi Eliezer clarifies he was referring to a specific type. Finally, Abaye resolves the needle question by saying the student was referring to unfinished needles (גולמי).

sub.desc_en: A student asks Rabbi Eliezer about a tradition that distinguishes between different types of rings.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that the distinction applies only to Shabbat, not to impurity, where all rings are the same.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a human's ring (impure) and an animal's ring (pure).
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer was referring only to human rings.
The Gemara objects further by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a finger ring (impure) and a belt ring (pure).
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer was referring only to finger rings.
The Gemara objects further by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a metal ring with a coral seal (impure) and a coral ring with a metal seal (pure).
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer was referring only to a ring entirely made of metal.
The student asks further about a tradition that distinguishes between different types of needles.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that the distinction applies only to Shabbat, not to impurity, where all needles are the same.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a needle whose eye or point is broken (pure) and an intact needle (impure).
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer was referring only to intact needles.
The Gemara objects further by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a rusty needle that impedes sewing (pure) and one that does not (impure).
The school of Rabbi Yannai adds that the distinction applies only when the rust's mark is visible.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Eliezer was referring only to smooth (rust-free) needles.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a pierced needle (impure) and an unpierced needle (pure) for impurity, but not for Shabbat.
Abaye resolves the needle question by explaining that the student was referring to unfinished needles (גולמי).

items.text: Mishnah on animals' ornaments on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah on animals' ornaments on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists which ornaments animals may wear on Shabbat, with disputes between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists which ornaments animals may wear on Shabbat: a donkey with a pack-saddle tied to it, males with a leather strap, ewes with a covering, a muzzle, and a woolen band, and goats with a tied teat.
Rabbi Yosei prohibits all these ornaments except the woolen band for ewes.
Rabbi Yehuda says goats may go out with a tied teat to dry up their milk, but not to preserve milk.

items.text: Shmuel's condition and Rav Nachman's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Shmuel's condition and Rav Nachman's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that the Mishnah's allowance applies only when the mardea was tied before Shabbat. Rav Nachman proves this from the Mishnah's wording, arguing that the case of 'not tied' must refer to not being tied from before Shabbat, implying the first clause requires it to be tied from before Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the Mishnah's allowance applies only when the mardea was tied before Shabbat.

Rav Nachman proves Shmuel's condition from the Mishnah's wording, arguing that the case of 'not tied' must refer to not being tied from before Shabbat, implying the first clause requires it to be tied from before Shabbat.

items.text: Supporting baraita with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.text_en: Supporting baraita with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states that a donkey may go out with a mardea if tied before Shabbat, but not with an ukaf. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits even an ukaf if tied before Shabbat, with conditions about not tying a rope or strap under the tail.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's condition, stating that a donkey may go out with a mardea only if tied before Shabbat, and adds restrictions on a saddle and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient opinion.
The baraita rules that a donkey may not go out with an ukaf even if tied before Shabbat.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits even an ukaf if tied before Shabbat, provided one does not tie a rope or strap under the tail.

items.text: Rav Asi's question and Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Asi's question and Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Asi bar Natan asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Ashi whether one may place a mardea on a donkey on Shabbat. He permits it, but is silent when asked about the difference from an ukaf. Rabbi Zeira defends him, citing Rav's ruling that one may hang a traskal on an animal on Shabbat, and a fortiori a mardea, since the latter is for pain relief.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi bar Natan asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Ashi whether one may place a mardea on a donkey on Shabbat, and receives a permissive answer.

sub.text: Rav Asi bar Natan's follow-up question
sub.text_en: Rav Asi bar Natan's follow-up question
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi bar Natan asks why a mardea is different from an ukaf, and Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Ashi remains silent.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that forbids even moving an ukaf on Shabbat, implying that placing one is certainly forbidden.
Rabbi Zeira defends Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav Ashi by citing Rav's ruling that one may hang a traskal on an animal on Shabbat, and a fortiori a mardea, since the latter is for pain relief.

items.text: Shmuel's opposing view and his criticism of Rav
items.text_en: Shmuel's opposing view and his criticism of Rav
items.desc_en: Shmuel permits a mardea but prohibits a traskal. When Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef reports Rav's view to Shmuel, Shmuel dismisses Rav as ignorant of Shabbat matters.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a mardea is permitted but a feeding basket (טרסקל) is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef's report and Shmuel's reaction
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef's report and Shmuel's reaction
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef reports Rav's ruling to Shmuel, who dismisses Rav as ignorant of Shabbat laws.
Shmuel dismisses Rav as ignorant of Shabbat matters for permitting the traskal.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's encounter with Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet and clarification
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's encounter with Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet and clarification
items.desc_en: Upon ascending to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Zeira finds Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet citing Rabbi Yochanan that one may place a mardea on a donkey on Shabbat. Rabbi Zeira approves, noting that 'Aryoch' (Shmuel) also interpreted it thus in Babylonia. The Gemara clarifies that Rav also said this, but the key point is that Shmuel's version included the prohibition of hanging a traskal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira ascends to Eretz Yisrael and finds Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet citing Rabbi Yochanan that one may place a מַרְדַּעַת (saddlecloth) on a donkey on שבת (Shabbat).
Rabbi Zeira approves, noting that 'אַרְיוֹךְ (Aryoch)' — i.e., Shmuel — also interpreted it thus in Babylonia.
The Gemara asks: Who is 'אַרְיוֹךְ (Aryoch)'? It is Shmuel. But didn't Rav also say this?

The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Zeira heard Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet conclude that one may not hang a טְרַסְקָל (fodder basket) on שבת (Shabbat), and it was that part — the prohibition — that Rabbi Zeira attributed to Shmuel, since Rav permitted it.

items.text: Distinguishing mardea from ukaf: two explanations
items.text_en: Distinguishing mardea from ukaf: two explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a mardea is permitted but an ukaf is not. It answers that an ukaf might fall off on its own, leading to carrying. Rav Pappa adds another distinction: placing a mardea is for warming the donkey (which causes pain), while an ukaf is for cooling (no pain), and a donkey feels cold even in summer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since everyone agrees that a saddlecloth (מַרְדַּעַת) is permitted, what distinguishes it from a saddle (אוּכָּף), which is prohibited?
The Gemara answers: The case of a saddle is different because it is possible for it to fall off on its own, so there is no need to permit removing it by hand.

Rav Pappa offers another distinction: placing a saddlecloth is to warm the donkey (which causes pain if not done), while a saddle is for cooling (no pain), and a donkey feels cold even in the summer season of Tammuz.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about traskalim and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about traskalim and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita lists items animals may not wear in the public domain, including 'syachin with traskalim in their mouths' in the public domain, implying it is permitted in a courtyard. The Gemara initially assumes this refers to large animals for pleasure, but concludes it refers to small animals for pain relief, thus not contradicting the earlier ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection by citing a baraita that lists items animals may not wear in the public domain, including 'syachin with traskalim in their mouths'.
The baraita continues by listing items that are permitted for animals in the courtyard, implying a distinction between public domain and courtyard.

The Gemara infers from the baraita that traskalim are forbidden only in the public domain but permitted in a courtyard, and asks whether this refers to large animals for pleasure, which would contradict the earlier ruling.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita refers to small animals for pain relief, not large animals for pleasure, so there is no contradiction.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that an amulet is permitted for an animal only if it is an expert amulet, but the Mishnah's language suggests otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that an amulet is permitted for an animal only if it is an expert amulet.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about expert amulets
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about expert amulets
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says 'not with an amulet that is not expert,' implying an expert amulet is permitted, but the baraita says 'even if it is expert.' The resolution is that the baraita refers to an amulet expert for humans but not for animals, because humans have a מזל that assists them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says 'not with an amulet that is not expert,' implying an expert amulet is permitted, but the baraita says 'even if it is expert.'
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to an amulet expert for humans but not for animals, because humans have a מזל (astrological fortune) that assists them.
