items.text: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah's 'stringency'
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah's 'stringency'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement 'this is a stringency for animals over humans,' and explains that it does not refer to amulets but to the sandal (a type of shoe).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'this is a stringency for animals over humans' in light of the previous reinterpretation.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's statement refers not to amulets but to the sandal (a type of shoe).

items.text: Anointing and massaging animals
items.text_en: Anointing and massaging animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that one may anoint and massage a human but not an animal, and suggests this is because of pain (צער), but the Gemara rejects this, saying it is because of pleasure (תענוג).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one may anoint and massage a human but not an animal.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita implies that the prohibition is due to pain (צער) when there is a wound.
The Gemara rejects this, explaining that the prohibition is due to pleasure (תענוג), not pain.

items.text: Cooling an animal with blood congestion
items.text_en: Cooling an animal with blood congestion
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that an animal with blood congestion may not be cooled in water, but a human may. Ulla explains this is a decree because of grinding herbs (שחיקת סממנין). The Gemara questions why the same decree does not apply to humans, and answers that a human appears to be cooling off, but an animal does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that an animal with blood congestion may not be cooled in water, but a human may.
Ulla explains that the prohibition is a decree because of grinding herbs (שחיקת סממנין).
The Gemara objects that the same decree should apply to humans as well.
The Gemara answers that a human appears to be cooling off, so the decree does not apply.
The Gemara objects that an animal also appears to be cooling off.
The Gemara resolves that there is no concept of cooling off for an animal.

items.text: Decree about bringing an animal from outside the techum
items.text_en: Decree about bringing an animal from outside the techum
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we decree for animals at all, citing a baraita that one may call an animal from outside the techum and it comes, without fear of bringing it. Ravina answers that the case is where the animal's techum is absorbed within the owner's techum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we decree for animals at all, citing a baraita that one may call an animal from outside the techum and it comes, without fear of bringing it.
Ravina answers that the case is where the animal's techum is absorbed within the owner's techum.

items.text: Dispute about grinding herbs for animals
items.text_en: Dispute about grinding herbs for animals
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the issue of grinding herbs is itself a dispute among Tannaim, citing a baraita where one may not run an animal that ate vetch in the courtyard to cure it, but Rabbi Oshaya permits it, and Rava rules like Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asserts that the issue of grinding herbs (שחיקת סממנין) is itself a dispute among Tannaim.
A baraita is cited: an animal that ate vetch may not be run in the courtyard to cure it, but Rabbi Oshaya permits it.
Rava publicly rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Oshaya's lenient position.

items.text: Contradiction about goats with udder bags
items.text_en: Contradiction about goats with udder bags
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says a zav may not go out with his bag, nor goats with their udder bags, but a baraita says goats may go out with udder bags. Rav Yehuda resolves this by distinguishing between tightly bound and loosely bound bags. Rav Yosef says it is a Tannaic dispute, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei forbids all except certain sheep, and Rabbi Yehuda permits for drying but not for milking. Alternatively, both are Rabbi Yehuda, distinguishing between drying and milking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a zav may not go out with his bag, nor goats with their udder bags.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita permits goats to go out with their udder bags.
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a tightly bound bag (forbidden) and a loosely bound bag (permitted).
Rav Yosef objects that the contradiction is not resolvable by a simple distinction; rather, it reflects a Tannaic dispute.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei forbids all goats except certain sheep, and Rabbi Yehuda permits goats bound for drying but not for milking.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: both sources follow Rabbi Yehuda, distinguishing between a bag for drying (permitted) and a bag for milking (forbidden).

items.text: Story of Antiochan goats
items.text_en: Story of Antiochan goats
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Yehuda said there was a case of goats in Antioch whose udders were large, and they made bags for them so their udders would not be scratched.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts Rabbi Yehuda's story of Antiochan goats with large udders that were given bags to prevent scratching.

items.text: Story of the man whose wife died and he nursed his son
items.text_en: Story of the man whose wife died and he nursed his son
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught a story of a man whose wife died and he had no money for a wet nurse, so a miracle occurred and his breasts opened like a woman's, and he nursed his son. Rav Yosef praises the man, but Abaye says he was degraded because the natural order was changed. Rav Yehuda says this shows how difficult sustenance is, and Rav Nachman adds that miracles happen but sustenance is not created.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis taught a story of a man whose wife died, and a miracle occurred: his breasts opened like a woman's and he nursed his son.
Rav Yosef praises the man, saying how great he is that such a miracle was performed for him.
Abaye objects, arguing that the man is actually degraded because the natural order was changed for him.
Rav Yehuda observes how difficult sustenance is, since the natural order was changed for this man.
Rav Nachman concludes that miracles happen but sustenance is not created, showing the difficulty of livelihood.

items.text: Story of the man who married a woman with a stump
items.text_en: Story of the man who married a woman with a stump
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught a story of a man who married a woman with a stump and did not recognize it until her death. Rav praises the woman's modesty, but Rabbi Chiyya says it was her nature, and instead praises the man's modesty for not recognizing it.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis taught a story about a man who married a woman with a stump and did not recognize it until her death.
Rav praises the woman's modesty for not being recognized by her husband.
Rabbi Chiyya objects that the woman's behavior was merely her nature, not modesty.
Rabbi Chiyya instead praises the man's modesty for not recognizing his wife's condition.

items.text: Meaning of 'לבובין' for male animals
items.text_en: Meaning of 'לבובין' for male animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says male animals go out 'לבובין.' Rav Huna says it means 'תותרי' (a type of ornament). Ulla says it is a skin tied against their heart to protect from wolves. The Gemara questions why wolves attack males more than females, and answers that males are fatter, but then questions that females are also fat, and that wolves do not distinguish. The Gemara concludes it is because males walk with their snouts raised like sick people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the Mishnah's term 'לבובין' for male animals.
Rav Huna explains that 'לבובין' means 'תותרי' (a type of ornament), citing the verse 'לִבַּבְתִּנִי' to show the root connotes closeness.
Ulla says 'לבובין' refers to a skin tied against their heart to protect from wolves.
The Gemara objects that wolves attack females too, and questions why they would specifically target males at the front of the herd.
The Gemara suggests males are fatter, but objects that females are also fat and wolves cannot distinguish.
The Gemara concludes that males are attacked because they walk with their snouts raised like sick people, making them vulnerable.

items.text: Alternative explanation of 'לבובין' and 'שחוזות'
items.text_en: Alternative explanation of 'לבובין' and 'שחוזות'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says 'לבובין' means a skin tied under their male organ to prevent them from mounting females, and 'שחוזות' (in the Mishnah's continuation) means lifting the tail so males can mount. The Gemara proves this from the contrast in the Mishnah and from the verse 'והנה אשה לקראתו'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'לבובין' refers to a skin tied under the males' organ to prevent them from mounting females.
The Gemara proves this interpretation from the Mishnah's continuation, where 'שחוזות' means lifting the tail so males can mount, showing a contrast.
The Gemara proves that 'שחוזות' is a term of exposure from the verse 'והנה אשה לקראתו' (and behold a woman came to meet him).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that sheep may go out 'כבולות' (bound). The Gemara begins to explain the meaning of this term.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that sheep may go out 'כבולות' (bound).

items.text: Explanation of 'כבולות' and 'ארץ כבול'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'כבולות' and 'ארץ כבול'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'כבולות' means binding the tail to prevent males from mounting. It then explores the etymology of 'כבול' from the verse about 'ארץ כבול', with Rav Huna and Rava debating its meaning, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offering an alternative explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'כבולות' means and answers that it refers to binding the tail downward to prevent males from mounting.
The Gemara cites a verse about 'ארץ כבול' to prove that 'כבול' connotes unfruitfulness.
The Gemara asks what 'ארץ כבול' means, and Rav Huna answers that it refers to people bound (wealthy) in silver and gold.
Rava objects that if the people were wealthy, why would the land be called 'כבול' negatively? Rav Huna responds that wealth led to idleness and unfruitfulness.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'ארץ כבול' was a swampy land where the foot sinks up to the ankle (כבלא), and people call it a binding land that does not produce fruit.

items.text: Explanation of 'כבונות'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'כבונות'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'כבונות' as sheep whose wool is combed for weaving, citing a baraita about the color of a leprous spot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the term 'כבונות' (bound).
The Gemara explains that 'כבונות' means combing the wool for spinning, citing a baraita about clean wool that is combed for spinning.
The Gemara cites a baraita about the color of a leprous spot (שאת) being like white wool, and Rav Bibi bar Abaye explains that this wool is clean, day-old wool that is combed for weaving.

items.text: Dispute about goats going out 'צרורות'
items.text_en: Dispute about goats going out 'צרורות'
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding the halakha for goats with bound udders, and then presents alternative versions of the tradition, including the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that goats may go out with bound udders.
Rav rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda (who permits), while Shmuel rules it follows Rabbi Yosei (who forbids).
Some transmit the dispute independently: Rav permits drying but not milking, Shmuel forbids both.

Some transmit the dispute on the Mishnah itself: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's position is that since one cannot distinguish, both are forbidden; Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, while Rabbi Yochanan rules like the first Tanna.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibitions for animals on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibitions for animals on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items with which a camel may not go out, and discusses the prohibition of tying camels together, while allowing leading them with ropes held in hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing prohibitions: a camel may not go out with a מטולטלת (a type of halter), nor עקוד (foreleg tied to hindleg) nor רגול (foreleg bent and tied to the upper arm), and similarly for all other animals.
The Mishnah continues: one may not tie camels together and lead them, but may insert ropes into his hand and lead, provided he does not tie a knot (כריכה).

items.text: Gemara on 'מטולטלת', 'עקוד', and 'רגול'
items.text_en: Gemara on 'מטולטלת', 'עקוד', and 'רגול'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the types of halters permitted for a camel, and then defines the terms 'עקוד' and 'רגול' from the Mishnah, with a debate about the correct definition of 'עקוד'.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that a camel may not go out with a saddlecloth tied only to its tail, but may go out with one tied to both its tail and its hump.
Rabba bar Rav Huna adds that a female camel may go out with a saddlecloth tied to its afterbirth.
Rav Yehuda defines 'עקוד' as binding one foreleg and one hindleg together like Isaac, and 'רגול' as bending the foreleg onto the upper foreleg and tying it.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that defines 'עקוד' as binding two forelegs and two hindlegs together, contradicting Rav Yehuda's definition.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Yehuda follows a different tanna who defines 'עקוד' as either one foreleg and one hindleg or two forelegs and two hindlegs.
The Gemara objects that the baraita still does not match Rav Yehuda's opinion, because the middle clause (two forelegs and two hindlegs) is problematic.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Yehuda follows a different tanna who defines 'עקוד' only as binding one foreleg and one hindleg, like Isaac.

items.text: Gemara on tying camels and rope restrictions
items.text_en: Gemara on tying camels and rope restrictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason for not tying camels together, and then discusses the permissibility of leading with ropes, focusing on kilayim and the amount of rope that may protrude from the hand, with a dispute between Shmuel and the Tanna of the school of Shmuel resolved by Abaye.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the mishna's prohibition of tying camels together.
Rav Ashi answers that it is because one appears like a merchant going to market, which is inappropriate on שבת (Sabbath).
Rav Ashi states that the mishna's restriction on intertwining ropes applies only to the prohibition of כלאים (diverse kinds), and the Gemara asks which type of כלאים is intended.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it refers to the diverse kinds of man and animal, citing a mishna that permits a person to plow or pull with any animal.
The Gemara suggests it refers to diverse kinds of ropes, but objects by citing a baraita that a single stitch does not constitute a connection for the prohibition of כלאים.
The Gemara resolves that the mishna refers to diverse kinds of ropes, and the prohibition is specifically when one intertwines and ties them together, which constitutes a significant connection.
Shmuel adds a restriction that no more than a handbreadth of rope may protrude from under one's hand on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that the Tanna of the school of Shmuel taught a baraita requiring two handbreadths, not one.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that Shmuel came to teach the practical halakha, ruling stringently that even one handbreadth is prohibited, despite the baraita's leniency up to two.

items.text: Resolving a contradiction about the height requirement
items.text_en: Resolving a contradiction about the height requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction between the Mishnah and a baraisa regarding the need to lift a burden a handbreadth off the ground. It resolves that the baraisa refers to a load carried between two people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraisa that requires lifting a burden a handbreadth off the ground, implying a stricter standard than the Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraisa refers to a load carried between two people, where the burden must be lifted a handbreadth.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibited animal ornaments
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibited animal ornaments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various ornaments and devices that animals may not wear on Shabbat, including a donkey's pack-saddle, bells, a ladder, a strap, and specific items for chickens, rams, ewes, calves, and cows. It concludes with a story about Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's cow that went out with a strap against the Sages' will.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibited animal ornaments on Shabbat, including a donkey's pack-saddle, bells, a ladder, a strap, and items for chickens, rams, ewes, calves, and cows, concluding with the story of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's cow.

items.text: Gemara's initial explanation for the first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's initial explanation for the first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly states that the reason for the first prohibition is as previously explained.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara briefly states that the reason for the first prohibition is as previously explained.

items.text: Explanations for the Mishnah's prohibitions
items.text_en: Explanations for the Mishnah's prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each prohibition: a bell is forbidden because it appears like going to a fair; a ladder (בי לועא) is for an animal with a wound; a strap is for a leash; chickens' threads are for identification; straps prevent them from breaking vessels; the wagon for rams prevents their tails from dragging; and the 'chanunot' for ewes is discussed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a bell is forbidden because it appears like going to a fair (חינגא).
Rav Huna identifies the ladder (סולם) as a 'בי לועא' (a device for an animal with a wound on its neck, to prevent it from turning and scratching).
The Gemara explains that the strap on the leg is used as a leash (גיזרא).
The Gemara explains that the threads on chickens serve as identification (סימנא) to prevent them from being swapped.
The Gemara explains that the strap on chickens prevents them from breaking vessels, and the wagon for rams prevents their tails from dragging.

items.text: Debate on the meaning of 'chanunot'
items.text_en: Debate on the meaning of 'chanunot'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Ulla suggests that 'chanunot' refers to anointing ewes with oil after shearing, but Rav Chisda objects that this would make them like 'Mar Ukva'. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel suggests it is for warming them during birth, but Rav Nachman objects that this would make them like 'Yalta'. Rav Huna explains that 'chanunot' refers to a wood called 'yachnun' used to make them sneeze and remove head lice. Shimon Nezira adds that it is a broom-wood. The Gemara concludes that 'chanunot' means we do something to have mercy on them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Ulla explains that 'chanunot' means anointing ewes with oil after shearing to prevent chilling.
Rav Chisda objects that this practice would make the ewe like 'Mar Ukva', implying excessive luxury.

sub.text: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel's alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel's alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel suggests that 'chanunot' refers to warming ewes during birth with oil on the forehead and womb.
Rav Nachman objects that this would make the ewe like 'Yalta', implying excessive pampering.
Rav Huna explains that 'chanunot' refers to a wood called 'yachnun' used to make ewes sneeze and remove head lice.
The Gemara objects that if this is for lice removal, male sheep would also need it, but the mishnah only mentions ewes.
The Gemara resolves that males do not need this because they butt each other, causing the lice to fall off naturally.
Shimon Nezira adds that the wood used is broom-wood (ריתמא).
The Gemara concludes that Rav Huna's explanation fits the term 'chanunot' (from 'chanun' meaning mercy), while the other rabbis' explanations mean we do something to have mercy on them.

items.text: Explanation of 'egel b'gimon'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'egel b'gimon'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that 'gimon' means a yoke. Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse 'halachof k'agmon rosho' that 'gimon' is a term for bending.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'egel b'gimon' means.
Rav Huna explains that 'gimon' means a yoke (בר נירא).
Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse 'halachof k'agmon rosho' that 'gimon' is a term for bending.

items.text: Explanations for cow's hide and strap
items.text_en: Explanations for cow's hide and strap
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the cow's hide (עור הקופר) is to prevent flies from bothering it. Regarding the strap between its horns, it notes a dispute between Rav and Shmuel: Rav forbids both for adornment and protection, while Shmuel forbids only for adornment but permits for protection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the cow's hide (עור הקופר) is placed to prevent flies from bothering the cow.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution of Rav and Shmuel's dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution of Rav and Shmuel's dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute regarding the strap between the cow's horns: Rav forbids both for adornment and protection, while Shmuel forbids only for adornment but permits for protection.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's cow and the principle of responsibility
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's cow and the principle of responsibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah could have only one cow when he tithed 12,000 calves annually. A baraisa explains it was his neighbor's cow, but because he did not protest, it was called by his name. The Gemara then cites a tradition from Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva that one who can protest against his household, city, or the entire world is held accountable. Rav Pappa applies this to the Exilarch's household, and Rabbi Chanina cites a verse about God judging the elders and officers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah could have only one cow when he tithed 12,000 calves annually from his herd.
A baraita answers that the cow was not his but his neighbor's, yet because he did not protest, it was called by his name.

sub.text: Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva's tradition
sub.text_en: Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva's tradition
sub.desc_en: A tradition from Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva teaches that one who can protest against his household, city, or the entire world and does not is held accountable for their sins.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's application and Rabbi Chanina's verse
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's application and Rabbi Chanina's verse
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa applies the principle to the Exilarch's household, and Rabbi Chanina cites a verse about God judging the elders and officers.

items.text: Opening question on the elders' sin
items.text_en: Opening question on the elders' sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what sin the elders committed, and answers that they failed to rebuke the people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what sin the elders committed.
The Gemara answers that the elders sinned by failing to rebuke the ministers.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel: rebuking the exilarch
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel: rebuking the exilarch
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda challenges Shmuel for ignoring a woman's cry, and Shmuel deflects, saying the exilarch Mar Ukva is the proper authority.

sub.desc_en: Sets the scene: Rav Yehuda was sitting before Shmuel when a woman cried out, but Shmuel ignored her.
Rav Yehuda challenges Shmuel by citing the verse that one who stops his ears from the poor man's cry will himself not be answered.
Shmuel deflects with a cryptic remark about cold and hot heads, then points out that Mar Ukva, the head of the court, is present and should handle the matter.

items.text: Prooftext for rebuke
items.text_en: Prooftext for rebuke
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse from Jeremiah commanding the house of David to judge justly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Jeremiah (21:12) commanding the house of David to judge justly, with a warning of divine punishment for evil deeds.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Simon: rebuking the house of the exilarch
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Simon: rebuking the house of the exilarch
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira urges Rabbi Simon to rebuke the house of the exilarch even if they won't listen.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira urges Rabbi Simon to rebuke the house of the exilarch.
Rabbi Simon objects that the house of the exilarch will not accept his rebuke.
Rabbi Zeira insists that Rabbi Simon should rebuke them even if they will not accept it.

items.text: The mark of the tav and the rebuke of the righteous
items.text_en: The mark of the tav and the rebuke of the righteous
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina teaches that God never retracted a good decree except regarding the mark of the tav. The Attribute of Justice argues that the righteous should be punished because they failed to rebuke the wicked, but God responds that the wicked would not have listened, and the Attribute retorts that this was not known to the righteous.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina opens by stating that God never retracted a good decree except regarding the mark of the tav, citing the verse from Ezekiel.
The Gemara elaborates that God instructed Gabriel to mark the righteous with a tav of ink and the wicked with a tav of blood.
The Attribute of Justice objects before God, arguing that the righteous are no different from the wicked because they failed to rebuke the sinners.
God responds that the wicked would not have accepted rebuke, but the Attribute retorts that this was not known to the righteous, leaving the decree unchanged.

items.text: Exegesis of Ezekiel's vision and the six angels
items.text_en: Exegesis of Ezekiel's vision and the six angels
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse about starting from the sanctuary, explaining that it means starting from those who are sanctified, i.e., those who fulfilled the entire Torah. It then identifies the six men as personifications of divine wrath.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of verse and Rav Yosef's teaching
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of verse and Rav Yosef's teaching
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Ezekiel and Rav Yosef's teaching that 'מקדשי' (My sanctuary) should be read as 'מקודשי' (My sanctified ones), referring to those who fulfilled the entire Torah from alef to tav.
The Gemara quotes the continuation of the verse describing the six men coming from the upper gate with weapons, standing by the copper altar.
The Gemara asks why the copper altar was mentioned, and answers that God commanded to start from the place where song is offered before Him.

The Gemara asks who the six men are, and Rav Chisda answers that they are personifications of divine wrath: קֶצֶף (rage), אַף (anger), חֵימָה (fury), מַשְׁחִית (destroyer), מְשַׁבֵּר (breaker), and מְכַלֶּה (finisher).

items.text: Interpretations of the letter tav
items.text_en: Interpretations of the letter tav
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim explain the meaning of the tav: Rav says it stands for 'tichyeh' (live) or 'tamut' (die); Shmuel says 'tammah zechut avot' (the merit of the fathers ended); Rabbi Yochanan says 'tachon zechut avot' (the merit of the fathers is gracious); Reish Lakish says it is the seal of God, which is 'Emet' (truth); Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says it refers to those who fulfilled the Torah from aleph to tav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the letter tav was specifically chosen for the mark.
Rav explains that tav stands for either 'tichyeh' (live) or 'tamut' (die), indicating the fate of the righteous and wicked.
Shmuel explains that tav stands for 'tammah zechut avot' (the merit of the fathers ended).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that tav stands for 'tachon zechut avot' (the merit of the fathers is gracious).
Reish Lakish explains that tav is the final letter of God's seal 'Emet' (truth), citing Rabbi Chanina.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that tav refers to those who fulfilled the entire Torah from aleph to tav.

items.text: When did the merit of the fathers end?
items.text_en: When did the merit of the fathers end?
items.desc_en: Amoraim debate when the merit of the patriarchs ceased: Rav says in the days of Hoshea ben Be'eri; Shmuel says in the days of Chazael; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says in the days of Elijah; Rabbi Yochanan says in the days of Hezekiah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from when the merit of the patriarchs ceased.
Rav says the merit ended in the days of Hoshea ben Be'eri, citing a verse about no one saving Israel.
Shmuel says the merit ended in the days of Chazael, citing a verse about God's mercy for the sake of the patriarchs.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the merit ended in the days of Elijah, citing a verse where Elijah invokes the patriarchs.
Rabbi Yochanan says the merit ended in the days of Hezekiah, citing a verse about zeal of the Lord of Hosts.

items.text: No death without sin, no suffering without transgression
items.text_en: No death without sin, no suffering without transgression
items.desc_en: Rav Ammi states that there is no death without sin and no suffering without transgression, and supports this with biblical verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ammi asserts that there is no death without sin and no suffering without transgression.
The gemara cites a verse from Ezekiel to prove that death requires sin, and a verse from Psalms to prove that suffering requires transgression.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: death without sin
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: death without sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where ministering angels question why Adam was punished with death for a minor sin, while Moses and Aaron, who kept the whole Torah, also died. God responds that death is a common decree for righteous and wicked alike. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar argues that Moses and Aaron died for their own sin at Mei Merivah, implying that without that sin they would not have died.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita in which the ministering angels question God about the death penalty imposed on Adam, and God responds that death is a common decree for all, righteous and wicked alike.

The Gemara explains that Rav Ami's view aligns with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that even Moses and Aaron died due to their own sin at Mei Merivah, implying that without sin they would not have died.

items.text: Four who died by the serpent's counsel
items.text_en: Four who died by the serpent's counsel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing four people who died due to the serpent's original sin: Benjamin, Amram, Jesse, and Kilab. It explains that Jesse is explicitly mentioned in a verse as 'son of Nahash,' meaning son of one who died by the serpent. The Gemara identifies the author of this baraita as Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, contradicting Rav Ammi's view that there is no death without sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing four people who died due to the serpent's counsel, with a scriptural proof for Jesse.
The Gemara questions how Abigail could be called 'daughter of Nahash' when she was actually the daughter of Jesse.
The Gemara explains that 'daughter of Nahash' means daughter of one who died due to the serpent's counsel, not literally the daughter of a man named Nahash.
The Gemara asks who is the tanna of this baraita, noting that it cannot be the tanna of the ministering angels because that view holds that Moses and Aaron also died without sin.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that there is death without sin, thereby refuting Rav Ammi's opinion.

items.text: Reuben did not sin
items.text_en: Reuben did not sin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan argues that anyone who says Reuben sinned with Bilhah is mistaken; the verse 'and he lay with Bilhah' actually means he disrupted his father's bed arrangement. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that Reuben was protected from that sin, and his action was to protest his mother's humiliation. Others say he disrupted two beds—one of the Shekhinah and one of his father.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan asserts that anyone who says Reuben sinned is mistaken, and explains the verse as referring to his rearranging his father's bed.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that Reuben was saved from the sin, and explains his action as a protest against the affront to his mother Leah.
Acherim offer an alternative explanation that Reuben disrupted two beds, one of the Divine Presence and one of his father, as indicated by the plural reading of 'yetzu'ai'.

items.text: Interpretations of 'Pachaz Kamayim'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'Pachaz Kamayim'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents various interpretations of the phrase 'Pachaz kamayim al tosar' from Jacob's blessing to Reuben. Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar HaModai, and Rava (or Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba) each offer different readings, interpreting the letters as acronyms for various meanings, such as 'you were hasty,' 'you sinned,' or 'you prayed.'

sub.desc_en: Introduces the dispute among Tanna'im over the interpretation of the phrase 'Pachaz kamayim al tosar'.
Rabbi Eliezer interprets the letters of 'pachaz' as 'you were impulsive, you were liable, you acted contemptuously'.
Rabbi Yehoshua interprets the letters as 'you trampled the law, you sinned, you were promiscuous'.
Rabban Gamliel interprets the letters as referring to Reuben's repentance: 'you prayed, you trembled, your prayer shone forth'.
Rabban Gamliel states that we still need the explanation of the Modaite.
Rabbi Elazar HaModai reverses the letters of 'pachaz' and interprets: 'you shook, you recoiled, sin flew from you'.
Rava (or Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba) reverses the letters and interprets: 'you remembered the punishment, you made yourself ill, you withdrew from sinning'.

items.text: The sons of Eli did not sin
items.text_en: The sons of Eli did not sin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan states that anyone who says the sons of Eli sinned is mistaken, as the verse equates Chofni and Pinchas, and Pinchas did not sin. Rav explains that the verse 'who lay with the women' means they delayed the women's offerings, and the Torah considers it as if they lay with them.

sub.desc_en: Introduces a mnemonic listing the names of biblical figures whose sins will be discussed.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan asserts that anyone who says the sons of Eli sinned is mistaken, citing the verse that lists both Chofni and Pinchas as priests of the Lord.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yonatan follows Rav's view that Pinchas did not sin, and the juxtaposition of Chofni to Pinchas implies Chofni also did not sin; the verse about lying with women is interpreted as delaying their offerings, which the Torah treats as if they lay with them.

items.text: Proof that Pinchas did not sin
items.text_en: Proof that Pinchas did not sin
items.desc_en: Rav argues that Pinchas did not sin, as the verse traces his lineage, implying he was righteous. The Gemara supports this with a verse about cutting off those who sin, and concludes that Pinchas is not included. It addresses apparent contradictions: the verse 'who lay' is read as 'yishkaven' (a different form), 'my sons' is read as 'beni' (my son), and 'they cause to pass' is read as 'ma'aviram' (they cause them to pass). The Gemara concludes that Pinchas is called a 'son of Belial' only because he failed to protest Chofni's actions.

sub.desc_en: Rav asserts that Pinehas did not sin, citing the verse that traces his lineage, implying his righteousness.
The Gemara supports Rav by citing the verse that those who sin will be cut off from having descendants who are scholars or priests, implying Pinehas did not sin.
The Gemara raises an objection from the verse 'who lay' in the plural, and resolves it by noting it is written as 'yishkaven' in the singular.
The Gemara objects with the verse 'my sons' in the plural, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that it is written as 'beni' (my son) in the singular.
The Gemara objects with the verse 'they cause to pass' in the plural, and Rav Huna answers that it is written as 'ma'aviram' in the singular.
The Gemara resolves the final objection by explaining that Pinehas is called a 'son of Belial' only because he failed to protest Chofni's actions, and the verse ascribes it to him as if he sinned.

items.text: Beginning of a new statement about the sons of Samuel
items.text_en: Beginning of a new statement about the sons of Samuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement by Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, but it is cut off. This section likely continues the pattern of defending biblical figures from accusations of sin.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani begins a statement in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, introducing a general principle about those who claim a biblical figure sinned, but the statement is cut off.

items.text: Defense of Samuel's sons
items.text_en: Defense of Samuel's sons
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that Samuel's sons did not sin, interpreting the verse 'they did not walk in his ways' to mean they did not follow his practice of traveling to judge, but they did not commit actual sin. Their 'turning after gain' refers only to their failure to emulate their father's selfless judging.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that anyone who says Samuel's sons sinned is mistaken, interpreting the verse 'they did not walk in his ways' to mean they did not follow his practice but did not actually sin.

The Gemara explains that the phrase 'they turned after gain' refers only to their failure to emulate their father Samuel, who traveled to judge in all places, while they stayed in their cities to increase fees for their officers and scribes.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on Samuel's sons' sin
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on Samuel's sons' sin
items.desc_en: A baraita presents four Tannaitic interpretations of 'they turned after gain': Rabbi Meir says they demanded their share verbally; Rabbi Yehuda says they imposed a burden on homeowners; Rabbi Akiva says they took an extra tithe basket by force; Rabbi Yosei says they took gifts by force.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute on the verse 'they turned after gain', citing Rabbi Meir's opinion that they demanded their portion verbally.
Rabbi Yehuda says they imposed a burden on homeowners.
Rabbi Akiva says they took an extra basket of tithe by force.
Rabbi Yosei says they took gifts by force.

items.text: Defense of David from sin with Bathsheba
items.text_en: Defense of David from sin with Bathsheba
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan argues that anyone who says David sinned is mistaken, citing the verse that God was with him. The verse 'why did you despise the word of God to do evil' is interpreted to mean he only sought to do evil but did not actually do it.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan asserts that anyone who says David sinned is mistaken, citing the verse that God was with David.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'Why did you despise the word of the Lord to do evil' means David intended to do evil but did not actually do it.

items.text: Rav's defense of David and the get for soldiers
items.text_en: Rav's defense of David and the get for soldiers
items.desc_en: Rav notes that Rabbi, a descendant of David, interprets the verse in David's favor: 'to do evil' implies he only intended but did not act. The verse about Uriah is explained: David should have tried him in Sanhedrin but didn't, and his marriage to Bathsheba was valid because soldiers in David's army gave conditional divorces, as taught by Rabbi Yonatan.

sub.desc_en: Rav introduces Rabbi's defense of David, interpreting the verse 'to do evil' as indicating David only intended but did not act.
Rabbi explains that David should have tried Uriah in Sanhedrin but didn't, and that his marriage to Bathsheba was valid.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan teaches that soldiers in David's army wrote conditional divorces (גט כריתות) for their wives, citing a verse about David's provisions.
Rav Yosef explains that 'עֲרֻבָּתָם' refers to matters mixed between husband and wife, i.e., the conditional divorce arrangement.

items.text: Defense regarding Uriah's death
items.text_en: Defense regarding Uriah's death
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that David was not punished for Uriah's death because Uriah was a rebel against the king, as evidenced by his statement 'my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are encamped in the open field,' implying he should have been with the army.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'and him you killed with the sword of the children of Ammon' to mean that just as one is not punished for killing with the sword of Ammon, so David is not punished for Uriah's death.
The Gemara explains the reason: Uriah was a rebel against the kingdom, as he said 'my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field'.

items.text: Rav's final assessment of David's sin
items.text_en: Rav's final assessment of David's sin
items.desc_en: Rav concludes that when you examine David, you find no sin except regarding Uriah, as the verse says 'only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.'

sub.desc_en: Rav concludes that when you examine David, you find no sin except the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

items.text: Dispute over whether David accepted slander
items.text_en: Dispute over whether David accepted slander
items.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction: Rav said David accepted slander (about Mephibosheth from Ziba), but earlier Rav defended David. The Gemara explains: Rav indeed said David accepted slander, but Shmuel argues he did not, because he saw clear signs (Mephibosheth's unkempt appearance) that corroborated Ziba's report.

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction: Rav said David accepted slander, but earlier Rav defended David.
Rav explains that David accepted Ziba's slander about Mephibosheth, citing verses where David gave Ziba Mephibosheth's property.
Shmuel argues David did not accept slander because he saw clear signs (Mephibosheth's unkempt appearance) that corroborated Ziba's report.

items.text: David's judgment of Mephibosheth and the Bat Kol
items.text_en: David's judgment of Mephibosheth and the Bat Kol
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts David's division of the field between Mephibosheth and Ziba, and Mephibosheth's response. A Bat Kol rebukes David, linking his action to the future division of the kingdom between Rehoboam and Jeroboam. The name 'Merib-baal' is explained as indicating Mephibosheth's quarrel with his master.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts David's judgment dividing the field between Mephibosheth and Ziba, and Mephibosheth's response blaming the one who brought David back in peace.
The Gemara explains that Mephibosheth's name 'Merib-baal' indicates his quarrel with his master, and a Bat Kol rebukes David, linking his action to the future division of the kingdom.

items.text: Bat Kol's prophecy about the divided kingdom
items.text_en: Bat Kol's prophecy about the divided kingdom
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that when David told Mephibosheth to divide the field with Ziba, a Bat Kol declared that Rehoboam and Jeroboam would divide the kingdom.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav reports that when David divided the field, a Bat Kol declared that Rehoboam and Jeroboam would divide the kingdom.

items.text: Consequences of David accepting slander
items.text_en: Consequences of David accepting slander
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav asserts that had David not accepted slander, the kingdom of David would not have been divided, Israel would not have worshipped idols, and they would not have been exiled.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that had David not accepted slander, the kingdom would not have split, Israel would not have worshipped idolatry, and they would not have been exiled.

items.text: Solomon's alleged sin: defense and reinterpretation
items.text_en: Solomon's alleged sin: defense and reinterpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan argues that Solomon did not sin, citing the verse that his heart was not fully with God 'like the heart of David his father.' The Gemara reconciles contradictory verses by explaining that Solomon's wives turned his heart to follow other gods, but he did not actually go; he only intended to build altars but did not. A difficulty is raised from Joshua, and the Gemara resolves it by citing a baraita that attributes the altars to a later king. Finally, the verse 'Solomon did evil' is explained as a result of his failure to rebuke his wives.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan asserts that anyone who says Solomon sinned is mistaken, citing the verse that his heart was not fully with God 'like the heart of David his father' — implying he did not sin.

The Gemara raises a difficulty from the verse that Solomon's wives turned his heart, and resolves it by citing Rabbi Natan's interpretation that the verse means they turned his heart to go after other gods, but he did not actually go.
The Gemara raises another difficulty from the verse that Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, and answers that he only intended to build but did not actually build.

The Gemara objects by analogy to Joshua: if 'then built' means only intended, then Joshua's building of an altar would also be only intended, which is impossible since he clearly built it; so Solomon must have built as well.

The Gemara resolves the objection by citing a baraita of Rabbi Yosei, which explains that the verse about Solomon's high places refers to a later king (Menasseh) who built them, and the verse attributes them to Solomon only as a literary device — comparing earlier kings to later ones for praise or blame.
The Gemara addresses the verse that Solomon did evil in God's eyes, explaining that because he failed to rebuke his wives, Scripture considers him as if he sinned, though he did not actually sin.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel on Solomon's reputation
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel on Solomon's reputation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel laments that it would have been better for Solomon to serve a different role than to have it written that he did evil.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel remarks that it would have been better for that righteous man (Solomon) to be a servant to something else than to have it written that he did evil in God's eyes.

items.text: Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter and its consequences
items.text_en: Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter and its consequences
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel describes how Solomon's wife, Pharaoh's daughter, brought a thousand musical instruments and taught him idolatrous practices, and he did not rebuke her. Another tradition states that when Solomon married her, Gabriel planted a reed in the sea, which grew into a sandbank that became the great city of Rome. A baraita adds that on the day Jeroboam set up the golden calves, a hut was built that became the Italy of Greece.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel reports that when Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter, she brought a thousand musical instruments and taught him idolatrous practices, and he did not rebuke her.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel (second tradition)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel (second tradition)
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel adds that when Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter, Gabriel planted a reed in the sea, which grew into a sandbank that became the great city of Rome.
A baraita adds that on the day Jeroboam set up the golden calves, a hut was built that became the Italy of Greece.

items.text: Josiah's righteousness and repentance
items.text_en: Josiah's righteousness and repentance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan argues that Josiah did not sin, citing the verse that he walked in the way of David. The verse about his repentance is explained as referring to his returning property from age eight to eighteen, giving from his own. This disagrees with Rav, who said Josiah was the greatest penitent of his generation. Rav Yosef adds another penitent in his generation, Ukban bar Nechemya, the Exilarch, and recounts a dream about him.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan declares that anyone who says Josiah sinned is mistaken, citing the verse that he walked in all the way of David his father.
The gemara asks how to reconcile the verse that says no king before Josiah repented as he did, if he never sinned.
The gemara explains that the repentance refers to returning property from age eight to eighteen, giving from his own, not from others.
Rav disagrees, stating that Josiah was the greatest penitent in his generation, and identifies another penitent in his own generation.
Rav Yosef adds another penitent in his generation, Ukban bar Nechemya the Exilarch, and recounts a dream about him.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Prohibited ornaments
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Prohibited ornaments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items a woman may not wear into the public domain on Shabbat, including wool and linen threads, straps, a totefet, sarbitin, a kabul, a golden city, a necklace, earrings, a signet ring, and a non-perforated needle. If she does go out with these, she is not liable to bring a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibited ornaments for a woman on Shabbat and states she is not liable for a sin-offering if she goes out with them.

items.text: Gemara's question on immersion and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's question on immersion and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions immersion (טְבִילָה) in the context of Shabbat. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the reason a woman may not go out with wool and linen threads is that the Sages said she may not immerse with them on a weekday until she loosens them; on Shabbat, she might need to perform a mitzvah immersion and untie them, leading her to carry them four cubits in the public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions immersion (טְבִילָה) in the context of Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the Mishnah's mention of immersion is the reason (מַה טַּעַם) why a woman may not go out with wool and linen threads: on a weekday she may not immerse with them until she loosens them, and on Shabbat she might need to perform a mitzvah immersion (טְבִילָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה) and untie them, leading her to carry them four cubits in the public domain.

items.text: Discussion of woven hairnets (תִּיכֵי חֲלִילָתָא)
items.text_en: Discussion of woven hairnets (תִּיכֵי חֲלִילָתָא)
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav about woven hairnets (תִּיכֵי חֲלִילָתָא). Rav responds that anything woven was not prohibited. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua confirms this, and an alternative version states that he observed his sisters were not particular about them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav about the status of woven hairnets (תִּיכֵי חֲלִילָתָא) regarding the prohibition of going out on Shabbat.
Rav responds that anything woven (אָרִיג) was not prohibited by the Sages' decree.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua confirms the same principle: anything woven was not prohibited.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Huna bar Yehoshua observed his sisters were not particular about these hairnets, implying they are not considered a significant adornment.

items.text: Distinction between the two versions of Rav Huna's statement
items.text_en: Distinction between the two versions of Rav Huna's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two versions of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's statement. It answers that the difference applies when the hairnets are dirty: according to the first version, since they are woven they are permitted; according to the second version, since she is particular about them when dirty, they are prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two versions of Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's statement.

The Gemara answers that the difference applies when the hairnets are dirty: according to the first version, since they are woven they are permitted; according to the second version, since she is particular about them when dirty, they are prohibited.

items.text: Baraita on interpositions and Rav Yosef's explanation
items.text_en: Baraita on interpositions and Rav Yosef's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing items that interpose (חוֹצְצִין) during immersion: wool and linen threads and straps on girls' heads. Rabbi Yehuda says wool and hair do not interpose because water flows through them. Rav Huna states that this applies only to the head. Rav Yosef challenges this, questioning what is excluded, and concludes that the reason is that a woman does not tighten them to the point of choking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing items that interpose (חוֹצְצִין) during immersion, including wool and linen threads and straps on girls' heads, with Rabbi Yehuda's exception for wool and hair.
Rav Huna states that all these items were taught only regarding the heads of girls, not other body parts.
Rav Yosef challenges Rav Huna's limitation, questioning what is excluded, and argues that if soft wool on hard head interposes, then soft on soft (neck) certainly should.
Rav Yosef alternatively argues that if hard linen on hard head interposes, then hard on soft (neck) certainly should.
Rav Yosef resolves that Rav Huna's reason is that a woman does not tighten the straps on her neck to the point of choking, so they do not interpose.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Ravina's response
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Ravina's response
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rav Yosef's reasoning by citing a baraita that girls may go out with threads in their ears but not with bands around their necks. If a woman does not choke herself, why are neck bands prohibited? Ravina begins to respond, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rav Yosef's reasoning by citing a baraita that girls may go out with threads in their ears but not with bands around their necks, arguing that if a woman does not choke herself, neck bands should also be permitted.
Ravina begins to respond to Abaye's objection, but the text cuts off before his full answer is recorded.

items.text: Context: the case of a woman choking herself
items.text_en: Context: the case of a woman choking herself
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier discussion involves a woman who tightens a strap around herself to appear plump, so it is not a permanent ornament.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case involves a woman tightening a strap (קטלא) around herself to appear plump, so it is not a permanent ornament and is forbidden.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on wool and hair threads
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on wool and hair threads
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that both wool and hair threads do not interpose because water penetrates them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that wool and hair threads do not form a חציצה (interposition) because water can penetrate them.

items.text: Rav Yosef's ruling and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding hair threads. Abaye questions whether this implies the Sages disagree, and the Gemara considers that Rabbi Yehuda might have said 'just as' to gain agreement on wool.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding hair threads.
Abaye challenges Rav Yosef: saying 'the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda' implies that the Sages disagree with him.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda may have said 'just as' to gain the Sages' agreement on wool threads, not that they originally disagreed on hair threads.

items.text: Rav Nachman's statement and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda on hair threads. A baraita confirms this, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves from the Mishnah that the Sages do not dispute hair threads.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states in the name of Shmuel that the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda regarding hair threads (חוטי שיער).
A baraita is cited that supports Rav Nachman's statement: wool threads interpose, hair threads do not, and Rabbi Yehuda says neither interpose.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves from the Mishnah itself that the Sages do not dispute hair threads, since the Mishnah permits a woman to go out with hair threads, which cannot be according to Rabbi Yehuda (who would permit even wool threads), so it must be according to the Sages.

items.text: Definition of טוטפת and related ornaments
items.text_en: Definition of טוטפת and related ornaments
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines טוטפת as a headband (אפוזייני) and cites a baraita listing permitted ornaments. Rabbi Avahu distinguishes between טוטפת (ear to ear) and סרביטין (reaching the cheeks). Rav Huna notes that poor women make them from colored materials, rich from silver and gold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'טוטפת' (headband) refers to.
Rav Yosef defines it as a 'חומרא דקטיפתא' (a type of ornamental headband).
Abaye objects that if it were a 'חומרא דקטיפתא', it would be like an expert amulet and thus permitted, contradicting the Mishnah's prohibition.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Abaye defines 'טוטפת' as a headband (אפוזייני).
A baraita supports this definition, listing 'טוטפת' and 'סרביטין' as permitted ornaments.
The Gemara asks for the distinction between 'טוטפת' and 'סרביטין'.
Rabbi Avahu explains: 'טוטפת' encircles from ear to ear, while 'סרביטין' reach down to the cheeks.
Rav Huna notes that poor women make these ornaments from colored materials, while rich women make them from silver and gold.

items.text: Definition of כבול and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling
items.text_en: Definition of כבול and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai questions whether כבול refers to a slave's chain or a wool cap. Rabbi Avahu concludes it is a wool cap, and a baraita states that a woman may go out with a כבול and איסטאמא in a courtyard, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits even in the public domain for items below the hairnet.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai questions whether the forbidden item כבול refers to a slave's chain (כבלא דעבדא) or a wool cap (כיפה של צמר), and whether the latter would be permitted.

Rabbi Avahu resolves that the Mishnah refers to a wool cap (כיפה של צמר), and a supporting baraita states that a woman may go out with a כבול and איסטאמא in a courtyard, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits even in the public domain for items below the hairnet.

items.text: Definition of איסטאמא and its halakhic properties
items.text_en: Definition of איסטאמא and its halakhic properties
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu defines איסטאמא as ביזיוני, which Abaye explains as a flying sieve. A baraita lists three halakhot about איסטאמא: no kilayim, no impurity from negaim, and it may not be worn in the public domain. Rabbi Shimon adds another ruling (cut off).

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks what the term 'איסטאמא' (a type of head covering) means.
Rabbi Avahu answers that איסטאמא is ביזיוני (a type of cheap head covering).
The gemara asks what 'ביזיוני' means.
Abaye explains in the name of Rav that ביזיוני is a flying sieve (a cheap, net-like head covering).
A baraita lists three halakhot about איסטאמא: no kilayim, no impurity from negaim, and it may not be worn in the public domain.
The baraita begins to add another ruling in the name of Rabbi Shimon, but the text is cut off here.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a bride's crown is not prohibited, setting the context for the discussion about seals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a bride's crown is not prohibited, setting the context for the discussion about seals.

items.text: Shmuel's statement and resolution of contradiction
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement and resolution of contradiction
items.desc_en: Shmuel says the Mishnah refers to a slave's collar, but a contradiction arises from his other statement. The Gemara resolves it by distinguishing between a seal made by the master and one made by the slave.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel asserts that the Mishnah refers to a slave's collar (כבלא דעבדא).
The Gemara questions Shmuel's consistency, citing his own ruling that a slave may go out with a seal on his neck but not on his garment.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a seal made by the master (permitted) and one made by the slave (forbidden).

items.text: Challenge to the resolution and support from Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef
items.text_en: Challenge to the resolution and support from Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution: if the seal is made by the master, why is a garment seal prohibited? It explains due to concern that the slave might fold it and carry it, citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's ruling about a folded cloak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution: if the seal is made by the master, why is a garment seal prohibited?
The Gemara explains the concern: the slave might fear the seal will break, fold the garment, and carry it on his shoulder.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports this concern by citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's ruling that one who goes out with a folded cloak on his shoulder on שבת (the Sabbath) is liable for a sin-offering.

items.text: Shmuel's instruction to Rav Chinana bar Sheilat
items.text_en: Shmuel's instruction to Rav Chinana bar Sheilat
items.desc_en: Shmuel tells Rav Chinana bar Sheilat that all the rabbis of the Exilarch's house should not go out with sealed cloaks except for him, as they are not particular about him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's instruction to Rav Chinana bar Sheilat that all the rabbis of the Exilarch's house should not go out with sealed cloaks except for him, as they are not particular about him.

items.text: Baraita supporting Shmuel and contradictory baraita
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Shmuel and contradictory baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Shmuel's ruling. Another baraita contradicts it, stating that a slave may not go out with any seal, and also discusses animal seals and bells.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Shmuel and supporting baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Shmuel and supporting baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's ruling that a slave may go out with a seal around his neck but not on his clothes, and a baraita supports this.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that prohibits a slave from going out with any seal, and discusses bells and ritual impurity.
The contradictory baraita further rules that an animal may not go out with any seal or bell, and none of these can become ritually impure.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction: metal vs. clay seals
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction: metal vs. clay seals
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests the distinction between master-made and slave-made, but rejects it. It resolves by distinguishing metal seals (prohibited) from clay seals (permitted), supported by Rav Nachman's principle and a proof from impurity laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the contradiction between the baraitot can be resolved by distinguishing between a seal made by the master (permitted) and one made by the slave himself (prohibited).

The Gemara rejects this suggestion, asserting that both baraitot refer to a seal made by the master, and instead distinguishes between a metal seal (prohibited) and a clay seal (permitted), citing Rav Nachman's principle about the master's concern.

The Gemara provides a proof from the baraita's statement that both seals cannot become ritually impure, arguing that if it were clay, even vessels of clay would not become impure, but the baraita implies that vessels of the same material can become impure, so it must be metal.
The Gemara objects: if the baraita referred to clay seals, then the inference that vessels of the same material can become impure would be impossible, since clay vessels cannot become impure.
The Gemara cites a baraita that vessels of stone, dung, and earth cannot become impure, concluding that the baraita must be referring to metal seals, and affirms this conclusion.

items.text: Discussion of the bell (zog) for a slave
items.text_en: Discussion of the bell (zog) for a slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a bell on the neck is prohibited but on the garment is permitted, and answers that it is securely attached (mumcha) and follows Rav Huna's principle that woven items are not subject to decree.

sub.desc_en: Mar states the baraita's ruling: a slave may not go out with a bell on his neck but may go out with a bell on his garment.
The Gemara questions why a bell on the neck is prohibited, suggesting the concern is that it might break off and the slave will bring it in his hand.
The Gemara objects that the same concern should apply to a bell on the garment, yet it is permitted.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a bell that is securely attached (מומחא), so it will not break off.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's principle
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara invokes Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's principle that anything woven into the garment was not subject to the rabbinic decree, explaining why a bell on the garment is permitted.

items.text: Animal seals and bells: impurity contradiction
items.text_en: Animal seals and bells: impurity contradiction
items.desc_en: The baraita states that animal bells do not receive impurity, but a contradictory source says they do. The Gemara begins to address this contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that an animal may not go out with a seal or bell on its neck or garment, and these items do not receive impurity.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: a bell of an animal is taught as impure, contradicting the baraita that says it does not receive impurity.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Bell impurity rules
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Bell impurity rules
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a door bell is pure, but if made for an animal it becomes impure. An animal bell repurposed for a door remains impure even if attached with nails, because vessels become impure through intention but only leave impurity through a physical change.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the impurity rules for bells: a door bell is pure, an animal bell is impure, and repurposing an animal bell for a door does not remove its impurity without a physical change.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: Bell with vs. without clapper
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: Bell with vs. without clapper
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between a bell with a clapper (עינבל) and one without. It cites Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan that a sound-producing metal vessel is impure, based on a verse about fire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a bell with a clapper (עינבל) and one without.
The Gemara objects: if it is a vessel, it should be impure even without a clapper; if not, can a clapper make it a vessel?

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara affirms, citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan, that a sound-producing metal vessel is impure based on the verse 'כל דבר אשר יבא באש' (everything that comes into fire), implying even sound is subject to impurity.

items.text: Challenge from the middle clause
items.text_en: Challenge from the middle clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution: if the bell lacks a clapper, how can the Mishnah say both types (neck bell and garment bell) are impure?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution: if the bell lacks a clapper (עינבל), how can the Mishnah's middle clause say both types (neck bell and garment bell) are impure?

items.text: Second baraita and resolution: Child vs. adult
items.text_en: Second baraita and resolution: Child vs. adult
items.desc_en: A baraita states that bells for a mortar, cradle, or book/towel covers are impure only if they have a clapper. The Gemara resolves: for a child, the bell is for sound, so without a clapper it is not a vessel; for an adult, it is an ornament and impure even without a clapper.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: bells made for a mortar, cradle, or book/towel covers are impure only if they have a clapper; if the clapper is removed, impurity remains.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: for a child, the bell is for sound, so without a clapper it is not a vessel; for an adult, it is an ornament and impure even without a clapper.

items.text: Abaye's explanation: Clapper can be reattached
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation: Clapper can be reattached
items.desc_en: The baraita says that if the clappers are removed, impurity remains. Abaye explains: because a layperson can reattach it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what purpose are the clappers still useful after being removed, such that they retain impurity?
Abaye answers: Because a layperson can reattach the clapper, it retains its status as a vessel and thus its impurity.

items.text: Rava's objection and Rabba's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Rabba's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a mishna that the bell and clapper are a 'connection' (חבור). Rabba explains that by Torah law, during use they are connected for both impurity and sprinkling, but not when not in use; a decree was made to unify the rules.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects by citing a mishna that states the bell and clapper are a 'connection' (חבור) for impurity.
The gemara suggests that the mishna might mean it is considered as if connected, but then cites a baraita that distinguishes between connection for impurity and for sprinkling.
The gemara questions the baraita: if it is a connection, it should apply to sprinkling too; if not, it should not apply to impurity either.
Rabba resolves that by Torah law, during use it is a connection for both impurity and sprinkling, but not when not in use; a decree was made to unify the rules.

items.text: Rava's alternative answer
items.text_en: Rava's alternative answer
items.desc_en: Rava offers his own resolution to the difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rava offers his own resolution to the difficulty.

items.text: Debate on the use of a shoe last
items.text_en: Debate on the use of a shoe last
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two opinions on why a shoe last is susceptible to impurity: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina says it is fit for striking earthenware, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is fit for giving water to an infant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the reason a shoe last is susceptible to impurity: because it is fit for striking earthenware.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that the shoe last is fit for striking earthenware.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the shoe last is fit for giving water to an infant.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan and the principle of 'stand and we will do our work'
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan and the principle of 'stand and we will do our work'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's view, citing a baraita that an object designated for sitting is impure only if it is not used as a temporary seat. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan debate whether this principle applies to midras impurity or also to impurity from a corpse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's view by citing a baraita that an object designated for sitting is impure only if it is not a temporary seat, implying that the principle of 'stand and we will do our work' applies.
Rabbi Elazar limits the principle of 'stand and we will do our work' to midras impurity, not to impurity from a corpse.
Rabbi Yochanan extends the principle of 'stand and we will do our work' also to impurity from a corpse.

items.text: Attempt to reverse the arguments
items.text_en: Attempt to reverse the arguments
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests reversing the earlier opinions, but questions why one would reverse the first set rather than the second.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes reversing the earlier opinions and questions why one would reverse the first set rather than the second.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Yochanan requires a use similar to the original craft
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Yochanan requires a use similar to the original craft
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a metal sandal for an animal, where Rabbi Yochanan says it is fit for running from battle over thorns, showing he requires a use akin to the original function.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that we have already heard that Rabbi Yochanan requires a use similar to the original craft (מעין מלאכה ראשונה).

The Gemara cites a baraita about a metal sandal for an animal, which is טמא (ritually impure), and the opinions of Rav, Rabbi Chanina, and Rabbi Yochanan on its use, with Rabbi Yochanan saying it is fit for running from battle over thorns and briars.

items.text: Differences between the opinions on the metal sandal
items.text_en: Differences between the opinions on the metal sandal
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes the practical differences between Rav and Rabbi Chanina (disgust) and between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina (weight).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rav and Rabbi Chanina regarding the metal sandal.
The Gemara answers that between Rav and Rabbi Chanina the difference is disgust (מאיס), and between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina the difference is weight (יקיר).

items.text: Introduction of the golden city of Jerusalem
items.text_en: Introduction of the golden city of Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss the mishnah's exclusion of a golden city ornament, citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it refers to a golden Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishnah's exclusion of a golden city ornament refers to.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites Rabbi Yochanan that the golden city ornament is a representation of Jerusalem made of gold.

items.text: Opening anecdote about Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a brief anecdote about what Rabbi Akiva did for his wife, setting the stage for the discussion on jewelry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a brief anecdote about what Rabbi Akiva did for his wife, setting the stage for the discussion on jewelry.

items.text: Baraita on the city of gold and the dispute
items.text_en: Baraita on the city of gold and the dispute
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute about a woman going out with a 'city of gold' (עיר של זהב). Rabbi Meir holds she is liable for a sin-offering, the Sages say she is exempt but it is forbidden, and Rabbi Eliezer permits it initially. The Gemara explains the reasoning behind each opinion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents three opinions: Rabbi Meir holds a woman is liable for a sin-offering if she goes out with a 'city of gold'; the Sages say she is exempt but it is forbidden; Rabbi Eliezer permits it לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara asks: On what basis do they disagree?

The Gemara explains: Rabbi Meir considers it a burden (משוי), the Sages consider it an ornament but fear she might remove and show it and come to carry it, and Rabbi Eliezer holds that a woman who wears a 'city of gold' is important and will not remove and show it.

items.text: Dispute about the wreath (כלילא)
items.text_en: Dispute about the wreath (כלילא)
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the 'wreath' (כלילא), with Rav forbidding it and Shmuel permitting it. It distinguishes between a 'woven' (אניסכא) and 'embroidered' (ארוקתא) wreath, with different opinions on which is the primary concern. Rav Ashi presents a lenient version of the dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a dispute about the wreath (כלילא): Rav forbids it and Shmuel permits it.

The Gemara explains that all agree a woven wreath (אניסכא) is forbidden; the dispute is about an embroidered wreath (ארוקתא), with one side considering the woven type primary and the other considering the embroidered type primary.

Rav Ashi presents a lenient version of the dispute: all agree the embroidered wreath is permitted; the dispute is about the woven wreath, with one side concerned she might remove and show it (leading to carrying) and the other side saying a distinguished woman does not remove and show it.
