items.text: Rav's lenient ruling and Levi's arrival
items.text_en: Rav's lenient ruling and Levi's arrival
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chanah reports that Rav explicitly permitted the wreath. The Gemara recounts that a great man (Levi) came to Nehardea and taught that the wreath is permitted, leading Rav to deduce that Rabbi Apas had died and Rabbi Chanina had succeeded him, based on a verse about the righteous.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chanah to Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chanah to Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar bar Chanah reports to Rav Yosef that Rav explicitly permitted the wreath (כלילא).
People tell Rav that a great man (Levi) came to Nehardea and taught that the wreath is permitted; Rav deduces that Rabbi Apas died and Rabbi Chanina succeeded him, so Levi came here.

The Gemara objects: perhaps Rabbi Chanina died and Rabbi Apas remained, and Levi came for another reason; the Gemara rejects this because Levi would have deferred to Rabbi Apas, and Rabbi Chanina was appointed by Rabbi's dying wish, as the verse about the righteous confirms.

items.text: Levi's and Rabbah bar Avuha's rulings
items.text_en: Levi's and Rabbah bar Avuha's rulings
items.desc_en: Levi taught in Nehardea that the wreath is permitted, resulting in 24 wreaths being removed. Rabbah bar Avuha taught similarly in Mechoza, resulting in 18 wreaths from one alley.

sub.text: Story of Levi and Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Story of Levi and Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Levi taught in Nehardea that a crown is permitted, and 24 crowns were removed; Rabbah bar Avuha taught similarly in Mechoza, and 18 crowns were removed from one alley.
Reports that Rabbah bar Avuha taught similarly in Mechoza, resulting in 18 wreaths from a single alley.

items.text: Discussion of קמרא (belt) and related items
items.text_en: Discussion of קמרא (belt) and related items
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah quotes Rav Shmuel permitting a 'קמרא' (belt). Two versions are given: one identifies it with an embroidered item (ארוקתא) on a gold-embroidered cloak, the other with a woven item (אניסכא) on a king's girdle. Ravina asks Rav Ashi about a קמרא above the belt, and Rav Ashi says that is two belts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah quotes Rav Shmuel permitting a קמרא (belt).
One version identifies the קמרא with an embroidered item (ארוקתא) on a gold-embroidered cloak, as explained by Rav Safra.
Another version identifies the קמרא with a woven item (אניסכא) on a king's girdle, as explained by Rav Safra.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi about the status of a קמרא worn above the belt.
Rav Ashi responds that wearing a קמרא above the belt constitutes two belts, implying it is prohibited.

items.text: Rav Ashi on רסוקא (garter)
items.text_en: Rav Ashi on רסוקא (garter)
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that a 'רסוקא' (garter) is permitted if it has 'מפרחייתא' (something that makes it fly?), otherwise it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules: Regarding a chain necklace (רסוקא), if it has a clasp (מפרחייתא) it is permitted; if not, it is forbidden.

items.text: Discussion of קטלא (necklace), rings, and impurity
items.text_en: Discussion of קטלא (necklace), rings, and impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions 'קטלא' (necklace), 'נזמים' (earrings), and a ring without a seal. The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita listing these as susceptible to impurity, including a ring with or without a seal. Rabbi Zeira resolves it by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Nechemiah and the baraita to the Rabbis, citing a dispute about following the seal or the band.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's 'קטלא' (necklace) means a nose-ring, and 'נזמים' (earrings) means nose-rings.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a ring with a seal is not considered a תכשיט (ornament) and thus one is liable for carrying it on Shabbat.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita listing women's ornaments susceptible to impurity, which includes a ring whether or not it has a seal.
Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Nechemiah and the baraita to the Rabbis.
A baraita is cited showing the dispute: the Rabbis rule that a ring's impurity follows the band, while Rabbi Nechemiah rules that it follows the seal, supporting the attribution.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rules for following the fastener
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rules for following the fastener
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a kolav (a type of key) one follows the nails, for a ladder one follows the rungs, and for a cradle one follows the chains. The Sages say everything follows the main support.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for following the fastener of a kolav, a ladder, and a cradle, with the Sages ruling that everything follows the main support.

items.text: Gemara: Rava and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak on the principle
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak on the principle
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah refers to sides: if a ring has a seal it is a man's ornament, if not it is a woman's ornament. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that impurity and Shabbat are different: for impurity the Torah said 'a vessel of work' and it is a vessel, but for Shabbat the Torah forbids a burden, so without a seal it is an ornament, with a seal it is a burden.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's ruling is relative to sides: a ring with a seal is a man's ornament, without a seal it is a woman's ornament.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that impurity and Shabbat are different domains: for impurity the Torah requires 'a vessel of work' and the ring is a vessel, but for Shabbat the Torah forbids a burden, so without a seal it is an ornament, with a seal it is a burden.

items.text: Discussion of a non-perforated needle
items.text_en: Discussion of a non-perforated needle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what a non-perforated needle is used for. Rav Yosef says because a woman parts her hair with it. Abaye objects that it should be like a pure birith and be permitted. Rav Adda Narshaha explains before Rav Yosef that a woman splits her hair with it. Rava explains its Shabbat use: she has a gold plate on her head; on weekdays she splits her hair with it, on Shabbat she places it opposite her forehead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what a non-perforated needle is used for, since it cannot be used for sewing.
Rav Yosef answers that a woman uses it to gather her hair.
Abaye objects that if the needle is used like a pure birith (a hairpin), it should be permitted as a woman's ornament.

sub.text: Rav Adda Narshaha's explanation before Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Adda Narshaha's explanation before Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda Narshaha explains before Rav Yosef that the needle is used for parting hair, not gathering it, thereby addressing Abaye's objection.
The Gemara asks what the needle is used for on Shabbat, since parting hair is a weekday activity.
Rava answers that a woman has a gold plate on her head; on weekdays she parts her hair with the needle, but on Shabbat she places it opposite her forehead as an ornament.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibitions on going out with certain items
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibitions on going out with certain items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man may not go out with a nailed sandal, nor with a single sandal if he has no wound on his foot, nor with tefillin, nor with an amulet that is not from an expert, nor with armor, helmet, or greaves. If he went out, he is not liable for a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions on going out with certain items on Shabbat, including a nailed sandal, a single sandal without a wound, tefillin, a non-expert amulet, armor, helmet, and greaves, with no sin-offering liability.

items.text: Gemara: The reason for the decree against nailed sandals
items.text_en: Gemara: The reason for the decree against nailed sandals
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a nailed sandal is forbidden. Shmuel recounts a story of persecution: people hid in a cave and agreed that whoever enters may enter but whoever leaves may not leave. One person's sandal turned over, they thought someone had left and been seen by enemies, they trampled each other and killed more than the enemies did. Rabbi Ila'i and Rami bar Yechezkel give similar accounts. At that time they decreed that one should not go out with a nailed sandal. The Gemara questions why it is not forbidden on weekdays too, and answers that the incident happened on Shabbat. It then asks why it is not permitted on Yom Tov, and notes that the Mishnah teaches it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a nailed sandal is forbidden to wear on Shabbat.
Shmuel recounts a story of persecution where people hid in a cave, and a turned-over sandal caused a panic that led to more deaths than the enemy caused.
Rabbi Ila'i gives a similar account of people hiding in a cave who panicked upon hearing a noise and killed each other.
Rami bar Yechezkel gives a similar account of people in a synagogue who panicked upon hearing a noise and killed each other.

The Gemara concludes that at that time they decreed against nailed sandals, then questions why it is not forbidden on weekdays and why it is not permitted on Yom Tov, noting that the Mishnah teaches it is forbidden.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Yom Tov one may send both sewn and unsewn garments, but not a nailed sandal or an unsewn shoe.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that on Yom Tov one may send sewn or unsewn garments, but not a nailed sandal or an unsewn shoe.

items.text: Gemara's question on the distinction between Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the distinction between Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah only prohibits the nailed sandal on Yom Tov, given that the concern for 'kinufya' (gathering of thorns) applies equally on Shabbat and fast days. It distinguishes between a gathering of prohibition and a gathering of permission, and notes that even Rabbi Chanina ben Akiva, who limited the decree to the Jordan River and a boat, would agree that Yom Tov and Shabbat are equivalent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah prohibits the nailed sandal only on Yom Tov, given that the concern for 'kinufya' (gathering of thorns) applies equally on Shabbat and fast days.
The Gemara answers that the incident involved a gathering of prohibition (kinufya de'issura), whereas here the gathering is one of permission (kinufya de'heteira).

items.text: Distinction between strengthening and decoration
items.text_en: Distinction between strengthening and decoration
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says the prohibition applies only to nails for strengthening, but for decoration it is permitted. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina debate the number of decorative nails: five or seven on each side, with Rabbi Yochanan explaining the arrangement.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel establishes the distinction: the prohibition of a nailed sandal applies only when nails are for strengthening, but for decoration it is permitted.
The Gemara asks how many decorative nails constitute 'for decoration'.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that five nails on each side are permitted for decoration.
Rabbi Chanina answers that seven nails on each side are permitted for decoration.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan to Rav Shemen bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan to Rav Shemen bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains to Rav Shemen bar Abba the arrangement of nails: for his own view, two on each side and one at the heel; for Rabbi Chanina's view, three on each side and one at the heel.

items.text: Supporting baraitot for the opinions
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot for the opinions
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Natan permits seven nails, Rabbi Mattir permits thirteen. The Gemara aligns Rabbi Chanina with Rabbi Natan, and Rabbi Yochanan with Rabbi Nehorai, who permits five and forbids seven.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Natan permits seven nails for a sandal that is being stitched, and Rabbi Mattir permits thirteen.
The Gemara aligns Rabbi Chanina with Rabbi Natan (seven nails), and Rabbi Yochanan with Rabbi Nehorai, who permits five and forbids seven.

items.text: Practical ruling between the opinions
items.text_en: Practical ruling between the opinions
items.desc_en: Eifa tells Rabba bar bar Chana that the disciples of Rabbi Yochanan should follow Rabbi Yochanan, but they (the Babylonians) will follow Rabbi Chanina.

sub.text: Eifa's statement to Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Eifa's statement to Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Eifa tells Rabbah bar bar Chanah that the disciples of Rabbi Yochanan should follow Rabbi Yochanan's lenient opinion, while they (the speaker's group) follow Rabbi Chanina's stricter opinion.

items.text: Inquiry about five and nine nails
items.text_en: Inquiry about five and nine nails
items.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rav Ashi about five nails: he says even seven is permitted. About nine: even eight is forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Huna's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rav Ashi: what is the ruling regarding five nails?
Rav Ashi answers that even seven nails are permitted.
Rav Huna asks further: what about nine nails?
Rav Ashi answers that even eight nails are forbidden.

items.text: Sandal sewn from inside
items.text_en: Sandal sewn from inside
items.desc_en: A cobbler asks Rabbi Ami about a sandal sewn from inside. Rabbi Ami permits it but does not know the reason. Rav Ashi explains that since it is sewn from inside, it is considered a shoe, and the rabbis decreed only on a sandal, not a shoe.

sub.desc_en: A cobbler asks Rabbi Ami about the permissibility of a sandal sewn from the inside.
Rabbi Ami permits it but admits he does not know the reason.
Rav Ashi explains that since it is sewn from inside, it is considered a shoe (מנעל), and the rabbis decreed only on a sandal (סנדל), not a shoe.

items.text: Sandal made like a kalkbos or covered with nails
items.text_en: Sandal made like a kalkbos or covered with nails
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda asks Rabbi Abba bar Avina about a sandal made like a kalkbos (a type of shoe): permitted. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina agrees. Rav Sheishet says if it is entirely covered with nails so that the ground does not wear it, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda asks Rabbi Abba bar Avina about the status of a sandal made like a kalkbos (a type of shoe).
Rabbi Abba bar Avina answers that such a sandal is permitted.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's supporting statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's supporting statement
sub.desc_en: It is also stated that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina independently rules that a sandal made like a kalkbos is permitted.
Rav Sheishet adds that if the sandal is entirely covered with nails so that the ground does not wear it, it is permitted.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Sheishet
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Sheishet
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Sheishet: a man may not go out with a nailed sandal, but it may be moved to cover a vessel or support a bed. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon forbids. If most nails fell out and four or five remain, it is permitted. Rabbi Mattir permits up to seven. If covered with leather below and nails above, or made like a kalkbos, or entirely covered with nails, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rav Sheishet, detailing various cases: one may not go out with a nailed sandal, but may move it to cover a vessel or support a bed; Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon prohibits; if most nails fell out and four or five remain, it is permitted; Rabbi Matir permits up to seven; if covered with leather underneath and nails on top, it is permitted; if made like a 'kalbus', a 'tas', a 'yated', or covered entirely with nails to prevent wear, it is permitted.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon forbids moving the nailed sandal even for these purposes.
If most nails fell out and four or five remain, it is permitted; Rabbi Mattir permits up to seven.
If covered with leather below and nails above, or made like a kalkbos, or entirely covered with nails, it is permitted.

items.text: Contradiction in the baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction in the baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the baraita says 'most nails fell out' (implying many remain) and then says 'four or five' (implying not more). Rav Sheishet resolves: one case is where they were worn down, the other where they were pulled out. The Gemara also questions why 'four or five' is needed (five is more lenient), and Rav Chisda explains: four for a small sandal, five for a large one. The contradiction regarding Rabbi Mattir (seven vs. thirteen) is resolved by distinguishing a 'nailed' sandal from a 'stitched' one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: it first says 'most nails fell out' (implying many remain) and then says 'four or five' (implying not more).
Rav Sheishet resolves the contradiction: one case is where nails were worn down (many remain, but they are short), the other where they were pulled out (only a few remain).
The Gemara questions why the baraita mentions both 'four' and 'five' — if five is permitted, four is certainly permitted.
Rav Chisda explains: four refers to a small sandal, five to a large one.
The Gemara notes a contradiction: one baraita says Rabbi Mattir permits up to seven nails, another says up to thirteen.
The Gemara resolves: the case of a 'nailed' sandal (מסומר) is different from a 'stitched' one (נוטה), so the numbers differ.

items.text: Halakha not like Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Halakha not like Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Matna says the halakha is not like Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara notes this is obvious (individual vs. majority), but it teaches that his reasoning is not accepted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Matnah (or alternatively Rav Achadvoi bar Matnah citing Rav Matnah) states that the halacha does not follow Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Matna states that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara asks: this is obvious, since the rule is that the halacha follows the majority over an individual!
The Gemara objects that this ruling is obvious, since the halakha always follows the majority over an individual.
The Gemara answers: lest you think that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is compelling, the statement teaches us that the halacha still follows the majority.
The Gemara explains that the statement was necessary to counter the assumption that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is compelling enough to follow him despite the majority.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya's lenient ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya's lenient ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya says he would permit many nails if not called 'Babylonian who permits prohibitions'. In Pumpedita they say 24, in Sura 22. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak gives a mnemonic: from Pumpedita to Sura, two are missing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya says: were it not that they call me 'Babylonian who permits prohibitions', I would permit many nails.
The Gemara asks: how many?
In Pumbedita they say twenty-four; in Sura they say twenty-two; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak gives a mnemonic: from Pumbedita to Sura, two are missing.

items.text: Exception for one with a foot wound
items.text_en: Exception for one with a foot wound
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds that the prohibition does not apply to an individual who has a wound on his foot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one may not go out with a single sandal when there is no wound on his foot.

items.text: Debate on which foot to shoe first when one foot is injured
items.text_en: Debate on which foot to shoe first when one foot is injured
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav argue about the purpose of a sandal—whether for pain or pleasure—and thus which foot to put on first when one foot has a wound.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: if one has a wound on one foot, which foot does he put the sandal on first?
Rav Huna answers: he puts the sandal on the wounded foot first, because a sandal is made for pain (protection).
Chiyya bar Rav answers: he puts the sandal on the healthy foot first, because a sandal is for pleasure, and the wound itself testifies to the need for protection.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's support for Rav Huna and his general rule
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's support for Rav Huna and his general rule
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan sides with Rav Huna, as shown by his request for a left shoe, and he compares shoes to tefillin, stating both should be put on the left first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rav Huna, citing an incident where Rabbi Yochanan asked Rav Shemen bar Abba for a shoe and criticized him for giving the right one first.
The Gemara objects that perhaps Rabbi Yochanan actually agrees with Chiyya bar Rav, and his criticism was that the left shoe was made into a wound (by being put on the wrong foot).

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan follows his own consistent reasoning, comparing shoes to tefillin (תפילין) — just as tefillin are put on the left arm, so too shoes are put on the left foot first.

items.text: Objection from a baraita: right shoe first
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita: right shoe first
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly states one should put on the right shoe first, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states one should put on the right shoe first, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's view that the left shoe is put on first like tefillin.

items.text: Resolution: both practices are valid, with a compromise
items.text_en: Resolution: both practices are valid, with a compromise
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says both practices are acceptable. Abaye suggests Rabbi Yochanan may not have known the baraita. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes a compromise: put on the right without tying, then the left with tying, then tie the right.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that both practices (right-first and left-first) are valid, since both the baraita and Rabbi Yochanan's view are authoritative.
Abaye objects that perhaps Rabbi Yochanan had not heard the baraita, or if he had, he held that the halacha does not follow it.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes a compromise: put on the right without tying, then the left with tying, then tie the right; Rav Ashi notes that Rav Kahana was not particular about this.

items.text: Baraita on order of dressing, washing, and anointing
items.text_en: Baraita on order of dressing, washing, and anointing
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches the proper order: putting on shoes (right first), removing (left first), washing and anointing (right first), and anointing the head first as it is king over all limbs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the proper order for putting on shoes (right first), removing (left first), washing and anointing (right first), and anointing the head first because it is king over all limbs.

items.text: Clarification on tefillin on Shabbat
items.text_en: Clarification on tefillin on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Safra explains that the Mishnah's prohibition of going out with tefillin on Shabbat applies even to those who hold Shabbat is a time for tefillin, due to concern of carrying in public; a variant teaching says one is not liable for a sin-offering because it is considered normal attire.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra clarifies that the Mishnah's prohibition of going out with tefillin on Shabbat applies even according to the view that Shabbat is a time for tefillin, due to concern that one might come to carry them into the public domain.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Safra's teaching
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Safra's teaching
sub.desc_en: An alternative version applies Rav Safra's statement to the Mishnah's end clause: one who goes out is not liable for a sin-offering, even according to the view that Shabbat is not a time for tefillin, because it is considered normal attire.

items.text: Definition of an expert amulet
items.text_en: Definition of an expert amulet
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that an amulet is considered 'expert' if the person is expert, even if the amulet itself is not proven; the Mishnah's wording supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'expert amulet' means the person is expert, not necessarily the amulet itself.
The Gemara proves Rav Pappa's interpretation from the Mishnah's wording: it says 'not from the expert' (מוּמְחֶה) referring to the person, not 'not expert' referring to the amulet.

items.text: Baraita on the criteria for an expert amulet and its use
items.text_en: Baraita on the criteria for an expert amulet and its use
items.desc_en: A baraita defines an expert amulet as one that healed three times, whether written or herbal, for any illness; it may be worn preventively, and one may tie and untie it even in public, provided it is not tied in a permanent knot.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by defining an expert amulet (קָמֵיעַ מוּמְחֶה) as one that healed three times, whether written or herbal, for any illness, whether life-threatening or not.
The baraita clarifies that the amulet is worn not after the illness has struck but preventively, to ward it off.
The baraita concludes that one may tie and untie the amulet even in a public domain, provided it is not tied in a permanent knot.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may go out with a strap and a ring, but not with an amulet that is not from an expert, due to mar'it ha'ayin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may go out with a strap and a ring into the public domain, but not with an amulet that is not from an expert, due to מראית העין (appearance of impropriety).

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on expert amulet
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on expert amulet
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the definition of an expert amulet from a baraita, and resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between the amulet's efficacy for the person and for itself.

items.text: Rav Pappa's analysis and unresolved query
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's analysis and unresolved query
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies the conditions for an amulet to be considered expert for the person or for itself, and raises an unresolved query about three amulets for one person.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies the conditions for an amulet to be considered expert for the person or for itself, distinguishing three cases: three amulets for three people three times each, three amulets for three people once each, and one amulet for three people.
Rav Pappa raises an unresolved query about three amulets for one person: whether the person is considered healed by the amulets or whether the person's luck receives the writing.
The Gemara concludes that the query remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: First inquiry: holiness of amulets for saving from fire
items.text_en: First inquiry: holiness of amulets for saving from fire
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether amulets have holiness, and attempts to answer from a baraita that they are not saved from a fire, implying no holiness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether amulets have sanctity, and attempts to answer by citing a baraita that they are not rescued from fire, implying no sanctity.

items.text: Second inquiry: holiness for genizah
items.text_en: Second inquiry: holiness for genizah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the inquiry is about genizah, and brings a baraita that writings on vessel handles must be cut and hidden, implying holiness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara redirects the question to burial (גניזה), citing a baraita that writing on vessel handles must be cut off and buried, implying sanctity.
The Gemara brings a baraita that writings on vessel handles and bed legs must be cut and hidden, implying they have holiness.

items.text: Third inquiry: entering a bathroom with an amulet
items.text_en: Third inquiry: entering a bathroom with an amulet
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may enter a bathroom with an amulet due to holiness, and attempts to answer from the Mishnah's ruling about a non-expert amulet, but deflects by saying the case is about an amulet of roots.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may enter a bathroom with an amulet, due to the question of whether amulets possess holiness.
The Gemara attempts to answer from the Mishnah's ruling that one may not go out with a non-expert amulet, implying that with an expert amulet one may go out, even into a bathroom.

The Gemara deflects the proof by explaining that the Mishnah's case involves an amulet of roots (עיקרים), which has no holiness, so the concern is only about carrying on Shabbat, not about entering a bathroom.

items.text: Final resolution: amulet for a life-threatening patient
items.text_en: Final resolution: amulet for a life-threatening patient
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the distinction between written and root amulets, and between dangerous and non-dangerous patients, concluding that since the amulet heals, carrying it is fine even if not from an expert.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that equates a written amulet with a root amulet, contradicting the previous distinction.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the contradiction by limiting the case to a life-threatening patient.
The Gemara objects again by citing a baraita that equates a dangerous patient with a non-dangerous patient, undermining the distinction.
The Gemara resolves that since the amulet heals, carrying it is fine even if not from an expert, regardless of type or patient condition.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about Rabbi Oshaya
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about Rabbi Oshaya
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita where Rabbi Oshaya says one may not hold a kovelet in hand and carry it four cubits in the public domain, contradicting the earlier leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Oshaya forbids holding a kovelet (a type of amulet) and carrying it four cubits in the public domain.

items.text: Resolution: kovelet is covered with leather, unlike tefillin
items.text_en: Resolution: kovelet is covered with leather, unlike tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the kovelet is covered with leather, but tefillin are also covered with leather yet must be removed before entering a bathroom. Abaye explains that the shin, dalet, and yod of tefillin are halakha from Sinai, making them more sacred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the kovelet is covered with leather, but notes that tefillin are also covered with leather yet must be removed before entering a bathroom.
Abaye explains that the shin, dalet, and yod of tefillin are halakha from Sinai, making them more sacred and thus requiring removal.

items.text: Explanation of terms: shiryon, kasda, maggafayim
items.text_en: Explanation of terms: shiryon, kasda, maggafayim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items a man may not wear; the Gemara explains the Aramaic terms: shiryon is zarda (armor), kasda is sanvarta (helmet), and maggafayim is puzmakei (greaves).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the items a man may not wear on Shabbat: shiryon, kasda, and maggafayim.
Rav explains the Aramaic terms: shiryon is zarda (armor), kasda is sanvarta (helmet), and maggafayim is puzmakei (greaves).

items.text: Mishnah: Items a woman may not wear out
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items a woman may not wear out
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items a woman may not wear into the public domain: a pierced needle, a signet ring, a kolyar, a kovelet, and a flask of balsam oil. Rabbi Meir holds she is liable for a sin-offering; the Sages exempt for kovelet and flask.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items a woman may not wear into the public domain on Shabbat.
Rabbi Meir holds a woman liable for a sin-offering if she goes out with these items; the Sages exempt her for the kovelet and flask of balsam oil.

items.text: Ulla's principle and Rav Yosef's challenge
items.text_en: Ulla's principle and Rav Yosef's challenge
items.desc_en: Ulla states that the prohibitions are reversed for men and women. Rav Yosef challenges this from a baraita that shepherds may wear sacks, and anyone may do so. Rav Yosef then explains that Ulla holds women are a separate nation.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the prohibitions of ornaments are reversed for men and women, meaning what is fit for one is forbidden for the other.
Rav Yosef challenges Ulla from a baraita that shepherds may wear sacks, and anyone may do so, implying that a garment fit for men is also fit for women.
Rav Yosef resolves the challenge by explaining that Ulla holds women are a separate nation, so their adornments are not interchangeable with men's.

items.text: Abaye's objection from tefillin and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from tefillin and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that if women are a separate nation, they should be exempt from tefillin, a time-bound positive commandment. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir holds night and Shabbat are times for tefillin, making it a non-time-bound commandment, so women are obligated.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if women are a separate nation, they should be exempt from tefillin, a time-bound positive commandment, yet the baraita says both men and women may bring in found tefillin.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir holds night and Shabbat are times for tefillin, making it a non-time-bound commandment, so women are obligated.

items.text: Objection: carrying is indirect, and resolution via Rava
items.text_en: Objection: carrying is indirect, and resolution via Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that carrying a ring is indirect. Rabbi Yirmeya suggests a woman treasurer, but Rabbi Yochanan asks about a man. Rava resolves that sometimes a man gives his wife a signet ring to take to a chest, and sometimes a woman gives her husband a plain ring to take to a craftsman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that carrying the ring is only an indirect act of הוצאה (carrying out).
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that we are dealing with a woman treasurer (גזברית), for whom carrying the ring is part of her job.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that the answer works for a woman, but what about a man who carries the ring?
Rava resolves that sometimes a man gives his wife a signet ring to take to a chest, and sometimes a woman gives her husband a plain ring to take to a craftsman, making the carrying direct for each.

items.text: Dispute about kovelet: Rabbi Meir, Sages, and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Dispute about kovelet: Rabbi Meir, Sages, and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms kolyar and kovelet. A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds it is a burden, the Sages consider it an adornment but worry she might show it and carry it, and Rabbi Eliezer permits it initially for a woman with bad odor. A contradiction about Rabbi Eliezer is resolved by distinguishing his rulings relative to Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the terms 'kolyar' and 'kovelet' mean, and Rav and Rav Asi explain them as a 'מכבנתא' (a type of headband) and 'חומרתא דפילון' (a heavy chain or necklace), respectively.

A baraita is cited recording the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds a woman is liable for a חטאת (sin-offering) if she goes out with a kovelet; the Sages say she is exempt but it is forbidden; Rabbi Eliezer permits it לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Meir considers the kovelet a משאוי (burden); the Sages consider it a תכשיט (adornment) but fear she might show it and carry it four cubits in the public domain; Rabbi Eliezer holds that a woman with bad odor will not show it and thus will not come to carry it.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita states that Rabbi Eliezer only exempts (פוטר) a woman who goes out with a kovelet, not permits it לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: when the baraita says Rabbi Eliezer exempts (פוטר), it is relative to Rabbi Meir who holds her liable for a חטאת (sin-offering); when it says he permits לכתחילה (the ideal standard), it is relative to the Sages who forbid it but exempt her from a sin-offering.

items.text: Opening Mishnah dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer regarding a woman going out with a key in her hand on Shabbat. Rabbi Meir holds her liable for a sin-offering, while Rabbi Eliezer exempts her in the case of a perfume box or flask.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer regarding a woman going out with a key in her hand on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the term 'כובלת' and then explains that the Mishnah is missing text. It clarifies that Rabbi Meir prohibits both items, while Rabbi Eliezer exempts, and adds a distinction: if they contain perfume, the woman is liable; if not, she is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'כובלת' (a type of ornament) refers to.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing text, and clarifies that Rabbi Meir prohibits both items, Rabbi Eliezer exempts, and adds a distinction: if they contain perfume, the woman is liable; if not, she is exempt.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Ashi on the principle of carrying less than a shiur in a vessel
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Ashi on the principle of carrying less than a shiur in a vessel
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava derives from the Mishnah that one who carries food less than the minimum measure in a vessel is liable, comparing it to a flask without perfume. Rav Ashi disagrees, arguing that in general one is exempt, but here the flask has no substance at all.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava derives from the Mishnah that one who carries food less than the minimum measure (פחות מכשיעור) in a vessel is liable, comparing it to a flask without perfume.
Rav Ashi disagrees, arguing that in general one is exempt, but here the flask has no substance at all (ליתיה לממשא כלל).

items.text: Discussion on Pilayton and the decree of Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
items.text_en: Discussion on Pilayton and the decree of Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about anointing oil, which Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel identifies as Pilayton. Rav Yosef challenges that Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava decreed against Pilayton and the Sages did not agree. Abaye responds that the Sages only decreed on items with both pleasure and joy, but not on those with pleasure alone.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel identifies the biblical 'first of oils' as Pilayton (a fragrant oil).
Rav Yosef objects that Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava decreed against Pilayton and the Sages did not agree, implying it is not permitted for pleasure.
Rav Yosef asks: if Pilayton is permitted for pleasure, why did the Sages not agree with Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's decree?

Abaye counters by citing a verse about drinking from bowls, which Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi interpret as a type of drink (קְנִישְׁקְנִין), and notes that Rabbah bar Rav Huna drank it without objection, showing that not all pleasurable items were forbidden.
Abaye resolves: the Sages decreed only on items with both pleasure (תַּעֲנוּג) and joy (שִׂמְחָה), but not on those with pleasure alone, explaining why Pilayton was not universally forbidden.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse about sleeping on ivory beds
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse about sleeping on ivory beds
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that the verse refers to people urinating naked before their beds. Rabbi Avahu objects, questioning why such a sin would lead to exile. He then offers an alternative interpretation: they ate and drank together, placed their beds close, exchanged wives, and defiled their beds with illicit seed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina interprets the verse as teaching that the people urinated naked before their beds.
Rabbi Avahu objects: if so, would they be exiled merely for urinating naked before their beds?
Rabbi Avahu offers an alternative interpretation: they ate and drank together, placed their beds close, exchanged wives, and defiled their beds with illicit seed.

items.text: Three things that bring poverty
items.text_en: Three things that bring poverty
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu or a baraita states three things that bring poverty: urinating naked before one's bed, being careless with hand-washing, and having one's wife curse him in his presence. Rava qualifies each: urinating is only problematic if facing the bed, but not if away; only if on the ground, not in a vessel. Carelessness is only if one does not wash at all. The wife's curse is about her jewelry if he can afford it but does not provide.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu (or a baraita) states three things that bring a person to poverty: urinating naked before one's bed, being careless with hand-washing, and having one's wife curse him in his presence.
Rava qualifies that urinating naked before the bed is only problematic if one faces the bed, but not if facing away.
Rava further qualifies that even facing the bed, it is only problematic if urinating on the ground, but not into a vessel.
Rava qualifies that carelessness with hand-washing is only problematic if one does not wash at all, but if one washes insufficiently it is not a concern.
Rav Chisda testifies that he washed his hands with two handfuls of water and received two handfuls of goodness, supporting the importance of proper hand-washing.
Rava explains that the wife's curse is about her jewelry, and this applies only when the husband can afford it but does not provide it.

items.text: Homiletical interpretation of the sins and punishment of the daughters of Zion
items.text_en: Homiletical interpretation of the sins and punishment of the daughters of Zion
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Illai expounds on the verse about the haughty daughters of Zion, describing their sinful behavior: walking upright, wearing anklets, applying eye makeup, and causing lust. Their punishment is described by Rabbah bar Ulla: their perfume becomes rot, their girdles become scabs, etc. Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of 'VaHashem Pothehen Ye'areh'.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Illai expounds on the verse about the haughty daughters of Zion, detailing their sinful behaviors: walking upright, applying eye makeup, and causing lust in young men.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Ulla's exposition of punishment
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Ulla's exposition of punishment
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ulla expounds the punishment for each sin: perfume becomes rot, girdles become scabs, and Rava adds a folk saying about beauty turning to pain.

Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina interprets the verse as meaning that leprosy broke out on their heads, using a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'וְסִפַּח' to the term 'סַּפַּחַת' in the Torah's leprosy passage.
Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of 'VaHashem Pothehen Ye'areh': one says their openings were poured out like a flask, the other says their openings became like a forest.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav describes the wealthy men of Jerusalem who would ask each other about the quality of their bread and wine.

items.text: Opening aggadic statements about Jerusalem's cinnamon and wine
items.text_en: Opening aggadic statements about Jerusalem's cinnamon and wine
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda comments on various types of wine and seating arrangements, all leading to licentiousness. Rachava quotes Rabbi Yehuda about the cinnamon wood of Jerusalem that was used for fuel and its fragrance, which was hidden after the destruction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all the listed factors—wine, seating, and companions—lead to licentiousness.
Rachava reports Rabbi Yehuda's tradition about Jerusalem's cinnamon wood, its fragrance, and its near-total disappearance after the destruction.

items.text: Mishnah: Weapons on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Weapons on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man may not go out with various weapons on Shabbat, and if he does, he is liable for a sin-offering. Rabbi Eliezer considers them ornaments, while the Sages consider them disgraceful, citing the verse about beating swords into plowshares. The Mishnah also discusses the status of a belt and chains.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man may not go out with weapons on Shabbat, and if he does, he is liable for a sin-offering.
Rabbi Eliezer considers weapons ornaments for a man.
The Sages consider weapons disgraceful, citing the verse about beating swords into plowshares.
The Mishnah rules that a belt is pure and one may go out with it on Shabbat.
The Mishnah rules that chains are impure and one may not go out with them on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Debate on weapons as ornaments in Messianic times
items.text_en: Gemara: Debate on weapons as ornaments in Messianic times
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the term 'אלָּה' as a club. It then presents a debate: Rabbi Eliezer is asked why weapons will be nullified in Messianic times if they are ornaments. He answers that they will not be needed, but Abaye objects that they could still be decorative. Shmuel holds that only political subjugation will differ in Messianic times, while Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says all prophecies are for that era, not the World to Come. An alternative version has Rabbi Eliezer claiming weapons will not be nullified even then.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'אלָּה' means and answers that it is a club.
Rabbi Eliezer states that weapons are ornaments for a man.
The Sages ask Rabbi Eliezer: if weapons are ornaments, why will they be nullified in Messianic times?
Rabbi Eliezer answers that weapons will not be needed in Messianic times, citing the verse 'nation shall not lift up sword against nation'.
Abaye objects that even if not needed, weapons could still serve as mere ornaments, like a lamp in the daytime.
Shmuel states that the only difference between this world and Messianic times is the subjugation to foreign kingdoms, citing the verse that the poor will never cease.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba supports Shmuel by saying that all prophecies are only for Messianic times, but for the World to Come, 'no eye has seen but You'.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.desc_en: An alternative version has Rabbi Eliezer responding that weapons will not be nullified even in Messianic times, which aligns with Shmuel and disputes Rabbi Chiya bar Abba.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's proof from Psalms and the principle of peshuto shel mikra
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's proof from Psalms and the principle of peshuto shel mikra
items.desc_en: Abaye asks for Rabbi Eliezer's source, and it is cited from Psalms: 'Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, your glory and your majesty.' Rav Kahana objects that this verse refers to words of Torah, but Mar bar Rav Huna responds that a verse never loses its plain meaning. Rav Kahana then reflects that he knew the entire Talmud at eighteen but only now learned this principle, implying one should first learn and then understand.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Dimi (or alternative tradents) for the scriptural source of Rabbi Eliezer's position that weapons are ornaments.
The answer cites the verse from Psalms (45:4) 'Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, your glory and your majesty' as Rabbi Eliezer's proof.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's objection to Mar bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection to Mar bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects that the verse refers to words of Torah, not to actual weapons.
Mar bar Rav Huna responds that a verse never loses its plain meaning, so the verse can simultaneously refer to Torah and to actual weapons.
Rav Kahana reflects that he knew the entire Talmud at eighteen but only now learned this principle, implying one should first learn and then understand.

items.text: Aggadic teachings on Torah scholars sharpening each other
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings on Torah scholars sharpening each other
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya quotes Rabbi Elazar that two Torah scholars who sharpen each other in halakha are granted success by God, as per the verse 'and your majesty be successful.' They also attain greatness. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that they merit things said in the right hand of the Torah, interpreting the verse about length of life in the right hand and wealth in the left.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic sign (סימן) 'זרות' is introduced to mark the following aggadic teachings.

Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Elazar teaches that two Torah scholars who sharpen each other in halakha are granted success and greatness by God, as derived from the verse 'והודרך צלח' (and your majesty be successful), with additional conditions of לשמה (for its own sake) and humility.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing Rava bar Rav Sheila / Rav Yosef bar Chama / Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing Rava bar Rav Sheila / Rav Yosef bar Chama / Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that such scholars merit the things said in the right hand of the Torah, interpreting the verse 'אורך ימים בימינה' (length of days in her right hand) to mean that those who turn to the right (למיימינים בה) get both long life and wealth, while those who turn to the left (למשמאילים בה) get only wealth.

items.text: More aggadic statements on Torah scholars' conduct
items.text_en: More aggadic statements on Torah scholars' conduct
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya quotes Reish Lakish that two Torah scholars who are gentle with each other are listened to by God. Rabbi Ami says even one who intends to do a mitzvah but is prevented is credited as if he did it. Rav Chinana bar Idi says one who performs a mitzvah properly will not receive bad news. Rav Asi says such a person can even annul a divine decree. Rabbi Abba quotes Reish Lakish that scholars who listen to each other are heard by God, and if they do not, they cause the Shechinah to depart. Another statement says scholars who 'raise banners' for each other are loved by God, provided they know the essence of the teaching and have no teacher in town.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya quotes Reish Lakish that two Torah scholars who are gentle with each other in halacha are listened to by God, citing a verse.
Rabbi Ami explains that even one who intended to perform a מצוה (commandment) but was prevented is credited as if he did it.
Rav Chinana bar Idi states that one who performs a מצוה (commandment) properly will not receive bad news.
Rav Asi (or Rabbi Chanina) adds that such a person can even annul a divine decree, citing a verse.
Rabbi Abba quotes Reish Lakish that scholars who listen to each other are heard by God.
Rabbi Abba quotes Reish Lakish that if scholars do not listen to each other, they cause the Shechinah (Divine Presence) to depart from Israel.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba quoting Reish Lakish, with Rava's gloss
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba quoting Reish Lakish, with Rava's gloss
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba quotes Reish Lakish that scholars who 'raise banners' for each other are loved by God, provided they know the essence of the teaching and have no teacher in town.

items.text: Final aggadic statements on charity, Torah scholars, and dogs
items.text_en: Final aggadic statements on charity, Torah scholars, and dogs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba quotes Reish Lakish that lending is greater than giving charity, and investing in business is greatest of all. Another statement says that if a Torah scholar is vengeful, gird him on your loins, but if an ignoramus is pious, do not live near him. Rav Kahana quotes Reish Lakish that one who raises a vicious dog in his home prevents kindness from entering his home.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba quotes Reish Lakish ranking lending above charity and business investment above both.
Rabbi Abba quotes Reish Lakish that a vengeful Torah scholar should be honored, but a pious ignoramus should be avoided.

sub.text: Rav Kahana citing Reish Lakish (or alternative tradents)
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana citing Reish Lakish (or alternative tradents)
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana (or Rav Asi or Rabbi Abba) quotes Reish Lakish that raising a vicious dog at home prevents kindness from entering.

items.text: Interpretation of 'mer'eihu chasid' and a story about a dog
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'mer'eihu chasid' and a story about a dog
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that a dog causes one to abandon fear of Heaven. A story is told of a woman who miscarried after a dog barked at her, despite the owner's assurance that the dog's teeth and claws were removed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the word 'mer'eihu' (his friend) is a Greek term for dog, and that a dog causes one to abandon fear of Heaven, citing the verse 'and the fear of the Almighty he will abandon'.

A story is told of a woman who entered a house to bake, a dog barked at her causing her to miscarry, and despite the owner's assurance that the dog's teeth and claws were removed, she replied that his kindness was already thrown behind the thorns, as the fetus had already moved.

items.text: Division of a verse between the evil and good inclinations
items.text_en: Division of a verse between the evil and good inclinations
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Reish Lakish debate the division of the verse from Ecclesiastes. Rav Huna says the first part is the words of the evil inclination and the latter part of the good inclination. Reish Lakish says the first part refers to words of Torah and the latter to good deeds.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets the verse from Ecclesiastes, dividing it between the words of the evil inclination and the good inclination.
Reish Lakish offers an alternative interpretation, assigning the first part of the verse to words of Torah and the latter part to good deeds.

items.text: Definition of 'birith' as an anklet
items.text_en: Definition of 'birith' as an anklet
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda identifies 'birith' as an 'etzadah' (anklet). Rav Yosef objects because a birith is pure and can be worn on Shabbat, while an etzadah is impure. The Gemara resolves that the birith is placed under the etzadah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a birith (anklet) is pure (טהורה) and may be worn on Shabbat.
Rav Yehuda identifies the birith as an etzadah (anklet).
Rav Yosef objects: the birith is pure and can be worn on Shabbat, but an etzadah is impure (טמאה), so they cannot be identical.
The Gemara resolves that the birith is placed under the etzadah, so the birith itself remains pure while the etzadah is impure.

items.text: Discussion of chains and anklets, and a story from Jerusalem
items.text_en: Discussion of chains and anklets, and a story from Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Ravin and Rav Huna sit before Rav Yirmeya, who is dozing. Ravin says a birith is one ring, and chains are two. Rav Huna says both are two, with a chain between them making them 'kevalim'. The Gemara questions the function of the chain, and answers with a story from Rabbi Yochanan about a family in Jerusalem that used chains to prevent miscarriages. Rav Yirmeya awakens and approves.

sub.desc_en: Ravin and Rav Huna sit before Rav Yirmeya, who is dozing.
Ravin states that a birith (anklet) is one ring, and kevalim (chains) are two rings.
Rav Huna objects that both are two rings, and a chain between them makes them kevalim.
The Gemara questions what function the chain serves in making the item a vessel susceptible to טומאה (ritual impurity).

sub.text: Citation of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Citation of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan that a sound-producing metal item is susceptible to טומאה (ritual impurity) from the verse 'כל דבר אשר יבא באש' (anything that comes into fire).
The Gemara objects that there the sound serves a function, but here what function does the chain serve?

sub.text: Resolution via story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Resolution via story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the chain does serve a function: a family in Jerusalem used chains between anklets to prevent miscarriages from wide strides, and Rav Yirmeya awakens and approves.

items.text: Source for impurity of a woven item and an ornament
items.text_en: Source for impurity of a woven item and an ornament
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a woven item of any size is impure, derived from the tzitz. Abaye objects that the tzitz is not woven but a plate. Rav Dimi later retracts and says the source for an ornament is the tzitz, and for a woven item is 'o beged'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the source for a woven item of any size being impure is the tzitz (the High Priest's forehead plate).

Abaye objects that the tzitz is not woven but a metal plate, citing a baraita describing it as a gold plate with two lines of inscription, and Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Yosi's testimony that he saw it in Rome with a single line.
Rav Dimi retracts his earlier statement and corrects: the source for an ornament of any size being impure is the tzitz, and for a woven item of any size being impure is from 'o beged' (or a garment).

items.text: Tannaic sources and Rava's derivation
items.text_en: Tannaic sources and Rava's derivation
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that a woven item of any size is impure, an ornament of any size is impure, and a combination is impure. Rava derives these from verses: woven from 'o beged', ornament from tzitz, and combination from 'kol kli ma'aseh'. A rabbi objects that the latter verse is about Midian, and Rava responds with a gezerah shavah.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach a baraita stating that a woven item of any size is impure, an ornament of any size is impure, a combination of both is impure, and a sack added to a garment is impure due to weaving.
Rava derives the three categories from verses: woven from 'אוֹ בֶגֶד' (or a garment), ornament from the tzitz (frontplate), and combination from 'כָּל כְּלִי מַעֲשֶׂה' (every work vessel).
A certain rabbi objects to Rava that the verse 'כָּל כְּלִי מַעֲשֶׂה' is written in the context of Midian, not general impurity.
Rava responds that he derives it via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), linking the verse to the general impurity context.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara connects the current discussion to the previous one by noting the repetition of the word 'kli'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the repetition of the word 'kli' from the previous daf to connect the discussion.

items.text: Addition of sack to a garment
items.text_en: Addition of sack to a garment
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a sack added to a garment can become impure even if not woven, and Rabbi Yochanan explains its use: a poor person braids three strands and hangs them around his daughter's neck.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a sack addition to a garment can be considered a separate vessel, since the garment itself is already woven.
The Gemara clarifies that the mishnah means a sack added to a garment even if not woven is still susceptible to impurity.
The Gemara asks what practical use such a sack addition serves.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that a poor person braids three strands and hangs them around his daughter's neck as a makeshift necklace.

items.text: Tannaic source for sack and similar materials
items.text_en: Tannaic source for sack and similar materials
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that the word 'or sak' includes kilkeli and chavak, but excludes ropes and cords, as sack is woven.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that derives from the verse 'or sack' that only woven items like sack are included for impurity, excluding ropes and cords.

items.text: Gezeirah shavah between sheretz and met
items.text_en: Gezeirah shavah between sheretz and met
items.desc_en: The Gemara uses a gezeirah shavah from the words 'beged' and 'or' in the contexts of sheretz and met to equate their impurity laws: both require woven material, and both include all goat hair products.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse regarding impurity of a corpse (met) that includes 'כל כלי עור וכל מעשה עזים' to include קילקלי (a coarse fabric) and חבק (a type of belt).
The Gemara raises an objection: one might think to include ropes and cords, but a logical inference (דין) from the impurity of a sheretz (creeping animal) shows that only woven material is impure.
The Gemara objects that the inference might be refuted because sheretz impurity is light, so one cannot analogize to the severe impurity of a corpse; therefore a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) is needed.
The Gemara resolves by applying the גזירה שוה: the words 'בגד' and 'עור' in both sheretz and met teach that only woven material is impure in both cases.
The Gemara adds that just as the גזירה שוה from met includes all goat hair products, so too in sheretz it includes all goat hair products.

items.text: Inclusion of horse and cow tail hair
items.text_en: Inclusion of horse and cow tail hair
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that materials from horse and cow tails are included via 'or sak', and resolves a contradiction by noting that the gezeirah shavah makes the earlier derivation superfluous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from the verse we only have material from goats; how do we include horse and cow tail hair? It answers: the verse says 'or sak' to include them.
The Gemara objects: but you already used the phrase 'or sak' to include קילקלי (goat hair fabric) and חבק (camel hair fabric)!

The Gemara resolves: that derivation was before the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) came; now that the verbal analogy came, the earlier derivation is superfluous, freeing 'or sak' for horse and cow tail hair.

items.text: Applying the inclusion to met impurity
items.text_en: Applying the inclusion to met impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara extends the inclusion of horse and cow tail hair to met impurity through another gezeirah shavah, despite a potential objection based on severity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that the inclusion of items from a horse's tail or cow's tail applies to the טומאה (ritual impurity) of a corpse, since only the case of a creeping animal was explicitly addressed?
The Gemara proposes a logical inference: just as the Torah included such items for a creeping animal, so too it should include them for a corpse.

The Gemara objects: the case of a creeping animal involves a lenient טומאת ערב (impurity until evening), which is extensive, so adding items is plausible; but a corpse involves a stringent טומאת שבעה (seven-day impurity), which is limited, so the inference may not hold.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing a גזֵירָה שָוָה (verbal analogy) from the terms 'בגד' and 'עור' in both contexts, establishing that the inclusion applies equally to corpse impurity.

items.text: The gezeirah shavah is superfluous
items.text_en: The gezeirah shavah is superfluous
items.desc_en: The Gemara demonstrates that the gezeirah shavah is superfluous (mufneh) in both directions, addressing the objection that sheretz is more severe because it impurifies by the size of a lentil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the verbal analogy were not superfluous (mufneh), it could be refuted: what is unique to a creeping animal is that it imparts impurity by the size of a lentil, which is more stringent than a corpse.

The Gemara answers that the terms 'בגד' and 'עור' (garment and leather) in the context of a creeping animal are indeed superfluous, because the halakhot of a creeping animal are juxtaposed to those of seminal emission, where the same terms already appear; thus the extra terms are free for the verbal analogy.

The Gemara objects that the verbal analogy is still only free from one side (the terms for a creeping animal are superfluous, but not for a corpse); according to the opinion that a one-sided free analogy can be refuted, what can be said?

The Gemara answers that the terms 'בגד' and 'עור' (garment and leather) in the context of a corpse are also superfluous, because the halakhot of a corpse are juxtaposed to those of seminal emission, where the same terms already appear; thus the verbal analogy is free from both sides.

items.text: Interpretation of the ornaments
items.text_en: Interpretation of the ornaments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rav Yosef explain the terms 'agil' and 'kumaz' from the verse about the Midianite spoils, with Rav Yosef noting the Aramaic translation and Rabbah deriving 'kumaz' as 'place of lewdness'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from the Midianite spoils listing the ornaments: chains, bracelets, rings, agil, and kumaz.
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) explains that 'עגיל (agil)' is a mold of the breasts and 'כומז (kumaz)' is a mold of the womb.
רב יוסף (Rav Yosef) notes that this explains why the Aramaic translation of 'כומז (kumaz)' is 'מחוך (maḥokh)', meaning something that leads to foolishness.
רבא (Rabbah) responds that the meaning is derived from the verse itself: 'כומז (kumaz)' is an acronym for 'כאן מקום זימה (here is the place of lewdness)'.

items.text: Moses' anger and the need for atonement
items.text_en: Moses' anger and the need for atonement
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak relates that Moses asked Israel if they had returned to their earlier sin; they replied they had not acted but had improper thoughts, so they brought an offering. The school of Rabbi Yishmael explains why that generation needed atonement.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak relates that Moses asked Israel if they had returned to their earlier sin; they replied they had not acted but had improper thoughts, so they brought an offering.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael explains why that generation needed atonement, introducing the reason for their offering.

items.text: Gemara's opening: reason for listing external and internal ornaments together
items.text_en: Gemara's opening: reason for listing external and internal ornaments together
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains why the biblical verse lists both external and internal ornaments together: to teach that looking at even a small finger of a woman is like looking at the place of nakedness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the biblical verse that describes those who 'strayed their eyes from nakedness' as the basis for the discussion.
Rav Sheshet explains that the verse lists external and internal ornaments together to teach that looking at even a small finger of a woman is like looking at the place of nakedness.

items.text: Mishnah: what a woman may wear into a courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah: what a woman may wear into a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permissible items: hair strings, a totefet, sewn-on sarbitin, a kabul, a pe'ah nokhrit, a wad in the ear or sandal, a wad for menstruation, pepper or salt in the mouth, and a false tooth. Rabbi permits a gold tooth, but the Sages forbid it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a woman may go out with hair strings, whether her own, her friend's, or an animal's.
The Mishnah lists additional permissible items: a totefet (headband) and sewn-on sarbitin (hair ribbons).
The Mishnah permits a kabul (head covering), a pe'ah nokhrit (false hairpiece) in a courtyard, a wad in the ear or sandal, and a wad prepared for menstruation.
The Mishnah permits pepper, a salt ball, and any item placed in the mouth, provided it is not placed לכתחילה (the ideal standard) on Shabbat, and if it falls out, she may not replace it.
The Mishnah concludes with a dispute: Rabbi permits a gold false tooth, but the Sages forbid it.

items.text: Gemara: necessity of listing all three types of hair strings
items.text_en: Gemara: necessity of listing all three types of hair strings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to list hair strings from the woman herself, her friend, and an animal: each case has a unique leniency that might otherwise be excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to list all three types of hair strings (from herself, her friend, and an animal), and explains that if only the woman's own hair were mentioned, one might think her friend's hair is forbidden because it is repulsive (מאיס).

The Gemara continues that if only the friend's hair were mentioned, one might think animal hair is forbidden because it is not of her species (לאו בר מינה), so the Mishnah needed to include animal hair as well.
The Gemara concludes that all three cases are necessary (צריכא) to prevent mistaken exclusions.

items.text: Baraita: restriction on a young girl wearing an old woman's hair strings
items.text_en: Baraita: restriction on a young girl wearing an old woman's hair strings
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a young girl may not wear an old woman's hair strings, and vice versa. The Gemara questions why a young girl would want to wear an old woman's strings, since it is degrading, and explains that the baraita simply pairs the cases.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a young girl may not go out with an old woman's hair strings, nor an old woman with a young girl's.

The Gemara asks: it is understandable that an old woman would want to wear a young girl's strings, as that is a credit to her, but why would a young girl wear an old woman's strings, since it is degrading?
The Gemara answers: since the baraita taught the case of an old woman with a young girl's strings, it also taught the reverse case for symmetry, even though it is not practically relevant.

items.text: Debate about kabul and pe'ah nokhrit: exceptions to the rule
items.text_en: Debate about kabul and pe'ah nokhrit: exceptions to the rule
items.desc_en: Rav states that anything forbidden in the public domain is also forbidden in a courtyard, except for kabul and pe'ah nokhrit. Rabbi Anani bar Sason says everything is like kabul (permitted). The Gemara reconciles the dispute by noting that Rabbi Anani bar Sason follows Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei, who disagrees. Ulla explains the reason for the exception: so that a woman does not become repulsive to her husband, citing a baraita about Rabbi Akiva's teaching on niddah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman may go out into a courtyard with a kabul (headband) and a pe'ah nokhrit (false hairpiece).
Rav states a general rule: anything forbidden in the public domain is also forbidden in a courtyard, except for kabul and pe'ah nokhrit.

sub.text: Rabbi Anani bar Sason in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Anani bar Sason in the name of Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Anani bar Sason says in the name of Rabbi Yishmael that everything is like kabul (permitted in a courtyard).
The Gemara objects: the Mishnah explicitly lists only kabul and pe'ah nokhrit, contradicting Rabbi Anani bar Sason's broader ruling.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Anani bar Sason follows Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei, who is a Tanna and disagrees with the Mishnah's ruling.
The Gemara asks Rav: why are kabul and pe'ah nokhrit specifically excepted from the general prohibition?
Ulla answers: so that a woman does not become repulsive to her husband, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva taught that a niddah may adorn herself to prevent her husband from divorcing her.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's principle: mar'it ha'ayin applies even in private
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's principle: mar'it ha'ayin applies even in private
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: wherever the Sages forbid something because of mar'it ha'ayin, it is forbidden even in the innermost rooms.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav that wherever the Sages forbid something because of מראית העין (appearance of impropriety), it is forbidden even in the innermost rooms.

items.text: Contradiction about a bell (zog) and resolution as a tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Contradiction about a bell (zog) and resolution as a tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah forbids a bell even if plugged, but a baraita permits a plugged bell in a courtyard. The Gemara resolves this as a dispute between tannaim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah forbids a woman from going out with a bell (זוג) even if it is plugged (פקוק), but a baraita permits her to plug a bell around her neck and walk with her in the courtyard.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that the two sources represent a dispute between different Tannaim (תנאים), and it introduces a supporting baraita that will follow.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Items a woman may wear out
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Items a woman may wear out
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items a woman may wear into a public domain on Shabbat, including a cloth for a wound, pepper, salt, and a false tooth, with disputes between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items a woman may wear out on Shabbat, including a cloth for a wound, pepper, salt, and a false tooth, with disputes between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Gemara: Conditions for the cloth and the handle
items.text_en: Gemara: Conditions for the cloth and the handle
items.desc_en: The Gemara specifies that the cloth must be tied to the ear or sandal, and Rava adds that even if not tied, it is permitted because it is repulsive. Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a handle, and Rabbi Abba permits it, supported by Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel teaches a baraita that the cloth (מוך) is permitted only if tied to the ear.
Rami bar Yechezkel teaches a baraita that the cloth on the sandal is permitted only if tied to the sandal.
Rami bar Chama assumed that the cloth prepared for menstruation is permitted only if tied between her thighs.
Rava answers that even if not tied, it is permitted because it is repulsive (מאיס) and she will not come to carry it.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Abba: if she made a handle (בית יד) for the cloth, what is the law?
Rabbi Abba answers that it is permitted.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Oshaya citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Oshaya citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: It is also stated that Rav Nachman bar Oshaya said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: if she made a handle, it is permitted.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about Rabbi Yochanan's practice
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about Rabbi Yochanan's practice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan went out with the cloth to the study hall, and his colleagues disagreed; Rabbi Yannai went out to a karmelit, and his entire generation disagreed. The Gemara resolves the contradiction with Rami bar Yechezkel's statement by distinguishing between a tight and loose cloth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yochanan went out with the cloth to the study hall and his colleagues disagreed, while Rabbi Yannai went out to a karmelit and his entire generation disagreed.
The Gemara objects by citing Rami bar Yechezkel's baraita that the cloth is only permitted when tied to the ear, contradicting the lenient practice of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a tight cloth (מִיהַדַּק) which is permitted even without tying, and a loose cloth (לָא מִיהַדַּק) which requires tying.

items.text: Mishnah: Pepper, salt, and other items
items.text_en: Mishnah: Pepper, salt, and other items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues listing items: pepper for bad breath, a lump of salt for a toothache, and any item placed in the mouth, like ginger or darsuna.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items a woman may carry on Shabbat: pepper for bad breath, a lump of salt for a toothache, and any item placed in the mouth, such as ginger or darsuna.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: The false tooth
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: The false tooth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a gold false tooth is permitted by Rabbi Meir but forbidden by the Sages. Rabbi Zeira clarifies that a silver tooth is universally permitted, and a baraisa supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a gold false tooth is permitted by Rabbi Meir but forbidden by the Sages.
Rabbi Zeira clarifies that the dispute applies only to gold, but a silver tooth is universally permitted.
A baraisa supports Rabbi Zeira's distinction between silver and gold teeth.

items.text: Gemara: Abaye's unifying principle
items.text_en: Gemara: Abaye's unifying principle
items.desc_en: Abaye states that Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar all hold that any item that is repulsive will not be carried. He cites examples: Rabbi Meir's ruling on the tooth, Rabbi Eliezer's exemption for a chain and flask, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's rule about items below the net.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar all hold that any repulsive item will not be carried out on Shabbat.
Abaye cites the earlier Mishnah where Rabbi Meir permits a gold tooth, illustrating the principle of repulsiveness.
Abaye cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer exempts a chain and a flask of perfumers' oil, items that are repulsive.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that items below the net may be worn out, but above the net are repulsive and not worn out.

items.text: Mishnah: Stone on a wound and other adornments
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stone on a wound and other adornments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits a woman to go out with a stone on a wound, young girls with threads or chips in their ears, Arab women with veils, and Median women with cloaks. It also allows covering a stone, nut, or coin, but not initially on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permitted adornments and items a woman may wear into a public domain on Shabbat, including a stone on a wound, threads for young girls, veils for Arab and Median women, and covering a stone or coin, provided it is not initially attached on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Why specifically a stone?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why specifically a stone?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what a צינית is (a wound) and why a stone is used. It considers alternatives like a potsherd or metal, but Abaye concludes that all are beneficial.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what a צינית (wound) is and answers that it is a 'בת ארעא' (a stone wound).
The Gemara asks why specifically a stone (סלע) is used for the wound, and suggests a potsherd (חספא) as an alternative.
