The Gemara objects that if the reason is for cooling (שוכתא), a metal plate (טסא) would be better.
The Gemara objects that if the reason is for the shape (צורתא), a coin (פולסא) would be better.
Abaye concludes that all these materials (stone, potsherd, metal, coin) are beneficial for the wound, so the mishna's choice of stone is not exclusive.

items.text: Gemara: Shmuel's father and the threads
items.text_en: Gemara: Shmuel's father and the threads
items.desc_en: Shmuel's father did not allow his daughters to go out with threads, but the Mishnah permits it. The Gemara explains that his daughters were colorful (attractive). He also did not let them sleep together, supporting Rav Huna's statement about women rolling on each other.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that young girls may go out with threads in their ears.
Shmuel's father did not allow his daughters to go out with threads, nor to sleep together, and he made them separate mikvaot in Nisan and Tishrei.
The Gemara questions how Shmuel's father could forbid what the Mishnah explicitly permits.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel's father's daughters were colorful (attractive), so the concern of attracting attention was greater.
The Gemara notes that Shmuel's father's prohibition against daughters sleeping together supports Rav Huna's statement that women who roll on each other may cause improper contact.

items.text: Opening statement from Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening statement from Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that certain women are disqualified from the priesthood.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that certain women are disqualified from the priesthood.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on Rav and Shmuel's dispute about flowing water
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on Rav and Shmuel's dispute about flowing water
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav holds that rainwater must not exceed flowing water in a mikveh, while Shmuel argues that a river is blessed from its source. Shmuel further states that only the Euphrates in Tishrei purifies through flowing water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav holds that rainwater must not exceed flowing water in a mikveh, to prevent learning from a foreign body.
Rav's practice of making a mikveh in Nisan supports his principle that rainwater must not exceed flowing water.
Shmuel argues that a river is blessed from its source, and further states that only the Euphrates in Tishrei purifies through flowing water.

items.text: Abaye's resolution of a contradiction in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution of a contradiction in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the latter clause of the Mishnah comes to teach about the law of immersion, not just covering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's use of the term 'פּוֹרֶפֶת' (she wraps) in the first clause.
Abaye explains that the latter clause of the Mishnah comes to teach about stamping (an impression).

items.text: Abaye's inquiry about a woman using a nut to carry her child
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry about a woman using a nut to carry her child
items.desc_en: Abaye asks whether a woman may use a nut as a pretext to carry her child on Shabbat. The Gemara considers the views of those who permit or forbid strategic actions in fire cases, and concludes with 'teiku' (undecided).

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks whether a woman may employ a stratagem (הערמה) by wrapping a nut to take out her small child on Shabbat.
The Gemara notes that the question applies both to those who permit stratagems and those who forbid them.
The Gemara objects that in the case of a fire, permitting a stratagem prevents extinguishing, but here there is no such concern.

The Gemara suggests that even for those who forbid stratagems in a fire, here it may be permitted because carrying a nut is not a normal way of carrying out a child; the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person with an amputated leg may go out with his wooden stump; this is the opinion of Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a cripple may go out with his wooden leg (קב) — the words of Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the laws of a wooden leg (kit'ea) and related items: Rabbi Yosei prohibits it; if it has a receptacle for crushed material, it is impure; its supports are impure with midras impurity and may be used on Shabbat and in the Temple courtyard; a chair with its supports is impure with midras but not used on Shabbat or in the courtyard; and a 'lukatmin' is pure and not used on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yosei's prohibition of the wooden leg.
The Mishnah states that if the wooden leg has a receptacle for crushed material, it is impure.
The Mishnah rules that the supports of the wooden leg are impure with midras impurity and may be used on Shabbat and in the Temple courtyard.
The Mishnah states that a chair with its supports is impure with midras but not used on Shabbat or in the courtyard.
The Mishnah concludes that lukatmin are pure and not used on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about the correct version of the Mishnah, but Rav Nachman does not know the answer or the halakha.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about the correct version of the Mishnah.
Rav Nachman responds that he does not know the correct version.
Rava asks Rav Nachman what the halakha (הלכה) is.
Rav Nachman again responds that he does not know the halakha (הלכה).

items.text: Shmuel and Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Shmuel and Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: It is stated that Shmuel and Rav Huna both rule that 'the amputee does not go out' (with his wooden leg), and Rav Yosef concludes that since both authorities agree, the Mishnah should be taught that way.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Shmuel and Rav Huna both rule that the amputee does not go out with his wooden leg.
Rav Yosef concludes that since both authorities agree, the Mishnah should be taught that the amputee does not go out.

items.text: Rava bar Shira's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rava bar Shira's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava bar Shira objects, citing a tradition from Rav Chanan bar Rava that Rabbi Meir permits the amputee to go out with his wooden leg and Rabbi Yosei prohibits it, but Rav reversed the version. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Shira objects to the previous ruling, asking whether they have not heard the tradition from Rav Chanan bar Rava.

sub.text: Tradition from Rav Chanan bar Rava
sub.text_en: Tradition from Rav Chanan bar Rava
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Shira cites the tradition that Rabbi Meir prohibits the amputee from going out with his wooden leg, and Rabbi Yosei permits it.
Rav reverses the version, indicating that Rabbi Meir permits and Rabbi Yosei prohibits.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a mnemonic (samekh samekh) to remember the correct version.

items.text: Shmuel's retraction
items.text_en: Shmuel's retraction
items.desc_en: Shmuel retracts his earlier position, as evidenced by a Mishnah about halitzah with a sandal that is not his own, where Shmuel identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Meir, who permits the amputee to go out with his wooden leg, while Rabbi Yosei prohibits it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Shmuel retracted his earlier position.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about halitzah with a sandal that is not one's own, which is valid.
The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of that Mishnah.
Shmuel identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Meir, who permits the amputee to go out with his wooden leg, while Rabbi Yosei prohibits it.

items.text: Rav Huna's retraction
items.text_en: Rav Huna's retraction
items.desc_en: Rav Huna also retracts, based on a baraita about a plasterer's sandal that is impure with midras and may be used for halitzah and on Shabbat according to Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages did not agree. Rav Huna explains that 'they did not agree' refers to Rabbi Yosei, while 'they agreed' refers to Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The stam reports that Rav Huna also retracted, citing a baraita about a plasterer's sandal that is impure with midras and may be used for halitzah and on Shabbat according to Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages did not agree.
The gemara objects that another baraita states 'they agreed with him', contradicting the first baraita.
Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'they agreed' refers to Rabbi Meir, while 'they did not agree' refers to Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Rav Yosef's identification of the dissenter
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's identification of the dissenter
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef identifies that the one who did not agree with Rabbi Akiva is Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, citing a Mishnah about a basket of straw and a reed tube where Rabbi Akiva declares them impure and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri declares them pure.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef identifies that the dissenter from the baraita is Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, citing a Mishnah about a basket of straw and a reed tube where Rabbi Akiva declares them impure and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri declares them pure.

items.text: Clarification of the plasterer's sandal
items.text_en: Clarification of the plasterer's sandal
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a plasterer's sandal is considered a vessel for midras impurity since it is not made for walking, and Rav Acha bar Rav Ulla explains that the plasterer walks in it until he reaches his home.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a plasterer's sandal can be susceptible to midras impurity since it is not made for walking.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ulla's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ulla's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ulla explains that the plasterer walks in the sandal until he reaches his home, thereby making it a walking vessel.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava about impurity
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava about impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's statement that if the wooden leg has a receptacle for crushed material, it is impure. Abaye says it is impure with corpse impurity but not midras, while Rava says it is also impure with midras. Rava supports his view from a Mishnah about a child's wagon, and Abaye distinguishes that there one leans on it, but here one does not. Abaye supports his view from a baraita about an old man's staff being pure, and Rava responds with a distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the wooden leg has a receptacle for crushed material, it is impure.
Abaye asserts that the leg is impure with טומאת מת (corpse impurity) but not with מדרס (midras impurity).
Rava counters that the leg is also impure with מדרס (midras impurity).
Rava cites a Mishnah that a child's wagon is impure with מדרס (midras impurity) to support his view.
Abaye distinguishes that in the case of the wagon one leans on it, but here one does not lean on the leg.
Abaye cites a baraita that an old man's staff is completely pure, supporting his view that the leg is not impure with מדרס (midras impurity).
Rava begins to respond with a distinction, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on sandals
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on sandals
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction about whether sandals made of certain materials are permitted for use on Shabbat and entering the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Yochanan corrects a Tanna who taught the wrong version of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about sandals is made to resolve a contradiction, distinguishing between sandals made for support and those made for leaning.
A baraita is cited stating that such sandals are susceptible to midras impurity, may not be worn on Shabbat, and may not be entered into the Temple courtyard.
A Tanna recites before Rabbi Yochanan a version of the Mishnah that says one may enter the Temple courtyard with these sandals.

Rabbi Yochanan corrects the Tanna, citing his own version that a woman may remove this sandal for חליצה (the levirate release ceremony), and insists the correct text is that one may not enter the Temple courtyard with them.

items.text: Definition of לוקטמין
items.text_en: Definition of לוקטמין
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the meaning of the term לוקטמין, with various Amoraim offering different interpretations: red clay, knots, or perfumes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term לוקטמין (a type of amulet) means.
Rabbi Abahu explains that לוקטמין means red clay (used as a seal).
Rava bar Pappa explains that לוקטמין means knots (tied amulets).
Rava bar Rav Huna explains that לוקטמין means perfumes (scented amulets).

items.text: Mishnah: Children and kings go out with knots and bells
items.text_en: Mishnah: Children and kings go out with knots and bells
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that children may go out with knots and kings with bells on Shabbat, and the principle that the Sages spoke in the present tense.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that children may go out with knots and kings with bells on Shabbat, and that the Sages spoke in the present tense (the rule applies to all, but the example reflects common practice).

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of knots and their properties
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of knots and their properties
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the knots mentioned in the Mishnah are 'קישורי פואה' (knots of a plant). Abaye's mother teaches the efficacy of different numbers of knots, and additional conditions are given for their effectiveness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the knots are, and Adda Mari in the name of Rav Nachman bar Baruch etc. answers that they are knots of a plant (פואה).
Abaye reports his mother's teaching about the efficacy of three, five, and seven knots for healing and even sorcery.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds conditions for the knots' effectiveness (not seeing sun, moon, rain, etc.), and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak comments that this is a rare case (a loaf falling into a well).

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's wording: 'sons' and 'knots'
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's wording: 'sons' and 'knots'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'sons' and not daughters, and 'small' and not adults. It explains that the knots are not ordinary knots but a specific remedy for a child who longs for his father, involving tying a strap from the right shoe on the left arm.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'sons' and 'small' rather than including daughters and adults.

sub.text: Avin bar Huna citing Rabbi Chama bar Gurya
sub.text_en: Avin bar Huna citing Rabbi Chama bar Gurya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets 'knots' as a specific remedy: a strap from the right shoe tied on the left arm for a child longing for his father.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a mnemonic: like tefillin (תפילין) on the left arm, but reversing sides is dangerous.

items.text: Various remedies and practices permitted on Shabbat
items.text_en: Various remedies and practices permitted on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A series of statements by Avin bar Huna in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya permit certain actions on Shabbat: covering a cup on the navel, anointing with oil and salt, choking, and wrapping a child. These are supported by stories of earlier sages.

sub.text: Avin bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.text_en: Avin bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.desc_en: Avin bar Huna in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya permits covering a cup on the navel on Shabbat.

sub.text: Avin bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.text_en: Avin bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.desc_en: Avin bar Huna in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya permits anointing with oil and salt on Shabbat.
The Gemara cites a story where earlier sages anointed themselves with oil and salt and recited a formula for protection, or used a wax seal in water as an alternative.

sub.text: Avin bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.text_en: Avin bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.desc_en: Avin bar Huna in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya permits choking on Shabbat.

sub.text: Avin bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.text_en: Avin bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Gurya
sub.desc_en: Avin bar Huna in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya permits wrapping a child on Shabbat.

items.text: Dispute over the version of the teaching and additional remedies
items.text_en: Dispute over the version of the teaching and additional remedies
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid differ on whether the Mishnah says 'sons' or 'son', and the attribution of the remedy. Abaye's mother provides rules for counting and tying knots.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid dispute the version of the Mishnah and the attribution of the remedy for a child's longing.
Abaye reports his mother's rule that all counting is done in the mother's name and all tying is done on the left side.
Abaye adds his mother's rule that specified counts are performed as specified, and unspecified counts are performed forty-one times.

items.text: Amulets for pregnancy and remedies for fever
items.text_en: Amulets for pregnancy and remedies for fever
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the use of an 'even tekumah' (stone of standing) for a woman who miscarries, with a debate about weighing it. Abaye's mother provides remedies for fever, including using a white zuz and salt, and a procedure involving a camel carrying something. The section ends with Rav Huna's statement.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one may go out on Shabbat with an 'even tekumah' (stone of standing) to prevent miscarriage, and Rabbi Meir adds that one may even go out with a weight of such a stone, for a woman who has not yet miscarried but is at risk.

sub.text: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya in the name of Abaye qualifies that the stone is effective only if it is specifically weighed and intended for the woman.
Abaye asks whether a woman who already has a stone may weigh another stone against it on Shabbat for the same purpose.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved with 'תיקו' (let it stand).

sub.text: Abaye in the name of his mother
sub.text_en: Abaye in the name of his mother
sub.desc_en: Abaye reports his mother's remedy for a one-day fever: take a white zuz (coin), go to the salt market, weigh an equal amount of salt, and tie it in the hollow of the neck with a blue thread.

sub.text: Abaye in the name of his mother (alternative remedy)
sub.text_en: Abaye in the name of his mother (alternative remedy)
sub.desc_en: Abaye's mother provides an alternative remedy: sit at a crossroads, take a load from a camel carrying something, throw it into a copper pot, seal it with lead, seal it with sixty seals, brand it, carry it, and say 'your burden is upon me and my burden is upon you'; Rav Acha bar Rav Huna corrects the formula to avoid harm.

sub.text: Abaye in the name of his mother (third remedy)
sub.text_en: Abaye in the name of his mother (third remedy)
sub.desc_en: Abaye's mother gives a third remedy: take a new jug, go to a river, ask the river for water for a guest, circle it over the head seven times, throw it backward, and return the water, saying the guest came and went on the same day.
Rav Huna begins a new statement, marking a transition to a new topic.

items.text: First remedy for fever
items.text_en: First remedy for fever
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a detailed recipe for a fever remedy involving seven items from seven sources, to be tied with a red string around the neck.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a detailed recipe for a fever remedy involving seven items from seven sources, to be tied with a red string around the neck.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's remedy for a persistent fever
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's remedy for a persistent fever
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan prescribes a different remedy for a persistent fever using an iron knife and a bramble bush, with specific verses recited over three days. Rav Acha bar Rava questions the order of verses, and the Gemara provides an alternative sequence. The incantation concludes with a prayer that the fire flee as it did from Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan prescribes a remedy for a persistent fever (אישתא צמירתא) using an iron knife and a bramble bush, tying a red thread to it.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's instructions for three days
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's instructions for three days
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan details the three-day procedure: each day cut a notch and recite a specific verse from the burning bush narrative.

Rav Acha bar Rava questions the order of verses and proposes an alternative sequence: on the first day recite the entire first encounter, on the second day the verse about God seeing Moses turn aside, and on the third day the verse 'Do not draw near'.

The Gemara concludes the remedy with an incantation addressed to the bramble bush, explaining that God's presence rested on it because it was lowly, and praying that the fever flee as fire fled from Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

items.text: Incantation for a simta (skin ailment)
items.text_en: Incantation for a simta (skin ailment)
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides a lengthy incantation for a simta, invoking angels and using obscure words, concluding with a curse that the ailment not grow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a lengthy incantation for a simta (skin ailment), invoking angels and using obscure words, concluding with a curse that the ailment not grow.

items.text: Incantation for a headache (kippa)
items.text_en: Incantation for a headache (kippa)
items.desc_en: A short incantation for a headache is given, invoking a drawn sword and a sling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a short incantation for a headache (כיפה), invoking a drawn sword and a sling.

items.text: Incantation for a demon (sheida)
items.text_en: Incantation for a demon (sheida)
items.desc_en: An incantation for a demon is provided, using obscure terms and curses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides an incantation to recite against a demon (שֵׁידָא), consisting of obscure curses and epithets.

items.text: Incantation for a toilet demon
items.text_en: Incantation for a toilet demon
items.desc_en: A specific incantation for a demon of the toilet is given, mentioning a lion's skull and dog's snout.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides an incantation for a toilet demon, invoking a lion's skull and a dog's snout.

items.text: Discussion on 'children of kings' and bells
items.text_en: Discussion on 'children of kings' and bells
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a Mishnah about children of kings going out with bells, identifying the Tanna as Rabbi Shimon who says all Israelites are children of kings. Rava offers an alternative explanation about a woven garment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna is the author of the Mishnah that permits children of kings to go out with bells.
Rabbi Oshaya answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that all Israelites are children of kings.
Rava offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah refers to a woven garment in one's cloak, and all agree.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on carrying amulets and Amorite practices
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on carrying amulets and Amorite practices
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may go out with a grasshopper's egg, a fox's tooth, and a nail from a crucifix for healing, according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages forbid even on weekdays due to Amorite practices. The Gemara explains the uses of these items. Abaye and Rava rule that anything with healing properties is not considered Amorite practice. The Gemara then discusses a baraita about a tree that sheds fruit, and a Tanna's statement that most practices are forbidden except for a specific remedy for a bone stuck in the throat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may go out with a grasshopper's egg, a fox's tooth, and a nail from a crucifix for healing, according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages forbid even on weekdays due to Amorite practices.
The Gemara explains the healing uses of each item: the grasshopper's egg for a fever, the fox's tooth for sleep (live for insomnia, dead for oversleeping), and the nail for inflammation.
The Mishnah's phrase 'for healing' is repeated, emphasizing Rabbi Meir's position.
Abaye and Rava rule that anything with healing properties is not considered Amorite practice.

The Gemara objects: does the inverse imply that anything without healing is Amorite practice, citing a baraita about a tree that sheds fruit being painted red and loaded with stones, questioning the healing value of painting.

The Gemara answers that the red paint is to attract attention so people pray for mercy, citing a baraita about a leper announcing his impurity, and Ravina notes that hanging baskets on a palm tree follows this Tanna's view.

sub.text: Tanna before Rabbi Chiya bar Avin
sub.text_en: Tanna before Rabbi Chiya bar Avin
sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rabbi Chiya bar Avin that all practices are forbidden as Amorite except for a specific remedy for a bone stuck in the throat, involving placing a bone of the same type on the head and reciting a formula.
The Gemara adds a formula for a bone stuck in the throat: 'It was pierced like a needle, it was locked like a shield, go down go down.'

items.text: First superstitious practice: saying 'Gad, my kid'
items.text_en: First superstitious practice: saying 'Gad, my kid'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists saying 'Gad, my kid' as a prohibited Amorite practice. Rabbi Yehuda argues that 'Gad' is a term for idolatry, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists saying 'Gad, my kid' as a prohibited Amorite practice.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that 'Gad' is a term for idolatry, citing the verse 'those who set a table for Gad'.

items.text: Second practice: calling a man by his wife's name and vice versa
items.text_en: Second practice: calling a man by his wife's name and vice versa
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that calling a man by his wife's name or a woman by her husband's name is prohibited as an Amorite practice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that calling a man by his wife's name or a woman by her husband's name is prohibited as an Amorite practice.

items.text: Third practice: saying 'Dunu Danai'
items.text_en: Third practice: saying 'Dunu Danai'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists saying 'Dunu Danai' as prohibited. Rabbi Yehuda explains that 'Dan' is a term for idolatry, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists saying 'דונו דני' (Dunu Danai) as prohibited due to דרכי האמורי (Amorite practices).
Rabbi Yehuda explains that 'דן' (Dan) is a term for idolatry, citing the verse 'חי אלהיך דן' (as your god Dan lives).

items.text: List of additional superstitious practices
items.text_en: List of additional superstitious practices
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates various superstitious acts involving animals, eggs, and cooking, all prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori. These include addressing a crow, slaughtering a rooster that crowed at evening, breaking eggs on a wall, dancing for chicks, and urinating into a pot to speed cooking.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the first superstitious practice: addressing a crow and a she-crow with specific incantations, which is prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori.
The Mishnah lists the second practice: slaughtering a rooster that crowed at evening or a hen that crowed like a rooster, prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori.
The Mishnah lists the third practice: saying 'I will drink and leave over' repeatedly, prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori.
The Mishnah lists the fourth practice: a woman cracking eggs on a wall, prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori.
The Mishnah lists the fifth practice: stirring (or dancing) in front of chicks, prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori.
The Mishnah lists the sixth practice: a woman dancing for chicks or counting seventy-one chicks to prevent their death, prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori.
The Mishnah lists the seventh practice: dancing for kutach (a dish), silencing for lentils, and shouting for grits, prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori.
The Mishnah lists the eighth practice: a woman urinating in front of her pot to speed cooking, prohibited as Darkhei HaEmori.

items.text: Permitted and prohibited aids for cooking
items.text_en: Permitted and prohibited aids for cooking
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits placing a mulberry twig or glass shards in a pot to speed cooking, but the Sages prohibit glass shards due to danger.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah permits placing a mulberry twig or glass shards in a pot to speed cooking.
The Sages prohibit glass shards due to the danger they pose.

items.text: Permitted practices for lamps
items.text_en: Permitted practices for lamps
items.desc_en: A Baraita teaches that one may put a lump of salt into a lamp to make it burn brighter, and clay or potsherds under a lamp to make it last longer.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita permits placing a lump of salt into a lamp to brighten it, and clay or potsherds under a lamp to prolong its burning.

items.text: Rav Zutra's ruling on covering an oil lamp
items.text_en: Rav Zutra's ruling on covering an oil lamp
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra says that one who covers an oil lamp and uncovers a naphtha lamp violates the prohibition of Bal Tashchit (waste).

sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra rules that one who covers an oil lamp and uncovers a naphtha lamp violates the prohibition of בל תשחית (do not destroy).

items.text: Permitted blessing: 'Wine and life for the Rabbis'
items.text_en: Permitted blessing: 'Wine and life for the Rabbis'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that saying 'Wine and life for the Rabbis' is not prohibited as an Amorite practice. A story is told of Rabbi Akiva who said this at his son's wedding feast.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that saying 'Wine and life for the Rabbis' is not prohibited as an Amorite practice.
A story is told that Rabbi Akiva, at his son's wedding feast, said this blessing over each cup of wine, providing a precedent for the practice.

items.text: Transition to next Mishnah: General principle of Shabbat liability
items.text_en: Transition to next Mishnah: General principle of Shabbat liability
items.desc_en: The daf concludes the previous chapter and begins a new Mishnah, which states the general rule: one who forgets the essence of Shabbat is liable for one sin-offering, while one who knows the essence but forgets it is liable for each Shabbat, and one who knows it is Shabbat is liable for each act.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule for Shabbat liability: one who forgets the essence of Shabbat is liable for only one sin-offering.
The Mishnah states the second case: one who knows the essence of Shabbat but forgets it is liable for each Shabbat.
The Mishnah states the third case: one who knows it is Shabbat is liable for each prohibited act.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a great principle regarding Shabbat: one who performs many labors of the same type is liable for only one sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states a great principle regarding Shabbat: one who performs many labors of the same type is liable for only one sin-offering.

items.text: Gemara's question about the term 'great principle'
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the term 'great principle'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the term 'great principle' for Shabbat, suggesting it might be to contrast with another principle, but notes that for tithes no such term is used.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the term 'כלל גדול' (a great principle) for Shabbat, noting that for tithes (מעשר) the Mishnah does not use this term.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's first answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's first answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin answers that Shabbat and Sabbatical year have 'fathers' and 'offshoots', so they are called 'great', unlike tithes. The Gemara then challenges this from Bar Kappara who uses 'great principle' for tithes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin answers that Shabbat and the Sabbatical year (שביעית) have primary categories (אבות) and subcategories (תולדות), so they use 'גדול', while tithes lack this structure, but then questions what Bar Kappara would say who uses 'כלל גדול' for tithes.
The Gemara objects that Bar Kappara uses 'great principle' for tithes, so what 'fathers' and 'offshoots' exist there?

items.text: Alternative answer: comparative severity
items.text_en: Alternative answer: comparative severity
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a different reason: Shabbat's punishment is greater than Sabbatical year's because it applies to both detached and attached items, and Sabbatical year's punishment is greater than tithes' because it applies to both human and animal food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative reason: the term 'גדול' reflects the greater scope of punishment for Shabbat compared to the Sabbatical year, and for the Sabbatical year compared to tithes.

items.text: Bar Kappara's view and the Mishnah of pe'ah
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's view and the Mishnah of pe'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Bar Kappara's use of 'great principle' for tithes: tithes apply to figs and vegetables, unlike pe'ah. It then cites the Mishnah's rules for pe'ah and tithes, showing the differences.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for Bar Kappara, who teaches 'great principle' regarding tithes, the principle is that the penalty of tithes is greater than that of pe'ah, because tithes apply to figs and vegetables while pe'ah does not.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule for pe'ah: any food that is guarded, grows from the ground, is harvested at once, and is stored for preservation is obligated in pe'ah.

The Mishnah explains each exclusion: 'food' excludes certain plants, 'guarded' excludes ownerless produce, 'grows from the ground' excludes mushrooms, 'harvested at once' excludes figs, and 'stored for preservation' excludes vegetables.

The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule for tithes: any food that is guarded and grows from the ground is obligated in tithes, but the conditions of 'harvested at once' and 'stored for preservation' are not taught, showing the difference from pe'ah.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel explain that the Mishnah's case of one who forgot the essence of Shabbat refers to a child captured among gentiles or a convert, but one who knew and then forgot is liable for each Shabbat. The Gemara questions the wording and clarifies that 'knows the essence' means one who knew it and then forgot.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both state that the Mishnah's case of one who forgot the essence of Shabbat refers to a child captured among gentiles or a convert, but one who knew and then forgot is liable for each Shabbat.
The Gemara questions the wording of the Mishnah: does 'one who forgot the essence of Shabbat' imply that he originally knew it?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah means one for whom the essence of Shabbat was forgotten from the outset, not one who knew and forgot.
The Gemara asks: if one knew and then forgot, is he liable for each Shabbat?
The Gemara objects: instead of teaching the case of one who knows the essence, the Mishnah should have taught the case of one who knew and forgot, which would be all the more so.
The Gemara resolves that 'one who knows the essence of Shabbat' in the Mishnah actually refers to one who knew it and then forgot it.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not teach the case of one who knows the essence of Shabbat but forgot it, which would certainly be liable for each act, and concludes that the Mishnah deals with one who knew and later forgot, and Rav and Shmuel's case is similar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not teach the case of one who knows the essence of Shabbat but forgot it, which would certainly be liable for each act, and concludes that the Mishnah deals with one who knew and later forgot, and Rav and Shmuel's case is similar.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's position and a challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's position and a challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish argue that only one who knew and forgot is liable, but a captive child or convert is exempt. A baraita is cited that seems to contradict them, stating that a captive child or convert is liable only for one sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish state that only one who knew and later forgot is liable, but a child captured among gentiles or a convert who converted among gentiles is exempt.

A baraita is cited that states a general rule: one who forgets the essence of Shabbat is liable only once, and it gives the example of a child captured among gentiles or a convert who converted among gentiles, with Monbaz exempting.

items.text: Monbaz's argument before Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Monbaz's argument before Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Monbaz argues before Rabbi Akiva that just as a deliberate sinner requires prior knowledge, so too an inadvertent sinner requires prior knowledge. Rabbi Akiva adds that the knowledge must be at the time of the act, and Monbaz agrees, but Rabbi Akiva then retorts that such a person is not called an inadvertent sinner but a deliberate one.

sub.desc_en: Monbaz argues before Rabbi Akiva that just as a deliberate sinner requires prior knowledge, so too an inadvertent sinner requires prior knowledge.
Rabbi Akiva adds that the knowledge must be at the time of the act.
Monbaz agrees, but Rabbi Akiva retorts that such a person is not called an inadvertent sinner but a deliberate one.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita teaches 'How? A child captive,' which is difficult for Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. They respond that Monbaz exempts such a person, and they hold like Monbaz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita explicitly says 'How so? A child,' which is difficult for Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish who exempt such a child.
Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish respond that Monbaz exempts, and they follow Monbaz's opinion.

items.text: Monbaz's scriptural basis
items.text_en: Monbaz's scriptural basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Monbaz's reasoning: he derives from the verse 'One Torah shall be for you for one who acts inadvertently' juxtaposed with 'the soul that acts with a high hand' that an inadvertent sinner is compared to a deliberate sinner, requiring prior knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Monbaz's reasoning: the verse 'תּוֹרָה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָכֶם לָעֹשֶׂה בִּשְׁגָגָה' (one law shall be for you for one who acts inadvertently) is juxtaposed with 'וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָד רָמָה' (the soul that acts with a high hand), comparing an inadvertent sinner to an intentional one, requiring prior knowledge.

items.text: The Rabbis' interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: The Rabbis' interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the verse 'One Torah,' and explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught his son that it is needed for a different derivation, as the verse continues.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis (who disagree with Monbaz) do with the verse 'תּוֹרָה אַחַת' (one law), and notes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught his son a different interpretation from it.

sub.text: Gemara's answer via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Rabbis need the verse for the teaching that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught his son, as the verse continues.

items.text: Opening derivation: all sins with karet are equated to idolatry
items.text_en: Opening derivation: all sins with karet are equated to idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse equating all commandments to idolatry, establishing that for any sin with karet for intentional violation, one brings a chatat for unintentional violation. This sets the framework for defining shogeg.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse equating all commandments to idolatry, establishing that for any sin with karet for intentional violation, one brings a chatat for unintentional violation.

items.text: Monbaz's view and Rabbanan's rejection
items.text_en: Monbaz's view and Rabbanan's rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Monbaz, shogeg means ignorance of the korban obligation, but the Rabbanan reject this, holding that ignorance of the korban is not considered shogeg.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion of Monbaz, what constitutes shogeg (unintentional error)?
The Gemara answers: for example, if one was unaware of the requirement to bring a korban (offering).
The Rabbis object: ignorance of the korban is not considered shogeg (unintentional error).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish debate the definition of shogeg
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish debate the definition of shogeg
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that shogeg requires ignorance of karet, even if one knows the prohibition (lav). Reish Lakish requires ignorance of both the lav and karet. Rava explains Reish Lakish's scriptural basis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the Rabbis, what constitutes shogeg?
Rabbi Yochanan answers: once one is unaware of the karet (divine excision) punishment, even if one was aware of the prohibition (לאו), it is considered shogeg.
Reish Lakish answers: one must be unaware of both the prohibition (לאו) and the karet (divine excision) punishment.
Rava explains Reish Lakish's reasoning by citing a verse that requires ignorance of both the prohibition and the karet.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse cited by Reish Lakish actually teaches that only one who repents from his knowledge brings a korban, excluding an apostate (meshummad).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: how does Rabbi Yochanan interpret the verse that Reish Lakish used?
The Gemara answers: the verse is needed to exclude an apostate (משומד) from bringing a korban.
A baraita is cited: one who repents from their knowledge brings a korban, but one who does not repent does not bring a korban.

items.text: Applying the debate to Shabbat: the case of multiple melachot
items.text_en: Applying the debate to Shabbat: the case of multiple melachot
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the dispute to the Mishnah's list of 39 melachot. Rabbi Yochanan's view allows liability for each melacha when one knows Shabbat is a lav but is ignorant of karet. Reish Lakish requires ignorance of both lav and karet, which is possible only if one knows Shabbat through techumim (according to Rabbi Akiva).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah listing the 39 אבות מלאכות (primary categories of forbidden labor) and Rabbi Yochanan's statement that if one performed them all in one lapse of awareness, one is liable for each individually.
The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yochanan, the case is possible when one knows Shabbat is a לאו (prohibition) but is ignorant of the כרת (karet) penalty.

The Gemara explains that according to Reish Lakish, who requires ignorance of both the לאו (prohibition) and the כרת (karet), the case is possible only if one knows Shabbat through תחומין (the Sabbath boundary prohibition) according to Rabbi Akiva's view.

items.text: A baraita defining shogeg and meizid, attributed to Monbaz
items.text_en: A baraita defining shogeg and meizid, attributed to Monbaz
items.desc_en: A baraita defines shogeg as ignorance of both Shabbat and melacha, and meizid as knowledge of both. Cases of mixed knowledge are still liable. The Gemara identifies this baraita as following Monbaz's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: who is the Tanna behind the baraita that the Rabbis taught?
The baraita is cited: one who is unaware of both Shabbat and the labors is the shogeg of the Torah; one who is aware of one but not the other is liable.
The Gemara answers: this baraita follows the opinion of Monbaz.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on shevu'at bitui and the novel korban
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on shevu'at bitui and the novel korban
items.desc_en: Abaye states that all agree (including Rabbi Yochanan) that for shevu'at bitui (an oath of utterance), one is liable only if ignorant of the lav, since there is no karet. The Gemara explains the concern: since this is a novel korban (the only lav that brings a korban), one might think ignorance of the korban itself should suffice, but Abaye rejects this.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that all agree regarding shevu'at bitui (an oath of utterance) that one is not liable for a korban unless one was ignorant of the lav (the prohibition itself).
The Gemara asks: 'All agree' — who is included? It clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan is the one who would need to agree, and questions why this is not obvious.
The Gemara explains the concern: since this is a novel korban (the only lav that brings a korban), one might think ignorance of the korban itself should suffice, but Abaye rejects this.

items.text: Gemara's objection to Abaye's view on Shavuot Bitui
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Abaye's view on Shavuot Bitui
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about Shavuot Bitui, suggesting it supports the Rabbis' view against Abaye. It then considers whether the baraita follows Monbaz or the Rabbis, concluding it is a refutation of Abaye.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita defining shigegat shevu'at bitui (unintentional violation of a verbal oath) and identifies its author as Monbaz.
The alternative version rejects the identification with Monbaz as obvious, concluding the baraita follows the Rabbis and constitutes a refutation of Abaye.

items.text: Abaye's statement on Terumah and the debate with Rava
items.text_en: Abaye's statement on Terumah and the debate with Rava
items.desc_en: Abaye asserts that all agree one is not liable for the additional fifth (chomesh) on terumah unless they are unaware of the prohibition. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's view applies only where karet is involved, and Rava argues that death stands in place of karet and the fifth in place of a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asserts that all agree one is not liable for the additional fifth (חומש) on תרומה (priestly portion) unless they are unaware of the prohibition itself.
The Gemara asks who is included in 'all agree,' and answers that it refers to Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's view is obvious, since he only spoke where כרת (karet) is involved, not where it is absent.
The Gemara explains that Abaye's statement is necessary to teach that death does not stand in place of כרת (karet) to impose liability for the fifth.
Rava argues that death stands in place of כרת (karet) and the fifth (חומש) stands in place of a sacrifice, so liability for the fifth applies only where a sacrifice would be required.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Chiya bar Rav on counting Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Chiya bar Rav on counting Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Chiya bar Rav argue about how one who loses track of Shabbat should count: Rav Huna says count six days and observe one, while Chiya bar Rav says observe one day and count six. The Gemara brings a baraita that supports Rav Huna, refuting Chiya bar Rav.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that one who loses track of Shabbat counts six days and observes one.
Chiya bar Rav counters that one should observe one day and then count six.
The Gemara explains the dispute: one opinion follows the creation of the world (starting with Sunday), the other follows Adam (who first observed Shabbat after six days).
A baraita is cited: one who loses track of Shabbat observes one day out of six.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita means 'counts six and observes one' (supporting Rav Huna).
The Gemara rejects the interpretation, saying the baraita means 'observes one and counts six' (supporting Chiya bar Rav).
The Gemara objects: if the baraita meant 'observes one and counts six', it should have said 'observes one and counts six' rather than 'observes one out of six'.
Another baraita is cited explicitly stating: 'counts six and observes one', supporting Rav Huna.
The Gemara concludes that this is a refutation of Chiya bar Rav's position.

items.text: Rava's ruling on daily sustenance for the lost traveler
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on daily sustenance for the lost traveler
items.desc_en: Rava rules that the traveler should do enough work each day for his sustenance, including the day he observes as Shabbat, by preparing from the previous day. He identifies the Shabbat day through Kiddush and Havdalah.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the lost traveler works each day for his sustenance, including the day he observes as Shabbat, by preparing from the previous day, and identifies the Shabbat day through Kiddush and Havdalah.

items.text: Rava's ruling on one who recognizes part of the day
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on one who recognizes part of the day
items.desc_en: Rava states that if one recognizes part of the day he left, he may work the entire day. The Gemara explains this is not obvious, as one might think he could work two days, but the ruling teaches that sometimes a caravan comes and he leaves.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one recognizes part of the day he left, he may work the entire day.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought he could work two days, but the ruling teaches that sometimes a caravan comes and he leaves.

items.text: Derivation of the law for one who knows the essence of Shabbat
items.text_en: Derivation of the law for one who knows the essence of Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuha deriving from two verses that one who knows the essence of Shabbat must observe each Shabbat individually. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, arguing the opposite derivation from the same verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where in the Torah are these matters derived?

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha answers by citing two verses: 'וְשָׁמְרוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת' (one observance for multiple Shabbatot) and 'וְאֶת שַׁבְּתֹתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ' (one observance for each Shabbat).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, arguing the opposite: 'וְשָׁמְרוּ' refers to one observance for each Shabbat, and 'וְאֶת שַׁבְּתֹתַי' refers to one observance for multiple Shabbatot.

items.text: Introduction of the next topic: one who knows it is Shabbat
items.text_en: Introduction of the next topic: one who knows it is Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the next case: one who knows that it is Shabbat, setting up the continuation of the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the next case: one who knows that it is Shabbat, setting up the continuation of the discussion.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes between one who knows it is Shabbat but not the labors and one who knows the labors but not Shabbat. Rav Safra and Rav Nachman offer explanations, with Rav Nachman ultimately attributing the distinction to the number of lapses of awareness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between one who knows it is Shabbat but not the labors and one who knows the labors but not Shabbat.
Rav Safra explains that in the first case the person refrains from Shabbat awareness, in the second from labor awareness.
Rav Nachman objects that refraining from Shabbat awareness is only because of labors, and refraining from labor awareness is only because of Shabbat, so the distinction collapses.
Rav Nachman explains that the distinction is based on the number of lapses of awareness: one lapse in the first case, multiple lapses in the second.

items.text: Source for division of labors from Shmuel
items.text_en: Source for division of labors from Shmuel
items.desc_en: Shmuel derives the principle that one is liable for each labor separately from the verse 'mechalileha mot yumat', interpreting it as applying to an unwitting transgressor, where 'yumat' means monetary liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that one is liable separately for each labor.
Shmuel derives from the verse 'מחלליה מות יומת' that the Torah multiplies many deaths for one desecration, implying separate liability for each labor.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'מחלליה מות יומת' is written about an intentional desecrator, not an inadvertent one.
The Gemara resolves that since the verse is not needed for an intentional case (already covered by 'כל העושה מלאכה יומת'), apply it to an inadvertent case, interpreting 'יומת' as monetary liability.

items.text: Objection: Why not derive from Rabbi Natan?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not derive from Rabbi Natan?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Shmuel could have derived the division of labors from Rabbi Natan's exposition of the thirty-nine labors from the verses in Exodus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shmuel did not derive the division of labors from the source used by Rabbi Natan.
A baraita cites Rabbi Natan who derives the thirty-nine labors from the repetition of 'דברים', 'הדברים', 'אלה הדברים' in the Torah.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's full derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's full derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rabbi Natan's complete derivation: from 'becharish uvaqatzir tishbot' and 'lo teva'aru esh' he learns that each primary labor is independently liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a hypothetical: if one performed all labors in a single lapse of awareness, perhaps he is liable only once.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'בחריש ובקציר תשבות' teaches that each distinct labor is separate.
The Gemara questions further: perhaps one is liable separately only for plowing and reaping (explicit in the verse), but for all other labors only once.

The Gemara answers that the verse 'לא תבערו אש' teaches that just as burning is an אב מלאכה (primary labor) and one is liable separately for it, so too for every primary labor one is liable separately.

items.text: Answer: Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Answer: Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yosei, who says that the verse about burning fire came out for a negative commandment, not for division, so Shmuel cannot use Rabbi Natan's derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yosei, who says that the prohibition of burning on Shabbat was singled out to teach a negative commandment (לאו), not to divide labors.

sub.text: Supporting baraita — Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Natan
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita — Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Natan
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei who says burning was singled out for a negative commandment, and Rabbi Natan who says it was singled out to divide labors.

items.text: Further objection: Rabbi Yosei's own source
items.text_en: Further objection: Rabbi Yosei's own source
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Shmuel could have derived division from Rabbi Yosei's own exposition of 've'asah me'achat mehenah', which implies multiple liabilities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shmuel did not derive the division of labors from the source used by Rabbi Yosei.

A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei who derives from the verse 'ועשה מאחת מהנה' that sometimes one is liable once for all, and sometimes separately for each, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains the derivation from the words 'אחת', 'מאחת', 'הנה', 'מהנה'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: the words 'אַחַת', 'מֵאַחַת', 'הֵנָּה', 'מֵהֵנָּה' teach that one (אַחַת) can be these (הֵנָּה), and these (הֵנָּה) can be one (אַחַת).

items.text: Incomplete continuation
items.text_en: Incomplete continuation
items.desc_en: The daf begins to explain the words 'achat' and 'me'achat' but is cut off.

sub.desc_en: An incomplete fragment begins to list the words 'אחת' and 'מאחת' as mnemonic devices (possibly for the names of the sages).

items.text: Shmuel's interpretation of the Mishnah's exegesis
items.text_en: Shmuel's interpretation of the Mishnah's exegesis
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's view that the Mishnah's derivations from the words 'henna' and 'mehenna' refer to primary categories (avot) and their subcategories (toladot). Shmuel rejects the interpretations of 'one that is henna' and 'henna that is one' as referring to combinations of intentionality and error.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's exegesis: 'henna' refers to primary categories (avot), 'mehenna' to subcategories (toladot), 'one that is henna' to intentional Sabbath violation with unintentional labor, and 'henna that is one' to unintentional Sabbath with intentional labor.
Shmuel rejects the Mishnah's interpretations of 'one that is henna' and 'henna that is one' as referring to combinations of intentionality and error.

items.text: Rava's inquiry to Rav Nachman about double unawareness
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry to Rav Nachman about double unawareness
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a case where one is unaware of both Shabbat and the forbidden labors. Rav Nachman initially says he is liable for only one, but Rava objects that he should be liable for each. Rav Ashi resolves by examining whether the person separates from Shabbat or from the labors. Ravina challenges this, arguing that one cannot separate from one without the other, concluding there is no difference.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: if one forgot both Sabbath and labor categories, what is the halacha (הלכה)?
Rav Nachman answers: since he forgot the Sabbath, he is liable only one sin-offering.
Rava objects: on the contrary, since he forgot the labor categories, he should be liable for each one separately.
Rav Ashi resolves: we examine whether he separated from the Sabbath or from the labor categories; if from Sabbath, he is liable only one; if from labor, he is liable for each.
Ravina objects: one only separates from Sabbath because of the labors, and from labors because of Sabbath — so there is no difference.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yochanan's statement about forty minus one labors
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yochanan's statement about forty minus one labors
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah listing thirty-nine primary labors and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation that if one performs them all in one lapse of awareness, he is liable for each. This supports the view that double unawareness leads to multiple liabilities, but if one is aware of Shabbat, he is only liable for one, which is only possible in a case of intentional Shabbat violation and unawareness of the labors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: the primary categories of labor are thirty-nine minus one.
The Gemara asks: why do we need the count?
Rabbi Yochanan answers: to teach that if one performed all of them in one lapse of awareness, he is liable for each one separately.
The Gemara infers: if one forgot both Sabbath and labor categories, he is liable for each — this fits well with Rabbi Yochanan's statement.
The Gemara objects: if one forgot only the Sabbath, he is liable only one — how can Rabbi Yochanan's case be found? Only in a case of intentional Sabbath violation with unintentional labor.

items.text: Reconciling with Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's view
items.text_en: Reconciling with Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if one holds like Rabbi Yochanan, the case is possible when one knows Shabbat only as a prohibition (lav). But if one holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who requires unawareness of both a negative commandment and karet, then one must know Shabbat only through the laws of techumim, in accordance with Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains: if the Tanna holds like Rabbi Yochanan, who says that if one was unaware of the karet penalty even though he was aware of the negative commandment, the case is found where he knew the Sabbath prohibition as a negative commandment.

The Gemara continues: if the Tanna holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who requires unawareness of both the negative commandment and the karet penalty, then how does he know the Sabbath? He knows it through the laws of Sabbath boundaries (תחומין), according to Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Rava's case of alternating awareness
items.text_en: Rava's case of alternating awareness
items.desc_en: Rava presents a scenario where one performs two sets of actions (reaping and grinding a fig-bulk each) with different combinations of awareness and unawareness, and then becomes aware of each set separately, setting up a question about liability for multiple sin-offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a case: one reaped and ground an olive's bulk in a state of unintentional Sabbath violation with intentional labor, and then again reaped and ground an olive's bulk in a state of intentional Sabbath violation with unintentional labor, and was informed about each act separately.

items.text: Opening statement on gerira
items.text_en: Opening statement on gerira
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a statement about the principle of 'gerira' (rolling) in the context of Shabbat labors: when one is aware of the sin of Shabbat but not the specific labor, reaping rolls reaping, but grinding stands alone. This sets up the debate between Abaye and Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the principle of gerira (rolling) for Shabbat labors: when one is aware of the sin of Shabbat but not the specific labor, reaping rolls reaping and grinding rolls grinding, but grinding that is opposite stands in its place.

items.text: Abaye and Rava debate gerira
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava debate gerira
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that grinding also rolls grinding, as they are the same category of labor. The Gemara questions Rava's position on gerira by citing a case of eating forbidden fat: Rava holds that a sacrifice for the first atones for the first and second, but not the third, while Abaye says any sacrifice atones for all. After hearing Abaye, Rava concedes that gerira exists but not double gerira.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that grinding also rolls grinding, because the category of grinding is one unified name.
The Gemara questions whether Rava actually holds the principle of gerira at all.

The Gemara cites a case where one ate two olive-bulks of forbidden fat in one lapse, then knew of one, then ate another: Rava ruled that bringing a sacrifice for the first atones for the first and second but not the third, showing limited gerira.
Rava continues: bringing a sacrifice for the third atones for the third and second but not the first; bringing for the middle atones for all.
Abaye argues that even if one brings a sacrifice for any one of the sins, all are atoned.
Abaye argues that even bringing a sacrifice for any one of them atones for all.
After hearing Abaye, Rava concedes that dragging exists, but only one level of dragging, not dragging of dragging.
The Gemara resolves: after Rava heard Abaye's view, he accepted gerira but not double gerira (gerira of gerira).
After hearing Abaye, Rava concedes that gerira exists but not double gerira.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question about combining half-measures
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question about combining half-measures
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Assi (or Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira) about a case where one reaped and ground half a fig-bulk with one type of error, then repeated with another type of error: do they combine? The answer is that they are divided for sins and do not combine.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Assi (or alternatively Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira): if one reaped and ground half a fig-bulk with ignorance of Shabbat but intent for the labor, then reaped and ground another half with intent for Shabbat but ignorance of the labor, do they combine?
Rabbi Assi answers: they are divided for sin-offerings and do not combine.
Rabbi Assi answers that the half-measures are divided for sins (חֲלוּקִין לַחֲטָאוֹת) and do not combine.

items.text: Challenge from a Mishnah about combining foods
items.text_en: Challenge from a Mishnah about combining foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that divided sins prevent combination, citing a Mishnah where eating half an olive of one type in two dishes combines for liability according to Rabbi Yehoshua. Resh Lakish explains that the case involves two dishes, and Rabbi Yehoshua holds that dishes divide only for leniency, not stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: is it always true that when divided for sin-offerings they do not combine? It cites a Mishnah where eating half an olive-bulk of one type and then another half of the same type in one lapse makes one liable, but from two types one is exempt.

The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needed to state that from one type one is liable, and Resh Lakish in the name of Bar Tuteni explains: it deals with eating from two dishes, and Rabbi Yehoshua holds that dishes divide; the Mishnah teaches that Rabbi Yehoshua only applies this stringently, not leniently.
The Gemara objects: here the cases are divided for sin-offerings, yet they combine (in the Mishnah's case of one type from two dishes).
Rabbi Zeira answers: Master (Rabbi Yirmeya) teaches the Mishnah from the beginning and it is difficult for him; we teach it from the end and it is not difficult for us.

Resh Lakish in the name of Bar Tuteni explains: the Mishnah's phrase 'from two types exempt' is necessary, and it deals with one type from two dishes, and Rabbi Yehoshua holds that dishes divide both leniently and stringently.

items.text: Resolution: different versions of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Resolution: different versions of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that Rabbi Zeira learned the Mishnah from the beginning, causing difficulty, while others learned it from the end, where the case is actually about one type in two dishes, and Rabbi Yehoshua holds that dishes divide for both leniency and stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: here the case involves different sin-offerings (חֲלוּקִין לַחֲטָאוֹת), yet the Mishnah says they combine (מִצְטָרְפִי) for liability, contradicting the earlier ruling that they do not combine.

Rabbi Zeira answers that the master (the questioner) learned the Mishnah from the beginning, causing the difficulty, while we (Rabbi Zeira and his circle) learned it from the end, and it poses no difficulty for us.

sub.text: Supporting baraita (Resh Lakish citing Bar Tuteni)
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita (Resh Lakish citing Bar Tuteni)
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Bar Tuteni explains that the Mishnah's case of 'two types' is actually one type in two dishes, and Rabbi Yehoshua holds that dishes divide (תַּמְחוּיִין מְחַלְּקִין) both for leniency and stringency, so the combination applies.

items.text: Conclusion from the end of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion from the end of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that from the end of the Mishnah, it is clear that the case involves one type and two dishes, supporting the version that Rabbi Yehoshua holds dishes divide for both leniency and stringency, thus resolving the challenge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the end of the Mishnah that it deals with one type and two dishes.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah's case of 'one type and one stew' refers to a situation where the person had intermediate knowledge, and follows Rabban Gamliel who holds that partial knowledge does not combine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's second clause needs to specify 'one type and one stew' when it is obvious.
Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah's case involves intermediate knowledge and follows Rabban Gamliel's view that partial knowledge does not combine.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue about a case where one ate two olive-sized portions of fat with a single awareness, then learned about the first and later the second. Rabbi Yochanan obligates two sin-offerings, citing the verse 'upon his sin... and bring'; Reish Lakish exempts, citing 'from his sin and it shall be forgiven'. The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish interprets the former verse as referring to after atonement, while Rabbi Yochanan's verse is explained as a case of eating one and a half olive-sized portions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: one ate two olive-sized portions of forbidden fat (חלב) with a single unawareness, then learned about the first and later about the second.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the person is liable to bring two sin-offerings.
Reish Lakish rules that the person is liable only for one sin-offering.
Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'על חטאתו... והביא' (upon his sin... and bring) to support his ruling.
Reish Lakish cites the verse 'מחטאתו ונסלח לו' (from his sin and it shall be forgiven) to support his ruling.
The Gemara objects to Reish Lakish: but the verse 'על חטאתו... והביא' is written, implying multiple offerings.
The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish interprets that verse as referring to after atonement (כפרה), not before.
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Yochanan: but the verse 'מחטאתו ונסלח לו' is written, implying a single offering.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's verse applies to a case where one ate one and a half olive-sized portions, and the verse teaches that the half does not combine with the whole.

items.text: Ravina's inquiry to Rav Ashi about the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Ravina's inquiry to Rav Ashi about the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether the dispute applies only when knowledge occurs before separation (with the point being whether knowledge or separation divides), or only after separation (with separation or atonement dividing), or in both cases. Rav Ashi concludes that the dispute applies in both cases, based on a logical argument from the verses. The Gemara then suggests that perhaps Rav Ashi was uncertain and spoke hypothetically.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish applies only when knowledge occurs before separation, only after separation, or in both cases.
Rav Ashi answers that the dispute applies in both cases, arguing from the verses: if the dispute were limited to one scenario, the verse could have been interpreted differently.
The Gemara suggests that perhaps Rav Ashi was uncertain and spoke hypothetically (אִם תִּמְצֵי לוֹמַר), explaining how each sage would interpret the verse under each scenario.

items.text: Ulla's statement on definite guilt-offering
items.text_en: Ulla's statement on definite guilt-offering
items.desc_en: Ulla states that according to the one who holds that a definite guilt-offering does not require initial knowledge.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that according to the one who holds that a definite guilt-offering (אשם ודאי) does not require initial knowledge.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rav Hamnuna's challenge
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rav Hamnuna's challenge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who performs five acts of intercourse with a designated slave-woman is liable only once. Rav Hamnuna challenges this: if one performed an act, set aside a sacrifice, and then said 'wait for me to perform another act,' would he also be liable only once? The Gemara responds that the case after setting aside the sacrifice is not being discussed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who performs five acts of intercourse with a designated slave-woman (שפחה חרופה) is liable only once.
Rav Hamnuna challenges: if one performed an act, set aside a sacrifice, and then said 'wait for me to perform another act,' would he also be liable only once?
The Gemara responds that the case after setting aside the sacrifice is not being discussed.

items.text: Rav Dimi's statement and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's statement and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that according to the opinion that a definite guilt-offering requires initial awareness, one is liable for each act. Abaye objects, noting that for a sin-offering, which also requires initial awareness, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree. Rav Dimi is silent, then Abaye suggests he might be referring to the case after setting aside the sacrifice, like Rav Hamnuna, and Rav Dimi confirms.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi says: according to the one who says that a definite guilt-offering (אשם ודאי) requires prior awareness, one who performs five acts with a designated slave-woman is liable for each one.
Abaye objects: consider the sin-offering (חטאת), which also requires prior awareness, yet Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish disagree about it.
Rav Dimi is silent, unable to respond.
Abaye asks: perhaps you are referring to the case after setting aside the sacrifice, like Rav Hamnuna? Rav Dimi confirms: yes.
Rav Dimi confirms Abaye's suggestion.

items.text: Ravin's resolution: everyone agrees in certain cases
items.text_en: Ravin's resolution: everyone agrees in certain cases
items.desc_en: Ravin reports that everyone agrees in some cases of the designated slave-woman: all agree one is liable only once (like Ulla), and all agree one is liable for each act (like Rav Hamnuna). The dispute (between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish) is only for the opinion that a definite guilt-offering requires initial awareness.

sub.desc_en: Ravin says: everyone agrees in the case of a designated slave-woman, and there is a dispute in the case of a designated slave-woman.
Everyone agrees that one is liable only once — in accordance with Ulla's view.
Everyone agrees that one is liable for each act — in accordance with Rav Hamnuna's view.
The dispute about a designated slave-woman — according to the one who says a definite guilt-offering requires prior awareness — is the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

items.text: Transition to further discussion
items.text_en: Transition to further discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals that the matter was stated (i.e., a related teaching will follow).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals a transition to a new statement or discussion.

items.text: Dispute between Rava and Abaye on intent
items.text_en: Dispute between Rava and Abaye on intent
items.desc_en: Rava and Abaye argue about a case where one intended to cut detached vegetation but cut attached vegetation. Rava holds he is exempt because he did not intend the prohibited cutting, while Abaye holds he is liable because he intended some cutting.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the case: one who intended to lift detached vegetation but cut attached vegetation is exempt.
The gemara presents a second case: one intended to cut detached vegetation but cut attached vegetation, and cites Rava's ruling of exemption.
Abaye argues that the person is liable because he intended some cutting in general.
Rava cites a baraita about the stringency of Shabbat over other commandments to support his position that intent for the specific prohibited act is required for liability.

items.text: Rava cites a baraita to support his position
items.text_en: Rava cites a baraita to support his position
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that states a stringency of Shabbat over other commandments: one is liable for each violation when two are done in one lapse of awareness. Conversely, for other commandments, unwitting action without intent is liable, unlike Shabbat. This supports Rava's view that intent matters for Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The gemara repeats the baraita's first clause about Shabbat's stringency regarding multiple acts in one lapse of awareness.
The gemara questions the baraita's comparison: if the case is reaping and grinding, the parallel in other commandments (eating forbidden fat and blood) also yields two liabilities.
The gemara reinterprets: the comparison is to a case of eating two portions of forbidden fat, where only one liability applies, paralleling two acts of reaping on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara questions the baraita's comparison
items.text_en: Gemara questions the baraita's comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the baraita's comparison works: if one performs two different forbidden acts (e.g., reaping and grinding), the same would apply to other commandments (e.g., eating forbidden fat and blood). The only way the baraita makes sense is if the comparison is between two identical acts (e.g., reaping twice vs. eating forbidden fat twice), where Shabbat would still require separate liability.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that the baraita actually refers to reaping and grinding, and the comparison is to idolatry, citing Rabbi Ami's rule that multiple acts of idolatry in one lapse yield only one liability.

items.text: Answer: The baraita refers to idolatry
items.text_en: Answer: The baraita refers to idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita's comparison is with idolatry, not other commandments in general. As Rabbi Ami said, one who performs multiple idolatrous acts (sacrificing, burning incense, libation) in one lapse of awareness is only liable once, unlike Shabbat where each act is separate.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions the application to idolatry by examining the baraita's second clause about inadvertent action without intent.

The gemara rejects possible examples: if one thought it was a synagogue and bowed, his heart is toward Heaven; if he saw an idol and bowed, either he accepted it as a god (intentional) or not (meaningless).

items.text: Gemara challenges the idolatry interpretation
items.text_en: Gemara challenges the idolatry interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the second clause of the baraita (unwitting action without intent) applies to idolatry. If one bows to a synagogue thinking it is a synagogue, his heart is to Heaven. If one sees an idol and bows, either he accepts it as a god (intentional) or not (meaningless). Thus the baraita's case is unclear.
