sub.desc_en: The gemara resolves: the case is one who bows to an idol out of love or fear, which is liable for idolatry; Abaye holds liable for Shabbat as well, but Rava exempts entirely.

items.text: Resolution: Cases of love/fear or 'permitted'
items.text_en: Resolution: Cases of love/fear or 'permitted'
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to one who worships idolatry out of love or fear (not intending it as a god), which fits Abaye's view that such action is liable. For Rava, who exempts, the case is where one mistakenly thinks the act is permitted. This explains why Shabbat exempts entirely.

sub.desc_en: The gemara clarifies that Rava's question to Rav Nachman was only about whether one is liable for one or two sin-offerings, not about complete exemption.

items.text: Conclusion: Rava's question to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Conclusion: Rava's question to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava's question to Rav Nachman was only about whether one is liable for one or two violations, but not about complete exemption. This clarifies the scope of the earlier dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava's question to Rav Nachman (about the case of intending to cut a detached object but cutting an attached one) was only about whether one is liable for one or two sin-offerings, but he never considered the possibility of complete exemption, which is now shown to be the case according to the baraita's second clause.

items.text: Abaye's examples of shogeg b'lo miskavein
items.text_en: Abaye's examples of shogeg b'lo miskavein
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Abaye's position by giving examples where one is liable for idolatry but exempt on Shabbat due to the principle that intending to cut detached but cutting attached is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: is the first clause about idolatry and the latter about other commandments, and what is an example of shogeg b'lo miskavein (unintentional without intent) in other commandments?
The Gemara answers: one thinks it is fat and eats it, which is liable for other commandments, but on Shabbat one is exempt because intending to cut detached but cutting attached is exempt.
The Gemara asks: what is Abaye's example of shogeg b'lo miskavein?
The Gemara answers: one thinks it is saliva and swallows it, which is liable for idolatry, but on Shabbat one is exempt because intending to lift detached but cutting attached is exempt.
The Gemara resolves: but if one intended to cut detached and cut attached, one is liable on Shabbat.

items.text: Dispute between Rava and Abaye on unintended throwing
items.text_en: Dispute between Rava and Abaye on unintended throwing
items.desc_en: Rava and Abaye argue about cases where one intended a lesser violation but performed a greater one, or thought the domain was private but it was public. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary to teach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: if one intended to throw two cubits but threw four, Rava says he is exempt (פטור) and Abaye says he is liable (חייב).
Rava explains his ruling: he is exempt because he did not intend the prohibited throwing of four cubits; Abaye counters that he is liable because he intended some throwing in general.
The Gemara presents a second case: one thought the domain was private but it was actually public; Rava says exempt, Abaye says liable.
Rava explains: he is exempt because he did not intend a prohibited throwing; Abaye counters: he is liable because he intended some throwing in general.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary to teach Rava's position, because each case might have led one to think he would concede to Abaye in the other.

items.text: Reconciling Rava's view with the Mishnah's count
items.text_en: Reconciling Rava's view with the Mishnah's count
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rava can explain the Mishnah's statement that one is liable for each melakhah if done in one lapse, given his view that unintended actions are exempt. It suggests Rava follows Rabbi Yochanan or Resh Lakish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rava, who holds that unintended actions are exempt, can explain the Mishnah's statement that one is liable for each melakhah if done in one lapse of awareness.

The Gemara resolves that Rava could follow Rabbi Yochanan's view that one is liable if they were aware of the prohibition but not the punishment, or Resh Lakish's view requiring ignorance of both, in which case the ignorance of Shabbat could be regarding the laws of techumin (Sabbath boundaries) according to Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Mishnah: The thirty-nine avot melakhot
items.text_en: Mishnah: The thirty-nine avot melakhot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the thirty-nine categories of forbidden labor on Shabbat, beginning with agricultural processes and continuing through textile, hide, writing, building, and other activities.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the primary categories of forbidden labor are thirty-nine, and lists the first group: agricultural and food-preparation labors from sowing through baking.
The Mishnah lists the second group: textile-related labors from shearing wool through tearing for the purpose of sewing.
The Mishnah lists the third group: hide-processing labors from hunting a deer through cutting the hide.

The Mishnah lists the fourth group: writing, building, demolishing, extinguishing, kindling, striking a hammer blow, and carrying out, and concludes that these are the thirty-nine primary categories of labor.

items.text: Gemara's question on the need for the count
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the need for the count
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the number of primary labors (forty minus one). Rabbi Yochanan answers that if one performs all of them in a single lapse of awareness, he is liable for each individually.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies the count of primary labors.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the count teaches that one who performs all labors in a single lapse of awareness is liable for each individually.

items.text: Order of plowing and sowing
items.text_en: Order of plowing and sowing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists sowing before plowing, contrary to the natural order. It answers that the Tanna is speaking about the practice in Eretz Yisrael, where they sow first and then plow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists plowing after sowing, when plowing normally precedes sowing.
The Tanna explains that the Mishnah follows the practice in the Land of Israel, where they sow first and then plow.

items.text: Grouping of planting-related labors
items.text_en: Grouping of planting-related labors
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that sowing, pruning, planting, bending a branch, and grafting are all one type of labor. The Gemara explains this teaches that performing multiple similar labors incurs only one liability. Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rabbi Ami states that a pruner is liable for planting, and a planter, etc., is liable for sowing. The Gemara corrects that it should say 'also for sowing'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that sowing, pruning, planting, bending, and grafting are all one category of labor.
The Gemara asks what novel point the baraita teaches.
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that one who performs many labors that are similar to one labor is liable only once.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha's statement in the name of Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha's statement in the name of Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha reports that pruning is liable as planting, and planting, bending, and grafting are liable as sowing.
The Gemara objects that the statement implies liability only for sowing, not for planting, which seems inconsistent.
The Gemara resolves that the statement should be read as 'also liable for sowing,' not exclusively.

items.text: Multiple liabilities for pruning with intent for wood
items.text_en: Multiple liabilities for pruning with intent for wood
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that one who prunes and needs the wood is liable for two: one for reaping and one for planting. Rav Yosef adds that one who cuts alfalfa is liable for two: reaping and planting. Abaye adds that one who cuts beets is liable for two: reaping and sowing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that one who prunes and needs the wood is liable for two labors: reaping and planting.
Rav Yosef rules that one who cuts alfalfa is liable for two labors: reaping and planting.
Abaye rules that one who cuts beets is liable for two labors: reaping and sowing.

items.text: Plowing and related labors
items.text_en: Plowing and related labors
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that plowing, digging, and making furrows are all one labor. Rav Sheshet rules that if one had a clod and removed it, in a house he is liable for building, in a field for plowing. Rava adds that if one had a pit and filled it, in a house he is liable for building, in a field for plowing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that plowing, digging, and making furrows are all one category of labor.
Rav Sheshet rules that removing a mound indoors is liable as building, but in the field as plowing.
Rava rules that filling a pit indoors is liable as building, but in the field as plowing.

items.text: Digging a pit only for its dirt
items.text_en: Digging a pit only for its dirt
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that one who digs a pit on Shabbat and only needs its dirt is exempt. Even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an unnecessary labor is liable, this case is different because the digger is destroying, not repairing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that one who digs a pit on Shabbat and only needs its dirt is exempt.
The Gemara explains that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable for a labor not needed for its own sake, this case is exempt because the digger is destroying, not improving.

items.text: Reaping and related labors
items.text_en: Reaping and related labors
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that reaping, grape-gathering, cutting dates, picking olives, and plucking figs are all one labor. Rav Pappa rules that one who throws a stone at a palm tree and causes dates to fall is liable for two: one for detaching and one for dismantling. Rav Ashi disagrees, saying this is not the normal way of detaching or dismantling.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that reaping, grape-harvesting, cutting, olive-harvesting, and fig-picking are all one category of labor.
Rav Pappa rules that one who throws a stone at a palm tree and causes dates to fall is liable for two labors: plucking and dismantling.
Rav Ashi objects that this action does not follow the normal manner of plucking or dismantling.

items.text: Gathering (me'amer) and its definition
items.text_en: Gathering (me'amer) and its definition
items.desc_en: Rava rules that one who gathers salt from a salt-pan is liable for the labor of gathering (me'amer). Abaye objects, saying that gathering applies only to produce of the ground.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one who gathers salt from a salt marsh is liable for the labor of gathering (מעמר).
Abaye objects that gathering (עימור) applies only to produce that grows from the ground.

items.text: Threshing and related labors
items.text_en: Threshing and related labors
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that threshing, beating flax, and combing wool are all one labor.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that threshing, winnowing, and sifting are all one category of labor.

items.text: Winnowing, selecting, grinding, and sifting
items.text_en: Winnowing, selecting, grinding, and sifting
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that winnowing, selecting, and sifting appear to be the same labor. Abaye and Rava both state that any act that was performed in the Tabernacle (Mishkan) is a primary labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that winnowing, selecting, and sifting seem to be the same labor.
Abaye and Rava both explain that these labors are distinct because each was performed in the construction of the Tabernacle.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission of pounding (כותש)
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission of pounding (כותש)
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why pounding (כותש) is not listed among the avot melachot. Abaye and Rava offer different explanations: Abaye says it is because a poor person eats his bread without pounding, while Rava attributes the list to Rabbi Yehuda who counts 39 melachot, and including pounding would make 40.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why pounding (כותש) is not listed among the avot melachot, given that similar acts are included.
Abaye answers that pounding is not a primary melacha because a poor person eats his bread without pounding it.
Rava answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who counts 39 avot melachot, and including pounding would make 40.
The Gemara objects that one could remove another melacha and include pounding instead.
The Gemara resolves that the correct explanation is like Abaye's, that pounding is not a primary melacha.

items.text: Baraita on selecting food and Ulla's interpretation
items.text_en: Baraita on selecting food and Ulla's interpretation
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if one has various foods before him, he may select and eat, select and put aside, but he should not select, and if he selected he is liable for a sin-offering. Ulla explains that this means he may select and eat or put aside for immediate use that day, but not for the next day. Rav Chisda objects, comparing it to baking or cooking for the same day.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one may separate (בורר) and eat or set aside food, but if one separates in a prohibited manner, he is liable for a sin-offering.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means.
Ulla explains that the baraita permits separating and eating immediately on the same day, but prohibits separating for the next day.
Rav Chisda objects that if separating for the same day is permitted, then baking and cooking for the same day would also be permitted, which is not the case.

items.text: Rav Chisda's and Rav Yosef's alternative interpretations
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's and Rav Yosef's alternative interpretations
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda suggests the baraita refers to selecting less than a shiur (the measure that incurs liability). Rav Yosef objects that even less than a shiur is prohibited for baking. Rav Yosef then proposes that the baraita distinguishes between selecting by hand (permitted) and using a sieve or sifter (liable for a sin-offering), with a basket or tray being prohibited but not liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the baraita refers to separating less than a shiur (minimum measure), which is permitted, but a full shiur is prohibited.
Rav Yosef objects that baking less than a shiur is also prohibited, so the distinction is invalid.
Rav Yosef explains that the baraita permits separating by hand, but prohibits using a sieve or sifter, with different levels of liability.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's and Abaye's interpretations, and Rava's approval
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's and Abaye's interpretations, and Rava's approval
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna objects that the baraita does not mention a basket or tray. He interprets it as permitting selecting food from waste, but not waste from food. Abaye objects that the baraita does not say 'food from waste'. Abaye then explains that the baraita permits selecting for immediate use, but not for later in the day, which is like selecting for storage and incurs liability. The Sages present this to Rava, who approves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna objects that the baraita does not mention a sieve or sifter.
Rav Hamnuna explains that the baraita permits separating food from waste, but prohibits separating waste from food.
Abaye objects that the baraita does not mention separating food from waste.
Abaye explains that the baraita permits separating immediately (for immediate use), but prohibits separating for later in the day, which is considered like storing.
Rava approves Abaye's explanation, saying that Nachmani (Abaye) spoke well.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Ashi and Rav Yirmeya from Difti
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Ashi and Rav Yirmeya from Difti
items.desc_en: The baraita discusses a case where one had two types of food and selected, ate, and put aside. Rav Ashi teaches that he is exempt, while Rav Yirmeya from Difti teaches that he is liable. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first case (exempt) is with a basket or tray, the second (liable) is with a sieve or sifter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one had two types of food and separated and ate, or separated and set aside.
Rav Ashi teaches that one is exempt from a sin-offering in this case.
Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti teaches that one is liable for a sin-offering in this case.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rav Ashi's exemption applies to using a basket or tray, while Rabbi Yirmeya's liability applies to using a sieve or sifter.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the exempt case refers to selection with a basket or tray (קנון ותמחוי), while the liable case refers to selection with a sieve or sifter (נפה וכברה).

items.text: Rav Dimi's story about Rav Bibi's Shabbat
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's story about Rav Bibi's Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that on Rav Bibi's Shabbat, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi visited, and Rav Bibi threw a basket of fruit before them. Rav Dimi is uncertain whether this was because Rav Bibi holds that selecting food from waste is prohibited, or because he was being generous.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that on Rav Beivai's Shabbat, he placed a basket of fruit before Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, and the Gemara is uncertain whether this was because separating food from waste is prohibited or because of generosity.

items.text: Chizkiya's ruling on selecting lupines
items.text_en: Chizkiya's ruling on selecting lupines
items.desc_en: Chizkiya states that one who selects lupines from their waste is liable. The Gemara questions whether this implies Chizkiya holds that selecting food from waste is prohibited, but distinguishes lupines because they are inedible without processing.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiya states that one who separates lupines from their waste is liable for a sin-offering.
The Gemara asks whether Chizkiya holds that separating food from waste is prohibited.
The Gemara answers that lupines are different, implying a distinction that justifies Chizkiya's ruling without adopting the general principle.

items.text: Clarification of Tochen (grinding) with beets and bran
items.text_en: Clarification of Tochen (grinding) with beets and bran
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's 'grinder' includes cutting beets into small pieces (Rav Pappa) and sifting bran (Rav Menasheh). Rav Ashi adds that if one is particular about the size of the cut, he is also liable for M'chatech (cutting to size).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's category of 'the grinder' and introduces Rav Pappa's explanation.
Rav Pappa rules that one who cuts beets into small pieces is liable for the labor of grinding (טוחן).
Rav Menasheh rules that one who sifts bran is liable for the labor of grinding (טוחן).
Rav Ashi adds that if one is particular about the size of the cut pieces, he is also liable for the labor of cutting to size (מחתך).

items.text: Why the Mishnah lists 'Lash' and 'Ofeh' separately
items.text_en: Why the Mishnah lists 'Lash' and 'Ofeh' separately
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa questions why the Mishnah lists both 'the kneader' and 'the baker' separately, since baking is included in the Mishkan's cooking of dyes. He answers that our Tanna is listing the order of bread-making, not the Mishkan's labors.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa questions why our Tanna omitted the Mishkan's cooking of dyes and instead listed 'the baker'.
Rav Pappa answers that our Tanna is merely listing the order of bread-making, not the Mishkan's labors.

items.text: Throwing a splinter into a furnace and boiling pitch
items.text_en: Throwing a splinter into a furnace and boiling pitch
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avira states that throwing a splinter into a furnace is liable for cooking (Mevashel). The Gemara notes this is obvious, but the teaching is that even though one intends to strengthen the vessel, the splinter first softens and then hardens. Rabbah bar Rav Huna says boiling pitch is liable for cooking, and the novelty is that even though it hardens again, it is still considered cooking.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avira states that throwing a splinter into a furnace is liable for cooking (Mevashel).
The Gemara objects that this ruling is obvious.
The Gemara explains the novelty: one might think the intent is to strengthen the vessel, but the splinter first softens and then hardens, so it is cooking.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna states that boiling pitch is liable for cooking.
The Gemara again objects that this is obvious.
The Gemara explains the novelty: one might think that since the pitch hardens again it is not cooking, but the teaching shows it is still considered cooking.

items.text: Liability for making a Chavita or a Tanura
items.text_en: Liability for making a Chavita or a Tanura
items.desc_en: Rava says one who makes a Chavita (a type of clay vessel) is liable for seven sin-offerings, and for a Tanura (oven) for eight. Abaye adds that making a Chalta (a type of bread) is liable for eleven, and if one sews its opening, for thirteen.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that one who makes a Chavita (a type of clay vessel) is liable for seven sin-offerings, and for a Tanura (oven) for eight.
Abaye adds that making a Chalta (a type of bread) is liable for eleven sin-offerings, and if one sews its opening, for thirteen.

items.text: Shearing wool from an animal and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Kahana
items.text_en: Shearing wool from an animal and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Kahana
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says one who spins wool directly from an animal on Shabbat is liable for three sin-offerings: for shearing, carding, and spinning. Rav Kahana objects that this is not the normal way of shearing, carding, or spinning. The Gemara cites a baraita from Rabbi Nechemya that spinning on an animal is called spinning, but distinguishes that Rabbi Nechemya had superior wisdom.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists shearing wool and whitening it as prohibited labors on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who spins wool directly from an animal on Shabbat is liable for three sin-offerings: for shearing, carding, and spinning.
Rav Kahana objects that this is not the normal way of shearing, carding, or spinning.
The Gemara challenges Rav Kahana by citing a baraita from Rabbi Nechemya that spinning on an animal is called spinning.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Nechemya's case is different because he possessed superior wisdom.

items.text: Plucking a wing and the three labors involved
items.text_en: Plucking a wing and the three labors involved
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who plucks a wing, cuts it, or pulls it out is liable for three sin-offerings. Resh Lakish specifies: plucking is liable for shearing, cutting for cutting to size, and pulling for smoothing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who plucks a wing, cuts it, or pulls it out is liable for three sin-offerings.
Resh Lakish specifies that plucking is liable for shearing, cutting for cutting to size, and pulling for smoothing.

items.text: The source for tying and untying in the Mishkan
items.text_en: The source for tying and untying in the Mishkan
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the prohibition of tying and untying in the Mishkan. Rava suggests it was for tying tent pegs, but Abaye objects that this is a temporary knot. Abaye suggests it was for weavers of curtains who tied broken threads. Rava counters that untying is not explained. After rejecting a suggestion, Rava (or Rabbi Illai) concludes it was from the hunters of the chilazon who tied and untied nets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where in the Mishkan there was an act of tying.
Rava answers that the tying was for tent pegs in the Mishkan.
The Gemara objects that tying tent pegs is a temporary knot, not a permanent one.
Abaye answers that the tying was done by weavers of the curtains who tied broken threads.
Rava objects that Abaye's explanation accounts for tying but not for untying.
The Gemara rejects a hypothetical suggestion that one could untie one knot and tie another, arguing it is disrespectful to do so before God.
Rava (or Rabbi Illai) concludes that the tying and untying in the Mishkan was done by hunters of the chilazon who tied and untied nets.

items.text: The requirement for two stitches and the source for tearing
items.text_en: The requirement for two stitches and the source for tearing
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'the one who sews two stitches' but this does not hold unless they are tied (Rabbi Yochanan). Then it asks where tearing existed in the Mishkan, and begins to cite Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira's answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'the one who sews two stitches' is problematic because two stitches do not hold unless tied.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the objection by stating that the Mishnah refers only to two stitches that are tied.
The Gemara asks where tearing existed in the Mishkan, since the Mishnah lists 'the one who tears in order to sew'.
Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira begin to provide an answer regarding the source of tearing in the Mishkan.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a curtain has a tear, one may tear it further and sew it on Shabbat, implying that such actions are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a curtain has a tear, one may tear it further and sew it on Shabbat, implying that such actions are permitted.

items.text: Rav's statement and the dispute about magicians
items.text_en: Rav's statement and the dispute about magicians
items.desc_en: Rav states that stretching a sewing thread on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering, learning from a magician is liable for death, and one who knows how to calculate seasons and constellations but does not is forbidden to speak with. A dispute between Rav and Shmuel arises about the meaning of 'amgush'ta' (magicians), with Rav holding it means blasphemers, supported by his earlier statement.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviah citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviah citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav states three halachot: stretching a sewing thread on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering, learning from a magician is liable for death, and one who knows how to calculate seasons and constellations but does not is forbidden to speak with.
The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about the meaning of 'amgush'ta' (magicians), with one saying sorcerers and the other saying blasphemers.

The Gemara concludes that Rav holds 'amgush'ta' means blasphemers, supported by his earlier statement that learning from a magician is liable for death, since if it meant sorcerers one could learn to understand and instruct.

items.text: The obligation to calculate seasons and constellations
items.text_en: The obligation to calculate seasons and constellations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara that one who knows how to calculate seasons and constellations but does not is condemned by a verse. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yochanan that it is a mitzvah to calculate, as it is a wisdom visible to the nations.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quotes a tradition that one who knows how to calculate seasons and constellations but does not is condemned by the verse 'וְאֵת פֹּעַל ה׳ לֹא יַבִּיטוּ וּמַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו לֹא רָאוּ'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yochanan that calculating seasons and constellations is a מצוה (commandment), derived from the verse 'וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם וַעֲשִׂיתֶם כִּי הִיא חָכְמַתְכֶם וּבִינַתְכֶם לְעֵינֵי הָעַמִּים', identifying this wisdom as the calculation of seasons and constellations.

items.text: Liability for hunting and killing a chilazon
items.text_en: Liability for hunting and killing a chilazon
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita: one who catches a chilazon and crushes it is liable for only one act. Rabbi Yehuda holds crushing is included in threshing, but the Sages disagree. Rava explains the Sages' reasoning that threshing applies only to produce of the ground. An objection is raised about taking a life, but Rabbi Yochanan answers that he crushed it dead. Rava counters that even if alive, it is a case of 'mit'asek' (unintentional), and the principle of 'p'sik reishei' does not apply because the animal's life is beneficial for extracting its dye.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who catches a chilazon and crushes it is liable for only one act; Rabbi Yehuda holds crushing is included in threshing, but the Sages disagree.
Rava explains the Sages' reasoning: threshing applies only to produce of the ground, not to a chilazon.
The Gemara objects: why is he not also liable for taking a life?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that he crushed it dead, so no separate life-taking liability applies.
Rava counters that even if crushed alive, it is a case of 'mit'asek' (unintentional) regarding taking a life.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Abaye and Rava's principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Abaye and Rava's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Abaye and Rava both rule that Rabbi Shimon agrees with 'p'sik reishei' (an inevitable consequence), so here crushing inevitably kills.
Rava resolves that the principle of 'p'sik reishei' does not apply because the animal's life is beneficial for extracting its dye, so the crushing is not purely inevitable.

items.text: Dispute about liability for slaughtering a chilazon
items.text_en: Dispute about liability for slaughtering a chilazon
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one who slaughters a chilazon is liable. Rav says it is due to dyeing, while Shmuel says it is due to taking a life.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one who slaughters a chilazon is liable for a sin-offering.
Rav answers that the liability is due to the forbidden labor of dyeing (צובע).
Shmuel answers that the liability is due to taking a life (נטילת נשמה).

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav's explanation for the labor of dyeing
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav's explanation for the labor of dyeing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists dyeing as a separate labor if it also involves taking a life (of the insect). Rav offers an explanation: the dyer benefits from the blood coloring the slaughter area, attracting customers, so the labor is indeed dyeing, not just killing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists dyeing as a separate labor if it also involves taking a life (of the insect), and suggests that it should be classified under both.
Rav explains that the dyer benefits from the blood coloring the slaughter area, attracting customers, so the labor is indeed dyeing, not just killing.

items.text: Salting and tanning: are they the same labor?
items.text_en: Salting and tanning: are they the same labor?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists both salting and tanning, but the Gemara notes they seem identical. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish resolve this by substituting one with 'smoothing' (sirtut). Rabba bar Rav Huna holds that salting meat is liable as tanning, but Rava objects that tanning does not apply to food. Rav Ashi limits Rabba's ruling to cases where the meat is needed for guests, not for household use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why salting and tanning are listed separately if they seem to be the same labor.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish answer that one of the two should be replaced with the labor of drawing lines (שירטוט).
Rabbah bar Rav Huna states that one who salts meat on Shabbat is liable for the labor of tanning (מעבד).
Rava objects that tanning (עיבוד) does not apply to food items.
Rav Ashi resolves that Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling applies only when one intends to preserve the meat for a journey, but for home use, one does not treat food like wood.

items.text: Smoothing and cutting: definitions and examples
items.text_en: Smoothing and cutting: definitions and examples
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the labors of smoothing (memachek) and cutting (mechatekh). Rabbi Acha bar Chanina rules that one who scrapes between pillars is liable for smoothing. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports three rulings from Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: scraping the tops of beams is liable for cutting, spreading a bandage is liable for smoothing, and chiseling a stone is liable for the final hammer blow. Rabbi Shimon ben Kisma adds that forming a shape in a vessel or blowing glass is liable for the final hammer blow. Rav Yehuda rules that removing threads from a garment is liable for the final hammer blow, provided one cares about them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina states that one who smooths between pillars on Shabbat is liable for the labor of smoothing (ממחק).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports three rulings from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: scraping poles is liable for cutting (מחתך), spreading a bandage is liable for smoothing (ממחק), and chiseling a stone is liable for the finishing blow (מכה בפטיש).

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Kisma citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Kisma citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Kisma citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish states that one who forms a shape in a vessel or blows glass is liable for the finishing blow (מכה בפטיש).
Rav Yehuda states that one who removes a splinter from a garment is liable for the finishing blow (מכה בפטיש), but only if he cares about the splinter.
Rav Yehuda rules that removing threads from a garment is liable for the final hammer blow, provided one cares about them.

items.text: Writing two letters: a baraita on large letters
items.text_en: Writing two letters: a baraita on large letters
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the case of writing one large letter that could contain two: one is exempt. Conversely, erasing a large letter that could contain two is liable. Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei notes this is a stringency for erasing over writing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one who writes one large letter where two could fit is exempt, but one who erases a large letter where two could fit is liable.

sub.text: Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei notes that this is a stringency in erasing compared to writing.
Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei notes that this is a stringency for erasing (מוחק) over writing (כותב).

items.text: The principle of 'makeh b'patish' (final hammer blow)
items.text_en: The principle of 'makeh b'patish' (final hammer blow)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists building, demolishing, extinguishing, kindling, and the final hammer blow. Rabba and Rabbi Zeira state a general principle: any action that completes a labor is liable as 'makeh b'patish'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rabbi Zeira state that anything that completes a labor is liable for the finishing blow (מכה בפטיש).
Rabba and Rabbi Zeira state a general principle: any action that completes a labor (גמר מלאכה) is liable as the final hammer blow (מכה בפטיש).

items.text: The word 'these' excludes Rabbi Eliezer; 'lacking one' excludes Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: The word 'these' excludes Rabbi Eliezer; 'lacking one' excludes Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's wording 'these are the avot melakhot' uses 'these' to exclude Rabbi Eliezer, who holds one liable for a toladah (sub-labor) in the place of an av (primary labor). The phrase 'lacking one' excludes Rabbi Yehuda, who adds the labors of shaking out and beating; the Sages respond that shaking out is included in warping and beating in weaving.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's wording
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's wording
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'אלו' (these) excludes Rabbi Eliezer's view, who holds one liable for a תולדה (sub-category) in place of an אב (primary category).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's wording
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's wording
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the phrase 'חסר אחת' (missing one) excludes Rabbi Yehuda's view, who adds the labors of shaking out (שובט) and darning (מדקדק), but the Sages respond that these are already included in the labors of stretching (מיסך) and weaving (אורג).

items.text: Mishnah: the rule of carrying based on storage suitability
items.text_en: Mishnah: the rule of carrying based on storage suitability
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states an additional principle: anything fit for storage and typically stored in that quantity, if carried out on Shabbat, one is liable for a sin-offering. Anything not fit for storage and not stored in that quantity is only liable for the one who stores it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states another rule: anything fit for storage and stored in that quantity, if carried out on Shabbat, one is liable for a sin-offering; otherwise, only the one who stored it is liable.

items.text: Gemara: what does 'fit for storage' exclude?
items.text_en: Gemara: what does 'fit for storage' exclude?
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates what the Mishnah's phrase 'fit for storage' excludes. Rav Pappa says it excludes menstrual blood; Mar Ukva says it excludes wood from an asherah (idolatrous tree). The one who says menstrual blood certainly excludes wood, while the one who says wood holds that menstrual blood is stored for a cat. The other opinion counters that since it is weak, it is not stored. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina notes that this Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Shimon, who holds that all shiurim are only for those who store them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'fit for storage' excludes.
Rav Pappa answers that it excludes menstrual blood.
Mar Ukva answers that it excludes wood from an asherah (idolatrous tree).
The Gemara notes that the one who says menstrual blood certainly excludes wood.
The Gemara explains that the one who says wood holds that menstrual blood is stored for a cat.
The other opinion counters that since menstrual blood is weak, it is not stored.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina notes that this Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Shimon, who holds that all shiurim are only for those who store them.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's concluding phrase 'and anything not fit for storage'.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's statement about Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's statement about Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar notes that the Mishnah's ruling does not follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that if an item is not normally stored but someone stored it, another who carries it out is liable due to the first person's intention.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that the Mishnah's ruling does not follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle that if an item is not normally stored but someone stored it, another who carries it out is liable due to the first person's intention.

items.text: Mishnah: Shiurim for carrying animal fodder
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shiurim for carrying animal fodder
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum measures for carrying various types of fodder on Shabbat: straw (mouthful of a cow), chaff (mouthful of a camel), grain stalks (mouthful of a lamb), herbs (mouthful of a kid), and garlic/onion leaves (wet: dried fig-bulk, dry: mouthful of a kid). These cannot combine because their measures differ.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum measures for carrying out various types of fodder on Shabbat, and states that different types do not combine because their measures are not equal.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of 'atzah' and dispute about carrying straw for a camel
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of 'atzah' and dispute about carrying straw for a camel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda defines 'atzah' as legume straw. Rav Dimi reports a dispute: carrying a cow's mouthful of straw for a camel — Rabbi Yochanan says liable, Reish Lakish says exempt. Rabbi Yochanan later retracted, and Rav Yosef and Abaye debate which view is correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'עָצָה' means, and Rav Yehuda answers that it is straw of leguminous plants.
Rav Dimi reports a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds one is liable for carrying straw the size of an ox's mouth for a camel, while Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds one is exempt.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan initially ruled one way but retracted, and Rav Yosef approves the retraction because the straw is not fit for a camel.
Abaye objects that the original ruling was correct because the straw is fit for an ox.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's support for the retraction
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's support for the retraction
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef supports the retraction, arguing that straw is not fit for a camel.
Abaye objects, arguing that the original view is more reasonable because the straw is fit for a cow.

items.text: Ravin's version of the dispute and the principle of eating under duress
items.text_en: Ravin's version of the dispute and the principle of eating under duress
items.desc_en: Ravin reports that all agree carrying straw for a camel is liable; the dispute is about carrying chaff for a cow. The opinions are reversed: Rabbi Yochanan says exempt because eating under duress is not considered eating, while Reish Lakish says liable because it is considered eating.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that all agree carrying straw for a camel is liable; the dispute is about carrying chaff for a cow.
The opinions are reversed: Rabbi Yochanan says exempt, Reish Lakish says liable.
Rabbi Yochanan explains his exemption: eating under duress (אכילה על ידי הדחק) is not considered eating.
Reish Lakish explains his liability: eating under duress (אכילה על ידי הדחק) is considered eating.

items.text: Reconciling the measure for grain stalks
items.text_en: Reconciling the measure for grain stalks
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says grain stalks are a mouthful of a lamb, but a baraita says a dried fig-bulk. It resolves that both are the same measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says the measure for עָמִיר (sheaves) is a lamb's mouthful, but a baraita says it is a dried fig's bulk, and resolves that both measures are the same.
The Gemara resolves that both measures are actually the same quantity.

items.text: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina on combining different measures
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina on combining different measures
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains that different items do not combine for the stricter measure, but they do combine for the more lenient measure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that moist garlic and onion leaves have a measure of a dried fig, dry ones a kid's mouthful, and they do not combine because their measures are not equal.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that they do not combine for the stricter measure, but they do combine for the more lenient measure.

items.text: Objection from the laws of impurity of fabrics
items.text_en: Objection from the laws of impurity of fabrics
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if measures differ, they cannot combine, as seen in the laws of fabric impurity where different materials combine only if they are fit for sitting. Rabbi Shimon explains the reason is their fitness for sitting, implying otherwise they do not combine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether items with different measures can combine, citing a baraita about different fabric types that combine for טומאת מושב (impurity of a seat).
The baraita states that different fabrics combine for טומאת מושב (impurity of a seat) because they are all fit for that purpose, implying that without such fitness they would not combine.

items.text: Rava's statement (unfinished)
items.text_en: Rava's statement (unfinished)
items.desc_en: Rava begins to speak, but the text cuts off, leaving his statement incomplete.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins a statement, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara connects the previous discussion to the Mishnah by stating that here too, the principle of a sample applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that here too, the items are fit as a sample, connecting the previous discussion to the Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Shiur for carrying food and exclusions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shiur for carrying food and exclusions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who carries food the size of a dried fig is liable, and different foods combine because they share the same shiur. Excluded are peels, pits, stalks, bran, and coarse flour. Rabbi Yehuda adds an exception for lentil peels that cook with them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who carries out food the size of a dried fig is liable, and foods combine due to equal measures, except for peels, pits, stalks, bran, and coarse bran; Rabbi Yehuda adds an exception for lentil peels that cook with them.
Rabbi Yehuda adds an exception for lentil peels that cook with them.

items.text: Gemara's question on bran and coarse flour
items.text_en: Gemara's question on bran and coarse flour
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why bran and coarse flour are excluded from combining, citing a baraita that they are included for the purpose of challah. Abaye answers that a poor person eats his bread with a moist dough, implying they are considered part of the food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why bran and coarse bran do not combine, citing a baraita that they are included in the measure for חלה (dough offering).
Abaye answers that a poor person eats his bread as a moist dough, so bran is considered part of the food for חלה but not for Shabbat carrying.
Abaye answers that a poor person eats his bread with a moist dough, so bran and coarse flour are considered part of the food for challah but not for Shabbat carrying.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on peels and the contradiction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on peels and the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah mentions only lentil peels, but a baraita includes bean peels as well. Rabbi Avahu resolves this by distinguishing between fresh and old peels; old peels are excluded because they look like flies in the dish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda mentions only lentil peels and not bean peels, citing a baraita where he includes both.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to fresh lentils, while the baraita refers to old ones.
The Gemara asks why old lentil peels are not included.
Rabbi Avahu answers that old lentil peels look like flies in the dish and are therefore not considered food.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The standard phrase 'Hadran alach Klal Gadol' marks the end of the chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard 'we return to you, Great Principle' formula.

items.text: Mishnah: Shiurim for liquids
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shiurim for liquids
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists shiurim for carrying various liquids: wine enough to mix a cup, milk for a swallow, honey for a wound, oil for a small limb, water for a kilor, and all other liquids in a revi'it. Rabbi Shimon says all are a revi'it, and these shiurim are only for those who store them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum measures for carrying out various liquids on Shabbat: wine for mixing a cup, milk for a swallow, honey for a wound, oil for anointing a small limb, water for rubbing a kilor, and all other liquids and slops in a revi'it; Rabbi Shimon says all are a revi'it, and these measures are only for those who store them.
The Mishnah states the shiur for milk: enough for a swallow.
The Mishnah states the shiur for honey: enough to put on a wound.
The Mishnah states the shiur for oil: enough to anoint a small limb.
The Mishnah states the shiur for water: enough to rub a kilor.
The Mishnah states that all other liquids have a shiur of a revi'it.
The Mishnah states that all other poured liquids have a shiur of a revi'it.
Rabbi Shimon says all liquids have a shiur of a revi'it.
Rabbi Shimon adds that these shiurim are only for those who store the liquids.

items.text: Gemara on the cup of blessing
items.text_en: Gemara on the cup of blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the wine shiur is for a 'good cup,' specifically the cup of blessing. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak quotes Rabbah bar Avuha that the cup of blessing must contain a quarter of a revi'it so that when diluted it stands at a revi'it. Rava adds that we also learn this from the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines the shiur for wine as 'the amount for mixing a good cup,' and the Gemara identifies this as the cup of blessing (כוס של ברכה).

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak quotes Rabbah bar Avuha that the cup of blessing must contain a רובע רביעית (quarter of a revi'it) so that when diluted it stands at a full revi'it.
Rava adds that we also learn this from the Mishnah, supporting the same shiur.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rava's principle
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rava's principle
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who carries wine on Shabbat is liable if he carries enough for mixing a cup. Rava explains that this measure is based on his principle that wine must be mixed with one-third water to be considered proper wine.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: one who carries wine on Shabbat is liable for the measure of a cup's mixing, and all other liquids for a revi'it.
Rava explains that his consistent principle is that any wine that does not carry one-third water is not considered proper wine, justifying the Mishnah's measure.

items.text: Abaye's two objections
items.text_en: Abaye's two objections
items.desc_en: Abaye raises two objections against Rava: first, a Mishnah states that diluted wine has two parts water and one part wine from the 'wine of the pitcher', implying a different ratio; second, water in a pitcher is not considered a significant measure for Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises two objections: first, a Mishnah states that mixed wine has two parts water and one part wine from the 'remaining wine'; second, water in the jug cannot combine with wine for the measure.
Abaye raises his second objection: water in a pitcher is not considered a significant measure for Shabbat, so why should it combine with wine to form the measure?

items.text: Rava's responses to Abaye
items.text_en: Rava's responses to Abaye
items.desc_en: Rava answers Abaye's objections: the Mishnah's ratio of two parts water to one part wine refers to appearance, not taste, which requires more wine; and regarding water in a pitcher, for Shabbat we require something significant, and this is indeed significant.

sub.desc_en: Rava responds: the 'remaining wine' is diluted and weak, requiring more for taste; regarding water in the jug, for Shabbat we require something significant, and this is indeed significant.
Rava answers Abaye's second objection: for Shabbat we require something significant (חשיב), and water in a pitcher is indeed significant.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's measure and Rav Yosef's comparison
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's measure and Rav Yosef's comparison
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that dried wine is liable in the measure of a kezayit, according to Rabbi Natan. Rav Yosef states that Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda said the same thing, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says that Beit Hillel only deemed blood of a neveila impure if it contains a revi'it, because it can congeal into a kezayit.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: dry [blood] is liable for a kezayit, according to Rabbi Nathan.

Rav Yosef identifies that Rabbi Nathan and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda said the same thing, citing the baraita about the six leniencies of Beit Shammai and stringencies of Beit Hillel regarding blood of a neveila.

items.text: Abaye's rejection of the comparison
items.text_en: Abaye's rejection of the comparison
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the cases are not parallel: Rabbi Natan's measure for wine (which is thin) requires a revi'it for a kezayit, but for blood (which is thick) a kezayit may not require a revi'it; conversely, Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's measure for blood may not apply to wine, which is thinner and thus a kezayit would be more than a revi'it.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rejects the comparison: Rabbi Nathan's case involves weak wine requiring a revi'it for a kezayit, but thick blood may not; conversely, Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's case involves thick blood where a kezayit suffices with a revi'it, but weak wine would require more than a revi'it for a kezayit.

items.text: The measure for milk and a textual ambiguity
items.text_en: The measure for milk and a textual ambiguity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for milk is 'kedei gemi'ah' (enough for a swallow). A question arises whether the word is spelled with a 'gimel' or an 'ayin'. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse to resolve the spelling.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that milk is liable for the measure of a gemi'ah (a swallow).
The Gemara asks whether the term is 'gemi'ah' (swallow) or 'gemi'ah' (sip).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the question by citing the verse 'הגמיאיני נא מעט מים מכדך' (give me a little water to drink from your jug), indicating the term is 'gemi'ah' (swallow).

items.text: Another unresolved question
items.text_en: Another unresolved question
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another unresolved question (איבעיא להו) but does not provide the content in this segment.

sub.desc_en: A new inquiry is raised (the text is incomplete, but it introduces another question).

items.text: Three spelling queries resolved by biblical verses
items.text_en: Three spelling queries resolved by biblical verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises three unresolved spelling questions (גר״א/גר״ע, אוממות/עוממות, מאמצין/מעמצין) and resolves each by citing a biblical verse that uses the same root.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the word for 'weevils' is spelled with an aleph or an ayin.
Rava bar Ulla resolves the spelling by citing the verse 'וְנִגְרַע מֵעֶרְכֶּךָ' (and he shall be deducted from your valuation), which uses the root with an ayin.
The Gemara asks whether the word for 'warts' is spelled with an aleph or an ayin.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi resolves the spelling by citing the verse 'אֲרָזִים לֹא עֲמָמֻהוּ' (the cedars in the garden of God did not overshadow him), which uses the root with an ayin.
The Gemara asks whether the word for 'closing the eyes' in the Mishnah is spelled with an aleph or an ayin.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves the spelling by citing the verse 'וְעֹצֵם עֵינָיו מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע' (and closes his eyes from seeing evil), which uses the root with an ayin.

items.text: Shiurim for milk, egg white, and honey; unresolved queries by Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Shiurim for milk, egg white, and honey; unresolved queries by Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: The Tosefta gives measures for carrying milk, egg white, and honey on Shabbat. Rav Ashi raises two unresolved questions: whether the measure for egg white is for rubbing or holding and rubbing, and whether honey's measure is for the entire wick or just its top.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta is cited, giving the measure for carrying milk (a mouthful), and for egg white (enough to put in a kilor's brush for rubbing with water).
Rav Ashi asks whether the measure for egg white is for rubbing alone or for holding and rubbing.
The gemara leaves the query unresolved (תיקו).
The Tosefta gives the measure for honey as enough to put on a wick (כתית), and a Tanna specifies it is for the mouth of the wick.
Rav Ashi asks whether the measure for honey applies to the entire wick or only its top, excluding the trailing part (הודרנא).
The gemara leaves the second query unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Everything created for a purpose: remedies from creatures
items.text_en: Everything created for a purpose: remedies from creatures
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that God created nothing in vain; each creature serves a medicinal purpose (e.g., snail for a wick, fly for a hornet, mosquito for a snake). The Gemara describes how to prepare a remedy from a black and white creature.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav declares that God created nothing in vain.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda lists specific creatures and their medicinal purposes: snail for a wick, fly for a hornet, mosquito for a snake, snake for a chafafit, and a spider for a scorpion.
The Gemara describes the preparation of a remedy from a black and a white creature: they are boiled and then rubbed on the affected area.

items.text: Five fears: weak over strong
items.text_en: Five fears: weak over strong
items.desc_en: A baraisa lists five instances where a weaker creature instills fear in a stronger one (e.g., mosquito over elephant). Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites a verse to support this phenomenon.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa lists five instances of fear of the weak over the strong: the mosquito over the lion, the gnat over the elephant, the spider over the scorpion, the swallow over the eagle, and the kilbit over the Leviathan.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites the verse 'המבליג שוד על עז' (He who makes the violent relent against the strong) as scriptural support for this phenomenon.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's questions to Rav Yehuda on natural phenomena
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's questions to Rav Yehuda on natural phenomena
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira finds Rav Yehuda in good spirits and asks him several questions about the order and features of animals (e.g., why goats walk before sheep, why some are covered and others uncovered, why the camel's tail is short, why the ant's horn is soft). Rav Yehuda answers with reasons based on their habits and needs.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: Rabbi Zeira found Rav Yehuda in good spirits at his father-in-law's door, so he could ask him anything.
Rabbi Zeira asks why goats walk before sheep in a flock.
Rav Yehuda answers that it corresponds to the order of creation: first darkness, then light (goats are dark, sheep are light).
Rabbi Zeira asks why some animals have covered genitals and others uncovered.
Rav Yehuda answers that animals whose genitals are used for human clothing are covered, and those not used are uncovered.
Rabbi Zeira asks why the camel's tail is short.
Rav Yehuda answers that the camel eats thorns, so a long tail would get tangled.
Rabbi Zeira asks why the ox's tail is long.
Rav Yehuda answers that the ox lives in marshes and needs a long tail to swat mosquitoes.
Rabbi Zeira asks why the ant's horn is soft.
Rav Yehuda answers that the ant lives in reeds, and if its horn were hard, it would break and blind the ant.
Shmuel provides supporting evidence: to blind an ant, one pulls out its horns.
Rabbi Zeira asks why the rooster's comb is raised upward.
Rav Yehuda answers that roosters live on beams, and if the comb were flat, dust would enter and blind them.

items.text: Folk etymologies of Aramaic words
items.text_en: Folk etymologies of Aramaic words
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides playful etymologies for various Aramaic words (e.g., דשא from דרך שם, דרגא from דרך גג, כוזא from כזה). It concludes with a baraisa listing three creatures that grow stronger with age: fish, snake, and pig.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides playful etymologies for a series of Aramaic words, breaking each into two Hebrew components.
A baraisa is cited listing three creatures that grow stronger with age: fish, snake, and pig.

items.text: Dispute over the measure of oil for anointing a small limb
items.text_en: Dispute over the measure of oil for anointing a small limb
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for oil is enough to anoint a small limb. The school of Rabbi Yannai specifies this means a small limb of a day-old infant. A challenge is raised from a baraisa, and the Gemara analyzes whether the dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Natan revolves around this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for carrying oil on Shabbat is enough to anoint a small limb.
The school of Rabbi Yannai specifies that the small limb is that of a day-old infant.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraisa that lists both 'a small limb' and 'a day-old infant' as separate measures.
The Gemara asks whether the baraisa means a small limb of an adult or a large limb of an infant.
The school of Rabbi Yannai rejects the objection, clarifying that they meant a small limb of a day-old infant.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Natan may revolve around this interpretation.
The Gemara analyzes whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds it is a small limb of an infant, while Rabbi Natan holds it is a small limb of an adult or a large limb of an infant.
The Gemara rejects this, concluding that all agree a small limb of a day-old infant is not the measure.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Nathan
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Nathan
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Nathan is not about Rabbi Yannai's principle but about whether a small limb of a large one-day-old and a large limb of a small one-day-old are equivalent. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds they are equivalent, while Rabbi Nathan disagrees. A baraisa is cited where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states the measure for oil is enough to anoint a small limb of a small one-day-old.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is not about Rabbi Yannai's principle but about a different point.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that a small limb of a large one-day-old and a large limb of a small one-day-old are equivalent.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Nathan's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Nathan's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nathan holds that a small limb of a large one-day-old is equivalent, but a large limb of a small one-day-old is not.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states the measure for oil is enough to anoint a small limb of a small one-day-old.

items.text: Abaye's principle for determining shiurim
items.text_en: Abaye's principle for determining shiurim
items.desc_en: Abaye states a general principle: for a substance that is sometimes used for its common purpose and sometimes for a less common purpose, the Sages follow the common purpose to be lenient. For a substance that is always used for its common purpose, they follow the common purpose to be stringent. He then applies this to wine, milk, and honey, explaining their shiurim.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states a general principle: for a substance used sometimes for its common purpose and sometimes for a less common purpose, the Sages follow the common purpose to be lenient; for a substance always used for its common purpose, they follow the common purpose to be stringent.
Abaye applies the principle to wine, milk, and honey, explaining their shiurim based on whether their common use is for consumption or for medicinal purposes.

items.text: Challenge regarding water and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge regarding water and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's principle regarding water: since drinking water is common but its medicinal use is not, why do the Sages follow the medicinal use to be stringent? Abaye answers that the baraisa was taught in the Galilee where water is commonly used for medicinal purposes. Rava offers an alternative explanation based on Shmuel's statement that all liquids cause swelling except water, which does not, so water's medicinal use is also common.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's principle: since water is commonly drunk but not commonly used for medicine, why do the Sages follow the medicinal use to be stringent?
Abaye answers that the baraisa was taught in the Galilee, where water is commonly used for medicinal purposes.
Rava offers an alternative explanation based on Shmuel's statement that all liquids cause swelling except water, which does not, so water's medicinal use is also common.

items.text: Shiur for blood and other liquids
items.text_en: Shiur for blood and other liquids
items.desc_en: A baraisa states that blood and all other liquids have a shiur of a revi'it. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says blood is enough to apply to one eye, as is done for a wild rooster. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says it is enough for one eye, as is done for a ya'rud bird, with a mnemonic: internal for internal, external for external.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa opens by stating that all other liquids have a shiur of a revi'it.
A second baraisa (תנו רבנן) reiterates that blood and all liquids have a shiur of a revi'it.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar gives a different shiur for blood: enough to apply to one eye, as is done for a wild rooster (ברקית).
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives a different shiur: enough for one eye, as is done for a ya'rud bird, with a mnemonic: internal for internal, external for external.

items.text: Distinction between one who carries out and one who stores
items.text_en: Distinction between one who carries out and one who stores
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that these shiurim apply to one who carries out, but for one who stores, any amount is liable. Rabbi Shimon says the opposite: these shiurim apply to one who stores, but for one who carries out, he is only liable for a revi'it. The Sages agree with Rabbi Shimon regarding carrying out slop water into the public domain, whose shiur is a revi'it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the shiurim apply to one who carries out, but for one who stores, any amount is liable.
Rabbi Shimon reverses the rule: the shiurim apply to one who stores, but for one who carries out, he is only liable for a revi'it.
The Sages agree with Rabbi Shimon regarding carrying out slop water into the public domain, whose shiur is a revi'it.

items.text: Clarification of the distinction between 'carrying out' and 'storing'
items.text_en: Clarification of the distinction between 'carrying out' and 'storing'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the distinction: isn't one who stores also carrying out? Abaye explains that the case is about a student who was told by his teacher to clear a place for a meal. If the item is significant to everyone, he is liable; if not, he is liable only if his teacher designated it as significant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the distinction between 'carrying out' (מוציא) and 'storing' (מצניע), asking: isn't one who stores also carrying out?

Abaye explains that the case involves a student whom his teacher told to clear a place for a meal; if the item is significant to everyone, he is liable, and if not, he is liable only if his teacher designated it as significant.

items.text: Purpose of slop water and resolution of a contradiction
items.text_en: Purpose of slop water and resolution of a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what slop water is used for. Rabbi Yirmeya says for mixing clay. A contradiction is noted from a baraisa that says the shiur for clay is enough to make a furnace opening. The Gemara resolves: one is for already mixed clay, the other for unmixed clay, because one does not trouble to mix clay just for a furnace opening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what slop water (שופכין) is used for, and Rabbi Yirmeya answers that it is for mixing clay (לגבל בהן את הטיט).
The Gemara objects by citing a baraisa that gives the shiur for clay as enough to make a furnace opening (פי כור), which seems to contradict the shiur for slop water.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one shiur refers to already mixed clay (מגבל) and the other to unmixed clay (לא מגבל), because one does not trouble to mix clay just for a furnace opening.

items.text: Mishnah: Shiurim for rope, reed, and paper
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shiurim for rope, reed, and paper
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists shiurim: one who carries out rope enough to make a handle for a basket; reed enough to make a hanger for a sieve or a sifter; Rabbi Yehuda says enough to take a measure for a child's shoe; paper enough to write a tax seal on it; and one who carries out a tax seal is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the shiurim for rope, reed, and paper, including Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and the liability for carrying out a tax seal.

items.text: Mishnah: Shiurim for paper, ink, and other materials
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shiurim for paper, ink, and other materials
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum measures for various materials: paper (to wrap a small perfume bottle), ink (to write two letters), and others like wax, clay, lime, etc., with dissenting opinions from Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum measure for paper (to wrap a small perfume bottle), leather (for an amulet), and other materials like ink (for two letters).
The Mishnah continues listing measures for kohl, glue, pitch, wax, clay, bran, and lime, with Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting opinion on the measure for clay and lime.
Rabbi Nechemya gives his own measure for lime: enough to whitewash a small 'undifi' (a type of small structure).

items.text: Gemara: Additional shiurim for rope, fibers, and wool
items.text_en: Gemara: Additional shiurim for rope, fibers, and wool
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why rope is not listed for making a handle for a sieve, answers that people don't do that, and then cites a baraita with shiurim for fibers (to make a basket handle), palm fiber (to filter wine), and wool (to make a small ball).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why rope is not included in the Mishnah with a measure for making a hanger for a sieve, and answers that people do not make such hangers because the rope is tightly tied to the vessel.

A baraita is cited providing measures for fibers (for a basket handle), palm fiber (for a funnel filter), and resin (for anointing under a small sponge), with the Gemara resolving a contradiction between two measures for resin.
A baraita is cited giving the shiur for fibers (הוּצִין) to make a handle for an Egyptian basket.
Acherim gives the shiur for palm fiber (סִיב) to place on a small funnel for filtering wine.
The baraita gives the shiur for wool (רְבָב) to anoint under a small sponge, and its measure is a סלע (sela).
The Gemara objects that another baraita states the measure is a גרוגרת (dried fig).
The Gemara resolves that both measures (סלע and גרוגרת) are the same shiur.

sub.text: Baraita's statement on wool for a ball
sub.text_en: Baraita's statement on wool for a ball
sub.desc_en: The baraita gives the shiur for wool fibers (מוֹכִין) to make a small ball, and its measure is an אגוז (walnut).

items.text: Dispute: Definition of 'two letters' for paper
items.text_en: Dispute: Definition of 'two letters' for paper
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says paper's shiur is to write a tax receipt (two letters of tax notation), but another source says 'two letters' without specification. Rav Sheshet and Rava offer different explanations: Rav Sheshet says it means two letters of tax notation, Rava says it means two of our letters plus a handle, which is the tax receipt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the measure for paper is enough to write a customs knot, and a Tanna explains that a customs knot consists of two letters.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that one who takes out blank paper is liable only if it can hold two letters, without specifying 'customs knot'.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by explaining that the 'two letters' in the baraita refer specifically to two letters of a customs knot.
Rava offers an alternative resolution: the measure is two of our letters plus a handle (בית אחיזה), which together constitute a customs knot.

items.text: Objection to Rava from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection to Rava from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that states liability for carrying erased paper if its blank space can hold two letters or its whole can wrap a bottle. This supports Rav Sheshet (who requires only two letters of tax notation) but challenges Rava (who requires a handle, which is not needed here). The Gemara concludes 'Kashya' (a difficulty).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about erased paper and a paid note, which mentions only the measure of two letters without a handle.
The Gemara notes that Rav Sheshet's explanation fits the baraita, but Rava's explanation requiring a handle is problematic because the baraita does not mention a handle.
The Gemara points out that for Rava, who requires a handle (בית אחיזה) in addition to two letters, the baraita does not mention a handle, posing a difficulty.
The Gemara declares the difficulty unresolved, concluding 'Kashya' (a difficulty).

items.text: Baraita: Carrying a tax receipt before and after showing
items.text_en: Baraita: Carrying a tax receipt before and after showing
items.desc_en: A baraita states that carrying a tax receipt before showing it to the tax collector incurs liability, but after showing it, one is exempt. Rabbi Yehuda holds one is liable even after showing because he still needs it. Abaye, Rava, and Rav Ashi debate what distinguishes the opinions: runners of the tax collector, a large vs. small tax collector, or a single tax collector needing to show a second one.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that one who takes out a customs knot is liable before showing it to the customs official, but exempt afterward; Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable even afterward because he still needs it.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the first Tanna and Rabbi Yehuda.
Abaye explains that the difference lies in the case of customs runners (רָהִיטֵי מוֹכְסָא) who run between stations.
Rava says the difference is between a high-ranking and a low-ranking customs official.
Rav Ashi says the difference is a single customs official, because Rabbi Yehuda holds he needs the knot to show to a second official, saying 'See, I am a customs man.'
Rav Ashi answers that the difference is a single tax collector, because Rabbi Yehuda holds one needs to show it to a second tax collector.

items.text: Baraita: Carrying a promissory note before and after payment
items.text_en: Baraita: Carrying a promissory note before and after payment
items.desc_en: A baraita states that carrying a promissory note before payment incurs liability, but after payment one is exempt. Rabbi Yehuda holds one is liable even after payment because he needs it. Rav Yosef says the dispute is about whether it is forbidden to keep a paid note; Abaye says both agree it is forbidden, but they dispute whether one who admits to writing the note needs to validate it in court.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that carrying a promissory note before payment incurs liability, but after payment one is exempt; Rabbi Yehuda holds one is liable even after payment because he needs it.
The gemara asks what practical difference lies between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Yosef answers that the dispute is about whether it is forbidden (אסור) or permitted (מותר) to keep a paid promissory note.
Abaye says both agree it is forbidden to keep a paid note, but they dispute whether one who admits to writing the note needs to validate it in court (קיום).

items.text: Gemara's opening discussion on the Mishnah's measurement for leather
items.text_en: Gemara's opening discussion on the Mishnah's measurement for leather
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a dispute about whether a borrower who claims repayment needs to produce a receipt. Rava explains that all agree a written document requires validation, but they argue about writing a receipt. Rav Ashi adds that the borrower must show the receipt to a second creditor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's statement that the borrower's claim of repayment is accepted until he says 'I repaid' or 'I did not repay'.
Rava explains that all agree a written document requires validation, and the dispute is about whether a receipt (שובר) is written for the borrower.
Rav Ashi adds that the borrower must show the receipt to a second creditor, saying 'See, I am a man who has repaid.'

items.text: Rava's inquiry about the shiur for carrying leather
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry about the shiur for carrying leather
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about the shiur for carrying leather. Rav Nachman answers that it is the same as the Mishnah's measurement: enough to make an amulet. Rava then asks about processed leather, and Rav Nachman says it is no different.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about the shiur (measurement) for carrying leather on Shabbat.
Rav Nachman answers that the shiur is the same as the Mishnah's measurement: enough to make an amulet.
Rava asks about the shiur for processed leather (מעובד).
Rav Nachman answers that it is no different — the shiur remains the same.

items.text: Proof from the laws of laundering and weaving
items.text_en: Proof from the laws of laundering and weaving
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a Mishnah about laundering and weaving: the shiur for those who process wool is the same as for the finished product.
