Similarly, the shiur for leather intended for processing is the same as processed leather. Rava then asks about leather not intended for processing, and Rav Nachman says it is no different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a proof that the shiur for leather intended for processing is the same as processed leather.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about laundering and weaving: the shiur for those who process wool is the same as for the finished product.
The Gemara concludes that just as the shiur for wool intended for weaving equals that of woven cloth, so too the shiur for leather intended for processing equals that of processed leather.
Rava asks about the shiur for leather not intended for processing.
Rav Nachman answers that it is no different — the same shiur applies even for leather not intended for processing.

items.text: Objection from the laws of dyes
items.text_en: Objection from the laws of dyes
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: is there really no difference between processed and unprocessed leather? It cites a Mishnah where the shiur for soaked dyes is different from dry dyes. Rav Nachman resolves this by saying that people do not bother to soak dyes for a small sample.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: is there really no difference between processed and unprocessed leather? It cites a Mishnah where the shiur for soaked dyes is different from dry dyes.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha resolves: the difference is because people do not bother to soak dyes for a small sample (דוגמא לאירא).

items.text: Second objection from garden seeds
items.text_en: Second objection from garden seeds
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: the shiur for garden seeds before planting is different from after planting. Rav Pappa resolves this by saying that people do not bother to take out a single thread for planting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the different shiurim for garden seeds before planting (less than a dried fig-bulk) versus after planting (enough to fertilize a cabbage stalk), citing the Mishnah and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and Rabbi Akiva and the Sages.

Rav Pappa resolves the objection by explaining that the two shiurim refer to different cases: one for seeds already planted (where the shiur is small because one does not bother to take out a single thread for planting) and one for seeds not yet planted (where the shiur is larger).

items.text: Third objection from mud
items.text_en: Third objection from mud
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects further: the shiur for liquid waste before mixing with mud is different from the shiur for mud itself. The Gemara answers that people do not bother to mix mud for making a furnace opening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the shiur for liquid waste before mixing (רביעית) differs from the shiur for mud itself (enough for a furnace opening), showing inconsistency.
The Gemara answers that people do not bother to mix mud specifically for making a furnace opening, so the larger shiur applies only to ready-made mud.

items.text: Baraita about three types of leather
items.text_en: Baraita about three types of leather
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ami cites Ulla: there are three types of leather: matza, chippa, and diftera. Their shiurim are given: matza for a small weight, chippa for an amulet, diftera for writing a get. The Gemara questions the shiur for matza, and Abaye gives a specific measurement. The Gemara then notes that this shiur is for cooked leather.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Chiyya bar Ammi in the name of Ulla
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Chiyya bar Ammi in the name of Ulla
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita citing Ulla's classification of three types of leather: matza, chippa, and diftera, defining matza as untreated leather.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the shiur for matza
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the shiur for matza
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the shiur (minimum measure) for matza leather.

sub.text: Tanna Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda's answer
sub.text_en: Tanna Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda teaches that the shiur for matza is enough to wrap a small weight.
Abaye specifies the exact size as a quarter of a quarter of a Pumbeditan measure.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the baraita for chippa and diftera
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the baraita for chippa and diftera
sub.desc_en: The Gemara continues the baraita: chippa is salted but not floured or tanned, with shiur for an amulet; diftera is salted and floured but not tanned, with shiur for writing a get.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from the baraita's shiur for matza
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from the baraita's shiur for matza
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the baraita states the shiur for matza as wrapping a small weight, and Abaye gave a specific measure, but this seems inconsistent with the earlier sugya.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita's shiur for matza refers to cooked leather, not raw leather.

items.text: Contradiction from the laws of impurity
items.text_en: Contradiction from the laws of impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a Mishnah states that the shiur for leather for impurity (five by five handbreadths) is the same as for carrying. The Gemara resolves that this refers to a kurtubla (a type of leather).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a Mishnah states that the shiur for leather for impurity (five by five handbreadths) is the same as for carrying.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to a kurtubla (a type of leather), not to ordinary leather.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial contradiction
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial contradiction
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that klaf must be large enough to write a small parashah. A contradiction is raised from a baraita that mentions klaf and duchsustos for a mezuzah, which is resolved by identifying 'mezuzah' as referring to tefillin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that klaf must be large enough to write a small parashah.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that gives the size of klaf and duchsustos for a mezuzah.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by interpreting 'mezuzah' in the baraita as referring to the mezuzah of tefillin.
The Gemara objects that tefillin are not normally called 'mezuzah'.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda and Rabbi Zakkai refer to the tefillin box as 'mezuzah', supporting the usage.

items.text: Refining the interpretation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Refining the interpretation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous resolution by noting that the latter clause specifies 'small parashah in tefillin,' implying the first clause deals with an actual mezuzah. It then reinterprets the Mishnah as stating the measure for duchsustos is for a mezuzah, and for klaf is for the small parashah in tefillin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the later clause of the Mishnah specifies tefillin, implying the earlier clause deals with an actual mezuzah.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah as a question about the sizes of klaf and duchsustos, with the answer distinguishing between them.

items.text: Rav's ruling on duchsustos
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on duchsustos
items.desc_en: Rav states that duchsustos is like klaf, meaning tefillin can be written on it. The Gemara questions this from the Mishnah, which only mentions klaf for tefillin, and resolves that it is only a matter of optimal practice (mitzvah).

sub.desc_en: Rav states that duchsustos is like klaf, meaning tefillin can be written on it.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that only klaf is mentioned for tefillin, not duchsustos.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's restriction is only for the ideal standard (למצוה), not absolute invalidity.
A baraita citing a law from Sinai specifies that tefillin are on klaf and mezuzah on duchsustos, supporting the distinction.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita's rule is also only for the ideal standard (למצוה).

items.text: Debate about changing the material
items.text_en: Debate about changing the material
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that changing the material invalidates a mezuzah, and another that invalidates both. It resolves that both refer to mezuzah but with different placements, and offers alternative explanations involving a tannaitic dispute and Rav's alignment with the school of Menashe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita that says if one deviates from the material, it is invalid.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to mezuzah, not tefillin.
The Gemara objects with another baraita that says deviation in either material is invalid.
The Gemara answers that both baraitot refer to mezuzah, but one case is writing klaf on the hair side or duchsustos on the flesh side.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the dispute about deviation in both materials is a disagreement among Tannaim.
A baraita records that Rabbi Acha validates deviation in both materials in the name of Rabbi Achai bar Chanina or Rabbi Yaakov bar Chanina.
Rav Pappa says that Rav's ruling aligns with the Tanna of the school of Menashe, who validates tefillin on klaf, gevil, or duchsustos.

items.text: Identifying the subject of the baraita
items.text_en: Identifying the subject of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what the baraita from the school of Menashe refers to, concluding it must be a Torah scroll, not tefillin or mezuzah. It then cites a supporting baraita about not downgrading holiness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'wrote it' refers to in the baraita of the school of Menashe.
The Gemara rejects that it refers to mezuzah, since mezuzah is not written on klaf.
The Gemara concludes it must refer to tefillin.
The Gemara objects that tefillin are also not written on gevil.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita of the school of Menashe refers to a Torah scroll.
A baraita supports that one cannot downgrade holiness, implying that if downgrading were allowed, a Torah scroll could be used for mezuzah.

items.text: Final resolution and reversal of Rav's statement
items.text_en: Final resolution and reversal of Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that if downgrading were permitted, one could make a mezuzah from tefillin written on duchsustos. It then rejects this and concludes that Rav's statement should be reversed: klaf is like duchsustos, meaning mezuzah can be written on klaf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if downgrading were permitted, one could make a mezuzah from a Torah scroll, implying the scroll was written on duchsustos.
The Gemara answers that the Torah scroll was written on klaf, not duchsustos.
The Gemara objects that mezuzah is not written on klaf.
The Gemara answers that a baraita states writing a mezuzah on klaf, paper, or patch is invalid, implying it is possible but invalid.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports that Rabbi Meir would write mezuzah on klaf because it is more durable.
The Gemara now revises Rav's statement: instead of duchsustos being like klaf, klaf is like duchsustos, meaning both can be used for mezuzah.

items.text: Transition to next Mishnah
items.text_en: Transition to next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly states the next Mishnah's topic: the measure of ink is enough to write.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that ink must be sufficient to write.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rava's question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rava's question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for carrying two letters written with ink, a quill, or a reed pen. Rava asks whether one letter written with all three materials is considered a single act of writing.

items.text: Rava's rulings on writing while walking and sequential acts
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on writing while walking and sequential acts
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one writes two letters while walking, he is liable because the writing itself is the placement. However, if he writes one letter, then later writes another, he is exempt because the second act lacks the minimum quantity at the time of the first.

items.text: Rava's rulings on half-fig quantities and removal
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on half-fig quantities and removal
items.desc_en: Rava discusses cases of carrying half a fig-bulk: if one places it and then another, the first is considered as if consumed or burned, exempting him. If he lifts the first before placing the second, he is exempt. But if he passes the second over the first within three handbreadths, he is liable.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding within three handbreadths
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding within three handbreadths
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rava himself said that within three handbreadths, according to the Rabbis, one needs placement on something. The resolution distinguishes between throwing and passing.

items.text: Baraita on half-fig quantities in one or two lapses
items.text_en: Baraita on half-fig quantities in one or two lapses
items.desc_en: A Baraita states that if one carries two half-fig bulks in one lapse of awareness, he is liable; in two lapses, exempt. Rabbi Yose adds that in one lapse to one domain, liable; to two domains, exempt. Rabba adds that this applies only when there is a liability for a sin-offering between them, but not if it is a karmelit.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on karmelit and pisla
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on karmelit and pisla
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that even a karmelit counts, but not a pisla (a public domain partition). Rava argues that even a pisla counts, consistent with his view that Shabbat domains are like divorce domains.

items.text: Discussion on the measure of eye-paint
items.text_en: Discussion on the measure of eye-paint
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for eye-paint is enough for one eye. The Gemara questions this, noting that women usually paint both eyes. Rav Huna explains that modest women paint only one eye. A Baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes between medicinal and cosmetic use. Hillel bar Shmuel bar Nachmani interprets this as referring to city women.

items.text: Measure for wax
items.text_en: Measure for wax
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for wax is enough to place on the mouth of a small hole. A Tanna specifies: the mouth of a small wine hole.

items.text: Measure for glue
items.text_en: Measure for glue
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for glue is enough to place on the head of a shafshaf. A Tanna specifies: the head of a shafshaf that is on the top of a hunter's reed.

items.text: Measure for tar and sulfur
items.text_en: Measure for tar and sulfur
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for tar and sulfur is enough to make a small hole. A Tanna specifies: to make a small hole.

items.text: Measure for clay and a difficulty with Rabbi Yehuda's measure
items.text_en: Measure for clay and a difficulty with Rabbi Yehuda's measure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for clay is enough to make the mouth of a bellows. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's measure is larger, since we know the Rabbis' measure is larger. It resolves that the Mishnah means enough to seal the opening of a small oven.

items.text: Measure for bran
items.text_en: Measure for bran
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for bran is enough to place on the mouth of a goldsmith's bellows.

items.text: Opening Tosefta on carrying hair and lime
items.text_en: Opening Tosefta on carrying hair and lime
items.desc_en: The Tosefta states the shiur for carrying hair is enough to mix with clay for a goldsmith's furnace, and for lime enough to lime a small finger. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that Israelite girls who have reached puberty but not age use lime, while rich girls use fine flour and royal girls use oil of myrrh, with a debate about what that oil is.

items.text: Story of Rav Bivi and his daughter's cosmetic treatment
items.text_en: Story of Rav Bivi and his daughter's cosmetic treatment
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi applied lime to his daughter limb by limb, spending 400 zuz, while a gentile neighbor applied it all at once, causing his daughter's death. Rav Nachman comments that Rav Bivi, who drinks beer, needs such treatment for his daughters, but we who do not drink beer do not need it.

items.text: Debate on Rabbi Yehuda's measure of lime and the terms kilkul and andifa
items.text_en: Debate on Rabbi Yehuda's measure of lime and the terms kilkul and andifa
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says the shiur is enough to lime a kilkul. Rav explains kilkul and andifa as tzid'a and bat tzid'a (a type of plaster). The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's measure is larger than the Rabbis', and raises a contradiction from a baraita where Rabbi says Rabbi Yehuda's words apply to beaten plaster and Rabbi Nechemya's to egg-lime. Rabbi Yitzchak resolves that the measure is for the andifa (a tool).

items.text: Rav Kahana's objection and alternative explanations
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection and alternative explanations
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects that a person does not make his money into broken pieces, so he explains that 'andifa' refers to 'shnatot' (years), as in a mishna about measures for offerings. Alternatively, he says 'andifa' means 'aputa' (face), citing a story of a Galilean who was struck on the face (andifei) and died.

items.text: Mishna: Shiurim for earth, dung, sand, and a reed
items.text_en: Mishna: Shiurim for earth, dung, sand, and a reed
items.desc_en: The Mishna states shiurim: earth like a seal of letters (Rabbi Akiva) or a seal of documents (Sages); dung and fine sand enough to fertilize a cabbage stalk (Rabbi Akiva) or a leek (Sages); coarse sand enough to put on a full spoon of lime; a reed enough to make a quill; if thick or brittle, enough to cook a light egg, beaten and placed in a pan.

items.text: Gemara on the measure of sand and its source
items.text_en: Gemara on the measure of sand and its source
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the measure of sand is enough to put on a plasterer's spoon. Rav Chisda says this follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that sand is harmful to lime, while Rava says even the Rabbis agree that its disadvantage is its advantage.

items.text: Gemara on the measure of a reed for a quill
items.text_en: Gemara on the measure of a reed for a quill
items.desc_en: The Tosefta states the quill must reach the joints of the fingers. Rav Ashi asks whether this refers to the upper or lower joint, and the Gemara concludes with teiku (let it stand).

items.text: Gemara on the 'light egg' and its measure
items.text_en: Gemara on the 'light egg' and its measure
items.desc_en: The Tosefta specifies the egg is beaten with oil and placed in a pan. Mar bar Ravina asks his son what a 'light egg' is; he suggests a chicken egg, but Mar bar Ravina questions why not a bird's egg. Rav Sheshet says it is a hen's egg, and the Gemara asks why all other Shabbat measures are k'grogeret (like a dried fig) but here it is k'beitzah (like an egg). Rav Nachman answers that k'grogeret is from a light egg.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Shiurim for bone, glass, and stone
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Shiurim for bone, glass, and stone
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum sizes for carrying bone, glass, and a pebble or stone on Shabbat, with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Yaakov offering alternative measurements.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum size for carrying bone, glass, and a pebble or stone on Shabbat, with the Tanna Kamma's measurements.
Rabbi Yehuda gives an alternative measurement for bone: enough to make a spoon (חף).
Rabbi Elazar bar Yaakov gives an alternative measurement for a pebble or stone: enough to throw at an animal.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's shiur and Ulla's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's shiur and Ulla's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's shiur is larger than the Rabbis', noting the opposite is known. Ulla explains that Rabbi Yehuda refers to a 'half-open hand' (חפי פותחת), and a baraita clarifies the halakha of such handles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's shiur is larger, noting that the opposite is known.
Ulla explains that Rabbi Yehuda refers to a 'half-open hand' (חפי פותחת).

A baraita clarifies the halakha of such handles, stating that those attached to the door are pure, but if fixed in the door they are impure, and those of a gate are pure even if attached, because anything connected to the ground is like the ground.

items.text: Baraita on glass shiur
items.text_en: Baraita on glass shiur
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that the shiur for glass is enough to cut two threads at once, clarifying the Mishnah's 'to scrape the head of a weaver's shuttle'.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that the shiur for glass is enough to cut two threads at once.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's condition and shiur for stone
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's condition and shiur for stone
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov quoting Rabbi Yochanan states that the stone must be one the bird feels, and a baraita gives Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's shiur of ten zuz weight.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the shiur for a stone to throw at a bird applies only when the bird feels it.
The Gemara asks what the shiur is.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov sets the shiur at the weight of ten zuz.
A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's shiur: the stone must weigh ten zuz.

items.text: Zunin's question on bathroom stones and the conclusion
items.text_en: Zunin's question on bathroom stones and the conclusion
items.desc_en: Zunin asks the Sages about the shiur for bathroom stones; they suggest kezayit, ke'egoz, and kebeitzah, but he objects. They conclude it is melo hayad, with a baraita citing Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon bar Yosei.

sub.desc_en: Zunin came to the study hall and asked the rabbis: What is the shiur for stones for the bathroom?
The rabbis answered: Like an olive, a nut, and an egg.
Zunin objected: Would one bring in large stones?
They counted and concluded: A handful.
A baraita records Rabbi Yosei's opinion: Like an olive, a nut, and an egg.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yosei's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yosei's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yosei says in his father's name: A handful.

items.text: Baraita on three angled stones and comparison to etrog
items.text_en: Baraita on three angled stones and comparison to etrog
items.desc_en: A baraita permits three angled stones for the bathroom, with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disputing their size. Rafram bar Pappa quoting Rav Chisda compares this dispute to that of the etrog, and the Gemara clarifies the source.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that three smoothed stones may be brought into the bathroom on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks: What is their shiur?
Rabbi Meir says: Like a nut.
Rabbi Yehuda says: Like an egg.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa quoting Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa quoting Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: The dispute here is like the dispute regarding an etrog.
The Gemara objects: There it is a Mishnah, here it is a baraita!
The Gemara resolves: Rather, the dispute regarding an etrog is like the dispute here.

items.text: Additional halakhot: pa'yeis, handling stones, and fixed place
items.text_en: Additional halakhot: pa'yeis, handling stones, and fixed place
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda prohibits certain stones (pa'yeis), identified by Rabbi Zeira as Babylonian beans. Rava forbids handling a stone on Shabbat as on a weekday; Mar Zutra objects but allows indirectly. Rabbi Yannai and Rav Sheshet give shiurim based on a fixed place or a witness.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says: But not the 'payeis'.
The Gemara asks: What is 'payeis'?
Rabbi Zeira explains: Babylonian beans.
Rava says: It is forbidden to handle a stone on Shabbat in the way one handles it on a weekday.
Mar Zutra objects: Is there a danger?
The Gemara resolves: It is permitted indirectly (כלאחר יד).
Rabbi Yannai says: If there is a fixed place for the bathroom, the shiur is a handful; if not, the shiur is like the small mortar of spices.
Rav Sheshet says: If there is a witness on it, it is permitted.

items.text: Objection from baraita on ten things causing hemorrhoids
items.text_en: Objection from baraita on ten things causing hemorrhoids
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita listing ten things that cause hemorrhoids, including wiping with a stone used by another. It resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between wet and dry, one side vs. two sides, or one's own vs. another's stone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita.
A baraita lists ten things that bring a person to hemorrhoids, including wiping with a stone that another used.
The Gemara resolves: This refers to a wet stone, that to a dry one.
Alternatively: Here from one side, there from two sides.
Alternatively: This is one's own stone, that is another's.

items.text: Abaye's question on stones washed by rain
items.text_en: Abaye's question on stones washed by rain
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef about stones whose markings were washed away by rain; Rav Yosef rules that if their impression remains, they are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asked Rav Yosef: If rain fell on the stones and they were washed away, what is the halakha?
Rav Yosef answered: If their impression is recognizable, it is permitted.

items.text: Rabba bar Rav Sheila's inquiry
items.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila's inquiry
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila asks a question of Rav, beginning a new discussion.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Sheila's question to Rav
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila's question to Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila asked Rav a question.

items.text: Question about moving excrement to the roof
items.text_en: Question about moving excrement to the roof
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether one may move excrement to the roof on Shabbat. The answer is given that human dignity overrides a negative commandment. Marimar states this ruling, and Ravina objects from a Mishnah about Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding taking a splinter from animal feed, but the Gemara distinguishes between fixing a place for a meal and for a toilet.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether one may move excrement to the roof on Shabbat.
The Gemara answers that human dignity overrides a negative commandment from the Torah.
Marimar states this ruling in a public teaching.
Ravina objects from a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer permits taking a splinter from animal feed and the Sages forbid it, implying human dignity does not override a rabbinic prohibition.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between fixing a place for a meal, where dignity is less urgent, and for a toilet, where dignity is paramount.

items.text: Prohibition of defecating in a plowed field on Shabbat
items.text_en: Prohibition of defecating in a plowed field on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Huna forbids defecating in a plowed field on Shabbat. The Gemara considers possible reasons: it is not due to trampling (which is permitted on weekdays), nor due to uprooting grass (since a clod with grass may be used for wiping, though uprooting is a capital offense), but rather because one might take earth from a mound and fill a pit, violating the prohibitions of building or plowing as per Rabbah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that it is forbidden to relieve oneself in a plowed field on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rav Huna's ruling.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the reason is trampling, since that would apply even on a weekday.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the reason is uprooting grass, citing Reish Lakish that a clod with grass may be used for wiping.
The Gemara adds that one who deliberately uproots grass on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering.
The Gemara resolves that the concern is that one might take earth from a mound and fill a hollow, violating the prohibition of building or plowing as per Rabbah.
Rabbah's principle is cited: filling a hole indoors is liable for building, in the field for plowing.

items.text: Law of a clod with grass and handling a potsherd
items.text_en: Law of a clod with grass and handling a potsherd
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that a clod with grass may be used for wiping, but uprooting from it on Shabbat incurs a sin-offering. Rav Pappi infers that a potsherd (parpisa) may be moved. Rav Kahana objects that this applies only for a need, not without need. Abaye then clarifies that if the potsherd was on the ground and placed on pegs, one is liable for uprooting; if on pegs and placed on the ground, liable for planting.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that a clod with grass may be used for wiping on Shabbat.
The Gemara adds that one who uproots grass from it on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering.
Rav Pappi infers from Reish Lakish that a piece of pottery (פרפסא) is permitted to be moved on Shabbat.
Rav Kahana objects: if they permitted it for a need, would they permit it without a need?
Abaye digresses to clarify the laws of moving a potsherd: if placed from ground onto pegs, one is liable for uprooting.
Abaye continues: if placed from pegs onto ground, one is liable for planting.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's prohibition of wiping with a shard on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's prohibition of wiping with a shard on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan forbids wiping with a shard on Shabbat. The Gemara rejects reasons of danger or sorcery (which would apply even on weekdays) and suggests it is due to smoothing the edges, which is an unintended act. Rav Nathan bar Oshaya explains that on weekdays it is forbidden due to danger, but on Shabbat, since it has the status of a vessel, it is permitted; the statement teaches that it is forbidden on weekdays but permitted on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that it is forbidden to wipe with a potsherd on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the reason is danger, since that would apply even on a weekday.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the reason is sorcery, since that would also apply on a weekday.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the reason is smoothing fibers, since that is an unintentional act.
Rav Nathan bar Oshaya resolves that on Shabbat it is forbidden because the potsherd has the status of a vessel, but on a weekday it is permitted.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan teaches us this distinction.

Rav Nathan bar Oshaya explains that on weekdays it is forbidden due to danger, but on Shabbat, since the shard has the status of a vessel, it is permitted; the statement teaches that it is forbidden on weekdays but permitted on Shabbat.

items.text: Rava's version and contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's views
items.text_en: Rava's version and contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's views
items.desc_en: Rava teaches the reason of smoothing the edges, and raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan forbids wiping with a shard, implying that an unintended act is forbidden, yet he also rules like an anonymous Mishnah that a nazir may rub but not comb, where unintended acts are permitted. The Gemara resolves that the correct version is like Rav Nathan bar Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: Rava teaches the ruling as being due to smoothing fibers, and raises a contradiction from Rabbi Yochanan against himself.
The Gemara asks: Did Rabbi Yochanan actually say it is forbidden to wipe with a potsherd on Shabbat?
The Gemara objects that this implies that an unintentional act is forbidden.
The Gemara cites that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that the law follows an unattributed Mishnah.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that a nazir may rub and part his hair but not comb, implying that an unintentional act is permitted.
The Gemara resolves that the correct explanation is like Rav Nathan bar Oshaya's.

items.text: Story about sorcery and the matron
items.text_en: Story about sorcery and the matron
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reference to sorcery with a story: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna were traveling on a boat, and a matron asked to join them but they refused. She spoke a spell and immobilized the boat; they spoke a spell and released it. She then asked what she could do to them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the sorcery concern?
The Gemara relates a story where a matron asked Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna to sit with her on a boat, but they refused.
The matron spoke a word and immobilized the boat through sorcery.
The rabbis spoke a word and released the boat from the sorcery.
The matron asked them: What can I do to you?

items.text: Rav Huna's rebuke to his son regarding Rav Chisda's wisdom
items.text_en: Rav Huna's rebuke to his son regarding Rav Chisda's wisdom
items.desc_en: Rav Huna asks his son Rabba why he does not attend Rav Chisda's lectures, as his teachings are sharp. Rabba replies that Rav Chisda discusses mundane matters like bathroom etiquette, but Rav Huna rebukes him, saying that since Rav Chisda deals with matters of life, Rabba should certainly go.

sub.desc_en: Rabba complains that Rav Chisda only teaches trivial bathroom etiquette, not deep Torah.
Rav Huna asks his son Rabba why he does not attend Rav Chisda's sharp lectures.
Rabba answers that Rav Chisda only discusses mundane bathroom safety, not Torah.
Rav Huna rebukes Rabba, saying that since Rav Chisda deals with matters of life, Rabba should certainly attend.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda on wiping with a pebble vs. a potsherd
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda on wiping with a pebble vs. a potsherd
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda disagree on whether one should wipe with a pebble or a potsherd. A baraita supports Rav Chisda, but Rafram bar Pappa resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rav Huna's ruling applies to the rims of vessels.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that when one has a pebble and a potsherd before him, he should wipe with the pebble and not with the potsherd.
Rav Chisda rules the opposite: one should wipe with the potsherd and not with the pebble.
A baraita is cited that supports Rav Chisda's view, presenting a challenge to Rav Huna.
Rafram bar Pappa resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rav Huna's ruling applies specifically to the rims of vessels.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna on wiping with a pebble vs. grass
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna on wiping with a pebble vs. grass
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna argue whether one should wipe with a pebble or grass. A baraita warns against using something that fire can burn, but the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between moist and dry grass.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna: one says wipe with a pebble but not grass, the other says wipe with grass but not a pebble.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that warns against wiping with something that fire can burn, implying grass is forbidden.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between moist grass (permitted) and dry grass (forbidden).

items.text: The danger of delaying excretion
items.text_en: The danger of delaying excretion
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Ravina disagree on whether one who needs to relieve himself but does not is afflicted by a bad spirit or a spirit of filth. A baraita supports the latter view, comparing it to a furnace heated over its ashes.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the case of one who needs to relieve himself but does not.
Rav Chisda and Ravina disagree: one says a bad spirit (רוח רעה) afflicts him, the other says a spirit of filth (רוח זוהמא) afflicts him.
A baraita supports the view that a spirit of filth (רוח זוהמא) afflicts him, comparing the person to a furnace heated over its ashes.

items.text: Remedies for one who cannot relieve himself
items.text_en: Remedies for one who cannot relieve himself
items.desc_en: Various sages offer advice for one who needs to relieve himself but cannot: standing and sitting repeatedly, moving to the side, rubbing with a pebble, or distracting his mind. Rav Acha bar Rava questions the last advice, but Rav Ashi clarifies that one should distract himself from other matters. Rav Yirmeya from Difti testifies to seeing a traveler succeed by standing and sitting.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the case of one who needs to relieve himself but cannot, and Rav Chisda advises standing and sitting repeatedly.
Rav Chanan from Nehardea advises moving to the side.
Rav Hamnuna advises rubbing the area with a pebble.
The Rabbis advise distracting one's mind.
Rav Acha bar Rava objects that distracting the mind would make one even less able to relieve himself.
Rav Ashi clarifies that one should distract himself from other matters, not from the need itself.
Rav Yirmeya from Difti testifies to seeing a traveler succeed by standing and sitting repeatedly until he relieved himself like a pot.

items.text: Baraita on preparing for a fixed meal
items.text_en: Baraita on preparing for a fixed meal
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that one entering a fixed meal should walk ten times of four cubits (or four times of ten cubits), relieve himself, and then enter and sit in his place.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one entering a fixed meal should walk a certain distance, relieve himself, and then enter and sit in his place.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the size of a potsherd
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the size of a potsherd
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three opinions on the minimum size of a potsherd: Rabbi Yehuda says enough to place between two beams, Rabbi Meir says enough to stir fire, and Rabbi Yosei says enough to hold a quarter-log. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei debate a proof from Isaiah. The Gemara questions which measure is larger, and Abaye explains that Rabbi Meir's measure is for a large fire. The Gemara then defends Rabbi Yosei's objection and explains Rabbi Meir's response.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three opinions on the minimum size of a potsherd: Rabbi Yehuda says enough to place between beams, Rabbi Meir says enough to stir fire, and Rabbi Yosei says enough to hold a quarter-log.
Rabbi Meir cites the verse 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא בִמְכִתָּתוֹ חֶרֶשׂ לַחְתּוֹת אֵשׁ מִיָּקוּד' (no potsherd will be found in its rubble to stir fire from a hearth) as a mnemonic for his measure.
Rabbi Yosei objects that the same verse also mentions 'וְלַחְשׂוֹף מַיִם מִגֶּבֶא' (to scoop water from a cistern), which could support his own measure of holding a quarter-log.
The Gemara asks which measure is larger: Rabbi Meir's or Rabbi Yosei's.
The Gemara reasons that by common sense Rabbi Yosei's measure is larger, but from the verse Rabbi Meir's measure appears larger, since the verse curses with a small vessel first and then a large one.
Abaye resolves that Rabbi Meir's measure of stirring fire refers to a large fire, so his measure is indeed larger than Rabbi Yosei's.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei's argument against Rabbi Meir from the verse seems valid.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir was using a 'לָא מִיבַּעְיָא' (not only) argument: not only will a valuable item not be found, but even a worthless item will not be found, so the verse does not prove which measure is larger.

items.text: Transition to a new chapter: Impurity of idolatry
items.text_en: Transition to a new chapter: Impurity of idolatry
items.desc_en: The daf concludes the previous chapter and begins a new one with a Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva derives from a verse that idolatry conveys impurity by carrying like a menstruating woman. The Gemara cites a related baraita about a house adjacent to idolatry that collapsed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך המוציא יין' (we return to you, 'He who brings out wine').
Rabbi Akiva opens the new chapter by deriving from the verse 'תִּזְרֵם כְּמוֹ דָוָה' that idolatry (עבודה זרה) conveys impurity by carrying (משא) like a menstruating woman (נדה).
The Gemara cites a related baraita about a house adjacent to idolatry that collapsed, ruling that one must retreat four cubits into his own property before rebuilding.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an idol's stones, wood, and dirt convey impurity like a sheretz, citing the verse 'Shakketz teshaktzenu'. Rabbi Akiva argues it is like a niddah, citing 'Tizrem kemodavah', implying impurity by carrying. Rabba explains the verse 'Tizrem' means to remove it as a stranger, and 'Tze tomar lo' means 'enter, do not say to him'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that stones, wood, and dirt of an idol convey impurity like a sheretz (creeping thing), citing the verse 'Shakketz teshaktzenu'.
Rabbi Akiva argues that an idol conveys impurity like a niddah (menstruant), based on the verse 'Tizrem kemodavah', implying impurity by carrying (משא).
Rabba explains the verse 'Tizrem' as meaning to remove the idol like a stranger, and 'Tze tomar lo' as 'enter, do not say to him'.

items.text: Rabba's analysis of the dispute: impurity by carrying
items.text_en: Rabba's analysis of the dispute: impurity by carrying
items.desc_en: Rabba clarifies that all agree an idol conveys impurity by carrying (masa), as it is compared to niddah. The dispute is about impurity via a stone that supports a load (even mesama). Rabbi Akiva holds it is like niddah, which conveys impurity via even mesama, while the Rabbis hold it is like sheretz, which does not.

sub.desc_en: Rabba states that all agree an idol conveys impurity by carrying (משא), since it is compared to a niddah.
Rabba explains that the dispute is about אבן מסמא (a stone used as a seat): Rabbi Akiva holds it conveys impurity like a niddah, while the Rabbis hold it does not, like a sheretz.

items.text: Purpose of the dual comparisons and a question about limbs
items.text_en: Purpose of the dual comparisons and a question about limbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For Rabbi Akiva, why is idolatry compared to sheretz? For the Rabbis, why to niddah? Answers: For Rabbi Akiva, it teaches that its accessories (meshamesheha) are impure like sheretz; for the Rabbis, it teaches impurity by carrying. The Gemara then questions why not compare to neveilah, and explains that niddah teaches that idolatry is not divided into limbs. Rav Chama bar Gurya's question about whether idolatry is divided into limbs is resolved for the Rabbis, but he asked according to Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Akiva, to what halachic purpose is the idol compared to a sheretz? It answers: for its accessories (משמשיה).
The Gemara asks: for the Rabbis, to what halachic purpose is the idol compared to a niddah? It answers: for impurity by carrying (משא).

The Gemara objects: why not compare the idol to a neveila (carcass)? It answers: indeed, but the comparison to niddah teaches that an idol, like a niddah, does not convey impurity in parts (אֵינָהּ לְאֵבָרִין).
The Gemara asks: what about Rav Chama bar Gurya's question whether an idol conveys impurity in parts? It could be resolved from here that according to the Rabbis it does not.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Chama bar Gurya asked his question according to Rabbi Akiva's opinion.
The Gemara resolves: Rav Chama bar Gurya asked his question according to Rabbi Akiva's position, not the Rabbis'.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's alternative interpretation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's alternative interpretation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar argues that all agree an idol does not convey impurity via even mesama. The dispute is about impurity by carrying (masa): Rabbi Akiva holds it is like niddah, which conveys impurity by carrying, while the Rabbis hold it is like sheretz, which does not. For Rabbi Akiva, the comparison to sheretz teaches about its accessories; for the Rabbis, the comparison to niddah teaches that idolatry is not divided into limbs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that all agree an idol does not convey impurity through אבן מסמא (a stone used as a seat).
Rabbi Elazar explains that the dispute is about impurity by carrying (משא): Rabbi Akiva holds it conveys impurity like a niddah, while the Rabbis hold it does not, like a sheretz.
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Akiva, to what halachic purpose is the idol compared to a sheretz? It answers: for its accessories (משמשיה).
The Gemara asks: for the Rabbis, to what halachic purpose is the idol compared to a niddah? It answers: to teach that an idol, like a niddah, does not convey impurity in parts (אֵינָהּ לְאֵבָרִים).

items.text: Question on Rabbi Akiva's analogy and Rav Chama's dilemma
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Akiva's analogy and Rav Chama's dilemma
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva compares idolatry to a menstruant (נִדָּה) rather than to a carcass (נְבֵלָה), and answers that the analogy teaches that idolatry does not transmit impurity by limbs (אֵינָהּ לְאֵבָרִין). It then notes that Rav Chama bar Gurya's question about whether idolatry transmits impurity by limbs is resolved by this, but explains that Rav Chama learned the Mishnah like Rabbah and asked according to Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva compared idolatry to a נִדָּה (menstruant) rather than to a נְבֵלָה (carcass).
The Gemara answers that the analogy teaches that idolatry does not transmit impurity by limbs (אֵינָהּ לְאֵבָרִין).
The Gemara objects that Rav Chama bar Gurya's dilemma about whether idolatry transmits impurity by limbs is resolved by this answer.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Chama learned the Mishnah like Rabbah and asked his question according to Rabbi Akiva's opinion.

items.text: First objection from a baraita and Rabbah's resolution
items.text_en: First objection from a baraita and Rabbah's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Akiva compares idolatry to a menstruant and its accessories to a reptile. This contradicts Rabbah's view, but Rabbah explains that the baraita means only that idolatry does not transmit impurity through a stone that serves as a seat (אֶבֶן מְסָמָא), not that it lacks limb-impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Akiva compares idolatry to a נִדָּה (menstruant), which is difficult for Rabbah's position.

Rabbah answers that the baraita's comparison to a שֶׁרֶץ (creeping thing) means only that it does not transmit impurity through a stone weight (אֶבֶן מְסָמָא), not that it transmits impurity by limbs.

items.text: Second objection from a baraita on היסט and Rabbah's counter
items.text_en: Second objection from a baraita on היסט and Rabbah's counter
items.desc_en: Another baraita is cited: a gentile and idolatry do not transmit impurity through היסט (carrying), but Rabbi Akiva says they do. This challenges Rabbah, but Rabbah retorts that the same baraita says gentiles do not transmit through היסט, yet a known tradition states that gentiles were decreed to be like zavim in all respects, implying they do transmit through היסט.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from a baraita about a gentile and idolatry, which is difficult for Rabbah's position.
Rabbah counters that the same difficulty applies to the gentile case, and cites a baraita that gentiles were decreed to be like זָבִין (those with a discharge) in all respects.

items.text: Rabbah and Rabbi Elazar reconcile the baraita
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rabbi Elazar reconcile the baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains the baraita according to his own view: a gentile transmits impurity through both היסט and a seat-stone, idolatry transmits through itself and its היסט but not through its seat-stone, and Rabbi Akiva adds the seat-stone. Rabbi Elazar explains according to his view: a gentile transmits through both, idolatry transmits through itself but not through its היסט, and Rabbi Akiva adds היסט.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the difficulty by explaining that for a gentile, both the person and their stone weight transmit impurity, but for idolatry, only the idol itself and its movement transmit impurity, not its stone weight, while Rabbi Akiva adds the stone weight.

Rabbi Elazar resolves the difficulty by explaining that for a gentile, both the person and their stone weight transmit impurity, but for idolatry, only the idol itself transmits impurity, not its movement, while Rabbi Akiva adds the movement.

items.text: Rav Ashi's reinterpretation of the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's reinterpretation of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges the previous explanations by asking what the word 'הֵן' means. He then reinterprets the baraita: a gentile and his gentile woman, whether they moved others or others moved them, are impure; idolatry that moved others is pure, but others who moved it are impure; its accessories are always pure. Rabbi Akiva says both gentile and idolatry are impure in both cases, while accessories are always pure.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions the meaning of the term 'הֵן' (they) in the baraita.

Rav Ashi explains that the baraita means: a gentile who moves others or is moved by them is impure; idolatry that moves others is pure but if moved by others is impure; its accessories are always pure; Rabbi Akiva says both gentile and idolatry are impure in both cases, while accessories are always pure.
Rabbi Akiva holds that both a gentile and idolatry are impure in both cases, while accessories are always pure.

items.text: Question on idolatry moving others and Rami's answer
items.text_en: Question on idolatry moving others and Rami's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how idolatry can move others (to transmit impurity), and Rami bar Rav Yeiva answers by citing a Mishnah about a zav on one scale pan causing foods on the other pan to become impure when the zav tilts the scale, illustrating indirect movement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how it is possible for idolatry to move others, as opposed to being moved by others.
Rami bar Rav Yeiva answers by citing a Mishnah about a זָב (one with a discharge) on a scale, where the זָב's movement causes impurity to foods and liquids.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita with Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita with Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a baraita states all moving impurities are pure except for the movement of a zav, implying no other source has such a law. It questions whether this contradicts Rabbi Akiva, who includes idolatry as a source of impurity via movement. The Gemara resolves that the baraita only excludes things similar to a zav, not idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a baraita stating that all moving impurities are pure except for the movement of a zav contradicts Rabbi Akiva, who includes idolatry as a source of impurity via movement.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita can align with Rabbi Akiva, as it only excludes things similar to a zav, not idolatry.

items.text: Rav Chama bar Gurya's query: Is idolatry subject to impurity by limbs?
items.text_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya's query: Is idolatry subject to impurity by limbs?
items.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya asks whether an idol that breaks into pieces retains impurity for each limb. He distinguishes between cases where a commoner can repair it (considered attached) and where not (considered broken). The Gemara presents two versions of the query, concluding with 'teiku' (undecided).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya asks whether idolatry is subject to impurity by limbs (אֵבָרִים) or not.
Rav Chama bar Gurya clarifies that when a commoner can restore the idol, it is considered attached and thus impure by limbs.
Rav Chama bar Gurya asks whether an idol that cannot be restored by a commoner is considered broken and thus not impure by limbs, or whether it still lacks nothing and remains impure.
An alternative version asks the opposite: when the idol cannot be restored it is clearly broken, but when it can be restored, is it considered attached or still currently detached?
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

items.text: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami's query: Idolatry less than an olive's bulk
items.text_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami's query: Idolatry less than an olive's bulk
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asks whether an idol smaller than an olive's bulk imparts impurity. Rav Yosef objects, noting that for prohibition, even a fly-sized idol is forbidden. The question is about impurity: is it compared to a creeping thing (requiring a lentil's bulk) or to a corpse (requiring an olive's bulk)?

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asks about the status of an idol smaller than an olive's bulk (כְּזַיִת) regarding impurity.
Rav Yosef objects that regarding prohibition, even a fly-sized idol of Ba'al Zevuv is forbidden, as shown by a baraita.
Rav Yosef clarifies that the question is about impurity: whether an idol is compared to a creeping thing (שֶׁרֶץ) requiring a lentil's bulk, or to a corpse (מֵת) requiring an olive's bulk.

items.text: Resolution from a baraita: Idolatry requires an olive's bulk
items.text_en: Resolution from a baraita: Idolatry requires an olive's bulk
items.desc_en: Rav Avya (or Rabba bar Ulla) cites a baraita that explicitly states an idol smaller than an olive's bulk has no impurity at all, deriving this from a verse comparing idolatry to a corpse. This resolves the query in favor of the olive's bulk requirement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya (or Rabba bar Ulla) cites a baraita that an idol smaller than an olive's bulk has no impurity at all, based on a verse comparing it to a corpse.

items.text: Explaining the multiple comparisons for idolatry
items.text_en: Explaining the multiple comparisons for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah compared idolatry to a creeping thing, a menstruating woman, and a corpse: each comparison teaches a leniency (e.g., not impure by carrying, not by limbs, not by a lentil's bulk). Since idolatry's impurity is rabbinic, we apply leniencies, not stringencies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the Rabbis hold that idolatry is compared to a corpse for the olive's bulk, why is it also compared to a creeping thing and a menstruating woman?
The Gemara answers that the comparisons are for leniencies (קוּלָּא), not stringencies (חוּמְרָא), since the impurity of idolatry is rabbinic.

items.text: Mishnah: Source for a ship being pure
items.text_en: Mishnah: Source for a ship being pure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a ship is pure from impurity, citing the verse 'the way of a ship in the heart of the sea' (Proverbs 30:19).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks: from where do we know that a ship is pure (טְהוֹרָה)? It answers with the verse 'דֶּרֶךְ אֳנִיָּה בְלֶב יָם' (the way of a ship in the heart of the sea).

items.text: Gemara: Derivation and alternative view of Chananya
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation and alternative view of Chananya
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse teaches that just as the sea is pure, so is a ship. A baraita cites Chananya who derives the purity of vessels from a sack: a vessel that is movable when full and empty is susceptible to impurity, excluding a ship which is not movable when full.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the obviousness of the verse and explains that it teaches a comparison: just as the sea is pure, so is a ship.
Chananya cites a baraita that derives purity from a sack (שַׂק): anything that can be moved when full and empty is pure, excluding a ship which cannot be moved when full.
A baraita cites Chananya who derives the purity of vessels from a sack: a vessel movable when full and empty is susceptible to impurity, excluding a ship which is not movable when full.

items.text: Difference between the two views: A clay ship
items.text_en: Difference between the two views: A clay ship
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two derivations. It answers: a clay ship. According to the verse derivation, it is pure like any ship in the sea. According to Chananya's sack derivation, it is impure because it is not movable when full, unlike a sack.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two derivations (the verse and the sack analogy).
The Gemara answers that the difference is a clay ship: according to the verse it is pure, but according to the sack analogy it is impure because it cannot be moved when full.

items.text: Another difference: A Jordan River ship and an aggadic conclusion
items.text_en: Another difference: A Jordan River ship and an aggadic conclusion
items.desc_en: Another difference is a Jordan River ship, which is movable when full because it is carried on land. Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya explains its impurity. The Gemara then records an aggadic teaching from Rav Yehuda citing Rav, and from Rabbi Yonatan and Resh Lakish, about the importance of Torah study even at the time of death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes another difference between the two derivations: a Jordan River ship, which is movable when full because it is carried on land.

Rabbi Yonatan teaches that one should never refrain from Torah study even at the time of death, citing the verse 'זֹאת הַתּוֹרָה אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל' (This is the Torah: a person who dies in a tent).
Resh Lakish teaches that words of Torah endure only for one who 'kills himself' over them, citing the same verse.

items.text: Baraitot on wagons and boxes as proof for Hananya
items.text_en: Baraitot on wagons and boxes as proof for Hananya
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Hananya considers moving via jumping as tilṭul, and cites a baraita about three types of wagons and another about three types of boxes, with Rabbi Yochanan's comment on the wagon's impurity status based on a receptacle for pomegranates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Hananya considers moving an object by means of jumping (שוורים) to be a prohibited form of tilṭul (carrying).
The Gemara answers affirmatively by citing a baraita listing three types of wagons and their impurity statuses, implying that movement via jumping is considered tilṭul.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that if the wagon has a receptacle for pomegranates, it is impure with corpse impurity, supporting the baraita's framework.
A second baraita lists three types of boxes and their impurity statuses, further illustrating the principle that movement via jumping is considered tilṭul.

items.text: Debate on midras of earthenware vessels and the boat
items.text_en: Debate on midras of earthenware vessels and the boat
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that midras of earthenware is pure, and Rabbi Yosei says even the boat is pure. Rav Zevid explains the statement, and Rav Pappa objects to the use of 'even', offering an alternative explanation involving wooden vessels and the Jordan boat.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that midras of earthenware vessels is pure, and Rabbi Yosei adds that even the boat is pure.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means.

Rav Zevid explains that the baraita means: midras of earthenware is pure but its touch is impure, and an earthenware boat is impure like Chananya; Rabbi Yosei says even the boat is pure like our Tanna.
Rav Pappa objects to Rav Zevid's use of 'even' in the explanation.

Rav Pappa offers an alternative explanation: midras of earthenware is pure but its touch is impure; for wooden vessels both midras and touch are impure; the Jordan boat is pure like our Tanna; Rabbi Yosei says even the boat is impure like Chananya.

items.text: Scriptural derivation for purity of earthenware midras
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation for purity of earthenware midras
items.desc_en: Hezekiah derives from a verse that a vessel's midras is like the person: if the person can be purified in a mikveh, so can the vessel, excluding earthenware which cannot. The school of Rabbi Yishmael similarly derives from another verse, and Rabbi Ila raises an objection about a mat in the context of a corpse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the midras (trampling) impurity of an earthenware vessel is pure (i.e., does not convey impurity)?

Hezekiah derives from the verse 'וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִגַּע בְּמִשְׁכָּבוֹ' (And a man who touches his bed) that the bed is compared to the person: just as the person has purification in a mikveh, so too his bed has purification in a mikveh, excluding earthenware which cannot be purified in a mikveh.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches a similar derivation from the verse 'כְּמִשְׁכַּב נִדָּתָהּ יִהְיֶה לָּהּ' (like the bed of her menstruation it shall be for her), comparing the bed to her: just as she has purification in a mikveh, so too her bed has purification in a mikveh, excluding earthenware which has no purification in a mikveh.
Rabbi Ila raises an objection: from where do we derive that a mat (מפץ) in the context of a corpse (i.e., a vessel that can become impure through contact with a corpse) is impure?

items.text: Kal vachomer and its refutation regarding the mat
items.text_en: Kal vachomer and its refutation regarding the mat
items.desc_en: A kal vachomer is proposed: if small vessels pure for a zav are impure for a corpse, then a mat impure for a zav should be impure for a corpse. Rabbi Chanina objects that the mat lacks purification in a mikveh. The Gemara then explains that two verses resolve the matter: one teaches impurity for a zav's bed, the other teaches that only items with a similar type are impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if small vessels that are pure for a zav are impure for a corpse, then a mat that is impure for a zav should certainly be impure for a corpse.
Rabbi Chanina objects that the mat lacks purification in a mikveh (ritual bath), and distinguishes the case because the mat has a similar type of item (a bed) that is impure for a zav.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Chanina's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Chanina's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rabbi Chanina's reasoning with a sharp expression ('May Heaven save us from that opinion!') and then explains that the true reason is based on two verses.

The Gemara resolves the matter by citing two verses: one teaches impurity for a zav's bed, and the other teaches that only items with a similar type (יש במינו) are impure, even without mikveh purification; items without a similar type are compared to the bed itself.

items.text: Rava's derivation about earthenware vessels
items.text_en: Rava's derivation about earthenware vessels
items.desc_en: Rava derives that a earthenware vessel used for treading (midras) is pure from the verse about an open vessel with a tight seal. The Gemara explains that the verse implies that if it has a tight seal, it is pure, even if designated for a menstruant wife.

sub.desc_en: Rava says: the midras (treading) of an earthenware vessel is pure from here:
Rava cites: 'And any open vessel that has no tight lid on it' — implying that if it HAS a tight lid, it is pure.
Rava asks: do we not deal with it designated for his menstruant wife, and yet the Merciful One says it is pure!
Rava answers: and the Merciful One says it is pure!

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the garden bed
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the garden bed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a garden bed of six by six handbreadths can contain five seeds: four at the corners and one in the middle, derived from the verse 'for as the earth brings forth its growth, and as a garden causes its seeds to sprout'. The Gemara explains that the word 'zir'eha' (its seeds) in the plural indicates two, and the other words in the verse yield a total of five.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule that a garden bed of six by six handbreadths can contain five seeds, four at the corners and one in the middle, and derives this from the verse 'for as the earth brings forth its growth, and as a garden causes its seeds to sprout', noting the plural form 'zir'eha' (its seeds).
The Gemara asks: what is the derivation from the verse?

Rav Yehuda explains the derivation: the word 'תּוֹצִיא' (brings forth) counts as one, 'צִמְחָהּ' (its growth) as one, totaling two; 'זֵרוּעֶיהָ' (its seeds) in the plural counts as two, totaling four; and 'תַּצְמִיחַ' (causes to sprout) as one, yielding a total of five seeds.

items.text: Opening principle: five in six do not draw nourishment
items.text_en: Opening principle: five in six do not draw nourishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the established principle that five species planted in a bed of six handbreadths do not draw nourishment from each other, setting up the basis for the subsequent discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the established principle that five species planted in a bed of six handbreadths do not draw nourishment from each other.

items.text: Source for the principle: biblical verses and the Horites
items.text_en: Source for the principle: biblical verses and the Horites
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the principle is valid, citing a verse about not moving boundaries. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yonatan explain that the early inhabitants (the Horites) were experts in land measurement, knowing exactly how much space each plant needs, and the term 'Chori' is interpreted as those who smell the earth or become free from their property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source that the rabbis' principle that five plants in six handbreadths do not draw from each other is valid.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'לֹא תַסִּיג גְּבוּל רֵעֲךָ' (Do not move your neighbor's boundary) and explains that it refers to boundaries set by the early inhabitants.
The Gemara asks who these 'early ones' are.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan identifies the early ones as the Horites (בני שעיר החורי), who were experts in land measurement, knowing exactly how much space each plant needs.
Rav Pappa explains the name 'חֹרִי' (Horite) as those who smell the earth, and 'חִוִּי' (Hivite) as those who taste the earth like a snake.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an alternative explanation: 'חֹרִי' means they became free (בני חורין) from their property.

items.text: Dimensions of the bed and its borders
items.text_en: Dimensions of the bed and its borders
items.desc_en: Rav Assi states that the bed itself is six handbreadths, excluding its borders. A baraita supports this. Rabbi Yehuda defines the border width as a handbreadth, based on a verse comparing irrigation to a foot, which is a handbreadth.

sub.desc_en: Rav Assi states that the bed (ערוגה) itself is six handbreadths, excluding its borders.
A baraita supports Rav Assi's ruling that the bed's interior is six handbreadths.
The Gemara asks: how wide are the borders of the bed?
Rabbi Yehuda defines the border width as a handbreadth, based on a verse comparing irrigation to a foot.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira / Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira / Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or alternatively Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: just as a foot is a handbreadth, so too the border is a handbreadth, derived from the verse 'וְהִשְׁקִיתָ בְרַגְלְךָ כְּגַן הַיָּרָק' (and you water with your foot like a garden of vegetables).

items.text: Rav's qualification: the bed in a ruin and the corners
items.text_en: Rav's qualification: the bed in a ruin and the corners
items.desc_en: Rav says that the rule of the bed (six handbreadths) was taught only regarding a ruin, not a full field. The Gemara objects about the corners, and the school of Rav answers that one fills the corners. The Gemara then questions why one should not plant outside and not fill inside.

sub.desc_en: Rav opens by stating that the mishnah's rule of the bed (six handbreadths) was taught only regarding a ruin (חורבה), not a full field.
The Gemara objects that even in a ruin, the corners (קרנות) of the bed remain unplanted, creating a gap.

sub.text: Bei Rav in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Bei Rav in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: The school of Rav (בי רב) answers in Rav's name that one fills the corners (ממלא את הקרנות) with soil to eliminate the gap.
The Gemara questions why one should not simply plant outside the bed (מאבראי) rather than filling the inside (מגואי) with soil.

items.text: Gemara's question about 'rosh tor'
items.text_en: Gemara's question about 'rosh tor'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the concern of filling the corners (קרנות) applies even to a 'rosh tor yarak' (a row end of vegetables), citing a Mishnah that permits such a case. It concludes that 'rosh tor' does not apply to a bed (ערוגה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the concern of filling the corners (קרנות) applies even to a 'rosh tor yarak' (a row end of vegetables), citing a Mishnah that permits such a case.
The Gemara resolves that the concept of 'rosh tor' does not apply to a bed (ערוגה).

items.text: Shmuel's interpretation: a bed between beds
items.text_en: Shmuel's interpretation: a bed between beds
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the Mishnah refers to a bed situated between other beds, and the concern of intermingling is resolved by arranging rows in opposite directions.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the Mishnah's ruling about a bed between beds refers to a case where one extends a row to one side and another row to the other side, preventing mixing.

items.text: Dispute about a single furrow across the entire bed
items.text_en: Dispute about a single furrow across the entire bed
items.desc_en: Ulla reports a query from the West: if one plows a single furrow across the entire bed, does it nullify the rows? Rav Sheshet and Rav Asi disagree, and Ravina challenges Rav Ashi with a baraita about planting rows of different vegetables, which is distinguished by the presence of 'sharacha' (a type of gourd).

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that the sages in the West asked: if one plowed a single furrow across the entire bed, what is the halacha (הלכה)?
Rav Sheishet answers that the mixing (עירבוב) caused by the furrow nullifies the row distinction.
Rav Asi answers that the mixing does not nullify the row distinction.
Ravina objects to Rav Ashi by citing a baraita that permits two rows of different species but forbids a single row of each species, implying that mixing does not nullify the row.
Rav Ashi rejects the objection, distinguishing the case because there are gaps (שראכא) between the rows.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's method for filling a garden with vegetables
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's method for filling a garden with vegetables
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana quotes Rabbi Yochanan: one who wants to fill his entire garden with vegetables should make a bed six by six handbreadths, round five handbreadths within it, and fill the corners with whatever he wishes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one who wishes to fill his entire garden with vegetables may make a bed of six by six handbreadths, round five within it, and fill the corners as desired.

items.text: Addressing the space between beds and Rav Ashi's solution
items.text_en: Addressing the space between beds and Rav Ashi's solution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the space between the beds. The school of Rabbi Yannai answers by destroying the intervening area, while Rav Ashi suggests alternating the planting direction (warp and woof). Ravina challenges Rav Ashi with a baraita about the required six handbreadths between different vegetables, and the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: but what about the spaces between the rounded areas?

sub.text: Answer from the school of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Answer from the school of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that one destroys (מחריב) the spaces between the rounded areas.
Rav Ashi answers that if the spaces were sown in warp (שתי) pattern, one sows them in woof (ערב) pattern, and vice versa.
Ravina objects to Rav Ashi by citing a baraita that the required distance for vegetable work between different vegetables is six handbreadths, and they are viewed as distinct.
The baraita continues with the phrase 'and one views them,' but the text is cut off, leaving the resolution incomplete.

items.text: Continuation of the square table discussion
items.text_en: Continuation of the square table discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the leniency of a square table applies only to that specific case, not to other similar situations, and explains that the leniency is to allow another leniency regarding the head of the ox that emerges from it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the leniency of a square table applies only to that specific case, not to other similar situations, and explains that the leniency is to allow another leniency regarding the head of the ox that emerges from it.

items.text: Mishnah: Sources for various halakhot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sources for various halakhot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists four halakhot derived from verses: a woman who emits semen on the third day is impure; circumcision may be washed on the third day even on Shabbat; a crimson thread is tied to the head of the scapegoat; anointing on Yom Kippur is like drinking, with a supporting verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists four derivations from verses: a woman who emits semen on the third day is impure, circumcision bathing on Shabbat, tying a crimson thread on the scapegoat, and anointing on Yom Kippur is like drinking.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's consistency
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's consistency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the first part of the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya while the latter part does, and explains that according to one approach the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, while according to another the first part is the Rabbis and the latter part is Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's inconsistency: the first clause does not follow Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, but the last clause does, since he holds a woman who emits semen is pure.

The Gemara resolves: one who does not posit multiple Tannaim reads the first clause as 'pure' and attributes the whole Mishnah to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya; one who posits multiple Tannaim assigns the first clause to the Rabbis and the last to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Another answer explains that the one who attributes the Mishnah to multiple Tannaim holds that the first part is the Rabbis and the latter part is Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute about the time of impurity
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute about the time of impurity
items.desc_en: A Baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says a woman who emits semen on the third day is pure; Rabbi Yishmael says the time varies between four, five, or six periods; Rabbi Akiva says it is always five periods, with a partial sixth if the first was partial.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting three opinions: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says a woman who emits semen on the third day is pure; Rabbi Yishmael says the time varies between four, five, or six watches; Rabbi Akiva says always five, with a partial sixth if the first watch was partial.
Rabbi Yishmael states that the time of impurity varies between four, five, or six periods.
Rabbi Akiva rules that it is always five periods, with a partial sixth if the first was partial.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Tannaitic positions
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Tannaitic positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara, reported before Rav Pappa or by Rav Pappa to Rava, aligns Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya with the Rabbis who say separation was on the fifth, Rabbi Yishmael with Rabbi Yose who says on the fourth, and explains Rabbi Akiva also follows Rabbi Yose based on Rav Adda bar Ahava's teaching that Moses ascended and descended at dawn.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask before Rav Pappa (or Rav Pappa asks Rava): Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya aligns with the Rabbis (who say separation at five watches), Rabbi Yishmael aligns with Rabbi Yosei (who says separation at four), but with whom does Rabbi Akiva align?
Rava answers that Rabbi Akiva always aligns with Rabbi Yosei, as Rav Adda bar Ahava said: Moses ascended early and descended early.

sub.text: Gemara's answer / Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer / Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva always follows Rabbi Yose, based on Rav Adda bar Ahava's teaching that Moses ascended and descended at dawn.

items.text: Proof for Moses' ascent and descent at dawn
items.text_en: Proof for Moses' ascent and descent at dawn
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides scriptural proof: Moses ascended early in the morning as per Exodus 34:4, and his descent is compared to his ascent by the verse 'Go, descend, and you shall ascend' (Exodus 24:12), teaching that descent was also at dawn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves the statement: Moses ascended early, as written 'וַיַּשְׁכֵּם מֹשֶׁה' (Moses rose early), and descended early, as the verse 'לֶךְ רֵד' (go down) equates descent to ascent, both being early.

items.text: Discussion on the permissibility of daytime relations
items.text_en: Discussion on the permissibility of daytime relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the teaching about Moses' times was necessary, given Rav Huna's statement that Jews are holy and do not engage in relations during the day. Rava answers that if the house is dark it is permitted, and a Torah scholar may darken his room with his tallit and it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the early descent needed to be stated, given Rav Huna's principle that Israelites are holy and do not engage in marital relations during the day.
Rava answers that if the house is dark it is permitted, and Rava (or Rav Pappa) adds that a Torah scholar may darken his house with his cloak and it is permitted.
Rava (or alternatively Rav Pappa) adds that a Torah scholar may darken his room with his tallit and it is permitted.

items.text: The status of טבול יום for receiving the Torah
items.text_en: The status of טבול יום for receiving the Torah
items.desc_en: Abaye bar Ravin and Rav Chanina bar Avin argue that the Torah was given to טבול יום. Marimar states this teaching, and Ravina questions whether he means it was actually given or was fitting to be given. Marimar clarifies he means it was fitting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: But they were טבולי יום (those who immersed but await sunset)? Abaye bar Ravin and Rav Chanina bar Avin both say the Torah was given to a טבול יום.
