Marimar sits and teaches this tradition; Ravina asks him: Do you mean it was actually given (נִיתְּנָה) or that it was fitting (רְאוּיָה)?
Marimar answers: I mean it was fitting (רְאוּיָה).

items.text: Why not immerse between sunset and nightfall or on Shabbat morning?
items.text_en: Why not immerse between sunset and nightfall or on Shabbat morning?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Israelites did not immerse between sunset and nightfall to receive the Torah. Rabbi Yitzchak answers with a verse indicating God did not speak in secret. Another suggestion to immerse on Shabbat morning is rejected because it would cause confusion between those going to receive the Torah and those going to immerse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Israelites did not immerse between sunset and nightfall and then receive the Torah at that same time.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers with a verse indicating that God did not speak in secret, implying the revelation had to be public, not at twilight.
The Gemara proposes an alternative: why not immerse on Shabbat morning and receive the Torah then?
Rabbi Yitzchak rejects this, explaining it would cause confusion between those going to receive the Torah and those going to immerse.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva, and the Sages on the period of niddah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva, and the Sages on the period of niddah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the previous ruling is according to Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages require six complete onot. Rav Chisda distinguishes between discharge from the woman (impure only when moist) and from the man. Rav Sheishet challenges this with a verse about semen, but the Gemara deflects the challenge.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the earlier ruling follows Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages require six complete onot (periods).
Rav Chisda distinguishes: the dispute applies only when the discharge came from the woman, but if it came from the man, it is impure only while still moist.
Rav Sheishet challenges with a verse that excludes dried semen, implying the impurity applies only to moist semen, which seems to contradict Rav Chisda's distinction.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by reinterpreting the verse: the exclusion of dried semen refers to discharge from the woman, not from the man.

items.text: Rav Pappa's query about semen in the belly of a gentile woman or animal
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's query about semen in the belly of a gentile woman or animal
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether semen of a Jew in the belly of a gentile woman is considered moist (and thus impure) because Jews are careful with mitzvot, or because gentiles eat repulsive things. He further asks about semen in the belly of an animal, questioning whether the lack of a vestibule causes decay. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether semen of a Jew in a gentile woman's belly is considered moist (and thus impure) because Jews are careful with mitzvot, or because gentiles eat repulsive things.
Rav Pappa further asks whether semen in an animal's belly decays due to the lack of a vestibule, or whether the same rule applies.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: The date of the giving of the Ten Commandments
items.text_en: The date of the giving of the Ten Commandments
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that the Ten Commandments were given on the sixth of Sivan, while Rabbi Yosei says the seventh. Rava explains that all agree they arrived at Sinai on Rosh Chodesh and that the Torah was given on Shabbat. The dispute is about the fixing of the month: Rabbi Yosei holds that the month was fixed on Sunday, and on Monday nothing was said due to travel fatigue, while on Tuesday the command about being a kingdom of priests was given.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the Ten Commandments were given on the sixth of Sivan.
Rabbi Yosei disputes the Sages, asserting that the Torah was given on the seventh of Sivan.
Rava resolves the dispute by explaining that all agree the Israelites arrived at Sinai on Rosh Chodesh and that the Torah was given on Shabbat, using verbal analogies (גזירה שווה) from the verses.

Rava explains that the dispute is about the fixing of the month: Rabbi Yosei holds that the month was fixed on Sunday, and on Monday nothing was said due to travel fatigue, while on Tuesday the command about being a kingdom of priests was given.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis on the dates of the giving of the Torah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis on the dates of the giving of the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the core dispute: Rabbi Yosei holds that the new moon was established on Sunday, so the commandment of boundary was given on Tuesday and separation on Wednesday; the Rabbis hold it was established on Monday, so the commandment of 'You shall be to Me' was given on Tuesday, boundary on Wednesday, and separation on Thursday. A challenge is raised against Rabbi Yosei from the verse 'Sanctify them today and tomorrow'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rabbi Yosei's position that the new moon was established on Sunday, so the commandment of boundary was given on Tuesday and separation on Wednesday, and the Rabbis' position that it was established on Monday, so the commandment of 'You shall be to Me' was given on Tuesday, boundary on Wednesday, and separation on Thursday.
The Gemara raises an objection against Rabbi Yosei from the verse 'Sanctify them today and tomorrow', which implies only two days of separation, not three.

items.text: Baraita: Three things Moses did on his own and God agreed
items.text_en: Baraita: Three things Moses did on his own and God agreed
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei holds Moses added one day on his own. A baraita lists three things Moses did on his own: adding a day of separation, separating from his wife, and breaking the tablets. For each, the Gemara explains Moses' reasoning and the proof that God agreed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei holds Moses added one day of separation on his own initiative.
A baraita lists three things Moses did on his own and with which God agreed: adding a day, separating from his wife, and breaking the tablets.
The Gemara asks what hermeneutical reasoning Moses used to add a day.

Moses reasoned from the verse 'today and tomorrow' that 'today' is like 'tomorrow' — just as tomorrow includes its preceding night, so today includes its preceding night, yielding two full days beyond the current one.
The Gemara proves God agreed because the Divine Presence did not descend until Shabbat morning, confirming Moses' added day.
The Gemara asks what reasoning Moses used to separate from his wife.
Moses reasoned a kal vachomer (a fortiori): if Israel, who only heard God once, were commanded to abstain from marital relations, then he, who spoke with God constantly, certainly must separate.
The Gemara proves God agreed through the verses 'go say to them: return to your tents' and 'you stand here with Me', and an alternative proof from 'mouth to mouth I speak with him'.
The Gemara asks what reasoning Moses used to break the tablets.
Moses reasoned a kal vachomer: if the Passover sacrifice, one of 613 commandments, forbids an apostate from eating it, then the entire Torah, now given to apostate Israel, certainly must be withheld.

sub.text: Gemara's proof of divine agreement (citing Resh Lakish)
sub.text_en: Gemara's proof of divine agreement (citing Resh Lakish)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves God agreed through the verse 'which you broke' and Resh Lakish's interpretation that God said 'may your strength be straight for breaking them'.

items.text: Challenge against the Rabbis from 'third day'
items.text_en: Challenge against the Rabbis from 'third day'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a challenge against the Rabbis from the verse 'Be ready for the third day', which implies the third of the month and the third day of the week, contradicting their view. The Gemara answers that this verse follows Rabbi Yosei's opinion.

sub.text: Gemara's further challenge against Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Gemara's further challenge against Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection against Rabbi Yosei from the verse 'And they were prepared for the third day', which seems to imply only two days of preparation, but the Gemara answers that Moses added one day on his own.

The Gemara raises an objection against the Rabbis from the verse 'third' meaning the third of the month and the third day of the week, which would imply the new moon was on Sunday, contradicting the Rabbis.
The Rabbis answer that the verse which says 'third' is according to Rabbi Yosei's opinion, not theirs.
The Rabbis answer that the verse follows Rabbi Yosei's opinion, not theirs, so it poses no difficulty to their view.

items.text: Interpretation of 'third day' and the verses 'Vayashev' and 'Vayaged'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'third day' and the verses 'Vayashev' and 'Vayaged'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the purpose of the 'third day' reference, citing a dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and Rabbi (and an alternative opinion) about whether Moses first explained the punishment or the reward of the boundary commandment, based on the two verses 'Vayashev' and 'Vayaged'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the purpose of the 'third day' reference is, and introduces a baraita.
The baraita cites two verses, 'וישב' (Vayashev) and 'ויגד' (Vayaged), to set up the dispute about what Moses communicated.
The Gemara asks what was said in the exchange between God, Moses, and Israel, framing the content of the verses.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda states that the exchange was about the commandment of boundary-setting (מצות הגבלה).
Rabbi argues that Moses first explained the punishment (עונשה) using the verse 'וישב' (words that unsettle), and then the reward (מתן שכרה) using 'ויגד' (words that attract like aggadah).
An alternative opinion reverses the order: Moses first explained the reward (מתן שכרה) via 'וישב' (words that restore the mind), and then the punishment (עונשה) via 'ויגד' (words as hard as sinews).

items.text: Challenge from 'sixth day' and Rava's statement
items.text_en: Challenge from 'sixth day' and Rava's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another challenge against the Rabbis from the phrase 'sixth day' (sixth of the month and sixth day of the week), and answers that this too follows Rabbi Yosei. It then asks what the 'sixth' refers to, and Rava begins to answer.

sub.text: Gemara's challenge against the Rabbis from 'sixth'
sub.text_en: Gemara's challenge against the Rabbis from 'sixth'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against the Rabbis from the verse 'sixth' meaning the sixth of the month and the sixth day of the week, which would imply the new moon was on Sunday.
The Rabbis answer that this verse too is according to Rabbi Yosei's opinion.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the purpose of 'sixth'
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the purpose of 'sixth'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'sixth' comes to teach, and Rava begins to answer.
Rava begins to answer the question about the meaning of 'sixth'.

items.text: Dispute about Marah: Shabbat vs. techumim
items.text_en: Dispute about Marah: Shabbat vs. techumim
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov and another Amora argue whether at Marah the Israelites were commanded about Shabbat or also about techumim (Sabbath boundaries). The dispute is based on the verse 'as the Lord your God commanded you' and Rav Yehuda's statement that this refers to Marah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov states that the verse refers to their journeys, not their encampments.
The Gemara explains that the dispute concerns the Shabbat (שבת) given at Marah (מרה).
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites the verse 'as the Lord your God commanded you' and identifies it as referring to Marah.
One Mar holds that at Marah they were commanded only about Shabbat (שבת), not about techumim (תחומין, Sabbath boundaries).
The other Mar holds that they were also commanded about techumim (תחומין).

items.text: Challenge to the Rabbis from the Exodus chronology
items.text_en: Challenge to the Rabbis from the Exodus chronology
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraisa stating that the 15th of Nisan, when the Israelites left Egypt, was a Thursday. This leads to a calculation that Rosh Chodesh Iyar was Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh Sivan was Sunday, which contradicts the Rabbis' view that the months were not intercalated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraisa about the Exodus chronology and calculates that Rosh Chodesh Iyar was Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh Sivan was Sunday, which contradicts the Rabbis' view that the months were not intercalated.

items.text: Rabbis' response: Iyar was intercalated
items.text_en: Rabbis' response: Iyar was intercalated
items.desc_en: The Rabbis answer that in that year, the month of Iyar was made full (intercalated) by adding a day, which would shift the days of the week. This resolves the contradiction from the previous section.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis respond that Iyar of that year was intercalated (made full), and they repeat the baraisa's chronology to show that Nisan was completed and Iyar began on Shabbat.

items.text: Refinement: The baraisa follows Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Refinement: The baraisa follows Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that if Iyar was deficient (29 days) and Sivan began on Sunday, the chronology still contradicts the Rabbis. Therefore, the baraisa must be according to Rabbi Yosei, who holds that months are intercalated differently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Iyar was deficient (29 days), Sivan would begin on Sunday, which still contradicts the Rabbis, and then identifies the baraisa as following Rabbi Yosei's view.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge from the manna
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge from the manna
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa brings a verse that the 15th of Iyar was Shabbat, based on the manna narrative. This would make Rosh Chodesh Sivan Sunday, again challenging the Rabbis. The Rabbis respond again that Iyar was intercalated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa brings a verse showing that the 15th of Iyar was Shabbat, which would make Rosh Chodesh Sivan Sunday, contradicting the Rabbis.
The Rabbis again respond that Iyar of that year was intercalated (made full).

items.text: Rav Chavivi's challenge from the Mishkan's dedication
items.text_en: Rav Chavivi's challenge from the Mishkan's dedication
items.desc_en: Rav Chavivi of Mehoza cites a tradition that the Mishkan was erected on the 1st of Nisan, which was a Sunday (based on the ten crowns). This leads to a calculation that Rosh Chodesh Iyar was Thursday, contradicting earlier assumptions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chavivi of Mehoza brings a baraisa about the ten crowns of the first of Nisan in the second year, and calculates that Rosh Chodesh Nisan was Sunday, which would make the 14th fall on Thursday.

Acherim's baraita states that the interval between Shavuot and Rosh Hashanah is only four days (or five in a leap year), which forces Rosh Chodesh Iyar to be Friday and Rosh Chodesh Sivan to be Shabbat, creating a difficulty for both Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis.

items.text: Final difficulty: Contradiction for both Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Final difficulty: Contradiction for both Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa of Acherim that the interval between Shavuot and Rosh Hashanah is only four days, leading to a calculation that Rosh Chodesh Iyar was Friday and Rosh Chodesh Sivan was Shabbat. This contradicts both Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis, as Rabbi Yosei holds that seven months are deficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to the baraisa of Acheirim, the interval between festivals is only four days, which would make Rosh Chodesh Iyar Friday and Rosh Chodesh Sivan Shabbat, contradicting both Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis, and notes that Rabbi Yosei's calendar has seven deficient months.
From Acherim's calculation, Rosh Chodesh Iyar falls on Friday and Rosh Chodesh Sivan on Shabbat, which contradicts both Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis.
The Gemara notes that for Rabbi Yosei, seven months are deficient, which would resolve the contradiction, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Dispute about the date of the giving of the Torah
items.text_en: Dispute about the date of the giving of the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from Seder Olam that implies the Torah was given on the sixth of Sivan, which contradicts Rabbi Yosei's view that it was given on the seventh. Rabbi Yosei deflects by saying the baraita follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei by citing a baraita from Seder Olam that calculates the date of the giving of the Torah as the sixth of Sivan, contradicting his view that it was the seventh.
Rabbi Yosei deflects the challenge by asserting that the baraita follows the opinion of the Rabbis, not his own.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yosei's own statement
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yosei's own statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another statement of Rabbi Yosei that Moses went up and down on the second, third, and fourth of Sivan, and on the fifth built an altar, implying the Torah was given on the sixth. The Gemara suggests this is because of the Torah, but Rabbi Yosei could say it was due to Shabbat preparation. A Galilean's homily supports the Rabbis' view that the Torah was given on the sixth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rabbi Yosei's own statement that Moses ascended and descended on the second, third, and fourth of Sivan, built an altar on the fifth, and had no time on the sixth, implying the Torah was given on the sixth, and asks whether this is because of the Torah.
The Gemara answers that the lack of time on the sixth was due to Shabbat preparation, and cites a Galilean's homily that supports the Rabbis' view that the Torah was given on the sixth of Sivan.

items.text: The coercion at Sinai and its acceptance in the days of Achashverosh
items.text_en: The coercion at Sinai and its acceptance in the days of Achashverosh
items.desc_en: Rav Avdimi bar Chama bar Chasa teaches that God held the mountain over Israel like a vat, threatening to bury them if they did not accept the Torah. Rav Acha bar Yaakov says this provides a strong objection to the Torah's validity. Rava counters that they later willingly accepted it in the days of Achashverosh.

sub.text: Rav Avdimi bar Chama bar Chasa
sub.text_en: Rav Avdimi bar Chama bar Chasa
sub.desc_en: Rav Avdimi bar Chama bar Chasa teaches that at Sinai God held the mountain over Israel like a vat, threatening to bury them if they did not accept the Torah.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that this coercion provides a strong objection (מודעא רבה) to the Torah's validity, since acceptance was under duress.

Rava resolves the objection by noting that despite the initial coercion, the Jews willingly accepted the Torah again in the days of Achashverosh, as implied by the verse 'קִיְּימוּ וְקִבְּלוּ' (they fulfilled what they had already accepted).

items.text: The earth's fear and silence at Sinai
items.text_en: The earth's fear and silence at Sinai
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah interprets a verse to mean that the earth initially feared at Sinai but later was calm. The fear is explained by Resh Lakish's teaching that God conditioned the existence of the world on Israel's acceptance of the Torah.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah questions the apparent contradiction in the verse 'אֶרֶץ יָרְאָה וְשָׁקָטָה' (the earth feared and was quiet), asking how it can be both afraid and calm.
Chizkiyah resolves the contradiction by explaining that initially the earth feared, but eventually it became calm.
Resh Lakish explains why the earth feared: God conditioned the existence of creation on Israel's acceptance of the Torah, threatening to return the world to chaos if they refused.

items.text: The crowns for 'na'aseh' before 'nishma' and their loss and restoration
items.text_en: The crowns for 'na'aseh' before 'nishma' and their loss and restoration
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simai teaches that when Israel said 'na'aseh' before 'nishma', 600,000 ministering angels placed two crowns on each Jew. After the sin of the golden calf, 1,200,000 destroying angels removed them. Rabbi Yochanan says Moses took them, and Resh Lakish says they will be restored in the future.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simai teaches that when Israel said 'na'aseh' before 'nishma', 600,000 ministering angels placed two crowns on each Jew.
After the sin of the golden calf, 1,200,000 destroying angels removed the crowns, as per the verse 'וַיִּתְנַצְּלוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת עֶדְיָם מֵהַר חוֹרֵב'.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's amplification
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's amplification
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina notes that at Chorev they received the crowns and at Chorev they were removed.
Rabbi Yochanan says Moses took all the crowns, as the verse 'וּמֹשֶׁה יִקַּח אֶת הָאֹהֶל' follows.
Resh Lakish says the Holy One will restore the crowns in the future, as per the verse 'וּפְדוּיֵי ה׳ יְשֻׁבוּן וּבָאוּ צִיּוֹן בְּרִנָּה וְשִׂמְחַת עוֹלָם עַל רֹאשָׁם'.

items.text: The Bat Kol and the apple metaphor
items.text_en: The Bat Kol and the apple metaphor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that when Israel said 'na'aseh' before 'nishma', a Bat Kol asked who revealed this secret of the angels, who also do before they hear. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina compares Israel to an apple tree, whose fruit precedes its leaves.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar reports that when Israel said 'na'aseh' before 'nishma', a Bat Kol (heavenly voice) asked who revealed to them the secret of the ministering angels, who also 'do' before they 'hear', as shown by the verse.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains why Israel is compared to an apple tree: just as the apple's fruit precedes its leaves, so Israel preceded 'na'aseh' (we will do) before 'nishma' (we will hear).

items.text: A heretic's challenge and Rava's response
items.text_en: A heretic's challenge and Rava's response
items.desc_en: A heretic sees Rava studying intently and biting his fingers, and mocks Israel for putting their mouths before their ears. Rava responds that they acted with integrity, unlike the heretic who would have rejected the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes a heretic seeing Rava studying intently, biting his fingers until they bleed.
The heretic mocks Israel as a hasty people who put their mouths before their ears, implying they should have listened first before accepting the Torah.
Rava responds that Israel acted with integrity (תמימים), unlike the heretic who would have rejected the Torah if given the chance.

items.text: Opening proverb on the righteous and the deceitful
items.text_en: Opening proverb on the righteous and the deceitful
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a proverb contrasting those who walk in integrity (the righteous) with those who walk in deceit (the treacherous), citing Proverbs 11:3.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a proverb contrasting those who walk in integrity with those who walk in deceit, citing Proverbs 11:3.

items.text: The bride's initial single eye and later two eyes
items.text_en: The bride's initial single eye and later two eyes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan interprets Song of Songs 4:9, saying that initially God was pleased with Israel's single eye (at Sinai), but later with both eyes. Ulla and Rav Mari add that the bride (Israel) was faithless under the canopy (the Golden Calf), yet Rav notes that God still calls it 'giving' not 'stinking'. The Tanna Kamma praises those who suffer silently.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan interprets Song of Songs 4:9, saying that initially God was pleased with Israel's single eye (at Sinai), but later with both eyes.
Ulla laments that the bride (Israel) was faithless under the canopy (the Golden Calf).
Rav Mari cites a verse (Song of Songs 1:12) to support the idea of Israel's faithlessness during the giving of the Torah.
Rav notes that despite the sin, God still calls it 'giving' not 'stinking', indicating enduring love.
The Tanna Kamma praises those who suffer silently and are insulted without retaliating, applying the verse about those who love God.

items.text: Each divine utterance divided into seventy languages
items.text_en: Each divine utterance divided into seventy languages
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that every word from God was divided into seventy languages, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael compares it to a hammer splitting rock. Rav Chananel bar Pappa adds that Torah words are like a 'nagid' (a prince) that can kill or revive.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that every divine utterance was divided into seventy languages.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael supports this with a metaphor: as a hammer splits into many sparks, so each divine word splits into seventy languages.
Rav Chananel bar Pappa adds that Torah words are compared to a 'nagid' (prince) that can both kill and revive.

items.text: Torah as life or death, and two crowns for each word
items.text_en: Torah as life or death, and two crowns for each word
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Torah is a potion of life for those who turn right and a potion of death for those who turn left. Another interpretation says each word from God was tied with two crowns. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets Song of Songs 1:13-14, and Mar Zutra explains the word 'karmei' as gathering.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Torah is a potion of life for those who turn right and a potion of death for those who turn left.
An alternative interpretation explains that each word from God was tied with two crowns.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets Song of Songs 1:13-14 as Israel's declaration that despite affliction, God dwells between her breasts and atones for the sin of the calf.
The Gemara asks how we know that the word 'karmei' (כרמי) means gathering.
Mar Zutra answers by citing a Mishnah where 'kormin' (כורמים) means gathering clothes on a launderer's stool.

items.text: Each word filled the world with fragrance
items.text_en: Each word filled the world with fragrance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that each word from God filled the world with fragrance, and God used wind from His treasuries to carry away the first word before the next, as per Song of Songs 5:13.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that each divine word filled the world with fragrance, and God used wind from His treasuries to carry away each word before the next, as per Song of Songs 5:13.

items.text: Israel's souls departed and were revived by dew
items.text_en: Israel's souls departed and were revived by dew
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that at each word from God, Israel's souls departed (Song of Songs 5:6), and God revived them with the dew that will resurrect the dead (Psalm 68:10). He also says that Israel retreated twelve mil and angels drew them back.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that at each divine utterance, Israel's souls departed, and God revived them with the dew of resurrection.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that at each utterance, Israel retreated twelve mil and angels drew them back.

items.text: Angels' objection and Moses' defense of the Torah
items.text_en: Angels' objection and Moses' defense of the Torah
items.desc_en: When Moses ascended to heaven, the angels objected to giving the Torah to a human. God told Moses to answer them. Moses, holding God's throne, argued that the Torah's commandments (e.g., 'I am the Lord your God who took you out of Egypt', 'You shall have no other gods') are irrelevant to angels who never were in Egypt or among idolaters.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports that when Moses ascended to heaven, the ministering angels objected to God giving the Torah to a human.
God responds to the angels that Moses came to receive the Torah.
The angels protest that the precious Torah, hidden for 974 generations, should not be given to flesh and blood.
God instructs Moses to answer the angels; Moses expresses fear, and God tells him to hold onto the throne of glory.
Rabbi Nachum cites a verse and explains that God spread His divine radiance and cloud over Moses.
Moses defends the Torah by arguing that its commandments, such as the exodus from Egypt and prohibition of other gods, are irrelevant to angels who never experienced Egypt or idolatry.

items.text: The angels' argument against giving the Torah to Israel
items.text_en: The angels' argument against giving the Torah to Israel
items.desc_en: The angels protest that the Torah should remain in heaven, arguing that Israel is unworthy because they engage in idolatry, labor, business, and have parents, jealousy, and the evil inclination. They cite the Ten Commandments to show that Israel violates them, but ultimately concede to God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the angels' argument: since Israel engages in idolatry, labor, business, and has parents, jealousy, and the evil inclination, they are unworthy of the Torah.
The angels immediately concede to God, as the verse says 'ה׳ אֲדֹנֵינוּ מָה אַדִּיר שִׁמְךָ' but not 'תְּנָה הוֹדְךָ עַל הַשָּׁמָיִם'.

items.text: The angels give gifts to Moses
items.text_en: The angels give gifts to Moses
items.desc_en: After conceding, each angel becomes a friend to Moses and gives him a gift, including the Angel of Death, who teaches him the power of incense to stop a plague.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes that each angel, including the Angel of Death, gave Moses a gift, and the Angel of Death taught him the power of incense to stop a plague.

items.text: Satan searches for the Torah and Moses' humility
items.text_en: Satan searches for the Torah and Moses' humility
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recounts that when Moses descended from heaven, Satan searched for the Torah everywhere—earth, sea, and the deep—but could not find it. God tells him to go to Moses. Moses humbly denies possessing the Torah, and God praises him for his modesty, naming the Torah after him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recounts that when Moses descended from heaven, Satan searched for the Torah in earth, sea, and the deep, but could not find it.
Satan reports his failure to find the Torah, and God tells him to go to Moses.
Moses humbly denies possessing the Torah, and God praises his modesty, naming the Torah after him.

items.text: Moses' encounter with God tying crowns to letters
items.text_en: Moses' encounter with God tying crowns to letters
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi relates that when Moses ascended to heaven, he found God tying crowns to the letters. God asks why Moses did not greet Him, and Moses explains that a slave does not greet his master. God then tells Moses he should have helped Him, and Moses prays for God's strength.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports that when Moses ascended to heaven, he found God tying crowns to the letters.
God asks Moses why he did not greet Him with 'שלום' (peace).
Moses explains that a slave does not greet his master, so he refrained from offering 'שלום'.
God rebukes Moses, saying he should have helped Him by greeting Him.
Moses immediately prays for God's strength, quoting the verse 'ועתה יגדל נא כח ה׳'.

items.text: The sin of the Golden Calf and Satan's deception
items.text_en: The sin of the Golden Calf and Satan's deception
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains the verse 'the people saw that Moses delayed' by reading 'boshaysh' as 'bau shesh' (the sixth hour). Moses told Israel he would return after forty days at the beginning of the sixth hour. Satan confused the world, showing them a vision of Moses' bier, leading them to say to Aaron, 'this man Moses...'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi opens by interpreting the verse 'the people saw that Moses delayed' (וַיַּרְא הָעָם כִּי בֹשֵׁשׁ מֹשֶׁה) as a wordplay: read not 'boshaysh' but 'bau shesh' (the sixth hour had come).
He explains that when Moses ascended to heaven, he told Israel he would return after forty days at the beginning of the sixth hour, but Satan confused the world at the end of the forty days.
Satan approached Israel, asked where Moses was, and when they said he had ascended, Satan showed them a vision of Moses' bier, leading them to say to Aaron 'this man Moses...'.

items.text: The etymology of 'Sinai'
items.text_en: The etymology of 'Sinai'
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rav Kahana the meaning of 'Har Sinai'. Rav Kahana suggests it means the mountain where miracles were performed for Israel, but is challenged. He then says it means a good sign for Israel. The rabbi criticizes him for not studying aggada with Rav Pappa and Rav Huna. Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna explain that 'Sinai' means the mountain where enmity descended upon the nations. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina lists five names for the mountain.

sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rav Kahana what 'Har Sinai' means.
Rav Kahana answers that Sinai is the mountain where miracles were performed for Israel.
The rabbi objects that if so, the mountain should have been called 'Har Nissai' (Mountain of Miracles).
Rav Kahana revises his answer: Sinai is the mountain that became a good sign for Israel.
The rabbi objects again: if so, it should be called 'Har Simanai' (Mountain of the Sign).
The rabbi rebukes Rav Kahana for not studying aggada with Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna explain that 'Sinai' means the mountain where enmity (שִׂנְאָה) descended upon the nations of the world.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina lists five names for the mountain, beginning with 'Midbar Tzin'.

items.text: The names of Mount Sinai
items.text_en: The names of Mount Sinai
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the mountain is called Sinai and Horeb, citing Rabbi Avahu's view that Sinai is its primary name and Horeb refers to the destruction that came upon the nations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Mount Sinai is named for the proliferation of Israel and the descent of hatred upon the nations.
Rabbi Avahu states that the mountain's primary name is Sinai, and it is called Horeb because destruction descended upon the nations there.

items.text: Interpretation of 'if your sins be as scarlet'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'if your sins be as scarlet'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak and Rava interpret the verse from Isaiah, explaining that the unusual phrasing teaches that God will tell Israel to go to their ancestors for rebuke, but ultimately they rely on God alone for forgiveness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording 'כַּשָּׁנִים' (like the years) instead of 'כַּשָּׁנִי' (like scarlet).
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that 'כַּשָּׁנִים' refers to sins accumulated from the six days of creation until now, which will be whitened like snow.

Rava questions the verse 'לְכוּ נָא וְנִוָּכְחָה יֹאמַר ה׳' (Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord), asking why it says 'לְכוּ' (go) instead of 'בּוֹאוּ' (come) and 'יֹאמַר' (will say) instead of 'אָמַר' (said).
Rava explains that in the future, God will tell Israel to go to their ancestors for rebuke.
Israel objects that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob each failed to pray for them despite God's promises.
God responds that since Israel has relied on Him, their sins will be whitened like snow.

items.text: The patriarchs' responses to Israel's sins
items.text_en: The patriarchs' responses to Israel's sins
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan describes a future dialogue where Abraham and Jacob suggest Israel be destroyed, but Isaac argues that they are his children and offers a calculation of their sins, leading to their forgiveness.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan introduces a future dialogue where God tells Abraham that Israel sinned, and Abraham responds by suggesting they be destroyed for the sanctification of God's name.
God then approaches Jacob, hoping his experience with raising children will lead him to mercy, but Jacob also suggests the people be destroyed for the sanctification of God's name.
God remarks that there is no reason in elders and no wisdom in youth, then turns to Isaac, who argues that Israel are his children and not God's, citing their acceptance of the Torah at Sinai.
Isaac calculates the actual amount of sin in a human life, subtracting non-culpable years, nights, and necessary activities, and offers to bear half or all the remaining sins himself.
The people begin to praise Isaac as their father, but he redirects them to praise God, and they lift their eyes to heaven and declare God as their father and redeemer.

items.text: Jacob's descent to Egypt
items.text_en: Jacob's descent to Egypt
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that Jacob deserved to go to Egypt in iron chains, but his merit caused him to be drawn with cords of love.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that Jacob deserved to go to Egypt in iron chains, but his merit caused him to be drawn with cords of love.

items.text: Mishnah: Shiurim for carrying wood and spices
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shiurim for carrying wood and spices
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum measures for carrying wood, spices, dye materials, and laundry agents on Shabbat, with Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on the measure for removing a stain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum measures for carrying various items on Shabbat, including wood for cooking an egg, spices for seasoning, and materials for dyeing or laundering.
The Mishnah lists measures for carrying dye materials and laundry agents on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda gives his own measure for laundry agents: enough to remove a stain.

items.text: Gemara: Why repeat the measure for wood?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why repeat the measure for wood?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah repeats the measure for wood when it was already taught elsewhere, and explains that it teaches that even thick or broken wood is measured by the same standard, not by any amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah repeats the measure for wood, citing a previous baraita about a reed for making a quill or cooking an egg.
The Gemara explains that the repetition teaches that even though wood is usable for a key, the measure for cooking an egg still applies.

items.text: Contradiction regarding spices
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding spices
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's measure for spices and a baraita that discusses combining different types of spices, citing Chizkiya's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's measure for spices and a baraita about forbidden mixtures of spices, citing Chizkiyah's statement.
The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita that discusses combining different types of spices.
The Gemara invokes Chizkiya's statement as part of the contradiction.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of sweeteners' measure
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of sweeteners' measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah's measure for sweeteners (any amount) is because they are used to sweeten a pot, implying that without this use, they would not be significant. It then applies this reasoning to other contexts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah's measure for sweeteners (any amount) is because they are suitable for sweetening a pot.
The Gemara infers that if the sweeteners were not suitable for sweetening, they would not be significant.
The Gemara applies the same reasoning to the current context: here too they are suitable for sweetening.

items.text: Contradiction regarding dye materials
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding dye materials
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the mishnah's measure for nut and pomegranate peels (to dye a small garment) and a baraita that says soaked dyes are measured for a small sample. Rav Nachman bar Rav Abba resolves this by explaining that one does not bother to soak dyes for a small sample.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the measure for nut and pomegranate peels, stes, and poah is enough to dye a small garment.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that sets the measure for soaked dyes as enough to dye a sample for a weaver's beam.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha resolves that one does not trouble to soak dyes for a sample for a weaver's beam.

items.text: Definitions of urine, natron, and borit
items.text_en: Definitions of urine, natron, and borit
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the substances listed in the mishnah: urine (up to 40 days), natron (Alexandrian, not Antipatrian), and borit. Rav Yehuda initially says borit is sand, but a baraita lists both borit and sand, so he redefines borit as kabrita (a type of alkali). A challenge from the laws of shevi'it forces a further redefinition to ahala (a plant), and a contradiction is resolved by positing two types of ahala.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna defines urine as valid only up to forty days old.
The Tanna defines natron as Alexandrian natron, not Antipatrian.
Rav Yehuda initially identifies borit as sand.
The Gemara objects that a baraita lists both borit and sand as separate items, so borit cannot be sand.
The Gemara redefines borit as kabrita (a type of alkali).
The Gemara challenges that a baraita lists borit alongside ahala, and kabrita is not subject to shevi'it laws, unlike ahala.
The Gemara argues that kabrita has no root and thus is exempt from shevi'it, but the baraita includes borit in a list of items subject to shevi'it.
The Gemara redefines borit as ahala (a plant).
The Gemara objects that a baraita lists both borit and ahala as separate items.
The Gemara resolves that there are two types of ahala, one called borit and one called ahala.

items.text: Definitions of kimolya and ashlag
items.text_en: Definitions of kimolya and ashlag
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda defines kimolya as shlof dotz (a type of dye). Shmuel defines ashlag as shunaga, found in a pearl hole and extracted with an iron needle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda identifies kimolya as shlof dots (a type of clay).
Shmuel reports that he asked all seafarers and they said its name is shunaga, found in a pearl hole, extracted with an iron rod.

items.text: Mishnah: Measures for various items
items.text_en: Mishnah: Measures for various items
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists items that are prohibited in any amount when carried on Shabbat: pepper, citron, spices, metals, altar stones, altar dust, book and cloth decay, and idolatry accessories (according to Rabbi Yehuda).

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists items whose measure for carrying on Shabbat is any amount, including pepper, coriander, spices, metals, altar stones, and book mold, with Rabbi Yehuda adding idolatry accessories.

items.text: Gemara: Uses for pepper, citron, and spices
items.text_en: Gemara: Uses for pepper, citron, and spices
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the uses for pepper (for bad breath), citron (for a headache), and spices (for bad smell). A baraita adds that carrying bad smell, good oil, argaman, and a rose bud each have their own measures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what pepper is used for and answers it is for bad breath.
The Gemara asks what coriander is used for and answers it is for a poultice.
A baraita lists additional items whose measure is any amount: bad smell, good oil, purple dye, and a rose bud.
The Gemara answers that citron is used for a headache.
A baraita lists additional items with their own minimal measures: bad smell, good oil, argaman, and a rose bud.

items.text: Gemara: Use for metals
items.text_en: Gemara: Use for metals
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what metals are used for, and a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar answers that they are suitable for making a small goad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what metals are used for, and cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that they are suitable for making a small goad.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar answers that metals are suitable for making a small goad.

items.text: Baraita: Measures for iron and copper in vows
items.text_en: Baraita: Measures for iron and copper in vows
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the minimum measure for one who vows to bring iron or copper. For iron, Acheirim says at least an amah by an amah (for a crow's cage, per Rav Yosef). For copper, Rabbi Eliezer says at least a small copper tube (for cleaning wicks, per Abaye).

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who vows to bring iron to the Temple must bring at least a cubit by a cubit.
The Gemara asks what such iron is used for, and Rav Yosef answers it is for a raven's trap.
An alternative version states that others say the minimum is a raven's trap.
The Gemara asks how large that is, and Rav Yosef answers a cubit by a cubit.
The baraita states that copper must be at least a ma'ah of silver, and Rabbi Eliezer says a small copper tube.
The Gemara asks what the copper tube is used for, and Abaye answers it is for poking wicks and cleaning lamps.
The baraita continues with the rule for copper: at least a ma'ah of silver in value.
Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the minimum for copper is a small copper tube.
The gemara asks what the copper tube is used for.
Abaye explains that the tube is used for poking wicks and cleaning lamps.

items.text: Gemara: Definitions of book and cloth decay
items.text_en: Gemara: Definitions of book and cloth decay
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda defines the decay of books, silk, grape clusters, fig mouths, and pomegranate mouths as dangerous. A story illustrates the danger: a student eating figs is warned by Rabbi Yochanan about the fig mouth.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda identifies book mold, silk decay, grape stalks, fig mouths, and pomegranate mouths as all dangerous.
A story about a student eating figs before Rabbi Yochanan, who warns that the fig mouth kills.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Yochanan and a student
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Yochanan and a student
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates the danger: a student eating figs is warned by Rabbi Yochanan about the fig mouth.

items.text: Mishnah: Measures for a peddler's box and garden seeds
items.text_en: Mishnah: Measures for a peddler's box and garden seeds
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who carries a peddler's box with many items is liable for only one sin-offering. For garden seeds, the measure is less than a dried fig. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says five seeds.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who carries a peddler's box is liable for only one sin-offering, and garden seeds are less than a dried fig-bulk, with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira saying five.
The mishnah states that for garden seeds, the measure is less than a dried fig.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira gives a different measure: five seeds.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Shiurim for seeds and insects
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Shiurim for seeds and insects
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum measurements for carrying various items on Shabbat: cucumber seeds (two), gourd seeds (two), Egyptian bean seeds (two), a live kosher locust (any amount), a dead locust (the size of a dried fig), and the bird 'tziporet keramim' (any amount, as it is stored for medicine). Rabbi Yehuda adds that one who carries a live non-kosher locust is liable for any amount, as it is stored for a child to play with.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the minimum shiurim (measurements) for carrying seeds and a live kosher locust on Shabbat.
The Mishnah adds the shiur for a dead locust (the size of a dried fig) and for the bird 'tziporet keramim' (any amount, as it is stored for medicine).
Rabbi Yehuda adds that one who carries a live non-kosher locust is liable for any amount, as it is stored for a child to play with.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's shiurim
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's shiurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that the measure for fine dung or sand is enough to fertilize a single cabbage stalk (according to Rabbi Akiva) or a leek (according to the Sages), which seems to conflict with the Mishnah's two seeds. Rav Pappa resolves: the Mishnah refers to seeds that have already been sown (where one would not bother to carry a single seed), while the baraita refers to seeds that have not yet been sown.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about the shiur for manure and fine sand, which differs from the Mishnah's shiurim.

Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between seeds that have been planted (where a larger shiur applies) and those not yet planted (where a smaller shiur applies), because one does not trouble to take out a single strand for planting.

items.text: Baraitot on additional shiurim
items.text_en: Baraitot on additional shiurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites baraitot: for carrying seeds, if for planting (two), if for eating (a pig's mouthful, which is one), if for fuel (enough to cook a light egg), if for counting (two, others say five). Also, carrying two hairs from a horse's or cow's tail is liable (stored for snares), a pig's bristle (one), palm fibers (two), palm shoots (one).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the shiur for carrying seeds depends on the intended use: for planting (two), for eating (the amount of a pig's mouthful, which is one), for fuel (enough to cook a light egg), or for counting (two).
Acherim (other sages) say the shiur for counting is five seeds.
Another baraita lists shiurim for carrying items like horse or cow tail hairs (two, for making loops), a pig's bristle (one), palm fibers (two), and palm shoots (one).
A second baraita lists shiurim for hairs: two from a horse's or cow's tail (liable, stored for snares), one pig's bristle.
The baraita concludes: palm fibers (two), palm shoots (one).

items.text: Identification and use of tziporet keramim
items.text_en: Identification and use of tziporet keramim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what 'tziporet keramim' is: Rav says it is the 'palya bi'ari' (a type of bird). Abaye describes its use for wisdom: one eats half of it (the right side), places the left half in a copper tube sealed with sixty seals, hangs it on the left arm, and studies as desired; otherwise, one's learning is uprooted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the identity of the bird 'tziporet keramim'.
Rav identifies it as 'palya bi'ari' (a type of bird).

Abaye describes a folk remedy using this bird: it is found in a single-branched palm tree, used for wisdom, involving eating half and sealing the other half in a copper tube with sixty seals, hung on the left arm, with a scriptural sign, enabling one to learn as much as desired.

items.text: Debate on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a non-kosher locust
items.text_en: Debate on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a non-kosher locust
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the first Tanna disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda: perhaps because one might eat it. But then the same concern applies to a kosher locust, yet Rav Kahana removed a locust from his mouth to avoid violating 'do not abominate yourselves'. Rather, the concern is that it might die and then be eaten; Rabbi Yehuda holds that a child would mourn a dead locust, so it is not stored for that purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna Kamma (first sage) disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda regarding the non-kosher locust.
The Gemara suggests that the Tanna Kamma is concerned that the child might eat the non-kosher locust.

The Gemara objects: if the concern is eating, then even a kosher locust should be forbidden, citing Rav Kahana who removed a locust from his mouth to avoid the prohibition of 'בל תשקצו' (do not abominate yourselves).
The Gemara refines the concern: the Tanna Kamma fears the child might eat the locust after it dies (when it becomes non-kosher).
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda holds that if the locust dies, the child will mourn it and not eat it, so the concern is removed.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The phrase 'Hadran alach Amar Rabbi Akiva' marks the end of the chapter, indicating the return to the study of the chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Stam concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you), marking the end of the chapter.

items.text: New Mishnah: The principle of designation
items.text_en: New Mishnah: The principle of designation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: One who designates an item for seed, a sample, or medicine, and then carries it on Shabbat, is liable for any amount. But for any other person, liability is only according to the standard shiur. If one then brings it back inside, he is only liable according to the standard shiur.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one who stores an item for seed, sample, or medicine and carries it on Shabbat is liable for any amount, while an ordinary person is liable only for the standard shiur; if he returns it, he is liable only for the standard shiur.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Why does the Mishnah say 'hamatznia' (one who designates)? It should say 'hamotzi' (one who carries)! Abaye answers: The case is where one designated the item but forgot why, and now carries it out without a specific intent; the Mishnah teaches that the original designation still determines liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the term 'המצניע' (one who stores) rather than simply 'המוציא' (one who carries).
Abaye answers that the case involves one who stored an item but forgot the purpose, and now carries it out without specific intent, so the shiur depends on the original storage intent.

items.text: Clarification of intent in carrying
items.text_en: Clarification of intent in carrying
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even if one's initial thought is nullified, the act is still considered based on the original intention, as one acts with the original thought in mind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that even if one nullifies his initial thought, the act is still governed by the original intention, as one acts on the first thought.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's liability for a single wheat grain
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's liability for a single wheat grain
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel states that Rabbi Meir would hold one liable for carrying a single wheat grain for sowing. The Gemara questions this, noting the Mishnah says 'any amount', but clarifies it excludes a fig-bulk, implying a minimum of an olive's bulk. Rav Yitzchak objects that if so, one would not be liable for carrying his entire house unless he takes it all out, but the Gemara dismisses this as his intention is nullified.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that Rabbi Meir would hold one liable for carrying out a single wheat kernel for sowing.
The Gemara questions why this is necessary, since the Mishnah already states 'any amount'.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'any amount' excludes the standard fig-bulk measure, but one might think a olive-bulk is still required; Shmuel's statement teaches that even a single kernel suffices.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak objects: if intention determines liability, then if one intended to carry out his entire house, would he not be liable until he carries it all out?
The Gemara rejects the objection: in that case, his intention is nullified in the eyes of all people, and people are only liable for the standard measure.

items.text: Mishnah not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Mishnah not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling does not align with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that if an item is not normally stored but someone stored it, another who takes it is liable based on the first person's intention.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, as a baraita teaches his ruling.

sub.text: Baraita citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: The baraita states Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle: if an item is not normally stored, but one person stored it and another carried it out, the latter is liable due to the former's intention.

items.text: Liability when changing intention for a fig-bulk
items.text_en: Liability when changing intention for a fig-bulk
items.desc_en: Rava quoting Rav Nachman rules that if one carries a fig-bulk for eating and then decides to use it for sowing, or vice versa, he is liable. The Gemara questions this, as there is always a sufficient size, but Rava clarifies that we might have thought both lifting and placing must be with the same intention, so this teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports in the name of Rav Nachman: if one carries out a fig-bulk for eating and then changes his mind to sowing, or vice versa, he is liable.
The Gemara questions why this is obvious: in either case there is a sufficient measure.
The Gemara explains that one might think we require the lifting and placing to be under a single intention; Rav Nachman's statement teaches that this is not necessary.

items.text: Rava's queries on changing size and intention
items.text_en: Rava's queries on changing size and intention
items.desc_en: Rava raises a series of questions: if one carries half a fig-bulk for sowing and it swells, then he decides to eat it; if one carries a fig-bulk for eating and it shrinks, then he decides to sow it; and if it shrinks and then swells again. The Gemara leaves the last question unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if one carries out half a fig-bulk for sowing and it swells, then changes his mind to eat it, what is the law?
Rava raises a second query: if one carries a fig-bulk for eating and it shrinks, then changes his mind to sow it, what is the law?
Rava raises a third query: if one carries a fig-bulk for eating, it shrinks, and then swells again, what is the law?
The Gemara leaves the third query unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rava's query about terumah thrown into a impure house
items.text_en: Rava's query about terumah thrown into a impure house
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about throwing an olive's bulk of terumah into an impure house: is one liable for Shabbat (which requires a fig-bulk) or for impurity (which requires an egg's bulk)? The Gemara clarifies it is about Shabbat where there is less than an egg's bulk of food, and this completes it. Rav Nachman cites a baraita of Abba Shaul that the showbread and two loaves have a fig-bulk measure, implying that for Shabbat, a fig-bulk is required.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: if one throws an olive-bulk of תרומה (priestly portion) into a ritually impure house, what is the law?
The Gemara clarifies the question: for Shabbat, a fig-bulk is needed; for impurity, an egg-bulk of food is needed.
The Gemara specifies: the case is regarding Shabbat, where there is less than an egg-bulk of food, and this olive-bulk completes it to an egg-bulk.
The Gemara presents the dilemma: since it combines for impurity, is he also liable for Shabbat, or do we require a fig-bulk for Shabbat?
Rav Nachman responds: you have already learned it (from a Mishnah).
Abba Shaul states that the two loaves and the showbread have a measure of a fig-bulk.
The Gemara questions why this is relevant, asking: should we say that since for impurity...

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's shiurim
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's shiurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah (91a) uses a k'zayit for carrying on Shabbat, comparing it to the laws of piggul where a k'zayit is the measure for disqualification. It distinguishes between the two: in piggul, the offering is disqualified when taken outside the Temple courtyard, while on Shabbat, liability only occurs when taken into the public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah uses a k'zayit for Shabbat carrying, and distinguishes between piggul (disqualified when taken outside the courtyard) and Shabbat (liable only when taken into the public domain).

items.text: Abaye's explanation of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states that if one reinserts the object, he is only liable for its original measure. Abaye explains that the case involves throwing the object into a storeroom where its place is recognizable. The Mishnah teaches that since he threw it into the storeroom, he has nullified its original placement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's statement that one who re-enters is only liable for the original shiur is obvious.

Abaye explains that the case involves throwing the item into a storage area where its place is recognizable, and the Mishnah teaches that since he threw it into storage, he has nullified its original placement.

items.text: Mishnah: Carrying food to the threshold
items.text_en: Mishnah: Carrying food to the threshold
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one carries food and places it on the threshold (אסקופה), whether he or another later takes it out, he is exempt because he did not complete the act in one action. Similarly, if a basket full of fruit is placed on the outer threshold, even if most fruit is outside, he is exempt until he removes the entire basket.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who places food on a threshold and then another takes it out is exempt, and similarly a basket of produce on the outer threshold is exempt unless the entire basket is taken out.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the threshold's status
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the threshold's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the nature of the threshold (אסקופה). If it is a public domain, why is he exempt? If it is a private domain, why is he exempt? It concludes that the threshold is a karmelit, and the Mishnah teaches that only if the object rests in a karmelit is he exempt; otherwise, he is liable. This Mishnah disagrees with ben Azzai, who holds that carrying from a store to a colonnade via a stoa is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the status of the threshold (אסקופה), first considering it a public domain and then a private domain, and rejecting both because the Mishnah's exemption would be inconsistent.
The Gemara resolves that the threshold is a karmelit (כרמלית), and the Mishnah teaches that only if the object rests in a karmelit is he exempt; otherwise, he is liable.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with ben Azzai, who holds that carrying from a store to a colonnade via a stoa is exempt.

items.text: Dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan on 'אגד כלי'
items.text_en: Dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan on 'אגד כלי'
items.desc_en: Chizkiya says the Mishnah's ruling about the basket applies only to a basket full of cucumbers and gourds, but if full of mustard seeds, he is liable, because 'אגד כלי' (the container's binding) is not considered a binding. Rabbi Yochanan says even if full of mustard seeds, he is exempt, because 'אגד כלי' is considered a binding.

sub.desc_en: Hezekiah states that the Mishnah's exemption applies only to a basket of cucumbers and gourds, but a basket of mustard seeds is liable because the binding of the vessel is not considered a binding.
Rabbi Yochanan says that even a basket of mustard seeds is exempt, because the binding of the vessel is considered a binding.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's proof that the Mishnah contradicts both opinions
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's proof that the Mishnah contradicts both opinions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira argues that the Mishnah's wording supports neither Chizkiya nor Rabbi Yochanan. The phrase 'until he removes the entire basket' implies that if all the fruit is outside, he is exempt, supporting Rabbi Yochanan. But the phrase 'even though most fruit is outside' implies that if all fruit is outside, he is liable, supporting Chizkiya.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira argues that the Mishnah supports neither Hezekiah nor Rabbi Yochanan: the phrase 'until he takes out the entire basket' implies that the binding of the vessel is considered a binding (against Hezekiah), while 'even though most produce is outside' implies that the binding is not considered a binding (against Rabbi Yochanan).

items.text: Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan reconcile the Mishnah with their views
items.text_en: Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan reconcile the Mishnah with their views
items.desc_en: Chizkiya explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'until he removes the entire basket' applies only to a basket of cucumbers and gourds, but for mustard seeds, it is as if he removed the entire basket, and he is liable. Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'even though most fruit is outside' includes even all fruit, and he is exempt until he removes the entire basket.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Hezekiah and Rabbi Yochanan each reconcile the Mishnah with their own positions: Hezekiah limits the Mishnah to cucumbers and gourds, while Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'even though most produce is outside' to include even all produce being outside.

Chizkiya explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'until he removes the entire basket' applies only to a basket of cucumbers and gourds, but for mustard seeds, it is as if he removed the entire basket, and he is liable.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'even though most fruit is outside' includes even all fruit, and he is exempt until he removes the entire basket.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita of the peddler's basket
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita of the peddler's basket
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought: one who carries a peddler's basket and places it on the outer threshold, even if most types are outside, is exempt until he removes the entire basket. The Gemara initially assumes this refers to tied bundles (צררי), which challenges Chizkiya. Chizkiya answers that it deals with large baskets (אורנאסי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a peddler's basket: even though most types are outside, one is exempt until the entire basket is taken out, which seems to contradict Hezekiah's position.
Hezekiah answers that the baraita deals with large containers (אורנסאי) where the items are not bound together, so it does not contradict his view.
Chizkiya answers that the baraita deals with large baskets (אורנאסי), not tied bundles, thus resolving the challenge.

items.text: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's challenge from the thief's case
items.text_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's challenge from the thief's case
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye challenges: if one steals a purse on Shabbat, he is liable because the prohibition of theft precedes Shabbat. But if he drags it out, he is exempt because both prohibitions occur simultaneously. If 'אגד כלי' is considered a binding, then the theft prohibition should precede Shabbat. The Gemara answers that the case is where he removes it through the bottom of the purse, not through its opening, so the container does not bind the contents.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye challenges: if one steals a purse on Shabbat, he is liable because the theft prohibition precedes Shabbat; but if he drags it out, both prohibitions arise simultaneously. If 'אגד כלי' is considered a binding, then the theft prohibition should precede Shabbat, contradicting the exemption.
The Gemara answers that the case is where he removes the purse through its bottom (שוליו), not through its opening (פיו), so the container does not bind the contents.

items.text: Resolving the difficulty about the basket with holes
items.text_en: Resolving the difficulty about the basket with holes
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an earlier difficulty about a basket with holes (שינצין) that allows one to extract fruit without being considered 'removing from the basket'. It offers two answers: either there are no holes, or if there are, they are wrapped around the basket so the fruit is not inside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty about the basket with holes (שינצין) by offering two alternative answers: either there are no holes, or if there are, the fruit is wrapped around the basket so it is not considered inside.

items.text: Dispute between Rava and Abaye on אגד כלי
items.text_en: Dispute between Rava and Abaye on אגד כלי
items.desc_en: Rava says that if the vessel is full of mustard (small items that can slip through), one is liable, because the vessel does not form a unified 'bundle' (אגד). Abaye says even then one is exempt, because the vessel itself constitutes a bundle. The Gemara notes that each Sage reversed his previous stance.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah's exemption applies only to a basket full of cucumbers and gourds, but if it is full of mustard (small items that slip through), one is liable, because the vessel does not form a unified bundle (אגד).
Abaye argues that even if the basket is full of mustard, one is exempt, because the vessel itself constitutes a bundle (אגד).
The Gemara notes that each Sage reversed his previous stance, creating an apparent contradiction within each Sage's own views.

items.text: Explicit dispute about carrying by hand vs. vessel
items.text_en: Explicit dispute about carrying by hand vs. vessel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a known dispute: Abaye says carrying fruit by hand makes one liable, but in a vessel exempt; Rava says the opposite — by hand exempt, in vessel liable. This is the background to their reversal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the explicit dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding carrying fruit by hand versus in a vessel.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah about the poor man
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah about the poor man
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's view (hand liable) from a Mishnah where the householder extends his hand outside, and the poor man takes from it — both are exempt. The answer: there the hand is above three handbreadths (a different domain).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's position that carrying in the hand is liable, citing a Mishnah where both the householder and the poor man are exempt when the hand is extended outside.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the Mishnah's case (hand above three handbreadths, a different domain) from Abaye's case (hand below three handbreadths).

items.text: Mishnah: Standard vs. unusual ways of carrying
items.text_en: Mishnah: Standard vs. unusual ways of carrying
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates which modes of carrying are normal (like in one's hand, on a shoulder) and therefore liable, and which are unusual (behind the hand, on foot, etc.) and exempt, because they are not the way of carriers (בני קהת).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists normal carrying modes (hand, chest, shoulder) that incur liability, and unusual modes (behind hand, foot, mouth, etc.) that are exempt, because they are not the way of carriers (בני קהת).

items.text: Gemara: Source for carrying above ten handbreadths
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for carrying above ten handbreadths
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives that carrying above ten handbreadths is a legitimate method (and thus liable) from the Levites' carrying of the Mishkan. The Gemara calculates the height from the boards (ten cubits), and the fact that the poles were attached one-third from the top, making the burden higher than ten handbreadths. An alternative derivation is from the Ark (nine cubits plus one for the lid, also ten). A potential derivation from Moses is rejected because Moses had exceptional height.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who carries a burden above ten handbreadths is liable, deriving this from the Levites' carrying of the Mishkan, and the Gemara explains the derivation by equating the height of the altar to the Mishkan's ten cubits.

The Gemara calculates the height of the Levites as ten cubits from the boards and the tent spread, and notes that a burden carried on poles is lifted one-third from the top, so the burden was above ten handbreadths.
An alternative derivation is offered from the Ark, which was nine cubits plus a one-tefach lid, totaling ten, and the poles lifted it above ten handbreadths.
The Gemara objects that one could derive from Moses, but rejects this because Moses was exceptional in height, as the Shekhinah only rests on a wise, mighty, wealthy, and tall person.

items.text: Carrying on one's head: dispute and resolution
items.text_en: Carrying on one's head: dispute and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav cites Rabbi Chiyya that carrying on one's head makes one liable, as the people of Hutzal do. The Gemara objects that Hutzal is not the majority of the world. It then corrects: 'one of the people of Hutzal' — but then his own city's practice might not be universal. Finally, it concludes that carrying on one's head is exempt (since it is not the ordinary way).

sub.desc_en: Rav cites Rabbi Chiyya that carrying a load on one's head on Shabbat makes one liable, because the people of Hutzal do so.
The Gemara objects that the people of Hutzal are not the majority of the world, so their practice cannot define the standard.
The Gemara corrects the citation: Rav said 'one of the people of Hutzal' who carries on his head is liable because his townspeople do so.
The Gemara objects that even if his townspeople do so, his individual practice should be nullified relative to the general custom of all people.
The Gemara resolves that the correct version is that carrying a load on one's head is exempt, because it is not the ordinary way of carrying.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if the people of Hutzal did this, their opinion is disregarded by everyone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even if the people of Hutzal acted this way, their opinion is disregarded by everyone.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of one who intends to carry in front but it ends up behind, and vice versa, with the ruling that a woman wearing a girdle is liable in both directions. Rabbi Yehuda adds those who receive documents.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who intends to carry an object in front of him but it ends up behind him is exempt.
The Mishnah states that one who intends to carry behind him but it ends up in front is liable.
The Mishnah states that a woman who girds herself with a sash is liable whether she carries in front or behind.
The Mishnah explains the reason: the sash is suitable to be turned around.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that even those who receive slips of paper are liable.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the distinction between the two cases, initially suggesting a contradiction. Rabbi Elazar says the Mishnah was taught by different Tannaim. Rava offers an alternative explanation based on quality of guarding. Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by explaining the Mishnah uses a 'not only' style.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah distinguishes between the two cases, since in both the person's intention was not fulfilled.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the Mishnah is inconsistent because it was taught by different Tannaim.

Rava offers an alternative explanation based on the quality of guarding: one who intended a high standard of guarding but achieved a low standard is exempt, while one who intended a low standard but achieved a high standard is liable.

The Gemara refines the question: the internal logic of the Mishnah's phrasing suggests a contradiction between the first clause and the second clause regarding the case of 'to his back and it came to his back'.
Rabbi Elazar again asserts that the Mishnah is inconsistent because it was taught by different Tannaim.

Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah uses a 'not only' style, teaching that even in the case of 'to his back and it came to his front' one is liable, because one intended a low standard of guarding and achieved a high standard.

items.text: Dispute regarding the case of 'behind and it came behind'
items.text_en: Dispute regarding the case of 'behind and it came behind'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case of 'behind and it came behind' is a dispute between Tannaim, as illustrated by a baraita about one who carries money in a pouch. Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages debate whether it is analogous to 'behind and came behind' or 'after his hand and foot'. The Gemara concludes that all agree on the basic cases, and the dispute is only about the pouch with its opening downward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara declares that the case of 'behind and it came behind' is a dispute between Tannaim.

A baraita is cited: one who carries money in a pouch with its opening upward is liable; with its opening downward, Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable and the Sages exempt him, and they debate whether it is analogous to 'behind and came behind' or 'after his hand and foot'.

The Gemara analyzes the baraita's dialogue, noting that Rabbi Yehuda's question implies the Sages exempt in the 'behind and came behind' case, and their counter-question implies Rabbi Yehuda holds liable in the 'after his hand and foot' case, but a baraita states that all agree 'after his hand and foot' is exempt.

The Gemara resolves: all agree that 'behind and came behind' is liable and 'after his hand and foot' is exempt; the dispute is only about the pouch with its opening downward, which one Sage compares to 'behind and came behind' and the other to 'after his hand and foot'.

items.text: Explanation of the Mishnah's phrase 'In truth'
items.text_en: Explanation of the Mishnah's phrase 'In truth'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that whenever the Mishnah says 'In truth', it is a halakha. A baraita explains that the woman's girdle is like the scribes of the kingdom who do so.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the term 'באמת' (truly) in the Mishnah indicates a halachic ruling.
