A baraita supports the Mishnah's reason: royal scribes do this (gird themselves with a sash to carry items).
A baraita explains that the woman's girdle is like the scribes of the kingdom who do so.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Carrying a loaf jointly
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Carrying a loaf jointly
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who carries a loaf into the public domain is liable, but if two carry it they are exempt unless one could not do it alone, in which case they are liable, though Rabbi Shimon exempts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who carries a loaf into the public domain is liable.
The Mishnah states that if two carry it out, they are exempt.
The Mishnah states that if one cannot carry it alone and two carry it, they are liable.
The Mishnah adds that Rabbi Shimon exempts even in the last case.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of joint carrying
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of joint carrying
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, or Abaye, or a baraita, explains the dispute: when both can carry alone, Rabbi Meir holds them liable, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon exempt; when neither can, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir hold them liable, Rabbi Shimon exempt; when one can and the other cannot, all agree they are liable. A baraita supports this, deriving from the verse 'ba'asotah' that one who does the entire act is liable, not one who does part.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav / Abaye / baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav / Abaye / baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav (or Abaye or a baraita) states the three-case dispute between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon regarding joint carrying.
A baraita supports the previous statement, citing the verse 'בַּעֲשֹׂתָהּ' (when it is done) to derive that one who does the entire act is liable, not one who does part of it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about joint carrying
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about joint carrying
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that if one person cannot carry an object alone and two carry it, they are liable; otherwise exempt. Rabbi Shimon holds they are always exempt, deriving from the verse that an individual who does it is liable, but two who do it are exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about joint carrying: Rabbi Yehuda holds liability depends on whether one person could carry the object alone, while Rabbi Shimon holds two are always exempt, citing the verse 'בַּעֲשֹׂתָהּ' (in its doing) to exclude joint action.

items.text: Gemara analysis: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara analysis: Scriptural basis for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the verse 'when she does it' as the source. Rabbi Shimon sees three exclusions: one who uproots while another places, one who can and one who can, one who cannot and one who cannot. Rabbi Yehuda uses the third exclusion for an individual acting on court instruction, but Rabbi Shimon holds that such an individual is liable. Rabbi Meir sees only two exclusions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what scriptural basis underlies the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Shimon holds that the verse contains three exclusionary terms, exempting cases where one lifts and another places, where each is capable alone, and where neither is capable alone.
Rabbi Yehuda uses the third exclusion for an individual who acts on a court ruling, exempting him, while Rabbi Shimon holds such an individual liable.
Rabbi Shimon states that an individual who sins based on a court ruling is liable, not exempt.
Rabbi Meir argues that only two exclusionary terms are written, used to exempt the case of one lifting and another placing, and an individual acting on a court ruling.

items.text: Question about one who can and one who cannot
items.text_en: Question about one who can and one who cannot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: when one can carry and one cannot, who is liable? Rav Chisda says the one who can, because the one who cannot does nothing. Rav Hamnuna objects that the weak one assists (mesayei'a). Rav Chisda retorts that assistance has no substance (ein bo mamash).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In the case where one can carry and one cannot, which of them is liable?
Rav Chisda answers: The one who can carry is liable, because the one who cannot does nothing of substance.
Rav Hamnuna objects: The one who cannot carry is assisting (מסייע) the other, so he is doing something.
Rav Chisda rejects the objection, stating that assistance (מסייע) has no substance (אין בו ממש).

items.text: Proof from the mishnah of the bed and cloths
items.text_en: Proof from the mishnah of the bed and cloths
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid quotes Rava: a mishnah about a bed on four cloths — if the bed cannot stand on three legs, the cloths are impure (they bear weight); if it can, they are pure, even though they assist each other. This supports the principle that assistance has no substance.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid cites a baraita about a bed and four cloths to support Rav Chisda's principle that assistance has no substance.

items.text: Objection and defense from bed/baggage and zav cases
items.text_en: Objection and defense from bed/baggage and zav cases
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta objects: the case is different because the bed constantly shifts weight, potentially rendering cloths impure like a zav who rolls on couches. But the Gemara rejects this, citing a zav case where uncertainty renders them impure. Ultimately it reaffirms that assistance has no substance, concluding with Rav Papi's citation of Rava.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda of Diskarta objects that assistance (מסייע) does have substance, and distinguishes the bed case because the bed shifts weight entirely, but then raises the counterexample of a zav rolling on couches where uncertainty renders them impure.
The Gemara rejects the objection, concluding that the reason is because we say assistance (מסייע) has no substance, and then cites Rav Papi in the name of Rava who supports this with a baraita.

items.text: Proof from Mishnayot that 'mesayei'a ein bo mamash'
items.text_en: Proof from Mishnayot that 'mesayei'a ein bo mamash'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yossi's ruling about a horse and donkey is not considered 'assistance' (mesayei'a), and then proves from three sources (Rabbi Eliezer's ruling, the case of receiving with right hand assisted by left, and the earlier Mishnah) that assistance has no legal substance.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yossi's ruling that a horse conveys impurity through its forelegs and a donkey through its hind legs.
The baraita presents Rabbi Yossi's position: a horse transmits impurity through its forelegs and a donkey through its hind legs, because a horse leans on its forelegs and a donkey on its hind legs.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yossi's ruling is not considered a case of mutual assistance (מסייע), which should affect the impurity status.
The Gemara objects: why does the leaning matter — the two legs are supporting each other!
The Gemara answers that this is because we say that assistance (מסייע) has no legal substance (אין בו ממש).
The Gemara resolves: it must be because we say that 'assistance' (מסייע) has no substance — hence the leaning leg's support is negligible.
Rav Ashi cites a baraita about Rabbi Eliezer's ruling regarding a priest standing on one foot, which also assumes that assistance has no substance.

Rav Ashi cites a baraita (on sacrificial service) where Rabbi Eliezer rules: if the priest places one foot on a vessel and one on the ground, we consider whether he could stand on one foot if the vessel were removed — showing that assistance (מסייע) is disregarded.
The Gemara again questions why this is not considered assistance.
Ravina cites a baraita: if the priest received (blood) with his right hand while his left hand assists him, the service is valid — confirming that assistance has no substance.
The Gemara confirms the principle: even though the left hand assists, the service is valid, so we infer conclusively that 'assistance has no substance.'
The Gemara repeats the principle that assistance has no legal substance.
Ravina cites a baraita about receiving with the right hand assisted by the left, which also demonstrates that assistance has no substance.
The Gemara questions this case as well.
The Gemara concludes that this too proves the principle.
The Gemara concludes that the principle is established: assistance has no legal substance.

items.text: Dispute over shiur for multiple actors: individual or combined
items.text_en: Dispute over shiur for multiple actors: individual or combined
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about whether multiple people performing a forbidden act together each need a full shiur, or one combined shiur suffices. Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna disagree, and Rav Pappa cites a proof from a Mishnah about a bed with four cloths under its legs, showing that a single shiur suffices for all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that when each person is individually capable, Rabbi Meir holds them liable.
The Gemara raises a question: do we require a full shiur for each person individually, or is one combined shiur sufficient for all?

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna's dispute
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna disagree: one requires a full shiur for each, the other says one shiur suffices for all.

sub.text: Rav Pappa citing Rava's proof from a Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa citing Rava's proof from a Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a Mishnah about a bed with four cloths under its legs, showing that one combined shiur suffices for all.

items.text: Further proofs for a single shiur from cases of trapping and theft
items.text_en: Further proofs for a single shiur from cases of trapping and theft
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Ravina bring additional proofs from Mishnayot: a deer trapped by two people, and partners who stole and slaughtered, showing that a single shiur applies to all participants, not individual shiurim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a Mishnah about a deer trapped by two people to prove that a single shiur applies to all participants, not individual shiurim.
Ravina adds a proof from a Mishnah about partners who stole and slaughtered, showing that a single shiur applies to all.

items.text: Proof from a weaver's reed and its rejection
items.text_en: Proof from a weaver's reed and its rejection
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a proof from a Mishnah about two people carrying out a weaver's reed, but Rav Acha bar Rava challenges it, suggesting the reed might contain sufficient material for each to weave a cloth, thus not proving the point. The Gemara concludes this proof is inconclusive.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a Mishnah about two people carrying out a weaver's reed, arguing that they are liable, implying a single measure suffices for all.
Rav Acha bar Rava objects that the reed might contain enough material for each to weave a cloth, so the proof is inconclusive.

items.text: Correction of a Tanna's statement about the weaver's reed
items.text_en: Correction of a Tanna's statement about the weaver's reed
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Nachman that two people carrying a weaver's reed are exempt, and Rabbi Shimon holds them liable. Rav Nachman corrects the statement, saying the correct version is that they are liable, and Rabbi Shimon exempts them.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Nachman that two people carrying a weaver's reed are exempt, and Rabbi Shimon holds them liable.
Rav Nachman objects that the Tanna's version is backwards (כְּלַפֵּי לְיָיא — against the prevailing view).
Rav Nachman corrects the statement: the correct version is that they are liable, and Rabbi Shimon exempts them.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on carrying food in a vessel and the principle of 'tafel'
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on carrying food in a vessel and the principle of 'tafel'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses carrying less than a shiur of food in a vessel, where the vessel is secondary (tafel) to the food, and the case of a live person in a bed versus a corpse. The Gemara begins to analyze the Mishnah, questioning whether one who carries two olive-sized portions of forbidden fat in one lapse is liable for two, and Rav Sheshet clarifies the context.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of carrying food less than a shiur in a vessel (exempt for vessel), carrying a living person in a bed (exempt for bed), carrying a corpse in a bed (liable), and other standard shiur items (liable except Rabbi Shimon who exempts).
A baraita of the Sages clarifies: one who carries food of standard shiur in a vessel is liable for the food but exempt for the vessel, unless he needs the vessel itself.

The Gemara infers: if one eats two olive-sized portions of forbidden fat (חלב) in one lapse of awareness, he is liable for two sin-offerings — suggesting the vessel is secondary and does not combine the portions.
Rav Sheshet answers: we are dealing here with a case where the food is less than a shiur but the vessel is significant, so the vessel is not secondary.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the mishnah's case
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves an apparent contradiction in the mishnah by explaining that the case involves forgetfulness regarding both the food and the vessel, with intermittent awareness, and ties it to a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the mishnah explicitly says 'even on the vessel,' contradicting the proposed distinction.
Rav Ashi resolves that the case involves forgetfulness about both food and vessel with intermittent awareness, tying it to the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

items.text: Analysis of the mishnah: 'one who carries a living being on a bed'
items.text_en: Analysis of the mishnah: 'one who carries a living being on a bed'
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah's ruling that one is exempt for carrying a living being on a bed aligns with Rabbi Natan, who holds that a living being carries itself. Rava defends the Rabbis, arguing that they only disagree with Rabbi Natan regarding animals that fidget, but they agree regarding a living person who carries himself.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks whether the mishnah's ruling that one is exempt for a live animal on a bed reflects only Rabbi Nathan's view, not the Rabbis'.
A baraita is cited: one who carries an animal (live or slaughtered) into the public domain is liable, but Rabbi Nathan exempts for live animals because they carry themselves.
Rava answers that even the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Nathan regarding a live human who carries himself, differing only on animals that fidget.

items.text: Challenge from Ben Beteira's ruling about a horse
items.text_en: Challenge from Ben Beteira's ruling about a horse
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges Rava's distinction by citing a baraita where Ben Beteira permits carrying a horse, and Rabbi Yochanan equates Ben Beteira with Rabbi Natan. If the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Natan regarding a person, why is the case of a horse attributed specifically to Ben Beteira and Rabbi Natan? The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan refers to a horse designated for bird-hunting, which does not carry itself.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's objection to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's objection to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah objects to Rava by citing the mishnah where Ben Beteira permits a horse, and Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Ben Beteira and Rabbi Nathan said the same thing.

Rav Adda bar Ahavah elaborates: a baraita states Ben Beteira permits a horse because it performs a labor for which one is not liable for a sin-offering, and Rabbi Yochanan equates Ben Beteira and Rabbi Nathan.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah argues: if the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Nathan on humans, why does Rabbi Yochanan specifically link Ben Beteira and Rabbi Nathan, since even the Rabbis would concede?
Rava answers that Rabbi Yochanan's statement refers specifically to a horse designated for bird-hunting, which fidgets like an animal.
The gemara questions whether such a horse exists, and answers that there is one in the Bei Ziyarin region.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's qualification: Rabbi Natan agrees regarding a bound animal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's qualification: Rabbi Natan agrees regarding a bound animal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Natan agrees that a bound animal does not carry itself. Rav Adda bar Matna challenges this by noting that Persian horses appear bound, yet Rabbi Yochanan still equated Ben Beteira and Rabbi Natan. The Gemara resolves that the Persians' horses are merely spirited, not truly bound.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Nathan concedes liability when the animal is bound.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Mattana's objection to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana's objection to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana objects to Abaye: Persian horses appear bound, yet Rabbi Yochanan equated Ben Beteira and Rabbi Nathan, implying exemption.
Abaye answers that there, the horse's spirit holds it, as illustrated by a story of a groom who ran three parasangs on foot when the king was angry with him.

items.text: Beginning of the discussion on carrying a corpse
items.text_en: Beginning of the discussion on carrying a corpse
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who carries a corpse on a bed is liable, and similarly for an olive's bulk of a corpse. The Gemara begins to cite a statement from Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding Rabbi Shimon's opinion on this matter.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Yosef in the name of Reish Lakish, state that Rabbi Shimon would exempt one who carries a corpse on a bed.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana / Rav Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana / Rav Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Yosef in the name of Reish Lakish, report that Rabbi Shimon would exempt one who carries a corpse on a bed.

items.text: Rava's statement on Rabbi Shimon's liability for melacha she'eina tzricha l'gufah
items.text_en: Rava's statement on Rabbi Shimon's liability for melacha she'eina tzricha l'gufah
items.desc_en: Rava asserts that Rabbi Shimon agrees one is liable for actions like using mortar to dig or a Torah scroll to read, even though these are melacha she'eina tzricha l'gufah. The Gemara questions how to find a case where Rabbi Shimon would hold liable for melacha she'tzricha l'gufah, and clarifies that the statement precludes the notion that only actions with dual purpose (e.g., mortar for a plate and digging) are liable.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak permits moving a corpse to a karmelit for burial
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak permits moving a corpse to a karmelit for burial
items.desc_en: A corpse was in a drokeret (a narrow alley), and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak permitted moving it to a karmelit. Rabbi Yochanan's brother questioned whether this follows Rabbi Shimon's lenient view, noting that even if exempt from a chatat, there is still a rabbinic prohibition. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak retorts that even according to Rabbi Yehuda it is permitted, because kavod habriyot (human dignity) overrides a negative commandment.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet on removing tumah signs
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet on removing tumah signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: if one removes one of two signs of tumah, he is liable; if one of three, Rav Nachman says liable (since his action is effective, as removing one leaves the tumah dependent on the others), while Rav Sheshet says exempt (since the tumah still remains).

items.text: Rav Sheshet's proof from a baraita about half an olive's worth
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's proof from a baraita about half an olive's worth
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet brings a proof from a mishna and a baraita: a half-olive from a corpse is exempt, but a baraita says liable. He resolves that the baraita refers to removing a half-olive from a full olive (effective), while the mishna refers to removing a half-olive from an olive and a half (ineffective). Rav Nachman counters that both are liable, and the mishna's 'exempt' refers to removing a half-olive from a large corpse.

items.text: Mishnah: Nail-cutting, hair-removal, and cosmetic actions on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Nail-cutting, hair-removal, and cosmetic actions on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists actions: cutting nails with hands or teeth, removing hair, mustache, beard, and women's cosmetic actions (plaiting, applying kohl, curling hair). Rabbi Eliezer holds one liable, while the Sages prohibit only as shevut (rabbinic decree).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar limits the dispute to using hands, not a tool
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar limits the dispute to using hands, not a tool
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that the dispute (between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages) applies only when using hands; but with a tool, all agree one is liable. The Gemara notes this is obvious from the mishnah's wording 'zo bazo', but clarifies that it precludes the notion that the Sages exempt even with a tool.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar limits the dispute to one's own nails, not another's
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar limits the dispute to one's own nails, not another's
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar further states that the dispute applies only to one's own nails; but for another person, all agree one is exempt. The Gemara notes this is obvious from the mishnah's wording 'tzipornav', but clarifies that it precludes the notion that Rabbi Eliezer holds liable even for another's nails.

items.text: The measure of 'full of the tweezers' and a contradiction resolved
items.text_en: The measure of 'full of the tweezers' and a contradiction resolved
items.desc_en: A baraita states that removing a 'full of the tweezers' of hair is liable. Rav Yehuda says this measure is two hairs. The Gemara notes a contradiction with another baraita that says 'for a bald spot, two', and resolves by emending to 'and similarly for a bald spot, two'.

items.text: Baraita on the measure and Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on plucking white hairs
items.text_en: Baraita on the measure and Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on plucking white hairs
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the measure of two hairs for liability. Rabbi Eliezer says one hair suffices, and the Sages agree with him when plucking white hairs from black ones, where even one is liable. This is also prohibited on weekdays due to the prohibition of cross-dressing.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling on a mostly detached nail or hair
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling on a mostly detached nail or hair
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules: if most of a nail or hair is detached, using hands is permitted ab initio, but with a tool one is liable for a chatat. The Gemara questions how a tool could be liable while hands are permitted, and reinterprets: if mostly detached, hands are permitted, tool is prohibited but exempt; if not mostly detached, hands are prohibited but exempt, tool is liable. Rav Yehuda rules like him, and Rabbi Yochanan adds that this applies only if they grow upward and cause pain.

items.text: The rationale for women's cosmetic actions: plaiting, kohl, curling
items.text_en: The rationale for women's cosmetic actions: plaiting, kohl, curling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why women who plait, apply kohl, or curl hair are liable. Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina says: plaiting is like weaving, kohl is like writing, curling is like spinning. The Sages object that these are not the usual methods of those melachot. Rabbi Avahu then says he received a different explanation from Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina.

items.text: Mishnah: Plaiting, painting, and building
items.text_en: Mishnah: Plaiting, painting, and building
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists actions that are prohibited on Shabbat: applying eye-paint (due to dyeing), plaiting hair and curling it (due to building). It cites Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's derivation from the creation of Eve that plaiting is a form of building. A baraita by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that doing these for oneself is exempt, but for another is liable, and prohibits a woman from applying rouge.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three prohibited actions on Shabbat: applying eye-paint (due to dyeing), plaiting hair, and curling it (due to building).
The Gemara questions how plaiting hair can be considered a form of building.
The Gemara answers yes, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's derivation from the creation of Eve that plaiting is called building in coastal cities.
A baraita by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that doing these actions for oneself is exempt, but for another is liable, and prohibits a woman from applying rouge due to dyeing.

items.text: Baraita: Milking, churning, and cheese-making
items.text_en: Baraita: Milking, churning, and cheese-making
items.desc_en: A baraita lists actions that are liable for a sin-offering on Shabbat: milking, churning, and cheese-making (each to the size of a dried fig), as well as sweeping, sprinkling, and removing honeycombs. Rabbi Eliezer holds that if done intentionally on a Festival, one receives lashes; the Sages say all are merely forbidden rabbinically.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing three prohibited labors on Shabbat: milking, churning, and cheese-making, each liable for a sin-offering when performed to the size of a dried fig.
The baraita adds three more actions liable for a sin-offering on Shabbat: sweeping, sprinkling, and removing honeycombs.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that if one intentionally performs these actions on a Festival, he receives lashes.
The Sages disagree and hold that all these actions are merely prohibited rabbinically (שבות), not Torah violations.

items.text: Gemara: The underlying categories for milking, churning, and cheese-making
items.text_en: Gemara: The underlying categories for milking, churning, and cheese-making
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Gurya is asked why each action is liable. He gives tautological answers, and is mocked. The academy later explains: milking is liable due to separating (מפרק), churning due to selecting (בורר), and cheese-making due to building (בונה).

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rav Nachman bar Gurya arrived in Neharde'a and was asked why milking is liable on Shabbat.
Rav Nachman bar Gurya gives tautological answers for milking, churning, and cheese-making, each time saying the liability is due to the action itself.
The questioners mock Rav Nachman bar Gurya, saying his teacher must have been a reed-cutter in the swamp (i.e., ignorant).
Rav Nachman bar Gurya asks the academy, which explains that milking is liable due to separating (מפרק), churning due to selecting (בורר), and cheese-making due to building (בונה).

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Eliezer's reason for honeycombs
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Eliezer's reason for honeycombs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: just as one who detaches from a forest on Shabbat is liable, so too one who removes honeycombs is liable, based on the verse 'and he dipped it in the forest of honey'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for the liability of one who removes honeycombs on Shabbat.

Rabbi Elazar explains the analogy: just as one who detaches from a forest on Shabbat is liable, so too one who removes honeycombs is liable, based on the verse 'and he dipped it in the forest of honey'.

items.text: Gemara: Sprinkling water on Shabbat
items.text_en: Gemara: Sprinkling water on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Amemar permits sprinkling in Machoza because there are no pits. Rava Tosfa'ah (or Mar Kashisha) finds Rav Ashi suffering from heat and cites a baraita: one may wash hands and feet in different corners, and the house becomes sprinkled incidentally. Rav Ashi says he was unaware of this.

sub.desc_en: Amemar permits sprinkling water (זילחא) in Machoza on Shabbat, reasoning that the rabbinic prohibition was only due to concern for creating pits, which does not apply there.

sub.text: Rava Tosfa'ah (or Mar Kashisha) citing a baraita
sub.text_en: Rava Tosfa'ah (or Mar Kashisha) citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rava Tosfa'ah (or Mar Kashisha) finds Rav Ashi suffering from heat and cites a baraita that permits washing hands and feet in different corners, causing the house to become sprinkled incidentally.
Rav Ashi responds that he was unaware of this baraita, implying he now accepts the leniency.

items.text: Gemara: A wise woman may sprinkle
items.text_en: Gemara: A wise woman may sprinkle
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a wise woman may sprinkle her house on Shabbat. Now that we hold like Rabbi Shimon, it is permitted even ab initio.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that a wise woman may sprinkle her house on Shabbat.
The Gemara concludes that since we now hold like Rabbi Shimon, sprinkling is permitted even לכתחילה (ab initio).

items.text: Mishnah: Uprooting from a perforated pot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Uprooting from a perforated pot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one who uproots from a perforated pot is liable, from an unperforated pot is exempt. Rabbi Shimon exempts in both cases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first ruling: one who uproots from a perforated pot is liable, from an unperforated pot is exempt.
Rabbi Shimon exempts in both cases, whether the pot is perforated or not.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's position
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's position
items.desc_en: Abaye (or Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav) raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says Rabbi Shimon exempts for both, implying he treats a perforated pot as unperforated. Yet another source quotes Rabbi Shimon saying there is no difference between a perforated and unperforated pot.

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says Rabbi Shimon exempts for both, implying he treats a perforated pot as unperforated.
Abaye cites another source where Rabbi Shimon explicitly says there is no difference between a perforated and unperforated pot, contradicting the Mishnah's implication.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Shimon's view on earthenware vessels
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Shimon's view on earthenware vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon considers a perforated vessel as detached for all purposes, except for impurity regarding seeds, as the Torah expanded purity for seeds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon considers a perforated vessel as detached for all purposes, except for impurity regarding seeds, because the Torah expanded purity for seeds as per the verse 'על כל זרע זרוע אשר יזרע' (upon all seed that is sown).

items.text: Question about root-sized perforation
items.text_en: Question about root-sized perforation
items.desc_en: An elder asks Rabbi Zeira about Rabbi Shimon's ruling on a root-sized perforation opposite the hole. Rabbi Zeira remains silent, but later states that Rabbi Shimon concedes if the perforation is the size for purification, prompting the elder's surprise.

sub.desc_en: An elder asks Rabbi Zeira about Rabbi Shimon's ruling regarding a root-sized perforation opposite the hole in a clay vessel.
Rabbi Zeira remains silent and does not answer the elder.
Rabbi Zeira later states that Rabbi Shimon concedes if the perforation is the size required for purification.

The elder objects, expressing surprise that Rabbi Zeira would not answer the simpler question about a root-sized perforation but now addresses the more obvious case of a purification-sized perforation.

items.text: Abaye's correction of Rabbi Zeira's statement
items.text_en: Abaye's correction of Rabbi Zeira's statement
items.desc_en: Abaye suggests that if Rabbi Zeira's statement was reported, it was actually that Rabbi Shimon concedes if the vessel was perforated below a quarter-log.

sub.desc_en: Abaye clarifies that if Rabbi Zeira's statement was indeed reported, it was that Rabbi Shimon concedes when the vessel was perforated below a quarter-log.

items.text: Rava's five measures for earthenware vessels
items.text_en: Rava's five measures for earthenware vessels
items.desc_en: Rava enumerates five degrees of perforation in earthenware vessels: from the size of a liquid outlet (still fit for purification water), to a liquid inlet (still fit for seeds), to a small root (still fit for olives), to an olive outlet (still fit for pomegranates), to a pomegranate outlet (completely pure). If sealed with a tight lid, it remains pure until most is broken.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating there are five measures for earthenware vessels, beginning with the first: a perforation the size of a liquid outlet renders the vessel pure from being a purification water container but still fit for sanctifying purification water.
Rava states the second measure: a perforation the size of a liquid inlet renders the vessel pure from sanctifying purification water but still fit for preparing seeds.
Rava states the third measure: a perforation the size of a small root renders the vessel pure from preparing seeds but still fit for receiving olives.
Rava states the fourth measure: a perforation the size of an olive outlet renders the vessel pure from receiving olives but still fit for receiving pomegranates.
Rava states the fifth measure: a perforation the size of a pomegranate outlet renders the vessel completely pure.
Rava concludes that if the vessel is sealed with a tight lid (צָמִיד פָּתִיל), it remains pure until most of it is broken.

items.text: Rav Asi's tradition and Rava's clarification
items.text_en: Rav Asi's tradition and Rava's clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Asi reports a tradition that the measure for an earthenware vessel is the size of a pomegranate outlet. Rava questions whether this applies only to a vessel sealed with a tight lid, and resolves the apparent contradiction with his own ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi reports a tradition that the measure for an earthenware vessel's disqualification is the size of a pomegranate outlet.
Rava questions whether Rav Asi's tradition applies only to a vessel sealed with a tight lid (מוקף צמיד פתיל).
The gemara objects that Rava himself ruled that a sealed vessel is disqualified only when most of it is broken, not at the pomegranate outlet size.
The gemara resolves the contradiction, indicating that the two rulings are not in conflict.

items.text: Concluding discussion on earthenware vessel shiurim
items.text_en: Concluding discussion on earthenware vessel shiurim
items.desc_en: Rav Asi distinguishes between the shiur for earthenware vessels (כונס משקה) and the exception of גיסטרא. Ulla reports a dispute between two Amoraim in the West: one says the shiur is כמוציא רימון, the other says כשורש קטן. Rav Chinana bar Kahana cites Rabbi Eliezer that the shiur is כמוציא זיתים, and Mar Kashisha adds that such vessels are like כלי גללים etc., not susceptible to impurity, and for צמיד פתיל require a majority break.

sub.desc_en: The gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between large vessels (רברבי) and small vessels (זוטרי).
Rav Asi states that the general shiur for earthenware vessels is כונס משקה (holds liquid), and the exception of מוציא משקה (lets liquid out) applies only to a גיסטרא (broken vessel).
Mar Zutra explains the reason: one does not say 'bring a גיסטרא to another גיסטרא' (i.e., a broken vessel is not used to repair another broken vessel).
Ulla reports that two Amoraim in the West dispute: one says the shiur is כמוציא רימון (the size of an olive's exit), the other says כשורש קטן (the size of a small root).
The gemara provides a mnemonic: 'one who increases and one who decreases' (both are valid).

sub.text: Rav Chinana bar Kahana citing Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Kahana citing Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Kahana cites Rabbi Eliezer that the shiur for earthenware vessels is כמוציא זיתים (the size of an olive's exit).
Mar Kashisha adds in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that such vessels are like כלי גללים etc., not susceptible to impurity, and for צמיד פתיל require a majority break.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The phrase הדרן עלך המצניע marks the end of the chapter 'HaMatznia' and the transition to the next Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The phrase 'הדרן עלך המצניע' marks the end of the chapter 'HaMatznia' and the transition to the next Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Throwing between domains on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Throwing between domains on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that throwing from a private domain to a public domain or vice versa incurs liability. Rabbi Akiva holds one liable for throwing from one private domain to another with a public domain in between, while the Sages exempt. It gives examples: two balconies opposite each other in the public domain—passing or throwing is exempt; if they are on the same story, passing is liable but throwing is exempt, as was the Levites' service. Two wagons in the public domain—they may pass planks but not throw.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: throwing between private and public domains on Shabbat incurs liability, and records the dispute between Rabbi Akiva (liable) and the Sages (exempt) regarding throwing across a public domain between two private domains.

The Mishnah illustrates with two balconies opposite each other in the public domain: passing or throwing is exempt; if on the same story, passing is liable but throwing is exempt, as was the Levites' service.
The Mishnah gives a second example: two wagons in the public domain may pass planks to each other but may not throw.

items.text: Derivation of hotza'ah from the Torah
items.text_en: Derivation of hotza'ah from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the prohibition of hotza'ah (carrying out) is written in the Torah. Rabbi Yochanan answers via a gezeirah shavah on the word 'ha'avarah' from Yom Kippur, establishing that the command to 'pass a call through the camp' occurred on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since throwing is a derivative of carrying out, where is the prohibition of carrying out itself written in the Torah?

Rabbi Yochanan answers by citing the verse 'וַיְצַו מֹשֶׁה וַיַּעֲבִירוּ קוֹל בַּמַּחֲנֶה' (Moses commanded and they passed a call through the camp), explaining that Moses was in the Levite camp (a public domain) and told Israel not to carry from their private domain to the public domain.
The Gemara objects: how do we know this occurred on Shabbat? Perhaps it was on a weekday, because the work was completed.
The Gemara resolves by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'העברה' (passing) from Yom Kippur: just as there it is forbidden on that day, so here it is forbidden on Shabbat.

items.text: Distinction between av and toldah for hotza'ah and hachnasah
items.text_en: Distinction between av and toldah for hotza'ah and hachnasah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives hachnasah (carrying in) by logic, but notes that hotza'ah is an av (primary category) while hachnasah is a toldah (subcategory). The practical difference is that performing two avot or two toldot incurs two sin-offerings, but an av and its toldah incur only one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found a source for hotza'ah (carrying out), but from where do we derive hachnasah (carrying in)?
The Gemara answers that it is logical: since both involve transferring between domains, hotza'ah is an av (primary category) and hachnasah is a toldah (subcategory).
The Gemara asks: since one is liable for both, why call one av and the other toldah?
The Gemara resolves: the practical difference is that performing two avot or two toldot incurs two sin-offerings, but an av and its toldah incur only one.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's view on av and toldah
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's view on av and toldah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why, according to Rabbi Eliezer who holds one liable for a toldah in place of an av, we still call one 'av' and the other 'toldah'. Two answers are given: either the one that was significant in the Mishkan is called 'av', or the one explicitly written in the Torah is called 'av'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds one liable for a toldah (subcategory) in place of an av (primary category), why do we still call one 'av' and the other 'toldah'?
First answer: the one that was significant in the Mishkan (Tabernacle) is called 'av', and the one that was not significant in the Mishkan is not called 'av'.
Second answer: the one explicitly written in the Torah is called 'av', and the one not written is called 'toldah'.

items.text: Source for liability for throwing four cubits in the public domain
items.text_en: Source for liability for throwing four cubits in the public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the source for liability for throwing an object four cubits in the public domain. Rabbi Yoshiyah suggests it is derived from the weavers of the curtains who threw needles to each other, but this is rejected. Rav Chisda suggests they threw a shuttle, but this too is rejected. Ultimately, the Gemara concludes that the liability for carrying four cubits in the public domain is a halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about throwing four cubits at a wall, distinguishing between above and below ten handbreadths.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive liability for throwing four cubits in the public domain?
Rabbi Yoshiyah suggests that liability is derived from the weavers of the curtains who threw needles to each other, corrected to the sewers of the curtains.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the sewers sat close together, within four cubits, so no liability for throwing four cubits is proven.
Rav Chisda suggests that the weavers threw a shuttle (בוכיאר) into the curtain, and the Gemara clarifies it was thrown by the last weaver.
The Gemara objects: the shuttle travels in an exempt area (the curtain), and perhaps the weavers sat close together within a handbreadth.
The Gemara objects further: perhaps they passed the shuttle hand-to-hand, and cites the baraita of Lud that each worker does only his own work, not his fellow's.
The Gemara concludes that the liability for carrying four cubits in the public domain is a הלכה למשה מסיני (a law transmitted to Moses at Sinai).

items.text: The identity of the mekoshesh and the practical difference
items.text_en: The identity of the mekoshesh and the practical difference
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel says the mekoshesh (wood-gatherer) was liable for carrying four cubits in the public domain. A baraitha says he was liable for uprooting, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov says he was liable for gathering. The practical difference is for the principle of Rav: if one performs all 39 melachot in one lapse, he is liable only for one, but Rabbi Yochanan holds he is liable for each.

sub.text: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel states that the mekoshesh was liable for carrying four cubits in the public domain, while a baraitha says he was liable for uprooting, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov says he was liable for gathering.
The Gemara asks what practical difference emerges from these three positions.

The Gemara explains that the difference relates to Rav's principle that performing all 39 melachot in one lapse incurs only one liability, versus Rabbi Yochanan's view that each melacha incurs separate liability.
The Gemara objects that the text should read 'he is not liable for any of them' rather than 'he is liable only for one'.

The Gemara resolves that each authority is certain about his own position but uncertain about the others, so the practical difference is only for someone who holds one view as certain and another as uncertain.

items.text: The mekoshesh identified as Tzelafchad
items.text_en: The mekoshesh identified as Tzelafchad
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that the mekoshesh was Tzelafchad, as per Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira rebukes him, saying that if he is correct, the Torah concealed Tzelafchad's identity and Rabbi Akiva reveals it; if not, he slanders a righteous man.

sub.desc_en: The baraita identifies the mekoshesh as Tzelafchad, citing a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'במדבר' (in the wilderness) to connect the incident with the daughters of Tzelafchad, per Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira rebukes Rabbi Akiva, arguing that if his identification is correct, he reveals what the Torah concealed; if incorrect, he slanders a righteous man.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the source for the dispute about Aaron's leprosy
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the source for the dispute about Aaron's leprosy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation of the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira regarding whether Aaron was also stricken with leprosy. It rejects a gezeirah shavah and instead derives the matter from the word 'וַיַּעְפִּילוּ'. A beraita supports the view that Aaron was indeed stricken, based on the verse 'וַיִּפֶן אַהֲרֹן אֶל מִרְיָם וְהִנֵּה מְצֹרָעַת'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation of the dispute, suggesting a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy), but then rejects it.
The Gemara answers that the derivation is from the word 'וַיַּעְפִּילוּ' (they presumed).
Rabbi Akiva states that the verse 'וַיִּחַר אַף ה׳ בָּם' teaches that Aaron was also stricken with leprosy.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira objects, arguing that if Aaron was stricken, the Torah concealed it and Rabbi Akiva reveals it; if not, he slanders a righteous person.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that 'בָּם' refers only to a mild rebuke, not leprosy.
A baraita supports the view that Aaron was stricken, citing the verse 'וַיִּפֶן אַהֲרֹן אֶל מִרְיָם וְהִנֵּה מְצֹרָעַת' and explaining that he turned away from his own leprosy.

items.text: Resh Lakish's principle: one who suspects the innocent is punished bodily
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's principle: one who suspects the innocent is punished bodily
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that one who suspects innocent people is punished in his body, citing Moses who suspected Israel and was struck with leprosy. The Gemara elaborates that Israel are believers and sons of believers, while Moses would ultimately not believe, as shown by the incident at the waters of Meribah.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that one who suspects innocent people is punished bodily, citing Moses who suspected Israel and was struck with leprosy.
The Gemara elaborates that Israel are believers and sons of believers, while Moses would ultimately not believe, as shown by the incident at the waters of Meribah.

items.text: Rava's principle: good measure comes more quickly than punishment
items.text_en: Rava's principle: good measure comes more quickly than punishment
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina) notes that the attribute of good comes more swiftly than the attribute of punishment, as demonstrated by the verses regarding Moses' hand: the leprous hand was only shown after being taken out, but the healed hand was shown immediately upon being taken from his bosom.

sub.text: Rava (or Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.text_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina) states that the attribute of good (מִדָּה טוֹבָה) comes more swiftly than the attribute of punishment (מִדַּת פּוּרְעָנוּת), citing the verses about Moses' hand: the leprous hand appeared only after being taken out, while the healed hand returned immediately upon being taken from his bosom.

items.text: Miracle within a miracle and the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Miracle within a miracle and the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar comments on the verse 'וַיִּבְלַע מַטֵּה אַהֲרֹן אֶת מַטֹּתָם' that it was a miracle within a miracle. The Mishnah's case is then stated: throwing from one private domain to another private domain through a public domain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar comments on the verse that the swallowing of the staffs was a miracle within a miracle.
The Mishnah's case is stated: throwing from one private domain to another private domain through a public domain.

items.text: Rabbah's dilemma: the dispute is below ten handbreadths or above?
items.text_en: Rabbah's dilemma: the dispute is below ten handbreadths or above?
items.desc_en: Rabbah raises a dilemma: do Rabbi Akiva and the Sages dispute when the throw is below ten handbreadths, based on the principle of 'קלוטה כמי שהונחה', or above ten handbreadths, based on whether we derive throwing from passing? He presents both possibilities.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah raises the first possibility: the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages is when the throw is below ten handbreadths, disagreeing about whether we apply the principle of קלוטה כמי שהונחה (an object in airspace is considered at rest), but above ten handbreadths all agree one is exempt and we do not derive throwing from passing.

Rabbah raises the second possibility: the dispute is when the throw is above ten handbreadths, disagreeing about whether we derive throwing from passing, but below ten handbreadths all agree one is liable because an object in airspace is considered at rest.

items.text: Rav Yosef resolves the dilemma from Rav Chisda's tradition
items.text_en: Rav Yosef resolves the dilemma from Rav Chisda's tradition
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Rav Chisda had a dilemma which Rav Hamnuna resolved from a baraita: Rabbi Akiva and the Sages dispute regarding throwing through the public domain itself, implying the dispute is below ten handbreadths. The Gemara confirms this by analyzing the baraita and concluding that the dispute is about the principle of 'קלוטה כמי שהונחה'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Rav Chisda had a dilemma which Rav Hamnuna resolved from a baraita: the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages regarding throwing through the public domain itself implies they disagree below ten handbreadths.

The Gemara questions the baraita's context: if it refers to passing, why would passing above ten handbreadths be exempt, given Rabbi Elazar's ruling that carrying above ten handbreadths is liable like the Levites?

The Gemara concludes that the baraita must refer to throwing, and the dispute is below ten handbreadths, confirming that the disagreement is about the principle of 'קלוטה כמי שהונחה' (an object in airspace is considered at rest).

items.text: Disputing opinions: Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Chilkiya bar Tovi, and a beraita
items.text_en: Disputing opinions: Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Chilkiya bar Tovi, and a beraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar holds that Rabbi Akiva would even impose liability above ten handbreadths. Rabbi Chilkiya bar Tovi distinguishes: within three handbreadths all agree liability, above ten all agree exemption, and between three and ten is the dispute. A beraita supports this, adding that if the domains are his own, it is permitted above ten handbreadths due to shevut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Elazar's position disputes the previous conclusion.
Rabbi Elazar states that Rabbi Akiva would impose liability even above ten handbreadths, and the mishnah's mention of 'the public domain itself' is to highlight the leniency of the Sages.
The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Chilkiya bar Tovi's position also disputes the previous conclusion.
Rabbi Chilkiya bar Tovi distinguishes: within three handbreadths all agree liability, above ten all agree exemption, and between three and ten is the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages.
A baraita supports Rabbi Chilkiya bar Tovi's position, adding that if the domains are his own, it is permitted above ten handbreadths due to shevut.

items.text: Challenge to Rav from the beraita about private domains
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav from the beraita about private domains
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's ruling that throwing between two houses on opposite sides of a public domain is forbidden, based on the beraita that says if the domains are his own, it is permitted. It suggests this is a refutation of Rav, but then notes the case was already resolved as one where the houses are at different heights, leading to concern about falling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the beraita's ruling that if the domains are his own, it is permitted, and proposes this as a refutation of Rav's position.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by noting that the case of Rav was already established as one where the houses are at different heights, leading to concern about falling and carrying.

items.text: The principle of lavud: less than three handbreadths is considered attached
items.text_en: The principle of lavud: less than three handbreadths is considered attached
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Hamnuna about the source for the rabbinic principle that anything less than three handbreadths is considered attached (lavud). Rav Hamnuna answers that it is because a public domain cannot be perfectly level. The Gemara questions this and brings a counterexample from a mishna about a sukka, concluding that the principle is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's question to Rav Hamnuna
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's question to Rav Hamnuna
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Hamnuna for the source of the rabbinic principle that anything less than three handbreadths is considered attached (lavud).
Rav Hamnuna answers that the principle derives from the fact that a public domain cannot be perfectly level.

The Gemara objects: if the reason is unevenness, why specifically three handbreadths? It brings a counterexample from a mishna about a sukka where a partition less than three handbreadths from the ground is valid.
The Gemara answers that the sukka case has a different reason (kids can break through), and concludes that the lavud principle is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.

items.text: Baraita on public to public with private in between, and Rav Chana's difficulty
items.text_en: Baraita on public to public with private in between, and Rav Chana's difficulty
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one throws from public domain to public domain with a private domain in between, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi imposes liability, while the Sages exempt. Rav and Shmuel both explain that Rabbi Yehuda only imposes liability if the private domain is roofed. Rav Chana reports in the name of Shmuel that Rabbi Yehuda would impose two liabilities: one for taking out and one for bringing in. Rav Chana sits and is troubled by this.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one throws from public domain to public domain with a private domain in between, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi imposes liability, while the Sages exempt.
Rav and Shmuel both explain that Rabbi Yehuda only imposes liability if the private domain is roofed, treating it like a full house.
Rav Chana reports in the name of Shmuel that Rabbi Yehuda would impose two liabilities: one for taking out and one for bringing in.
Rav Chana sits and is troubled by this statement, setting up a difficulty.

items.text: Gemara's initial question: Does Rabbi Yehuda hold liable for a toladah?
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question: Does Rabbi Yehuda hold liable for a toladah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable for a toladah in the place of an av, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda lists additional labors. The baraita seems to imply that Rabbi Yehuda considers these as avot, not toladot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable for a toladah (sub-category) in the place of an av (primary category), citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda lists additional labors, implying he considers them avot.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: Two versions of the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: Two versions of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the difficulty arises only in the version taught by Mar Aha, where Rabbi Yehuda's statement conflicts with itself. In the version taught by Rav Yehuda, there is no contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the problematic version to Mar Aha's teaching, while in Rav Yehuda's version there is no difficulty.

items.text: Baraita about carrying four cubits in the public domain
items.text_en: Baraita about carrying four cubits in the public domain
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda holds liable for carrying from a private domain to a public domain and then walking four cubits, while the Sages exempt. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says Rabbi Yehuda held liable for two violations: one for hotza'ah (taking out) and one for ha'avarah (carrying). The Gemara initially assumes this implies Rabbi Yehuda holds liable for a toladah in the place of an av, but then rejects this, suggesting the case involves a specific scenario where the object rests only upon entering the public domain.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting a case of carrying from a private domain to a public domain and walking four cubits, where Rabbi Yehuda holds liable and the Sages exempt.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that Rabbi Yehuda held liable for two violations: one for hotza'ah (taking out) and one for ha'avarah (carrying).
The Gemara initially assumes that if Rabbi Yehuda held liable for only one violation, the Sages would be completely exempt, but the object was already taken out into the public domain.
The Gemara rejects this, suggesting that Rabbi Yehuda might still hold liable for only one violation, in a case where the person said 'let it rest only upon entering the public domain.'
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about the principle of קְלוּטָה כְּמָה שֶׁהוּנְּחָה (catching is like placing), and that Rabbi Yehuda does not hold liable for a toladah in place of an av.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's additions: shovet and medakdek
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's additions: shovet and medakdek
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda adds the labors of shovet (beating) and medakdek (sizing) to the list. The Gemara initially argues that if he performed both together, this shows he holds liable for a toladah in the place of an av. However, the Gemara rejects this, suggesting that Rabbi Yehuda considers these as avot themselves, not toladot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda adds the labors of shovet (beating) and medakdek (sizing) to the list of forbidden labors.
The Sages object that shovet is already included in the av of meseikh (smoothing) and medakdek in the av of oreg (weaving).
The Gemara infers that Rabbi Yehuda must have performed both labors together, proving he holds one liable for a toladah (sub-category) in the place of an av (primary category).
The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting Rabbi Yehuda performed each labor separately and considers them avot (primary categories), not toladot (sub-categories).

items.text: Support from the language 'adds' and the ruling of Rabbah and Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Support from the language 'adds' and the ruling of Rabbah and Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the term 'adds' (מוסיף) implies adding avot, not toladot. This is supported by Rabbah and Rav Yosef who both state that Rabbi Yehuda only held liable for one violation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the term 'adds' (מוסיף) implies adding avot (primary categories), not toladot (subcategories).

sub.text: Supporting statement of Rabbah and Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Supporting statement of Rabbah and Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both state that Rabbi Yehuda only held liable for one violation, supporting the interpretation that he does not hold liable for a toladah (subcategory) in place of an av (primary category).

items.text: Ravina's question to Rav Ashi: The case of 'wherever you want, let it rest'
items.text_en: Ravina's question to Rav Ashi: The case of 'wherever you want, let it rest'
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about the earlier assumption that Rabbi Yehuda held liable for two violations. Rav Ashi explains that the case involves a person who says 'wherever you want, let it rest,' meaning the object is considered to rest immediately upon leaving the hand.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi about the earlier assumption that Rabbi Yehuda would be liable for two violations, noting the inconsistency in where the object is considered to rest.
Rav Ashi answers that the case involves a person who says 'wherever you want, let it rest,' meaning the object is considered to rest immediately upon leaving the hand.

items.text: Analogy to writing a name: Intending to throw eight and throwing four
items.text_en: Analogy to writing a name: Intending to throw eight and throwing four
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers a case where one intended to throw eight cubits but only threw four, comparing it to writing part of a name. The Gemara questions whether the object is considered to have been placed (since it left the hand) or not (since it didn't reach its intended destination). The Gemara rejects the analogy to writing a name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where one intended to throw eight cubits but threw four, comparing it to writing part of a name, and then asks about the reverse case where one intended to throw four but threw eight.
The Gemara rejects the analogy to writing a name, arguing that in the writing case the incomplete name is not the full name, whereas in the throwing case the object does travel the full distance.

items.text: Baraita: Throwing from public domain to public domain with a private domain in between
items.text_en: Baraita: Throwing from public domain to public domain with a private domain in between
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who throws from one public domain to another with a private domain in between, a distance of four cubits, is liable.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who throws from one public domain to another with a private domain in between, a distance of four cubits, is liable.

items.text: Opening statement: exemption for less than four cubits
items.text_en: Opening statement: exemption for less than four cubits
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling that one who carries less than four cubits in the public domain is exempt teaches that multiple domains can combine, and we do not say that a carried object is considered as if placed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling that one who carries less than four cubits in the public domain is exempt teaches that multiple domains can combine, and we do not say that a carried object is considered as if placed.

items.text: Rav's ruling on covered public domain
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on covered public domain
items.desc_en: Rav rules that one who carries four cubits in a covered public domain is exempt because it does not resemble the banners of the wilderness. The Gemara objects from the case of the Tabernacle's wagons, which were covered and yet their undersides, between them, and sides are considered public domain.

sub.text: Rav's ruling via Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav's ruling via Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that one who carries an object four cubits in a covered public domain is exempt, because it does not resemble the camp standards in the wilderness.
The Gemara objects: covered wagons are considered a public domain underneath, between, and alongside them, contradicting Rav's exemption.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's ruling applies specifically to a covered courtyard (דָרָאתָא), not to wagons.

items.text: Calculation of wagon dimensions and the principle of לבוד
items.text_en: Calculation of wagon dimensions and the principle of לבוד
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the dimensions of the wagon and the planks: the wagon is five cubits long, each plank is one and a half cubits wide, three planks are placed, leaving half a cubit between them, which would be considered connected by the principle of לבוד. The Gemara answers that the planks were placed on their sides, not flat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier objection by calculating the wagon's dimensions and arguing that the space between planks is considered connected (לבוד).
The Gemara rejects the calculation, explaining that the planks were placed on their edges, not flat, changing the spacing.

items.text: Further calculation and dispute about plank thickness
items.text_en: Further calculation and dispute about plank thickness
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues: the thickness of the plank is one cubit, four planks are placed, leaving one cubit between them, which would be considered connected by לבוד. This works according to the opinion that the planks were one cubit thick at the bottom and tapered to a finger's breadth at the top, but not for the opinion that they were one cubit thick throughout.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recalculates with planks on their edges, finding a cubit gap that would be considered connected (לבוד).

sub.text: Gemara's question for the second opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's question for the second opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the calculation works for the opinion that planks taper from a cubit at the bottom to a finger at the top, but questions how it works for the opinion that planks are a full cubit thick throughout.
But according to the opinion that the planks were one cubit thick throughout, the calculation fails, leaving an unresolved difficulty.

items.text: Rav Kahana's resolution: rings on the wagon
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's resolution: rings on the wagon
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana answers that the planks were placed on rings, and the rings were placed on the back of the wagon, but the wagon itself was covered, resolving the difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana answers that the planks were placed on rings (אַטְבְּעֵי) on the wagon's back, and the wagon itself was covered, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Shmuel's statement on the boards' pegs
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement on the boards' pegs
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that the boards of the Tabernacle were joined by pegs (יתדות). This brief statement introduces the topic of the boards' construction.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the boards of the Tabernacle were joined by pegs (יתדות).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya on board thickness
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya on board thickness
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma (Rabbi Yehuda) says the boards were one cubit thick at the bottom and tapered to a finger's breadth at the top, citing the verse 'they shall be complete at its head.' Rabbi Nechemya argues they were one cubit thick throughout, citing the verse 'together.' The Gemara resolves the apparent contradictions in the verses.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's position that the boards were one cubit thick at the bottom and tapered to a finger's breadth at the top, citing the verse 'they shall be complete at its head' and the parallel verse 'they were completely cut off.'
Rabbi Nechemya argues that the boards were one cubit thick throughout, citing the verse 'together.'
The Gemara objects: but the verse says 'complete' (תַּמִּים), which seems to support Rabbi Yehuda's view that they tapered.
The Gemara answers: that verse refers to the boards being complete (not split) and not having a plank-like shape.
The Gemara objects: but the other verse says 'together' (יַחְדָּו), which seems to support Rabbi Nechemya's view of uniform thickness.
The Gemara answers: that verse means that the boards should not be interchanged with each other (they must remain paired as originally made).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute regarding the corner boards
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute regarding the corner boards
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Nechemya, the uniform thickness allows the corner boards to fill the gap, while according to Rabbi Yehuda, the tapering boards would leave a gap, which is resolved by shaping them like mountains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Nechemya, who holds the boards are uniformly one cubit thick, the width of the corner boards fills the gap at the western end.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Yehuda, whose boards taper to a fingerbreadth, the corner boards would leave a gap because one board enters and the other exits.
The Gemara resolves that the boards were shaped like mountains, tapering to fit together and fill the gap.

items.text: The middle bar stood by a miracle
items.text_en: The middle bar stood by a miracle
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught that the middle bar (הבריח התיכון) stood by a miracle, as it passed through the boards lengthwise.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught that the middle bar (הבריח התיכון) stood by a miracle, as it passed through the boards lengthwise.

items.text: Calculation of the inner curtains' coverage
items.text_en: Calculation of the inner curtains' coverage
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates how the ten inner curtains (each 28 cubits long) cover the Tabernacle. When placed widthwise, they cover the roof and leave nine cubits on each side, covering the boards (according to Rabbi Nechemya) or the sockets (according to Rabbi Yehuda). When placed lengthwise, they cover the roof and leave ten cubits, covering the sockets (Rabbi Yehuda) or exposing them (Rabbi Nechemya).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that when the ten inner curtains (each 28 cubits long) are placed widthwise across the Tabernacle, they cover the roof and leave nine cubits on each side, covering the sockets (according to Rabbi Yehuda) or the boards (according to Rabbi Nechemya).
The Gemara then calculates that when the curtains are placed lengthwise, they cover the roof and leave ten cubits, covering the sockets (Rabbi Yehuda) or exposing them (Rabbi Nechemya).

items.text: Calculation of the outer curtains' coverage
items.text_en: Calculation of the outer curtains' coverage
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates how the eleven outer curtains of goat hair (each 30 cubits long) cover the Tabernacle. When placed widthwise, they cover the roof and leave ten cubits on each side, covering the sockets (Rabbi Yehuda) or exposing them (Rabbi Nechemya). A baraita supports this: the extra cubit on each side covers the cubit of the sockets (Rabbi Yehuda) or the boards (Rabbi Nechemya). When placed lengthwise, they cover the roof and leave fourteen cubits; after doubling the sixth curtain, twelve cubits remain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that when the eleven goat-hair curtains (each 30 cubits long) are placed widthwise across the Tabernacle, they cover the roof and leave ten cubits on each side; according to Rabbi Yehuda this covers the cubit of the sockets, while according to Rabbi Nechemya it exposes the cubit of the sockets.

A baraita supports the calculation: the extra cubit on each side covers the cubit of the sockets (Rabbi Yehuda) or the boards (Rabbi Nechemya); when placed lengthwise, after doubling the sixth curtain, twelve cubits remain.

items.text: Explanation of the verse 'half the curtain shall hang over'
items.text_en: Explanation of the verse 'half the curtain shall hang over'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the verse 'half the curtain shall hang over' refers to the extra curtain hanging down. For Rabbi Nechemya, it means the curtain protrudes from its companions. A Tanna from the school of Rabbi Yishmael compares the Tabernacle to a woman walking in the market with her skirts trailing behind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yehuda, the verse 'half the curtain shall hang over' is explained, but according to Rabbi Nechemya, what does 'תסרח' mean?
The Gemara answers: it means the curtain protrudes from its companions.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: A Tanna from the school of Rabbi Yishmael compares the Tabernacle to a woman walking in the market with her skirts trailing behind, illustrating the protruding curtain.

items.text: Boards were grooved and sockets were hollow
items.text_en: Boards were grooved and sockets were hollow
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the boards were grooved (חרוצים) and the sockets were hollow (חלולים), likely to receive the pegs mentioned by Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that the boards were grooved (חרוצים) and the sockets were hollow (חלולים), supporting Shmuel's statement about pegs.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the hooks appear in the loops like stars in the sky, describing the visual effect of the Tabernacle's structure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the visual effect of the hooks in the loops appearing like stars in the sky.

items.text: Baraita on the curtains' wisdom
items.text_en: Baraita on the curtains' wisdom
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the lower curtains were of blue, purple, and scarlet, while the upper ones were of goat hair, and greater wisdom was said about the upper ones, as they were spun directly from the goats, per Rabbi Nehemiah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita details the materials of the Tabernacle curtains and notes that greater wisdom was attributed to the upper curtains, citing verses and a tradition from Rabbi Nechemya about the goats being spun directly from the goats.
The baraita states that the upper curtains were of goat hair and that greater wisdom was said about them than the lower ones.

The baraita contrasts the verses: for the lower curtains it says 'every wise-hearted woman spun with her hands,' while for the upper ones it says 'all the women whose hearts lifted them spun the goats.'
Rabbi Nehemiah explains that the upper curtains were spun directly from the goats while still wet, demonstrating greater wisdom.

items.text: Dimensions of wagons and boards
items.text_en: Dimensions of wagons and boards
items.desc_en: Rav in the name of Rabbi Chiyya states that the wagons' undersides, between them, and their sides are public domain. Abaye specifies the space between wagons as the length of a wagon (five cubits) to avoid crowding the boards. Rava adds that the sides of the wagon are the width of a wagon (two and a half cubits) to prevent the boards from moving.

sub.text: Rav in the name of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rav in the name of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rav in the name of Rabbi Chiyya states that the undersides of the wagons, the spaces between them, and their sides are public domain.
Abaye specifies that the space between wagons is the length of a wagon (five cubits) to prevent the boards from being crowded.
Rava adds that the sides of the wagon are the width of a wagon (two and a half cubits) to prevent the boards from moving.

items.text: Reconciling the width of public domain
items.text_en: Reconciling the width of public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the public domain's width is sixteen cubits when the Tabernacle's was only fifteen, and answers that the extra cubit was for a Levite to stand and hold the boards when they were pulled out.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the standard public domain width is sixteen cubits, but derived from the Tabernacle it would be only fifteen cubits.
The Gemara resolves that the extra cubit was occupied by a Levite standing there to catch the planks when they were pulled out.

items.text: Mishnah: The well's rim and rock
items.text_en: Mishnah: The well's rim and rock
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a well's rim or a rock that is ten handbreadths high and four wide constitutes a private domain; one who takes from or places on it is liable, but if smaller, exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a well-rim or rock ten handbreadths high and four wide makes one liable for carrying from or onto it on Shabbat; less than that is exempt.

items.text: Gemara: The well's rim combines with the well
items.text_en: Gemara: The well's rim combines with the well
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions 'the well's rim' and not just 'the well', and supports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the well and its rim combine to reach ten handbreadths. A baraita confirms this: a well ten deep and four wide in public domain may not be drawn from on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies 'well-rim' and 'rock' rather than just 'well' and 'rock'.
The Gemara notes that this supports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the well and its rim combine to reach ten handbreadths.
A baraita confirms that a well ten handbreadths deep and four wide in public domain may not be drawn from on Shabbat.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that a well in a courtyard requires a partition ten handbreadths high, and one may only drink from it on Shabbat if one inserts one's head and most of one's body. The well and its rim combine to make the ten handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the rule about a well in a courtyard requiring a partition and the combination of well and rim to reach ten handbreadths.

items.text: Rav Mordechai's question about a pillar in the public domain
items.text_en: Rav Mordechai's question about a pillar in the public domain
items.desc_en: Rav Mordechai asks Rava whether throwing an object onto a pillar ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide in the public domain is liable. Rava and others initially answer that the mishnah already resolves it, but Rav Mordechai objects, citing a mishnah that one is liable for taking from and placing on such a pillar. They suggest the mishnah refers to a needle, which is small, but counter that even a needle has a slight protrusion or is placed in a groove.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai asks Rava whether throwing an object onto a pillar ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide in the public domain is liable, since the object comes from a place of exemption.

sub.text: Rava, Rav Yosef, and Abaye's answer
sub.text_en: Rava, Rav Yosef, and Abaye's answer
sub.desc_en: Rava, Rav Yosef, and Abaye each answer that the mishnah already resolves the question, but Rav Mordechai dismisses them as repeating the same point.
The sages object, citing a mishnah that one is liable for taking from and placing on such a pillar.
Rav Mordechai answers that the mishnah might refer to a needle, which is small and thus different from a pillar.
The gemara rejects this, arguing that even a needle has a slight protrusion or is placed in a groove, so it still has a significant resting place.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question about a wall in the public domain
