items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question about a wall in the public domain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks about a wall ten handbreadths high but less than four handbreadths wide, surrounded by a karmelit and made into a private domain: if one throws an object and it lands on top, is one liable? Ulla argues a fortiori that if it serves as a partition for others, surely it does for itself. Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi and Rabbi Yitzchak report that Rabbi Yochanan himself rules one is liable.

sub.text: Rav Meysha citing Rabbi Yochanan's question
sub.text_en: Rav Meysha citing Rabbi Yochanan's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks about a wall in the public domain, ten handbreadths high but less than four wide, surrounded by a karmelit and made into a private domain: if one throws an object and it lands on top, is one liable?
Ulla argues a fortiori that if the wall serves as a partition for others, surely it does for itself, implying liability.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi and Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi and Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi and Rabbi Yitzchak report that Rabbi Yochanan himself rules one is liable, reinforcing Ulla's argument.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question about a nine-handbreadth well and a rim
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question about a nine-handbreadth well and a rim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks: if a well is nine handbreadths deep and one removes a rim from it to complete it to ten, does the simultaneous removal of the object and creation of the partition incur liability? Similarly, if a well is ten handbreadths and one places a rim inside to reduce it, does the simultaneous placement and removal of the partition incur liability?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks two cases: a nine-handbreadth well where one removes a rim to complete ten, and a ten-handbreadth well where one adds a rim to reduce it, questioning liability when object removal and partition creation or removal occur simultaneously.

items.text: Attempt to resolve from a mishnah about throwing at a wall
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from a mishnah about throwing at a wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve Rabbi Yochanan's question from a mishnah about throwing four cubits at a wall: above ten handbreadths is like throwing into the air (exempt), below ten is like throwing on the ground (liable). Rabbi Yochanan explains that the mishnah deals with a soft fig cake that sticks, but the Gemara objects that it reduces the four cubits. The resolution is that there the cake is not nullified, while here the rim is nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve Rabbi Yochanan's question from a mishnah about throwing four cubits at a wall, noting the distinction between above and below ten handbreadths, and then raises the difficulty that the object did not actually rest.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the mishnah deals with a soft fig cake that sticks to the wall, but the Gemara objects that this reduces the four cubits.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing that in the mishnah the fig cake is not nullified (it remains a separate entity), while here the rim is nullified (it becomes part of the wall).

items.text: Rava's question about throwing a board onto pegs
items.text_en: Rava's question about throwing a board onto pegs
items.desc_en: Rava asks: if one throws a board and it lands on pegs, is the simultaneous placement of the object and creation of a partition liable? The Gemara notes this is similar to Rabbi Yochanan's question, but Rava's actual query is when one throws a board with an object on it: does the simultaneous arrival count as placement and partition, or since the board lands slightly before the object, is it partition then placement? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if one throws a board and it lands on pegs, is the simultaneous placement of the object and creation of a partition liable? The Gemara notes this is similar to Rabbi Yochanan's question.

Rava refines his question: when one throws a board with an object on it, does the simultaneous arrival count as placement and partition, or since the board lands slightly before the object, is it partition then placement? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rava's ruling on water and a nut
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on water and a nut
items.desc_en: Rava states that it is obvious that water on water constitutes placement, but a nut on water is a question that is not resolved here.

sub.text: Rava's question about water and a nut
sub.text_en: Rava's question about water and a nut
sub.desc_en: Rava states that water on water is clearly considered placement, but then questions the case of a nut on water.

items.text: Rava's question about a nut in a floating vessel
items.text_en: Rava's question about a nut in a floating vessel
items.desc_en: Rava asks about a case where a nut is inside a vessel that floats on water: do we follow the nut (which has come to rest) or the vessel (which has not)? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a nut inside a floating vessel is considered to have come to rest (following the nut) or not (following the vessel), and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Oil floating on wine: dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Oil floating on wine: dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if oil floats on wine and a טבול יום touches only the oil, only the oil is rendered impure. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri argues that they are considered connected. This dispute is cited as relevant to the previous question about floating objects.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the Sages regarding oil floating on wine.
The baraita states that when oil floats on wine and a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) touches only the oil, only the oil is rendered impure; Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri argues both are connected.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri argues that the oil and wine are considered connected, so touching the oil renders both impure.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on a pit in the public domain with a mat
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on a pit in the public domain with a mat
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that if one throws a mat into a pit ten handbreadths deep and eight wide, he is liable. If he divided the pit with the mat, he is exempt. The Gemara contrasts Abaye's view with Rabbi Yochanan's uncertainty regarding a ring (חוליא).

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that throwing a mat into a public-domain pit ten handbreadths deep and eight wide makes one liable, but dividing the pit with the mat exempts.
The gemara contrasts Abaye's clear position that a mat nullifies the partition with Rabbi Yochanan's doubt about a ring nullifying it, implying the mat certainly does not nullify for Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara contrasts that for Rabbi Yochanan, who is uncertain about the ring, it is obvious that a mat does not nullify the partition.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on a pit filled with water vs. fruit
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on a pit filled with water vs. fruit
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that throwing into a pit filled with water is liable because water does not nullify the partitions, but throwing into a pit filled with fruit is exempt because fruit does nullify them. A baraita supports this with a case of throwing from the sea to a river or vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that throwing into a pit filled with water makes one liable, but into a pit filled with fruit exempts, because water does not nullify the partition while fruit does.
A baraita supports Abaye: throwing from the sea to a river or vice versa is exempt, but Rabbi Shimon says if the place is ten deep and four wide, one is liable.

items.text: Mishnah: Throwing four cubits at a wall
items.text_en: Mishnah: Throwing four cubits at a wall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one throws an object four cubits and it hits a wall above ten handbreadths, it is like throwing into the air (exempt); if below ten handbreadths, it is like throwing on the ground (liable). Throwing four cubits on the ground is liable.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that throwing four cubits at a wall above ten handbreadths is like throwing into the air (exempt), below ten is like throwing on the ground (liable).

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer about the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer about the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: but the object did not come to rest? Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Mishnah deals with a moist fig-cake that sticks to the wall.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: the object thrown at the wall did not come to rest, so why is one liable?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the mishnah deals with a thick fig cake that sticks to the wall, thus coming to rest.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya's ruling on throwing above ten into a hole
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's ruling on throwing above ten into a hole
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya states that if one throws above ten handbreadths and the object lands in any small hole, the liability depends on the dispute between Rabbi Meir (who says we consider the hole as if it extends to complete ten) and the Rabbis (who do not). A baraita supports this.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya explains that if one throws above ten handbreadths and the object lands in a small hole, liability depends on the dispute between Rabbi Meir (who says we consider the hole as if carved to complete the height) and the Sages (who do not).
A baraita supports this: throwing above ten handbreadths into a small hole — Rabbi Meir holds liable, the Sages exempt.
The gemara explains that according to the Rabbis, who hold that we do not consider the hole as extending, the thrower is exempt.
A baraita is cited that explicitly supports the ruling: Rabbi Meir holds liable and the Sages exempt in this case.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a mound that slopes ten within four cubits
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a mound that slopes ten within four cubits
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that if a mound rises ten handbreadths within four cubits and one throws an object that lands on top, he is liable. A baraita and Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel support this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that a mound that rises ten handbreadths within four cubits is a valid partition, and throwing onto it makes one liable.

A baraita supports this: an alleyway that slopes to the public domain or inward needs no side-post or beam; Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel explicitly rules that a mound rising ten within four makes one liable for throwing onto it.
Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel explicitly states the same ruling as Rav, providing additional support.

items.text: Mishnah: Throwing and rolling beyond four cubits
items.text_en: Mishnah: Throwing and rolling beyond four cubits
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one throws within four cubits and the object rolls outside, he is exempt; if he throws outside four cubits and it rolls inside, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules: if one throws within four cubits and the object rolls outside, he is exempt; if thrown outside and it rolls inside, he is liable.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer about rolling
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer about rolling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: but the object did not come to rest? Rabbi Yochanan answers that it applies when it rests on something. A baraita elaborates: if the wind pushed it in and then out, he is exempt; if the wind held it momentarily, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: the object did not come to rest, so why is one liable?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the mishnah applies only when the object rests momentarily on something.
A baraita supports this: if wind pushes the object outside four cubits and then brings it back, he is exempt; but if the wind holds it momentarily, even if it later brings it back, he is liable.

items.text: Rava's ruling on within three handbreadths and Marimar's teaching
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on within three handbreadths and Marimar's teaching
items.desc_en: Rava states that within three handbreadths, according to the Rabbis, the object must rest on something. Marimar was teaching this halakha, and Ravina questioned him.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that within three handbreadths, according to the Sages, the object must rest on something to incur liability.
The gemara notes that Marimar was sitting and teaching this ruling, and Ravina addressed him.
Ravina questions Marimar about the ruling.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the earlier Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the earlier Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction between the earlier Mishnah and Rabbi Yochanan's statement, explaining that the case involves an object that will eventually come to rest, even if it hasn't yet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case is identical to Rabbi Yochanan's statement.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a rolling object (which will not come to rest) and the Mishnah's case (which will eventually come to rest).

items.text: Mishnah: Throwing into the sea and a water reservoir
items.text_en: Mishnah: Throwing into the sea and a water reservoir
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who throws four cubits into the sea is exempt, but if it is a shallow water reservoir (less than ten handbreadths deep) where the public walks, one is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who throws an object into the sea four cubits is exempt, but if the water is less than ten handbreadths deep and the public walks there, he is liable.
The Mishnah repeats the case of shallow water with public passage to emphasize the liability for throwing within it.

items.text: Gemara's question about the repetition of 'rekak'
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the repetition of 'rekak'
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rava why the Mishnah repeats the word 'rekak' twice, explaining that one instance refers to summer and one to winter, and both are necessary.

sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rava why the Mishnah repeats the word 'הילוך' (walking) twice, explaining that it teaches that walking under duress is still considered walking, but use under duress is not considered use.
The rabbi asks why the Mishnah repeats the word 'רקק' (shallow water) twice, and suggests one is for summer and one for winter, explaining the necessity of both.

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the repetition is needed to teach that even when the water is four cubits wide, people do not walk around it but through it.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the repetition is needed to counter the assumption that if the water is four cubits wide, people would walk around it rather than through it.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the repetition teaches that even when the water is less than four cubits wide, people step over it, and he supports this with his own principle about throwing and resting on a camel's hump.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the repetition is needed to counter the assumption that if the water is less than four cubits wide, people would step over it rather than walk through it.
Rav Ashi supports his explanation with his own principle that one who throws an object that lands on a camel's hump is liable because the public cuts through that space.

items.text: Mishnah: Throwing from sea to land and between ships
items.text_en: Mishnah: Throwing from sea to land and between ships
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who throws from sea to land, from land to sea, or between ships is exempt, but if ships are tied together, one may carry between them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that throwing from sea to land, land to sea, or between boats is exempt, but if boats are tied together one may transfer between them.
The Mishnah adds that if ships are tied together, one may move objects between them; if not, even if they are adjacent, one may not.

items.text: Dispute about drawing water from a ship
items.text_en: Dispute about drawing water from a ship
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says one may extend a small projection (ziz) from the ship to draw water, while Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna require a four-handbreadth area. The Gemara explains their reasoning about the measurement of the karmelit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rav Huna permits drawing water from a ship via a minimal projection (זיז), while Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna require a four-handbreadth area.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Huna's view: the karmelit (כרמלית) is measured from the seabed, so the air above is a place of exemption (מקום פטור), and the projection is only needed as a reminder (היכרא).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the opposing view: the karmelit is measured from the water's surface, so without a four-handbreadth area one would be carrying from a karmelit (כרמלית) to a private domain (רשות היחיד).

items.text: Rav Nachman's challenge to Rav Huna
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's challenge to Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbah bar Avuha how Rav Huna's view works when the water is less than ten handbreadths deep, and is answered that a ship always sails in at least ten handbreadths, with scouts going ahead.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's objection to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna that sometimes the water is less than ten handbreadths deep, so one would be transferring from a neutral domain to a private domain.
Rabbah bar Avuha answers that a boat does not sail in water less than ten handbreadths deep, and Rav Safra adds that scouts go ahead of it to ensure depth.
Rav Safra answers that scouts (sounding boats) go ahead of the ship to ensure sufficient depth.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question about disposing of water
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question about disposing of water
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rav Chiya bar Avin how one disposes of waste water according to Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna, and the answer is to throw it against the ship's side, as force in a karmelit is not prohibited.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rav Chiya bar Avin
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rav Chiya bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rav Chiya bar Avin how one disposes of waste water according to Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's opinion.
Rav Chiya bar Avin answers that one throws the water against the side of the boat, and the force of one's throw in a neutral domain was not decreed forbidden.
A baraita is cited to support the principle that one's force in a neutral domain is not forbidden, stating that one may not transfer directly from a boat to the sea or vice versa.
The Gemara cites a baraita that one may not move objects from the ship to the sea or from the sea to the ship, supporting the leniency regarding force in a karmelit.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on a pit and the sea
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on a pit and the sea
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that if a pit is ten handbreadths deep but not ten high, one may carry from inside it to the sea but not from the sea into it. The Gemara questions the inconsistency, concluding that the pit is considered a single domain with the sea, and that one's force in a karmelit is not prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that a pit ten handbreadths deep but not ten high allows carrying from inside to the sea but not from the sea into it.

The Gemara questions the inconsistency: why is carrying from the sea into the pit forbidden but from the pit to the sea permitted, since both involve transfer between a private domain (רשות היחיד) and a karmelit (כרמלית)?
The Gemara resolves that the pit is considered a single domain (אחודה) with the sea, and that one's force (כוחו) in a karmelit is not prohibited by rabbinic decree.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on islands of Meishan
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on islands of Meishan
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the islands of Meishan are considered karmelit, and one may only carry within them four cubits. He adds exceptions: if the island is less than three handbreadths above water, or if reeds and rushes surround it, the restriction does not apply.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the ponds of Meishan may only be carried within four cubits.
Rav Huna qualifies that this applies only when there is no area of three by four handbreadths; if there is, the restriction does not apply.
Rav Huna adds that if reeds and rushes fill the pond, the restriction does not apply.

items.text: Rav Nachman's objection: apply gud achit
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection: apply gud achit
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna's ruling, arguing that the principle of "gud achit mechitzata" (extend the partition downward) should apply, making the island a private domain. He cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda applies this principle to a cane in the public domain.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects, arguing that the principle of גוד אחית מחיצתא (extend the partition downward) should apply here, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda applies this principle.
The baraita states that if one stuck a cane in the public domain with a basket on top and threw an object that landed on it, he is liable, showing that the principle of גוד אחית מחיצתא is applied.
Rav Nachman concludes that just as the principle applies in the baraita, it should apply here, making the island a private domain.

items.text: Rav Yosef's counter-objection and Abaye's support
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's counter-objection and Abaye's support
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, citing a tradition from Rav Yehuda quoting Rav. Abaye counters with a baraita about a pillar in the public domain that supports the principle of gud achit, arguing it should apply here as well.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects, citing a tradition from Rav Yehuda quoting Rav, with a baraita stating that the Sages exempt in the case of the cane and basket.

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef, citing a baraita about a pillar in the public domain that supports the principle of גוד אחית מחיצתא, implying the Sages' exemption in the cane case is not a general rejection.

items.text: Distinction: partition that kids can breach vs. not
items.text_en: Distinction: partition that kids can breach vs. not
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a partition that kids can breach (the pillar) and one that they cannot (the island). Rav Acha bar Rav Acha questions whether fish breaching the water counts, but Rav Ashi responds that fish breaching is not considered breaching, citing a precedent about a hanging partition in a ruin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy, distinguishing between a partition that kids (goats) can breach (מחיצה שהגדיים בוקעין בה) and one they cannot, implying the pillar case has a valid partition while the pond does not.
Rav Acha bar Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi whether the breach of fish (בקיעת דגים) in a ship should be considered a breach, and Rav Ashi responds that fish breach is not considered a breach.

The Gemara supports this by citing Rabbi Tavla's inquiry to Rav about whether a hanging partition (מחיצה תלויה) permits carrying in a ruin, and Rav's answer that it does not, implying that only a partition that reaches the ground is valid.

sub.text: Supporting precedent from Rabbi Tavla and Rav
sub.text_en: Supporting precedent from Rabbi Tavla and Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites a precedent: Rabbi Tavla asked Rav about a hanging partition in a ruin, and Rav ruled it does not permit carrying, establishing that fish breaching is not considered breaching.

items.text: Clarification about water and fish breaches
items.text_en: Clarification about water and fish breaches
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why water is considered a weak partition, given that fish can breach it, and concludes that a fish breach is not considered a valid breach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why water is considered a weak partition, given that fish can breach it.
The Gemara concludes that a fish breach is not considered a valid breach, so water remains a weak partition.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's ruling about tied boats is not obvious; it is necessary to permit carrying between them via the space between them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling about tied boats is necessary, as it seems obvious.
Rava answers that the Mishnah is needed to permit carrying in the space between the boats.

items.text: Rav Safra's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Safra's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Safra objects to Rava's explanation, pointing out that the Mishnah explicitly says 'one may carry from one to another,' so Rava's interpretation is unnecessary. Instead, Rav Safra explains that the Mishnah permits carrying after an eruv, citing a baraita about tied boats and partitions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra objects to Rava's explanation, arguing that the Mishnah's explicit language 'one may carry from one to another' makes Rava's interpretation unnecessary.
Rav Safra explains that the Mishnah permits carrying only after an עירוב (eruv), citing a baraita about tied boats and partitions.

items.text: Parallel ruling for mats in the public domain
items.text_en: Parallel ruling for mats in the public domain
items.desc_en: The baraita extends the same principle to mats spread in the public domain: they can be used for an eruv and carrying, but if rolled up they are forbidden, and if re-spread they return to their original permissibility, as any partition made on Shabbat is valid.

sub.desc_en: The baraita extends the ruling from boats to mats in the public domain, stating that they permit eruv and carrying, but if rolled up they are forbidden, and if re-spread they return to their original permissibility, as any partition made on Shabbat is valid.

items.text: Rav Nachman's distinction between throwing and carrying
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's distinction between throwing and carrying
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Nachman's statement that the leniency applies only to throwing but not to carrying, and resolves that Rav Nachman's ruling was specifically about intentional actions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman's statement by citing his own earlier ruling that the leniency applies only to throwing (לזרוק) but not to carrying (לטלטל).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rav Nachman's restrictive ruling was specifically stated regarding intentional (מזיד) actions, not unintentional ones.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling about the type of connection
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling about the type of connection
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that even a weak connection like a cloak string suffices for carrying between boats. The Gemara clarifies that this applies when the boats can stand independently, and distinguishes between impurity and Shabbat laws.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that even a weak connection like a cloak string suffices for carrying between boats.
The Gemara asks under what circumstances Shmuel's ruling applies: if the boats can stand independently it is obvious, and if they cannot, why would a string suffice?
The Gemara answers that the boats can indeed stand independently, and Shmuel's statement comes to exclude a mistaken inference from his own earlier ruling.
The Gemara cites a baraita about impurity: a connection that holds a vessel brings impurity, but a weak connection does not.
Shmuel adds that the baraita's ruling applies only when the vessel is tied with an iron chain, indicating a strong connection.

The Gemara resolves that the impurity law requires a strong connection due to the verse 'בחלל חרב' (by the hollow of a sword), but for Shabbat, since the boats can stand independently, even a weak cloak string suffices as a mere marker.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one throws an object on Shabbat and remembers after it leaves his hand, or if another person or a dog catches it, or it is burned, he is exempt. It also rules that one who throws to make a wound and remembers before the wound is made is exempt. The general principle is that one is liable for a sin-offering only if both the beginning and end of the act are unintentional.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that one is exempt from a sin-offering if he remembers after throwing, or if another catches it, or if it is burned, and that liability requires both beginning and end to be unintentional.

items.text: Gemara's first question and Rav Kahana's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and Rav Kahana's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the object lands, is one liable? But the Mishnah says one is exempt unless both beginning and end are unintentional! Rav Kahana answers that the Mishnah's case is one who throws a 'locket' (a type of ornament) and it lands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Does the Mishnah imply that if the object lands (and he remembers only after landing) he is liable? But the Mishnah itself says one is exempt unless both beginning and end are unintentional.
Rav Kahana answers that the Mishnah's end clause comes to teach about a case of a 'laktah' (a type of basket) and a 'mitna' (a shoulder load).

items.text: Objection to Rav Kahana and Rava's first answer
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Kahana and Rava's first answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: A locket is held in one's hand! Rav Kahana's case must be where he intended to make a wound. But the Mishnah already covers that case! Rava therefore says the case is one of 'carrying' (מעביר), not throwing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: A 'laktah' and 'mitna' are held in one's hand, and the Mishnah already taught that case in the clause about throwing to make a wound, which is also exempt.
Rava answers that the Mishnah is dealing with a case of 'ma'avir' (carrying across a domain), not throwing.
Rava resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah's case is one of 'carrying' (מעביר), not throwing.

items.text: Rava's second answer: two cases in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's second answer: two cases in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's 'this is the rule' refers to throwing. Rava therefore says the Mishnah teaches two cases: one who throws and remembers after it leaves his hand, or even if he does not remember but another catches it, etc., he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: The Mishnah's general principle ('zeh haklal') is stated in the context of throwing, not carrying.
Rava answers that the Mishnah teaches two cases: one where he remembers after throwing, and another where he does not remember but another catches it or it is burned.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution: the Mishnah is missing a clause
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution: the Mishnah is missing a clause
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the Mishnah is missing a clause and should read: One who throws and remembers after it leaves his hand, and another catches it, etc., is exempt. But if it lands, he is liable. This applies only if he later forgot, but if he did not forget, he is exempt, since all sin-offerings require both beginning and end to be unintentional.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the Mishnah is missing a clause and should read: if he threw and remembered after it left his hand, or another caught it, etc., he is exempt; but if it landed, he is liable, provided he forgot again afterward.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rava on partial intent
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rava on partial intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case: two cubits unintentionally, two cubits intentionally, two cubits unintentionally. Rabbah says he is exempt, Rava says he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbah and Rava regarding a case of two amot (cubits) unintentionally, two intentionally, and two unintentionally.
Rabbah rules that the person is exempt from a חטאת (sin-offering).
Rava rules that the person is liable for a חטאת (sin-offering).

items.text: Rabbah's reasoning and the Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Rabbah's reasoning and the Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: Rabbah says he is exempt even according to Rabban Gamliel who says there is no awareness for half a measure, because there the completion is unintentional, but here the middle part is intentional. The Gemara asks: In what case? If throwing, it is unintentional! Rather, it is carrying.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that he exempts the case even according to Rabban Gamliel, because there the completion was unintentional, but here the middle part was intentional.
The Gemara asks: In what case is this? If throwing, it is unintentional!
The Gemara answers: Rather, it is carrying.

items.text: Rava's reasoning and the Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Rava's reasoning and the Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: Rava says he is liable even according to the Rabbis who say there is awareness for half a measure, because there it is in his control, but here it is not in his control. The Gemara asks: In what case? If carrying, it is in his control! Rather, it is throwing.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains his ruling: even according to the Rabbis who hold there is awareness for a half-measure, here the middle segment is not in his control (since it is thrown), so it is considered unintentional.
The Gemara asks: in what type of act? If it is carrying (העברה), the person has control over the entire action, so why would Rava hold him liable?
The Gemara answers: the case must be throwing (זריקה), where the final landing is beyond the thrower's control.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling on unusual landing places
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling on unusual landing places
items.desc_en: Rabbah says: If one throws and the object lands in a dog's mouth or a furnace's mouth, he is liable. The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that says if a dog catches it, he is exempt. Rabbah distinguishes: there he did not intend, here he intended.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if one throws and the object lands in a dog's mouth or a furnace's mouth, he is liable.
The Gemara objects: But we learned in the Mishnah that if a dog catches it, he is exempt.
Rabbah resolves: there (in the Mishnah) he did not intend for the dog to catch it; here he intended for it to land in the dog's mouth.

items.text: Rav Beivai's support from a baraita
items.text_en: Rav Beivai's support from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye brings support from a baraita: There is one who eats a single meal and is liable for four sin-offerings and one guilt-offering, e.g., a tamei person eating chelev that is notar from sacrifices on Yom Kippur. Rabbi Meir adds: If it was Shabbat and he carried it out in his mouth, he is liable. The Sages said this is not from the same category. The Gemara explains: Since he intends, his thought designates it as a place. Here too, since he intends, his thought designates it as a place.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye cites a baraita about one who eats a single meal and is liable for four sin-offerings and one guilt-offering, involving a tamei person eating chelev that is notar from sacrifices on Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Meir adds that if it was Shabbat and he carried it out in his mouth, he is liable.
The Sages object that this case is not from the same category.
The Gemara questions why the Sages object, since there is no normal way of carrying out in that manner.
The Gemara answers that since he intends, his thought designates it as a place.
The Gemara applies the same principle here: since he intends, his thought designates it as a place.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the labors of building, chiseling, striking with a hammer, and drilling, stating that any amount renders one liable. It adds a general rule: any labor whose effect endures on Shabbat is liable, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel includes striking the anvil with a sledgehammer as a form of 'repairing'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measure for building liability, lists related labors (chiseling, striking with a hammer, drilling), gives a general rule that any enduring labor is liable, and adds Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion that striking the anvil is like repairing.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'any amount' and two explanations
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'any amount' and two explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose a minimal building serves. Rabbi Yirmeya suggests a poor person digging a small hole to hide coins, paralleling the Tabernacle's tent-stitchers. Abaye rejects this, noting that stitchers don't dig holes, and instead proposes a poor person making a small stove ledge. Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that there is no poverty in the Tabernacle context, and offers the case of a homeowner sealing a crack in his mansion, paralleling a plank with a wormhole sealed with lead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose a minimal building (כל שהוא) serves.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that a poor person digs a small hole to hide coins, paralleling the Tabernacle's tent-stitchers who dig holes for their needles.
Abaye objects that stitchers do not dig holes because they use awls, not needles.
Abaye instead proposes that a poor person makes a small stove ledge (פיטפוטי כירה) for a small pot, paralleling the Tabernacle's dyers who make such ledges for their small cauldrons.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that there is no poverty in the Tabernacle context, so the poor-person analogy is invalid.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's alternative answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's alternative answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov instead offers the case of a homeowner sealing a crack in his mansion, paralleling a Tabernacle plank with a wormhole sealed with lead.

items.text: Shmuel's statement on chiseling a stone and the resolution
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement on chiseling a stone and the resolution
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that one who chisels a stone (מצדד) is liable. An objection is raised from a baraita where only the one who applies mortar is liable, not the one who places the stone. The Gemara resolves that there are three layers in building: the bottom layer requires chiseling and earth, the middle requires mortar, and the top requires only placement.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that one who chisels a stone (מצדד) on Shabbat is liable for the labor of building.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that only the one who applies mortar is liable, not the one who places the stone, contradicting Shmuel's ruling.

sub.text: Gemara's further objection from Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Gemara's further objection from Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that the baraita's continuation (Rabbi Yosei) also seems to contradict Shmuel, as it holds one liable even for mere placement on a stone pile.

The Gemara resolves that there are three distinct layers in building: the bottom requires chiseling and earth, the middle requires mortar, and the top requires only placement, thus reconciling the sources.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the category of 'smoothing' (מסתת)
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the category of 'smoothing' (מסתת)
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the liability category for smoothing (מסתת): Rav says it is a subcategory of building (בונה), while Shmuel says it is a subcategory of striking with a hammer (מכה בפטיש). They extend the dispute to making a hole in a chicken coop and inserting a handle into an axe. The Gemara explains why all three cases are necessary to fully delineate their disagreement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks under which prohibited labor category the smoother (מסתת) is liable.
Rav rules that the smoother is liable under the category of building (בונה).
Shmuel rules that the smoother is liable under the category of striking with a hammer (מכה בפטיש).

sub.text: Extension of the dispute to making a hole in a chicken coop
sub.text_en: Extension of the dispute to making a hole in a chicken coop
sub.desc_en: The dispute is extended to making a hole in a chicken coop, with Rav and Shmuel repeating their respective positions.

sub.text: Extension of the dispute to inserting a handle into an axe
sub.text_en: Extension of the dispute to inserting a handle into an axe
sub.desc_en: The dispute is extended to inserting a handle into an axe, with Rav and Shmuel repeating their respective positions.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of necessity for the first case
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of necessity for the first case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first case (smoothing) was necessary because Rav's ruling there is based on the typical building process, but in the chicken coop case, which is not typical building, one might think Rav would concede to Shmuel.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of necessity for the second case
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of necessity for the second case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the second case (chicken coop) was necessary because Rav's ruling there is based on creating an airspace, but in the axe handle case, which does not resemble building, one might think Rav would concede to Shmuel; and the third case was necessary because Shmuel's ruling there might otherwise be thought to apply only to that case, but not to the first two.

items.text: Rav Nathan's inquiry and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.text_en: Rav Nathan's inquiry and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Oshaya asks Rabbi Yochanan about the category for smoothing. Rabbi Yochanan gestures that it is 'striking with a hammer'. The Gemara notes a difficulty: the Mishnah lists both 'the smoother' and 'the striker with a hammer' separately. Rabbi Yochanan reinterprets the Mishnah as 'the smoother who strikes with a hammer' (i.e., one category). The Gemara then introduces a baraita to further clarify.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Oshaya asks Rabbi Yochanan: for which category is the smoother liable?
Rabbi Yochanan gestures with his hand that the smoother is liable under the category of 'the striker with a hammer'.
The Gemara objects: but we learned in the Mishnah that 'the smoother' and 'the striker with a hammer' are listed separately, implying they are distinct categories.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the objection by reinterpreting the Mishnah: 'the smoother who strikes with a hammer' — a single category.
The Gemara says 'Come and hear' to introduce a baraita that will further clarify the matter.

items.text: Gemara's question on the measure for boring
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the measure for boring
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that any amount of boring incurs liability, contrasting the views of Rav and Shmuel. It resolves that the case involves boring with an iron rod and leaving it in place, which completes the labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's ruling that any amount of boring incurs liability fits with Shmuel's view that the labor is not complete unless it serves a constructive purpose.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves boring with an iron rod and leaving it in place, which completes the labor.

items.text: The general rule: including a specific case
items.text_en: The general rule: including a specific case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'this is the rule' comes to include, and answers that it includes the case of pressing a measure into a kab (a dry measure).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'this is the rule' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes the case of pressing a measure into a kab (a dry measure).

items.text: Debate on the reason for liability for striking an anvil
items.text_en: Debate on the reason for liability for striking an anvil
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef say the striker is liable because he trains his hand. The children of Rachava object that if so, one who sees a craft and completes it would be liable. Abaye and Rava say the reason is that the Tabernacle workers did so to hammer plates. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constructive action is performed by striking the anvil.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef answer that the striker is liable because he trains his hand for the craft.
The children of Rachava object that if the reason is training the hand, then one who merely observes a craft and completes it mentally would also be liable.
Abaye and Rava answer that the striker is liable because the Tabernacle workers who hammered plates did so, establishing the prototype of the prohibited labor.
A baraita is cited that supports Abaye and Rava's position, stating that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules the striker liable because the Tabernacle workers did so.

items.text: Mishnah: measures for plowing and related labors
items.text_en: Mishnah: measures for plowing and related labors
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who plows, weeds, prunes, or trims any amount is liable. For gathering wood or herbs, the measure depends on the purpose: for improvement any amount, for fuel enough to cook an egg, for animal food a mouthful for a kid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the measures for plowing, weeding, pruning, trimming, and gathering wood or herbs, with liability depending on the purpose.

items.text: Gemara: purpose of gathering herbs
items.text_en: Gemara: purpose of gathering herbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the gathered herbs are for, and answers that they are for pumpkin seeds, corresponding to the Tabernacle where they were used for a single bundle of dyes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the gathered herbs are used for.
The Gemara answers that the herbs are for pumpkin seeds, corresponding to the Tabernacle where they were used for a single bundle of dyes.

items.text: Baraita on measures for weeding and trimming
items.text_en: Baraita on measures for weeding and trimming
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that for pulling weeds or trimming branches, the measure depends on the purpose: for eating a fig-bulk, for animal food a mouthful for a kid, for fuel enough to cook an egg, for beautifying the ground any amount.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that for pulling weeds or trimming branches, the measure depends on the purpose: for eating a fig-bulk, for animal food a mouthful for a kid, for fuel enough to cook an egg, for beautifying the ground any amount.

items.text: Debate on the baraita's distinction
items.text_en: Debate on the baraita's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita distinguishes between purposes, since all are for beautifying the ground. Rabbah and Rav Yosef say it was taught about a marsh. Abaye says even in a field where one does not intend to beautify, and the Gemara notes that Abaye and Rava agree on 'pesik reishei' but here it is in another's field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita distinguishes between purposes, since all actions seem to beautify the ground.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef answer that the baraita was taught about a marsh, where the primary intent is not beautification.
Abaye offers an alternative answer: even in a field that is not a marsh, the baraita applies when one does not intend to beautify.
The Gemara objects that Abaye and Rava agree on the principle of 'פסיק רישא' (an inevitable consequence), which would seem to contradict Abaye's answer.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the case is in another's field, where the person does not care about beautification and the action is not intended.

items.text: Mishnah: writing two letters on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: writing two letters on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who writes two letters, whether with right or left hand, from one name or two, with two inks, in any language, is liable. Rabbi Yosi says the liability is due to marking, as they wrote on Tabernacle planks to pair them. Rabbi Yehuda notes that a small name can be derived from a large one.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who writes two letters on Shabbat is liable, regardless of hand, ink, or language.
Rabbi Yosi explains that the liability for two letters is due to the act of marking, as was done on the Tabernacle planks to pair them.
Rabbi Yehuda notes that a small name can be derived from a large one, citing examples like 'שם' from 'שמעון' and 'נח' from 'נחור'.

items.text: Gemara: liability for writing with the left hand
items.text_en: Gemara: liability for writing with the left hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why writing with the left hand is liable, since writing is normally done with the right. Rabbi Yirmeya says it was taught about a left-handed person. Abaye says it is about one who is ambidextrous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why writing with the left hand is liable, since writing is normally done with the right hand.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the mishnah was taught about a left-handed person, for whom the left is the dominant hand.
The Gemara objects that if the left-handed person's left is like everyone else's right, then writing with his right should not be liable.
Abaye answers that the mishnah refers to an ambidextrous person, who is equally skilled with both hands.

items.text: Attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Yosi
items.text_en: Attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Yosi
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov bar Bat Yaakov says the Mishnah is Rabbi Yosi's, who holds that liability for two letters is due to marking. The Gemara notes that since the latter clause is Rabbi Yosi, the first clause must also be his, so the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yosi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov bar Bat Yaakov attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Yosi, who holds that liability for two letters is due to marking (רושם).
The Gemara objects: since the latter clause is Rabbi Yosi, the first clause cannot be his.
The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yosi's, including the first clause.

items.text: Question on Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda only holds one liable for two letters that are two names, but not for two letters that are one name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda only holds one liable for two letters that are two names, but not for two letters that are one name.

items.text: Derivation from the verse 'me'achat'
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse 'me'achat'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 've'asah me'achat' that one is liable for a single act, but not necessarily for completing the entire object. It then limits this to a minimum of two letters or two threads.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְעָשָׂה מֵאַחַת' to teach that one is liable for a single act, not necessarily for completing the entire object.
The baraita limits the derivation: one is not liable for a single letter or thread, but only for a minimum of two letters or two threads (or one house in a sieve).

items.text: Opening dispute on writing liability
items.text_en: Opening dispute on writing liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the Tanna Kamma's view that one is liable only when writing a small name derived from a large one (e.g., 'Shem' from 'Shimon'). Rabbi Yehuda argues that even two letters that form a single name (like 'Shash' or 'Tat') render one liable.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that one is liable only when writing a small name derived from a large one, giving examples like 'Shem' from 'Shimon'.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that even writing two letters that form a single name, like 'Shash' or 'Tat', renders one liable.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's objection: liability for marking, not writing
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's objection: liability for marking, not writing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei argues that the liability is not for writing but for marking, as was done on the Tabernacle boards. Therefore, one is liable for scratching one mark on two boards or two marks on one board.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei objects that liability is not for writing but for marking, as was done on the Tabernacle boards, so one is liable for scratching one mark on two boards or two marks on one board.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's derivation from 'achat' and 'me'achat'
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's derivation from 'achat' and 'me'achat'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon derives from the verses that one is liable only for a melakhah that is substantial and enduring, not for a single letter or thread. The verse 'achat' and 'me'achat' together indicate a middle ground.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon opens by citing the verse 'וְעָשָׂה אַחַת' and the limiting term 'מֵאַחַת' to define the threshold of liability.
Rabbi Shimon raises the possibility that one might be liable only for completing an entire name, garment, or sieve, then rejects it with 'מֵאַחַת'.
Rabbi Shimon raises the opposite extreme that even a single letter or thread might suffice, then rejects it with 'אַחַת'.
Rabbi Shimon resolves that one is liable only for a melakhah that is substantial and enduring, a middle ground between the two extremes.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's principle: 'achat' and 'henah'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's principle: 'achat' and 'henah'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that sometimes one is liable once for all actions, and sometimes liable for each individually, based on the verses 've'asah achat' and 've'asah henah'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that the verses 've'asah achat' and 've'asah henah' teach that sometimes one is liable once for all actions, and sometimes liable for each individually.

items.text: Resolving Rabbi Yehuda's statement: his own vs. his teacher's
items.text_en: Resolving Rabbi Yehuda's statement: his own vs. his teacher's
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda's statement about two letters forming a name is not his own but from Rabban Gamliel, resolving a potential contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a potential contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the Mishnah that one is liable for writing two letters that form a name seems to conflict with another source.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah's statement is Rabbi Yehuda's own opinion, while the baraita attributes the same ruling to Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Clarifying Rabbi Shimon's position vs. Tanna Kamma
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabbi Shimon's position vs. Tanna Kamma
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon is more lenient or stringent than the Tanna Kamma, considering the case of 'alef alef' in 'a'azzerkha'. It concludes that Rabbi Shimon requires writing the entire name, but then corrects to 'the entire verse' based on a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Shimon's opinion is identical to the Tanna Kamma, and suggests a possible difference regarding the letters 'alef alef' in the word 'a'azzerkha', implying Rabbi Shimon might be more stringent.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon is lenient, requiring completion of the entire action for liability, contradicting the notion that he is stringent.
The Gemara initially answers that Rabbi Shimon teaches that one must write the entire name to be liable.
The Gemara rejects the first answer by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon explicitly says that the verse 'from one' precludes requiring the entire name.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting Rabbi Shimon's statement: one might think he must write the entire verse, but 'from one' teaches that writing less than a verse suffices.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei's opinion that the verse's phrasing teaches that sometimes one is liable for one sin-offering for all, and sometimes for each individually.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's principle explained by Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's principle explained by Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yosei's derivation: 'achat' and 'me'achat' teach about writing a small name from a large one; 'henah' and 'mehenah' teach about avot and toldot; 'achat shehi henah' and 'henah shehi achat' teach about combinations of intent and error.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Yosei's principle, citing the key terms 'achat', 'me'achat', 'henah', and 'mehenah'.

Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains the derivation: 'achat' teaches writing a complete name like Shimon, 'me'achat' teaches writing a small name like Shem from Shimon; 'henah' teaches primary categories (avot), 'mehenah' teaches subcategories (toldot); 'achat shehi henah' teaches cases of intent regarding Shabbat with error regarding labors, and 'henah shehi achat' teaches the reverse.

items.text: Question on the form of the letter mem
items.text_en: Question on the form of the letter mem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda questions whether a small name can be derived from a large one, noting that the mem in 'Shem' is closed while in 'Shimon' it is open. Rav Chisda answers that a closed mem made open is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda questions the derivation of a small name from a large one, noting that the mem in 'Shem' is closed while in 'Shimon' it is open.
Rav Chisda answers that a closed mem made open is valid, resolving the discrepancy.

items.text: Objection from baraita on letter forms
items.text_en: Objection from baraita on letter forms
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists many letter substitutions that invalidate a Torah scroll, including closed mems made open. This seems to contradict Rav Chisda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists many letter substitutions invalidating a Torah scroll, including closed mems made open, which seems to contradict Rav Chisda's ruling.

items.text: Resolution: Rav Chisda follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
items.text_en: Resolution: Rav Chisda follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rav Chisda's view aligns with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who derives a hint for the water libation from the varying spellings of 'niskehem' etc., implying that a closed mem made open is valid. The Gemara then infers that the reverse (open made closed) is also valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rav Chisda's view aligns with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who derives a hint for the water libation from the varying spellings of 'niskehem' etc.
The Gemara infers that just as an open mem made closed is valid, so too a closed mem made open is valid.

items.text: Final question on the comparison
items.text_en: Final question on the comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the cases are comparable, as an open mem made closed is different from a closed mem made open.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the cases are comparable, as an open mem made closed is different from a closed mem made open.

items.text: The miracle of the mem and samekh and the origin of final letters
items.text_en: The miracle of the mem and samekh and the origin of final letters
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mem and samekh on the tablets stood miraculously, and that the final forms of letters (מנצפך) were established by the prophets (צופים). It addresses the objection that prophets cannot innovate, concluding that the letters were forgotten and then re-established.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the mem and samekh on the tablets stood miraculously, as their central parts would have fallen out when carved.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the final letter forms (מנצפך) were established by the prophets (צופים).
The Gemara objects that a prophet cannot innovate a new halacha, citing the verse 'אלה המצות' (these are the commandments).
The Gemara resolves that the final letters already existed but were forgotten, and the prophets re-established them.
The Gemara objects again: even re-establishing forgotten letters would be an innovation, which a prophet cannot do.
The Gemara concludes that the letters were entirely forgotten and then re-established by the prophets, which is not considered innovation but restoration.

items.text: Rav Chisda's statements on the tablets
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's statements on the tablets
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the mem and samekh on the tablets stood miraculously, and that the writing on the tablets could be read from both sides, giving examples like נבוב/בובן.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the letters mem and samekh on the tablets stood miraculously.
Rav Chisda adds that the writing on the tablets could be read from both sides, giving examples like נבוב/בובן.

items.text: Children's homily on alef-beit
items.text_en: Children's homily on alef-beit
items.desc_en: The rabbis tell Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that children in the study hall said things not said even in Joshua's time: they interpret the letters alef to dalet as moral lessons about giving charity discreetly.

sub.text: The rabbis to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: The rabbis to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: The rabbis report to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that children today said things not said even in Joshua's time.
The children interpret alef to dalet as moral lessons about giving charity discreetly.

items.text: Interpretations of letters he to tzadi
items.text_en: Interpretations of letters he to tzadi
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues the homiletical interpretations: he-vav represents God's name; zayin-chet-tet-yud-kaf teaches reward; mem open and closed represent open and closed statements; nun bent and straight represent faithful bent and straight; samekh-ayin means support the poor; pe bent and straight represent open and closed mouth; tzadi bent and straight represent righteous bent and straight, with an added bent indicating the Torah was given with difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the letters he to nun: he-vav is God's name, zayin-chet-tet-yud-kaf teaches reward, mem open and closed represent open and closed statements, nun bent and straight represent faithful bent and straight.
The Gemara offers two interpretations for samekh-ayin: support the poor, or make signs in the Torah and acquire it.
The Gemara interprets pe bent and straight as open and closed mouth, and tzadi bent and straight as righteous bent and straight.
The Gemara questions why tzadi's interpretation is needed, since it seems identical to nun's interpretation of faithful bent and straight.
The Gemara answers that the Torah added an extra bend to tzadi, teaching that the Torah was given with difficulty (מנוד ראש, a shaking of the head).

items.text: Interpretation of kuf and reish
items.text_en: Interpretation of kuf and reish
items.desc_en: Kuf represents holy, reish represents wicked. The Gemara explains why the kuf turns its face from the reish, why its crown faces the reish, and why its leg is suspended, indicating that if the wicked repents, God will crown him and let him enter. This supports Resh Lakish's statement that one who comes to be impure is given an opening, but one who comes to be pure is helped.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the letter kuf (ק) represents holy (קדוש) and reish (ר) represents wicked (רשע), and interprets the shapes: the kuf turns its face away from the reish because God cannot look at the wicked; its crown faces the reish to indicate that if the wicked repents, God will crown him like Himself; and its leg is suspended to allow the penitent to enter.
The Gemara asks: why not let the penitent enter through the same opening (the suspended leg) rather than needing a separate entrance?
The Gemara notes that this interpretation supports Resh Lakish's statement that one who comes to be impure (טמא) is given an opening, but one who comes to be pure (טהר) is helped.

Resh Lakish cites the verse 'If to scoffers He scoffs, but to the humble He gives grace' (משלי ג:לד) to teach that one who comes to defile himself is given an opening, but one who comes to purify himself is assisted.

items.text: Interpretation of shin and tav
items.text_en: Interpretation of shin and tav
items.desc_en: Shin represents falsehood (שקר), tav represents truth (אמת). The Gemara explains why falsehood's letters are close together and truth's are far apart, and why falsehood stands on one leg while truth has stable foundations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the letter shin (ש) represents falsehood (שקר) and the letter tav (ת) represents truth (אמת).
The Gemara asks why the letters of falsehood (ש,ק,ר) are close together in the alphabet while the letters of truth (א,מ,ת) are far apart.
The Gemara answers that falsehood is common and truth is rare, so falsehood's letters are placed close together for convenience while truth's letters are spread out.
The Gemara asks why falsehood stands on one leg (the letter shin has one base) while truth has a solid foundation (the letter tav has a broad base).
The Gemara answers that truth stands firm and endures, while falsehood does not stand and ultimately collapses.

items.text: Atbash interpretations for the wicked and the righteous
items.text_en: Atbash interpretations for the wicked and the righteous
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an atbash (א״ת ב״ש) interpretation: for the wicked, the letters spell out their rejection; for the righteous, the letters spell out their reward and protection. It concludes with a dialogue between Gehinnom and God about the righteous and the nations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the atbash (א״ת ב״ש) interpretation for the wicked, where each letter pair spells out their rejection and punishment.

The Gemara shifts to the atbash (א״ת ב״ש) interpretation for the righteous, where the letters spell out their reward and protection, concluding with Gehinnom's complaint that the righteous are taken from it.
God responds to Gehinnom, explaining that He has mercy on the righteous because they are humble and truthful, and Gehinnom then asks to be sustained from the seed of Sheth.

sub.text: Holy One Blessed be He and Gehinnom
sub.text_en: Holy One Blessed be He and Gehinnom
sub.desc_en: God tells Gehinnom that the righteous will go to the Garden of Eden, and Gehinnom complains of exhaustion, so God offers it the nations of the world instead.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Liability for writing on Shabbat
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Liability for writing on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who writes two letters in one lapse is liable, listing valid writing materials (ink, gum, red dye, etc.) and surfaces (two walls at an angle, two tablets of a notebook that read together). It then lists cases of exemption: writing with non-durable substances, with the back of the hand, foot, mouth, or elbow; writing one letter adjacent to existing writing; writing over existing writing; intending to write a 'chet' but writing two 'zayins'; writing on two walls of a house or two pages of a notebook that do not read together. Rabbi Eliezer holds one liable for scratching on one's skin, while the Sages exempt. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira holds one liable for writing a single letter as a notarikon, while the Sages exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule that writing two letters in one lapse is liable, lists valid materials and surfaces, and then presents the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer (liable for scratching on skin) and the Sages (exempt).

The Mishnah lists cases of exemption: writing with non-durable substances, with unusual body parts, one letter adjacent to writing, writing over writing, intending a chet but writing two zayins, writing on two walls or pages that do not read together, and the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira (liable for a notarikon) and the Sages (exempt).

items.text: Gemara: Defining the writing materials
items.text_en: Gemara: Defining the writing materials
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms from the Mishnah: 'dyo' is ink, 'sam' is a type of gum, 'sikra' is red dye (called 'skarta'), 'komos' is gum, and 'kankantum' is a black ink used by shoemakers, as taught by Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins defining the writing materials from the Mishnah, explaining that 'dyo' is ink and 'sam' is a type of gum.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah explains that 'sikra' is called 'skarta' in Aramaic, a red dye.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Shmuel explains that 'kankantum' is the black ink used by shoemakers.

items.text: Gemara: Expanding 'any substance that makes a mark'
items.text_en: Gemara: Expanding 'any substance that makes a mark'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional substances are included by the Mishnah's phrase 'and any substance that makes a mark.' It answers that it includes the case taught by Rabbi Chananya: writing with 'mei tarya' (a type of liquid) and 'af'tza' (a plant) is valid. Rabbi Chiya adds that writing with 'avar' (lead), 'sh'chor' (black), and 'shichor' (another black substance) is also valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional cases the Mishnah's phrase 'and with anything that makes a mark' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes the baraitot of Rabbi Chananya (writing with מי טריא ואפצא is valid) and Rabbi Chiyya (writing with אבר, שחור, or שיחור is valid).
Rabbi Chiya adds that writing with 'avar' (lead), 'sh'chor' (black), and 'shichor' (another black substance) is also valid.

items.text: Gemara: The dispute about scratching on skin and the Ben Stada story
items.text_en: Gemara: The dispute about scratching on skin and the Ben Stada story
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts Rabbi Eliezer arguing to the Sages that scratching on skin should be liable, citing Ben Stada who brought sorcery from Egypt through scratching on his skin. The Sages respond that he was a fool, and no proof is brought from fools. The Gemara then discusses Ben Stada's identity: he is Ben Pandira, and Rav Chisda explains that 'Stada' refers to his mother's paramour, while 'Pandira' is her husband. It clarifies that his mother was Miriam, the women's hairdresser, and the name 'Stada' comes from a popular saying that she 'strayed' from her husband.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Eliezer's argument to the Sages that Ben Stada brought sorcery from Egypt through scratching on his skin, and the Sages' rejection that he was a fool and one does not bring proof from fools.
The Gemara digresses to clarify the identity of Ben Stada: Rav Chisda explains that 'Stada' refers to his mother's paramour, and the popular saying in Pumpedita is that she strayed from her husband.
The Sages reject the proof, saying Ben Stada was a fool and no evidence is brought from fools.
The Gemara questions the identification of Ben Stada, noting he is actually Ben Pandira.
Rav Chisda explains that 'Stada' refers to her paramour and 'Pandira' to her husband.
The Gemara questions whether her husband was actually Papus ben Yehuda.
The Gemara resolves that 'Stada' refers to his mother, who was Miriam the women's hairdresser.
The Gemara concludes with the popular saying in Pumpedita that she 'strayed' from her husband, explaining the name 'Stada'.

items.text: Gemara: Analyzing the case of writing one letter adjacent to writing
items.text_en: Gemara: Analyzing the case of writing one letter adjacent to writing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the tanna is for the Mishnah's ruling that writing one letter adjacent to existing writing is exempt. Rava bar Rav Huna says it is not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, because Rabbi Eliezer holds that one who completes a single thread on a loom is liable, implying he would also hold one liable for adding a single letter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna is the source of the Mishnah's ruling that writing one letter adjacent to existing writing is exempt.
Rava bar Rav Huna answers that it is not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that even one letter on a woven fabric is liable.

items.text: Gemara: Analyzing the case of writing over existing writing
items.text_en: Gemara: Analyzing the case of writing over existing writing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the tanna is for the Mishnah's ruling that writing over existing writing is exempt. Rav Chisda says it is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, as a baraita teaches: if one needed to write God's name but intended to write 'Yehuda' and omitted the 'dalet', Rabbi Yehuda says he can pass his quill over it to sanctify it, implying that writing over existing writing is effective. The Sages disagree, saying the name is not from the chosen (i.e., it is not valid).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna is the source of the Mishnah's ruling that writing over existing writing is exempt.
Rav Chisda answers that it is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who in a baraita holds that one can sanctify a name written as 'Yehuda' by adding a dalet, while the Sages disagree.

A baraita is cited: if one needed to write God's name but intended to write 'Yehuda' and omitted the 'dalet', Rabbi Yehuda says he can pass his quill over it to sanctify it, implying that writing over existing writing is effective.
The Sages disagree, saying the name is not from the chosen (i.e., it is not valid).

items.text: Gemara: The case of completing a book or garment with one letter or thread
items.text_en: Gemara: The case of completing a book or garment with one letter or thread
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who writes a single letter and thereby completes a book, or weaves a single thread and thereby completes a garment, is liable. The Gemara asks who the tanna is. Rava bar Rav Huna says it is Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that completing a single thread on a loom is liable. Rav Ashi says it could even be the Rabbis, because completing is different (i.e., the final act of completion is significant).

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who writes a single letter and completes a book, or weaves a single thread and completes a garment, is liable.
The Gemara asks which Tanna is the source of this baraita.
Rava bar Rav Huna answers that it is Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one letter on a woven fabric is liable.
Rav Ashi objects that even if one says it is the Rabbis, completing a book is different.

items.text: Gemara: Writing one letter in Tiberias and one in Tzippori
items.text_en: Gemara: Writing one letter in Tiberias and one in Tzippori
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami says that one who writes one letter in Tiberias and another in Tzippori is liable, because it is writing, just lacking proximity. The Gemara objects from the Mishnah which exempts one who writes on two walls of a house or two pages of a notebook that do not read together. The Gemara resolves: there, the writing lacks an act of bringing together (the walls or pages are separate), but here, no act of bringing together is lacking (the letters are already in their proper place).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that one who writes one letter in Tiberias and one in Tzippori is liable, as it is writing but merely lacking proximity.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that writing on two walls of a house that do not read together is exempt.
The Gemara resolves that there the writing lacks an act of bringing together, while here it does not lack an act of bringing together.

items.text: Gemara: The case of correcting a single letter
items.text_en: Gemara: The case of correcting a single letter
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who corrects a single letter is liable. The Gemara questions this: if writing a single letter is exempt (as per the Mishnah), how can correcting one letter be liable? Rav Sheshet explains: we are dealing with a case where one removed the roof of a 'chet' and made it into two 'zayins' (i.e., he created two letters from one). Rava explains: one removed the crown of a 'dalet' and made it into a 'resh' (i.e., he changed one letter into another).

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who corrects a single letter is liable.
The Gemara questions the contradiction: writing one letter is exempt, yet correcting one letter is liable.
Rav Sheshet answers that we are dealing with a case where one removed the roof of a חית and made it into two זיינים.
Rava answers alternatively that it is a case where one removed the crown of a דלת and made it into a ריש.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of a contradiction about writing two letters
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of a contradiction about writing two letters
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between a mishnah that holds one liable for writing two letters and a baraita that exempts. The distinction is based on whether the letters require additional ornamentation (זיוני) or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the mishnah holds one liable for writing two letters, but a baraita exempts.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between letters that require ornamentation (זיוני) and those that do not.

items.text: Notarikon interpretations of biblical verses
items.text_en: Notarikon interpretations of biblical verses
items.desc_en: Various amoraim expound on the concept of notarikon (acronymic interpretation) from the Torah. Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra deriving it from the verse about Abraham, and other rabbis offer their own notarikon readings of verses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who writes a single letter as a notarikon (acronym) is liable according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira, but the Sages exempt him.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra derives the concept of notarikon from the Torah, interpreting the verse 'כי אב המון גוים נתתיך' as an acronym for multiple attributes.
Rabbi Yochanan offers his own notarikon interpretation of the word 'אנכי' as 'אנא נפשי כתבית יהבית' (I Myself wrote and gave).
The Rabbis interpret 'אנכי' as 'אמירה נעימה כתיבה יהיבה' (pleasant speech, writing, giving).
