Some interpret 'אנכי' in reverse order as 'יהיבה כתיבה נאמנין אמריה' (giving, writing, faithful are its words).
Beit Rabbi Natan interprets 'כי ירט הדרך לנגדי' as 'יראה, ראתה, נטתה' (feared, saw, turned aside).
Beit Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'כרמל' as 'כר מלא' (a full field).
Rav Acha bar Yaakov interprets 'והוא קללני קללה נמרצת' as 'נואף הוא, מואבי הוא, רוצח הוא, צורר הוא, תועבה הוא' (an adulterer, a Moabite, a murderer, an enemy, an abomination).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak interprets 'מה נדבר ומה נצטדק' as 'נכונים אנחנו, צדיקים אנחנו, טהורים אנחנו, דכים אנחנו, קדושים אנחנו' (we are correct, righteous, pure, humble, holy).

items.text: Mishnah: Writing two letters in two unawarenesses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Writing two letters in two unawarenesses
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who writes two letters in two separate unawarenesses—one in the morning and one in the evening—is liable according to Rabban Gamliel but exempt according to the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who writes two letters in two lapses (morning and evening) is liable according to Rabban Gamliel, but the Sages exempt.

items.text: Gemara: The dispute over partial measure awareness
items.text_en: Gemara: The dispute over partial measure awareness
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabban Gamliel holds that there is no awareness for a partial measure (so the two acts combine), while the Sages hold that there is awareness for a partial measure (so they do not combine).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what principle do they disagree?

The Gemara explains: Rabban Gamliel holds that there is no awareness for a half-measure (so two half-measures combine), while the Sages hold that there is awareness for a half-measure (so they do not combine).

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter 'HaBoneh'
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter 'HaBoneh'
items.desc_en: The standard formula marking the end of the chapter 'HaBoneh' is recited.

sub.desc_en: The scribe marks the end of the chapter 'HaBoneh'.

items.text: Mishnah: Weaving and sewing measures
items.text_en: Mishnah: Weaving and sewing measures
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents disputes about the minimum measure for weaving: Rabbi Eliezer says three threads at the start and one on the fabric, while the Sages say two threads in both cases. It also lists other liable acts: making two loops, sewing two stitches, and tearing to sew two stitches.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah cites Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that one who weaves three threads at the start and one on the fabric is liable, while the Sages say the measure is two threads both at the start and end.
The mishnah lists additional liable actions: making two heddle loops, sewing two stitches, and tearing with intent to sew two stitches.

items.text: Gemara: Resolving the contradiction between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Gemara: Resolving the contradiction between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yitzchak taught 'two' threads, while the mishnah says 'three'. It resolves by distinguishing between thick threads (אלימי) and thin threads (קטיני), with two explanations offered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yitzchak taught 'two' threads, but our mishnah says 'three'.
The Gemara resolves: one refers to thick threads, the other to thin threads, with two explanations about structural stability and recognizability.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between thick threads (אלימי) and thin threads (קטיני).
One explanation: for thick threads, three do not unravel but two do; for thin threads, even two do not unravel.
Another explanation: for thin threads, three are noticeable but two are not; for thick threads, even two are noticeable.

items.text: Two baraitot supporting Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.text_en: Two baraitot supporting Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one supports Rabbi Eliezer's view (three threads at the start), and the other supports the Sages' view (two threads). Each baraita also discusses the measure for the selvage (שפה).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Eliezer's view: one who weaves three threads at the start and one on the fabric is liable, and the baraita concludes anonymously in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer.
A second baraita is cited that supports the Sages' view: one who weaves two threads on the warp and on the woof is liable, and it concludes anonymously in accordance with the Sages.

items.text: Gemara: Definitions of 'Nirim' and 'Keiros'
items.text_en: Gemara: Definitions of 'Nirim' and 'Keiros'
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the mishnah's phrase 'two loops in the heddles' (בנירים) as two in the heddle and one in the rod. Rav explains 'Keiros' as a type of weaving tool (מצוביתא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is meant by 'in the heddles' (בנירים)?
Abaye explains: two loops in the heddle rod and one in the heddle.
The Gemara asks: What is meant by 'in the kairos' (בקירוס)?
Rav explains: it refers to a weaver's comb (מצוביתא).

items.text: Gemara: Why the mishnah repeats sewing and tearing
items.text_en: Gemara: Why the mishnah repeats sewing and tearing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah repeats 'the one who sews two stitches' and 'the one who tears' when they were already taught in the list of primary labors. It explains that the repetition is to introduce the new case of tearing in anger or for the dead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah repeats 'the one who sews two stitches' when it was already taught in the list of primary labors.
The Gemara answers that the repetition is necessary to introduce the continuation about tearing.
The Gemara further asks why 'the one who tears' is also repeated, since it too was already listed among the primary labors.
The Gemara answers that the repetition of tearing is to introduce the new case of tearing in anger or for the dead.
The Gemara asks how one can find a case of tearing in order to sew two stitches that is not already covered by the primary labor.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who tears in anger, for his dead, or any destroyer is exempt; but one who destroys with intent to repair is liable according to the measure of repair. It lists the measures for laundering, carding, dyeing, weaving, and sewing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who tears in anger, for his dead, or any destroyer is exempt, but one who destroys with intent to repair is liable according to the measure of repair, listing the measures for laundering, carding, dyeing, weaving, and sewing.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: a baraita says one who tears in anger, in mourning, or for his dead is liable. It resolves that the Mishnah refers to a stranger's death, while the baraita refers to one's own relative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that one who tears in anger, in mourning, or for his dead is liable and has fulfilled the obligation of tearing.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah refers to a non-relative's death, while the baraita refers to one's own relative.

items.text: Refining the exemption: exceptions for a sage, a worthy person, and at the moment of death
items.text_en: Refining the exemption: exceptions for a sage, a worthy person, and at the moment of death
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the Mishnah says 'his dead' (מֵתוֹ), implying his own. It answers that it refers to those not obligated to mourn, but if the deceased is a sage, a worthy person, or if one is present at the moment of death, one is liable to tear. Each case is supported by a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah says 'his dead' (מֵתוֹ), implying the deceased is his own relative, contradicting the earlier resolution.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah indeed refers to one's own dead, but only to those who are not obligated to mourn (e.g., a minor or a wicked person).
The Gemara cites a baraita that if the deceased is a sage, everyone is considered his relative and must tear, but the Mishnah's exemption applies only when the deceased is not a sage.
The Gemara cites a baraita that if the deceased is a worthy person (אָדָם כָּשֵׁר), one is liable to tear, but the Mishnah's exemption applies only when the deceased is not worthy.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that one standing at the moment of death is liable to tear, but the Mishnah's exemption applies only when one is not present at that moment.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction regarding tearing in anger
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction regarding tearing in anger
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the contradiction about tearing in anger, resolving it by attributing the Mishnah (exempt) to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an unnecessary labor is exempt, and the baraita (liable) to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds it is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the case of 'his dead' is resolved, but the contradiction regarding 'in his anger' remains.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who exempts for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה (unnecessary labor), while the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable.
The Gemara explains the principle: Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה (unnecessary labor), while Rabbi Shimon exempts.

items.text: Objection and defense: tearing in anger as a constructive act
items.text_en: Objection and defense: tearing in anger as a constructive act
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda only holds liable for a constructive act, but tearing in anger is destructive. Rabbi Avin answers that it is constructive because it calms his temper. A baraita then condemns such anger as akin to idolatry, citing a verse about the evil inclination.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda's liability applies only to a constructive act, not a destructive one.
Rabbi Avin answers that tearing in anger is also constructive, as it gives satisfaction to his evil inclination.
The Gemara objects: is such behavior permitted?
A baraita teaches that one who tears in anger is like an idol worshipper, as the evil inclination escalates.
Rabbi Avin cites a verse to prove that the evil inclination is a 'strange god' within a person.

items.text: Permissible destruction for imposing household discipline
items.text_en: Permissible destruction for imposing household discipline
items.desc_en: The Gemara qualifies that tearing in anger is permitted when done to instill fear in one's household, citing examples of rabbis who broke vessels for this purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's exemption applies when one tears to instill fear in his household.
Examples are given of rabbis who broke objects to instill fear in their households.

items.text: Aggadic teachings on mourning and eulogizing
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings on mourning and eulogizing
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents aggadic statements: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi says God stores tears for the worthy; Rav Yehuda says one who delays eulogizing a sage deserves to die; Rabbi Yochanan says such a person will not live long. A challenge from the verse about Joshua's elders is answered, and a new teaching begins about a brother who dies.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi teaches that God stores the tears shed for a worthy person in His treasury, citing the verse 'נֹדִי סָפַרְתָּה...' (You have stored my tears in Your bottle).
Rav Yehuda says that one who delays eulogizing a sage deserves to be buried alive, as the mountain 'גָּעַשׁ' (shook) to kill the elders who delayed burying Joshua.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that one who delays eulogizing a sage will not live long, as a measure-for-measure punishment, citing the verse 'בְּסַאסְּאָה בְּשַׁלְּחָהּ תְּרִיבֶנָּה' (in measure, when you send her forth, you will contend with her).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba challenges Rabbi Yochanan by citing the verse that the elders who outlived Joshua 'הֶאֱרִיכוּ יָמִים' (lengthened days), contradicting the claim that delaying eulogy shortens life.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse only says they lengthened 'יָמִים' (days), not 'שָׁנִים' (years), so the punishment of shortened years still applies.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ יְמֵיכֶם' (that your days may be multiplied) also says 'יָמִים' (days), yet it clearly promises long life.
The Gemara resolves that a ברכה (blessing) is different and can include years, unlike the punishment context.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba introduces a new teaching from Rabbi Yochanan about a brother who dies, shifting the topic.

items.text: Opening statement on mourners and damage
items.text_en: Opening statement on mourners and damage
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a general rule that all mourners are concerned, and then states that all who cause damage on Shabbat are exempt, setting the stage for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general rule that all mourners are concerned for each other, and then states that all who cause damage on Shabbat are exempt.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's baraita and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's baraita and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu teaches a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan stating that all who cause damage are exempt except for one who wounds and one who burns. Rabbi Yochanan rejects this, saying that wounding and burning are not in the Mishnah, and if they were, they would be explained as cases where the person needs the blood for his dog or the ashes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu teaches a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan stating that all who cause damage are exempt except for one who wounds (חובל) and one who burns (מבעיר).
Rabbi Yochanan dismisses the baraita, telling Rabbi Avahu to teach outside, because wounding and burning are not in the Mishnah.

Rabbi Yochanan nevertheless concedes that if the Mishnah included such cases, wounding would only be liable if one needs the blood for his dog, and burning would only be liable if one needs the ashes.

items.text: Reconciliation of Mishnah and baraita
items.text_en: Reconciliation of Mishnah and baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can say all who cause damage are exempt, and answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda while the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon. It then explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: since the Torah needed to permit circumcision (which involves wounding), it implies that wounding in general is liable; similarly, since the Torah forbade burning in the case of a priest's daughter, it implies that burning in general is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can state that all who cause damage are exempt, given the baraita that includes wounding and burning as exceptions.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, while the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: since the Torah needed to permit circumcision (which involves wounding), it implies that wounding in general is liable.
The Gemara continues Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: since the Torah forbade burning in the case of a priest's daughter, it implies that burning in general is liable.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda would respond, and answers that in those cases (circumcision and burning a priest's daughter) the person is performing a constructive act, as per Rav Ashi's principle: just as one is liable for repairing a vessel or cooking dyes, so too one is liable for these acts because they are constructive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda would respond to the proof from circumcision and the burning of a priest's daughter.
The Gemara answers that in those cases the person is performing a constructive act (מתקן), not a destructive one.
Rav Ashi supports this by equating the constructive acts of circumcision and burning a priest's daughter to repairing a vessel or cooking dyes, all of which are liable.

items.text: Shiur for laundering
items.text_en: Shiur for laundering
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the shiur (measurement) for the act of laundering: Rav Yosef demonstrates it as folded, while Rav Chiyya bar Ami demonstrates it as spread out.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the shiur (measurement) for the act of laundering.
Rav Yosef demonstrates the shiur as folded (כפול).
Rav Chiyya bar Ami demonstrates the shiur as spread out (פשוט).

items.text: Mishnah on trapping
items.text_en: Mishnah on trapping
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one who traps a bird into a dovecote or a deer into a house is liable, while the Sages say a bird into a dovecote is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehuda's position: one who traps a bird into a dovecote or a deer into a house is liable.
The Sages counter: trapping a bird into a dovecote is exempt (and the Mishnah cuts off here, implying the deer case is disputed or omitted).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for trapping a deer that is in a garden, courtyard, or enclosure, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that not all enclosures are equal: if the animal lacks trapping (i.e., it is not fully confined), one is exempt; if it does not lack trapping, one is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: trapping a deer in an enclosure is liable, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies that liability depends on whether the animal lacks trapping (is not fully confined).

items.text: Gemara's contradiction between baraitot
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction between baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two baraitot regarding trapping from enclosures on Yom Tov: one permits trapping animals and birds but not fish, while another prohibits all. It initially resolves the contradiction for animals by attributing the rulings to Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, but struggles with birds, suggesting a distinction between a roofed and unroofed enclosure, which is rejected because a house is roofed yet birds in a house are not considered trapped.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Yom Tov that permits trapping animals and birds from enclosures but prohibits fish.
The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing another baraita that prohibits trapping any animal, bird, or fish from enclosures on Yom Tov.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for animals by attributing the permissive baraita to the Rabbis and the prohibitive one to Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara notes that the contradiction for birds remains unresolved.
The Gemara suggests that the contradiction for birds can be resolved by distinguishing between a roofed enclosure (where birds are considered trapped) and an unroofed one (where they are not).
The Gemara rejects this distinction because a house is roofed, yet both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis agree that a bird in a house is not considered trapped unless it is in a cage.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's resolution with צפור דרור
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's resolution with צפור דרור
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by explaining that the discussion involves the צפור דרור (a type of bird that does not accept dominion), which lives in a house as if in a field. He then extends the resolution to animals, distinguishing between a large enclosure and a small one.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by explaining that the discussion involves the צפור דרור (sparrow-like bird) which does not accept dominion, and then extends the resolution to animals by distinguishing between large and small enclosures.

items.text: Definitions of large and small enclosures
items.text_en: Definitions of large and small enclosures
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi provides multiple definitions for a small enclosure: one where one can run after the animal and catch it in a single lunge, or where the shadows of the walls meet, or where there are no hiding places. A large enclosure is the opposite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the precise definitions of a large enclosure versus a small enclosure.

Rav Ashi provides three criteria: a small enclosure is one where one can catch the animal in a single run, or where the shadows of the walls overlap, or where there are no hiding places; otherwise it is large.
Rav Ashi alternatively defines a small enclosure as one where the shadows of the walls meet; otherwise it is large.
Rav Ashi further defines a small enclosure as one without hiding places; otherwise it is large.

items.text: Halakhic ruling and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Abaye questions whether this implies there is a dispute, and Rav Yosef retorts that the ruling is merely a practical matter, not a theoretical debate.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports in the name of Shmuel that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling.
Abaye questions whether stating the הלכה implies that the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel actually disagree.
Rav Yosef dismisses Abaye's question, asking what practical difference it makes, and Abaye retorts that one should complete the study properly rather than being dismissive.

items.text: Baraita on trapping a blind, sleeping, or sick deer
items.text_en: Baraita on trapping a blind, sleeping, or sick deer
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one is liable for trapping a blind or sleeping deer, but exempt for a lame, old, or sick deer. Abaye questions the distinction, and Rav Sheshet resolves it by distinguishing between a feverish sick person (liable) and one sick from cold (exempt).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who traps a blind or sleeping deer is liable, but trapping a lame, old, or sick deer is exempt.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef to explain the distinction between the two categories, and Rav Yosef answers that the first group is capable of being trapped (can be chased), while the second is not.
Abaye objects by citing another baraita that states a sick deer is liable, contradicting the first baraita.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a sick deer due to fever (which is weak and not easily trapped) and one due to cold (which is still capable of being trapped).

items.text: Baraitot on trapping locusts and insects
items.text_en: Baraitot on trapping locusts and insects
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding liability for trapping locusts, wasps, and mosquitoes. Another baraita distinguishes between trapping locusts in dew (exempt) and in heat (liable), with Elazar ben Mahabai adding an exemption if they come in streams. The Gemara questions whether Elazar's ruling applies to the first or second clause.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir holds one liable for trapping locusts, crickets, wasps, and mosquitoes on Shabbat, while the Sages rule based on whether the species is normally trapped.
Another baraita is cited: trapping locusts during dew is exempt, during heat is liable; Elazar ben Mahabai adds that even during heat, if they come in swarms, one is exempt.
The Gemara asks whether Elazar ben Mahabai's statement refers to the first clause (exemption during dew) or the second clause (liability during heat).
The Gemara resolves the question by citing the full baraita, showing that Elazar ben Mahabai's statement applies even to the second clause (during heat).

items.text: Mishnah: Trapping a deer by locking it in a house
items.text_en: Mishnah: Trapping a deer by locking it in a house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a deer enters a house and one person locks the door, he is liable; if two lock it, they are exempt; if one cannot lock it and two do, they are liable; Rabbi Shimon exempts in the latter case.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of trapping a deer by locking it in a house: one person locking alone is liable, two locking are exempt unless one could not do it alone, and Rabbi Shimon exempts in all cases.

items.text: Gemara: Trapping a lion
items.text_en: Gemara: Trapping a lion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba quotes Shmuel that one who traps a lion on Shabbat is not liable until he brings it into its enclosure (גורזקי).

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who traps a lion on Shabbat is not liable until he brings it into its enclosure (גורזקי).

items.text: Mishnah: Sitting at the entrance and trapping
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sitting at the entrance and trapping
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses cases where one person sits at the entrance without filling it, and a second fills it (the second is liable); or the first fills it and the second sits beside him (the first is liable, the second exempt), comparing it to locking one's house for security and finding a deer trapped inside.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses cases where one person sits at the doorway without filling it, and a second fills it: the second is liable; if the first fills it and the second sits beside him, the first remains liable even if he later leaves, analogous to locking one's house for protection and finding a deer trapped inside.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on trapping a bird under one's wing
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on trapping a bird under one's wing
items.desc_en: Rav states that if a bird enters under one's wing, he may sit and guard it until dark. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges this from a mishnah about two people sitting at a doorway, where the second is exempt but possibly forbidden. The Gemara concludes that the second is exempt and permitted, as shown by the analogy of locking one's house and finding a deer inside.

sub.text: Rav via Rabbi Abba and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav via Rabbi Abba and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav states that if a bird enters under one's wing on Shabbat, one may sit and guard it until dark.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects from a mishnah where the second person is exempt but possibly forbidden, challenging Rav's lenient ruling.
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the mishnah means exempt and permitted, as shown by the analogy of locking one's house and finding a deer inside.
The Gemara concludes that the second person is indeed exempt and permitted, supporting Rav's ruling.
An alternative version presents Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's own statement that the mishnah supports Rav, concluding that the second is exempt and permitted.

items.text: Shmuel's rule: three exceptions to 'exempt but forbidden'
items.text_en: Shmuel's rule: three exceptions to 'exempt but forbidden'
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that all exemptions on Shabbat are exempt but forbidden, except for three cases which are exempt and permitted: trapping a bird under one's wing, lancing a boil, and catching a snake. Each is supported by a mishnah or baraita showing permission.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states a general rule: all exemptions on Shabbat are exempt but forbidden, except for three specific cases which are exempt and permitted.
The Gemara identifies the first exception (trapping a bird under one's wing) and proves it is permitted from the mishna's analogy of locking a house and finding a deer inside.
The Gemara identifies the second exception (lancing a boil to drain fluid) and proves it is permitted from the mishna allowing a needle to remove a thorn.
The Gemara identifies the third exception (catching a snake to prevent a bite) and proves it is permitted from the mishna allowing overturning a bowl on a scorpion to prevent a sting.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter (hadran)
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter (hadran)
items.desc_en: This segment marks the end of the chapter 'HaOreg' with the formulaic 'hadran alach haOreg'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard closing formula 'we return to you, chapter HaOreg'.

items.text: Mishnah: Eight creeping things and their laws
items.text_en: Mishnah: Eight creeping things and their laws
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that for the eight creeping things mentioned in the Torah, one who traps or wounds them is liable. For other vermin, wounding is exempt, and trapping is liable only if done for a need. Animals and birds in one's domain are exempt from trapping but liable for wounding.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the eight creeping creatures (שמונה שרצים) mentioned in the Torah, stating that trapping or wounding them incurs liability, while for other vermin, wounding is exempt and trapping is liable only if done for a need; for one's own domesticated animals and birds, trapping is exempt but wounding is liable.

items.text: Gemara: Who holds that these creeping things have skin?
items.text_en: Gemara: Who holds that these creeping things have skin?
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah that the eight creeping things have skin. Shmuel identifies the tanna as Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who says they have skins. Rabba bar Rav Huna argues that even the Rabbis agree regarding Shabbat, though they disagree regarding impurity. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita where the Rabbis explicitly disagree on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah's statement that one who wounds these creeping things is liable, implying they have skin.
The Gemara asks which tanna holds this position.
Shmuel identifies the tanna as Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that these eight creeping things have skin.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri explicitly states that the eight creeping things have skins.
Rabba bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav argues that even the Rabbis could agree regarding Shabbat, though they disagree regarding impurity.
Rabba bar Rav Huna explains that the Rabbis only disagree with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding טומאה (ritual impurity), where the verse includes their skins, but regarding Shabbat they concede.
The Gemara objects: Do the Rabbis really not disagree regarding Shabbat?
The Gemara cites a baraita where the Rabbis explicitly disagree with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding Shabbat, stating there is no skin.

items.text: Dispute about the skin of the eight creeping creatures
items.text_en: Dispute about the skin of the eight creeping creatures
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate the meaning of the Mishnah's statement about the skin of the eight creeping creatures. Rava clarifies that the skin is not considered like flesh for impurity only regarding those listed by the Sages, implying that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's additional creatures are impure. Rav Adda bar Matna resolves the contradiction by stating that the Sages disagree only regarding impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: If the Mishnah says 'for those the Sages listed,' then on the contrary, those listed have no skin at all (since the Sages exclude them from the skin rule).
Abaye explains that the Mishnah means: the skin is not considered distinct from flesh except for those the Sages did NOT list (i.e., Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's additional creatures).
Rava objects: the Mishnah explicitly says 'for those the Sages listed,' not 'for those they did not list.'
Rava explains: the Mishnah means that the skin does not transmit impurity like flesh except for those the Sages listed (i.e., the eight creeping creatures).
The Gemara asks: Does this imply that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri considers those not listed by the Sages as impure (i.e., their skin transmits impurity)?
The Gemara objects with a baraita: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri explicitly says that the eight creeping creatures have skins but do not transmit impurity.
Rav Adda bar Matna resolves: the Sages' statement applies only to matters of impurity — the skin is not considered flesh for impurity regarding those the Sages listed.

items.text: Question about Shabbat liability
items.text_en: Question about Shabbat liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Sages also disagree regarding Shabbat, citing a baraita that states one is liable for trapping or wounding the eight creeping creatures that have skin. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri agrees that these eight have skin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Sages also disagree regarding Shabbat, citing a baraita that states one is liable for trapping or wounding the eight creeping creatures that have skin, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri agrees that these eight have skin.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the first tanna is Rabbi Yehuda, who follows the 'type' (גישתא) of the creature. The Sages who disagree with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding impurity agree with him regarding Shabbat. The Gemara notes that the text should read 'the words of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and his dispute'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi identifies the first tanna as Rabbi Yehuda, who follows the 'type' (גישתא) of the creature.
Cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda classifies the lizard (לטאה) by its type, supporting the identification.
Rav Ashi explains that the Sages who dispute Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding impurity agree with him regarding Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that the text should read 'the words of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and his dispute' rather than just 'the words of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri'.
The Gemara resolves that the correct reading is 'the words of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and his dispute'.

items.text: Source for a wound that does not heal
items.text_en: Source for a wound that does not heal
items.desc_en: Levi asks Rabbi about the source for a wound that does not heal. The answer is derived from the verse about the leopard's spots, comparing it to the skin of a Cushite that does not change.

sub.desc_en: Levi asks Rabbi for the biblical source of a wound that does not heal.
Rabbi cites the verse about the Cushite's skin and the leopard's spots as the source.
The Gemara objects that the word 'חֲבַרְבֻּרֹתָיו' cannot mean spots, because then the verse should have said 'נָמֵר גְּווֹנָיו'.
The Gemara resolves that the verse compares the wound to the skin of a Cushite, which does not change color back, so the wound does not heal.

items.text: Who is the tanna for killing other vermin?
items.text_en: Who is the tanna for killing other vermin?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who kills other vermin is liable. Rabbi Yirmeya identifies this as Rabbi Eliezer's view, who holds that killing a louse is like killing a camel. Rav Yosef objects that the Sages only disagree regarding lice, which do not reproduce, but agree regarding other vermin that do.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna behind the Mishnah's ruling that one who kills other vermin is liable.
Rabbi Yirmeya identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that killing a louse on Shabbat is like killing a camel.
Rav Yosef objects that the Sages only disagree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding lice, which do not reproduce, but agree regarding other vermin that do reproduce.

items.text: Derivation from rams
items.text_en: Derivation from rams
items.desc_en: Both Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages derive their positions from the rams of the Tabernacle. Rabbi Eliezer focuses on the taking of life, while the Sages focus on reproduction. Abaye questions whether lice do not reproduce, citing that God sustains even lice eggs, but the Gemara explains that 'lice eggs' is just a name for a type of creature.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that both Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages derive their positions from the rams of the Tabernacle, with Rabbi Eliezer focusing on the taking of life and the Sages on reproduction.
Abaye questions whether lice do not reproduce, citing that God sustains even lice eggs.
The Gemara explains that 'lice eggs' is just a name for a type of creature, not actual eggs, so lice do not reproduce.

items.text: Flea reproduction and trapping
items.text_en: Flea reproduction and trapping
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the distinction, noting that fleas reproduce and yet Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree about trapping a flea. Rav Ashi explains that their dispute is about trapping, not killing; regarding killing, even Rabbi Yehoshua agrees one is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that mentions 'droplets and lice eggs', implying lice do reproduce, contradicting the earlier claim.
The Gemara raises a second objection: a flea reproduces, yet Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree about trapping it, implying a dispute exists despite reproduction.
Rav Ashi resolves that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua concerns trapping (צידה), not killing; regarding killing, even Rabbi Yehoshua agrees one is liable.

items.text: Tanna for trapping for need
items.text_en: Tanna for trapping for need
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who traps for a need is liable. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies this as Rabbi Shimon's view, who holds that an unnecessary labor is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who traps for a need is liable.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה (unnecessary labor) is exempt.

items.text: Alternative version: lancing a boil
items.text_en: Alternative version: lancing a boil
items.desc_en: Some teach the same attribution regarding lancing a boil: if to make an opening, liable; if to drain pus, exempt. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says this is Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: Presents an alternative version of the teaching, applying the same distinction to lancing a boil: if to make an opening, liable; if to drain pus, exempt.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Identifies the Tanna of this alternative version as Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה (unintended labor) is exempt.

items.text: Alternative version: trapping a snake
items.text_en: Alternative version: trapping a snake
items.desc_en: Others teach the same attribution regarding trapping a snake: if to prevent it from biting, exempt; if for medicine, liable. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says this is Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: Introduces an alternative version of the teaching, applied to trapping a snake: if to prevent it from biting, exempt; if for medicine, liable.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies the Tanna of this ruling as Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה (labor not needed for its own sake) is exempt.

items.text: Liability for removing a fish from the sea
items.text_en: Liability for removing a fish from the sea
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who removes a fish from the sea is liable once a spot the size of a sela dries on it. Rabbi Yosei bar Avin adds that this includes between its fins. Rav Ashi clarifies that this includes even if it becomes slimy, not necessarily completely dry.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who removes a fish from the sea on Shabbat is liable once a spot the size of a sela (coin) dries on it.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin adds that the dried spot includes the area between the fish's fins.
Rav Ashi clarifies that the liability applies even if the fish becomes slimy, not necessarily completely dry.

items.text: Liability for removing a fetus from the womb
items.text_en: Liability for removing a fetus from the womb
items.desc_en: Mar bar Hamdurei in the name of Shmuel rules that one who reaches into an animal's womb and removes a fetus is liable. Rava explains the reason: just as one is liable for uprooting a thorn from a hedge because it is uprooting something from its growth, so too here. Abaye adds that one who uproots...

sub.text: Mar bar Hamdurei in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Mar bar Hamdurei in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Hamdurei citing Shmuel rules that one who reaches into an animal's womb and removes a fetus is liable on Shabbat.
Rava explains that the reason is analogous to uprooting a thorn from a hedge, which is liable because it is uprooting something from its growth.
Rava invokes Rav Sheshet's ruling that one who uproots a thorn from a hedge is liable for uprooting something from its growth.
Abaye begins to add a parallel case of uprooting, but the text cuts off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening discussion: pulling from a perforated pot
items.text_en: Opening discussion: pulling from a perforated pot
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that pulling a mushroom from a perforated pot is liable because it is considered uprooting from its place of growth, unlike a non-perforated pot where it is not considered attached.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that pulling a mushroom from a perforated pot is liable for uprooting from its place of growth.
Rav Oshaya objects by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a perforated and non-perforated pot regarding liability for uprooting.
The Gemara resolves that in the baraita the non-perforated pot is not the plant's place of growth, whereas here the perforated pot is.

items.text: Rav Huna: writing tefillin on bird skin
items.text_en: Rav Huna: writing tefillin on bird skin
items.desc_en: Rav Huna permits writing tefillin on the skin of a kosher bird. Rav Yosef questions the novelty, but Abaye explains that without Rav Huna, one might think the many holes in bird skin disqualify it; the Gemara notes that any hole through which ink passes is not considered a hole.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna permits writing tefillin on the skin of a kosher bird.
Rav Yosef questions the novelty, noting that the Mishnah already states that one who wounds a bird is liable, implying it has skin.
Abaye explains that Rav Huna teaches that despite the many holes in bird skin, any hole through which ink passes is not considered a hole, so tefillin may be written on it.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection from the verse 'biknafav'
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection from the verse 'biknafav'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges Rav Huna from the verse 'biknafav' which includes the skin of a bird for ritual impurity. If bird skin is considered skin, why would a verse be needed to include it? Abaye responds that it is indeed skin, and the Torah included it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects to Rav Huna's ruling by citing the verse 'biknafav' (in its wings) that includes the skin of a bird for ritual impurity, arguing that if bird skin is considered skin, why would a verse be needed to include it?
Abaye responds that bird skin is indeed considered skin, and the Torah included it through the verse.

items.text: Alternative version: Rabbi Zeira's proof
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rabbi Zeira's proof
items.desc_en: In an alternative version, Rabbi Zeira argues that the verse 'biknafav' proves bird skin is skin, because otherwise why would the Torah need to include it? Abaye counters that even if it is not skin, the verse is needed to teach that despite its many cracks, it is not repulsive.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces an alternative version of the discussion, attributing the proof to Rabbi Zeira.
Rabbi Zeira argues that if bird skin were not considered skin, the verse 'biknafav' would be unnecessary to include it.
Abaye responds that even if bird skin is not considered skin, the verse is needed to teach that despite its many cracks, it is not repulsive and is fit for tefillin.

items.text: Mar bar Ravina's inquiry about fish skin
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravina's inquiry about fish skin
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether tefillin may be written on the skin of a kosher fish. Rav Nachman responds that this depends on whether Elijah will come and clarify if the fish's foul odor can be removed.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina asks Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether tefillin may be written on the skin of a kosher fish.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's initial answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's initial answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds cryptically that the answer depends on whether Elijah will come and clarify.
The Gemara asks what Rav Nachman meant by his cryptic response.
The Gemara objects that it is obvious fish have skin, as evidenced by the Mishnah that fish skin and bones convey protection in a tent with a corpse.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Nachman's doubt was whether the fish's foul odor (זוהמא) can be removed from its skin, a matter requiring Elijah's clarification.

items.text: The story of Shmuel, Karna, and Rav
items.text_en: The story of Shmuel, Karna, and Rav
items.desc_en: Shmuel and Karna sit by the river; Shmuel predicts Rav's arrival. Karna asks Rav the source for writing tefillin only on kosher animal hide. Rav cites 'lema'an tihyeh torat Hashem befikha' — from what is permitted in your mouth. Rav also derives that blood is red from the verse about Moab, and that circumcision is performed on the organ that produces fruit. Karna is cursed by Rav for causing him distress, and Shmuel later cares for Karna.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel and Karna sit by the river; Shmuel predicts Rav's arrival and sends Karna to attend to him.

Karna asks Rav for the source that tefillin may only be written on kosher animal hide; Rav answers with the verse 'לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה תּוֹרַת ה׳ בְּפִיךָ' (from what is permitted in your mouth) and also derives that blood is red from the Moab verse.

Karna asks for the source that circumcision is performed on the organ that produces fruit; Rav answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'ערלתו' (his foreskin) to 'ערלתו' in the context of fruit trees, rejecting alternative interpretations.
Rav curses Karna for causing him distress, but Shmuel later cares for Karna; Rav's curse that Karna's children should not survive is fulfilled.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the source for circumcision
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the source for circumcision
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita: Rabbi Yoshiya derives the place of circumcision from a verbal analogy of 'orlato', while Rabbi Nathan says it is unnecessary because the verse 'et besar orlato' indicates the place where male and female are distinguishable.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a question about the source for the place of circumcision, and presents Rabbi Yoshiya's derivation from a verbal analogy of 'ערלתו' (his foreskin).
Rabbi Nathan argues that no verbal analogy is needed, because the verse 'ואת בשר ערלתו' explicitly indicates the place where male and female are distinguishable.

items.text: Baraita on materials for tefillin
items.text_en: Baraita on materials for tefillin
items.desc_en: The baraita states that tefillin may be written on the hide of a kosher animal, including neveilot and treifot of kosher species, and are wrapped in their hair and sewn with their sinews. They may not be written on the hide of a non-kosher animal.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that tefillin may be written on the hide of a kosher animal, including neveilot and treifot of kosher species, and are wrapped in their hair and sewn with their sinews, but not on the hide of a non-kosher animal.

items.text: The Baityosi's question and Rabbi Yehoshua's parable
items.text_en: The Baityosi's question and Rabbi Yehoshua's parable
items.desc_en: A Baityosi asks Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi why tefillin cannot be written on non-kosher hide. Rabbi Yehoshua cites 'lema'an tihyeh torat Hashem befikha'. The Baityosi then asks why neveilot and treifot are permitted, and Rabbi Yehoshua gives a parable of two condemned men, one killed by the king and one by an executioner. The Baityosi further asks why they may not be eaten, and Rabbi Yehoshua cites the prohibition of neveilah.

sub.desc_en: A Baityosi asks Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi for the source that tefillin may not be written on the hide of a non-kosher animal, and Rabbi Yehoshua cites the verse 'לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה תּוֹרַת ה׳ בְּפִיךָ' (so that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth), deriving that it must come from something permitted in your mouth.

The Baityosi objects: if the rule is 'from what is permitted in your mouth,' then why are tefillin permitted on the hide of neveilot (carcasses) and treifot (torn animals), which are forbidden to eat?

Rabbi Yehoshua answers with a parable of two condemned men, one killed by the king and one by an executioner, explaining that the one killed by the king is more praiseworthy — so too, neveilot and treifot, though forbidden to eat, are from a kosher species and thus their hide is permitted for tefillin.
The Baityosi presses further: if the hide is permitted, why not permit eating the meat itself?
Rabbi Yehoshua rejects the objection by citing the explicit Torah prohibition 'לֹא תֹאכְלוּ כׇל נְבֵלָה' (you shall not eat any carcass), showing that the meat is forbidden regardless.
The Baityosi concedes, saying 'קָאלוֹס' (well said / beautiful), accepting Rabbi Yehoshua's answer.

items.text: Mishnah: no making helmei on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: no making helmei on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not make helmei (a type of medicinal compress) on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition against making helmei (a medicinal compress) on Shabbat.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Permitted and prohibited brine
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Permitted and prohibited brine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not make concentrated brine on Shabbat, but may make diluted brine to dip bread or put into a dish. Rabbi Yosei argues that both are the same action (הילמי), and then defines permitted brine as one where oil is added first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one may not make concentrated brine on Shabbat, but may make diluted brine for dipping bread or adding to a dish; Rabbi Yosei objects that both are the same action (הילמי), and then defines permitted brine as one where oil is added first.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah and Rabbi Yosei's intent
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah and Rabbi Yosei's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah distinguishes between concentrated and diluted brine. It then debates whether Rabbi Yosei's statement is to prohibit or permit, with Rav Yehuda and Rabbah disagreeing, and Rabbi Yochanan concluding that Rabbi Yosei prohibits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by its ambiguous phrasing.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that the Mishnah means: one may not make concentrated brine, but may make diluted brine.
The Gemara raises a question: does Rabbi Yosei intend to forbid or permit the diluted brine?
Rav Yehuda argues that Rabbi Yosei permits, because the Mishnah does not use the phrase 'Rabbi Yosei forbids'.
Rabbah objects that the Mishnah's later clause 'these are permitted brine' implies that Rabbi Yosei forbids the diluted brine.
Rabbah concludes that Rabbi Yosei forbids, and Rabbi Yochanan agrees.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yosei's prohibition
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yosei's prohibition
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly states Rabbi Yosei prohibits both concentrated and diluted brine, arguing that if one is prohibited and the other permitted, people would mistakenly think that a large amount of work is prohibited but a small amount is permitted. The baraita then defines permitted brine as one where oil and salt or oil and water are mixed first.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbah's conclusion: it states the same rule about concentrated and diluted brine, and Rabbi Yosei argues that both are forbidden, then defines permitted brine as one where oil and salt or oil and water are mixed, but not water and salt לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Definition of concentrated brine (מי מלח עזין)
items.text_en: Definition of concentrated brine (מי מלח עזין)
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'strong brine' (מי מלח עזין) as that in which an egg floats, and Abaye quantifies it as two-thirds salt and one-third water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a mnemonic sign for the following three topics: strong brine, radish, and etrog.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ḥaviva
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ḥaviva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ḥaviva teaches a baraita that one may not make strong brine on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks for the definition of 'strong brine' (מי מלח עזין).

sub.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef bar Abba both define strong brine as any brine in which an egg floats.
Abaye quantifies the brine as two-thirds salt and one-third water.

items.text: Salting radish and egg on Shabbat
items.text_en: Salting radish and egg on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the prohibition of salting radish and egg on Shabbat, with Rav Ḥizkiya distinguishing between radish (prohibited) and egg (permitted). Rav Naḥman recounts his practice of not salting radish but dipping it in salt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what such strong brine is used for.
Rabbi Avahu answers: for making murias (a fish brine).

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chaviva
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chaviva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Chaviva teaches that one may not salt radish or egg on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Chizkiya in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Chizkiya in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Chizkiya in the name of Abaye distinguishes: radish is forbidden, egg is permitted.

Rav Nachman recounts his evolving practice with radish: initially he salted it, then stopped because Shmuel said salt ruins its pungency, and after hearing that in the West they salt 'kishrei kishrei', he now only dips it in salt rather than salting it directly.

items.text: Properties of etrog, radish, and egg
items.text_en: Properties of etrog, radish, and egg
items.desc_en: A baraita states that etrog, radish, and egg, if not for their outer peel, would never leave the intestines.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chaviva
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chaviva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Chaviva teaches that etrog, radish, and egg, without their outer peel, would never pass through the intestines.

items.text: The Dead Sea and its unique properties
items.text_en: The Dead Sea and its unique properties
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that no man ever sank in the Dead Sea. Rav Yosef questions this, and Abaye explains that even a man who sinks in all other waters does not sink there. The Gemara then discusses using its water for washing on Shabbat, which is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi says: no man ever drowned in the Dead Sea.
Rav Yosef objects: the statement is inverted — a man didn't drown, but a wall did? That makes no sense.
Abaye explains that Rav Dimi meant: not only does a wall not drown anywhere, but even a man who drowns elsewhere does not drown in the Dead Sea.
The Gemara asks what practical halachic difference this makes.

sub.text: Story of Rabin and Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.text_en: Story of Rabin and Rabbi Yirmeya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara illustrates with a story: Rabin asked Rabbi Yirmeya whether one may wash with Dead Sea water on Shabbat, and he permitted it.

items.text: Medical treatments on Shabbat: wine and saliva for the eye
items.text_en: Medical treatments on Shabbat: wine and saliva for the eye
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether one may apply wine or saliva to the eye on Shabbat. One opinion permits wine on the outside of the eye but prohibits it inside, while another prohibits even tasteless saliva on the outside. The Gemara concludes that Shmuel heard one ruling from his father and the other from Levi, but it is unknown which is which.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may squeeze and open (the eye) on Shabbat, and Ravin replies that he did not hear about this but heard about a similar case.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Mattana and Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Mattana and Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports two conflicting traditions in the names of Avuh deShmuel and Levi: one permits wine on the outside of the eye but prohibits it inside, and the other prohibits even tasteless saliva on the outside.
The Gemara concludes that Shmuel heard one ruling from his father and the other from Levi, but it is unknown which is which.

items.text: Soaking a cloth in wine on Shabbat eve for the eye
items.text_en: Soaking a cloth in wine on Shabbat eve for the eye
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva reports in Shmuel's name that one may soak a cloth (קילורין) on Shabbat eve and place it on the eye on Shabbat. However, when Mar Ukva saw someone blinking excessively, he limited the permission. Rabbi Yannai requests the remedy, but Shmuel's response is that a cold drop in the morning and washing hands and feet in hot water in the evening are better than any remedy.

sub.text: Mar Ukva in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Mar Ukva in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva in the name of Shmuel rules that one may soak a collyrium cloth on Shabbat eve and apply it to the eyes on Shabbat without concern.
Bar Levai sees Mar Ukva squeezing and opening his eyes with the cloth and objects that Shmuel did not permit such active manipulation.

sub.text: Rabbi Yannai's request and Mar Ukva's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's request and Mar Ukva's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai asks Mar Ukva to send him some of Shmuel's collyrium; Mar Ukva responds that a cold drop in the morning and washing hands and feet in warm water in the evening are better than any collyrium.
A baraita supports this: Rabbi Muna in the name of Rabbi Yehuda says the same thing about the cold drop and washing.
A supporting baraita is cited in which Rabbi Muna says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that a cold drop in the morning and washing hands and feet in the evening are better than any remedy.

items.text: Prohibition of touching certain body parts on Shabbat
items.text_en: Prohibition of touching certain body parts on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who touches the eye, nose, mouth, ear, wound, penis, or anus should have his hand cut off, as these actions are prohibited on Shabbat due to the concern of causing bleeding or other violations.

sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva says: a hand that touches the eye, nose, mouth, ear, wound, penis, or anus should be cut off.

items.text: Permitted and forbidden uses of eye-paint (pukh) on Shabbat
items.text_en: Permitted and forbidden uses of eye-paint (pukh) on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a free woman who insists on washing her hands three times, and Rabbi Yochanan states that eye-paint (pukh) removes a tear, increases eyelash hair, and is permitted for a princess. A supporting baraita from Rabbi Yosei is cited.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists forbidden uses of hands on Shabbat, and Rabbi Natan adds that a free woman insists on washing her hands three times.
Rabbi Yochanan states that eye-paint (pukh) removes a tear, increases eyelash hair, and is permitted for a princess.
A supporting baraita cites Rabbi Yosei repeating the same statement about eye-paint.

items.text: Herbs without healing concern (ein bahen mishum refu'ah)
items.text_en: Herbs without healing concern (ein bahen mishum refu'ah)
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva citing Shmuel, Rav Yosef, and Rav Sheshet list specific herbs (alim, kusbarta, keshut) that are permitted on Shabbat because they are not considered healing. Rav Yosef questions kusbarta, and Rav Sheshet adds gargira as beneficial. Mar Ukva further permits all types of keshut except taruza.

sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva in the name of Shmuel permits alim (leaves) on Shabbat because they are not considered healing.
Rav Yosef adds that kusbarta (coriander) is also permitted as it has no healing status.
Rav Sheshet adds that keshut (cucumbers) are also permitted as they are not considered healing.
Rav Yosef questions his own ruling, noting that kusbarta (coriander) is difficult even for him.
Rav Sheshet adds that gargira (a type of herb) is beneficial even for him, implying it is healing and thus prohibited.
Mar Ukva in the name of Shmuel permits all types of keshut (cucumbers) except taruza (a specific variety).

items.text: Roasted shirka and egg poultices; Ze'iri's principle
items.text_en: Roasted shirka and egg poultices; Ze'iri's principle
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda permits roasted shirka but forbids egg poultices. The story of Ze'iri's wife preparing such for Chiyya bar Ashi is told, and Ze'iri's general principle is cited: just as one may pour clear wine and water into a strainer on Shabbat because it is not considered a prohibited act, so too here the poultice is not a prohibited act.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that roasted shirka (a type of gourd) is permitted on Shabbat, but egg poultices are forbidden.

sub.text: Story about Ze'iri and Chiyya bar Ashi
sub.text_en: Story about Ze'iri and Chiyya bar Ashi
sub.desc_en: The story is told that Ze'iri's wife prepared such a poultice for Chiyya bar Ashi, who refused to eat it, and she rebuked him saying that she had prepared it for his teacher (Ze'iri) who ate it.

Ze'iri's general principle is cited: just as one may pour clear wine and water into a strainer on Shabbat without concern, so too here the poultice is not considered a prohibited act because it is intended for consumption.

items.text: Wine for a wound; vinegar vs. wine; Rava's leniency for the pampered
items.text_en: Wine for a wound; vinegar vs. wine; Rava's leniency for the pampered
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva permits compressing a wounded hand or foot with wine on Shabbat. A dilemma is raised about vinegar (challa). Rav Hillel reports that in Rav Kahana's academy they said vinegar is forbidden. Rava states that the pampered people of Mechoza are healed even by wine, implying it is permitted for them.

sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva permits compressing a wounded hand or foot with wine on Shabbat without concern.
The Gemara raises a dilemma about whether vinegar (חַלָּא) is permitted for compressing a wound.
Rav Hillel reports that in Rav Kahana's academy they ruled that vinegar is forbidden.
Rava states that the pampered people of Mechoza are healed even by wine, implying it is permitted for them.

items.text: Ravina's incident: back of hand/foot is different
items.text_en: Ravina's incident: back of hand/foot is different
items.desc_en: Ravina visited Rav Ashi and saw him compressing the back of his foot with vinegar. Ravina questioned him based on Rav Hillel's ruling, but Rav Ashi answered that the back of the hand and foot are different. An alternative version has Rav Ashi using wine, and Ravina citing Rava's leniency for the pampered, but Rav Ashi again distinguishes the back of the hand/foot, citing Rav Adda bar Matna's ruling that they are like a life-threatening wound and override Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Ravina visited Rav Ashi and saw him compressing the back of his foot with vinegar.
Ravina questioned Rav Ashi based on Rav Hillel's ruling that vinegar is forbidden.
Rav Ashi answered that the back of the hand and foot are different.
An alternative version has Rav Ashi using wine, and Ravina citing Rava's leniency for the pampered.
Rav Ashi again distinguishes the back of the hand/foot, citing Rav Adda bar Matna's ruling that they are like a life-threatening wound and override Shabbat.

items.text: Contradiction about the Great Sea for ritual bathing
items.text_en: Contradiction about the Great Sea for ritual bathing
items.desc_en: A baraita permits bathing in certain waters (Gerar, Hamtan, Asya, Tiberias) but not in the Great Sea, steeping water, or the Sea of Sodom. A contradictory baraita permits the Great Sea. Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the first to Rabbi Meir and the second to Rabbi Yehuda, citing a Mishnah about their dispute. Rabbi Yosei adds that all seas purify by flowing water but are invalid for zavim, metzoraim, and sanctifying hatat water. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists permitted and forbidden waters for bathing: Gerar, Hamtan, Asya, and Tiberias are permitted, but the Great Sea, steeping water, and the Sea of Sodom are not.
The gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita permits bathing in the Great Sea, conflicting with the first baraita's prohibition.

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Meir (who invalidates all seas as a mikveh) and the second to Rabbi Yehuda (who validates the Great Sea), citing a Mishnah about their dispute.
Rabbi Yosei adds that all seas purify by flowing water (זוחלין) but are invalid for zavim, metzoraim, and sanctifying hatat water.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects to Rabbi Yosei's statement, though the objection is not elaborated in the surviving text.

items.text: Resolving contradictions about bathing waters on Shabbat
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions about bathing waters on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between cases where one delayed (אישׁתַּהִי) and where one did not. The Gemara then questions this resolution, citing a baraita that permits bathing in Tiberias water and brine even without delay, and concludes that the distinction between good and bad parts of the Great Sea and between delayed and not delayed applies to brine as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute about the Mediterranean Sea regarding impurity and purity can be applied to the laws of שבת (Sabbath).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases where one delayed in the water (אישְׁתַּהִי) and where one did not.
The Gemara objects that if the later baraita is about not delaying, then even bathing in מי משׁרה (water in which flax was soaked) should be permitted.
A baraita is cited that permits bathing in the waters of Tiberias, מי משׁרה (water in which flax was soaked), and the Sodom Sea, even with wounds, provided one does not delay; delaying is prohibited.

The Gemara resolves the contradictions: for the Great Sea, the distinction is between good and bad parts; for מי משׁרה (water in which flax was soaked), the distinction is between delaying and not delaying.

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted and forbidden foods for healing on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted and forbidden foods for healing on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not eat אֵיזֹבְיוֹן (a type of hyssop) on Shabbat because it is not food for healthy people, but one may eat יוֹעֶזֶר and drink אַבּוּבְרוֹאֶה. All foods may be eaten for healing, and all drinks may be drunk, except for מי דקלים and כוס עיקרים, which are for jaundice. However, one may drink מי דקלים for thirst and anoint with שמן עיקרים not for healing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists which foods and drinks are permitted or forbidden for healing on Shabbat, distinguishing between those that are regular food and those used specifically as remedies.

items.text: Identifying אֵזוֹב and אֵיזֹבְיוֹן
items.text_en: Identifying אֵזוֹב and אֵיזֹבְיוֹן
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef identifies אֵזוֹב as אברתה בר המג and אֵיזֹבְיוֹן as אברתה בר הינג. Ulla says it is מָרְוָא חִיוָּרָא, and Rav Pappi says it is שׁוּמְשׁוּק. Rav Yirmeya from Difti supports Rav Pappi based on a Mishnah about hyssop having three stalks and three calyxes. The Gemara then explains that it is eaten for intestinal worms, with seven black dates, and is made from barley flour left for forty days.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef identifies אֵזוֹב (hyssop) as 'אברתה בר המג' and אֵיזֹבְיוֹן (hyssop-like plant) as 'אברתה בר הינג'.
Ulla identifies it as מָרְוָא חִיוָּרָא (white marva), and when brought to him at Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's house, he confirms it is the hyssop of the Torah.
Rav Pappi identifies it as שׁוּמְשׁוּק (shumshuk), and Rav Yirmeya from Difti supports him based on a Mishnah that hyssop has three stalks and three calyxes, which matches shumshuk.
The Gemara explains that this plant is eaten for intestinal worms (קוּקְאיָנֵי), prepared with seven black dates, and made from barley flour left for forty days.

items.text: Identifying יוֹעֶזֶר and remedies for jaundice
items.text_en: Identifying יוֹעֶזֶר and remedies for jaundice
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies יוֹעֶזֶר as פותנק (a type of plant) eaten for jaundice, with seven white dates, and lists various preparations from different ingredients. If that fails, it recommends swallowing white תַחְלֵי, fasting, eating fatty meat on coals, sucking a bone, and drinking חַלָּא (though some say it harms the liver). As a last resort, one should scrape an aspen tree from top to bottom, boil it in beer, seal the openings, and drink it the next day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what יוֹעֶזֶר (the plant mentioned in the Mishnah) is.
The Gemara answers that יוֹעֶזֶר is פותנק (a type of plant).
The Gemara asks for what ailment this plant is eaten.
The Gemara answers that it is eaten for jaundice (אַרְקָתָא).
The Gemara asks with what accompaniment the plant is eaten.
The Gemara answers that it is eaten with seven white dates.
The Gemara asks from what ingredients the remedy is made.

The Gemara lists various preparations: from a certain plant and water on an empty stomach, from fatty meat, from beef, from nuts, from a type of legume, all on an empty stomach, followed by drinking water.
If the first remedy fails, the Gemara recommends swallowing white תַחְלֵי (a type of plant).
If that fails, the Gemara recommends fasting, then eating fatty meat on coals, sucking a bone, and drinking חַלָּא (a type of drink).
Some say that חַלָּא is not recommended because it is harmful to the liver.
As a last resort, the Gemara instructs scraping an aspen tree from top to bottom, boiling it in beer, sealing the openings, and drinking it the next day, because of the aspen's properties.

items.text: Identifying אַבּוּבְרוֹאֶה and remedies for dropsy
items.text_en: Identifying אַבּוּבְרוֹאֶה and remedies for dropsy
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies אַבּוּבְרוֹאֶה as חוּמַטְרִיָּא, a single rod, used for dropsy. If that fails, one should take five כְּלִילֵי and five cups of beer, boil them together until reduced, and drink. The mother of Rav Achadvoi bar Ami prepared this for a man, gave it to him, heated an oven, placed him inside, and he expelled a green substance like a thorn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what אַבּוּבְרוֹאֶה (the drink mentioned in the Mishnah) is, and answers that it is חוּמַטְרִיָּא (a single rod).
The Gemara further asks what חוּמַטְרִיָּא is, and answers that it is a single rod (used for a remedy).
The Gemara asks what the remedy is used for, and answers that it is for dropsy (גִילּוּיָא).
The Gemara provides an alternative remedy: take five כְּלִילֵי (crown-like herbs) and five cups of beer, boil them together until reduced, and drink.

sub.text: Story about the mother of Rav Achadvoi bar Ami
sub.text_en: Story about the mother of Rav Achadvoi bar Ami
sub.desc_en: The mother of Rav Achadvoi bar Ami prepared a single crown and cup of beer for a man, gave it to him, heated an oven, placed him inside, and he expelled a green substance like a thorn, demonstrating the remedy's effectiveness.

items.text: Various remedies for snakebite, scorpion sting, and dropsy
items.text_en: Various remedies for snakebite, scorpion sting, and dropsy
items.desc_en: Rav Avya recommends a quarter-log of milk from a white goat. Rav Huna bar Yehuda recommends a citron hollowed out, filled with honey, and placed in fire. Rabbi Chanina says urine of a forty-day-old child: a barley grain for a wasp, a quarter-log for a scorpion, half a quarter for dropsy, and a quarter even for witchcraft. Rabbi Yochanan says אניגרון, אבנגר, and תירייקה are good for both dropsy and witchcraft. For one who swallowed a snake, eat כְּשׁוּתָא with salt and run three mil. Rav Shimi bar Ashi saw a man who swallowed a snake, appeared as a horseman, ate כְּשׁוּתָא with salt and ran three mil, and the snake came out in pieces. Another version says Rav Shimi bar Ashi himself swallowed a snake, and Eliyahu appeared as a horseman. For one bitten by a snake, take the fetus of a white donkey, tear it open, and place it on the wound, provided it is not a treifa.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya recommends a quarter-log of milk from a white goat as a remedy.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda recommends hollowing out a citron, filling it with honey, placing it in fire, and eating it.
Rabbi Chanina prescribes urine of a forty-day-old child in varying amounts for wasp sting, scorpion sting, dropsy, and even witchcraft.
Rabbi Yochanan says אניגרון, אבנגר, and תירייקה are effective for both dropsy and witchcraft.
The gemara states that one who swallowed a snake should eat כְּשׁוּתָא with salt and run three mil.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi saw a man who swallowed a snake, appeared as a horseman, ate כְּשׁוּתָא with salt, ran three mil, and the snake came out in pieces.
An alternative version says Rav Shimi bar Ashi himself swallowed a snake, and Eliyahu appeared as a horseman to administer the same remedy.
The gemara states that for one bitten by a snake, take the fetus of a white donkey, tear it open, and place it on the wound, provided it is not a טריפה (ritually unfit animal).

items.text: Story of the snake that bit a scholar
items.text_en: Story of the snake that bit a scholar
items.desc_en: A story is told about a scholar from Pumbedita who was bitten by a snake. Abaye suggests that the snake was sent by the Rabbis as a punishment for the scholar's transgression, citing the verse about a snake biting one who breaks down a fence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara tells a story about a scholar from Pumbedita who was bitten by a snake after causing thirteen white donkeys to be declared טריפה (ritually unfit) and a lion ate another donkey.
Abaye suggests that the snake was sent by the Rabbis as a punishment, citing the verse 'וּפֹרֵץ גָּדֵר יִשְּׁכֶנּוּ נָחָשׁ' (one who breaks down a fence will be bitten by a snake).

The sages confirm Abaye's explanation, recounting that the scholar had violated a decree of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna forbidding bringing myrtle and palm branches to a wedding feast on a table, and was bitten by a snake and died.

items.text: Remedies for snake encounters
items.text_en: Remedies for snake encounters
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides various remedies for someone who has been encircled by a snake, bitten by a snake, or is being chased by a snake. It also gives advice for a woman who sees a snake and is unsure if it has taken an interest in her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy for someone encircled by a snake: go into water, place a palm branch on one's head, push the snake away, and when it rises, throw it into the water and escape.

The Gemara provides remedies for someone bitten by a snake: ride four cubits, jump over a log, cross a river, or at night sleep on a bed over four barrels with cats and pots, and for someone chased by a snake, run in a zigzag path.

items.text: Remedies for a woman with a snake inside her
items.text_en: Remedies for a woman with a snake inside her
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the remedy for a woman who has a snake inside her. It suggests a procedure involving placing her on barrels, burning fatty meat, and using a mixture of leeks and wine to lure the snake out, then burning it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what remedy is available for a woman who has a snake inside her, and suggests she engage in intercourse before it.
Some object that intercourse would only strengthen the snake's desire, making the situation worse.
Instead, she should take some of her hair and nails, throw them at the snake, and say 'I am menstruating' to repel it.

The Gemara prescribes a detailed procedure: seat her on barrels, burn fatty meat on coals, place leeks and wine nearby, and when the snake emerges, seize it with tongs and burn it in fire so it does not return.

items.text: Mishnah: All foods and drinks are permitted for healing
items.text_en: Mishnah: All foods and drinks are permitted for healing
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's statement that all foods and drinks are permitted for healing on Shabbat. It specifies that the Mishnah includes spleen for teeth and vetch for the bowels, and includes מי צלפין בחומץ. Ravina asks Rava about drinking urine on Shabbat, and Rava says it is not included because people do not drink it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all foods and drinks are permitted for healing on Shabbat, and the Gemara specifies that this includes spleen for teeth, vetch for bowels, and מי צלפין בחומץ (a certain brine in vinegar).
Ravina asks Rava whether drinking urine is permitted on Shabbat for healing.
Rava answers that the Mishnah's rule 'all drinks one may drink' excludes urine because people do not normally drink it.

items.text: Exception: מי דקלים
items.text_en: Exception: מי דקלים
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the exception of מי דקלים (palm water) from the Mishnah's list. It explains the dispute between those who say מי דקרים and those who say מי דקלים. Rabba bar Barona describes the location of the palm water, and Ulla says that Babylonian beer is better.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating the exception of מי דקלים (palm water) from the permitted drinks.
A baraita is cited, recording a variant version of the Mishnah that reads מי דקרים instead of מי דקלים.
The Gemara explains the two versions: מי דקרים means they pierce the gall bladder, and מי דקלים means they come from two palm trees.
The Gemara asks for the identity of מי דקלים (palm water).
Rabba bar Barona describes the location of the palm water: two palm trees in the West with a spring between them, and the effects of drinking successive cups.
Ulla states that Babylonian beer is better than palm water, provided one has not drunk it for forty days.

items.text: Recipe for זיתום המצרי
items.text_en: Recipe for זיתום המצרי
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef and Rav Pappa give recipes for זיתום המצרי, a medicinal drink. Rav Yosef says it is one-third barley, one-third safflower, and one-third salt.
