Rav Pappa says it is one-third wheat, one-third safflower, and one-third salt and cumin, with the mnemonic סיסאני. It is drunk between the lamb and the festival.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef gives his recipe for זיתום המצרי (Egyptian olive drink): one-third barley, one-third safflower, one-third salt.
Rav Pappa gives an alternative recipe: one-third wheat, one-third safflower, one-third salt and cumin, with the mnemonic סיסאני.
The gemara concludes that the drink is consumed between the lamb and the festival, and it has a regulating effect: it loosens a constipated person and constricts a loose one.

items.text: Recipe for כוס עקרין
items.text_en: Recipe for כוס עקרין
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the recipe for כוס עקרין, a medicinal drink. Rabbi Yochanan gives a recipe involving specific amounts of various ingredients. The drink is prepared differently for a זבה (a woman with a discharge) and for ירקונא (jaundice).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the nature of the 'cup of roots' (כוס עקרין) mentioned in the Mishnah.

Rabbi Yochanan provides a recipe for the cup of roots, specifying ingredients and their proportions, and distinguishes between its preparation for a זבה (woman with a discharge) and for ירקונא (jaundice).
The Gemara adds an alternative instruction: if the first method fails, one should bring three (additional units of the mixture).

items.text: Remedies for a woman with a discharge (zov)
items.text_en: Remedies for a woman with a discharge (zov)
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists a sequence of escalating remedies for a woman suffering from a persistent discharge (zov), starting with a drink of wine and a command to cease, and progressing through various potions, rituals, and charms, culminating in a specific hair treatment that guarantees a cure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins listing remedies for a woman with a discharge (zov), starting with a drink of wine and a command to cease.
The Gemara provides a second remedy: seating her at a crossroads and startling her.
The Gemara gives a third remedy: a potion of cumin, saffron, and fenugreek roots boiled in wine.
The Gemara offers a fourth remedy: sixty wicks of a wax candle boiled and drunk.
The Gemara gives a fifth remedy: a certain herb (פשיטנא) boiled in wine.
The Gemara provides a sixth remedy: a Roman rooster, roasted and taken with flax or vine wool.
The Gemara gives a seventh remedy: digging seven pits, roasting a shoot of an orlah tree, and moving her between pits.
The Gemara offers an eighth remedy: fine flour placed from her navel downward.
The Gemara gives a ninth remedy: an ostrich egg, roasted and taken with flax or vine wool.
The Gemara gives a tenth remedy: opening a barrel of wine in her name.
The Gemara concludes with a final remedy: a hair from a white donkey's hoof, which guarantees a permanent cure.

items.text: Remedies for jaundice (yarkona) and a story about Rabbi Acha bar Yosef
items.text_en: Remedies for jaundice (yarkona) and a story about Rabbi Acha bar Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides remedies for jaundice, including a drink of beer with certain ingredients, and then recounts that Rabbi Acha bar Yosef suffered from this ailment and was cured by Rabbi Kahana using a method involving a cloth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents remedies for jaundice (yarkona), including a drink of beer with certain ingredients, and recounts that Rabbi Acha bar Yosef suffered from this ailment and was cured by Rabbi Kahana using a method involving a cloth.

items.text: Additional remedies and a story about a traveler
items.text_en: Additional remedies and a story about a traveler
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues with more remedies for unspecified ailments, including a mixture of dates, clay, and wormwood, and a procedure involving a donkey foal. It then tells a story of a traveler who was cured by eating leeks from a certain place, and the subsequent healing of his garment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara prescribes a remedy of three measures of Persian dates, clay, and wormwood boiled in beer.
The Gemara prescribes a remedy using a donkey foal's blood placed on the head while guarding the eyes.
The Gemara prescribes a remedy of a fish head preserved in brine boiled in beer.
The Gemara prescribes a remedy of a thorny plant split and placed on the heart.
The Gemara prescribes a remedy of leeks from the beds of Meishar.

A traveler suffering from the ailment asked Ginna'i to take his cloak and give him leeks from Meishar, ate them, then borrowed back the cloak to sleep in it, and when he got up, small pieces fell from it.

items.text: Discussion on the permissibility of causing sterilization indirectly
items.text_en: Discussion on the permissibility of causing sterilization indirectly
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the remedy for jaundice that causes sterilization is permitted, citing a baraita that prohibits causing sterilization in humans. It resolves that the remedy is allowed because it is indirect (causes self-sterilization), citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle regarding a rooster, and concludes with a distinction from Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the remedy for jaundice (two [eggs?] in beer) that causes sterilization is permitted.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from a verse that causing סירוס (sterilization) in a human is forbidden.
The Gemara distinguishes: the prohibition applies only when one intends to cause sterilization, but here the remedy causes self-sterilization (מעצמו) indirectly.
Rabbi Yochanan's principle is cited: one who wants to sterilize a rooster may take its crest and it becomes sterilized by itself, showing indirect action is permitted.
Rav Ashi objects that the rooster case is not about sterilization but about a spirit of swelling (רָמוּת רוּחָא) that afflicts it, so the principle does not apply here.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a further statement from Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, likely to resolve the objection, but the text cuts off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening discussion on leavening and castration
items.text_en: Opening discussion on leavening and castration
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a general principle about leavening after leavening and castration after castration, citing verses. It then questions the case of an old man, leading to a discussion about women and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general principle that all agree one is liable for leavening after leavening and castration after castration, citing verses.
The Gemara questions the case of an old man, implying a difficulty with the previous principle.
Rabbi Yochanan objects, citing his own statement that certain things restored his youth, challenging the applicability to an old man.
The Gemara resolves that the case refers to a woman, not an old man.

sub.text: Gemara's question regarding Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.text_en: Gemara's question regarding Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection based on Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's view that the verse 'פרו ורבו' applies to both men and women, questioning what can be said in that case.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves an old woman or a barren woman, where the commandment of procreation does not apply.

items.text: Mishnah: Tooth and back pain remedies
items.text_en: Mishnah: Tooth and back pain remedies
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one with tooth pain may not gargle vinegar on Shabbat, but may dip food normally. For back pain, one may not apply wine and vinegar, but may apply oil, except rose oil. Rabbi Shimon says all Israelites are like royalty.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the rule for tooth pain: one may not gargle vinegar but may dip food normally, and if healed incidentally it is permitted.
The mishnah states the rule for back pain: one may not apply wine and vinegar but may apply oil, except rose oil.
The mishnah explains that royalty anoint with rose oil on wounds, as that is their normal practice even on weekdays.
Rabbi Shimon states that all Israelites are considered royalty, thereby permitting rose oil for everyone.

items.text: Gemara's question on vinegar for teeth
items.text_en: Gemara's question on vinegar for teeth
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Pappa challenges Rav Avahu: The mishnah implies vinegar is good for teeth, but a verse says vinegar is harmful. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between when there is a wound (healing) and when there is no wound (damaging), or between fruit vinegar and wine vinegar.

sub.text: Rav Acha Arikha (Rav Acha bar Pappa) to Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Rav Acha Arikha (Rav Acha bar Pappa) to Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Pappa challenges Rabbi Avahu: the mishnah implies vinegar is beneficial for teeth, yet the verse says vinegar is harmful to teeth like smoke to eyes.
Rabbi Avahu resolves: the verse refers to vinegar from fruit (harmful), while the mishnah refers to vinegar from leavened grain (beneficial).
An alternative resolution: both refer to grain vinegar; when there is a wound it heals, when there is no wound it loosens the teeth.

items.text: Dispute on gargling method
items.text_en: Dispute on gargling method
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the mishnah (which forbids gargling) and a baraita (which permits gargling and swallowing but not spitting). Abaye says the mishnah also refers to gargling and spitting. Rava distinguishes between before dipping (permitted) and after dipping (forbidden).

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions the mishnah's prohibition of gargling, citing a baraita that permits gargling and swallowing but forbids gargling and spitting.
Abaye explains that the mishnah also refers to gargling and spitting, consistent with the baraita.
Rava answers that even if the mishnah means gargling and swallowing, the baraita refers to before the meal (permitted) and the mishnah to after the meal (forbidden).

items.text: Rava's 'ho'il' principle
items.text_en: Rava's 'ho'il' principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that according to Rava's logic, if before dipping is permitted, after dipping should also be permitted due to the 'ho'il' principle. Rava's principle states that anything permitted on Shabbat is also permitted on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since before dipping is permitted, after dipping should also be permitted, because Rava holds the 'ho'il' principle.
Rava states that anything permitted on Shabbat is also permitted on Yom Kippur, due to the 'ho'il' principle.

items.text: Rava's retraction
items.text_en: Rava's retraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rava retracted from that 'ho'il' principle. It proves this from a baraita that allows all obligated in immersions to immerse on Yom Kippur, implying the principle was abandoned.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes that Rava retracted that principle, as a baraita permits all obligated in immersion to immerse normally on both Tisha b'Av and Yom Kippur, contradicting the 'הואיל (since it is permitted)' extension.
The Gemara questions how we know Rava retracted from that specific principle, suggesting he might have retracted from a different one.
The Gemara rejects this possibility as inconceivable.
A baraita is cited that all obligated in immersions may immerse as usual, even on Yom Kippur, which contradicts Rava's principle and shows he retracted from it.

items.text: Halakha like Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Halakha like Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Abba bar Zavda says in the name of Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara questions this, citing a statement from Rav Shimi bar Chiyya in the name of Rav about a certain type of oil.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda reports in the name of Rav that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon regarding rose oil.
The gemara questions whether Rav indeed holds like Rabbi Shimon, citing a conflicting statement from Rav Shimi bar Chiyya in Rav's name about a certain ointment.

sub.text: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiyya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a contradictory statement from Rav Shimi bar Chiyya in Rav's name regarding a certain type of oil (מסוכריא דנזייתא), implying Rav may not follow Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya: R' Shimon's position and the halakha
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya: R' Shimon's position and the halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction about R' Shimon's view regarding 'פסיק רישיה', then clarifies a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about the halakha. Rava explains that the halakha follows R' Shimon but not for his reason, and the Gemara explores what that means.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case of crushing medicine on a festival is forbidden even for Rabbi Shimon, because he concedes in a case of 'פסיק רישיה' (an inevitable consequence).
The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon, and a version without names also records this dispute.
Rava resolves the dispute by stating that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, but not for his reason.
The Gemara asks what it means that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon but not for his reason, and proposes that Rabbi Shimon permits healing oil while Rav forbids it.
The Gemara objects that Rav cannot hold that oil heals, because a baraita about princes anointing with rose oil implies that oil does heal.
The Gemara resolves that the difference is about availability: Rabbi Shimon permits even when rose oil is not commonly available, while Rav permits only where it is common.

items.text: Closing formula for the previous chapter
items.text_en: Closing formula for the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing phrase 'הדרן עלך' marks the end of the previous chapter, 'שמנה שרצים'.

sub.desc_en: The standard closing phrase marks the end of the previous chapter.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Knots for which one is liable
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Knots for which one is liable
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists knots that incur liability on Shabbat: the camel-driver's knot and the sailor's knot, and states that one is liable for tying and untying them. R' Meir exempts any knot that can be untied with one hand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the camel-driver's knot and the sailor's knot as liable for tying and untying on Shabbat, with Rabbi Meir exempting any knot that can be untied with one hand.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the camel-driver's and sailor's knots
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the camel-driver's and sailor's knots
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what these knots are, rejecting the possibility that they are the knots tied to the nose-ring or the oar, as those are not permanent knots. It concludes they are the knots of the nose-ring itself and the oar itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the camel-driver's and sailor's knots are, and rejects the possibility that they are the knots tied to the nose-ring or the oar, since those are not permanent knots.
The Gemara concludes that the knots are the knots of the nose-ring itself and the oar itself.

items.text: Gemara: R' Meir's opinion on a bow knot
items.text_en: Gemara: R' Meir's opinion on a bow knot
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi asks whether a bow knot (עניבה) is considered a knot according to R' Meir. The Gemara presents two possible reasons for R' Meir's exemption: either because it can be untied with one hand (which a bow knot can), or because it is not tight (but a bow knot is tight). The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi asks whether a bow knot (עניבה) is considered a knot according to R' Meir.
The Gemara suggests one possible reason for R' Meir's exemption: the knot can be untied with one hand, and a bow knot also meets that criterion.
The Gemara offers an alternative reason: R' Meir exempts knots that are not tight, but a bow knot is tight, so it would be prohibited.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Permitted knots
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Permitted knots
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists knots that are not liable like the camel-driver's or sailor's knot, including a woman tying her garment opening, hairnet strings, belt, sandal straps, wine and oil skins, and a meat pot. R' Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that one may tie a rope in front of an animal to prevent it from escaping. The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah first says these are not liable (implying prohibition), but then lists them as permitted even initially. It resolves that the Mishnah means there are knots that are not liable like those, and these are the examples.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists knots that are not liable like the camel-driver's or sailor's knot, including a woman tying her garment opening, hairnet strings, belt, sandal straps, wine and oil skins, and a meat pot; Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds that one may tie a rope in front of an animal to prevent it from escaping.
The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah first says these are not liable (implying prohibition), but then lists them as permitted even לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah means there are knots that are not liable like those, and these are the examples.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara on permitted knots
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara on permitted knots
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists knots that are prohibited but not liable for a sin-offering, and those that are permitted ab initio, such as a woman tying her cloak strings. The Gemara clarifies that the case of a cloak with two openings is included to prevent the assumption that one opening nullifies the other, and the case of net strings is included because a woman is careful about her hair and will untie rather than pull.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists knots that are prohibited but not liable for a sin-offering, and those that are permitted לכתחילה (the ideal standard), such as a woman tying her cloak strings.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to specify the case of a cloak opening, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a cloak with two openings, and the Mishnah teaches that one opening does not nullify the other.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to specify the case of net strings, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a loose net, and the Mishnah teaches that a woman is careful about her hair and will untie rather than pull.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot on sandal straps
items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot on sandal straps
items.desc_en: Three baraitot are cited regarding one who unties sandal straps on Shabbat: one says he is liable for a sin-offering, one says he is exempt but it is prohibited, and one says it is permitted ab initio. This creates an apparent contradiction between the rulings for sandals and for shoes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites three contradictory baraitot regarding one who unties sandal straps on Shabbat: one holds him liable for a sin-offering, one holds him exempt but prohibited, and one permits it ab initio.
The Gemara notes the apparent contradiction between the baraitot regarding both sandals and shoes.

items.text: Resolution of contradictions for shoes and sandals
items.text_en: Resolution of contradictions for shoes and sandals
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradictions: for shoes, the liability for a sin-offering applies to those with buckles, exemption but prohibition applies to those with straps, and permission applies to the people of Mehoza who tie loosely. For sandals, the liability applies to Arabian sandals with buckles, exemption to those with a heel-strap, and permission to a sandal used by two people, as illustrated by the story of Rav Yehuda and his child.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding shoes by distinguishing three types: those with buckles (liable for a sin-offering), those with straps (exempt but prohibited), and those of the people of Mehoza who tie loosely (permitted לכתחילה).

The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding sandals by distinguishing three types: Arabian sandals with buckles (liable), those with a heel-strap (exempt but prohibited), and a sandal used by two people (permitted לכתחילה).
The Gemara illustrates the permitted sandal with the story of Rav Yehuda, who shared a sandal with his child, and Abaye ruled that such a sandal is liable for a sin-offering if tied on Shabbat.

items.text: Abaye's question and Rav Yehuda's response
items.text_en: Abaye's question and Rav Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: Abaye questions Rav Yehuda: if a sandal used by two people is permitted, why did he rule that it is liable for a sin-offering? Rav Yehuda explains that since he himself sometimes uses it, it is considered his vessel, but Abaye counters that if so, it should be permitted ab initio.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yehuda: if a sandal used by two people is only פטור אבל אסור (exempt but forbidden), why did you rule it is חייב חטאת (liable for a sin-offering)?
Rav Yehuda explains that since he himself sometimes uses the sandal on weekdays, it is considered his personal vessel, making its use on Shabbat a full-fledged violation.
Abaye counters that if the sandal is indeed Rav Yehuda's personal vessel, then using it on Shabbat should be מוּתָּר לְכַתְּחִילָּה (permitted ab initio), not liable for a sin-offering.

items.text: Practical rulings for a broken sandal strap
items.text_en: Practical rulings for a broken sandal strap
items.desc_en: Two incidents are recounted: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Avahu what to do when his sandal strap breaks on Shabbat, and is told to wrap a moist reed around it. Abaye asks Rav Yosef the same question and is told to leave it. The Gemara explains the difference: in Rabbi Yirmeya's case, the sandal was not guarded (it might fall off), while in Abaye's case it was guarded. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's resolution of a dispute implies the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.text: Narrative: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Avahu what to do when his sandal strap breaks on Shabbat, and is told to wrap a moist reed around it.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef the same question and is told to leave the broken sandal.
The Gemara explains the difference: in Rabbi Yirmeya's case the sandal was not guarded (might fall off), while in Abaye's case it was guarded.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's resolution of a dispute implies the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Sages regarding a broken sandal
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Sages regarding a broken sandal
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if both ears or both loops of a sandal are broken, it is pure; if only one is broken, it is impure. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between the inner and outer ear. Ulla or Rabbah bar bar Chanah says that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that the same dispute applies to Shabbat but not to chalitza. The Gemara analyzes this: if the dispute is like the Sages, then for Shabbat it is a vessel, but for chalitza it is not; if like Rabbi Yehuda, then for Shabbat it is not a vessel, but for chalitza it is. The Gemara resolves that the statement means that the halakha for chalitza follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that a sandal with a broken outer ear is still a vessel for chalitza.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding the impurity status of a sandal with broken ears or loops.

sub.text: Ulla / Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ulla / Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the same dispute applies to Shabbat but not to chalitza.
The Gemara asks: according to which opinion (Sages or Rabbi Yehuda) did Rabbi Yochanan apply the dispute to Shabbat but not to chalitza?
The Gemara objects that if the dispute follows Rabbi Yehuda, then for Shabbat the sandal is not a vessel, but for chalitza it is, yet a left sandal on the right foot is valid for chalitza.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement means the halakha for chalitza follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that a sandal with a broken outer ear is still a vessel for chalitza, unlike the Sages.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about a vessel that is not considered a vessel for its purpose applies here, given his own statement that the halakha follows an anonymous mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the vessel is considered a vessel for its purpose in this case, distinguishing between its general status and its specific function here.

items.text: Citing the mishnah about a sandal with broken straps
items.text_en: Citing the mishnah about a sandal with broken straps
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah stating that if one strap of a sandal is broken and repaired, it remains impure with midras impurity; if the second is broken and repaired, it is pure from midras but impure from contact with midras. The Gemara assumes this applies to both the inner and outer strap, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing a mishnah about a sandal with broken straps, arguing that the mishnah applies equally to inner and outer straps, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's view.

items.text: Distinguishing inner and outer straps
items.text_en: Distinguishing inner and outer straps
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the mishnah specifically refers to the inner strap, not the outer one. Rav Yitzchak ben Yosef explains the mishnah as referring to a sandal with four straps to avoid contradicting Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishnah specifically refers to the inner strap, not the outer one, and questions what the outer strap's status would be.
The Gemara objects that if the mishnah only discusses the inner strap, it should have explicitly distinguished between inner and outer straps.
Rav Yitzchak ben Yosef resolves the contradiction by explaining that the mishnah refers to a sandal with four straps, so that Rabbi Yochanan's position is not contradicted.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on Rabbi Yehuda's halakha
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on Rabbi Yehuda's halakha
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's consistency, as he earlier reconciled a mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda's view. The Gemara resolves that there are two different amora'im explaining Rabbi Yochanan's position.

sub.text: Ravin's report via Rav Chanan bar Abba in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Ravin's report via Rav Chanan bar Abba in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's consistency, since he earlier reconciled a mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda's view, implying he agrees with Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara resolves that there are two different amora'im explaining Rabbi Yochanan's position, so the contradiction is only apparent.

items.text: Rabbi Chizkiya's question and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Chizkiya's question and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chizkiya asks about a vessel that is punctured multiple times and sealed, eventually reaching the size of a pomegranate. Rabbi Yochanan responds by citing the sandal case, where repairing the second strap introduces a new entity, and applies the same principle here.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chizkiya asks: if a vessel was punctured to the size of an olive, sealed, then punctured again and sealed repeatedly until the total opening reaches the size of a pomegranate, what is the halachic status?

Rabbi Yochanan responds by citing the Mishnah of the sandal: when one strap breaks and is repaired, the sandal remains טמא מדרס (impure with midras impurity); when the second strap breaks and is repaired, it becomes טהור (pure) from midras but still טמא מגע מדרס (impure by contact). He then poses the question: why is the first repair different from the second?

Rabbi Yochanan resolves: in the sandal case, the second repair introduces 'פָּנִים חֲדָשׁוֹת' (a new entity), and the same principle applies here — each successive sealing of the vessel's puncture is treated as a new entity, so the vessel does not regain its original impurity status.

items.text: Assessment of later generations' stature
items.text_en: Assessment of later generations' stature
items.desc_en: The Gemara comments on the relative wisdom of generations, with Rabbi Zeira quoting Rava bar Zimuna that if earlier sages were angels, later ones are humans; if earlier were humans, later are like donkeys, but not the special donkeys of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement about the relative stature of generations, quoting Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rava bar Zimuna that later generations are inferior to earlier ones, comparing them to donkeys.

items.text: Clarifications on wine and oil skins and a meat pot
items.text_en: Clarifications on wine and oil skins and a meat pot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah's ruling about wine and oil skins is necessary when the skin has two openings, lest one think that repairing one nullifies the other. Similarly, a meat pot with a handle requires clarification that repairing the handle does not nullify the pot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah's ruling about wine and oil skins is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary when the skin has two openings, lest one think that repairing one nullifies the other; the mishnah teaches that it does not.
The Gemara asks why the mishnah's ruling about a meat pot is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary when the pot has a handle, lest one think that repairing the handle nullifies the pot; the mishnah teaches that it does not.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion on tying
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion on tying
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the necessity of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling about tying, and explains it applies when there are two straps, lest one think that repairing one nullifies the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishna's ruling of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov (רבי אליעזר בן יעקב) that one may tie a rope across an entrance, and then questions why this ruling is necessary.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary only when the entrance has two ropes, lest one think that repairing one rope nullifies the other, thereby making the knot permanent and prohibited.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion and ruling
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion and ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the earlier statement teaches that one may nullify a knot by loosening it. Rav Yosef reports in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. Abaye questions whether this implies there was a dispute, and Rav Yosef responds sharply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that one of the earlier statements teaches that loosening a knot nullifies it.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Abaye questions whether the ruling implies there was a dispute among the sages.
Rav Yosef rebukes Abaye, asking why he cares and telling him to finish his studies.

items.text: Mishnah: Tying a bucket with a belt
items.text_en: Mishnah: Tying a bucket with a belt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may tie a bucket with a belt but not with a rope. Rabbi Yehuda permits it, stating a principle: any knot that is not permanent does not incur liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may tie a bucket with a belt but not with a rope, and Rabbi Yehuda permits it, stating that any knot which is not permanent does not incur liability.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of rope is forbidden. If it is an ordinary rope, Rabbi Yehuda would permit it because it is a permanent knot. Rather, it is a weaver's rope. The Gemara infers that the Rabbis decree against a weaver's rope due to ordinary rope, while Rabbi Yehuda does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of rope is forbidden in the Mishnah, suggesting it cannot be an ordinary rope because Rabbi Yehuda would permit it as a permanent knot.
The Gemara answers that the forbidden rope is a weaver's rope (חֶבֶל דְּגַרְדִּי), not an ordinary one.
The Gemara infers that the Rabbis decree against a weaver's rope due to ordinary rope, while Rabbi Yehuda does not decree.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding tying a bucket rope
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding tying a bucket rope
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that contradicts both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara resolves the contradiction for the Rabbis: a rope with a rope is confused, but a bow with a knot is not. For Rabbi Yehuda, a bow itself is considered a knot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that contradicts both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda regarding tying a bucket rope.
The Gemara states that the baraita poses a difficulty for both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, as their positions appear contradictory.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: for the Rabbis, a rope tied to a rope is confused with a knot, but a bow is not; for Rabbi Yehuda, a bow itself is considered a knot.

items.text: Bringing a rope from home to tie to an ox and a crib
items.text_en: Bringing a rope from home to tie to an ox and a crib
items.desc_en: Rav states that one may bring a rope from home and tie it to an ox and a crib. Rabbi Acha bar Pappa challenges this with a baraita that forbids bringing a rope from home. The Gemara distinguishes: there it is an ordinary rope, here it is a weaver's rope.

sub.text: Rav (via Rabbi Abba and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi)
sub.text_en: Rav (via Rabbi Abba and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi)
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a person may bring a rope from home and tie it to an ox and a crib on Shabbat.
Rabbi Acha bar Pappa challenges Rav by citing a baraita that forbids bringing a rope from home to tie to an ox and a crib.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the baraita refers to an ordinary rope (חֶבֶל דְּעָלְמָא), while Rav's ruling concerns a weaver's rope (חֶבֶל דְּגַרְדִּי), which is permitted.

items.text: Moving vessels used for pressing olives
items.text_en: Moving vessels used for pressing olives
items.desc_en: Shmuel permits moving vessels used for pressing olives on Shabbat. A question about the upper and lower weights is left unresolved. Rav Nachman clarifies that even those weights are permitted, but not the pillars. Rava questions this, and the Gemara distinguishes between a field and a house regarding making holes. Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi and is told they are not moved because they are not handled.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel permits moving vessels used for pressing olives on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks Rav Yehuda about the status of the upper and lower weights of the press.
The question remains unresolved, with Rav Yehuda giving no definitive answer.
Rav Nachman clarifies that even the weights are permitted, but not the pillars of the press.
Rava questions why the pillars are treated differently from the weights.
The Gemara rejects the idea that the pillars cause holes, citing a baraita about burying vegetables under a vine where holes form naturally and are permitted.
The Gemara distinguishes between a field, where one does not come to make holes, and a house, where one might intentionally make holes, explaining the prohibition on pillars.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question to Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question to Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi about moving the weights of the press on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Levi rules that they are not moved because they are not handled (i.e., not designated for use).

items.text: Mishnah: Folding garments and making beds
items.text_en: Mishnah: Folding garments and making beds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may fold garments even four or five times and make beds from Friday night to Shabbat, but not from Shabbat to Saturday night. Rabbi Yishmael permits folding from Yom Kippur to Shabbat. The Mishnah discusses which sacrifices are offered when Shabbat and Yom Kippur coincide.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule: one may fold garments and make beds from Friday night to Shabbat, but not from Shabbat to Saturday night.
Rabbi Yishmael adds a leniency: one may fold garments and make beds from Yom Kippur to Shabbat.
The Tanna Kamma rules on sacrifices: fats of Shabbat are offered on Yom Kippur, but not those of Yom Kippur on Shabbat.
Rabbi Akiva disagrees and rules that neither Shabbat fats are offered on Yom Kippur nor Yom Kippur fats on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Restrictions on folding garments and honor of Shabbat
items.text_en: Gemara: Restrictions on folding garments and honor of Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara limits the Mishnah's leniency to one person, new garments, white garments, and when one has no change of clothes. The house of Rabban Gamliel did not fold white garments because they had changes. Rav Huna says if one has a change, he should change; if not, he should let his garments hang. Rav Safra objects that this appears haughty, but the Gemara responds that since he does not do so on weekdays, it is not haughty. The Gemara expounds verses from Isaiah regarding honoring Shabbat with special clothing and speech.

sub.desc_en: Bei Rabbi Yannai limits the Mishnah's leniency of folding garments to one person, new garments, white garments, and when one has no change of clothes.
A baraita reports that the house of Rabban Gamliel did not fold white garments because they had changes of clothes, supporting the limitation.
Rav Huna rules that if one has a change of clothes he should change, and if not he should let his garments hang loose.
Rav Safra objects that letting garments hang appears haughty.
The Gemara resolves that since he does not do so on weekdays, it is not haughty.
The Gemara expounds verses from Isaiah regarding honoring Shabbat with special clothing and speech.

items.text: Restrictions on Shabbat speech and walking
items.text_en: Restrictions on Shabbat speech and walking
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that speech is forbidden on Shabbat but thought is permitted. It then questions what constitutes prohibited walking on Shabbat, citing Rav Huna's ruling about crossing a water channel: one may step if the first foot is placed before the second is lifted, otherwise it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that on Shabbat, speech is forbidden but thought is permitted.
The Gemara asks what constitutes prohibited walking on Shabbat, analogous to the speech restriction.

sub.text: Rav Huna citing Rav (or Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna)
sub.text_en: Rav Huna citing Rav (or Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna)
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that when crossing a water channel on Shabbat, one may step only if the first foot is placed before the second is lifted; otherwise it is forbidden.

items.text: Rava's objection and Rabbi's question on taking large strides
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Rabbi's question on taking large strides
items.desc_en: Rava objects to the previous ruling, arguing that any attempt to cross the water leads to either excessive walking or squeezing water from clothes, but since it is unavoidable, it is permitted. Then Rabbi asks Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei about taking large strides on Shabbat, who responds that it is forbidden even on weekdays because it damages eyesight, though it can be restored through Kiddush at sunset.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to the previous ruling, arguing that any attempt to cross the water leads to either excessive walking or squeezing water from clothes, but since it is unavoidable, it is permitted.

Rabbi asks Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei about taking large strides on Shabbat, who responds that it is forbidden even on weekdays because it damages eyesight, though it can be restored through Kiddush at sunset.

items.text: Eating earth on Shabbat and the status of Babylonian soil
items.text_en: Eating earth on Shabbat and the status of Babylonian soil
items.desc_en: Rabbi asks Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei about eating earth on Shabbat. He responds that it is forbidden even on weekdays because it is harmful. Rabbi Ami adds that eating earth from Babylon is like eating the flesh of one's ancestors, and others say it is like eating creeping things, citing the verse about the flood.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi asks Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei whether eating earth is permitted on שבת (the Sabbath).

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei responds that eating earth is forbidden even on weekdays because it is harmful (מלקה).
Rabbi Ami adds that eating earth from Babylon is like eating the flesh of one's ancestors.
Yesh Omrim (some say) that eating Babylonian earth is like eating creeping things, citing the verse about the flood wiping out all life.

items.text: Etymologies of Shinar and Metzulah, and the rabbinic decree on earth
items.text_en: Etymologies of Shinar and Metzulah, and the rabbinic decree on earth
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains that Shinar is so named because all the dead of the flood were shaken there, and Rabbi Yochanan says Metzulah is so named because they were drowned there. The Gemara questions how eating earth can be like eating creeping things if they were destroyed, and answers that since it is harmful, the rabbis decreed against it, citing a story of a man who ate garlic and leeks and died.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains that Shinar is so named because all the dead of the flood were shaken there.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Metzulah is so named because all the dead of the flood were drowned there.
The Gemara questions how eating earth can be like eating creeping things if they were already destroyed.
The Gemara answers that since it is harmful, the rabbis decreed against it.
The Gemara cites a story of a man who ate garlic and leeks and died, illustrating the harm.

items.text: Shabbat garments and the wisdom of Ruth and Samuel
items.text_en: Shabbat garments and the wisdom of Ruth and Samuel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse about washing and anointing as referring to Shabbat clothes. He then applies the verse 'Give to the wise and he will be wiser' to Ruth and Samuel, showing how they exceeded the instructions given to them: Ruth did more than Naomi commanded, and Samuel did not repeat Eli's exact words when God called him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse about washing and anointing as referring to Shabbat garments.
Rabbi Elazar applies the verse 'Give to the wise and he will be wiser' to Ruth and Samuel, showing they exceeded instructions.
The gemara demonstrates that Ruth exceeded Naomi's instructions by going to the threshing floor before putting on the garments.
The gemara demonstrates that Samuel exceeded Eli's instructions by omitting the divine name when responding to God's call.

items.text: Boaz's recognition of Ruth's modesty and virtue
items.text_en: Boaz's recognition of Ruth's modesty and virtue
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Ruth's repeated going and coming showed she sought dignified company. Boaz's question about her was because he saw wisdom in her: she picked two stalks but not three. A baraita adds that he saw modesty: standing stalks were left standing, fallen ones were seated. Boaz's instruction to stay with his girls was because he saw her loyalty to Naomi.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Ruth's repeated going and coming showed she sought dignified company.
The gemara questions why Boaz would ask about a young woman, implying it was unusual for him.
Rabbi Elazar answers that Boaz saw wisdom in Ruth: she picked two stalks but not three.
A baraita adds that Boaz saw modesty in Ruth: standing stalks were left standing, fallen ones were seated.
The gemara questions why Boaz would instruct Ruth to stay with his girls, as it was not his usual behavior.
Rabbi Elazar answers that Boaz saw Ruth's loyalty to Naomi and therefore deemed it appropriate to associate with her.

items.text: Hints of Davidic dynasty and the bitterness of Menashe
items.text_en: Hints of Davidic dynasty and the bitterness of Menashe
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets Boaz's words 'come here' as a hint that the Davidic kingdom would come from Ruth, citing David's use of 'halom'. The vinegar dip hints that vinegar is good for heatstroke. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says it hints at a son whose deeds would be bitter as vinegar—Menashe. The seating 'beside the reapers' hints that the Davidic kingdom would be divided.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets Boaz's words 'come here' (גֹּשִׁי הֲלֹם) as a hint that the Davidic kingdom would come from Ruth, citing David's use of 'הלום' in his prayer.
Rabbi Elazar adds that the vinegar dip hints that vinegar is good for heatstroke.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani offers an alternative interpretation: the vinegar hints at a son whose deeds would be bitter as vinegar—Menashe.
Rabbi Elazar interprets the seating 'beside the reapers' as a hint that the Davidic kingdom would be divided.

items.text: Allegorical interpretations of Ruth's eating
items.text_en: Allegorical interpretations of Ruth's eating
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets 'she ate' as referring to the days of David, 'she was satisfied' to Solomon, and 'she left over' to Hezekiah. Others say 'ate' refers to David and Solomon, 'satisfied' to Hezekiah, and 'left over' to Rabbi's time, as Rabbi's steward was wealthier than King Shapur. A baraita interprets these as referring to this world, the days of the Messiah, and the world to come.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the three verbs in the verse as allegorically referring to the days of David, Solomon, and Hezekiah.
An alternative interpretation assigns 'ate' to David and Solomon, 'satisfied' to Hezekiah, and 'left over' to the time of Rabbi, citing that Rabbi's steward was wealthier than King Shapur.
A baraita interprets the three verbs as referring to this world, the days of the Messiah, and the world to come.

items.text: Interpretations of 'instead of glory' and the burning of Aaron's sons
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'instead of glory' and the burning of Aaron's sons
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'instead of his glory' as not literal glory, consistent with his calling his garments 'my honors'. Rabbi Elazar says it means literal glory. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani compares it to the burning of Aaron's sons, where the soul burns but the body remains, so here too the soul burns but the body remains.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'instead of his glory' (תחת כבודו) as not literal glory, consistent with his calling his garments 'my honors' (מכבדותי).
Rabbi Elazar says 'instead of his glory' means literal glory.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani compares it to the burning of Aaron's sons, where the soul burns but the body remains, so here too the soul burns but the body remains.

items.text: Introduction to a new statement by Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Introduction to a new statement by Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement attributed to Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Acha bar Abba, but the content is cut off, serving as a transition to the next part of the discussion.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new statement attributed to Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Acha bar Abba, but the content is cut off, serving as a transition.

items.text: Source for changing clothes from the Torah
items.text_en: Source for changing clothes from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse that teaches the concept of changing clothes, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives a lesson in proper conduct: one should not use the same clothes for cooking and for serving wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a Torah source for the concept of changing clothes.
The Gemara cites the verse 'He shall remove his garments and put on other garments' as the source.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives a lesson in proper conduct: one should not use the same clothes for cooking and for serving wine.

items.text: A scholar should not wear patched shoes
items.text_en: A scholar should not wear patched shoes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that it is disgraceful for a Torah scholar to go out in patched shoes. The Gemara questions this based on Rabbi Acha bar Chanina's practice, and resolves that the patches were layered one on top of another.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that it is disgraceful for a Torah scholar to go out in patched shoes.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Acha bar Chanina went out in patched shoes, contradicting the ruling.
Rabbi Acha bar Rav Nachman resolves that the patches were layered one on top of another, which is not disgraceful.

items.text: A scholar with a stain on his garment is liable to death
items.text_en: A scholar with a stain on his garment is liable to death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a Torah scholar found with a stain on his garment is liable to death, based on a verse. Ravina and the Gemara distinguish between a cloak and a shirt.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a Torah scholar found with a stain on his garment is liable to death, citing a verse.
Ravina suggests the correct reading is 'רְבָד' (a patch) rather than 'רְבָב' (a stain).
The Gemara resolves that the two readings are not in dispute: one refers to a cloak (גלימא) and the other to a shirt (לבושא).

items.text: Interpretation of Isaiah's nakedness and barefoot
items.text_en: Interpretation of Isaiah's nakedness and barefoot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'naked' refers to worn-out clothes, and 'barefoot' refers to patched shoes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'naked' as worn-out clothes and 'barefoot' as patched shoes, explaining the prophet Isaiah's behavior.

items.text: Mishnah: Stains on a yoke and garments as a barrier
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stains on a yoke and garments as a barrier
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses when a stain on a yoke or garment constitutes a barrier for immersion. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives a size limit, and Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yishmael says even on one side it is a barrier.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a stain on a yoke is a barrier for immersion, and on garments, a stain on one side is not a barrier but on two sides it is.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds a size limit for the stain on a yoke: up to the size of an Italian issar coin.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Yishmael's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Yishmael's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yishmael rules that even a stain on one side of a garment is a barrier.

items.text: Reish Lakish's inquiry about the yoke
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's inquiry about the yoke
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Chanina whether the yoke's stain is a barrier on one or two sides. Rabbi Chanina says he did not hear that, but heard a similar ruling: for builders it is on one side, for a boor on two sides, and the yoke is not more significant than a boor's garment.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Chanina whether the yoke's stain (רבב) is a barrier on one side or two sides.
Rabbi Chanina says he did not hear the answer to that specific question, but heard a similar ruling.
Rabbi Chanina cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose rules that for builders the stain is a barrier on one side, for a boor on two sides.
Rabbi Chanina concludes that the yoke's stain cannot be more significant than a boor's garment, implying it is a barrier on two sides.

items.text: Definitions of a Torah scholar
items.text_en: Definitions of a Torah scholar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines a Torah scholar as one who is meticulous about his garment, who can be appointed as a leader, and who prioritizes heavenly matters. The Gemara elaborates on the criteria for appointing a leader.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'builders' (בַּנָּאִין) in the previous Mishnah refers to.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that 'builders' refers to Torah scholars who engage in building the world (studying Torah) all their days.
Rabbi Yochanan defines a Torah scholar as one who is meticulous about his garment, turning it over to avoid stains, so that lost items can be returned by visual identification.
Rabbi Yochanan defines a Torah scholar worthy of being appointed a communal leader as one who can answer a halachic question anywhere, even in a minor tractate like Kallah.
Rabbi Yochanan defines a Torah scholar whose townspeople are obligated to do his work as one who prioritizes heavenly matters over his own affairs, but only for providing his bread.

Rabbi Yochanan defines a Torah scholar as one who can answer a halachic question anywhere, and explains the practical difference: if in one tractate, he is appointed a leader in his town; if in the entire corpus, he is appointed head of the academy.

items.text: Discussion of colored garments
items.text_en: Discussion of colored garments
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish identifies certain garments as 'olyairin' from overseas. The Gemara questions whether they are white, based on Rabbi Yannai's instruction to his sons, and concludes they are red, distinguishing between cloaks and shirts.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish identifies certain garments as 'olyairin' (colored cloaks) that come from overseas.
The Gemara questions whether these garments are white, based on the term 'olyairin'.
Rabbi Yannai instructed his sons not to bury him in white or black garments, but specifically in 'olyairin' garments from overseas.
The Gemara concludes that 'olyairin' garments are red, not white, based on Rabbi Yannai's burial instructions.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between cloaks (גלימי) and shirts (לבושי), explaining that the term 'olyairin' applies differently to each.

items.text: Sacrifices on Shabbat, Yom Kippur, and Festivals
items.text_en: Sacrifices on Shabbat, Yom Kippur, and Festivals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva debate which sacrifices can be offered on Shabbat, Yom Kippur, and Festivals. Rabbi Zeira summarizes their positions regarding vows and voluntary offerings.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yishmael's position that the verse 'עולת שבת בשבתו' teaches that the fats of Shabbat sacrifices may be offered on Yom Kippur, but not vice versa.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the same verse teaches that Shabbat fats may be offered on a Festival (יום טוב), but excludes Yom Kippur.

Rabbi Zeira summarizes the practical halachic difference: according to Rabbi Yishmael, vows and voluntary offerings (נדרים ונדבות) may be brought on Festivals, while according to Rabbi Akiva they may not.

items.text: Opening dispute about the identity of the mishnah
items.text_en: Opening dispute about the identity of the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that in Babylonia they said the mishnah about Yom Kippur on Friday is the opinion of everyone. Upon ascending to Eretz Yisrael, the narrator found Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi teaching that it is Rabbi Akiva's view, because Rabbi Yishmael would require blowing the shofar to publicize that Shabbat fats are offered on Yom Kippur. The narrator objects that priests are vigilant and do not need such a reminder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that in Babylonia they said the mishnah about Yom Kippur on Friday is the opinion of everyone.

sub.text: Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.text_en: Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.desc_en: Upon ascending to Eretz Yisrael, the narrator found Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi teaching that the mishnah is Rabbi Akiva's view, because Rabbi Yishmael would require blowing the shofar to publicize that Shabbat fats are offered on Yom Kippur.
The narrator objects that priests are vigilant and do not need such a reminder.

items.text: Question about the principle 'priests are vigilant'
items.text_en: Question about the principle 'priests are vigilant'
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha asks Rav Ashi: Do we say 'priests are vigilant'? He cites a mishnah about three blasts to separate between sacred and profane, and Abaye's explanation that those blasts were for the general public of Jerusalem. Here too, the blasts would be for the general public, not just priests.

sub.text: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha challenges Rav Ashi's principle that 'priests are vigilant' by citing a mishnah about three blasts to separate sacred and profane, and Abaye's explanation that those blasts were for the general public of Jerusalem, arguing that here too the blasts would be for the general public, not just priests.

items.text: Alternative reason: no shofar because of shevut
items.text_en: Alternative reason: no shofar because of shevut
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Let them blow the shofar so people know that cutting vegetables is permitted from mincha time onward. Rav Yosef answers: Because we do not push aside a rabbinic prohibition (shevut) to permit something.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why they do not blow the shofar so that people will know that cutting vegetables is permitted from mincha time onward.
Rav Yosef answers that one does not push aside a rabbinic prohibition (שבות) to permit something.

items.text: Rav Shisha's distinction: near shevut vs. far shevut
items.text_en: Rav Shisha's distinction: near shevut vs. far shevut
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi says: A near rabbinic prohibition (blowing shofar on Friday) they permitted, but a far one (blowing on Saturday night) they did not permit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi distinguishes between a near rabbinic prohibition (blowing shofar on Friday), which was permitted, and a far one (blowing on Saturday night), which was not permitted.

items.text: Refutation of Rav Shisha from a baraita
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Shisha from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Shisha: Did they permit a near shevut? A baraita states that when a festival falls on Friday they blow the shofar but do not recite havdalah, and on Saturday night they recite havdalah but do not blow. Why not blow to publicize that slaughter is permitted immediately? This shows that the explanation is like Rav Yosef's (that shevut is not pushed aside).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Did they really permit a near shevut (a rabbinic prohibition close to the permitted act)?
The Gemara cites a baraita: On a festival that falls on Friday they blow the shofar but do not recite havdalah; on Saturday night they recite havdalah but do not blow.
The Gemara asks: Why not blow the shofar on Saturday night to publicize that slaughter is permitted immediately?
The Gemara concludes that the explanation is like Rav Yosef's: shevut (rabbinic prohibitions) are not pushed aside even for a public need.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling: Yom Kippur on Shabbat forbids cutting vegetables
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling: Yom Kippur on Shabbat forbids cutting vegetables
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Abba) quotes Rav Huna: Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat prohibits cutting vegetables. Rav Mana teaches a baraita deriving this from the word 'Shabbaton' — it adds a shevut prohibition beyond melacha. The Gemara concludes that this refers to cutting vegetables.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira / Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira / Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that Yom Kippur falling on Shabbat prohibits cutting vegetables.
Rav Mana cites a baraita that derives the prohibition from the word 'שַׁבָּתוֹן' (Shabbaton), implying a shevut restriction.
The Gemara questions the purpose of the extra word: if it refers to melacha, the verse already prohibits melacha explicitly.
The Gemara concludes that the word 'שַׁבָּתוֹן' must refer specifically to the prohibition of cutting vegetables.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's opposing ruling and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's opposing ruling and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan: Yom Kippur on Shabbat permits cutting vegetables. The Gemara raises an objection from the baraita that forbids it, and resolves that the baraita refers to the additional prohibition of a positive and negative commandment for melacha itself, not for cutting vegetables.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat, cutting vegetables is permitted.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that derives from the verse 'שַׁבָּתוֹן' that Yom Kippur on Shabbat forbids cutting vegetables.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita actually refers to melacha itself, teaching that one violates both a positive commandment (עשה) and a negative commandment (לא תעשה) for performing melacha on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat, not to cutting vegetables.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's view that cutting vegetables is permitted on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's view that cutting vegetables is permitted on Yom Kippur that falls on Shabbat.

items.text: Opening anecdote about permitted activities on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about permitted activities on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that on Yom Kippur that falls on a weekday, one may crack nuts and peel pomegranates from mincha onwards due to emotional distress. It then relates that the households of Rav Yehuda and Rabba engaged in similar activities, but when Rav Yehuda saw people disparaging, he forbade it based on a letter from Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that on Yom Kippur, one may crack nuts and peel pomegranates from mincha onwards due to emotional distress.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that on Yom Kippur falling on a weekday, one may crack nuts and peel pomegranates from mincha onward due to emotional distress.
The Gemara relates that the households of Rav Yehuda and Rabba engaged in similar activities (cracking nuts and peeling pomegranates).
When Rav Yehuda saw people disparaging the practice, he forbade it based on a letter from Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Transition to new chapter
items.text_en: Transition to new chapter
items.desc_en: A brief statement marking the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of the next.

sub.desc_en: The gemara marks the end of the previous chapter and the beginning of the new one with the standard formula הדרן עלך (we return to you).

items.text: Mishnah: Rescuing sacred writings from a fire
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rescuing sacred writings from a fire
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all sacred writings may be rescued from a fire on Shabbat, whether or not they are read publicly, even if written in any language. They require burial. The reason they are not read is due to neglect of the study hall.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that all sacred writings may be rescued from a fire on Shabbat, regardless of language or public reading status, and they require burial; the reason they are not read is due to neglect of the study hall.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rav Huna says writings in translation are not rescued, Rav Chisda says they are. They agree that if one holds they may be read, all agree they are rescued. The dispute is only according to the view that they may not be read. A challenge is brought from the Mishnah, which seems to support Rav Chisda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda regarding writings in Aramaic or any other language.

The Gemara clarifies that the dispute applies only according to the opinion that these writings were not given to be read; Rav Huna prohibits rescue, while Rav Chisda permits rescue due to the disgrace of sacred writings.
The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the Mishnah, which states that all sacred writings are rescued, implying even those in any language, which contradicts Rav Huna's position.
Rav Chisda explains that they are rescued due to the disgrace of holy writings (ביזיון כתבי הקודש).
The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the Mishnah, which states that all holy writings are rescued even if written in any language, implying support for Rav Chisda.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda reconcile the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda reconcile the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna responds by pointing out a contradiction in the Mishnah: if they are rescued, why require burial? He and Rav Chisda each reinterpret the Mishnah to support their own positions. Rav Huna limits rescue to Hebrew texts; Rav Chisda extends it to all languages.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rejects the challenge by pointing to the Mishnah's statement that these writings require burial, arguing that if they are rescued, burial is obviously needed, so the Mishnah must be interpreted differently.

Each Amora resolves the Mishnah according to his own position: Rav Huna limits rescue to Hebrew writings, while Rav Chisda permits rescue of all languages and explains that even the decayed remains require burial.
Rav Huna limits the Mishnah's rescue to Hebrew-script scrolls; translations in any other language are not rescued, though they still require burial (גניזה).
Rav Chisda extends the Mishnah's rescue to all languages, and explains that the burial requirement applies only to the decayed remains (מקוק) of the scrolls.

items.text: Further challenges and resolution
items.text_en: Further challenges and resolution
items.desc_en: Additional baraitot are brought to challenge Rav Huna. One baraita explicitly states that writings in translation are rescued, and another lists specific languages. Rav Huna deflects by attributing the first to a different Tanna and the second to a dispute between Tannaim, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei prohibits rescue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that explicitly permits rescuing writings in Aramaic or any language, challenging Rav Huna.
Rav Huna deflects by claiming that baraita follows the opinion that these writings were given to be read, which is not his position.
The Gemara cites another baraita listing specific foreign scripts that are rescued even though not given to be read, again challenging Rav Huna.
Rav Huna responds that the dispute is between Tannaim, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei prohibits rescue, supporting his view.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's story and Rabbi's critique
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's story and Rabbi's critique
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei recounts a story about Abba Chalafta visiting Rabban Gamliel in Tiberias, who was reading a translated Book of Job. Abba Chalafta recalls that Rabban Gamliel's grandfather ordered such a book to be buried under a course of stones. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that a pot of clay was placed over it. Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) raises two objections: there was no clay on the Temple Mount, and it is forbidden to destroy them by hand; rather, they should be left to decay.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei recounts a story where Abba Chalaphta saw Rabban Gamliel reading a translated Book of Job and ordered it buried, supporting the prohibition.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's version
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's version
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds that a clay pot was placed over the book to bury it.
Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) raises two objections: there was no clay on the Temple Mount, and it is forbidden to destroy sacred writings by hand; instead, they should be left to decay naturally.
The Gemara asks which Tanna is the subject of the dispute.
Rabbi rules that instead of burying, one should leave the books in a place of decay so they rot on their own.

items.text: Rejecting the first Tanna and identifying the dispute
items.text_en: Rejecting the first Tanna and identifying the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that the first Tanna of Rabbi Yosei is the one who permits saving sacred writings, suggesting instead that the dispute is about whether they were given to be read. It then identifies the actual disputants as Rabbi Yosei and the Tanna of Gifit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the first Tanna of Rabbi Yosei is the one who permits saving sacred writings, but then suggests the dispute is actually about whether they were given to be read.
The Gemara resolves that the actual disputants are Rabbi Yosei and the Tanna of Gifit.

items.text: Baraita on blessings and amulets
items.text_en: Baraita on blessings and amulets
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that blessings and amulets containing divine names are not saved from a fire but are burned in place, and that writing blessings is like burning the Torah. A story about Rabbi Yishmael illustrates the severity of the offense.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that blessings and amulets containing divine names are not saved from a fire but are burned in place.
The baraita declares that those who write blessings are considered as if they burn the Torah.

A story is told about a man writing blessings in Tzidon; Rabbi Yishmael tests him, and the man sinks the blessings in water, prompting Rabbi Yishmael to say that the latter punishment is greater than the former.

items.text: Inquiry about writings in non-durable ink
items.text_en: Inquiry about writings in non-durable ink
items.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rabbah bar Rav Huna whether writings in various inks but in Hebrew are saved from a fire. The Gemara explores the issue from both sides, and Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules they are not saved, despite a conflicting teaching by Rav Hamnuna. Rav Ashi resolves the conflict with a baraita distinguishing between scrolls and a Megillah.

sub.text: Reish Galuta's question to Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Reish Galuta's question to Rabbah bar Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rabbah bar Rav Huna whether writings in non-durable inks (סם, סיקרא, קומוס, קנקנתום) but in Hebrew are saved from a fire.

The Gemara analyzes the question from both sides: for one who says non-Hebrew writings are saved, perhaps here the ink is non-durable; for one who says they are not saved, perhaps Hebrew writings are saved.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that such writings are not saved from a fire.
The Gemara objects that Rav Hamnuna taught a baraita that such writings are saved.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's initial response
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's initial response
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna responds that if it is taught, it is taught, without further explanation.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's resolution with a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution with a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the conflict by citing a baraita that distinguishes between scrolls (which may be written in any language) and a Megillah (which must be written in Ashurit on parchment with ink), implying that the baraita of Rav Hamnuna refers to a Megillah, not general scrolls.

items.text: Inquiry about a Torah scroll lacking eighty-five letters
items.text_en: Inquiry about a Torah scroll lacking eighty-five letters
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chalvu asks Rav Nachman whether a Torah scroll that lacks eighty-five consecutive letters, like the section of 'Vayehi Binsoa HaAron', is saved from a fire. Rav Nachman clarifies that the question is about a scroll that lacks the entire section, and rules that it is not saved.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chalvu asks Rav Nachman whether a Torah scroll lacking eighty-five consecutive letters, like the section of 'Vayehi Binsoa HaAron', is saved from a fire.
Rav Nachman clarifies that the question is about a scroll lacking the entire section, and rules that it is not saved.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about Targum
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about Targum
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita that permits saving Targum written in Hebrew, even if it lacks eighty-five letters, such as 'Yegar Sahaduta'. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to completing a scroll, not to the minimum requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that permits saving Targum written in Hebrew, even if it lacks eighty-five letters, such as 'Yegar Sahaduta'.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to completing a scroll, not to the minimum requirement of eighty-five letters.

items.text: Dispute about whether the letters must be consecutive
items.text_en: Dispute about whether the letters must be consecutive
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether the eighty-five letters must be consecutive or can be scattered. Rav Huna says consecutive, Rav Chisda says even scattered. A baraita supports Rav Chisda, and Rav Chisda explains it in Rav Huna's favor as referring to words.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a question whether the eighty-five letters must be consecutive (מכונסות) or can be scattered (מפוזרות).
Rav Huna answers that the letters must be consecutive (מכונסות).
Rav Chisda answers that even scattered (מפוזרות) letters suffice.
A baraita is cited that a Torah scroll that is worn is saved only if it has eighty-five letters to gather, like the section of 'ויהי בנסוע הארון', which implies scattered letters, refuting Rav Huna.
The gemara declares that the baraita is a refutation (תיובתא) of Rav Huna's position.

Rav Chisda explains the baraita in accordance with Rav Huna, interpreting that the eighty-five letters must be in words (בתיבות), i.e., consecutive within each word but the words themselves can be scattered.

items.text: Baraita on the section of Vayehi Binsoa
items.text_en: Baraita on the section of Vayehi Binsoa
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the section of 'Vayehi Binsoa HaAron' was marked by the Holy One with signs above and below, indicating its special status.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the section of 'Vayehi Binsoa HaAron' was marked by the Holy One with signs above and below, indicating its special status.

items.text: The dispute about the placement of the paragraph of Vayihi Binsoa HaAron
items.text_en: The dispute about the placement of the paragraph of Vayihi Binsoa HaAron
items.desc_en: Rabbi holds that the paragraph is not in its proper place because the book is significant in its own right. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman cites Rabbi Yonatan that the seven pillars refer to the seven books of the Torah, aligning with Rabbi. The Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says the paragraph will eventually be moved to its proper place among the banners, and was placed here to separate two punishments.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens by citing Rabbi's position that the paragraph of Vayihi Binsoa HaAron is not in its proper place, because the book is significant in its own right.
The gemara asks whose opinion aligns with Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman's statement that the seven pillars refer to the seven books of the Torah, and answers that it aligns with Rabbi.

The gemara identifies Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi, explaining that the paragraph will eventually be moved to its proper place among the banners and was placed here to separate two punishments.

items.text: First inquiry: margins of a Torah scroll
items.text_en: First inquiry: margins of a Torah scroll
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the margins (gilyonin) of a Torah scroll are saved from fire. It attempts to bring a proof from a baraita about a worn-out Torah scroll: if it has 85 letters like the paragraph of Vayihi Binsoa HaAron, it is saved; otherwise not. The Gemara deflects: a worn-out scroll is different because its margins are not considered significant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the margins (גליונין) of a Torah scroll are saved from fire on Shabbat.

sub.text: First attempted proof from a baraita
sub.text_en: First attempted proof from a baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove the matter from a baraita about a worn-out Torah scroll: it is saved only if it has 85 letters like the paragraph of ויהי בנסוע הארון, implying margins are not saved.
The Gemara objects that the baraita should have saved the scroll because of its margins, and deflects: a worn-out scroll is different because its margins are not considered significant.

items.text: Second inquiry: margins of a Torah scroll that was erased
items.text_en: Second inquiry: margins of a Torah scroll that was erased
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries another proof from a baraita about a Torah scroll that was erased: if it has 85 letters, it is saved; otherwise not. The Gemara clarifies: the question is not about the place of writing, which loses sanctity when the writing is gone, but about the margins above and below, between paragraphs, between pages, and at the beginning and end of the scroll. The Gemara deflects: those margins are like cut-off and discarded material.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a Torah scroll that was erased, which states that if it retains 85 letters it is saved from fire, implying that the margins (גליונים) themselves are not saved, thus answering the inquiry.

The Gemara objects: why does the baraita not save the scroll for the sake of its margins? It then clarifies that the question is not about the place of writing, which loses sanctity when the writing is gone.
The Gemara specifies that the inquiry concerns the margins above and below, between paragraphs, between pages, and at the beginning and end of the scroll.
The Gemara deflects the proof by arguing that those margins are like cut-off and discarded material (גיז ושדי), so they do not retain sanctity.
