items.text: Third inquiry: margins that impart impurity to hands
items.text_en: Third inquiry: margins that impart impurity to hands
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries a proof from a baraita that the margins of a Torah scroll impart impurity to hands, implying they are sacred. The Gemara deflects: perhaps they are different because they are attached to a Torah scroll.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that margins of a Torah scroll are sacred by citing a baraita that they impart impurity to hands.
The Gemara deflects the proof by suggesting that the margins are different because they are attached to a Torah scroll.

items.text: Fourth inquiry: margins of heretical books
items.text_en: Fourth inquiry: margins of heretical books
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries a proof from a baraita that gilyonin and sifrei minim are not saved from fire. The Gemara initially assumes gilyonin of a Torah scroll, but rejects this: it refers to gilyonin of heretical books. The Gemara then clarifies that sifrei minim themselves are like gilyonin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove the status of Torah scroll margins by citing a baraita that gilyonin and heretical books are not saved from fire.
The Gemara initially assumes that 'gilyonin' refers to the margins of a Torah scroll.
The Gemara rejects the assumption and clarifies that 'gilyonin' refers to the margins of heretical books, not a Torah scroll.
The Gemara objects: if heretical books themselves are not saved, why mention their margins separately?
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita means heretical books themselves are treated like margins — not saved from fire.

items.text: The law of heretical books and the statements of Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Tarfon, and Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: The law of heretical books and the statements of Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Tarfon, and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita: gilyonin and sifrei minim are not saved from fire. Rabbi Yosei says one may cut out the Divine names and bury them, burning the rest. Rabbi Tarfon says he would burn them even with the names, because heretics are worse than idolaters. Rabbi Yishmael argues a fortiori: if for peace between husband and wife the Torah allows erasing God's name, then for these books that cause enmity between Israel and God, certainly they should be burned. They are not saved from fire, collapse, water, or any destructive force.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that gilyonin and heretical books are not saved from fire.
Rabbi Yosei rules that on a weekday one may cut out the Divine names and bury them, burning the rest.
Rabbi Tarfon declares he would burn even the Divine names in heretical books, because heretics are worse than idolaters, and cites a verse condemning them.

Rabbi Yishmael argues a fortiori: if for peace between husband and wife the Torah allows erasing God's name, then for these books that cause enmity between Israel and God, certainly they should be burned.
The baraita concludes that just as these books are not saved from fire, they are also not saved from collapse, water, or any destructive force.

items.text: The books of the Avidan academy and the practices of the Sages
items.text_en: The books of the Avidan academy and the practices of the Sages
items.desc_en: Yosef bar Chanin asks Rabbi Avahu whether the books of the Avidan academy are saved from fire, but the matter remains unresolved. The Gemara relates that Rav did not go to the Avidan academy, and certainly not to the Nitzrefei academy. Shmuel did not go to Nitzrefei but did go to Avidan. Rava avoided Avidan by pretext. Mar bar Yosef, who was from them, was once endangered. Rabbi Meir called them 'aven gilyon' (iniquity of the margin), and Rabbi Yochanan called them 'avon gilyon' (sin of the margin).

sub.desc_en: Yosef bar Chanin asks Rabbi Avahu whether the books of the Avidan academy (ספרי דבי אבידן) are saved from fire on Shabbat.
Rabbi Avahu gives an equivocal answer — both yes and no — and the matter remains unresolved in his hand.

sub.text: Gemara's report on Rav and Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara's report on Rav and Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav never went to the Avidan academy and certainly not to Nitzrefei, while Shmuel did not go to Nitzrefei but did go to Avidan.
When asked why he does not attend the Avidan academy, Rava avoids by claiming a palm tree or its location is difficult for him.

sub.text: Mar bar Yosef's claim and danger
sub.text_en: Mar bar Yosef's claim and danger
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Yosef, who was from them, claims he is not afraid, but once when he went they sought to endanger him.

sub.text: Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Yochanan's epithets
sub.text_en: Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Yochanan's epithets
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir called the Avidan books 'aven gilyon' (iniquity of the margin) and Rabbi Yochanan called them 'avon gilyon' (sin of the margin).

items.text: The story of Ima Shalom and the philosopher
items.text_en: The story of Ima Shalom and the philosopher
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Ima Shalom, the wife of Rabbi Eliezer and sister of Rabban Gamliel, who had a philosopher neighbor. This section sets up the narrative that will continue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Ima Shalom, wife of Rabbi Eliezer and sister of Rabban Gamliel, and notes that a philosopher lived in her neighborhood.

items.text: Story of the bribed judge
items.text_en: Story of the bribed judge
items.desc_en: A judge who refused bribes was tricked with a golden lamp and then a donkey. The judge initially ruled based on a forged document (עוון גליון) that gave equal inheritance to sons and daughters, but later reversed his decision citing another part of the same document that upheld the Torah's law.

sub.desc_en: The gemara tells the story of a judge known for refusing bribes, who was tricked by a woman with a golden lamp and then ruled based on a forged document (עוון גליון) that gave equal inheritance to sons and daughters.
The next day, the judge reversed his decision after receiving a donkey, citing another part of the same document that upheld the Torah's law of inheritance.
Rabban Gamliel comments that the donkey came and extinguished the lamp, alluding to the judge's corruption.

items.text: Dispute about reading Scriptures on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about reading Scriptures on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether one may read from the Writings (Ketuvim) on Shabbat. Rav permits it outside of study hall hours, while Shmuel forbids it entirely. The Gemara notes a practice in Nehardea that contradicts Shmuel's view, leading to a revised version of the dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's question about why one may not read from the Writings on Shabbat.
Rav rules that the prohibition applies only during study hall hours, but outside those hours one may read.
Shmuel rules that even outside study hall hours one may not read from the Writings on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects: Nehardea, Shmuel's own locale, practices reading from the Writings on Shabbat afternoon, contradicting his ruling.

sub.text: Gemara's revised version of the dispute
sub.text_en: Gemara's revised version of the dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by revising the dispute: Rav's prohibition applies only in a place where a study hall is present, but elsewhere one may read.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution and Rabbi Nehemya's reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution and Rabbi Nehemya's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Shmuel's original statement aligns with Rabbi Nehemya's view, who says that Scriptures are not read to prevent people from treating them like mundane documents. A baraita supports this, allowing study and looking up verses when needed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the dispute by asserting that Shmuel's original statement stands, and Shmuel actually follows Rabbi Nehemya's view.
A baraita is cited to support the permissibility of studying and looking up verses in sacred writings, even though reading them for leisure is prohibited.
Rabbi Nehemya explains the reason for the prohibition: to prevent people from treating sacred writings as casually as mundane documents.

items.text: Mishnah: Saving a book cover with the book
items.text_en: Mishnah: Saving a book cover with the book
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may save a book cover (tik) together with the book, and a tefillin bag with the tefillin, even if money is inside. They are saved to a non-public alleyway; Ben Beteira permits even a public alleyway.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may save a book cover (tik) together with the book, and a tefillin bag with the tefillin, even if money is inside.
The Mishnah specifies that these items are saved to a non-public alleyway (מבוי שאינו מפולש).
Ben Beteira permits saving them even to a public alleyway (מבוי מפולש).

items.text: Gemara: Skinning the Paschal lamb on Shabbat
items.text_en: Gemara: Skinning the Paschal lamb on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita about skinning the Paschal lamb on Shabbat when the 14th of Nisan falls on Shabbat. Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka limits skinning to the chest, while the Sages permit skinning the entire animal. The Gemara explains the Sages' reasoning based on the verse 'כל פעל ה' למענהו' to prevent spoilage or disgrace.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka permits skinning the Paschal lamb only up to the chest on Shabbat, while the Sages permit skinning the entire animal.
The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yishmael's position is understandable because the chest is needed for the sacrificial service, but what is the Sages' reasoning for permitting full skinning?

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Sages derive their permission from the verse 'כל פעל ה' למענהו' (Everything God made for His purpose).
The Gemara asks: In this context, what specific purpose (למענהו) is served by skinning the entire animal?
Rav Yosef answers: The purpose is to prevent the meat from spoiling (שלא יסריח).
Rava answers: The purpose is to prevent the sacred offerings from being left like a carcass (disgrace).
The Gemara asks: What is the practical difference between Rav Yosef's and Rava's explanations?
The Gemara answers: The difference is in cases where the meat is placed on a gold table (which does not spoil quickly) or on a hot day (where spoilage is rapid but disgrace is less).
The Gemara asks: How does Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka interpret the verse 'כל פעל ה' למענהו'?

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Natan's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Natan's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Natan answers: Rabbi Yishmael applies the verse to prevent removing the sacrificial portions (אימורין) before skinning, because of the small fibers (נימין) that would be lost.

items.text: Comparison between saving a cover and skinning the lamb
items.text_en: Comparison between saving a cover and skinning the lamb
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's leniency about saving a book cover can be applied to skinning the lamb. Rav Chisda and Mar Ukva explain that the colleagues argued with Rabbi Yishmael: if one can save a cover, why not skin the lamb? Rav Ashi clarifies that the two cases differ: one involves carrying (טלטול) and the other involves a prohibited labor (מלאכה).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Mar Ukva asks what the colleagues replied to Rabbi Yishmael: if one may save a book cover, why not skin the lamb?
The Gemara objects that the cases are not comparable: saving a cover involves טלטול (carrying), while skinning involves מלאכה (prohibited labor).

Rav Ashi resolves that the dispute involved two issues: they argued about both טלטול (carrying) and מלאכה (labor), and the colleagues' reply was: if one may save a cover, should we not carry the skin together with the meat?

items.text: Refining the comparison: base for forbidden vs. permitted items
items.text_en: Refining the comparison: base for forbidden vs. permitted items
items.desc_en: The Gemara refines the earlier comparison between saving a book cover with money inside and moving a hide with meat. It distinguishes between a base set for both forbidden and permitted items (the cover) and one set solely for a forbidden item (the hide). The Gemara then proposes a stronger comparison: if one may bring a money-containing cover from elsewhere to save a Torah scroll, surely one may move a hide with meat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refines the comparison between a book cover with money and a hide with meat, distinguishing between a base set for both forbidden and permitted items (the cover) and one set solely for a forbidden item (the hide), then proposes a stronger comparison from bringing a money-containing cover from elsewhere to save a Torah scroll.

items.text: Source for bringing a cover with money
items.text_en: Source for bringing a cover with money
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for the allowance to bring a cover containing money. It initially suggests a proof from the fact that one does not throw out the money, but rejects this due to the difference in urgency. Mar bar Rav Ashi resolves that the original reasoning stands, and the difficulty about labor vs. carrying is answered by the case where the hide is not fixed (i.e., not attached).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source of the comparison, initially suggesting it derives from the fact that one does not throw out the money from the cover, but rejects this due to the difference in time pressure.

Mar bar Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by maintaining the original comparison and explaining that the hide is not fixed as a base, so moving it is merely טלטול (carrying) not מלאכה (forbidden labor).
Mar bar Rav Ashi resolves that the original reasoning stands, and the difficulty about labor vs. carrying is answered by the case where the hide is not fixed (i.e., not attached).

items.text: Abaye and Rava on Rabbi Shimon's principle
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava on Rabbi Shimon's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Abaye and Rava both agree that Rabbi Shimon would concede in a case of 'psik reishei' (an inevitable consequence), such as removing the hide with a knife (which involves cutting). This clarifies the earlier distinction between permitted and forbidden actions.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava object that Rabbi Shimon would agree to the principle of 'פסיק רישיה ולא ימות' (an inevitable consequence), as when one removes the hide with a knife, it inevitably severs the meat.

items.text: Defining a mavui mefulash according to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Defining a mavui mefulash according to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses where to save items. Rav Chisda defines a mavui that is not mefulash as having three walls and two side-posts, and a mavui mefulash as having three walls and one side-post. Both definitions are according to Rabbi Eliezer, who requires two side-posts for an alleyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to define a 'מפולש' (open alley) versus a 'שאינו מפולש' (closed alley), and Rav Chisda answers with definitions based on partitions and side-posts.
The Gemara notes that both definitions align with Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, citing a Mishnah where he requires two side-posts for an alley.
The Gemara notes that both definitions align with Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, who requires two side-posts for an alleyway, as cited from a Mishnah.

items.text: Rabbah's objection and alternative definition
items.text_en: Rabbah's objection and alternative definition
items.desc_en: Rabbah objects to Rav Chisda's definition: a mavui with three walls and one side-post should not be called mefulash, and according to the Rabbis, one could save food and drink there. Rabbah instead defines a mavui that is not mefulash as having two walls and two side-posts, and a mavui mefulash as having two walls and one side-post.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects to Rav Chisda's definition, arguing that an alley with three partitions and one side-post is not truly 'מפולש', and proposes his own definition based on two partitions and two side-posts.
Rabbah completes his definition: an alley with two partitions and one side-post is 'מפולש' (open).

items.text: Both definitions according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Both definitions according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that both definitions (Rav Chisda's and Rabbah's) are according to Rabbi Yehuda, who permits a side-post on each side of a public domain. The Rabbis disagree, saying one cannot merge a public domain in this way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that both definitions align with Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, citing a baraita where he permits carrying between two houses on opposite sides of a public domain using side-posts or beams, but the Sages reject this.

items.text: Abaye's challenge to Rabbah
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge to Rabbah
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah: according to your own definition, according to the Rabbis, one could save food and drink in such an alleyway? This question challenges the practical implication of Rabbah's definition.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rabbah's definition, asking that according to the Rabbis (who reject Rabbi Yehuda's view), one could not save food and drink into such an alley, contradicting the Mishnah's allowance.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution of the mavoy dispute
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution of the mavoy dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that a mavoy with three partitions and one lechi is not a mavoy mefulash, while three partitions without a lechi is a mavoy mefulash. He adds that even Rabbi Eliezer, who requires two lechis for foods and drinks, would agree that one lechi suffices for a Torah scroll.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the mavoy dispute by distinguishing between a mavoy with three partitions and one lechi (not mefulash) and three partitions without a lechi (mefulash).

sub.text: Rav Ashi's extension regarding Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's extension regarding Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi adds that even Rabbi Eliezer, who requires two lechis for foods and drinks, would agree that one lechi suffices for a Torah scroll.

items.text: Mishnah: Saving food on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Saving food on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may save enough food for three meals on Shabbat, with the quantity depending on the time of the fire. Rabbi Yosei says one may always save three meals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may save food for three meals on Shabbat, specifying that what is fit for humans is saved for humans and what is fit for animals is saved for animals.
The Mishnah elaborates with examples: if a fire breaks out on Shabbat eve, one saves three meals; in the morning, two meals; in the afternoon, one meal.
Rabbi Yosei states that one may always save food for three meals, regardless of the time of the fire.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one may not save more food, given that saving is permitted. Rava answers that due to panic over money, allowing more would lead to extinguishing the fire. Abaye objects with a baraita about a broken barrel, and the Gemara explains the concern is bringing a vessel through a public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since one is already engaged in permitted saving, why not allow saving more food?
Rava answers that because a person is panicked about his money, allowing more saving would lead him to extinguish the fire.
Abaye objects by citing a baraita about a broken barrel on a roof, where one may place a vessel under it but not bring another vessel to catch or collect the wine.
The Gemara explains that there too the concern is a decree lest one bring a vessel through a public domain, just as in the fire case.

items.text: Baraita: Broken barrel and guests
items.text_en: Baraita: Broken barrel and guests
items.desc_en: The baraita details that if a barrel breaks on one's roof, one may place a vessel under it, but not bring additional vessels to catch or collect the wine. However, if guests arrive, one may bring additional vessels. One must invite guests before collecting, and according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, one may employ הערמה (legal circumvention).

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the basic rule: if a barrel breaks on one's roof, one may place one vessel under it but may not bring additional vessels to catch or collect the wine.
The baraita adds an exception: if guests arrive, one may bring additional vessels, but must invite them before collecting the wine.
The baraita records a dispute: the anonymous first Tanna forbids הערמה (legal circumvention), while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda permits it.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute about הערמה in the baraita parallels a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding saving animals from a pit. Rabbi Eliezer allows only one animal to be saved, while Rabbi Yehoshua allows הערמה to save both. The Gemara rejects this parallel, noting differences in the cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute in the baraita about הערמה (trickery) parallels the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding saving animals from a pit, and cites the relevant baraita.

The Gemara rejects the parallel, arguing that Rabbi Eliezer's leniency there was due to the possibility of providing sustenance, which is absent here, and Rabbi Yehoshua's leniency there was due to צער בעלי חיים (animal suffering), which is absent here.

items.text: Baraita: Saving bread and other foods
items.text_en: Baraita: Saving bread and other foods
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one has clean bread and coarse bread, one may save the coarse bread to save the clean bread. One may save food from Yom Kippur to Shabbat, but not from Shabbat to Yom Kippur, and certainly not from Shabbat to a festival or the next Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one saves clean bread over coarse bread, and may save food from Yom Kippur to Shabbat but not vice versa, nor from Shabbat to a festival or the next Shabbat.

items.text: Baraita: Bread forgotten in the oven
items.text_en: Baraita: Bread forgotten in the oven
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses saving bread forgotten in the oven when Shabbat begins. One may save three meals and invite others to save for themselves. When removing the bread, one should use a knife rather than a baker's peel, as the peel is a usual tool. The Gemara notes that removing bread is considered wisdom, not labor, but one should still vary the method.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one who forgot bread in the oven when Shabbat began may save three meals and invite others to save for themselves.
The baraita adds that when removing the bread, one should use a knife rather than a baker's peel (מרדה).
The Gemara objects: but the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that removing bread (רדיית הפת) is wisdom, not labor, so why require a change?
The Gemara resolves: nevertheless, we vary the method as much as possible to avoid even the appearance of a prohibited act.

items.text: Laws of Shabbat meals and bread
items.text_en: Laws of Shabbat meals and bread
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that one should prepare for Shabbat early. Rabbi Abba states that one must break bread over two loaves on Shabbat, as per the verse 'lechem mishneh'. Rav Ashi observes that Rav Kahana holds two loaves but breaks only one, citing the verse 'laketu'. Rabbi Zeira breaks bread over the entire meal. Ravina questions if this looks gluttonous, but Rav Ashi explains it is not, since he does not do so on weekdays. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi begin with the eiruv bread, citing the principle of performing a mitzvah with an item already used for a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that one should always rise early to prepare for Shabbat, citing the verse 'וְהָיָה בַּיּוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי וְהֵכִינוּ אֵת אֲשֶׁר יָבִיאוּ' (and it shall be on the sixth day, they shall prepare what they bring), implying immediate preparation.
Rabbi Abba states that on Shabbat one is obligated to break bread over two loaves, as it is written 'לֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה' (double bread).
Rav Ashi reports that Rav Kahana holds two loaves but breaks only one, citing the verse 'לָקְטוּ' (they gathered).
Rabbi Zeira breaks bread over the entire meal (all the bread before him).
Ravina questions Rav Ashi whether Rabbi Zeira's practice appears gluttonous.
Rav Ashi answers that since Rabbi Zeira does not do so on weekdays, it does not appear gluttonous.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi begin their Shabbat meal with the bread used for the eiruv (עירוב), citing the principle that a מצוה (commandment) item should be used for another מצוה.

items.text: Number of Shabbat meals
items.text_en: Number of Shabbat meals
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one is obligated to eat three meals on Shabbat, while Rabbi Chidka says four. Rabbi Yochanan explains that both derive their views from the same verse, with Rabbi Chidka counting three instances of 'hayom' excluding the night, and the Rabbis including the night. The Gemara then cites the Mishnah's case of a fire on Friday night.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: the Tanna Kamma obligates three Shabbat meals, while Rabbi Chidka says four.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that both sides derive their positions from the same verse, with Rabbi Chidka counting three instances of 'hayom' excluding the night, and the Rabbis including the night.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case of a fire on Friday night to connect the dispute to the earlier discussion.

items.text: Gemara's initial analysis of the Mishnah's three meals
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of the Mishnah's three meals
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's mention of saving three meals at dusk implies one has not yet eaten, but rejects this, suggesting one has already eaten. It then applies the same logic to morning and afternoon, but the pattern is challenged by the Mishnah's continuation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's allowance to save three meals at dusk implies one has not yet eaten.
The Gemara rejects the implication, stating that one has already eaten.
The Gemara applies the same logic to the morning meal, asking if saving two meals implies one has not eaten.
The Gemara again rejects the implication, stating one has already eaten.
The Gemara applies the same logic to the afternoon meal, asking if saving one meal implies one has not eaten.
The Gemara again rejects the implication, stating one has already eaten.

items.text: Resolution: the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Ḥidka
items.text_en: Resolution: the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Ḥidka
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's continuation (Rabbi Yosei says one always saves three meals) implies the first Tanna holds three meals are saved at all times, contradicting the earlier interpretation. It concludes that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Ḥidka, who holds one saves only one meal at night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's continuation, where Rabbi Yosei always saves three meals, implies the first Tanna also holds three meals are required, contradicting the earlier interpretation.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is a clarification (מחוורתא) and does not follow Rabbi Chidka's opinion.

items.text: Analysis of a baraita on charity portions
items.text_en: Analysis of a baraita on charity portions
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a baraita stating one with two meals may not take from the tamḥui, and one with fourteen meals may not take from the kuppah. It questions whose opinion this follows, noting that the Rabbis would require fifteen meals and Rabbi Ḥidka sixteen. It resolves that it is the Rabbis, as one is told to eat on Shabbat what he would have eaten after Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about who may take from the charity fund, which sets thresholds of two and fourteen meals.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this baraita follows, noting it fits neither the Rabbis (who require 15 meals) nor Rabbi Chidka (who requires 16).
The Gemara answers that it follows the Rabbis, who tell the poor person to eat on Shabbat what they would have eaten at the end of Shabbat.

items.text: Alternative attribution: Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Alternative attribution: Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the baraita could follow Rabbi Ḥidka, suggesting one is told to eat on Friday night what he would eat on Friday day. It objects that one would then fast all Friday, and concludes the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who says make your Shabbat a weekday rather than depend on others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita must follow the Rabbis and not Rabbi Chidka.
The Gemara counters that even if it follows Rabbi Chidka, one could be told to eat on Friday night what they would have eaten on Friday day.
The Gemara objects that one cannot be expected to fast all of Friday to save the meal.
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who says to make your Shabbat a weekday rather than depend on others.

items.text: Analysis of a baraita on a traveling poor person
items.text_en: Analysis of a baraita on a traveling poor person
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a baraita that gives a poor traveler one loaf, and if he stays overnight, lodging, and if he spends Shabbat, three meals. It questions whether this follows the Rabbis or Rabbi Ḥidka, and resolves that it can be Rabbi Ḥidka if the traveler already has a meal with him, and they give him another meal to take along.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about giving a traveling poor person three meals if they stay for Shabbat.
The Gemara asks whether this baraita follows the Rabbis and not Rabbi Chidka.
The Gemara answers that it follows Rabbi Chidka, who tells the poor person to eat the meal they already have with them.
The Gemara objects that the poor person would not travel empty-handed, as they are provided with a meal to take along.
The Gemara asks what 'overnight sustenance' (פרנסת לינה) means.
Rav Pappa explains that it means a bed and a pillow.

items.text: Baraita on washing dishes on Shabbat
items.text_en: Baraita on washing dishes on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one washes dishes used for one meal to use for the next, but after minḥa one does not wash. However, cups and flasks are washed all day because drinking has no fixed time.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the order of washing dishes for Shabbat meals and that drinking vessels may be washed all day.
The baraita rules that after minḥa one no longer washes dishes, but cups and flasks may be washed all day because drinking has no fixed time.

items.text: Aggadic reward for three Shabbat meals
items.text_en: Aggadic reward for three Shabbat meals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara teaches that one who fulfills three Shabbat meals is saved from three punishments: the birth pangs of the Messiah, the judgment of Gehinnom, and the war of Gog and Magog, each derived from a verse with 'day'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi transmits that one who fulfills three Shabbat meals is saved from three calamities: the birth pangs of the Messiah, the judgment of Gehinnom, and the war of Gog and Magog.
The Gemara provides scriptural support for each of the three salvations by linking the word 'day' in the verse about Shabbat to verses about each calamity.

items.text: Reward for delighting in Shabbat
items.text_en: Reward for delighting in Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei teaches that one who delights in Shabbat is given a boundless inheritance, as it is written: 'Then you shall delight in the Lord, and I will cause you to ride on the high places of the earth, and I will feed you...'

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei teaches that one who delights in Shabbat receives an inheritance without borders, citing the verse 'Then you shall delight in the Lord...'

items.text: Opening: Inheritance like Jacob
items.text_en: Opening: Inheritance like Jacob
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse about Jacob's inheritance, contrasting it with Abraham and Isaac, to show that Jacob's blessing was more expansive.

items.text: Rewards for Oneg Shabbat
items.text_en: Rewards for Oneg Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that oneg Shabbat saves from exile. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says that one who delights in Shabbat is granted his heart's desires. The Gemara then discusses what constitutes oneg Shabbat, with various opinions on specific foods.

items.text: Forgiveness for Shabbat Observers
items.text_en: Forgiveness for Shabbat Observers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that one who properly observes Shabbat is forgiven even for idolatry, based on a homiletic reading of a verse.

items.text: Redemption through Shabbat
items.text_en: Redemption through Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says that if Israel had kept the first Shabbat, no nation would have ruled them. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says that if Israel kept two Shabbatot properly, they would be redeemed immediately.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's Desires: Three Meals and Hallel
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's Desires: Three Meals and Hallel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei expresses his wish to be among those who eat three Shabbat meals and complete Hallel daily. The Gemara questions the latter, noting that daily Hallel is blasphemy, and resolves that it refers to Pesukei Dezimra.

items.text: Praying at Sunset
items.text_en: Praying at Sunset
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei wishes to be among those who pray at sunset. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states it is a mitzvah to pray at sunset, and Rabbi Zeira cites a verse.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's Desires: Death and Shabbat Practices
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's Desires: Death and Shabbat Practices
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei expresses wishes to die from intestinal illness (as most righteous do), to die while engaged in a mitzvah, to usher in Shabbat in Tiberias and end it in Tzippori, and to be among those who seat people in the study hall rather than those who stand them up.

items.text: Charity and Being Suspected
items.text_en: Charity and Being Suspected
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei wishes to be among charity collectors rather than distributors, and among those who are suspected without cause. Rav Pappa testifies that he was suspected but was innocent.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's Five Sons
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's Five Sons
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states he performed five marital acts and planted five cedars in Israel, listing his sons. The Gemara questions if he neglected the mitzvah of onah, and resolves that he meant he repeated the act five times.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's Euphemisms
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's Euphemisms
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says he never called his wife 'my wife' or his ox 'my ox', but rather 'my home' and 'my field'.

items.text: Modesty and Humility
items.text_en: Modesty and Humility
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says he never looked at his circumcision. The Gemara notes that Rabbi also said this, but with an additional stringency. Rabbi Yosei also says the beams of his house never saw the edges of his garment.

items.text: Deference and Consistency
items.text_en: Deference and Consistency
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says he never transgressed his colleagues' words, would ascend the platform if asked even though he is not a priest, and never retracted a statement.

items.text: Sages' Merits
items.text_en: Sages' Merits
items.desc_en: Various sages express their merits: Rav Nachman for three Shabbat meals, Rav Yehuda for focused prayer, Rav Huna for not walking bareheaded, Rav Sheishet for tefillin, and Rav Nachman again for tzitzit.

items.text: Abaye's Merit and Conclusion
items.text_en: Abaye's Merit and Conclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks his son about his father's stringency, and is told it was regarding tzitzit. Abaye expresses his merit for honoring Torah scholars who complete a tractate.

items.text: Rava and Mar bar Rav Ashi on judging Torah scholars
items.text_en: Rava and Mar bar Rav Ashi on judging Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rava states that he does not even rest his head on a pillow before finding merit for a Torah scholar who comes before him for judgment. Mar bar Rav Ashi disqualifies himself from judging a Torah scholar because the scholar is as dear to him as himself, and a person cannot see a fault in themselves.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a general statement about honoring Torah scholars on Shabbat.
Rava declares that he does not rest his head on a pillow before finding merit for a Torah scholar who comes before him for judgment.
Mar bar Rav Ashi disqualifies himself from judging a Torah scholar because the scholar is as dear to him as himself, and a person cannot see a fault in themselves.

items.text: Customs of the early sages in honoring Shabbat
items.text_en: Customs of the early sages in honoring Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina would wrap himself and stand at sunset on Shabbat eve, saying 'Come, let us go out to greet the Shabbat Queen.' Rabbi Yannai would don fine garments and say 'Come, bride, come, bride.' Rabba bar Rav Huna visited Rabba bar Rav Nachman and was served three se'ah of fat fish, and they explained they always prepare for Shabbat regardless of guests. Rabbi Abba would buy meat from thirteen butchers and give it to the door, saying 'Hurry, hurry.' Rabbi Avahu would sit on an ivory stool and fan the fire. Rav Anan wore a cloak, citing a baraita that one should not use garments that cooked for the master to pour a cup for the master.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina wraps himself and stands at sunset on Shabbat eve, inviting others to go out to greet the Shabbat Queen.
Rabbi Yannai dons fine garments and says 'Come, bride, come, bride' to welcome Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rabba bar Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rabba bar Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna visits Rabba bar Rav Nachman, is served three se'ah of fat fish, and is told they always prepare for Shabbat regardless of guests.
Rabbi Abba buys meat from thirteen butchers and gives it to the door, saying 'Hurry, hurry' to honor Shabbat.
Rabbi Avahu sits on an ivory stool and fans the fire in honor of Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Anan citing Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rav Anan citing Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rav Anan wears a cloak, citing a baraita that one should not use garments that cooked for the master to pour a cup for the master.

items.text: Various sages' preparations for Shabbat
items.text_en: Various sages' preparations for Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Safra would roast a head, Rava would salt a fish, Rav Huna would light candles, Rav Pappa would braid wicks, Rav Chisda would cut beets, Rabba and Rav Yosef would chop wood, Rabbi Zeira would kindle small sticks, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak would carry items in and out, saying that if Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were coming, he would certainly carry for them. An alternative version has Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi carrying items, saying they would do so for Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra would roast a head in honor of Shabbat.
Rava would salt a fish in preparation for Shabbat.
Rav Huna would light candles for Shabbat.
Rav Pappa would braid wicks for Shabbat lamps.
Rav Chisda would cut beets for Shabbat.
Rabba and Rav Yosef would chop wood for Shabbat.
Rabbi Zeira would kindle small sticks for Shabbat.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak would carry items in and out for Shabbat.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that he carries items as if for Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, whom he would honor.
An alternative version states that Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi carried items, saying they would do so for Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: The story of Yosef Mokir Shabbat
items.text_en: The story of Yosef Mokir Shabbat
items.desc_en: Yosef, who honored Shabbat, had a gentile neighbor with vast wealth. Chaldeans predicted that Yosef would consume all his wealth. The gentile sold everything and bought a pearl, placing it in his hat. A wind blew it into the water, a fish swallowed it, and it was caught and brought to market on Shabbat eve. The sellers directed the fish to Yosef, who bought it, found the pearl, and sold it for thirteen attics of gold dinars. An elder commented that one who borrows from Shabbat, Shabbat repays.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Yosef Mokir Shabbat and his wealthy gentile neighbor, whose Chaldean astrologers predicted Yosef would consume all the gentile's wealth.
The gentile sells all his property, buys a pearl, and places it in his hat, but a wind blows it into the water where a fish swallows it.
The fish is caught and brought to market on Shabbat eve; sellers direct it to Yosef, who buys it and finds the pearl inside.
Yosef sells the pearl for thirteen attics of gold dinars, and an elder comments that one who borrows from Shabbat is repaid by Shabbat.

items.text: What merits wealth for Jews in different lands
items.text_en: What merits wealth for Jews in different lands
items.desc_en: Rabbi asked Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi what merits the wealthy in Eretz Yisrael, and he answered tithing, citing the verse 'Aser te'aser' (tithe so that you become wealthy). For Babylonia, it is honoring the Torah. For other lands, it is honoring Shabbat. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba recounts staying with a host in Ludkiya who had a golden table carried by sixteen people, with silver chains and vessels, and when set they said 'The earth is the Lord's' and when removed 'The heavens are the Lord's'. The host was a butcher who set aside the finest animal for Shabbat, and Rabbi Chiya blessed him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi asks Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi what merit causes the wealthy in Eretz Yisrael to be wealthy.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael answers that they merit wealth through tithing, citing the verse 'עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר' (tithe so that you become wealthy).
Rabbi asks what merit causes the wealthy in Babylonia to be wealthy.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael answers that the wealthy in Babylonia merit wealth through honoring the Torah.
Rabbi asks what merit causes the wealthy in other lands to be wealthy.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael answers that the wealthy in other lands merit wealth through honoring Shabbat.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba recounts a story of a wealthy host in Ludkiya who honored Shabbat by setting aside the finest animal, and was blessed for it.

items.text: The spice of Shabbat and honoring it through timing and dress
items.text_en: The spice of Shabbat and honoring it through timing and dress
items.desc_en: The emperor asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya why Shabbat food has a fragrant smell. He replied that there is a spice called 'Shabbat' that we put in, and it works only for those who observe Shabbat. The Exilarch asked Rav Hamnuna about the verse 'and to the holy of the Lord, honored', and he explained it refers to Yom Kippur, which has no eating or drinking, so honor it with clean clothes. Rav and Shmuel debate whether 'vechibadto' means to advance or delay the meal. The sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba asked what distinguishes Shabbat for them since they have meat and wine daily, and he said to change the timing. Rav Sheishes would seat the sages in the sun in summer and in the shade in winter so they would rise quickly.

sub.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya why Shabbat food has a fragrant smell.
Rabbi Yehoshua replies that there is a spice called 'Shabbat' which only works for those who observe Shabbat.
The Exilarch asks Rav Hamnuna about the meaning of the verse 'and to the holy of the Lord, honored'.
Rav Hamnuna explains that the verse refers to Yom Kippur, which has no eating or drinking, so one honors it with clean clothes.
Rav and Shmuel debate whether 'vechibadto' means to advance or delay the Shabbat meal.

sub.text: Sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba's question
sub.text_en: Sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba's question
sub.desc_en: The sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba ask their father what distinguishes Shabbat for them since they have meat and wine daily.
Rav Pappa advises them to change the timing of the meal: if they usually eat early, delay it; if late, advance it.
Rav Sheishes would seat the sages in the sun in summer and in the shade in winter so they would rise quickly.

items.text: Opening story about Rav Huna
items.text_en: Opening story about Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Huna, while arranging his coins for the Rabbis, adjures them not to violate Shabbat.

items.text: The obligation to recite Vayechulu
items.text_en: The obligation to recite Vayechulu
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) states that even an individual praying on Friday night must recite Vayechulu, as Rav Hamnuna teaches that doing so makes one a partner with God in creation. Rabbi Elazar adds a proof that speech is like action.

items.text: The accompanying angels on Friday night
items.text_en: The accompanying angels on Friday night
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quoting Mar Ukva says that one who prays and recites Vayechulu is blessed by two ministering angels. A baraisa of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda describes how a good angel and an evil angel accompany a person home from synagogue on Friday night, and their responses based on whether the home is prepared for Shabbat.

items.text: Setting the table for Shabbat and Motzaei Shabbat
items.text_en: Setting the table for Shabbat and Motzaei Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Chanina advise setting the table even for a small meal on Friday night and Motzaei Shabbat. The Gemara relates that Rabbi Avahu would eat a kidney from a calf prepared for Motzaei Shabbat, and when his son Avimi suggested saving it for Friday night, a lion ate it.

items.text: The power of answering Amen
items.text_en: The power of answering Amen
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that answering 'Amen, yehei shmei rabba' with full force tears up one's decree. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan says even an idolater is forgiven. Reish Lakish says it opens the gates of Eden, and Rabbi Chanina explains 'Amen' stands for 'El Melech Ne'eman'.

items.text: Fire and Shabbat desecration
items.text_en: Fire and Shabbat desecration
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav says fire only occurs where Shabbat is desecrated, citing a verse. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains 'lo tichbeh' means when no one is around to extinguish it. Abaye says Jerusalem was destroyed because they desecrated Shabbat.

items.text: Jerusalem destroyed for neglecting Shema
items.text_en: Jerusalem destroyed for neglecting Shema
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu says Jerusalem was destroyed because they neglected the recitation of Shema morning and evening, citing verses from Isaiah.

items.text: Jerusalem destroyed for neglecting schoolchildren
items.text_en: Jerusalem destroyed for neglecting schoolchildren
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna says Jerusalem was destroyed because they neglected schoolchildren. Ulla says it was due to lack of mutual shame. Rabbi Yitzchak says it was because they treated small and great alike.

items.text: Jerusalem destroyed for lack of rebuke and disrespect for scholars
items.text_en: Jerusalem destroyed for lack of rebuke and disrespect for scholars
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says Jerusalem was destroyed because they did not rebuke each other, comparing them to deer. Rabbi Yehuda says it was because they disgraced Torah scholars, and Rav Yehuda quoting Rav says one who disgraces scholars has no cure.

items.text: The importance of schoolchildren and Torah scholars
items.text_en: The importance of schoolchildren and Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav interprets a verse as referring to schoolchildren and Torah scholars. Reish Lakish quoting Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah says the world exists only for the breath of schoolchildren. Rav Pappa questions Abaye about their own study, and Abaye distinguishes between breath with and without sin. Reish Lakish further says schoolchildren are not interrupted even for building the Temple, and any city without schoolchildren is destroyed.

items.text: Jerusalem destroyed for lack of trustworthy men, and a contradiction
items.text_en: Jerusalem destroyed for lack of trustworthy men, and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rava says Jerusalem was destroyed because trustworthy men ceased, citing a verse. The Gemara objects with Rav Katina who says trustworthy men never ceased even in Jerusalem's downfall, citing another verse about a man offering his brother to be a ruler.

items.text: Opening aggadic exposition on the verse 'Katzin tihyeh lanu'
items.text_en: Opening aggadic exposition on the verse 'Katzin tihyeh lanu'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse from Isaiah, explaining that 'yisa' refers to an oath, and 'lo eheyeh chovesh' means one who does not bind himself to Torah study. It then questions whether this applies only to Torah matters or also to business, concluding that the verse refers to Torah, not business.

items.text: Mishnah: Rescue of food and clothing on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rescue of food and clothing on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may rescue a basket of bread even if it contains a hundred meals, a cake of dried figs, and a barrel of wine, and may call others to rescue for themselves. It discusses where to rescue (to a courtyard that is an eruv) and the dispute between Ben Betera and the Sages. Rabbi Yosei limits the number of garments to eighteen.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between saving and folding, and the case of a large vessel
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between saving and folding, and the case of a large vessel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance of a hundred meals against the earlier rule of three meals. Rav Huna distinguishes between one who comes to save (all) and one who comes to fold (only three meals). Rabbi Abba bar Zavda distinguishes between the same courtyard and another courtyard. Rava's story about Rav Sheizvi and Rav Chisda clarifies that one may not bring a vessel larger than three meals, but may fill the same vessel as much as he wants.

items.text: Gemara: The calculation after Shabbat and the issue of payment
items.text_en: Gemara: The calculation after Shabbat and the issue of payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a calculation is needed after Shabbat if the food was ownerless. Rav Chisda says it is a matter of piety. Rava objects that pious people do not take Shabbat wages, and explains that the owner is God-fearing and does not want to benefit from others, nor does he want to trouble them for free. The Mishnah means that if the rescuers are clever, they make a calculation after Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Difference between 'for yourselves' and 'with me'
items.text_en: Gemara: Difference between 'for yourselves' and 'with me'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'for yourselves' regarding food and 'with me' regarding clothing. The answer is that for food, only three meals are permitted, so the rescuer does not need them, but for clothing, the rescuer may need them for the entire day.

items.text: Baraita: The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei on the number of garments
items.text_en: Baraita: The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei on the number of garments
items.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Meir allows one to wear, remove, and re-wear garments all day, while Rabbi Yosei limits to eighteen specific garments, listing them.

items.text: Mishnah: Making partitions and using vessels to prevent fire
items.text_en: Mishnah: Making partitions and using vessels to prevent fire
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may spread a goat-skin over a chest that caught fire because it singes, and one may make a partition with any vessels, full or empty, to stop the fire. Rabbi Yosei forbids new earthenware vessels full of water because they will burst and extinguish the fire.

items.text: Gemara: Rava's ruling on a garment that caught fire
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's ruling on a garment that caught fire
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav rules that if a garment caught fire on one side, one may pour water on the other side. A baraita is cited that one may spread the garment and cover himself, and similarly for a Torah scroll, one may spread it and read from it.

items.text: Opening: Rabbi Shimon ben Nanas vs. Rabbi Yosei on indirect extinguishment
items.text_en: Opening: Rabbi Shimon ben Nanas vs. Rabbi Yosei on indirect extinguishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a dispute: Rabbi Shimon ben Nanas permits indirect extinguishment (e.g., shaking a table to cause a lamp to fall), while Rabbi Yosei forbids it. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Shimon's reasoning is that the action is a 'cause' (gerama), not direct labor, and thus permitted.

items.text: Tanna Kamma vs. Rabbi Yosei on new clay vessels
items.text_en: Tanna Kamma vs. Rabbi Yosei on new clay vessels
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: Tanna Kamma permits making partitions with empty vessels to prevent fire spread, but Rabbi Yosei forbids using new clay vessels filled with water because they might burst and extinguish the fire. The Gemara infers that Tanna Kamma permits indirect extinguishment (gerama), while Rabbi Yosei forbids it.

items.text: Rabbi's ruling on a lamp behind a door
items.text_en: Rabbi's ruling on a lamp behind a door
items.desc_en: A baraita: If a lamp is behind a door, one may open and close it normally; if it goes out, it goes out. Rav curses this ruling. Ravina/Rav Acha asks why Rav curses it — perhaps because Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda (who forbids indirect extinguishment), while the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon (who permits). But Rav curses even a baraita that follows Rabbi Shimon?

items.text: Abaye and Rava agree: Rabbi Shimon admits in 'cutting off head' case
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava agree: Rabbi Shimon admits in 'cutting off head' case
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava both state that Rabbi Shimon would agree that cutting off a head (direct killing) is forbidden, even though it is a 'cause' (gerama). This clarifies that Rabbi Shimon's leniency applies only to indirect actions that are not equivalent to direct labor.

items.text: Rav Yehuda vs. Abaye on opening a door against a fire
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda vs. Abaye on opening a door against a fire
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda permits opening a door opposite a fire on Shabbat, but Abaye curses him. The Gemara analyzes whether the dispute is about a common wind (which might spread fire) or an uncommon one. Rav Yehuda permits because he does not decree a prohibition, while Abaye forbids because he does decree.

items.text: Sages vs. Rabbi Yosei on partitions with vessels
items.text_en: Sages vs. Rabbi Yosei on partitions with vessels
items.desc_en: A baraita: Sages permit making partitions with empty vessels or with full vessels that are unlikely to break (metal vessels). Rabbi Yosei forbids even vessels from Kfar Shihin and Kfar Hananya (which are fragile). The Gemara notes that this seems to invert the earlier dispute: Sages permit gerama (indirect extinguishment), Rabbi Yosei forbids it. But the Gemara resolves by saying the baraita is entirely Rabbi Yosei's view, and the Sages' leniency is only for vessels that won't break.

items.text: Rami bar Yeva's contradiction: Sages vs. Sages, Rabbi Yosei vs. Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rami bar Yeva's contradiction: Sages vs. Sages, Rabbi Yosei vs. Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yeva points out contradictions: Sages permit indirect extinguishment in one baraita but forbid it in another (regarding a name written on flesh). Similarly, Rabbi Yosei permits in one baraita (regarding a name on flesh) but forbids in another (regarding partitions). The Gemara resolves: the 'name on flesh' case involves a direct prohibition (writing), not gerama.

items.text: Rami bar Yeva's second contradiction: Sages vs. Sages on bathing
items.text_en: Rami bar Yeva's second contradiction: Sages vs. Sages on bathing
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yeva raises another contradiction: Sages forbid bathing with a name on flesh (because it might erase), but permit bathing for a mitzvah even if it might erase. The Gemara resolves: the mitzvah case is permitted because the person is anxious about money (and might come to scrub), but here the person is not anxious.

items.text: Rami bar Yeva's third contradiction: Sages vs. Sages on extinguishing
items.text_en: Rami bar Yeva's third contradiction: Sages vs. Sages on extinguishing
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yeva notes: Sages permit indirect extinguishment (gerama) in one case, but forbid it in another (where a person might come to directly extinguish). The Gemara resolves: the difference is whether the person is 'anxious about money' (which might lead to direct action) or not.

items.text: Rami bar Yeva's fourth contradiction: Sages vs. Rabbi Yosei on partitions
items.text_en: Rami bar Yeva's fourth contradiction: Sages vs. Rabbi Yosei on partitions
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yeva notes: Sages permit partitions with vessels that won't break, but Rabbi Yosei forbids even those. The Gemara resolves: the dispute is about 'gerama' — Sages permit indirect extinguishment, Rabbi Yosei forbids it.

items.text: Rami bar Yeva's fifth contradiction: Rabbi Yosei vs. Rabbi Yosei on partitions
items.text_en: Rami bar Yeva's fifth contradiction: Rabbi Yosei vs. Rabbi Yosei on partitions
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yeva notes: Rabbi Yosei forbids partitions with fragile vessels, but permits them with metal vessels. The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yosei's own view is that gerama is forbidden, but he permits metal vessels because they won't break and thus won't cause extinguishment.

items.text: Rami bar Yeva's sixth contradiction: Rabbi Yosei vs. Rabbi Yosei on bathing
items.text_en: Rami bar Yeva's sixth contradiction: Rabbi Yosei vs. Rabbi Yosei on bathing
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yeva notes: Rabbi Yosei forbids bathing with a name on flesh (because it might erase), but permits bathing for a mitzvah even if it might erase. The Gemara resolves: the mitzvah case is permitted because the person is not anxious about money (and won't scrub), while the general case is forbidden because the person might scrub.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Sheila's explanation: Sages permit standing naked before the Name
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Sheila's explanation: Sages permit standing naked before the Name
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Sheila explains the Sages' leniency in the 'name on flesh' case: they permit standing naked before the Name because the prohibition is only against 'doing' (writing), not against 'causing' (gerama). Rabbi Yosei, however, forbids even gerama.

items.text: Final resolution: Sages vs. Rabbi Yosei on gerama
items.text_en: Final resolution: Sages vs. Rabbi Yosei on gerama
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: The Sages permit gerama (indirect extinguishment) because they do not decree a prohibition where the person might come to direct action, while Rabbi Yosei forbids gerama because he does decree such a prohibition. The dispute about partitions with vessels is similarly resolved: Sages permit if vessels won't break, Rabbi Yosei forbids even those.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry into Rabbi Yosei's view on timely immersion
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry into Rabbi Yosei's view on timely immersion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei holds that timely immersion is a mitzvah, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei exempts a ba'al keri from immersing after minchah. It resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah, who holds that immersion on the seventh day suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei holds that timely immersion is a mitzvah, based on a previous assumption.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei exempts a ba'al keri from immersing after minchah, contradicting the view that timely immersion is a mitzvah.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah, who holds that immersion on the seventh day suffices, not Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Mishnah: Gentile and minor extinguishing a fire
items.text_en: Mishnah: Gentile and minor extinguishing a fire
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a gentile comes to extinguish a fire on Shabbat, one may not instruct him to do so or not, because his rest is not incumbent upon them. However, if a minor comes to extinguish, one must prevent him, because his rest is incumbent upon them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a gentile comes to extinguish a fire on Shabbat, one may not instruct him to do so or not, because his rest is not incumbent upon them; but if a minor comes to extinguish, one must prevent him, because his rest is incumbent upon them.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Ammi's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Ammi's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi says that in a fire one may say 'whoever extinguishes does not lose.' The Gemara attempts to support this from the Mishnah, but then refutes the proof by noting that the Mishnah's language implies one may not even hint at extinguishing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi states that in a fire one may say 'whoever extinguishes does not lose.'
The Gemara proposes to support Rabbi Ammi from the Mishnah about a gentile coming to extinguish.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that while one may not say 'extinguish' to a gentile, one may say 'whoever extinguishes does not lose.'
The Gemara objects by citing the end of the Mishnah, which also forbids saying 'do not extinguish,' implying that even a hint is prohibited.
The Gemara concludes that no support for Rabbi Ammi can be derived from this Mishnah.

items.text: Story of Yosef ben Simai and the fire
items.text_en: Story of Yosef ben Simai and the fire
items.desc_en: A story is told about Yosef ben Simai, whose courtyard caught fire on Shabbat. Non-Jewish soldiers came to extinguish it, but he prevented them due to Shabbat honor. A miracle occurred and rain extinguished the fire. The Sages said he need not have paid them, as the Mishnah permits not intervening.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts the story of Yosef ben Simai, whose courtyard caught fire on Shabbat; non-Jewish soldiers came to extinguish it, but he prevented them due to Shabbat honor, and a miracle occurred with rain extinguishing the fire.

After the event, Yosef ben Simai paid the soldiers, but the Sages ruled he need not have done so, citing the Mishnah that one does not instruct a gentile to extinguish or not extinguish a fire on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's inference about a minor eating neveilot
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about a minor eating neveilot
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a minor eating neveilot must be prevented by the court. Rabbi Yochanan limits this to a minor acting on his father's instructions. The Gemara questions whether a gentile acting on a Jew's behalf would be permitted, and answers that a gentile acts for himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a minor eating neveilot must be prevented by the court.
Rabbi Yochanan limits the inference to a minor acting on his father's instructions.
The Gemara questions whether a gentile acting on a Jew's behalf would be permitted.
The Gemara answers that a gentile acts for himself, not on the Jew's behalf.

items.text: Mishnah: Covering a flame and other precautions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Covering a flame and other precautions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits covering a lamp with a vessel to prevent it from catching a beam, and covering a child's excrement or a scorpion to prevent harm. Rabbi Yehudah relates that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was concerned about a sin-offering in such a case.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first ruling: one may cover a lamp with a bowl to prevent it from catching the beam.
The Mishnah adds two more permitted coverings: covering a child's excrement and covering a scorpion to prevent it from biting.
Rabbi Yehudah relates a story: a case came before Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai in Arav, and he said he was concerned about a sin-offering in such a case.

items.text: Gemara's story of rabbis visiting Avin of Neshikya
items.text_en: Gemara's story of rabbis visiting Avin of Neshikya
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rav Yehudah, Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba, and Rav Chanan bar Rava who visited Avin of Neshikya. The narrative is cut off, but it likely relates to the previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a story about Rav Yehudah, Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba, and Rav Chanan bar Rava who visited Avin of Neshikya.

items.text: Opening story about Rav Chanan bar Rava and the child's waste
items.text_en: Opening story about Rav Chanan bar Rava and the child's waste
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava was not brought a bed, and found his son being taught a mishnah about moving child's waste on Shabbat. He objects that the waste itself is already prepared for dogs, and questions the ruling by citing a baraita about rivers and springs having the status of everyone's feet.

items.text: Correction of the mishnah to chicken waste
items.text_en: Correction of the mishnah to chicken waste
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah must have been about chicken waste, not child's waste, to avoid the objection.

items.text: Objection from the status of גרף של רעי
items.text_en: Objection from the status of גרף של רעי
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that chicken waste is itself a גרף של רעי and should be forbidden. It distinguishes between waste in a vessel (permitted) and waste itself (forbidden), citing a story about Rav Ashi and a mouse found in a spice box, which was removed by its tail and thrown into the garbage. The Gemara resolves that the waste is in a garbage pit in the courtyard, not in the open.

items.text: Baraita on five creatures killed on Shabbat and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Baraita on five creatures killed on Shabbat and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The mishnah mentions killing a scorpion lest it sting. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says all harmful creatures may be killed on Shabbat. Rav Yosef objects with a baraita listing only five specific creatures that may be killed, implying others may not. The Gemara analyzes whether the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda (who holds that unnecessary labor is forbidden) or Rabbi Shimon (who permits it), concluding it must be Rabbi Shimon, and only those five are permitted.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution of the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya questions whether the baraita is correctly formulated. Rav Yosef asserts that he himself teaches it and resolves it: the baraita refers to cases where the creature is running after him, and it is the opinion of everyone (both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon).

items.text: Dispute about killing snakes and scorpions: the pious and the sages
items.text_en: Dispute about killing snakes and scorpions: the pious and the sages
items.desc_en: A tanna taught before Rava bar Rav Huna that one who kills snakes and scorpions on Shabbat is not favored by the spirit of the pious. Rava bar Rav Huna retorts that such pious ones are not favored by the spirit of the sages. This disagrees with Rav Huna, who rebuked a man for killing a hornet, implying it is forbidden.

items.text: Baraita about encountering snakes and scorpions
items.text_en: Baraita about encountering snakes and scorpions
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught: If snakes and scorpions came upon him, if he killed them it is known they were sent to be killed; if he did not kill them, it is known they were sent to kill him and a miracle occurred. Ulla (or others) say this applies only when they are hissing at him.

items.text: Story of a snake in the study hall and Rabbi's ruling
items.text_en: Story of a snake in the study hall and Rabbi's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana relates that a snake fell in the study hall and a Nivti (a type of snake-charmer) killed it. Rabbi said: He encountered one like himself (i.e., a fellow snake).

items.text: Inquiry about Rabbi's statement and the permissibility of killing snakes and scorpions
items.text_en: Inquiry about Rabbi's statement and the permissibility of killing snakes and scorpions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi's statement 'he encountered one like himself' means he acted properly or not. It brings a story where Rabbi Yannai was asked about killing snakes and scorpions on Shabbat. He said he kills a hornet, so a snake or scorpion is certainly permitted. But perhaps it is only by stepping on them inadvertently, as per Rav Yehuda, Rav Sheishet, and Rav Katina who each said certain creatures can be killed by stepping on them inadvertently.

items.text: Story of Abba bar Marta and the spitting incident
items.text_en: Story of Abba bar Marta and the spitting incident
items.desc_en: Abba bar Marta (also known as Abba bar Minyomei) was being pressured by the house of the Exilarch for money. They brought him and were tormenting him. He spat. The Exilarch ordered a vessel to be placed over it. Abba bar Marta said it was unnecessary, citing Rav Yehuda that spittle can be stepped on inadvertently. The Exilarch recognized him as a Torah scholar and released him.

items.text: Ruling about moving large benches on Shabbat
items.text_en: Ruling about moving large benches on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said in the name of Rabbi Chanina that large benches of the house of Rabbi may be moved on Shabbat. Rabbi Zeira asked whether they are lifted with one hand or two hands.

items.text: Discussion about carrying poles on Shabbat
items.text_en: Discussion about carrying poles on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana reports that Rabbi Chanina permitted carrying poles (קרונות) of the house of Rabbi on Shabbat. Rabbi Zeira asks whether this applies to poles carried by one or two people, and the answer is given by analogy to the poles of the house of Rabbi's father. The Gemara then discusses a related ruling about drinking wine from a non-Jew's poles with a single seal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana answers Rabbi Zeira's question by comparing the poles to those of the house of Rabbi's father.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana reports that Rabbi Chanina permitted moving the poles of the house of Rabbi on Shabbat.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether the poles are carried by one person or two.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana answers by analogy to the poles of Rabbi's father's house.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana adds that Rabbi Chanina permitted the house of Rabbi to drink wine from non-Jews' poles with a single seal, but the reason is uncertain.

items.text: Mishnah: Non-Jew's actions on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Non-Jew's actions on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a non-Jew lights a candle, fills water, or makes a gangplank for his own purposes, a Jew may benefit from it; but if done for a Jew, it is prohibited. It recounts a story of Rabban Gamliel and the elders who descended via a gangplank made by a non-Jew.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a non-Jew lights a lamp for himself, an Israelite may use its light; if for the Israelite, it is forbidden, and similarly for water and a gangplank, with a story about Rabban Gamliel and the elders.
The Mishnah adds the contrasting case: if the non-Jew acted for a Jew, it is forbidden.
The Mishnah states that if a non-Jew fills water for his own animal, a Jew may water his animal afterward.
The Mishnah adds the forbidden case for water done for a Jew.
The Mishnah states that if a non-Jew makes a gangplank for his own descent, a Jew may descend after him.
The Mishnah adds the forbidden case for a gangplank made for a Jew.
The Mishnah recounts that Rabban Gamliel and the elders descended via a gangplank made by a non-Jew, illustrating the permitted case.

items.text: Gemara: Need for all three cases
items.text_en: Gemara: Need for all three cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah lists three cases: candle, water, and gangplank. For candle, one might think it's always permitted because light for one is light for a hundred; for water, one might fear the non-Jew might add water for the Jew; the gangplank case is needed to introduce the story of Rabban Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to list all three cases: lamp, water, and gangplank, and that the story of Rabban Gamliel teaches a practical lesson.
The Gemara questions why the water case is also needed, since one might fear the non-Jew might add water for the Jew.
The Gemara answers that the gangplank case is needed to introduce the story of Rabban Gamliel and the elders.

items.text: Baraita: Non-Jew gathering herbs and filling water
items.text_en: Baraita: Non-Jew gathering herbs and filling water
items.desc_en: A Baraita teaches that if a non-Jew gathers herbs or fills water for his animal, a Jew may feed his animal afterward, but if done for the Jew, it is prohibited. This applies only when the non-Jew does not know the Jew; if he knows him, it is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a non-Jew gathers herbs or draws water for his animal, an Israelite may benefit afterward, but only if the non-Jew does not know the Israelite.
The Baraita continues: If a gentile filled water to water his animal, a Jew may drink after him; but if done for the Jew, it is forbidden.
The Baraita specifies: These rulings apply when the gentile does not know the Jew; but if he knows him, it is forbidden.

items.text: Objection from Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Objection from Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rav Huna said that one may stand his animal on grass on Shabbat, but not on מוקצה. This seems to permit benefiting from grass without concern for the non-Jew's intent, contradicting the Baraita. The Gemara resolves that the animal stands and eats on its own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Rav Huna's statement that one may place his animal on grass on Shabbat, implying that benefiting from the non-Jew's action is permitted even when the non-Jew knows the Israelite.
The Gemara resolves: The animal stands facing the herbs and goes and eats them, so it is not considered set-aside.

items.text: Challenge from Rabban Gamliel's case
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabban Gamliel's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Baraita says if the non-Jew knows the Jew, it is prohibited, yet Rabban Gamliel was known to the non-Jew. Abaye answers that the non-Jew acted in his absence; Rava says that even if in his presence, light for one is light for a hundred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabban Gamliel's action in the Mishnah is consistent with the baraita, since the non-Jew knew him.
Abaye answers that the non-Jew acted in Rabban Gamliel's absence, so the permission applies.
Rava answers that even if the non-Jew acted in his presence, the principle that a lamp for one is a lamp for a hundred applies.

items.text: Support from Rabban Gamliel's statement
items.text_en: Support from Rabban Gamliel's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a version where Rabban Gamliel said: 'Since he did it not in our presence, let us descend.' This supports Abaye's answer that the non-Jew acted in their absence. The Gemara suggests a corrected version: 'Since he did it, let us descend.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Rabban Gamliel's own statement that they may descend because the non-Jew acted not in their presence, contradicting Rava's view.
The Gemara resolves by reinterpreting Rabban Gamliel's statement to mean 'since he made it, let us descend,' removing the condition of absence.

items.text: Further proofs from majority cases
items.text_en: Further proofs from majority cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings two proofs: a city with a bathhouse heated on Shabbat, and a lamp lit in a banquet hall. In both, the ruling depends on the majority: if most are non-Jews, it is permitted; if most are Jews, it is prohibited. The Gemara explains that in these cases, the action is done for the majority.

sub.text: Gemara's proof from a city with a bathhouse
sub.text_en: Gemara's proof from a city with a bathhouse
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a city with a mixed population and a bathhouse heated on Shabbat, where the ruling depends on the majority: if most are non-Jews, one may bathe immediately; if most are Jews, one must wait.
The Gemara explains that in the bathhouse case, the heating is done for the sake of the majority, so the ruling follows the majority.

sub.text: Gemara's proof from a lamp in a banquet hall
sub.text_en: Gemara's proof from a lamp in a banquet hall
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita about a lamp lit in a banquet hall, where the ruling again depends on the majority: if most are non-Jews, it is permitted; if most are Jews, it is prohibited; if equal, it is prohibited.
The Gemara explains that in the lamp case as well, the lighting is done for the sake of the majority.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: All vessels are movable on Shabbat, even if broken
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: All vessels are movable on Shabbat, even if broken
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all vessels, including their doors, can be taken on Shabbat even if they were dismantled during the week, unlike house doors which are not prepared for Shabbat use.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all vessels, including their doors, may be moved on Shabbat even if dismantled, unlike house doors which are not prepared (מוכן).

items.text: Mishnah continuation: Specific tools and their uses
items.text_en: Mishnah continuation: Specific tools and their uses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists specific tools (nutcracker, axe, saw, rake, winnowing fan, needle) and their permitted uses on Shabbat for non-prohibited tasks.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists specific tools and their permitted uses on Shabbat: a hammer for nuts, an axe for dried figs, a saw for cheese, a rake for dried figs, a winnowing shovel and pitchfork for a child, a spindle and weaving stick for inserting, a hand needle for thorns, and a sack needle for opening a door.
