Rabbi Avahu in the name of Reish Lakish cites a verse to show that first tithe taken in sheaves is exempt from תרומה גדולה (the great terumah), only requiring תרומת מעשר (the terumah of the tithe).
Rav Pappa challenges Abaye that if the exemption applies to sheaves, it should also apply when the tithe is taken in a heap (כרי), but Abaye cites a verse requiring the separation from all gifts.
Abaye resolves the distinction: the sheaves have not undergone grain processing (אידגן), while the heap has, so the exemption applies only to the former.

items.text: Mishnah: moving second tithe and consecrated items
items.text_en: Mishnah: moving second tithe and consecrated items
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case is where one paid the principal but not the added fifth, teaching that the fifth does not prevent moving the item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: it is obvious that one may move second tithe and redemption money — why is this stated?
The Gemara explains: the case is where one paid the principal (of the redemption) but not the additional fifth (חומש), teaching that the fifth does not impede the redemption.

items.text: Mishnah: dry lupine
items.text_en: Mishnah: dry lupine
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that only dry lupine may be moved, not moist, because it is bitter and inedible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah permits moving dry lupine, but not moist.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: moist lupine is too bitter for animals, so it is unfit for food on Shabbat (fit only for human use, which is not permitted here).

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's exceptions for untithed produce
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's exceptions for untithed produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to list items like טבל and מעשר ראשון, since they are obviously forbidden. It explains that the cases involve Rabbinic-level טבל (grown in an unperforated pot) and מעשר ראשון that was taken before תרומה גדולה, where one might have thought it is permitted. The Gemara also addresses מעשר שני and הקדש that were redeemed improperly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that one may not move טבל (untithed produce), since it is obviously forbidden.
The Gemara explains that the case involves Rabbinic-level טבל, grown in an unperforated pot, where one might have thought it is permitted.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that one may not move מעשר ראשון (first tithe), since it is obviously forbidden.
The Gemara explains that the case involves מעשר ראשון taken before תרומה גדולה (the large priestly portion), where one might have thought it is permitted.
The Gemara references a prior exchange between Rav Pappa and Abaye to support the need for the Mishnah's ruling.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state that one may not move מעשר שני (second tithe) and הקדש (consecrated property), since they are obviously forbidden.

The Gemara explains that the cases involve items that were redeemed improperly: מעשר שני redeemed with a coin lacking a royal stamp, and הקדש redeemed with land, where one might have thought they are permitted.

items.text: Baraita on moving animal feed and Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's addition
items.text_en: Baraita on moving animal feed and Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's addition
items.desc_en: A Baraita states that one may move חצב (a plant) because it is food for deer, and חרדל because it is food for doves. Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel adds that one may also move broken glass because it is food for ostriches. Rabbi Nathan objects, arguing that if so, one should be able to move bundles of twigs for elephants. The Gemara explains that ostriches are common, while elephants are not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists items that may be moved on Shabbat because they are food for animals: חצב (wild endive) for deer, חרדל (mustard) for doves, and according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, broken glass for ostriches.
Rabbi Nathan objects that if the criterion is potential food for any animal, one could move bundles of twigs as food for elephants, which is absurd.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel responds that ostriches are common in that region, whereas elephants are not, so the comparison fails.
The Gemara resolves that ostriches (נעמיות) are common, while elephants are not, so the ruling is limited to common animals.

items.text: Amemar and Rav Ashi's refinement of the ruling
items.text_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi's refinement of the ruling
items.desc_en: Amemar qualifies that the permission to move broken glass applies only if one actually has ostriches. Rav Ashi objects that Rabbi Nathan's question about elephants would also apply if one has elephants. The Gemara resolves that the ruling is based on the item being fit for the animal, not necessarily having it present.

sub.desc_en: Amemar adds that the permission to move broken glass applies only if one actually owns ostriches.
Rav Ashi objects that if one does have elephants, why should moving twigs for them be forbidden?
Rav Ashi resolves that the criterion is whether the item is fit for the animal, not whether one actually owns it; here too, broken glass is fit for ostriches.

items.text: Abaye's statement that all Israel are princes
items.text_en: Abaye's statement that all Israel are princes
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yishmael, and Rabbi Akiva all hold that all Jews are considered royalty. He provides sources: Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel from the previous ruling, Rabbi Shimon from a Mishnah about anointing with rose oil, and Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva from a Baraita about a debtor's garment.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yishmael, and Rabbi Akiva all hold the principle that all Israelites are considered royalty.

sub.text: Supporting citation for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Supporting citation for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling about broken glass for ostriches reflects this principle.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon rules that all Israelites may anoint wounds with rose oil on Shabbat, because they are all considered royalty.

sub.text: Supporting citation for Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Supporting citation for Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva rule that a debtor wearing an expensive cloak is stripped and given a suitable one, because all Israelites are worthy of fine garments.

items.text: Baraita on moving bundles of straw and herbs
items.text_en: Baraita on moving bundles of straw and herbs
items.desc_en: A Baraita discusses moving bundles of straw, wood, and twigs: if prepared for animal food, they may be moved; otherwise not. Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel permits bundles that can be carried in one hand. Another Baraita addresses moving bundles of סיאה, אזוב, and קורנית: if for wood, one may not take from them on Shabbat; if for animal food, one may. The Gemara identifies the plants and clarifies a confusion about קורנית.

sub.desc_en: The Baraita rules that bundles of straw, wood, and twigs may be moved only if prepared for animal food; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits bundles that can be carried in one hand.

A second Baraita addresses bundles of סיאה, אזוב, and קורנית: if for wood, one may not take from them; if for animal food, one may, with restrictions on cutting and rubbing, according to Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages.
The Gemara identifies the plants: אמיתא is ניניא, סיאה is צתרי, אזוב is אברתא, and קורנית is called קורניתא.
The Gemara resolves a confusion: the plant called קורניתא in the Baraita is actually חשאי (a different plant), while the true קורניתא is something else.

items.text: Dispute about moving salted and unsalted meat
items.text_en: Dispute about moving salted and unsalted meat
items.desc_en: An argument is presented: Rav Huna permits moving salted meat on Shabbat, while Rav Chisda forbids it. The Gemara questions Rav Huna's position because he follows Rav, who holds like Rabbi Yehuda regarding מוקצה. It resolves that Rav Huna distinguishes between מוקצה for eating (which he forbids) and מוקצה for handling (which he permits). Rav Chisda's position is challenged by an incident where he allowed moving a goose, but the Gemara explains that goose is fit for a cushion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rav Huna permits moving unsalted meat on Shabbat, while Rav Chisda forbids it.
The Gemara objects: Rav Huna was a student of Rav, who follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that מוקצה (set-aside items) is forbidden, so how can he permit moving unsalted meat?

The Gemara resolves: Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding מוקצה לאכילה (set aside from eating) but follows Rabbi Shimon regarding מוקצה לטלטל (set aside from handling), thus permitting moving the meat.

The Gemara objects to Rav Chisda's position: Rav Yitzchak bar Ami visited Rav Chisda's house and saw them moving a goose from sun to shade, and Rav Chisda only commented on the financial loss, not forbidding the moving.
The Gemara resolves: A goose is different because it is fit for use as a cushion (אומצא), so moving it is permitted even according to Rav Chisda.

items.text: Baraita on moving fish and bones
items.text_en: Baraita on moving fish and bones
items.desc_en: A Baraita states that salted fish may be moved, but unsalted fish may not. However, both salted and unsalted meat may be moved, aligning with Rabbi Shimon's view. Another Baraita permits moving bones because they are food for dogs.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that salted fish may be moved on Shabbat, but unsalted fish may not.
The same baraita permits moving meat whether salted or unsalted, and notes that this anonymous ruling aligns with Rabbi Shimon's lenient view on מוקצה (set-aside items).
A second baraita permits moving bones on Shabbat because they are food for dogs.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Prohibited foods due to danger
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Prohibited foods due to danger
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists foods that are forbidden to be kept because they pose a danger, such as tainted meat and uncovered water. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that all such items are forbidden to be kept due to danger.

items.text: Mishnah: Moving animals and children on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Moving animals and children on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the permissibility of moving a basket for chicks, pushing a runaway hen, and leading calves and foals. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between lifting and placing one leg at a time (permitted) and dragging (forbidden).

items.text: Gemara: Rescuing an animal from a water channel
items.text_en: Gemara: Rescuing an animal from a water channel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav permits bringing pillows and blankets under a fallen animal to help it climb out. The Gemara objects from a baraita that only allows providing food in place. The resolution distinguishes between when food is possible and when it is not. The Gemara then justifies overriding the rabbinic prohibition of nullifying a vessel's use due to the Torah law of preventing animal suffering.

items.text: Gemara: Leading a hen vs. other animals
items.text_en: Gemara: Leading a hen vs. other animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah allows pushing a hen but not leading it. A baraita states that one may lead animals in a courtyard but not a hen. Abaye explains that a hen lifts its feet, causing it to move in a way that resembles carrying. Two contradictory baraitot are reconciled by Abaye: the latter part refers to a hen.

items.text: Abaye: How to slaughter a hen to avoid tearing simanim
items.text_en: Abaye: How to slaughter a hen to avoid tearing simanim
items.desc_en: Abaye advises that when slaughtering a hen, one should press its feet into the ground or lift them to prevent it from placing its claws on the ground and tearing the simanim (windpipe and gullet).

items.text: Mishnah: Assisting birth on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah: Assisting birth on Shabbat and Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not assist an animal in birth on Yom Tov but may support it. For a woman, one may assist birth on Shabbat, call a midwife, desecrate Shabbat, and tie the umbilical cord. Rabbi Yose permits cutting it. All needs of circumcision are done on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: How to assist an animal in birth
items.text_en: Gemara: How to assist an animal in birth
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman debate the meaning of 'supporting' an animal in birth: Rav Yehuda says holding the newborn to prevent it from falling, Rav Nachman says pressing the flesh to help the offspring emerge. A baraita supports Rav Yehuda's view, adding that one may blow into its nose and give it a teat to suckle.

items.text: Gemara: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's practice for a pure animal
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's practice for a pure animal
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel relates that they would show mercy to a pure animal on Yom Tov by placing salt in its womb and sprinkling placental water on the offspring to encourage the mother to accept it. This is only for a pure animal, as an impure animal does not reject its young.

items.text: Gemara: Extending the Mishnah's ruling on a woman in labor
items.text_en: Gemara: Extending the Mishnah's ruling on a woman in labor
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional leniencies are included by the Mishnah's phrase 'and they desecrate Shabbat for her.' It cites a baraita that allows lighting a candle and bringing oil, even through hair to avoid squeezing. The Gemara explains that even a blind woman may have a candle lit for her to reassure her. The issue of squeezing oil from hair is resolved by Rabba and Rav Yosef (no squeezing in hair) and Rav Ashi (even if there is, one changes the normal method).

items.text: Gemara: Desecrating Shabbat for a woman in labor
items.text_en: Gemara: Desecrating Shabbat for a woman in labor
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that as long as the womb is open, one desecrates Shabbat for a woman in labor whether she says she needs help or not. Once the womb is closed, the ruling is different (the text is cut off).

items.text: Dispute on when to desecrate Shabbat for a woman in childbirth
items.text_en: Dispute on when to desecrate Shabbat for a woman in childbirth
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi and Mar Zutra present two versions of Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Shmuel. According to Rav Ashi, if the woman says she needs help, Shabbat is desecrated only while the grave is open; if she does not say so, it is not. Mar Zutra's version rules more leniently: while the grave is open, Shabbat is desecrated regardless of her statement; after it closes, only if she says she needs help.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's version of Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's version of Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi presents a version of Rav Yehuda's ruling: Shabbat is desecrated for a woman in childbirth only while the grave is open and she says she needs help.

sub.text: Mar Zutra's version of Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra's version of Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra presents a more lenient version: while the grave is open, Shabbat is desecrated regardless of her statement; after it closes, only if she says she needs help.

items.text: Ruling in favor of the lenient version
items.text_en: Ruling in favor of the lenient version
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Marimar which version is the halakha. Marimar rules like Mar Zutra's lenient version, citing the principle that in cases of doubt regarding life-saving, we are lenient.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Marimar which version of the ruling is the halakha — Mar Zutra's lenient version or Rav Ashi's stringent version.
Marimar rules like Mar Zutra's lenient version, citing the principle that in cases of doubt regarding life-saving, we are lenient.

items.text: Defining the duration of the 'open grave'
items.text_en: Defining the duration of the 'open grave'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks when the 'open grave' period begins and ends. Abaye says it begins from the time she sits on the birthstool; Rav Huna bar Yehoshua says from when blood flows. Regarding its end, Abaye says three days, Rava says seven in the name of Rav Yehuda, and some say thirty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks when the 'open grave' period begins, and Abaye answers that it starts from the time the woman sits on the birthstool.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua gives an alternative beginning: from when the blood flows, and some say from when her friends carry her on their arms.
The Gemara asks when the 'open grave' period ends, and Abaye answers that it lasts three days.

sub.text: Rava's answer in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rava's answer in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rava says in the name of Rav Yehuda that the period is seven days, and some say thirty days.

items.text: Nehardeans' ruling on the three periods
items.text_en: Nehardeans' ruling on the three periods
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that for the first three days, Shabbat is desecrated regardless of her statement; for the next seven days, only if she says she needs help; for the next thirty days, even if she says she needs help, Shabbat is not desecrated, but actions may be done through a non-Jew, as per Rav Ulla and Rav Hamnuna's principles.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that for a woman in childbirth (חיה), the first three days Shabbat is desecrated regardless of her statement, the next seven days only if she says she needs help, and after thirty days even if she says she needs help Shabbat is not desecrated.

sub.text: Supporting principles of Rav Ulla and Rav Hamnuna
sub.text_en: Supporting principles of Rav Ulla and Rav Hamnuna
sub.desc_en: The gemara supports the Nehardeans' ruling for the thirty-day period by citing Rav Ulla's principle that all needs of a sick person may be done through a non-Jew on Shabbat, and Rav Hamnuna's principle that for a non-life-threatening matter one may instruct a non-Jew to act.

items.text: The thirty-day period for immersion
items.text_en: The thirty-day period for immersion
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that a woman after childbirth is exempt from immersion for thirty days. Rava clarifies this applies only when her husband is not with her; if he is, he warms her. A story about Rav Chisda's daughter illustrates this.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in Shmuel's name that a woman after childbirth (חיה) is exempt for thirty days, and the Nehardeans clarify this applies to immersion (טבילה).
Rava qualifies that the exemption applies only when her husband is not with her; if he is, he warms her.
A story illustrates the ruling: Rav Chisda's daughter immersed within thirty days without her husband present and became chilled, so they carried her bed after Rava to Pumpedita.

items.text: Making a fire for a woman in childbirth on Shabbat
items.text_en: Making a fire for a woman in childbirth on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that a fire may be made for a woman in childbirth on Shabbat during the rainy season. The Gemara initially limits this, but then broadens it to include any sick person and any season, citing Rav Chiya bar Avin's statement about bloodletting.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that a fire may be made for a woman in childbirth on Shabbat during the rainy season.
The Gemara initially assumes the ruling is limited to a woman in childbirth and to the rainy season, excluding a general sick person and the dry season.
The Gemara rejects the initial limitation and broadens the ruling to apply to any sick person and any season.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin cites Shmuel that one who bled and became chilled may have a fire made for him even during the summer solstice, supporting the broadened ruling.

items.text: Practices and stories related to bloodletting
items.text_en: Practices and stories related to bloodletting
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts various practices of Sages after bloodletting: Shmuel had a roasted sheep's head, Rav Yehuda had a pigeon's dish, Rabbah had a calf's leg. Abaye questions Rabbah about wasting food, but Rabbah prioritizes his body. Rav Yehuda says one should sell house beams for shoes, and if poor, sell shoes for food. Rav and Shmuel debate whether the food should be meat or wine. Further stories describe the Sages' drinking habits and precautions after bloodletting, including a story about Shmuel lying in the sun and a discussion about the day of the summer solstice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that after bloodletting, Shmuel was given a roasted sheep's head, Rav Yehuda a pigeon's dish, and Rabbah a calf's leg.
Abaye questions Rabbah, noting that eating a calf's leg after bloodletting violates the prohibition of בל תשחית (wasteful destruction).
Rabbah replies that the prohibition of בל תשחית (wasteful destruction) of his own body takes priority over wasting food.
Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that one should sell house beams for shoes, and if needy after bloodletting, even sell shoes for food.
The Gemara asks what constitutes 'food needs' for a bloodletter.
Rav says meat is needed because life for life, while Shmuel says wine because red for red.
A mnemonic sign (סִימָן) is inserted to aid memory of the following traditions.
The Gemara records the personal practices of Sages after bloodletting: Shmuel ate a spleen dish, Rabbi Yochanan drank until his head ached, Rav Nachman until his spleen floated, etc.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak requests that on bloodletting day, his household be told he is coming, to secure special treatment.

The Gemara states that all ruses (deceitful tricks) are forbidden except this one: a bloodletter who cannot afford food may take a coin to a shop to get a quarter-log of wine, eat seven black dates, rub oil on his temple, and lie in the sun.
Ablet finds Shmuel lying in the sun and asks if bad can be good; Shmuel explains it is his bloodletting day.
The Gemara notes that actually there is one day a year — the summer solstice — when the sun is beneficial, but Shmuel did not reveal this to Ablet.

items.text: Warnings and precautions after bloodletting
items.text_en: Warnings and precautions after bloodletting
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both state that one who is lenient with the meal after bloodletting will have his sustenance reduced from heaven. They also warn against sitting in a draft after bloodletting, as it can cause danger. A story about Shmuel illustrates the danger of missing a brick in the wall. Finally, they advise tasting something before going out after bloodletting to avoid harm from spirits or murderers.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel state that one who is lenient with the meal after bloodletting will have his sustenance reduced from heaven.
Rav and Shmuel warn against sitting in a draft after bloodletting, as it can cause danger.
A story about Shmuel illustrates the danger of missing a brick in the wall after bloodletting.
Rav and Shmuel advise tasting something before going out after bloodletting to avoid harm from spirits or murderers.

items.text: The danger of standing up after certain activities
items.text_en: The danger of standing up after certain activities
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both teach that one who performs a certain activity should wait a bit before standing up, because standing immediately after five activities (eating, drinking, sleeping, bloodletting, marital relations) is perilous, as these are closer to death than to life.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav and Shmuel who both say that one who performs certain actions should wait a bit before standing, as these actions bring one closer to death. The five actions are eating, drinking, sleeping, bloodletting, and marital relations.

items.text: Shmuel on intervals for bloodletting
items.text_en: Shmuel on intervals for bloodletting
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that the interval between bloodletting sessions is thirty days. Between seasons (tequfot) one should reduce the amount, and between seasons one should again reduce (i.e., do it less frequently or in smaller quantity).

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the interval for bloodletting is every thirty days, and between intervals one should reduce and then return to reducing.

items.text: Shmuel on preferred days for bloodletting
items.text_en: Shmuel on preferred days for bloodletting
items.desc_en: Shmuel teaches that bloodletting should be done on Sunday, Wednesday, or Friday, but not on Monday or Thursday. Monday and Thursday are favorable for those with ancestral merit because the upper and lower courts are in session. The Gemara questions why Wednesday is allowed while Friday is also problematic due to Mars being in the same angle, and answers that since many people are busy on Friday, God protects the simple.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that bloodletting should be done on Sunday, Wednesday, or Friday, but not on Monday or Thursday, because those days have merit from the Patriarchs.
The Gemara asks why Wednesday is not included, and explains that it is because Mars is in the ascendant at that hour.
The Gemara objects that Friday also has Mars in the ascendant, yet Shmuel permits it.
The Gemara resolves that since many people are accustomed to bloodletting on Friday, 'the Lord protects the simple.'

items.text: Shmuel's cryptic rule on bloodletting danger
items.text_en: Shmuel's cryptic rule on bloodletting danger
items.desc_en: Shmuel states a series: four that is four, four that is fourteen, four that is twenty-four, and four with no four after it — that is dangerous. This cryptic statement refers to specific dates in the month.

sub.text: Shmuel's ruling on dangerous bloodletting dates
sub.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on dangerous bloodletting dates
sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that bloodletting on the fourth day of a month that has four days after it is dangerous, and similarly for other patterns.

items.text: Dangerous and weak days for bloodletting
items.text_en: Dangerous and weak days for bloodletting
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists weak and dangerous days for bloodletting: Rosh Chodesh and the second day are weak, the third is dangerous; the eve of a festival is weak, the eve of Shavuot is dangerous. The Sages decreed that all festival eves are weak because of the eve of Shavuot, which is dangerous because if Israel had not accepted the Torah, the 'slaughterer' (טבח) would have slain them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that bloodletting on Rosh Chodesh and the second day is weakening, on the third day is dangerous, and on the eve of Shavuot is dangerous, and the rabbis decreed on all festival eves because of Shavuot.

items.text: Shmuel on timing of eating and drinking relative to bloodletting
items.text_en: Shmuel on timing of eating and drinking relative to bloodletting
items.desc_en: Shmuel says that if one ate a wheat grain and then bled, it is as if he bled only for that grain — this is for medical benefit, but for general relief it indeed relieves. The Gemara then states the rule: after bloodletting, drinking should be immediate, but eating can be delayed up to half a mil.

items.text: Unresolved questions about drinking and eating after bloodletting
items.text_en: Unresolved questions about drinking and eating after bloodletting
items.desc_en: Two inquiries: regarding drinking, whether it is beneficial only immediately and harmful later, or neither harmful nor beneficial; regarding eating, whether it is beneficial only within half a mil and harmful before or after, or neither. Both end with teiku (let it stand unresolved).

items.text: Rav's proclamation about cheap leeks and beards
items.text_en: Rav's proclamation about cheap leeks and beards
items.desc_en: Rav announces: a hundred large onions for a zuz, a hundred heads for a zuz, a hundred mustaches — worthless. Rav Yosef recalls that in Rav Huna's study hall, on the day when the rabbis would be idle, they would say it is 'the day of mustaches' (meaning beards are cut), but he did not understand what they meant.

sub.text: Rav's proclamation and Rav Yosef's recollection
sub.text_en: Rav's proclamation and Rav Yosef's recollection
sub.desc_en: Rav proclaims a hundred gourds for a zuz, a hundred heads for a zuz, a hundred mustaches for nothing, and Rav Yosef recalls that at Rav Huna's house on a day when the rabbis were idle, they said it was a day of mustaches, but he did not know what they meant.
Rav Yosef recalls that in Rav Huna's study hall, on idle days the rabbis would call it a 'day of mustaches,' but he did not understand what they meant.

items.text: Tying and cutting the umbilical cord on Shabbat
items.text_en: Tying and cutting the umbilical cord on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Tosefta teaches that the umbilical cord may be tied on Shabbat; Rabbi Yosei says even cut. The Sages agree with Rabbi Yosei in the case of two newborns whose cords might cause a danger. Rav Nachman bar Rav Huna cites Rav that the law follows Rabbi Yosei. The Gemara adds that all that is mentioned in the rebuke passage (Ezekiel 16) is done for a woman in childbirth on Shabbat.

items.text: Proof from Ezekiel that all childbirth procedures are permitted on Shabbat
items.text_en: Proof from Ezekiel that all childbirth procedures are permitted on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Huna cites Rav: everything mentioned in the rebuke passage (Ezekiel 16:4) is done for a woman in childbirth on Shabbat. The verse provides proof for delivering the baby, cutting the umbilical cord, washing, salting, and swaddling the newborn on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Huna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Huna reports in the name of Rav that everything stated in the rebuke passage (Ezekiel 16) is performed for a woman in childbirth on שבת (Shabbat).
Rav cites the verse from Ezekiel 16:4 that lists the procedures not performed on the abandoned newborn, implying they are normally done.
The Gemara derives from the verse that one may deliver the baby on שבת (Shabbat).
The Gemara derives from the verse that one may cut the umbilical cord on שבת (Shabbat).
The Gemara derives from the verse that one may wash the newborn on שבת (Shabbat).
The Gemara derives from the verse that one may salt the newborn on שבת (Shabbat).
The Gemara derives from the verse that one may swaddle the newborn on שבת (Shabbat).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva on circumcision and Shabbat
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva on circumcision and Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Eliezer's lenient view that if a knife was not brought before Shabbat, it may be brought uncovered on Shabbat, and in a time of danger, covered on the testimony of witnesses. Rabbi Eliezer also permits cutting wood to make charcoal for iron tools. Rabbi Akiva states a general principle: any labor that can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, but circumcision, which cannot be done beforehand, does.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that if a knife was not brought before Shabbat, one may bring it uncovered on Shabbat, and in a time of danger, covered on the testimony of witnesses.
Rabbi Eliezer further permits cutting wood on Shabbat to make charcoal for forging iron tools.
Rabbi Akiva states a general principle: any labor that can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat, but circumcision, which cannot be done beforehand, does.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry: Rabbi Eliezer's rationale – love of mitzvah or suspicion?
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry: Rabbi Eliezer's rationale – love of mitzvah or suspicion?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is due to love of the commandment (חבובי מצוה) or to avoid suspicion (חשדא). The practical difference is whether the knife may be brought covered. Rabbi Levi resolves that it is for love of the commandment, and a baraita supports that it is brought uncovered, not covered. Rav Ashi confirms from the Mishnah's mention of covering only in a time of danger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Eliezer's leniency is due to חבובי מצוה (love of the commandment) or due to חשדא (suspicion), and explores the practical difference regarding bringing the knife covered.
Rabbi Levi states that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is solely due to חבובי מצוה (love of the commandment), and a supporting baraita and Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah confirm this.
A baraita supports Rabbi Levi's position, stating that the knife is brought uncovered, not covered, according to Rabbi Eliezer.
Rav Ashi confirms from the Mishnah's mention of covering only in a time of danger that the rationale is love of the commandment.

items.text: Alternative baraita: Rabbi Yehuda's version
items.text_en: Alternative baraita: Rabbi Yehuda's version
items.desc_en: A second baraita presents a variant: Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that in a time of danger they would bring the knife covered on the testimony of witnesses, implying a different nuance.

sub.desc_en: A second baraita records Rabbi Yehuda's version in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, stating that in a time of danger they would bring it covered on the testimony of witnesses.

items.text: Clarification: How many witnesses?
items.text_en: Clarification: How many witnesses?
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether 'on the testimony of witnesses' means the person and one other, or the person and two others. It concludes from the term 'witnesses' that it must be the person and two others, as 'witnesses' implies those fit to testify elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether 'witnesses' in the Mishnah means the person himself plus one other, or himself plus two others.
The Gemara resolves that 'witnesses' means himself plus two, because the plural 'עדים' implies at least two, and the phrase 'who are fit to testify elsewhere' supports this.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's other ruling and the story of Levi and chicken with milk
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's other ruling and the story of Levi and chicken with milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about Rabbi Eliezer's place where they cut wood for iron tools on Shabbat, and Rabbi Yose HaGelili's place where they ate chicken with milk. A story follows: Levi visited Yosef the bird-catcher, was served a chicken head in milk, and did not eat. When he came before Rabbi, he explained he did not ban them because it was Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's place, and they might follow Rabbi Yose HaGelili's lenient view. The baraita of Rabbi Yose HaGelili is cited, who permits chicken with milk based on a scriptural derivation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that in Rabbi Eliezer's place they cut wood for iron tools on Shabbat, and in Rabbi Yose HaGelili's place they ate chicken with milk.

A story recounts that Levi visited Yosef the bird-catcher, was served a chicken head in milk, and did not eat; when he came before Rabbi, he explained he did not ban them because it was Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's place, and they might follow Rabbi Yose HaGelili's lenient view.

The baraita of Rabbi Yose HaGelili is cited, who permits chicken with milk based on a scriptural derivation: the verse 'בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ' (in its mother's milk) excludes a bird, which has no mother's milk.

items.text: Stories of devotion to mitzvot: circumcision and tefillin
items.text_en: Stories of devotion to mitzvot: circumcision and tefillin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak tells of a city that followed Rabbi Eliezer's lenient practices and were rewarded by being spared from a decree against circumcision. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains that mitzvot accepted with joy, like circumcision, are still performed with joy, while those accepted with contention, like forbidden relations, are still contentious. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that mitzvot for which Jews gave their lives, like idolatry and circumcision, remain firmly held, while tefillin, for which they did not, are weak. The Gemara recounts the story of Elisha, the man of wings, who risked his life for tefillin and was miraculously saved, comparing Israel to a dove whose wings protect it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak recounts that a city which followed Rabbi Eliezer's lenient practices regarding circumcision was spared from a royal decree against circumcision.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains that mitzvot accepted with joy, like circumcision, are still performed with joy, while those accepted with contention, like forbidden relations, are still contentious.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that mitzvot for which Jews gave their lives, like idolatry and circumcision, remain firmly held, while tefillin, for which they did not, are weak.
Rabbi Yannai says tefillin require a clean body like Elisha, with Abaye and Rava explaining this means not passing gas or sleeping in them.
The Gemara recounts the story of Elisha, who risked his life for tefillin and was miraculously saved, earning the nickname 'man of wings'.
The Gemara explains that Elisha specifically said 'dove's wings' because Israel is compared to a dove, whose wings protect it, just as mitzvot protect Israel.

items.text: Final story: Bringing a scalpel through roofs and courtyards
items.text_en: Final story: Bringing a scalpel through roofs and courtyards
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rav Adda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak recounts that once they forgot to bring a scalpel before Shabbat, and they brought it on Shabbat through roofs and courtyards, demonstrating a lenient practice.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Rav Adda's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rav Adda's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Rav Adda reports in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak that once they forgot to bring a scalpel before Shabbat and brought it on Shabbat through roofs and courtyards.

items.text: Opening statement: the action was against Rabbi Eliezer's will
items.text_en: Opening statement: the action was against Rabbi Eliezer's will
items.desc_en: The segment states that the bringing of the knife was not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer's will, setting up the contradiction to be resolved.

sub.desc_en: The segment states that the bringing of the knife was not in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer's will, setting up the contradiction to be resolved.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and attempted resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and attempted resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects: Rabbi Eliezer permits carrying the knife, so the action was actually in his will. He suggests the phrase means it was against the Sages' will, but then cites a baraita that prohibits bringing the knife even through roofs, courtyards, and karpafs, contradicting the Sages' supposed leniency.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that the phrase 'contrary to the wishes of Rabbi Eliezer' is wrong, because Rabbi Eliezer actually permits carrying the scalpel.
Rav Yosef suggests the phrase means it was against the Sages' will, but then questions whether the Sages actually permitted carrying via roofs, courtyards, and enclosures.
A baraita is cited that prohibits bringing the knife via roofs, enclosures, or courtyards, contradicting the Sages' supposed leniency.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution: it was against Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants, but in accordance with Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution: it was against Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants, but in accordance with Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the action was against Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants (the Sages), but in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that roofs, courtyards, and karpafs are a single domain for vessels that rested within them, but not for vessels from the house.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by explaining that the action was against Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants, but in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that roofs, enclosures, and courtyards are a single domain for vessels that rested within them, but not for vessels from the house.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about an alleyway without shituf
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about an alleyway without shituf
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi whether one may carry throughout an alleyway that has not been joined (shituf). He compares it to a courtyard, which permits carrying even without an eruv, but notes differences: an alleyway lacks four walls and has no residents. Rabbi Asi remains silent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi whether an alleyway without shituf is like a courtyard (permitting carrying throughout) or different due to lacking four walls and residents.
Rabbi Asi remains silent and offers no response.

items.text: A story about bringing the knife on Shabbat and the difficulty with Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: A story about bringing the knife on Shabbat and the difficulty with Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish reports in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that once they forgot to bring the circumcision knife before Shabbat and brought it on Shabbat, which was difficult for the Sages because they acted against the majority opinion and followed Rabbi Eliezer, who is a 'Shamuti' (excommunicated).

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish reports in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that once they forgot to bring the circumcision knife before Shabbat and brought it on Shabbat.
The Sages found it difficult: how could they abandon the words of the Sages and act according to Rabbi Eliezer?
The Gemara explains two reasons for the difficulty: Rabbi Eliezer is a 'Shamuti' (excommunicated), and the rule is that the halakha follows the majority against an individual.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's clarification: the alleyway had no shituf, and Rabbi Zeira's earlier question is resolved
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's clarification: the alleyway had no shituf, and Rabbi Zeira's earlier question is resolved
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya asked Rabbi Yehuda HaGozer, who said the alleyway had no shituf and they carried the knife from one end to the other. Rabbi Zeira then asks if this implies carrying is permitted throughout such an alleyway, and Rabbi Yehuda confirms. Rabbi Zeira notes he had asked this before and received no answer; Rabbi Yehuda attributes his earlier silence to forgetfulness due to the pressure of his studies.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya reports that he asked Rabbi Yehuda HaGozer about the incident, who said the alleyway had no shituf and they carried the scalpel from one end to the other.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Yehuda HaGozer whether this implies that carrying is permitted throughout an alleyway that had no shituf.
Rabbi Yehuda HaGozer confirms that yes, carrying is permitted throughout such an alleyway.
Rabbi Zeira objects that he had previously asked Rabbi Yehuda HaGozer this very question and received no such answer.
Rabbi Yehuda HaGozer explains that his earlier silence was due to forgetfulness caused by the pressure of his studies, and now his knowledge has been restored.

items.text: Rav's ruling: an alleyway without shituf is limited to four cubits
items.text_en: Rav's ruling: an alleyway without shituf is limited to four cubits
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports in the name of Rav that in an alleyway without shituf, one may only carry within four cubits.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports in the name of Rav that in an alleyway without shituf, one may only carry within four cubits.

items.text: Abaye's clarification: Rav's ruling depends on whether courtyards made an eruv with houses
items.text_en: Abaye's clarification: Rav's ruling depends on whether courtyards made an eruv with houses
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that Rabbi Zeira stated this ruling without explanation until Rabbah bar Avuh explained it: Rav said that if courtyards made an eruv with houses, carrying is limited to four cubits; if not, carrying is permitted throughout the alleyway.

sub.desc_en: Abaye notes that Rabbi Zeira stated the ruling without explanation until Rabbah bar Avuh came and explained it.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh citing Rav explains that if courtyards made an eruv with houses, carrying is limited to four cubits; if not, carrying is permitted throughout the alleyway.

items.text: Rav Chanina's question about the logic of Rav's distinction
items.text_en: Rav Chanina's question about the logic of Rav's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina Chozah asks Rabbah why, when courtyards made an eruv with houses, the alleyway is treated differently, and explains that Rav holds that an alleyway is only permitted with a side-post or beam when there are houses opening into it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina Chozah asks Rabbah why, when courtyards made an eruv with houses, the alleyway is treated differently, and explains that Rav holds that an alleyway is only permitted with a side-post or beam when there are houses opening into it.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about courtyards and houses
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about courtyards and houses
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction: if there are houses but no courtyards, or courtyards but no houses, the earlier argument fails. Various solutions are proposed—nullifying permission to one person, or dividing the day—but each is rejected. Rav Ashi concludes that the houses are the cause of the courtyards' prohibition, and here there are no houses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if there are houses but no courtyards, or courtyards but no houses, the earlier argument about nullification fails.
The Gemara proposes that all residents nullify their permission to one person, but rejects it because a house still exists while houses are absent.
The Gemara proposes dividing the day between two people, but rejects it because at any given time only one person has permission.
Rav Ashi resolves that the houses are the cause of the courtyards' prohibition, and here there are no houses.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan limits Rabbi Eliezer's principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan limits Rabbi Eliezer's principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Eliezer did not teach that all mitzvah preparations override Shabbat; rather, he derived the rule for the two loaves via a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) from the omer. The baraita shows the analogy, and the Gemara notes that the gezerah shavah is 'free' (mufneh) because the superfluous phrase 'from the day you bring' indicates it.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan limits Rabbi Eliezer's principle: the rule that mitzvah preparations override Shabbat was not universal, but derived specifically for the two loaves (שתי הלחם) via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the omer.
A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Eliezer explicitly derives the rule for the two loaves via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the omer, using the shared term 'הבאה' (bringing).

The Gemara notes that the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) is 'free' (מופנה) because the superfluous phrase 'מיום הביאכם' (from the day you bring) in the omer passage indicates it is available for the analogy, preventing a potential refutation.

items.text: Objection: one-sided analogy is refutable
items.text_en: Objection: one-sided analogy is refutable
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the gezerah shavah is only one-sided (mufneh mi-tzad echad), and Rabbi Eliezer himself holds that such an analogy can be refuted. The Gemara answers that the word 'tavi'u' (you shall bring) is a ribbui (extension), so the analogy is not needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the gezerah shavah is only one-sided (mufneh mi-tzad echad), and Rabbi Eliezer himself holds that such an analogy can be refuted.
The Gemara answers that the word 'תָּבִיאוּ' (you shall bring) is a ribbui (extension), so the analogy is not needed.

items.text: Attempts to exclude lulav, sukkah, matzah, shofar
items.text_en: Attempts to exclude lulav, sukkah, matzah, shofar
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the ribbui excludes. It considers lulav, sukkah, matzah, and shofar, but each is rejected because baraitot explicitly state that Rabbi Eliezer holds their preparations override Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the exclusion (מיעוט) from the ribbui 'תביאו' comes to exclude, beginning by suggesting lulav.
The Gemara rejects lulav because a baraita states lulav and its preparations override Shabbat according to Rabbi Eliezer, so it cannot be excluded.
The Gemara suggests sukkah, but rejects it via a baraita stating sukkah and its preparations override Shabbat according to Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara suggests matzah, but rejects it via a baraita stating matzah and its preparations override Shabbat according to Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara suggests shofar, but rejects it via a baraita stating shofar and its preparations override Shabbat according to Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Exclusion of tzitzit and mezuzah
items.text_en: Exclusion of tzitzit and mezuzah
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah explains that the ribbui excludes tzitzit for one's garment and mezuzah for one's door. A baraita supports this: they agree that if one already attached tzitzit or made a mezuzah, he is liable. Rav Yosef explains the reason: these have no fixed time. Abaye objects that precisely because they have no fixed time, they should be more lenient.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah explains that the exclusion (מיעוט) from the ribbui refers to tzitzit for one's garment and mezuzah for one's door.
A baraita supports this: they agree that if one already attached tzitzit or made a mezuzah, he is liable.
The Gemara asks for the reason why these are excluded.
Rav Yosef explains the reason: these have no fixed time.
Abaye objects that precisely because they have no fixed time, they should be more lenient.

items.text: Gemara's question on the opening Mishnah's ruling about lulav
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the opening Mishnah's ruling about lulav
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that lulav and its preparations override Shabbat according to Rabbi Eliezer, asking why it is permitted at any time. Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak answers that since one can declare the lulav ownerless, it is considered his possession.

items.text: Derivation for lulav's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Derivation for lulav's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer derives that lulav's preparations override Shabbat. It rejects a derivation from the omer or two loaves because they are for God's needs. Instead, Rabbi Eliezer uses the verse 'bayom' (on the day) to include Shabbat. The Gemara clarifies that this applies to preparations, not the lulav itself.

items.text: Sages' objection and Rabbi Eliezer's response for lulav
items.text_en: Sages' objection and Rabbi Eliezer's response for lulav
items.desc_en: The Sages argue that the verse 'bayom' teaches that lulav is taken by day, not at night, not that it overrides Shabbat. Rabbi Eliezer derives the night exclusion from the verse 'vesemachtem lifnei Hashem Eloheichem shiv'at yamim'—days, not nights. The Sages counter that this verse is needed to prevent a comparison to sukkah, which includes nights.

items.text: Why not derive from lulav itself?
items.text_en: Why not derive from lulav itself?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah did not write the law explicitly in the lulav section so that other mitzvot could learn from it. It answers that lulav is unique because it requires four species, making it an unsuitable source for analogy.

items.text: Derivation for sukkah's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Derivation for sukkah's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer derives that sukkah's preparations override Shabbat. It rejects derivations from the omer, two loaves, or lulav due to their unique features. Instead, he learns via a gezerah shavah from 'shiv'at yamim' in lulav. The Gemara then asks why not write it explicitly in sukkah, and answers that sukkah is unique because it applies at night as well as day.

items.text: Derivation for matzah's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Derivation for matzah's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer derives that matzah's preparations override Shabbat. It rejects derivations from the omer, two loaves, lulav, or sukkah. Instead, he learns via a gezerah shavah from 'chamishah asar' in the festival of sukkot. The Gemara then asks why not write it explicitly in matzah, and answers that matzah is unique because it applies to women as well as men.

items.text: Derivation for shofar's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Derivation for shofar's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer derives that shofar's preparations override Shabbat. It rejects derivations from all previous cases. Instead, he uses the verse 'yom teruah yihyeh lachem'—'yom' even on Shabbat. The Gemara clarifies this applies to preparations, not the blowing itself, as the school of Shmuel already exempts shofar blowing from labor. The Sages argue the verse teaches day, not night; Rabbi Eliezer derives night exclusion from the verse on Yom Kippur. The Gemara then asks why not write it explicitly in shofar, and answers that shofar blowing on Rosh Hashanah brings remembrance, and on Yom Kippur it frees slaves and returns fields.

items.text: Beginning of derivation for milah's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Beginning of derivation for milah's preparations overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to ask how Rabbi Eliezer derives that milah and its preparations override Shabbat. It suggests he might learn from all the previous cases, but notes that those have unique features not shared by milah.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's source for circumcision overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's source for circumcision overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is based on the verse 'on the eighth day he shall circumcise the flesh of his foreskin,' implying even on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for circumcision overriding Shabbat is derived from the verse 'on the eighth day he shall circumcise the flesh of his foreskin,' implying even on Shabbat.

items.text: Challenge: Why not derive from circumcision alone?
items.text_en: Challenge: Why not derive from circumcision alone?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah did not just write about circumcision and let other laws be derived from it, and answers that circumcision has a unique stringency—thirteen covenants were made regarding it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah did not just write about circumcision and let other laws be derived from it.
The Gemara answers that circumcision has a unique stringency—thirteen covenants were made regarding it—so it cannot serve as a source for other laws.

items.text: Source for circumcision itself overriding Shabbat
items.text_en: Source for circumcision itself overriding Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer is only about the accessories of circumcision, but the act itself overrides Shabbat. Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak state this is a halachah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer is only about the accessories of circumcision, but the act itself overrides Shabbat according to all.
Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak state that the source for circumcision overriding Shabbat is a halachah (received tradition).

items.text: Objection: Kal vachomer from halachah is invalid
items.text_en: Objection: Kal vachomer from halachah is invalid
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya derives that saving a life overrides Shabbat via a kal vachomer from circumcision. The Gemara objects: if circumcision is a halachah, one cannot derive a kal vachomer from a halachah, as shown by another baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya derives that saving a life (פיקוח נפש) overrides Shabbat via a kal vachomer from circumcision, and then notes that if circumcision is a halachah (הלכה), one cannot derive a kal vachomer from a halachah, as shown by another baraita where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya himself rejects such a derivation.

items.text: Gezeirah shavah attempts and resolution
items.text_en: Gezeirah shavah attempts and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar proposes a gezeirah shavah from 'ot' to 'ot', but is challenged that tefillin would also override Shabbat. Then 'brit' to 'brit' is proposed, challenged by the great (animal). Then 'dorot' to 'dorot', challenged by tzitzit. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that we derive from all three terms together, excluding those with only one.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar proposes a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'אות' (sign) to 'אות' to derive that circumcision overrides Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that if the גזירה שווה from 'אות' is valid, then תפילין (phylacteries), which also have 'אות', would override Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar shifts to a גזירה שווה from 'ברית' (covenant) to 'ברית'.
The Gemara objects that the great (animal), which also has 'ברית', would override Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar shifts to a גזירה שווה from 'דורות' (generations) to 'דורות'.
The Gemara objects that ציצית (ritual fringes), which also has 'דורות', would override Shabbat.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that we derive from all three terms together ('אות', 'ברית', 'דורות'), excluding those with only one of them.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation from 'bayom' and defense
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation from 'bayom' and defense
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the verse 'bayom' teaches even on Shabbat. Resh Lakish challenges that those lacking atonement also have 'bayom' but do not override Shabbat; it is needed to exclude night. The Gemara defends that for circumcision, 'bayom' is still needed despite other verses, to include even when the baby is weak.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse 'בַּיּוֹם' (on the day) that circumcision is performed even on Shabbat.
Resh Lakish objects that those lacking atonement (מחוסרי כפרה) also have the word 'בַּיּוֹם' in their verses, yet they do not override Shabbat.
The Gemara answers that for those lacking atonement, 'בַּיּוֹם' is needed to teach that the offering is brought by day and not by night.
Resh Lakish counters that for circumcision too, 'בַּיּוֹם' is needed to exclude night, but that is already derived from 'בֶּן שְׁמֹנַת יָמִים' (an eighth-day-old).
Resh Lakish further objects that the day requirement for those lacking atonement is derived from 'בְּיוֹם צַוּוֹתוֹ' (on the day He commanded), so 'בַּיּוֹם' there is superfluous.

The Gemara defends that even though the day requirement is derived from 'בְּיוֹם צַוּוֹתוֹ', the word 'בַּיּוֹם' is still needed for circumcision to include the case of a weak baby, lest one think it should be delayed until night.

items.text: Ravina's counter-challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Ravina's counter-challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges that if 'bayom' is the source, then a non-priest or an onen should be valid for circumcision, but the verse excludes them.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects that if 'bayom' (on the day) is the source for circumcision overriding Shabbat, then a non-priest (זר) or an onen (אונן) should also be valid for circumcision, but the verse excludes them.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's derivation from 'shemini' and rejection
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's derivation from 'shemini' and rejection
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov says 'shemini' implies even on Shabbat. The Gemara objects that 'shemini' is needed to exclude the seventh day, but that is already from 'ben shemonat yamim'. Another verse excludes the ninth, but the Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's approach is clearer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov derives from the word 'שמיני' (eighth) that circumcision is performed even on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that 'שמיני' is needed to exclude the seventh day, but that exclusion is already derived from 'בן שמנת ימים'.
The Gemara resolves that one verse excludes the seventh day and another excludes the ninth, but concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's approach is clearer.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Rava's analysis
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan and Rava's analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan and not Rav Acha bar Yaakov, teaching that 'shemini yimol' applies even on Shabbat, and 'mechalleleha mot yumat' refers to other labors. Rava questions the baraita's internal logic, and the Gemara explains that the baraita initially thought a kal vachomer from leprosy (which overrides Temple service) would suffice, but then required the verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's position, teaching that 'שמיני ימול' applies even on Shabbat, and 'מחלליה מות יומת' refers to other labors.
Rava questions the internal logic of the baraita: what was the Tanna's initial reasoning and what later difficulty led to the conclusion?
The Gemara explains that the baraita initially thought a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from leprosy (which overrides Temple service) would suffice, but then required the verse.

items.text: Opening kal vachomer argument
items.text_en: Opening kal vachomer argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a kal vachomer: if Temple service overrides Shabbat, then circumcision (which is less severe) should also override Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a kal vachomer argument: if Temple service overrides Shabbat, then circumcision (which is less severe) should also override Shabbat.

items.text: Challenge to the kal vachomer
items.text_en: Challenge to the kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the premise: perhaps Shabbat is more severe than leprosy, or the argument is about the person being unfit, and concludes with a verse that circumcision is even on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'or not' means, suggesting that perhaps Shabbat is more severe than leprosy.
The Gemara raises an alternative objection: perhaps the severity is not about leprosy itself but about the person being unfit for service.
The Gemara resolves by citing the verse 'on the eighth day he shall be circumcised' and the word 'ביום' (by day) to teach that circumcision is performed even on Shabbat.

items.text: Baraita on circumcision overriding leprosy and Festivals
items.text_en: Baraita on circumcision overriding leprosy and Festivals
items.desc_en: A baraita states that circumcision overrides leprosy both in its time and not in its time, but overrides a Festival only in its time.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that circumcision overrides leprosy both in its proper time and not in its proper time, but overrides a Festival only in its proper time.

items.text: Source for circumcision overriding leprosy
items.text_en: Source for circumcision overriding leprosy
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'יִמּוֹל בְּשַׂר עׇרְלָתוֹ' that circumcision is performed even if there is a leprous spot, and the verse 'הִשָּׁמֶר בְּנֶגַע הַצָּרַעַת' applies elsewhere. An alternative interpretation is rejected by the word 'בָּשָׂר'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that circumcision overrides leprosy.

The baraita cites the verse 'יִמּוֹל בְּשַׂר עׇרְלָתוֹ' (Leviticus 12:3) to teach that even if there is a leprous spot, one cuts it, and the prohibition in 'הִשָּׁמֶר בְּנֶגַע הַצָּרַעַת' (Deuteronomy 24:8) applies elsewhere, not to circumcision.
The tanna raises an alternative: perhaps the prohibition applies even to circumcision, and the verse 'יִמּוֹל בְּשַׂר עׇרְלָתוֹ' applies only when there is no leprous spot.
The Gemara resolves that the superfluous word 'בָּשָׂר' (flesh) teaches that circumcision is performed even when there is a leprous spot.

items.text: Rava's analysis of the baraita's logic
items.text_en: Rava's analysis of the baraita's logic
items.desc_en: Rava questions the baraita's initial assumption and final difficulty, explaining that the baraita first uses a kal vachomer from Shabbat to leprosy, then questions whether Shabbat is indeed more severe, concluding with the verse 'בָּשָׂר'.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks what the tanna initially found acceptable and what ultimately troubled him in the baraita.
The Gemara explains that the tanna initially held that circumcision overrides leprosy via a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference) from שבת (Sabbath), which is more stringent.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the tanna's reconsideration
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the tanna's reconsideration
sub.desc_en: The tanna then questions whether שבת (Sabbath) is indeed more stringent, suggesting that צרעת (leprosy) might be more severe since it overrides the Temple service, and concludes with the verse 'בָּשָׂר' (flesh) to establish that circumcision overrides leprosy.

items.text: Alternative explanation: positive commandment overrides prohibition
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: positive commandment overrides prohibition
items.desc_en: Another version: circumcision overrides leprosy because a positive commandment overrides a prohibition, but here it is a positive and a prohibition combined, so the verse 'בָּשָׂר' is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another version: circumcision overrides leprosy because a positive commandment overrides a prohibition.
The Gemara asks what the tanna meant by 'or perhaps' and then reconsiders.
The Gemara objects: the principle that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition applies only to a simple prohibition, but here it is a positive and a prohibition combined.

The Gemara resolves: the verse 'יִמּוֹל בְּשַׂר עׇרְלָתוֹ' would apply only when there is no bright spot, but the extra word 'בָּשָׂר' teaches that circumcision overrides leprosy even when there is a bright spot.

items.text: Derivation for intermediate cases
items.text_en: Derivation for intermediate cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about an intermediate case (not an adult or infant) and Abaye derives it from a common feature of adult and infant circumcision.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for an adult and infant the derivation from the word 'בשר' (flesh) works, but from where do we derive that circumcision overrides leprosy for an intermediate case (a child between eight days and adulthood)?
Abaye derives the intermediate case from the common feature (הצד השוה) of adult and infant circumcision: both are circumcised and both override leprosy, so any circumcised male overrides leprosy.

items.text: Rava's kal vachomer and Rav Safra's challenge
items.text_en: Rava's kal vachomer and Rav Safra's challenge
items.desc_en: Rava says circumcision in its time needs no verse, derived from Shabbat. Rav Safra challenges: perhaps leprosy is more severe because it overrides Temple service. Rava responds that the person is unfit, not the leprosy.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that circumcision performed at its proper time needs no verse to override leprosy, as it is derived by a kal vachomer (a fortiori) from Shabbat.
Rav Safra challenges Rava: how do we know Shabbat is more severe? Perhaps leprosy is more severe because it overrides Temple service, which itself overrides Shabbat.
Rava responds that the leper's exclusion from Temple service is not because leprosy is severe, but because the person is unfit due to being מחוסר טבילה (lacking immersion).

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution for pure leprous spots
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution for pure leprous spots
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi addresses pure leprous spots, explaining that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition only when the prohibition is uprooted and the positive is fulfilled, which is not the case here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the case of pure leprous spots is settled, but what about pure leprous spots (where the kohen is not disqualified)?
Rav Ashi explains that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition only when the prohibition is uprooted and the positive is fulfilled, which is not the case here for pure leprous spots.

items.text: Incomplete segment
items.text_en: Incomplete segment
items.desc_en: The segment begins a reference to Rava and Rav Safra but is cut off; it likely continues the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara begins a reference to Rava and Rav Safra but is cut off, likely continuing the discussion.

items.text: Tannaic dispute on circumcision with a baheret
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute on circumcision with a baheret
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yoshiya says the verse 'basar' teaches that circumcision is performed even if there is a baheret (leprous spot) on the foreskin, implying it overrides the prohibition of cutting the spot. Rabbi Yonatan argues it is unnecessary, reasoning that since Shabbat (a severe prohibition) is overridden, certainly tzara'at (a lesser prohibition) is overridden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita: Rabbi Yoshiya derives from the word 'basar' that circumcision is performed even if there is a baheret on the foreskin.
Rabbi Yonatan argues that no verse is needed, reasoning that since Shabbat (a severe prohibition) is overridden by circumcision, certainly tzara'at (a lesser prohibition) is overridden.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed for Rabbi Yoshiya's view, since cutting the baheret is a 'davar she'eino mitkavein' (unintended act), which is permitted. Abaye answers that the verse is necessary for Rabbi Yehuda, who prohibits unintended acts. Rava counters that even for Rabbi Shimon (who permits unintended acts), the case is a 'pesik reishei' (inevitable result), which Rabbi Shimon concedes is forbidden. The Gemara notes that Abaye later accepted this reasoning after hearing it from Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed for Rabbi Yoshiya's view, since cutting the baheret is a דבר שאינו מתכוון (unintended act), which is permitted.
Abaye answers that the verse is necessary for Rabbi Yehuda, who prohibits unintended acts.
Rava counters that even for Rabbi Shimon (who permits unintended acts), the case is a פסיק רישא (inevitable result), which Rabbi Shimon concedes is forbidden.
The Gemara objects that Abaye himself elsewhere agrees with the principle of פסיק רישא (inevitable result).
The Gemara resolves that Abaye only accepted this reasoning after hearing it from Rava.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute regarding a different verse
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute regarding a different verse
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the dispute is presented, based on the verse 'Hishamer binega hatzara'at'. The Gemara again questions why a verse is needed, since it is a 'davar she'eino mitkavein'. Abaye and Rava repeat their explanations, and the Gemara again notes that Abaye later accepted Rava's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version of the dispute, citing the verse 'הִשָּׁמֶר בְּנֶגַע הַצָּרַעַת' (take heed of the plague of leprosy) and the ruling that one may perform actions that might incidentally cause the leprous spot to be removed.
The Gemara questions why a verse is needed, since the action is a דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין (an unintended consequence) and such actions are generally permitted.
Abaye explains that the verse is necessary according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין (unintended consequence) is forbidden.
Rava answers that even according to Rabbi Shimon, the verse is needed because Rabbi Shimon concedes in a case of פְּסִיק רֵישֵׁיהּ וְלָא יְמוּת (an inevitable consequence).
The Gemara objects that Abaye himself holds the principle that Rabbi Shimon concedes in a case of פְּסִיק רֵישֵׁיהּ וְלָא יְמוּת (an inevitable consequence).
The Gemara resolves that Abaye only accepted this principle after hearing it from Rava.

items.text: Explanation of the verse for Rabbi Shimon and the principle of aseh doche
items.text_en: Explanation of the verse for Rabbi Shimon and the principle of aseh doche
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Abaye, who follows Rabbi Shimon, interprets the verse 'basar'. Rav Amram answers that it refers to a case where the person intends to cut the baheret. The Gemara then questions the case of a minor, and Rav Mesharshiya answers that the father intends to cut his son's baheret. The Gemara further asks why another person cannot perform the circumcision, and cites Resh Lakish's principle: where there is both a positive and negative commandment, if both can be fulfilled, that is preferable; otherwise, the positive commandment overrides the negative. Here, there is no other person available.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Abaye, who follows Rabbi Shimon, interprets the verse 'basar' (flesh) in the context of circumcision overriding Shabbat.
Rav Amram answers that the verse applies when the person intends to cut the baheret (skin lesion) during circumcision.
The Gemara questions the case of a minor (infant) who cannot have intent to cut the baheret.
Rav Mesharshiya answers that the father intends to cut his son's baheret during the circumcision.
The Gemara asks why another person cannot perform the circumcision to avoid violating Shabbat.

The Gemara cites Resh Lakish's principle that where a positive and negative commandment conflict, if both can be fulfilled that is preferable; otherwise, the positive overrides the negative, and here there is no other person available.

items.text: Sources that Yom Tov does not override Shabbat for non-timely circumcision
items.text_en: Sources that Yom Tov does not override Shabbat for non-timely circumcision
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the rule that Yom Tov overrides Shabbat only for its own offerings, not for other matters. Four amoraim provide derivations: Chizkiyah from the verse 'Lo totiru' regarding the Pesach offering; Abaye from 'Olat Shabbat b'Shabbato'; Rava from 'Hu l'vado yei'aseh lachem'; and Rav Ashi from the word 'Shabbaton', which is a positive commandment, and a positive commandment does not override both a negative and positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that Yom Tov only overrides Shabbat for its own timely offerings.

Chizkiyah derives from the verse 'לֹא תוֹתִירוּ' (do not leave over) regarding the Pesach offering that a second morning is given for its burning, implying Yom Tov does not override Shabbat for non-timely matters.
Abaye derives from 'עוֹלַת שַׁבָּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ' (the Shabbat offering on its Shabbat) that only the Shabbat offering, not a weekday offering, is brought on Shabbat or Yom Tov.
Rava derives from 'הוּא לְבַדּוֹ יֵעָשֶׂה לָכֶם' (it alone shall be done for you) that only the Yom Tov offering itself, not its accessories or non-timely circumcision, is done on Shabbat.

Rav Ashi argues that 'שַׁבָּתוֹן' (a day of rest) is a positive commandment, and Yom Tov involves both a positive and a negative commandment, so a positive commandment does not override both a negative and a positive commandment.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's principle and its application to circumcision and Pesach
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's principle and its application to circumcision and Pesach
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Akiva's principle: any work that can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat; only work that cannot be done beforehand overrides. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva. A similar ruling is cited for Pesach. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: for circumcision, one might think it does not override because there is no karet, but for Pesach, which has karet, it might override; conversely, for Pesach, one might think it does not override because thirteen covenants were not cut for it, but for circumcision, which has thirteen covenants, it might override.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Akiva's principle that any work which can be done before Shabbat does not override Shabbat.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Akiva's principle.
A parallel Mishnah is cited for Pesach, stating the same principle, and Rav Yehuda again rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Akiva.

The Gemara explains why both cases (circumcision and Pesach) are necessary: each addresses a potential counterargument based on the presence or absence of כרת (karet) and the thirteen covenants of circumcision.

items.text: Mishnah: All necessary preparations for circumcision on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: All necessary preparations for circumcision on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the actions permitted on Shabbat for circumcision: circumcising, tearing, sucking, and applying a bandage and cumin. If spices were not ground before Shabbat, one may chew them with teeth and apply. If wine and oil were not mixed, each is applied separately. A protective covering (chaluk) is not made initially, but a rag may be wrapped. If not prepared beforehand, one may wrap it on a finger and bring it, even from another courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the actions permitted on Shabbat for circumcision: circumcising, tearing, sucking, and applying a bandage and cumin.
The Mishnah provides alternative procedures for spices and wine-oil mixtures that were not prepared before Shabbat.
The Mishnah concludes with rules for a protective covering (חָלוּק) and bringing a rag from another courtyard.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's inclusive phrase
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's inclusive phrase
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase "all needs of circumcision" comes to include. It cites a baraita that distinguishes between essential and non-essential foreskin threads: while the circumciser may return to cut essential threads, he does not return for non-essential ones.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who says one does not return
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who says one does not return
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna that holds one does not return for non-essential threads. Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan identifies it as Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, citing a baraita about skinning a Paschal offering on Shabbat.

items.text: Rejecting the identification based on the principle of beautifying mitzvot
items.text_en: Rejecting the identification based on the principle of beautifying mitzvot
