items.desc_en: A baraita taught by Yaakov Korcha is introduced, which will be discussed in the continuation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah permits placing an egg in a strainer on Shabbat, and a baraita attributed to Yaakov Korcha is introduced.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not soak asafoetida in warm water, but may place it in vinegar. It also discusses the treatment of vetch and straw.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not soak asafoetida in warm water, but may place it in vinegar, and discusses the treatment of vetch and straw.

items.text: Dispute about mustard preparation
items.text_en: Dispute about mustard preparation
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue whether mustard prepared before Shabbat can be stirred by hand or only with a utensil. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan then dispute whether any stirring is permitted, with Abaye and Rava initially ruling against Rabbi Yochanan, then reversing.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about mustard prepared before Shabbat: Rav permits stirring only with a utensil, not by hand.
Shmuel objects to Rav's ruling, arguing that mustard is animal feed and normally stirred by hand, so on Shabbat one may stir by hand but not with a utensil.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar forbids both methods, Rabbi Yochanan permits both, and Abaye and Rava initially rule against Rabbi Yochanan.
The gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan aligns with Rabbi Elazar's position and Rabbi Elazar with Shmuel's, and Abaye and Rava reverse their ruling to follow Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Stories of refusing mustard
items.text_en: Stories of refusing mustard
items.desc_en: Abaye's mother and Ze'ira's wife prepared mustard for them but they did not eat, while Rav Chiyya bar Ashi ate. Rava bar Sheva recounts standing before Ravina who ate mustard mixed with garlic.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Abaye's mother and Ze'ira's wife prepared mustard for them but they refused to eat, while Rav Chiyya bar Ashi ate, prompting a rebuke.
Rava bar Sheva testifies that he stood before Ravina, who ate mustard mixed with garlic, providing a precedent for leniency.

items.text: Mar Zutra's ruling and other preparations
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's ruling and other preparations
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that the halakha follows none of the previous statements but rather that mustard can be stirred by hand or utensil with honey. The Gemara then discusses preparing purslane and garlic on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that the halakha follows none of the previous statements but rather that mustard can be stirred by hand or utensil with honey, and one should mix (מערב) rather than beat (טרוף).
The Gemara discusses preparing purslane (שחליים) and garlic on Shabbat, including the use of a wick (אמיתא) and Abaye's comment that the wick is beneficial for garlic.

items.text: Enomelin and Aluntit
items.text_en: Enomelin and Aluntit
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may make enomelin (wine, honey, pepper) on Shabbat but not aluntit (old wine, water, balsam). Rav Yosef recounts drinking such a mixture and feeling its effects from head to toe.

sub.desc_en: The baraita permits making enomelin (wine, honey, pepper) on Shabbat but prohibits aluntit (old wine, water, balsam), explaining the latter is used for a bathhouse to cool.

Rav Yosef recounts drinking a cup of such a mixture after following Mar Ukva to the bathhouse, feeling its effects from head to toe, and explains that Mar Ukva could drink it daily because he was accustomed to it.

items.text: Mishnah on asafoetida and vetch
items.text_en: Mishnah on asafoetida and vetch
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not soak asafoetida in warm water but may put it in vinegar, and one may not boil or crush vetch but may put it in a sieve or basket.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not soak asafoetida in warm water but may put it in vinegar, and one may not boil or crush vetch but may put it in a sieve or basket.

items.text: Gemara on soaking asafoetida
items.text_en: Gemara on soaking asafoetida
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether soaking asafoetida is biblically prohibited or rabbinically. Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai about cold water, and a baraita resolves the dispute. A story follows about Rav Acha bar Yosef's medicinal use of asafoetida.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether soaking asafoetida in hot water on Shabbat is prohibited.

sub.text: Rav Adda Narshah's answer before Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Adda Narshah's answer before Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda Narshah explains that soaking asafoetida in hot water incurs a sin-offering, implying a biblical prohibition.
Abaye objects that if soaking asafoetida is biblically prohibited, then soaking a medicinal herb (אומצא) in water would also be liable, which is unreasonable.
Abaye resolves that the prohibition is only rabbinic, to prevent one from acting as on a weekday.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question to Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question to Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai whether soaking asafoetida in cold water on Shabbat is permitted.
Rabbi Yannai answers that it is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection from the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection from the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects that the Mishnah explicitly forbids only warm water, implying cold water is permitted.

sub.text: Rabbi Yannai's answer citing a baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's answer citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai explains that the Mishnah reflects an individual opinion (Rabbi Yosei), while a baraita forbids both hot and cold water.

sub.text: Gemara's digression on the use of asafoetida
sub.text_en: Gemara's digression on the use of asafoetida
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that asafoetida is used for heart palpitations (יוקרא דליבא).

sub.text: Story of Rav Acha bar Yosef and Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Acha bar Yosef and Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva instructs Rav Acha bar Yosef, who suffers from heart palpitations, to drink three measures of asafoetida over three days.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yosef's inquiry at the study hall
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef's inquiry at the study hall
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef drinks five measures over Shabbat eve and Shabbat, then asks the study hall whether drinking large amounts is permitted; they cite a baraita that one may drink a kav or two without concern.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yosef's second question
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef's second question
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef clarifies that his question is about soaking asafoetida, not drinking it.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin's answer citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin's answer citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin reports that Rav Huna said in the name of Rav: one may soak asafoetida in cold water and then place it in warm water.

The Gemara resolves that even for the one who forbids soaking, in this case it is permitted because Rav Acha bar Yosef had already drunk five measures and would be endangered if he did not drink on Shabbat.

items.text: Crushing flax on Shabbat
items.text_en: Crushing flax on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef asks Rav Safra whether crushing flax on Shabbat is permitted, and Rav Safra rules it is fine. The Gemara distinguishes this from the case of a scarf, where it appears like whitening.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Safra
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef's question to Rav Safra
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef, leaning on Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, asks Rav Safra whether crushing flax on Shabbat is permitted, considering whether the intent is to soften it (permitted) or to whiten it (forbidden).
Rav Safra rules that the intent is to soften the flax, so it is permitted.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rav Acha bar Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rav Acha bar Yosef
sub.desc_en: After leaving, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rav Acha bar Yosef what he asked Rav Safra, and Rav Acha bar Yosef reports the question and the permissive answer.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's follow-up question
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's follow-up question
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks why Rav Acha bar Yosef did not also ask about a scarf (סוּדָרָא), and Rav Acha bar Yosef replies that he already asked Rav Huna and received a ruling.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges that the case of flax should be inferred from the scarf case, and Rav Acha bar Yosef distinguishes: with a scarf it appears like whitening, but with flax it does not.

items.text: Rava's ruling on removing a knife from a reed
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on removing a knife from a reed
items.desc_en: Rava distinguishes between removing a knife from its sheath (permitted) and removing the sheath from the knife (forbidden), with an exception for a container used for storage.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the general rule: removing a knife from a reed (sheath) is permitted, but removing the reed from the knife is forbidden.
Rava adds an exception: if the container is used for storage (כלי קיואי), it is permitted to remove the sheath from the knife.

items.text: Rav Chisda on moving vegetable stalks
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on moving vegetable stalks
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that vegetable stalks may be moved on Shabbat if they are fit for animal food, otherwise they are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules: a vegetable stalk fit for animal food may be moved; otherwise it is forbidden.

items.text: Rav on moving meat and fish hooks
items.text_en: Rav on moving meat and fish hooks
items.desc_en: Rav permits moving a meat hook but forbids moving a fish hook on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi quoting Rav: a meat hanging may be moved; a fish hanging is forbidden.

items.text: Rav Katina's rejected statement about standing in the middle of a bed
items.text_en: Rav Katina's rejected statement about standing in the middle of a bed
items.desc_en: Rav Katina compares standing in the middle of a bed to standing in a woman's womb, but the Gemara dismisses this as baseless.

sub.desc_en: Rav Katina says: standing in the middle of a bed is like standing in a woman's womb; it is not a real statement.
The Gemara dismisses Rav Katina's statement as baseless.

items.text: Rav Chisda's advice for students and his daughters
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's advice for students and his daughters
items.desc_en: A series of practical and ethical instructions from Rav Chisda: students should buy long vegetables and reeds, avoid vegetables if bread is scarce, break bread properly, avoid waste, and more. He also advises his daughters on modesty and conduct.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda advises a student to buy long vegetables, as the stalk comes with the vegetable.
Rav Chisda advises a student to buy long reeds, as the bundle comes with the length.
Rav Chisda advises a student with scarce bread not to eat vegetables because they are appetite-stimulating (גָרֵיר), and recounts his own practice of avoiding vegetables in both poverty and wealth.
Rav Chisda advises a student with scarce bread not to break it wastefully, and recounts his own practice of checking the entire loaf before breaking.

Rav Chisda says one who can eat barley bread but eats wheat violates 'בל תשחית' (the prohibition against waste), and Rav Pappa extends this to beer versus wine, but the gemara rejects this, saying preserving one's body is more important.
Rav Chisda advises a student without oil to anoint himself with brine water.
Rav Chisda advises a student buying a tripe to buy the neck (אוּנְקָא) which contains three types of meat.
Rav Chisda advises a student buying a 'כיתוניתא' (a fine wheat) to buy from the Nahrava region, whiten it every thirty days, and it will last twelve months, with a guarantee.
Rav Chisda advises a student not to sit on a new cushion because it wears out his clothes.
Rav Chisda advises a student not to send his clothes to his host for laundering, as the host might see a defect and embarrass him.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's advice to his daughters
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's advice to his daughters
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs his daughters to be modest before their husbands and not to eat bread in their presence.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's advice to his daughters
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's advice to his daughters
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs his daughters not to eat vegetables, dates, or drink beer at night, and not to relieve themselves where their husbands do.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's advice to his daughters
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's advice to his daughters
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs his daughters that when someone knocks at the door, they should say 'מַנִּי' (who is it for me?) rather than 'מַנּוּ' (who is it?).

sub.text: Rav Chisda's advice to his daughters
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's advice to his daughters
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs his daughters to show a pearl first and a pitcher only after the guests are distressed, to test their character.

items.text: Mishnah and baraita on sifting beans
items.text_en: Mishnah and baraita on sifting beans
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not sift beans on Shabbat, and a baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who forbids any use of a sieve.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda notes: the Mishnah says 'one may not remove chickpeas' — this is not like that Tanna, for it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: one does not supervise the sieve at all.
The gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov forbids any use of a sieve on Shabbat.

items.text: Mishnah: sweeping before a fattened animal
items.text_en: Mishnah: sweeping before a fattened animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Rabbi Dosa permits sweeping and moving dung to the side on Shabbat, while the Sages forbid it. Taking food from one animal and giving to another is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Mishnah: one may sweep before a fattened animal and move aside due to dung — Rabbi Dosa permits, Sages forbid. One may take from before one animal and give to before another on Shabbat.
The Sages forbid sweeping and removing dung before the animal.
The Mishnah concludes with a permitted action: taking food from before one animal and giving it to another on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: analysis of the dispute and Rav Chisda's clarification
items.text_en: Gemara: analysis of the dispute and Rav Chisda's clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether the dispute is about the first clause, the last clause, or both. A baraita clarifies that the Sages forbid both. Rav Chisda initially distinguishes between a ground trough and a vessel trough, but then corrects himself: the dispute is only about a vessel trough, while a ground trough is universally forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Sages' dispute with Rabbi Dosa applies to the first clause, the last clause, or both.
A baraita is cited to clarify that the Sages forbid both the first and last clauses.
Rav Chisda initially distinguishes: the dispute applies only to a ground trough, but for a vessel trough, all agree it is permitted.
The Gemara objects: who would permit a ground trough, since it involves making pits (forbidden on Shabbat)?
Rav Chisda corrects himself: the dispute is only about a vessel trough, while a ground trough is universally forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: resolving contradictory baraitot on feeding animals
items.text_en: Gemara: resolving contradictory baraitot on feeding animals
items.desc_en: Two baraitot contradict each other: one says take from a good-mouthed animal to a bad-mouthed one, the other says the opposite. Abaye resolves: one may take from a donkey (no saliva) to an ox, but not from an ox to a donkey.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two contradictory baraitot: one says take from a good-mouthed animal to a bad-mouthed one, the other says the opposite.

Abaye resolves the contradiction: one may take from a donkey (no saliva) to an ox, but not from an ox to a donkey; the baraita about taking from a good-mouthed animal refers to a donkey, and giving to a bad-mouthed one refers to an ox.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah about feeding animals
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah about feeding animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about taking food from before an animal with a bad mouth applies to a donkey, which does not eat carefully, while giving food to an animal with a good mouth applies to a cow, which eats carefully.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's ruling about taking food from before an animal with a bad mouth applies to a donkey, which does not eat carefully, while giving food to an animal with a good mouth applies to a cow, which eats carefully.

items.text: Mishnah: Straw on a bed and the press
items.text_en: Mishnah: Straw on a bed and the press
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that straw on a bed may be moved only with one's body, not directly by hand, unless it is animal food or has a pillow/sheet on it. Regarding a householder's press, one may loosen but not press clothes; for a launderer's press, one may not touch it at all. Rabbi Yehuda permits loosening and removing it if it was already loosened before Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that straw on a bed may be moved only with one's body, not directly by hand, unless it is animal food or has a pillow or sheet on it.
The Mishnah rules that a householder's press may be loosened but not pressed on Shabbat, while a launderer's press may not be touched at all.
Rabbi Yehuda permits loosening and removing the entire press if it was already loosened before Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Indirect movement and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Indirect movement and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that moving a palm branch from top to bottom is permitted, but from bottom to top is prohibited. Rav Adda bar Abba cites a teaching that contradicts Rav Nachman, proving from the Mishnah that indirect movement (טלטול מן הצד) is not considered prohibited movement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that moving a palm branch from top to bottom is permitted, but from bottom to top is prohibited.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Abba citing a teaching
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Abba citing a teaching
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Abba cites a teaching that contradicts Rav Nachman, proving from the Mishnah that indirect movement (טלטול מן הצד) is not considered prohibited movement.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Rava on grinding pepper
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rava on grinding pepper
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda permits grinding one peppercorn at a time with a knife handle, but prohibits two. Rava argues that since the action is unusual, even many are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that grinding one peppercorn at a time with a knife handle is permitted, but two are forbidden.
Rava argues that since the action is performed in an unusual manner (משני), even many peppercorns are permitted.

items.text: Drying after bathing and the concern for carrying
items.text_en: Drying after bathing and the concern for carrying
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda advises drying oneself before leaving the water to avoid carrying water four cubits in a karmelit. The Gemara objects that descending also pushes water four cubits, but responds that the force of one's movement in a karmelit was not decreed prohibited.

items.text: Cleaning mud from one's foot: debate between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Cleaning mud from one's foot: debate between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: Abaye (or Rav Yehuda) says one may wipe mud off one's foot on the ground but not on a wall. Rava objects that wiping on a wall appears like building, but since it is a field wall, it is not. Rava then reverses: wiping on a wall is permitted, but on the ground is prohibited lest one come to level pits. Mar bar Ravina prohibits both, while Rav Pappa permits both; Mar bar Ravina suggests wiping on a beam.

sub.desc_en: Abaye (or Rav Yehuda) states that one may wipe mud from one's foot on the ground but not on a wall.
Rava objects that the reason for prohibiting wiping on a wall is that it appears like building, but this is a field wall, which is not a building.
Rava reverses the ruling: one may wipe on a wall but not on the ground, lest one come to level pits.

sub.text: Mar bar Ravina and Rav Pappa's dispute
sub.text_en: Mar bar Ravina and Rav Pappa's dispute
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina prohibits both wiping on ground and wall, while Rav Pappa permits both.
Mar bar Ravina suggests that one may wipe the mud on a beam.

items.text: Rava's three additional prohibitions
items.text_en: Rava's three additional prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rava prohibits sitting at the mouth of a drain lest an object fall and one come to carry it; prohibits leveling a pit (or similar) lest one come to make pits; and prohibits crushing a clod of earth at the mouth of a glass vessel lest one come to squeeze.

sub.desc_en: Rava prohibits sitting at the mouth of a drain lest an object fall and one come to carry it.
Rava prohibits leveling a pit (or similar) lest one come to make pits.
Rava prohibits crushing a clod of earth at the mouth of a glass vessel lest one come to squeeze.

items.text: Cleaning mud from clothing and shoes
items.text_en: Cleaning mud from clothing and shoes
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana permits scraping mud from inside a garment but not from outside. A baraita is cited that permits scraping mud from a shoe with the back of a knife and from a garment with a fingernail, provided one does not scrape vigorously; the Gemara clarifies that scraping vigorously is prohibited only on the outside. Rabbi Abahu quotes Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Yannai that one may scrape a new shoe but not an old one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that one may scrape mud from inside a garment but not from outside.
The Gemara raises a baraita that permits scraping mud from a garment with a fingernail, provided one does not scrape vigorously, seemingly contradicting Rav Kahana.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita's prohibition of scraping vigorously applies absolutely, i.e., even from inside.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita's restriction applies only to scraping vigorously from outside, not from inside, aligning with Rav Kahana.

sub.text: Rabbi Abahu quoting Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abahu quoting Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu transmits a tradition from Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yannai that one may scrape a new shoe but not an old one.

items.text: Scraping a shoe on Shabbat
items.text_en: Scraping a shoe on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a question about how to scrape a shoe on Shabbat. Rabbi Avahu suggests using the back of a knife, but an elder challenges this with a baraita of Rabbi Chiya that prohibits scraping altogether. Rav Chisda then clarifies that the prohibition applies only to smoothing the leather, not to cleaning it, but the Gemara questions this distinction and rephrases Rav Chisda's statement to refer to the amount of scraping.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one may scrape a shoe on Shabbat, and Rabbi Avahu answers using the back of a knife.
An elder challenges Rabbi Avahu by citing a baraita of Rabbi Chiya that prohibits scraping any shoe on Shabbat.
Rav Chisda clarifies that the prohibition applies only to smoothing the leather (לעַבְּדוֹ), not to cleaning it (לצַחְצְחוֹ).
The Gemara objects that smoothing is obviously forbidden, and asks who would permit cleaning.
The Gemara rephrases Rav Chisda's statement to refer to the amount of scraping: a small amount for cleaning is permitted, but a large amount for smoothing is forbidden.

items.text: Laws of wearing shoes on Shabbat
items.text_en: Laws of wearing shoes on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught: a child may not go out in a large shoe, but may go out in a large cloak; a woman may not go out in a patched shoe, and if she performed chalitzah with it, it is valid; one may not go out in a new shoe, specifically a woman's shoe. Bar Kappara adds that this is only if she had not worn it before Shabbat, but if she had worn it on Friday, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited listing restrictions on wearing shoes on Shabbat: a child may not wear a large shoe, a woman may not wear a patched shoe, and one may not wear a new shoe (specifically a woman's shoe).
Bar Kappara qualifies that the restriction on new shoes applies only if the woman had not worn them before Shabbat; if she had worn them on Friday, it is permitted.
The baraita rules: one may not go out in a new shoe, specifically a woman's shoe.
Bar Kappara qualifies the prohibition: it applies only if she had not worn the shoe before Shabbat, but if she had worn it on Friday, it is permitted.

items.text: Removing a shoe from a last on Shabbat
items.text_en: Removing a shoe from a last on Shabbat
items.desc_en: There is a contradiction between two baraitot: one permits removing a shoe from a last on Shabbat, the other prohibits it. The Gemara resolves this by attributing the lenient view to Rabbi Eliezer and the stringent view to the Rabbis, based on a Mishnah about impurity of a shoe on a last.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one permits removing a shoe from a last (אימוּס), the other prohibits it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the lenient view to Rabbi Eliezer and the strict view to the Sages, citing a Mishnah about ritual impurity of a shoe on a last.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer declares a shoe on a last pure (lenient) and the Sages declare it impure (stringent), supporting the attribution.

items.text: Rava and Abaye on the permissibility of using a shoe-last
items.text_en: Rava and Abaye on the permissibility of using a shoe-last
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the dispute between Rava and Abaye regarding a vessel whose primary function is prohibited: Rava permits moving it for any need, while Abaye permits only for its own use but not for its place. The Gemara initially assumes the case is about a loose last, citing Rabbi Yehuda who permits it when loose. It then notes that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling follows Rabbi Eliezer, and the Gemara reconciles the positions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that according to Rava, who permits moving a vessel whose primary function is for a prohibited use both for its own sake and for its place, the earlier ruling about removing a shoe from a last works out well.
The Gemara questions how the ruling works according to Abaye, who permits moving such a vessel only for its own use but not for its place.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a shoe that is loose on the last, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda permits moving it when loose.
The Gemara infers that only a loose shoe is permitted, and confirms that this works well for Abaye's position.
The Gemara objects that according to Rava, who permits moving the vessel even for its place, the restriction to a loose shoe is unnecessary — even a tight shoe should be permitted.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds the shoe is not a completed vessel, so the restriction to a loose shoe is specific to that opinion.
The Gemara marks the conclusion of the chapter 'תולין' (Hanging) with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Mishnah: Carrying a child with a stone
items.text_en: Mishnah: Carrying a child with a stone
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person may carry his child with a stone in the child's hand, and a basket with a stone inside it. One may also move impure terumah together with pure terumah and with non-sacred produce. Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may even elevate a mixture of terumah and non-sacred produce in a ratio of one to one hundred.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person may carry his child with a stone in the child's hand, and a basket with a stone inside it, and one may move impure תרומה (priestly portion) together with pure תרומה and with non-sacred produce.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may even elevate a mixture of תרומה and non-sacred produce in a ratio of one to one hundred.

items.text: Gemara: Carrying a child with a purse
items.text_en: Gemara: Carrying a child with a purse
items.desc_en: Rava rules: if one carries a live child with a purse around its neck, he is liable for the purse but not for the child, following Rabbi Nathan that a live being carries itself. The Gemara questions why the purse is not nullified to the child, and distinguishes between a bed and a purse. For a dead child, Rava holds one is exempt even for the child, following Rabbi Shimon that an unnecessary labor is exempt. The Gemara then reconciles the Mishnah with the case of a child who is attached to his father.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules: one who carries a live child with a purse around its neck is liable for the purse; for a dead child with a purse, he is exempt.
The Gemara asks: why is the carrier not also liable for the live child itself?
Rava follows Rabbi Nathan's principle that a live being carries itself, so the child is not considered a burden.
The Gemara objects: why is the purse not nullified to the child, just as a bed is nullified to a live person carried on it?
The Gemara distinguishes: a bed is nullified to a live person, but a purse is not nullified to a child.
Rava follows Rabbi Shimon that one is exempt for a labor not needed for its own sake, so carrying a dead child (unnecessary) incurs no liability.
Beit Rabbi Yannai resolves the Mishnah's allowance of carrying a child with a stone by limiting it to a child who is attached to his father.

items.text: Rava's distinction between a stone and a dinar
items.text_en: Rava's distinction between a stone and a dinar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifically mentions a stone, suggesting a dinar should be similar. Rava explains that a stone, if it falls, the father will not come to retrieve it, but a dinar, if it falls, the father will come to retrieve it, making it forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifically mentions a stone, suggesting that a dinar should be similarly forbidden.
Rava explains that a stone, if it falls, the father will not retrieve it, but a dinar, if it falls, the father will retrieve it, making it forbidden.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rava's view: one who carries folded garments on his shoulder or sandals and rings in his hand is liable, but if he is wearing them, he is exempt. Similarly, one who carries a person with his garments on him is exempt, but if he carries them as they are, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava by distinguishing between carrying folded garments on the shoulder (liable) and wearing them (exempt), and similarly for a person with his clothes on (exempt) versus carrying them as they are (liable).

items.text: The case of a basket with a stone inside
items.text_en: The case of a basket with a stone inside
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah permits moving a basket with a stone inside, as the basket becomes a base for a forbidden object. Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that we are dealing with a basket full of fruits. The Gemara questions why not shake out the fruits and stone, and Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rava answers that the basket is perforated, and the stone itself serves as a wall for the basket.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah permits moving a basket with a stone inside, since the basket becomes a base (בסיס) for a forbidden object.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that the case involves a basket full of fruits, so the basket is not a base for the stone alone.
The Gemara objects: why not simply shake out the fruits and the stone, and then carry the basket empty?

sub.text: Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rav answers that the fruits are of the type that become soiled (מטנפין), so one cannot shake them out.
The Gemara objects further: why not just tilt the basket and let the stone fall out by itself?

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rava answers that the basket is perforated (פחותה), and the stone itself serves as a wall (דופן) for the basket, so it is needed structurally.

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction regarding terumah
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction regarding terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the Mishnah's allowance to move impure terumah with pure terumah applies only when the pure is below and the impure above; but if pure is above and impure below, one may take the pure and leave the impure. The Gemara objects that even when pure is below, one could shake them out, and Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rav answers that we are dealing with fruits that become soiled. A baraita is brought that contradicts Rav Chisda, and Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by saying the Mishnah is for the sake of the object itself, while the baraita is for the sake of the place.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda distinguishes the Mishnah's allowance: it applies only when pure terumah is below and impure above; if pure is above and impure below, one takes the pure and leaves the impure.
The Gemara objects that even when pure is below, one could simply shake off the fruits and take them.

sub.text: Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ilai in the name of Rav answers that we are dealing with fruits that become soiled, so shaking is not feasible.
The Gemara brings a baraita that contradicts Rav Chisda, stating that impure terumah may be moved with pure terumah in either arrangement.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah permits moving for the sake of the object itself (לצורך גופו), while the baraita permits moving for the sake of the place (לצורך מקומו).

items.text: Rava's support for Rav Chisda's interpretation
items.text_en: Rava's support for Rav Chisda's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what compelled Rav Chisda to interpret the Mishnah as for the sake of the object itself. Rava answers that the Mishnah's continuation supports this: the case of money on a pillow, where Rabbi Yochanan said that only for the sake of the object itself may one shake it, but for the sake of the place, one may move it with the money still on it. Since the latter clause is for the sake of the object itself, the former clause is also for the sake of the object itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what compelled Rav Chisda to interpret the Mishnah as referring to moving the object for the sake of the object itself (לצורך גופו).

Rava answers that the Mishnah's continuation supports Rav Chisda: the case of money on a pillow, where Rabbi Yochanan ruled that only for the sake of the object itself may one shake it, proves that the first clause also deals with the sake of the object itself.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's leniency and its source
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's leniency and its source
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda permits moving terumah up to a loft, as it involves fixing a vessel. It suggests Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that terumah is considered as if it is already designated. But the Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's stringency does not imply leniency. Then it suggests Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Shimon, who permits when terumah falls into a mixture. But the Gemara questions the reasoning. Finally, it suggests Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who permits by focusing on one side and eating from the other. The Gemara concludes by questioning whether Rabbi Yehuda indeed holds like him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehuda can permit moving terumah up to a loft, since this involves fixing a vessel (תיקון כלי).
The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that terumah is considered as if it is already designated (תרומה בעיניה מחתא).
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that terumah that fell into less than 100 parts renders the mixture as definite terumah, while the Sages disagree.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's stringency (חומרא) does not imply leniency (קולא) in the case of moving terumah.
The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Shimon, who permits when terumah falls into a mixture before it can be separated.
The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Shimon's leniency may be based on a different reasoning (sequential vs. simultaneous fall), not on the principle of treating terumah as already designated.
The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who permits focusing on one side of the mixture and eating from the other.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda actually holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, leaving the matter unresolved.

items.text: Gemara's question on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar already disagree about the nullification of mixed produce (medumma), and explains that Rabbi Yehuda's opinion is more lenient than Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar already disagree about nullifying mixed produce (medumma), and explains that Rabbi Yehuda's opinion is more lenient.

items.text: Mishnah: Moving a stone or coins on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Moving a stone or coins on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if a stone is on the mouth of a barrel, one may tilt the barrel and the stone will fall; if between barrels, one may lift and tilt. For coins on a pillow, one may shake the pillow; if on a leather pillow, one may wipe it with a cloth or pour water until the coins are gone.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of moving a stone on a barrel and coins on a cushion on Shabbat.
The Mishnah states the rule for coins on a pillow: shake the pillow, and if on a leather pillow, wipe with a cloth or pour water until the coins are gone.

items.text: Rav Huna's distinction: forgetful vs. intentional placement
items.text_en: Rav Huna's distinction: forgetful vs. intentional placement
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says in the name of Rav that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when one forgot the stone or coins, but if one intentionally placed them, the object becomes a base (basis) for a forbidden item and may not be moved.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav distinguishes between a forgetful case (שוכח), where moving is permitted, and an intentional one (מניח), where the stone becomes a base (בסיס) for a forbidden object.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah regarding forbidden and permitted items
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah regarding forbidden and permitted items
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that when there is both a forbidden and a permitted element, we exert effort for the permitted but not for the forbidden. Rabba bar bar Chana says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, based on a baraita about separating legumes on Yom Tov. The Gemara then analyzes why the case of the stone is like a case where the waste is more than the food.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yosei's ruling on moving a barrel with a stone
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yosei's ruling on moving a barrel with a stone
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei who says that if a barrel is in a storeroom or glass vessels are underneath, one may lift the barrel to another place, tilt it, take what is needed, and return it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei's ruling that if a barrel is in a storeroom or under glass vessels, one may lift it to another place, tilt it, take what is needed, and return it.

items.text: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on coins on a pillow: forgetful vs. intentional, and need of the object vs. place
items.text_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on coins on a pillow: forgetful vs. intentional, and need of the object vs. place
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi says in the name of Rav that the Mishnah's leniency for coins on a pillow applies only when one forgot them. Rabba bar bar Chana says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it applies only when one needs the pillow itself, but if one needs the place, one may move the pillow with the coins still on it. Chiya bar Rav from Diftei teaches the same.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi reports in Rav's name that the Mishnah's leniency for shaking coins off a pillow applies only when one forgot them, but if one placed them intentionally, the pillow becomes a base (בסיס) for a forbidden object.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana states in Rabbi Yochanan's name that the leniency applies only when one needs the pillow itself, but if one needs the place, one may move the pillow with the coins still on it.
Chiya bar Rav from Diftei teaches the same ruling as Rabbi Yochanan, confirming the distinction between needing the object and needing the place.

items.text: Stories of forgetting a purse or brick: using a bread or child to move it
items.text_en: Stories of forgetting a purse or brick: using a bread or child to move it
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya, Rav Yitzchak, and Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheila in the name of Rabbi Asi relate cases where one forgot a purse or brick in the courtyard, and the solution was to place a loaf or child on it to permit moving it. Rabbi Yochanan ruled similarly for a forgotten sack of money in the street.

sub.text: Rabbi Oshaya, Rav Yitzchak, Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheila said Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya, Rav Yitzchak, Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheila said Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya, Rav Yitzchak, and Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheila in the name of Rabbi Asi each report that when a purse or brick of coins is forgotten in a courtyard, one may place a loaf or a child on it to move it, and Rabbi Yochanan ruled similarly.
Rav Yitzchak applies the same rule to a forgotten brick (לבנה) in the courtyard.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheila in the name of Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheila in the name of Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Sheila reports a case where a forgotten sack of money in the street was brought before Rabbi Yochanan, who ruled to place a loaf or child on it and move it.

items.text: Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi: halakha regarding forgetful placement
items.text_en: Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi: halakha regarding forgetful placement
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that the halakha follows all these teachings in cases of forgetfulness. Rav Ashi disagrees, saying that even in a case of forgetfulness, the method of placing a loaf or child was only said for a corpse, not for money.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra rules that the halacha follows all these traditions in a forgetful case, while Rav Ashi limits the use of a loaf or child to a corpse alone.
Rav Ashi disagrees, arguing that even in a case of forgetfulness, the method of placing a loaf or child was only said for a corpse, not for money.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's practices and the dispute with Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's practices and the dispute with Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Abaye would place a cup on pillows and Rava a knife on a pigeon to move them. Rav Yosef criticizes them, noting that the Sages only permitted such actions when one forgot, not ab initio. Abaye and Rava defend themselves by saying they are important people and the items are usable for other purposes. The Gemara questions whether Rava holds like Rabbi Yehuda, and cites a story where Rava ordered a goose to be cooked and its innards thrown to a cat.

sub.desc_en: Describes Abaye's practice of placing a cup on pillows and Rava's practice of placing a knife on a pigeon to move them on Shabbat.
Rav Yosef objects that the Sages only permitted moving a base for a forbidden object when one forgot (בשוכח), not לכתחילה (ab initio).
Abaye defends himself by saying he is an important person and the pillows are usable for sitting, so moving them is permitted.
Rava defends himself by saying he is an important person and the knife is usable as a support (אומצא) for eating, so moving it is permitted.
The Gemara questions whether Rava's reasoning implies he holds like Rabbi Yehuda, who permits moving a base only if the item is usable for a permitted purpose.
The Gemara rejects the implication by citing a story where Rava ordered a goose to be cooked and its innards thrown to a cat, showing he does not hold like Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Conclusion of Rava's ruling on using broken wood on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Conclusion of Rava's ruling on using broken wood on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rava holds like Rabbi Yehuda, as Rava taught that a woman may not enter a wood shed to take a splinter, and a broken splinter may not be used for fuel on Yom Tov, because one may burn vessels but not broken vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the earlier case, since the wood becomes putrid, one's mind was on it from yesterday, distinguishing it from the current case.

The Gemara concludes that Rava indeed holds like Rabbi Yehuda, citing Rava's own teaching that a woman may not enter a wood shed for a splinter and a broken splinter may not be used for fuel on Yom Tov.

items.text: Mishnah: Removing bones, peels, crumbs, and sponge from the table
items.text_en: Mishnah: Removing bones, peels, crumbs, and sponge from the table
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Beit Shammai say one may remove bones and peels from the table, while Beit Hillel say one must lift the entire table and shake it off. It then discusses removing crumbs smaller than an olive, bean and lentil stalks (animal food), and the rule for a sponge with or without a handle.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Beit Shammai say one may remove bones and peels from the table, while Beit Hillel say one must lift the entire table and shake it.
The Mishnah adds that one may remove crumbs smaller than a kezayit and hair of legumes from before the table, as they are animal food.
The Mishnah rules on a sponge: if it has a handle, one may wipe with it; otherwise not; the Sages say it may be handled on Shabbat and does not contract impurity.

items.text: Rav Nachman's identification of the Mishnah's positions
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's identification of the Mishnah's positions
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that Beit Shammai follows Rabbi Yehuda (who prohibits moving items that are not set aside) and Beit Hillel follows Rabbi Shimon (who permits moving any item that is not muktzeh).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that Beit Shammai follows Rabbi Yehuda and Beit Hillel follows Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Analysis of crumbs and stalks: support for Rabbi Yochanan and identification of Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Analysis of crumbs and stalks: support for Rabbi Yochanan and identification of Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the ruling on crumbs supports Rabbi Yochanan, who said that crumbs without an olive's bulk may not be destroyed by hand. It then asks who holds that bean and lentil stalks are permitted, answering that it is Rabbi Shimon, who does not accept the concept of muktzeh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling on crumbs supports Rabbi Yochanan, who said that crumbs without an olive's bulk may not be destroyed by hand.
The Gemara asks who holds that bean and lentil stalks are permitted to be moved.
The Gemara answers that it is Rabbi Shimon, who does not accept the concept of מוקצה (set-aside).

items.text: Sponge ruling: Rabbi Yehuda and the principle of 'Pesik Reishei'
items.text_en: Sponge ruling: Rabbi Yehuda and the principle of 'Pesik Reishei'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the sponge ruling (prohibiting use without a handle) aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids an unintended but inevitable consequence. It then clarifies that even Rabbi Shimon agrees in a case of 'Pesik Reishei' (an inevitable outcome), as stated by Abaye and Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out that the sponge ruling (requiring a handle) aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids an unintended but inevitable consequence (דבר שאין מתכוין).
The Gemara resolves that even Rabbi Shimon agrees in a case of 'Pesik Reishei' (an inevitable outcome), as stated by Abaye and Rava.

items.text: Practical rulings on moving date pits on Shabbat
items.text_en: Practical rulings on moving date pits on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the status of date pits: those of Aramaean dates are permitted to be moved because they are still attached to the fruit, while Persian date pits are forbidden. Various Amoraim (Shmuel, Rabbah, Rav Huna bar Yehoshua, Rav Sheishet, Rav Pappa, Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas) offer different methods for moving or disposing of them, such as using bread, a water vessel, a dung shovel, or throwing them behind the bed.

sub.desc_en: The anonymous voice distinguishes between Aramaean date pits, which are permitted to be moved (שרי לטלטולי) since they remain useful alongside their fruit, and Persian date pits, which are forbidden.
Rav Ashi objects to Rabbah's use of a dung shovel (גרף של רעי) for date pits, questioning whether one may prepare such a designated vessel לכתחילה (as an ideal standard).

The gemara lists three additional approaches: Rav Sheishet threw the pits with his tongue, Rav Pappa threw them behind the bed, and Rabbi Zecharya ben Avkulas would turn his face away and throw them, demonstrating that each Amora found a permissible method for disposal.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a broken barrel on Shabbat: one may save enough for three meals and invite others to save for themselves, provided one does not soak up the liquid. It then states the general prohibition of squeezing fruit to extract liquids, with Rabbi Yehuda distinguishing between fruit intended for eating (permitted) and for drink (forbidden). Finally, it discusses honeycombs crushed before Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a broken barrel on Shabbat: one may save enough for three meals and invite others to save for themselves, provided one does not soak up the liquid.
The Mishnah states the general prohibition of squeezing fruit to extract liquids on Shabbat, and that liquid that exudes on its own is forbidden.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between fruit intended for eating (permitted) and for drink (forbidden).
The Mishnah concludes with the case of honeycombs crushed before Shabbat: the exuded honey is forbidden, but Rabbi Eliezer permits it.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on the Mishnah's prohibition of soaking
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on the Mishnah's prohibition of soaking
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's phrase 'provided that one does not soak' by citing a Tanna: one should not soak in wine or dab in oil, as that would resemble weekday practice. It then cites a baraita about gathering scattered fruit in a courtyard: one may pick and eat piece by piece, but not into a basket or box, to avoid appearing as on a weekday.

sub.desc_en: A baraita elaborates on the Mishnah's prohibition of soaking: one may not soak up wine or dab oil, to avoid acting as on a weekday.
Another baraita rules that if fruits scatter in the courtyard, one may pick them up one by one and eat, but not into a basket, to avoid weekday-like activity.

items.text: Debate on Rabbi Yehuda's position regarding olives and grapes
items.text_en: Debate on Rabbi Yehuda's position regarding olives and grapes
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the Mishnah's dispute about squeezing fruit. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that Rabbi Yehuda conceded to the Sages regarding olives and grapes, because since they are primarily for squeezing, one is mindful. Ulla in the name of Rav argues that Rabbi Yehuda disputed even regarding olives and grapes. Rabbi Yochanan rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda for other fruits but not for olives and grapes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule and then quotes Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: Rabbi Yehuda agreed with the Sages regarding olives and grapes.
The Gemara explains the reason: since olives and grapes are primarily for squeezing, one is mindful of them and they are considered designated for drink.
Ulla in the name of Rav disputes this, asserting that Rabbi Yehuda disagreed even regarding olives and grapes.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda for other fruits but not for olives and grapes.

items.text: Rabba's alternative tradition on the dispute
items.text_en: Rabba's alternative tradition on the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabba in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel presents a different version: Rabbi Yehuda conceded to the Sages regarding olives and grapes, and the Sages conceded to Rabbi Yehuda regarding other fruits. This suggests a compromise where each side agrees with the other on different categories.

sub.text: Rabbah citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbah citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbah reports in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: Rabbi Yehuda conceded to the Sages regarding olives and grapes, and the Sages conceded to Rabbi Yehuda regarding other fruits.

items.text: Question about the actual point of dispute
items.text_en: Question about the actual point of dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Abba: if they agree on olives and grapes and on other fruits, then on what do they disagree? Rabbi Abba responds that he does not know. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak suggests that they disagree about berries and pomegranates.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Abba: if they agree on olives/grapes and other fruits, on what do they disagree? Rabbi Abba replies that he does not know.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak suggests that the dispute is about berries and pomegranates.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves: they likely disagree on berries and pomegranates.

items.text: Baraita supporting the dispute about berries and pomegranates
items.text_en: Baraita supporting the dispute about berries and pomegranates
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that clarifies the dispute: for olives and grapes, the liquid that emerges is always forbidden. For berries and pomegranates, Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between intent for eating (permitted) and for drink (forbidden), while the Sages forbid in all cases. This supports Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's suggestion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: for olives and grapes that have been pressed, the exuded liquid is forbidden whether intended for food or drink.
The baraita continues: for berries and pomegranates, Rabbi Yehuda permits the exuded liquid if intended for food, but forbids it if intended for drink or unspecified.
The Sages disagree, forbidding the exuded liquid whether intended for food or drink.

items.text: Challenge from a Mishnah about milk and a kal vachomer
items.text_en: Challenge from a Mishnah about milk and a kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's statement that Rabbi Yehuda considers 'stam' (unspecified intent) as forbidden, citing a Mishnah about human milk and animal milk. Rabbi Akiva's kal vachomer argument there suggests that animal milk should be impure even without intent, but the Sages refute this by comparing to blood. This section is cut off mid-argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Yehuda considers 'stam' (unspecified intent) as forbidden, citing a Mishnah about human milk and animal milk.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva uses a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) to argue that animal milk should be impure even without intent, but the Sages refute this by comparing to blood.

items.text: Challenge from olives and grapes
items.text_en: Challenge from olives and grapes
items.desc_en: The Sages challenge Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that milk is more stringent than blood, arguing that liquids from olives and grapes are pure when they come out unwillingly, so the same should apply to milk from other fruits.

sub.desc_en: The Sages challenge Rabbi Yehuda by arguing that liquids from olives and grapes are pure when they come out unwillingly, so the same should apply to milk from other fruits.

items.text: Gemara's initial understanding
items.text_en: Gemara's initial understanding
items.desc_en: The Gemara assumes that 'willingly' means he wants it, and 'unwillingly' means he is indifferent. If so, olives and grapes, which are typically squeezed, are pure when unwillingly produced, so other fruits, which are not typically squeezed, should certainly be pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Sages' proof from olives and grapes implies that for fruits not typically squeezed, liquid that comes out unwillingly is even more certainly pure.

items.text: Refined interpretation and alternative answer
items.text_en: Refined interpretation and alternative answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the initial understanding: 'willingly' means he is indifferent, and 'unwillingly' means he explicitly says he does not want it. Alternatively, olives and grapes are different because they are destined for waste, so they are considered abandoned from the start.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference by reinterpreting the terms: 'לרצון' means the owner is indifferent, and 'שלא לרצון' means he explicitly rejects it; alternatively, olives and grapes are unique because they are destined for disposal.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: olives and grapes are different because they are destined for waste, so they are considered abandoned from the start.

items.text: Seeking a source for Sages' agreement
items.text_en: Seeking a source for Sages' agreement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with the Sages regarding olives and grapes, but asks: from where do we derive that the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda regarding other fruits? It cites a baraita that begins to address this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda concedes to the Rabbis regarding olives and grapes, but asks how we know the Rabbis concede to Rabbi Yehuda regarding other fruits.
The Gemara cites a baraita that begins to address the halacha of squeezing fruits on Shabbat.

items.text: Attribution of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Attribution of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's leniency regarding squeezing certain fruits reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view or the Rabbis'. It concludes that since these fruits are not typically squeezed, even the Rabbis permit squeezing them ab initio, confirming the Mishnah is according to the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists fruits that may be squeezed on Shabbat, including figs and grapes, but not pomegranates, except for the household of Menashya bar Menachem who squeezed pomegranates.
The Gemara questions how we know the Mishnah's leniency reflects the Rabbis' view; perhaps it follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.
The Gemara rejects the possibility: even if Rabbi Yehuda permits squeezing when juice comes out on its own, he would not permit squeezing לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara resolves: since these fruits are not typically squeezed, even the Rabbis permit squeezing them לכתחילה (the ideal standard), confirming the Mishnah follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules in accordance with the practice of the house of Menashya bar Menachem, who squeezed pomegranates. Rava challenges this, questioning whether Menashya bar Menachem is a Tanna whose opinion can be followed, and whether his practice constitutes a majority.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah cites the practice of the house of Menashya bar Menachem, who squeezed pomegranates on Shabbat.
Rav Nachman rules that the halacha follows the practice of the house of Menashya bar Menachem.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman, questioning whether Menashya bar Menachem is a Tanna whose opinion can be followed, and whether his practice constitutes a majority.

items.text: First attempted proof from the Mishnah of kilayim
items.text_en: First attempted proof from the Mishnah of kilayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a minority practice can establish halakha, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that one who sustains thorns in a vineyard renders it forbidden, because in Arabia they sustain field thorns for camels. The Gemara rejects this, noting that Arabia is a specific place, whereas here the practice is not widespread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a minority practice can establish halakha by citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that sustaining thorns in a vineyard renders it forbidden, because in Arabia they sustain field thorns for camels.
The Gemara rejects the proof, noting that Arabia is a specific place where the practice is widespread, whereas here the minority practice is nullified against the majority.

items.text: Rav Chisda's principle of significance
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's principle of significance
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the house of Menashya bar Menachem's practice is valid because they considered pomegranates significant for squeezing, similar to Rav Chisda's ruling that radishes squeezed into a mikveh disqualify it due to change of appearance, since they are considered significant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by invoking Rav Chisda's principle that pomegranates, once deemed significant, produce liquid that disqualifies a mikveh through change of appearance.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the disqualification of the mikveh is because the liquid is a substance from which one does not make a mikveh ab initio, and any such substance disqualifies the mikveh when it changes its appearance.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the disqualification of the mikveh is because the liquid is a substance from which one does not make a mikveh לכתחילה (the ideal standard), and any such substance disqualifies the mikveh when it changes its appearance.

items.text: Debate about the status of must (מוחל)
items.text_en: Debate about the status of must (מוחל)
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a Mishnah about wine, vinegar, and must (מוחל) falling into a mikveh and disqualifying it. Abaye attributes the ruling to Rabbi Yaakov, who considers must a liquid, while Rabbi Shimon disagrees, holding that must is not a liquid except when mixed with oil residue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about wine, vinegar, or must (מוחל) falling into a mikveh and disqualifying it if it changes its appearance.
The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that must (מוחל) is considered a liquid.
Abaye attributes the Mishnah's ruling to Rabbi Yaakov, who holds that must is like a liquid, and explains why must that first emerges is pure.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, holding that must is not a liquid, and explains that must from the olive press is impure only because it inevitably contains oil residue.

items.text: Practical difference and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Practical difference and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the practical difference between Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon: must that comes after pressing. Rava then rules that the disqualification is because it is a substance from which one does not make a mikveh, and it disqualifies through change of appearance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the practical difference is between Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon regarding the status of מוחל (olive lees), and answers that it concerns מוחל that comes after pressing.
Rava rules that the disqualification of the mikveh is because it is a substance from which one does not make a mikveh לכתחילה (the ideal standard), and it disqualifies through change of appearance.

items.text: Squeezing grapes into a pot vs. bowl and the principle of liquid for food
items.text_en: Squeezing grapes into a pot vs. bowl and the principle of liquid for food
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that one may squeeze a cluster of grapes into a pot (where the juice will be absorbed in food) but not into a bowl (where it remains liquid). Rav Chisda extends this to milking a goat into a pot, indicating that liquid destined for food is considered food. Rami bar Chama challenges this from a law about a zav, and the Gemara resolves it with Rabbi Yochanan's explanation about a droplet on the teat.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that one may squeeze a cluster of grapes into a pot (where the juice will be absorbed in food) but not into a bowl (where it remains liquid).
Rav Chisda extends the principle to milking a goat into a pot, concluding that liquid destined for food is considered food (משקה הבא לאוכל — אוכל הוא).
Rami bar Chama challenges from the law of a zav (זב) who milks a goat: the milk is ritually impure, but if it is considered food, how can it become susceptible to impurity?

The Gemara resolves the challenge by citing Rabbi Yochanan's explanation that the impurity is due to a droplet of milk already on the teat, which is a liquid, not the milk that is being milked into the pot.

items.text: Ravina's objection from a corpse-impure person
items.text_en: Ravina's objection from a corpse-impure person
items.desc_en: Ravina raises an objection from the case of a corpse-impure person who squeezes olives and grapes, implying that the juice becomes susceptible to impurity, challenging the principle that liquid for food is considered food.

sub.desc_en: Ravina raises an objection from the case of a corpse-impure person who squeezes olives and grapes, implying that the juice becomes susceptible to impurity, challenging the principle that liquid for food is considered food.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that an egg-sized portion of food is pure, but more than that is impure, challenging the principle that liquid destined for food is considered food. It answers that the case involves squeezing into a bowl (where the liquid is not intended for the food).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that an egg-sized portion is pure but more is impure, challenging the principle that liquid destined for food is considered food.
The Gemara answers that the case involves squeezing into a bowl, where the liquid is not intended for the food.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's suggestion: a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's suggestion: a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya suggests that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda regarding smoothing grapes (whether it renders them susceptible to impurity) hinges on whether liquid destined for food is considered food.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya suggests that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda regarding smoothing grapes hinges on whether liquid destined for food is considered food.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative: dispute over liquid destined for waste
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative: dispute over liquid destined for waste
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rejects Rabbi Yirmeya's explanation, arguing that all agree liquid destined for food is not food; rather, the dispute is about liquid destined for waste. He supports this with a baraita about olives, where the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda disagree on whether liquid destined for waste is considered liquid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rejects Rabbi Yirmeya's explanation, arguing that all agree liquid destined for food is not food; rather, the dispute is about liquid destined for waste.
Rav Pappa cites a baraita about olives cut with impure hands, where the Tanna Kamma holds that liquid destined for waste does not render food susceptible to impurity.
The baraita continues with a case of testing olives for ripeness, where Rabbi Yehuda holds that liquid destined for waste is considered liquid, while the Tanna Kamma disagrees.

items.text: Rav Huna's resolution: two distinct disputes
items.text_en: Rav Huna's resolution: two distinct disputes
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua clarifies that the two sets of Tannaim dispute different issues: one set argues about liquid destined for waste, the other about liquid destined for polishing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing the two disputes: one set of Tannaim argues about liquid destined for waste, the other about liquid destined for polishing.

items.text: Rav's ruling on squeezing grapes and fish brine
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on squeezing grapes and fish brine
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports in the name of Rav that one may squeeze a cluster of grapes into a pot but not into a bowl, and fish for its brine even into a bowl. Abaye challenges Rav Dimi, noting a contradiction from Shmuel's ruling on pickled and boiled vegetables, and Rav Dimi defends his tradition by tracing it back to Rav.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that one may squeeze a cluster of grapes into a pot but not into a bowl.
Rav adds that one may squeeze fish for its brine even into a bowl.
Abaye challenges Rav Dimi, noting a contradiction from Shmuel's ruling on pickled and boiled vegetables.
Rav Dimi defends his tradition by tracing it back through a chain of transmission to Rav.

items.text: The core dispute: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan on squeezing
items.text_en: The core dispute: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan on squeezing
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the fundamental dispute: Rav permits squeezing pickled vegetables for their own sake but forbids for their liquid; Shmuel agrees but adds that boiled vegetables are the same; Rabbi Yochanan holds that squeezing any vegetable for its liquid incurs a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rav's position: squeezing pickled vegetables for their own sake is permitted, but for their liquid is exempt but forbidden.
Rav adds that boiled vegetables are permitted whether squeezed for their own sake or for their liquid.
Shmuel rules that both pickled and boiled vegetables are treated the same: squeezing for their own sake is permitted, for their liquid is exempt but forbidden.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that squeezing any vegetable for its liquid incurs a sin-offering, unlike Rav and Shmuel who only exempt but forbid.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita with each opinion
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita with each opinion
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may squeeze pickled vegetables for Shabbat but not for after Shabbat, and squeezing olives and grapes incurs a sin-offering. This challenges all three opinions. Each Amora resolves it according to his own view: Rav distinguishes between for their own sake and for their liquid; Shmuel includes boiled vegetables; Rabbi Yochanan equates all vegetables to olives and grapes for their liquid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita that permits squeezing pickled vegetables for Shabbat but not for after Shabbat, and prohibits squeezing olives and grapes with liability for a sin-offering, challenging the positions of Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan.

Rav resolves the baraita according to his view: the permission for pickled vegetables applies only to squeezing for their own sake (לְגוּפָן), while for their liquid (לְמֵימֵיהֶן) it is exempt but forbidden; boiled vegetables are permitted in all cases; olives and grapes incur a sin-offering.

Shmuel resolves the baraita according to his view: the permission includes both pickled and boiled vegetables, but only for their own sake (לְגוּפָן); for their liquid (לְמֵימֵיהֶן) it is exempt but forbidden; olives and grapes incur a sin-offering.

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the baraita according to his view: both pickled and boiled vegetables are permitted for Shabbat only for their own sake (לְגוּפָן); for their liquid (לְמֵימֵיהֶן) one who squeezes is treated like one who squeezed olives and grapes and is liable for a sin-offering.

items.text: Biblical law: only olives and grapes
items.text_en: Biblical law: only olives and grapes
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quotes Rav that Torah law only prohibits squeezing olives and grapes, and the school of Menashe teaches the same. The daf ends with a note about the validity of testimony.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quotes Rav that Torah law only imposes liability for squeezing olives and grapes.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from the school of Menashe
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from the school of Menashe
sub.desc_en: The school of Menashe teaches the same ruling, confirming Rav's statement.
The daf ends with a note about the validity of testimony, unrelated to the preceding halacha.

items.text: Testimony from a witness for firstborn animals
items.text_en: Testimony from a witness for firstborn animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a witness who heard from another witness is valid for testimony about a firstborn animal. Rav Ami forbids it, Rav Asi permits it, and Rav Yemar permits it, with the halakha following the lenient view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of testimony from a witness who heard from another witness, limiting it to testimony about a woman (for her husband's death).
The Gemara raises a question: is a witness who heard from another witness valid for testimony about a firstborn animal (בכור)?
Rav Ami forbids it, while Rav Asi permits it.
Rav Ami objects to Rav Asi, citing a baraita from the school of Menashe that limits witness-from-witness testimony to the case of a woman.
Rav Asi reinterprets the baraita: it means only that a woman is a valid witness for her own testimony, not that witness-from-witness is limited to her case.
Rav Yemar permits witness-from-witness for a firstborn, Marimar cites a verse in support, and the halakha (הלכה) follows the lenient view.

items.text: Honeycombs and the status of pressed olives and grapes
items.text_en: Honeycombs and the status of pressed olives and grapes
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya brings a baraita about olives and grapes crushed before Shabbat that exuded liquid on Shabbat: they are forbidden, but Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon permit. Rav Yosef and Abaye discuss the novelty of this ruling compared to the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya brings a baraita from Nehardea: olives and grapes crushed before Shabbat that exuded liquid on Shabbat are forbidden, but Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon permit.
Rav Yosef dismisses the baraita as teaching nothing new, calling it a 'superfluous man' who came to inform us.

Abaye defends the baraita's novelty: from the Mishnah one might think the leniency applies only when the item remains food throughout, but here the olives become liquid (משקה), so the baraita teaches that the leniency applies even in this case.

items.text: Mishnah: Soaking and rinsing foods on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Soaking and rinsing foods on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that foods which were in hot water before Shabbat may be soaked in hot water on Shabbat, but those that were not may only be rinsed, except for certain salted fish. The Gemara asks for an example, and Rav Safra provides one.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: foods that were in hot water before Shabbat may be soaked in hot water on Shabbat, while those that were not may only be rinsed, except for certain salted fish whose rinsing is the completion of their preparation.
The Gemara asks for an example of a food that was in hot water before Shabbat.
Rav Safra provides an example: the chicken of Rabbi Abba, and recounts a personal anecdote about eating it and being saved from danger by Rabbi Abba's wine.

items.text: Discussion on the Mishnah's ruling and liability for rinsing
items.text_en: Discussion on the Mishnah's ruling and liability for rinsing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan spits out Babylonian kutach, and Rav Yosef compares it to Rav Abba's chicken. Rav Gazza relates making kutach in Babylonia. The Gemara then discusses that rinsing the prohibited fish on Shabbat incurs a sin-offering, as their rinsing completes the melakha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yochanan would spit out Babylonian kutach (a dairy condiment).
Rav Yosef responds that they would spit out Rabbi Abba's chicken (a similarly repulsive dish).
Rav Gazza testifies that he once made Babylonian kutach and all the bolts of the West (a large crowd) asked for it, showing its desirability.
The Gemara asks: regarding the Mishnah's list of fish that may only be rinsed, what is the liability if one actually washes them on Shabbat?
Rav Yosef answers that one who washes them is liable to bring a sin-offering (חטאת).
Mar bar Ravina cites the Mishnah itself as proof: the Mishnah says 'their rinsing is the completion of their melakha (labor),' implying liability.

items.text: Aggadic questions: Why are Babylonian birds fat?
items.text_en: Aggadic questions: Why are Babylonian birds fat?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi sit before Rabbi Yochanan, who is dozing. They discuss why Babylonian birds are fat, and Rabbi Yochanan rebukes them for speaking without certainty. He explains that the birds are fat because they never went into exile, unlike the birds of Eretz Yisrael.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi sit before a dozing Rabbi Yochanan.

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba asks Rabbi Asi four aggadic questions: why Babylonian birds are fat, why Babylonian festivals are joyful, why Babylonian Torah scholars are distinguished, and why gentiles are repulsive.

Rabbi Asi gives dismissive or folk answers: birds are fatter elsewhere, festivals are joyful because the people are poor, scholars are distinguished because they are not learned, and gentiles are repulsive because they eat abominations.
Rabbi Yochanan wakes and rebukes them, citing the verse 'Say to wisdom: You are my sister' — only speak a matter if it is as clear to you as that your sister is forbidden to you.
