sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi's request
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi's request
sub.desc_en: They ask Rabbi Yochanan to tell them the correct answer to one of the questions.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Babylonian birds are fat because they never went into exile, citing the verse about Moab being at ease from youth.
The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says that for 52 years no person passed through Judah, proven by the gematria of 'בהמה' (52) in the verse about birds and beasts fleeing.

Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan concludes that all birds returned except the קולייס האיספנין (a specific fish), because its spine is not firm enough to swim upstream from Babylon to the spring of עין עיטם (Eitam).

items.text: Aggadic questions: Why are Babylonian festivals joyful and other phenomena?
items.text_en: Aggadic questions: Why are Babylonian festivals joyful and other phenomena?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Babylonian festivals are joyful because they were not subject to the curse of cessation of joy. It also explains that Babylonian Torah scholars are distinguished because they are not in their place, and that gentiles are repulsive because they did not stand at Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Babylonian festivals are joyful.
The Gemara answers that Babylonian festivals are joyful because they were not subject to the curse of cessation of joy, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar explains that God found Israel's festivals burdensome because they forced Him to determine harsh decrees.
Rabbi Yitzchak adds that every festival brought a Roman garrison to Tzippori.
Rabbi Chanina adds that every festival brought various Roman officials to Tiberias.
The Gemara asks why Babylonian Torah scholars are distinguished.
The Gemara answers that Babylonian scholars are distinguished because they are not in their place, citing a folk saying.
Rav Yosef teaches that Babylonian Torah scholars make blossoms and flowers for the Torah.
The Gemara asks why gentiles are repulsive.
The Gemara answers that gentiles are repulsive because they did not stand at Mount Sinai.

items.text: The serpent's zohama and its cessation
items.text_en: The serpent's zohama and its cessation
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi about converts: did their zohama cease? Rav Ashi answers that although they were not at Sinai, their guardian angels were, citing Deuteronomy 29:14. This is disputed by Rabbi Abba bar Kahana, who says the zohama did not cease from the patriarchs until three generations later, as Abraham fathered Ishmael, Isaac fathered Esau, and Jacob fathered the twelve tribes without blemish.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the principle that the serpent's zohama (impurity) was cast upon Eve, ceased for Israel at Sinai, but did not cease for gentiles.
Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi about the status of converts regarding the cessation of zohama.
Rav Ashi answers that although converts were not physically at Sinai, their guardian angels were, citing Deuteronomy 29:14.

Rabbi Abba bar Kahana disputes this, asserting that the zohama did not cease from the patriarchs until three generations, as Abraham fathered Ishmael, Isaac fathered Esau, and Jacob fathered the twelve tribes without blemish.

items.text: Mishnah: Breaking a barrel and piercing a stopper
items.text_en: Mishnah: Breaking a barrel and piercing a stopper
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may break a barrel to eat dried figs, provided he does not intend to make a vessel. One may not pierce a stopper of a barrel, according to Rabbi Yehuda, but the Sages permit it, though not from the side. If it was already pierced, one may not put wax on it because that would be smoothing. Rabbi Yehuda recounts a case before Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai in Arav, who was concerned about a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may break a barrel to eat dried figs, provided he does not intend to make a vessel.
The Mishnah records Rabbi Yehuda's position that one may not pierce a barrel's stopper.
The Mishnah records the Sages' position that piercing is permitted, but not from the side.
The Mishnah adds that if the stopper was already pierced, one may not put wax on it because that constitutes smoothing.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts a case before Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai in Arav, who expressed concern about a sin-offering.

items.text: Gemara: Dried figs pressed together vs. loose
items.text_en: Gemara: Dried figs pressed together vs. loose
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya limits the Mishnah to figs pressed together (דְּרוּסוֹת), not loose ones (מְפוֹרָדוֹת). An objection is raised from Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, who permits bringing a barrel of wine and cutting off its top with a sword on Shabbat. The Gemara deflects that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Nechemiah. Rava explains the difficulty: why teach 'dried figs' specifically? It implies they are pressed together.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya limits the Mishnah's allowance to dried figs that are pressed together (דְּרוּסוֹת), excluding loose ones (מְפוֹרָדוֹת).
The Gemara questions whether loose figs are indeed excluded, implying a challenge to Rabbi Oshaya's distinction.

An objection is raised from Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's baraita, which permits bringing a barrel of wine and cutting off its top with a sword on Shabbat, seemingly contradicting the limitation to pressed figs.
The Gemara deflects the objection by asserting that the baraita follows the Sages (רבנן), while the Mishnah follows Rabbi Nechemiah's stricter view.

The Gemara questions why Rabbi Oshaya went to the trouble of interpreting the Mishnah as Rabbi Nechemiah and about pressed figs, rather than simply interpreting it as about loose figs and following the Sages.

Rava explains that the Mishnah itself forced Rabbi Oshaya's interpretation: why specify 'dried figs' (גרוגרות) rather than 'fruits' (פירות)? This implies the figs are pressed together, a distinct case.

items.text: Baraitot about baskets of figs and dates
items.text_en: Baraitot about baskets of figs and dates
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one permits loosening, untying, and cutting baskets of figs and dates; the other permits only loosening. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one follows the Sages, the other follows Rabbi Nechemiah, who holds that even a ladle, cloak, or knife may only be used for their intended purpose.

sub.desc_en: A baraita permits loosening, untying, and cutting baskets of figs and dates on Shabbat.
A second baraita permits only loosening, but not untying or cutting.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one baraita follows the Sages, the other follows Rabbi Nechemiah.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Nechemiah's position
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Nechemiah's position
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Nechemiah's ruling that even a ladle, cloak, or knife may only be used for their intended purpose, explaining the stricter baraita.

items.text: Piercing a barrel with a drill on Shabbat
items.text_en: Piercing a barrel with a drill on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet whether one may pierce a barrel with a drill on Shabbat: is he intending to make an opening (forbidden) or for a pleasing appearance (permitted)? Rav Sheshet rules it is forbidden. An objection is raised from Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel's case of cutting off the top with a sword, but the Gemara distinguishes: there it is clearly for appearance, while here if it were for appearance, one would simply open it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet whether piercing a barrel with a drill on Shabbat is forbidden because one intends to make an opening, or permitted because one intends for a pleasing appearance.
Rav Sheshet rules that one intends to make an opening, so it is forbidden.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that one may cut off the top of a barrel with a sword on Shabbat, implying that such an action is permitted.

The Gemara resolves that in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's case, the intent is clearly for a pleasing appearance, whereas here, if the intent were for appearance, one would simply open the barrel normally.

items.text: Dispute about piercing the stopper: top vs. side
items.text_en: Dispute about piercing the stopper: top vs. side
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages is only about piercing the top, but from the side all agree it is forbidden, as the Mishnah says 'do not pierce it from the side.' Rav Chisda says the dispute is about the side, but on top all agree it is permitted, and the Mishnah's 'from the side' refers to the side of the barrel itself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages is only about piercing the top of the stopper, but from the side all agree it is forbidden, citing the Mishnah's phrase 'do not pierce it from the side.'

Rav Chisda counters that the dispute is about piercing from the side, but on top all agree it is permitted, and explains that the Mishnah's 'from the side' refers to the side of the barrel itself, not the stopper.

items.text: Making a new hole vs. adding to an old one
items.text_en: Making a new hole vs. adding to an old one
items.desc_en: A baraita states: one may not make a new hole on Shabbat, but if one wants to add to an existing hole, he may add. Some say one may not add. All agree that one may open an old hole from the start. The first Tanna asks: why is a new hole different? Because he is making an opening; adding also makes an opening! Rabba explains that by Torah law, any opening not for entering and exiting is not an opening, but the Sages decreed due to a chicken coop hole, which is for air. Adding is permitted because one is unlikely to add to a chicken coop.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rules: one may not make a new hole on Shabbat, but may add to an existing one; some say one may not add; all agree one may open an old hole.
The first Tanna asks: why is a new hole different from adding? Both involve making an opening.

Rabba explains that by Torah law, an opening not for entering and exiting is not considered an opening; the Sages decreed only due to a chicken coop hole for air, and adding is permitted because one is unlikely to add to a chicken coop.

items.text: Dispute about adding to a vessel and ruling by Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Dispute about adding to a vessel and ruling by Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute about whether one may add to a vessel on Shabbat due to the concern of 'richsha' (a type of work). Rav Nachman rules in accordance with the lenient opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute about adding to a vessel on Shabbat due to the concern of 'richsha' (a type of work), with one opinion forbidding and another permitting.
Rav Nachman rules in accordance with the lenient opinion that one may add to a vessel.

items.text: Distinction between reinforcing and preserving a barrel
items.text_en: Distinction between reinforcing and preserving a barrel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel distinguishing between piercing a barrel in a place meant for preserving (permitted) and reinforcing (forbidden). Rav Chisda and Rava debate the definition of these places.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all agree one may pierce an old hole in a barrel לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel distinguishing between a hole in a place meant for preserving (permitted) and reinforcing (forbidden).
The Gemara asks for the practical definitions of a preserving place versus a reinforcing place.
Rav Chisda defines: above the wine level is for preserving, below the wine level is for reinforcing.
Rava argues that even below the wine level is for preserving, and only below the lees is for reinforcing.

items.text: Abaye supports Rava with a baraita about a sealed house
items.text_en: Abaye supports Rava with a baraita about a sealed house
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a baraita to support Rava's view, comparing the laws of a sealed house to the barrel case, showing that a partition that serves as a guard is significant.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about a sealed house to support Rava's position, showing that a partition that serves as a guard is significant.

items.text: Dispute about cutting a reed (gubta) on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about cutting a reed (gubta) on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree about cutting a reed that is not properly prepared. The Gemara explains the reasoning: one fears it may lead to cutting for its own sake, the other does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding cutting a reed (גובְתָּא) that is not properly prepared, explaining that the one who forbids fears it may lead to cutting for its own sake, while the one who permits does not.

items.text: Support from a baraita and Rabbi Yoshiya's leniency
items.text_en: Support from a baraita and Rabbi Yoshiya's leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about cutting a reed on Yom Tov and Shabbat, with Rabbi Yoshiya being lenient. It clarifies that the dispute is about a cut that is not properly prepared, and Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi rules like Rabbi Yoshiya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that forbids cutting a reed on Yom Tov, and certainly on Shabbat, with Rabbi Yoshiya being lenient.
The Gemara asks to which part of the baraita Rabbi Yoshiya's leniency applies, rejecting both the first part (cutting) and the last part (returning) as implausible.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is about a cut that is not properly prepared, where one side decrees a prohibition lest one come to cut for the ideal standard, and the other does not.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi rules in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yoshiya's lenient position.

items.text: Dispute about oil in a perforated vessel
items.text_en: Dispute about oil in a perforated vessel
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree about using oil in a vessel that was perforated before Shabbat. Rav forbids due to a decree lest one come to use wax, while Shmuel permits. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Chanah reports that Rav explicitly permitted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah's case of a perforated vessel and presents Rav's prohibition versus Shmuel's permission regarding oil.
The gemara explains the reasoning: the one who forbids decrees due to wax, while the one who permits does not decree.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Chanah to Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Chanah to Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Chanah reports to Rav Yosef that Rav explicitly permitted oil in a perforated vessel.

items.text: Dispute about using a myrtle branch (tarfa de'asa) on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about using a myrtle branch (tarfa de'asa) on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Shmuel forbids using a myrtle branch due to a decree. Rav Yeimar and Rav Ashi debate the reason: one says it is because of a drainpipe, the other says lest one break it. The difference is if it is already broken and placed.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel forbids using a myrtle branch (טרפא דאסא) on Shabbat.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Shmuel's prohibition.
Rav Yeimar explains the prohibition is a decree due to a drainpipe (מרזב).
Rav Ashi explains the prohibition is a decree lest one break the branch (שמא יקוטם).
The Gemara notes the practical difference between the two explanations: a branch that is already broken and placed (דקטים ומנח).

items.text: Dispute about sitting on a bench (bei sadya) and Rav's practice
items.text_en: Dispute about sitting on a bench (bei sadya) and Rav's practice
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree about sitting on a bench on Shabbat. The Gemara explains the distinction between soft, hard, and medium benches. It then clarifies that Rav's own practice was not due to prohibition but out of respect for his teachers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about sitting on a bench (bei sadya) on Shabbat: Rav forbids and Shmuel permits, with the distinction between soft, hard, and medium benches.
The Gemara clarifies that Rav's own practice of not sitting on a bench was not due to prohibition but out of respect for his teachers, Rav Kahana and Rav Asi.

items.text: Mishnah: Placing food in water and drying clothes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Placing food in water and drying clothes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permitted actions on Shabbat: placing a cooked dish in a pit to preserve it, mixing good water with bad to cool it, warming cold water in the sun, and drying wet clothes in the sun but not in public.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permitted actions on Shabbat: placing a cooked dish in a pit, mixing good water with bad, warming cold water in the sun, and drying wet clothes in the sun but not in public.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's rulings
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why each ruling is necessary, explaining that the Mishnah teaches that there is no decree lest one come to dig a pit or to hide food in embers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's ruling about placing a dish in a pit is necessary, suggesting it might be obvious.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that there is no decree lest one come to level holes in the pit.
The Gemara questions why the ruling about placing good water in bad water is necessary, noting it is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the latter clause about placing cold water in the sun is necessary.
The Gemara questions why the ruling about placing cold water in the sun is necessary, suggesting it is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that there is no decree lest one come to insulate the water in hot ashes.

items.text: Dispute about drying clothes in private due to mar'it ha'ayin
items.text_en: Dispute about drying clothes in private due to mar'it ha'ayin
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that wherever the Sages prohibited due to mar'it ha'ayin, it is forbidden even in private. The Mishnah's ruling that one may dry clothes in the sun but not in public is presented as a dispute with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon who forbid entirely.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that wherever the Sages prohibited due to מראית העין (appearance of prohibition), it is forbidden even in the innermost chambers.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah, which permits drying clothes in the sun but not in public, implying that in private it is allowed.
The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute between Tannaim: the first Tanna permits in private, while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon forbid entirely, supporting Rav's ruling.

items.text: Rav Huna begins a new statement
items.text_en: Rav Huna begins a new statement
items.desc_en: Rav Huna begins to speak, but the text cuts off, indicating the start of a new discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna begins a statement, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening ruling on shaking a garment
items.text_en: Opening ruling on shaking a garment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who shakes out a garment on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering, but this only applies to new black garments that one is particular about.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that shaking out a garment on Shabbat incurs a sin-offering, but only for new black garments that one is particular about.

items.text: Stories of Ulla and Abaye regarding shaking garments
items.text_en: Stories of Ulla and Abaye regarding shaking garments
items.desc_en: Ulla saw rabbis shaking their cloaks and declared them desecrators of Shabbat, but Rav Yehuda and Abaye argued that since they were not particular about the dust, it was permitted.

sub.desc_en: Ulla arrives in Pumbedita, sees rabbis shaking their cloaks, and declares they are desecrating Shabbat.
Rav Yehuda tells the rabbis to continue shaking their cloaks in Ulla's presence, since they are not particular about the dust.
Abaye hesitates to give Rav Yosef his hat due to dew, but Rav Yosef instructs him to shake it off, as they are not particular about cleanliness.

items.text: The law of a folded garment on the shoulder
items.text_en: The law of a folded garment on the shoulder
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who goes out with a folded garment on his shoulder on Shabbat is liable, and this is supported by a baraita about merchants. The same applies to a storekeeper going out with money tied in his cloth, and to rags-men going out with kerchiefs on their shoulders.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) rules that one who goes out with a folded cloak resting on his shoulder on שבת (Shabbat) is חייב חטאת (liable to bring a sin-offering).
A ברייתא (baraita) supports this, stating that clothing merchants who go out with folded cloaks on their shoulders on שבת (Shabbat) are liable, and the rule applies to all people, not just merchants.

The same rule applies to a חנוני (shopkeeper) who goes out with coins bound in his cloth, and to רטנים (runners) who go out with kerchiefs on their shoulders, with the generalization that the rule applies to all people.

items.text: The story of Hurqanos and the ruling on a kerchief
items.text_en: The story of Hurqanos and the ruling on a kerchief
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda relates that Hurqanos went out with a kerchief on his shoulder with a fringe wound around his finger, and the Sages ruled that even without the fringe it is permitted. Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda rules that the halacha is that it is permitted even without the fringe.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda relates the story of Hurqanos who went out on Shabbat with a kerchief on his shoulder, with a fringe wound around his finger.
When the matter came before the Sages, they ruled that it is permitted even without the fringe wound around the finger.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda teaches in the name of Rav Chisda that the הלכה (binding law) is that it is permitted even without the fringe wound around his fingers.

items.text: The prohibition of making a marzev on Shabbat
items.text_en: The prohibition of making a marzev on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Ulla was asked about making a marzev on Shabbat and ruled it forbidden, with Rabbi Zeira explaining it refers to Babylonian purses. Rabbi Yirmeya then asked about various cases, and Rav Pappa gave a general rule: anything intended for gathering is forbidden, but for adornment is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Ulla is asked whether one may make a marzev on Shabbat.
Ulla rules that making a marzev is forbidden, citing Rabbi Ilai.
The gemara asks what a marzev is.
Rabbi Zeira explains that a marzev refers to Babylonian purses.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about various cases of making a marzev.
Rabbi Zeira answers that each case is forbidden.
Rav Pappa gives a general rule: anything intended for gathering (לכּנופי) is forbidden, but for adornment (להתנאות) is permitted, citing Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi who adorned himself with his cloak.

items.text: Dispute about Rabbi's action with his garment
items.text_en: Dispute about Rabbi's action with his garment
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi and Ravin report different versions of a story where Rabbi went out with both ends of his garment on his shoulder, and was questioned by Yehoshua ben Ziruz or Yehoshua ben Kefusai about whether this was prohibited. Rabbi responded that the earlier sages were not so stringent, and then let his garment down.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi went out with both ends of his garment on his shoulder, and Yehoshua ben Ziruz questioned whether Rabbi Meir would have deemed this liable for a sin-offering; Rabbi responded that Rabbi Meir was not so stringent, and then let his garment down.
Ravin reports a different version: the questioner was Yehoshua ben Kefusai, who asked about Rabbi Akiva's position, and Rabbi gave the same response and let his garment down.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda's clarification
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda's clarification
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda clarifies that the incident was reported with the word 'נשאל' (was asked), implying the question was posed as a halachic inquiry rather than a challenge.

items.text: Mishnah: Bathing and drying on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bathing and drying on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who bathes in cave or Tiberias water may dry himself even with ten towels, but may not carry them in his hand. However, ten people may dry themselves with one towel and carry it. It also lists various prohibited activities like rubbing, scraping, and setting bones.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins analyzing the Mishnah, noting that cave water is compared to Tiberias water in that both are hot, and that the Mishnah's phrasing implies it is only permitted after the fact, not initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by analyzing the Mishnah's comparison of cave water to Tiberias water, noting both are hot, and infers from the Mishnah's phrasing that bathing in them is only permitted בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה (a-priori).

items.text: Dispute about immersing the whole body in water on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about immersing the whole body in water on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous mishnah permitting immersing the whole body even initially as following Rabbi Shimon, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir prohibits, Rabbi Shimon permits, and Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between hot and cold water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous mishnah permitting immersing the whole body even לכתחילה (the ideal standard) as following Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir prohibits, Rabbi Shimon permits, and Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between hot and cold water.

items.text: Explanation of the mishnah about drying with a towel
items.text_en: Explanation of the mishnah about drying with a towel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the mishnah states both that one may dry with a single towel and that one may not bring ten towels: the first clause teaches that even a single towel might lead to wringing, and the second that even with many towels, the many people remind each other not to wring.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah's first clause teaches a leniency (even one towel might lead to wringing) and the second clause teaches a stringency (even many towels, the many people remind each other not to wring).

items.text: Baraita about drying with a towel and handing it to attendants
items.text_en: Baraita about drying with a towel and handing it to attendants
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may dry with a towel and leave it in a window, but should not give it to bath attendants because they are suspected of wringing it out. Rabbi Shimon permits drying with one towel and bringing it into one's house.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one may dry with a towel and leave it in a window, but not give it to bath attendants who might wring it; Rabbi Shimon permits drying with one towel and bringing it home.

items.text: Abaye asks about the halakha; four opinions cited
items.text_en: Abaye asks about the halakha; four opinions cited
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef for the halakha. Rav Yosef lists four authorities: Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan. The Gemara then elaborates each: Rabbi Shimon permits; Rabbi recounts bringing oil and towels on Shabbat; Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan both rule that one may dry with a towel and bring it into the house.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef for the halakha regarding drying with a towel on Shabbat.
Rav Yosef lists four authorities whose rulings bear on the question: Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon's position is the one already stated earlier (permitting drying with a towel).
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi recounts that when studying with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa, they would carry oil and towels across domains on Shabbat to reach a spring for bathing.
The Gemara cites Shmuel's ruling via Rav Yehuda: one may dry with a towel and bring it into the house.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: the halakha is that one may dry with a towel and bring it into the house.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's position resolved
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's position resolved
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's ruling because he elsewhere holds that the halakha follows an anonymous mishnah, which forbids bringing ten towels. The resolution is that the mishnah was taught by Ben Chachinai, not as an anonymous mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's ruling because he elsewhere holds that the halakha follows an anonymous mishnah, which forbids bringing ten towels.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah was taught by Ben Chachinai, not as an anonymous mishnah, so Rabbi Yochanan's principle does not apply.

items.text: Laws about bath attendants and garments
items.text_en: Laws about bath attendants and garments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that bath attendants may bring women's garments to the bathhouse provided they cover the head and most of the body. A סִכְנִיתָא requires tying both ends below the shoulders. Rava instructs the people of Mechoza to tie garments below the shoulders when bringing them to soldiers.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that bath attendants (אולירין) may bring women's garments to the bathhouse, provided the garments cover the woman's head and most of her body.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan adds that a סִכְנִיתָא (a specific type of garment) requires tying both ends below the shoulders.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that 'below' means below the shoulders.
Rava instructs the people of Mechoza to tie garments below the shoulders when bringing them to soldiers.

items.text: Rubbing the stomach on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rubbing the stomach on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita permits anointing and rubbing the stomach on Shabbat as long as it is not done in the weekday manner. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says one anoints first then rubs; Rabbi Yochanan says one anoints and rubs simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The baraita permits anointing and rubbing the stomach on Shabbat, provided it is not done in the weekday manner.
The gemara asks how one should perform the anointing and rubbing.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says one anoints first and then rubs.
Rabbi Yochanan says one anoints and rubs simultaneously.

items.text: Prohibition of standing in the Diomsit bath and its duration
items.text_en: Prohibition of standing in the Diomsit bath and its duration
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan forbids standing on the floor of the Diomsit bath because it acts as a laxative. Rav says the Diomsit season lasts 21 days including the עצרת. A question arises whether the עצרת is at the beginning or end; Shmuel's statement suggests it is at the end, but the Gemara questions if that applies here due to heat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not perform עמילה (rubbing/working the body) on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan forbids standing on the floor of the Diomsit bath because it acts as a laxative and healer (i.e., it is a prohibited medical treatment).
Rav states that the Diomsit season lasts 21 days, including the עצרת (the festival of Shavuot).
The Gemara raises a question: is the עצרת counted at the beginning or the end of the 21-day period?
The Gemara brings Shmuel's statement that all irrigation waters improve from the time of the slaughter (of the Passover offering) until the עצרת, suggesting the עצרת is at the end.
The Gemara rejects the proof: in Shmuel's case, cold weather improves the water, but here the Diomsit bath's benefit is from heat, so the timing may differ.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Arach and the danger of wine and water of Diomsit
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Arach and the danger of wine and water of Diomsit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo says the wine of Perugita and the water of Diomsit caused the ten tribes to be exiled. Rabbi Elazar ben Arach was drawn to them and forgot his learning; when he tried to read 'החודש הזה לכם' he said 'החרש היה לבם'. The rabbis prayed for him and his learning returned. This is the basis for Rabbi Nehorai's teaching to flee to a place of Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo states that the wine of Perugita and the water of Diomsit caused the ten tribes to be exiled from Israel.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Arach
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Arach
sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rabbi Elazar ben Arach was drawn to these places, forgot his learning, and mistakenly read 'החרש היה לבם' instead of 'החודש הזה לכם', until the rabbis prayed for his return of knowledge.

The gemara cites the mishnah of Rabbi Nehorai (identified as Rabbi Nechemya or Rabbi Elazar ben Arach) who teaches to flee to a place of Torah, and explains his name means 'one who enlightens the eyes of the sages in halacha.'

items.text: Prohibition of scraping with a scraper on Shabbat
items.text_en: Prohibition of scraping with a scraper on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita prohibits scraping with a scraper on Shabbat. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits scraping normally if one's feet are dirty with mud. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's mother made him a silver scraper.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the general prohibition against scraping with a scraper on Shabbat, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permitting scraping normally if one's feet are dirty.
A brief anecdote reports that Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's mother made him a silver scraper, illustrating practical use.

items.text: Reason for not descending into the קורדימא
items.text_en: Reason for not descending into the קורדימא
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the reason one may not descend into the קורדימא (a type of bath) is because of פיקא (a type of impurity or danger).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's prohibition against descending into the קורדימא (a type of bath).
The Gemara answers that the prohibition is due to פיקא (a type of impurity or danger).

items.text: Making אפיקטויזין (emetics) on Shabbat
items.text_en: Making אפיקטויזין (emetics) on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the prohibition of making אפיקטויזין applies only with a spice, but with the hand it is permitted. Rabbi Nechemya adds that even on a weekday it is forbidden because it spoils food.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not make אפיקטויזין (emetics) on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan limits the prohibition: it applies only with a spice (סם), but using the hand is permitted.
A baraita adds that Rabbi Nechemya forbids making אפיקטויזין even on a weekday because it spoils food.

items.text: Setting a child's limb on Shabbat
items.text_en: Setting a child's limb on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan permits setting a child's limb on Shabbat. The Gemara questions this against the mishnah that prohibits it, and resolves that the mishnah refers to the vertebrae, which looks like building.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one may not set a child's limb on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan permits setting a child's limb on Shabbat.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's ruling against the mishnah that forbids it.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah refers to the vertebrae, which looks like building, while Rabbi Yochanan permits setting other limbs.

items.text: Setting a broken bone on Shabbat
items.text_en: Setting a broken bone on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss the prohibition of setting a broken bone on Shabbat, citing a statement from Rabbi Chana Bagdata'ah in the name of Shmuel, but the segment ends abruptly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not set a broken bone on Shabbat.
Rabbi Chana Bagdata'ah begins to cite a statement from Shmuel regarding the Mishnah's ruling, but the text breaks off.

items.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's challenge to Rav Yehudah's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's challenge to Rav Yehudah's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah arrives in Pumbedita and avoids Rav Yehudah's lecture. Rav Yehudah sends an attendant to embarrass him, but during the lecture Rav Yehudah teaches that one may not reset a broken bone. Rabbah bar bar Chanah then cites a tradition from Shmuel that the halakhah permits it, and Rav Yehudah objects that he was not informed of this tradition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah teaches that one may not reset a broken bone on Shabbat.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites a tradition from Shmuel that the halakhah permits resetting a broken bone.
Rav Yehudah objects that he was not informed of this tradition and questions whether he was rightfully embarrassed.

items.text: Rav Avya's hand injury and Rav Yosef's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Avya's hand injury and Rav Yosef's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Avya dislocates his hand while sitting before Rav Yosef and asks about treatment. Rav Yosef initially rules it is forbidden, but then Rav Avya's hand heals on its own. Rav Yosef cites the Mishnah that one may not treat a dislocation with cold water but may bathe normally, and then questions the contradiction with Shmuel's lenient ruling. Rav Yosef resolves that each ruling applies in its own context.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya dislocates his hand while sitting before Rav Yosef and asks twice whether he may reset it, receiving a prohibition each time, and his hand swells.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's question to Rav Avya
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's question to Rav Avya
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites the Mishnah that one may not treat a dislocation with cold water but may bathe normally, and if it heals, it heals.
Rav Avya objects that the Mishnah forbids resetting a broken bone, but Shmuel's tradition permits it.
Rav Yosef dismisses the objection, stating that Shmuel's ruling applies only where it was explicitly stated, not to all cases.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The standard formula 'Hadran alach Chavit' marks the end of the chapter.

sub.desc_en: Opening: The standard formula 'Hadran alach Chavit' marks the end of the chapter.

items.text: Mishnah: Borrowing and lending on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Borrowing and lending on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one may ask a friend for jars of wine or oil on Shabbat, provided one does not use the word 'loan' (הלויני). Similarly, a woman may ask for loaves. If the friend does not trust him, he may leave his cloak as collateral and settle accounts after Shabbat. The same applies on Passover eve that falls on Shabbat in Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may borrow wine or oil from a friend on Shabbat without using the word 'loan', and similarly a woman may borrow loaves; if the lender does not trust the borrower, the borrower may leave a garment as collateral and settle accounts after Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between 'borrow' and 'loan'
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between 'borrow' and 'loan'
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye why the Mishnah distinguishes between 'borrow' (השאילני) and 'loan' (הלויני). Abaye explains that 'borrow' does not lead to writing, while 'loan' might. The Gemara questions why the same concern does not apply on weekdays, and Abaye answers that on Shabbat the distinction is noticeable because the Sages only permitted 'borrow', so one will not come to write.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye: why does the Mishnah distinguish between 'borrow' (השאילני) and 'loan' (הלויני)? Abaye answers: 'borrow' does not lead to writing, while 'loan' might lead to writing (a promissory note), which is forbidden on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Why women do not change their water-drawing practice on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Gemara: Why women do not change their water-drawing practice on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye why women do not vary their method of drawing water on Yom Tov, given the principle to make changes where possible. Abaye explains that any change would either increase walking or increase carrying, so no change is feasible.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye why women do not change their usual practice when filling jugs with water on Yom Tov, given the principle that one should make changes to distinguish Yom Tov from weekdays.
Abaye answers that it is impossible to change because using a smaller jug increases walking, and using a larger jug increases carrying, so no alternative is feasible.

items.text: Covering a barrel with a cloth
items.text_en: Covering a barrel with a cloth
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers covering a barrel with a cloth, which might lead to squeezing, or with a lid, which might break and lead to tying. It concludes that it is impossible to do so on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers covering a barrel with a cloth (leading to squeezing) or a lid (leading to tying), concluding it is impossible on Shabbat.

items.text: The principle of leaving Israelites alone
items.text_en: The principle of leaving Israelites alone
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye why people clap and dance on Yom Tov despite the prohibition, and why women sit at the entrance of an alley. Abaye responds that it is better for them to act inadvertently than intentionally, and this applies even to Torah law, as seen with Yom Kippur additions.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye why people clap and dance on Yom Tov despite the mishna's prohibition, and why women sit at the alley entrance despite Rava's ruling.
Abaye responds that it is better for Israelites to act inadvertently than intentionally, so we do not rebuke them.
The Gemara considers whether this principle applies only to rabbinic prohibitions but not to Torah prohibitions.
The Gemara concludes that the principle applies equally to Torah prohibitions, as seen with the Torah-mandated addition to Yom Kippur where people eat until dark and we do not rebuke them.

items.text: Lending loaves and the opinion of Hillel
items.text_en: Lending loaves and the opinion of Hillel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits a woman to lend loaves to her friend on Shabbat, but the Gemara questions whether this contradicts Hillel's ruling against lending without setting a price due to potential usury. It resolves that Hillel's concern applies only where prices fluctuate, not where they are fixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's allowance for a woman to borrow loaves from her friend on Shabbat implies that on a weekday it is permitted, which would contradict Hillel's ruling that one must set a price to avoid usury.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Hillel rules that a woman may not lend a loaf without first setting its monetary value, lest wheat prices rise and she come to violate the prohibition of interest.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a place where prices are fixed, where the Mishnah's leniency applies, and a place where prices fluctuate, where Hillel's concern about usury applies.

items.text: Dispute over a loan on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Dispute over a loan on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef and Rabbah argue whether a loan given on Yom Tov can be collected in court. Rav Yosef says no, to prevent writing, while Rabbah says yes, to avoid preventing joy. The Mishnah's case of leaving a cloak as collateral supports Rav Yosef's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about a loan given on Yom Tov: Rav Yosef says it cannot be collected in court.
Rabbah argues that the loan can be collected, otherwise people would refrain from lending and miss the joy of Yom Tov.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case of leaving a cloak as collateral, which supports Rav Yosef's view that the loan cannot be collected immediately.
The Gemara objects: if the loan can be collected, why does the Mishnah require leaving a cloak rather than simply giving the money and suing?
Rav Yosef explains that the borrower prefers not to go to court, so he leaves a cloak as collateral instead.

items.text: Support from the case of a cow slaughtered on Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Support from the case of a cow slaughtered on Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin brings a baraita about a cow slaughtered on Rosh Hashanah where the meat is considered a loan that is remitted in the Sabbatical year. The Gemara analyzes this to support Rav Yosef's view, distinguishing between cases where the debtor must declare remission and where he need not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin cites a baraita about a cow slaughtered on Rosh Hashanah, where the meat is subject to shemittah remission if the month is intercalated, otherwise not.
The Gemara questions how the baraita can use the term 'משמט' (remits) if the loan is not subject to collection at all, as per Rav Yosef's view.
The Gemara answers that the case is different because it became revealed that the day was actually a weekday (the month was not intercalated), so the loan is a regular one.
The Gemara challenges from the baraita's second clause: if the month is not intercalated, the meat is not remitted; this supports Rav Yosef's view that the loan is not subject to collection.
The Gemara answers that even if the loan is not subject to collection, if the debtor voluntarily pays, the creditor may accept it.
The Gemara objects: does this imply that in the first clause (intercalated month) if the debtor pays, the creditor may not accept?
The Gemara resolves that in the first case the debtor must verbally declare remission, while in the second case he need not, citing the mishnah about returning a debt in the Sabbatical year.

items.text: Practices of Rav Avya and Rabbah bar Ulla
items.text_en: Practices of Rav Avya and Rabbah bar Ulla
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Avya would take a pledge for a loan, while Rabbah bar Ulla would employ a legal stratagem to avoid the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Avya would take a pledge for a loan on Yom Tov, while Rabbah bar Ulla would employ a legal stratagem to avoid the prohibition.

items.text: Dedicating a Paschal lamb on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dedicating a Paschal lamb on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one may dedicate his Paschal lamb on Shabbat and his Festival offering on Yom Tov. The Gemara supports this from the Mishnah, explaining that it applies when others join in, and that the dedication is only rabbinic. It resolves a contradiction with another mishnah by distinguishing between obligations with a fixed time and those without.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one may dedicate his Paschal lamb on Shabbat and his Festival offering on Yom Tov.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's case of one who leaves his cloak as a pledge on Shabbat eve of Passover supports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah deals with one who already designated the animal and merely enrolls others to join, so the animal is already consecrated from the outset.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly prohibits enrolling partners on an animal for the first time on Yom Tov.
The Gemara distinguishes that since the person is a regular customer of the shepherd, it is as if he enrolled from the outset.
Rabbi Hoshaya teaches a baraita that one may go to a regular shepherd, take a lamb, consecrate it, and fulfill his obligation with it on Shabbat.
The Gemara answers that there too, since he is a regular customer, he effectively consecrated it from the outset.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly says 'consecrates', implying a new act of consecration.
The Gemara answers that the consecration referred to is only a rabbinic 'consecration of value' (הקדש עילוי), not a full biblical consecration.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Yochanan's own principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Yochanan's own principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan himself rules that the halacha follows an anonymous Mishnah, which prohibits consecrations on Yom Tov and all the more so on Shabbat.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between obligations with a fixed time (like the Paschal lamb), which may be consecrated on Shabbat, and those without a fixed time, which may not.

items.text: Mishnah: Counting guests and casting lots
items.text_en: Mishnah: Counting guests and casting lots
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may count his guests and dishes orally but not from writing, and may cast lots with his family over portions, provided he does not intend to exchange large for small portions. Lots may be cast for sacred matters on Yom Tov but not for portions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for counting guests and casting lots on Shabbat and Yom Tov.

items.text: Debate on the reason for the prohibition
items.text_en: Debate on the reason for the prohibition
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi and Abaye offer two reasons for the Mishnah's prohibition: concern that one might erase the writing (Rav Bibi) or that one might read mundane documents (Abaye). The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between them and answers: writing on a wall that is high up—according to Rav Bibi there is no concern, but according to Abaye there is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's prohibition.
Rav Bibi answers that the prohibition is a decree (גזירה) lest one erase the writing.
Abaye answers that the prohibition is a decree lest one read mundane documents (שטרי הדיוטות).
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two reasons.
The Gemara answers: the difference is writing on a high wall — according to Rav Bibi there is no concern, but according to Abaye there is.

items.text: Objection to Rav Bibi from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Bibi from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Bibi's position: if the concern is erasing, why not also worry about reading? Moreover, is there no concern for erasing? A baraita prohibits reading by candlelight even at a great height, implying concern for tilting the lamp, which could lead to erasing. This challenges Rav Bibi's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Bibi's position: if the concern is erasing, why not also worry about reading? Moreover, is there no concern for erasing?
The Gemara cites a baraita that prohibits reading by candlelight even at a great height, implying concern for tilting the lamp, which could lead to erasing.

items.text: Refined distinction: writing on a wall that can be erased
items.text_en: Refined distinction: writing on a wall that can be erased
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises the practical difference: writing on a wall that can be erased—according to Rav Bibi there is concern, but according to Abaye there is no concern, since a wall is not confused with a document.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises the practical difference: writing on a wall that can be erased—according to Rav Bibi there is concern, but according to Abaye there is no concern, since a wall is not confused with a document.

items.text: Further distinction: writing on a tablet or pinax
items.text_en: Further distinction: writing on a tablet or pinax
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes another difference: writing engraved on a tablet or pinax—according to Rav Bibi there is no concern, but according to Abaye there is concern. An objection is raised: a baraita permits counting from writing on a wall but not from a tablet or pinax, implying concern for reading even on a tablet, which challenges Rav Bibi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to the opinion that the concern is lest one read, why not also worry lest one erase?

The Gemara resolves: the practical difference between the two opinions is a case of writing engraved on a tablet or pinax—according to Rav Bibi there is no concern, but according to Abaye there is concern.
The Gemara objects: according to Rav Bibi, why not also worry lest one read from the tablet?
The Gemara suggests a possible answer: a tablet or pinax is not confused with a document, so reading from it does not lead to reading documents.
A baraita is cited: one may count from writing on a wall but not from writing on a tablet or pinax, implying concern for reading even on a tablet, which challenges Rav Bibi.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbah's statement reflects a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbah's statement reflects a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that Rabbah's statement (that reading is prohibited even at a great height) is itself a matter of Tannaitic dispute. A baraita records that Rabbi Acha permits reading from writing on a wall, implying that the concern for erasing is not universally accepted. Thus, Rav Bibi's position aligns with the Tanna who permits reading from a high wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances of the baraita? If the writing is engraved, why distinguish between a wall and a tablet?
The Gemara deduces that the baraita must refer to writing that is merely etched (not engraved), where the concern for erasing applies only to a tablet, not a wall.
The Gemara resolves: actually the case is writing high on a wall, and the difficulty from Rabbah is resolved because Rabbah's statement reflects a Tannaitic dispute.
A baraita is cited: one may count guests orally but not from writing, yet Rabbi Acha permits reading from writing on a wall, showing a dispute.
The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances of this baraita? If the writing is low, why not worry about erasing?
The Gemara concludes: it must be writing high on a wall, and thus Rabbah's statement is indeed a Tannaitic dispute, as proven.

items.text: Analogy to the dispute about mirrors on Shabbat
items.text_en: Analogy to the dispute about mirrors on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara draws an analogy to a Tannaitic dispute about looking in a mirror on Shabbat: Rabbi Meir permits a fixed mirror but not a portable one. The Gemara explains that the issue is with a metal mirror, which one might use to trim loose hairs, as per Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara draws an analogy between the dispute about reading from a wall and a Tannaitic dispute about mirrors on Shabbat, where Rabbi Meir permits a fixed mirror but not a portable one.
The Gemara questions why a fixed mirror is different from a portable one, since in both cases one might forget and come to trim hairs.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the dispute concerns a metal mirror, which is forbidden because one might use it to trim loose hairs, as per Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha.

items.text: Prohibition of reading writing under images and gazing at idols
items.text_en: Prohibition of reading writing under images and gazing at idols
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that writing that runs under a figure or portrait is forbidden to read on Shabbat, and looking at the portrait itself is forbidden even on weekdays due to the verse 'Do not turn to idols,' interpreted by Rabbi Chanin as 'do not turn your mind to them.'

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that writing running under a figure or portrait is forbidden to read on Shabbat.
The baraita adds that gazing at the portrait itself is forbidden even on weekdays, citing the verse 'Do not turn to idols.'
Rabbi Chanin interprets the verse homiletically: 'Do not turn your mind to them,' explaining the prohibition of gazing at idols.

items.text: Mishnah continuation: casting lots with family vs. others
items.text_en: Mishnah continuation: casting lots with family vs. others
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may cast lots with his sons and household members but not with others. The Gemara explains the reason: as per Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, members of a group who are particular with each other violate prohibitions of measures, weights, counting, and lending and repaying on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may cast lots with his sons and household members but not with others.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's distinction.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel explains that members of a group who are particular with each other violate prohibitions of measures, weights, counting, and lending and repaying on Yom Tov.

items.text: Permissibility of casting lots with family and the exception for large portions
items.text_en: Permissibility of casting lots with family and the exception for large portions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the leniency for casting lots with family extends to large portions, and explains that the Mishnah is incomplete: it permits even a large portion against a small one with family, but with others it is prohibited due to gambling (קוביא).

items.text: Clarification of 'but not on portions' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarification of 'but not on portions' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Bat Yaakov explains that the Mishnah's restriction 'but not on portions' refers to portions of non-sacred food on a Festival, countering a possible derivation from the verse that would forbid even non-sacred portions.

items.text: One who causes another's punishment is excluded from God's presence
items.text_en: One who causes another's punishment is excluded from God's presence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Bat Yaakov states that one who causes another to be punished is not admitted into God's presence. The Gemara seeks a proof, initially considering the spirit of Naboth in Ahab's story, but rejects it. It then derives the principle from verses about Nebuchadnezzar and Zedekiah, and finally from 'also punishing the righteous is not good'.

items.text: Etymology of 'chalashim' as lots
items.text_en: Etymology of 'chalashim' as lots
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that 'chalashim' means lots from the verse about the fall of Heilel ben Shachar, and Rabba bar Rav Huna explains that Nebuchadnezzar cast lots to determine which noble to sodomize.

items.text: Nebuchadnezzar's punishment and the fate of the wicked
items.text_en: Nebuchadnezzar's punishment and the fate of the wicked
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that no one laughed during Nebuchadnezzar's reign. Rabbi Yitzchak says it is forbidden to stand in his house. Rav Yehuda describes how Nebuchadnezzar's foreskin was stretched 300 cubits when he sought to harm Zedekiah, and how the wicked trembled when he descended to Gehinnom, but a heavenly voice declared his place is with the uncircumcised.

items.text: Opening Aggadah about Solomon's greatness
items.text_en: Opening Aggadah about Solomon's greatness
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an aggadic tradition about King Solomon's dominion over animals, citing a verse to support the claim that he rode a lion and bound a serpent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an aggadic tradition about King Solomon's dominion over animals, citing a verse to support the claim that he rode a lion and bound a serpent.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition of hiring workers on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition of hiring workers on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not hire workers on Shabbat, nor ask a friend to hire workers, and one may not go to the boundary to hire workers or bring produce, but may go to guard and bring produce in hand. Abba Shaul adds a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: One may not hire workers on Shabbat, nor ask a friend to hire workers; one may not darken the techum to hire workers or bring produce, but may darken to guard and bring produce in hand. Abba Shaul's rule: whatever I am entitled to say, I may darken for.
Rav Papa answers: the friend is a non-Jew (gentile), so the prohibition of hiring on Shabbat does not apply.
Rav Ashi objects: even speaking to a gentile on Shabbat is a shevut (rabbinic prohibition), so how can hiring be permitted?

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about the friend
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about the friend
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the distinction between 'himself' and 'his friend', initially suggesting the friend is a gentile, but Rav Ashi objects that speaking to a gentile is a rabbinic prohibition. Rav Ashi then explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who permits hinting to a friend.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah distinguishes between 'himself' and 'his friend' regarding hiring workers on Shabbat.
Rav Pappa answers that 'his friend' refers to a gentile, for whom speaking is permitted.
Rav Ashi objects that speaking to a gentile is itself a rabbinic prohibition (שבות), so the distinction is not justified.
Rav Ashi resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who permits hinting to a friend, so the distinction is between a direct command and a hint.

items.text: Ruling and rationale of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
items.text_en: Ruling and rationale of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who derives from a verse that speech is prohibited but thought is permitted on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who derives from the verse 'ממצוא חפצך ודבר דבר' that speech is prohibited but thought is permitted on Shabbat.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding thought in holy places
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding thought in holy places
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan permits thought everywhere except the bathhouse and latrine, implying thought is like speech, yet he also says thought is permitted on Shabbat. The Gemara resolves that the exception is due to the requirement of holiness, and the verse about nakedness is needed for Rav Yehuda's ruling about a naked gentile.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan permits thought everywhere except the bathhouse and latrine, implying thought is like speech, yet he also says thought is permitted on Shabbat.
Rava answers that the exception is due to the requirement of holiness (וְהָיָה מַחֲנֶיךָ קָדוֹשׁ), which is absent in the bathhouse and latrine.
The Gemara objects that the same holiness requirement applies here due to the verse 'וְלֹא יִרְאֶה בְךָ עֶרְוַת דָּבָר' (and no nakedness be seen in you).
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the verse is needed for Rav Yehuda's ruling that one may not recite Shema (קריאת שמע) in front of a naked gentile.
The Gemara questions why the ruling specifically mentions a gentile, as the same prohibition would apply to a naked Israelite.

The Gemara answers that the ruling uses a 'לָא מִיבַּעְיָא' (it is not necessary to say) structure: it is obvious for an Israelite, but for a gentile, whose flesh is compared to a donkey, one might think it is permitted, so the verse teaches it is forbidden.
The Gemara objects: one might still say that the gentile's nakedness is indeed considered proper (and thus permitted)?

The Gemara resolves the objection by citing the verse 'וְעֶרְוַת אֲבִיהֶם לֹא רָאוּ' (and they did not see their father's nakedness), which teaches that even the nakedness of a gentile is considered עֶרְוָה (nakedness) and is forbidden.

items.text: Proof that speech for mitzvah purposes is permitted
items.text_en: Proof that speech for mitzvah purposes is permitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the notion that speech is prohibited, citing numerous examples where rabbis permitted speaking about mitzvah matters on Shabbat, such as calculating mitzvah accounts, arranging charity, and attending to communal needs. The verse is reinterpreted to forbid only one's own affairs, not heavenly matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the premise that speech is prohibited on Shabbat, asking rhetorically whether speech is indeed forbidden.
Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna both rule that calculating mitzvah-related accounts is permitted on Shabbat, implying speech for mitzvah purposes is allowed.
Rabbi Elazar adds that one may allocate charity to the poor on Shabbat, another example of permitted speech for mitzvah purposes.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan permits attending to life-saving matters and communal needs on Shabbat, including going to synagogues to oversee public affairs.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan further permits going to theaters, circuses, and basilicas on Shabbat to attend to communal needs.
The Tanna of the school of Menashe permits arranging betrothals for children and teaching a child a trade on Shabbat, further demonstrating permitted speech.

The Gemara resolves the challenge by reinterpreting the verse 'מִמְּצוֹא חֶפְצְךָ וְדַבֵּר דָּבָר' (from pursuing your business and speaking a matter) to forbid only one's own affairs (חפציך), while heavenly matters (חפצי שמים) are permitted.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on permissible calculations
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on permissible calculations
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that calculations of 'what if' and 'already spent' are permitted on Shabbat, and a baraita supports this distinction.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda (in name of Shmuel) — final ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda (in name of Shmuel) — final ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel gives the final ruling: calculations for royal or governmental accounts are permitted on Shabbat.
A baraita confirms: calculations of past or future events are forbidden, but those of royal accounts are permitted.

items.text: Mishnah: Calculating expenses on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Calculating expenses on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may calculate expenses that have already been incurred, but not future expenses. The Gemara questions this distinction and explores the reasoning behind it.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's logic: why is it permissible to calculate past expenses but not future ones? It suggests that the difference lies in whether the worker's wages are already owed (past) or not yet owed (future).

items.text: Story of a pious man who refrained from repairing a breach on Shabbat
items.text_en: Story of a pious man who refrained from repairing a breach on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A story is told about a pious man who decided not to repair a breach in his field on Shabbat, and a miracle occurred: a caper bush grew and provided sustenance for him and his household. This illustrates the reward for honoring Shabbat.

items.text: Permitted speech on Shabbat: stating intent to go to a specific place
items.text_en: Permitted speech on Shabbat: stating intent to go to a specific place
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Shmuel teaches that one may tell a friend on Shabbat that he intends to go to a certain place tomorrow, provided there are guards (burganim) to prevent violation of the Sabbath boundary.

items.text: Mishnah: No darkening of the Sabbath boundary to hire workers or bring produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: No darkening of the Sabbath boundary to hire workers or bring produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one should not darken (i.e., light lamps) within the Sabbath boundary to hire workers or bring produce. The Gemara clarifies that hiring workers is forbidden because one cannot pay them on Shabbat, but bringing produce is permitted if there is a partition (mechitzah) to allow carrying.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's teaching: no darkening for straw and hay
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's teaching: no darkening for straw and hay
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya teaches that one should not darken the Sabbath boundary to bring straw or hay. The Gemara questions how one can bring straw if it is detached (not connected to the ground), and explains that it is possible with dry straw (seriah) that can be carried.

items.text: Mishnah: Darkening permitted for bride and deceased
items.text_en: Mishnah: Darkening permitted for bride and deceased
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may darken (light lamps) within the Sabbath boundary for the needs of a bride or a deceased person. The Gemara explains that for a bride, one may bring a myrtle branch (asa), and for a deceased, one may bring an ark and shrouds. However, for other needs, it is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: why bride and deceased are exceptions
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: why bride and deceased are exceptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a bride and a deceased are exceptions. For a bride, one can find a myrtle branch (asa) to bring; for a deceased, one needs an ark and shrouds. The Gemara suggests that if there is a partition (mechitzah), one could bring these items even for other needs, but the Mishnah specifically permits only for bride and deceased.

items.text: Further reasoning: why other needs are forbidden despite possible partitions
items.text_en: Further reasoning: why other needs are forbidden despite possible partitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues to analyze: why are other needs forbidden even if there are partitions? It suggests that for a bride, one may need to bring a myrtle branch that is not attached (not mechubar), and for a deceased, one may need to bring a shroud that is not attached. The Gemara then questions whether one can bring these items if they are attached, and concludes that the prohibition stands.

items.text: Discussion on the requirement of Havdalah before performing tasks
items.text_en: Discussion on the requirement of Havdalah before performing tasks
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the requirement to perform Havdalah (separation between holy and profane) before doing any work on Saturday night. It cites Rabbi Elazar ben Antigonus in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, stating that one must not do tasks before Havdalah. The Gemara then questions whether Havdalah can be done in prayer or over a cup, and addresses the practical issue of having a cup in the field.

items.text: Alternative Havdalah formula: 'Who separates between holy and profane'
items.text_en: Alternative Havdalah formula: 'Who separates between holy and profane'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba tells Rav Asi that in the West (Eretz Yisrael), they use the formula 'Who separates between holy and profane' (hamavdil bein kodesh lechol) for Havdalah, and they also perform other necessary tasks. Rav Asi confirms that when he was at Rav Kahana's, they said this formula and then sifted (siltei) something.

items.text: General principle by Abba Saul: all that I etc.
items.text_en: General principle by Abba Saul: all that I etc.
items.desc_en: Abba Saul states a general principle: 'All that I...' (the full phrase is not provided in the excerpt). The Gemara then asks: who is Abba Saul? It suggests either the first Tanna (Arisha) or the later one, and discusses the context of the Mishnah about not darkening the Sabbath boundary to hire workers.

items.text: Clarifying Abba Shaul's statement
items.text_en: Clarifying Abba Shaul's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the wording of Abba Shaul's statement, suggesting it should be reversed. It explains that Abba Shaul is referring to the latter clause of the Mishnah and is arguing with the first Tanna about the permissibility of asking another to guard produce within their respective techums.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Abba Shaul's wording, arguing that the statement should logically be reversed: 'All that I am not entitled to say, I am not entitled to darken for.'
The Gemara answers that Abba Shaul is referring to the latter clause of the Mishnah, and his statement should be read as 'All that I am entitled to darken for, I am entitled to say.'

The Gemara resolves that Abba Shaul is arguing with the first Tanna, citing Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Shmuel that one may ask another to guard produce within their respective techums, and Abba Shaul challenges the first Tanna to admit this is permitted.

items.text: The 'rule' of Abba Shaul and its application
items.text_en: The 'rule' of Abba Shaul and its application
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Abba Shaul's rule: anything one is permitted to say (ask another to do) on Shabbat, one may darken to the techum to do. It then explains that the word 'rule' in the Mishnah includes the case of bringing an animal from outside the techum by calling it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the wording of Abba Shaul's rule, asking what the word 'כלל' (rule) comes to include.
The Gemara answers that the word 'כלל' includes the case of bringing an animal from outside the techum by calling it, as taught by the Rabbis.

items.text: Darkening for the needs of a bride or a corpse
items.text_en: Darkening for the needs of a bride or a corpse
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may darken to the techum to attend to the needs of a bride or a corpse, including bringing a coffin and shrouds. One may instruct a messenger to go to a specific place, and if not found there, to another, and to pay more if necessary. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that one should not mention a specific sum.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may darken to the techum to attend to the needs of a bride or a corpse, including bringing a coffin and shrouds.
The Mishnah details that one may instruct a messenger to go to a specific place, and if not found there, to another, and to pay more if necessary.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that one should not mention a specific sum when instructing the messenger.

items.text: Mishnah: Darkening for bride and corpse, and gentile's actions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Darkening for bride and corpse, and gentile's actions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah reiterates that one may darken to the techum for a bride or corpse. If a gentile brought flutes on Shabbat, a Jew may not eulogize with them unless they came from a nearby place. If a gentile made a coffin or dug a grave for a Jew, the Jew may be buried in it, but if done specifically for a Jew, it may never be used.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on 'nearby place'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on 'nearby place'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'nearby place' means. Rav says it means literally nearby (within the techum). Shmuel says we are concerned that the flutes may have come from outside the wall (the techum), so they are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'nearby place' means in the Mishnah.
Rav says 'nearby place' means literally nearby, within the techum.
Shmuel says we are concerned that the flutes may have come from outside the wall (the techum), so they are forbidden.

items.text: Support for Shmuel from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Support for Shmuel from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah supports Shmuel, as it says if a gentile made a coffin or dug a grave, a Jew may be buried in it, implying it is permitted due to doubt (perhaps it was not done for the Jew). Similarly, regarding flutes, the doubt allows leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's ruling that if a gentile made a coffin or dug a grave for a Jew, the Jew may be buried in it, that the leniency is based on doubt, supporting Shmuel's position.

items.text: Support for Rav from a baraita about a bathhouse
items.text_en: Support for Rav from a baraita about a bathhouse
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav: in a city with Jews and gentiles, if a bathhouse heated on Shabbat, one may bathe immediately after Shabbat if the majority are gentiles, but must wait if the majority are Jews. Rabbi Yehuda adds a condition about a small bathhouse with a prominent person. The Gemara explains 'reshut' as a person with ten slaves who heat ten kettles at once.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What does 'reshut' mean? Rav Yehuda citing Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda explains: If there is an important person with ten slaves heating ten kettles simultaneously in a small bath — it is permitted to bathe immediately.
Rabbi Yehuda adds a condition: in a small bathhouse with a 'reshut' (prominent person), one may bathe immediately.
The Gemara asks what 'reshut' means in Rabbi Yehuda's statement.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that 'reshut' refers to a prominent person with ten slaves who heat ten kettles at once in a small bathhouse, permitting immediate bathing.

items.text: Why no waiting for the coffin and grave?
items.text_en: Why no waiting for the coffin and grave?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not require waiting for the coffin and grave to be made (like the bathhouse case). Ulla answers that the case is where the grave is already standing by the roadside. Rabbi Abahu adds that the coffin is already placed on the grave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah permits immediate burial without waiting for the coffin and grave to be made, analogous to the bathhouse case.
Ulla answers that the case is where the grave is already standing by the roadside.
The Gemara objects that while the grave's readiness is explained, the coffin's readiness remains unaddressed.
Rabbi Abahu answers that the coffin is already placed on the grave.

items.text: Mishnah: Preparing the corpse on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Preparing the corpse on Shabbat
