items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all needs of the dead may be done on Shabbat: anointing and washing, but without moving a limb. The pillow is removed from under the corpse and it is placed on sand so it decomposes quickly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that all needs of the dead may be performed on Shabbat, including anointing and washing without moving a limb, and removing the pillow to place the corpse on sand for faster decomposition.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Tying a jaw or supporting a beam
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Tying a jaw or supporting a beam
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may tie a jaw (of a corpse) not to raise it but to prevent it from sagging further, and similarly support a broken beam with a bench or bed legs not to raise it but to prevent further collapse.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from a bathhouse incident
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from a bathhouse incident
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's leniency by citing Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel: a student of Rabbi Meir entered a bathhouse after him and was told not to wash or anoint the floor, implying that even preventing deterioration is prohibited on Shabbat.

items.text: Clarification: 'All' includes vessels for a corpse
items.text_en: Clarification: 'All' includes vessels for a corpse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's inclusive language comes to include the practice of bringing metal and cooling vessels to place on a corpse's stomach to prevent bloating, and plugging its orifices to prevent air entry.

items.text: Solomon's allegory and the fate of gluttons
items.text_en: Solomon's allegory and the fate of gluttons
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets Solomon's verses about old age as referring to the spine, genitals, stomach, and feces. It then cites a teaching that those who abandon Torah and live in constant festivity will have their stomachs burst after three days, with the stomach rebuking them.

items.text: Mishnah: No closing the eyes of a dying person
items.text_en: Mishnah: No closing the eyes of a dying person
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not close the eyes of a dying person on Shabbat or even on a weekday at the moment of death, as doing so is considered shedding blood.

items.text: Gemara: The parable of the candle and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's method
items.text_en: Gemara: The parable of the candle and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's method
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the Mishnah with a parable of a flickering candle, and cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who permits a method to close a corpse's eyes by blowing wine into its nose and applying oil to its eyelids.

items.text: A living infant vs. a dead king: Desecrating Shabbat
items.text_en: A living infant vs. a dead king: Desecrating Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that one desecrates Shabbat for a day-old infant but not for King David after death, because a living person can observe many Shabbatot, while a dead person is free from commandments.

items.text: A living infant vs. a dead giant: Fear of animals
items.text_en: A living infant vs. a dead giant: Fear of animals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that a day-old infant needs no protection from weasels or mice, but the dead giant Og needs protection, because a living person inspires fear in creatures, while a dead person does not.

items.text: A lion does not fall on two, and the danger of sleeping alone
items.text_en: A lion does not fall on two, and the danger of sleeping alone
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that a lion does not attack two people, but an objection notes that we see lions attacking two. The Gemara resolves that a person is only vulnerable when they resemble an animal. Rabbi Chanina adds that sleeping alone in a house is forbidden because Lilith seizes one.

items.text: Exhortation to do good while young, and the days of the Messiah
items.text_en: Exhortation to do good while young, and the days of the Messiah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar urges one to do good while able, citing Solomon's verse about old age and the days of the Messiah, which have no merit or liability. This disagrees with Shmuel, who says the only difference between this world and the Messianic era is subjugation to kingdoms.

items.text: The wheel of fortune and the scholar's poverty
items.text_en: The wheel of fortune and the scholar's poverty
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar teaches that one should always pray for mercy regarding poverty, as it cycles through generations. Rav Yosef states that a Torah scholar does not become poor, but if he does, he does not return to his former state.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya's advice on charity and the principle of mercy
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya's advice on charity and the principle of mercy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya tells his wife to give bread to a poor person first so that her children will be treated likewise. He cites the verse and the teaching about the wheel of fortune. Rabbi Gamliel bar Rabbi teaches that one who shows mercy to creatures receives mercy from heaven.

items.text: Allegorical interpretation of old age and the efficacy of eye remedies
items.text_en: Allegorical interpretation of old age and the efficacy of eye remedies
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse about the darkening of sun, moon, and stars as referring to the forehead, nose, soul, and cheekbones. Shmuel says tears return until age forty, and Rav Nachman says eye shadow helps until forty, after which it only holds but does not widen.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's stoicism and the six types of tears
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's stoicism and the six types of tears
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina did not cry at his daughter's death, explaining that two losses (a hen and a lamp) are worse. He follows Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that there are six types of tears: three good and three bad (smoke, weeping, and...).

items.text: Opening allegory: the house of old age
items.text_en: Opening allegory: the house of old age
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a list of items that are good or bad for the body, then immediately interprets the verses of Kohelet 12 as allegories for the aging body: the guards are the loins and ribs, the strong men are the legs, the grinders are the teeth, and the women looking through the windows are the eyes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists items that are bad (house of the toilet) and good (spice, laughter, fruit) for the body.
The Gemara interprets the verses of Kohelet 12 as allegories for the aging body: guards are loins and ribs, strong men are legs, grinders are teeth, women looking through windows are eyes.

items.text: Caesar's question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
items.text_en: Caesar's question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
items.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya why he did not attend the Avidan (a place of debate or entertainment). Rabbi Yehoshua responds with a cryptic riddle about a snowy mountain, its merchants frozen, its dogs not barking, and its mills not grinding, which the Gemara explains as a reference to old age.

sub.text: Caesar's question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.text_en: Caesar's question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya why he did not attend the house of debate.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's poetic answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's poetic answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya answers with a poetic description of old age: snowy mountain, frozen merchants, silent dogs, idle mills, and the saying that before losing, one feels pain.
Bei Rav explains the riddle: 'While we have not yet lost ourselves, we are already in decline' — a reference to the weakening of old age.

items.text: The value of youth and the decline of old age
items.text_en: The value of youth and the decline of old age
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma says two are better than three, and woe to the one that goes and does not return, which Rav Chisda identifies as youth. Rav Dimi adds that youth is like a rose crown, old age like a thorn crown. Rabbi Meir advises to examine the teeth to find the age, citing a verse. Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda to loosen his sack and bring bread, as until forty eating is good, after forty drinking is good.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma
sub.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma saying: two out of three are good, woe to the one that goes and does not return.
Rav Chisda identifies the lost thing as youth, and Rav Dimi adds that youth is a rose crown, old age a willow crown.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: A Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir advises to examine the teeth and find in the gums, citing a verse about satisfaction with bread and goodness.
Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda: until forty, eating is beneficial; after that, drinking is beneficial.
Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda to loosen his sack and bring bread, as until forty eating is good, after forty drinking is good.

items.text: The barber's riddles and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's retort
items.text_en: The barber's riddles and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's retort
items.desc_en: A barber asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha about the distance from his place to Korchin, and Rabbi Yehoshua answers with a riddle. The barber then insults him, and Rabbi Yehoshua responds with a sharp retort. The barber then comments on the dignity of different modes of travel, and Rabbi Yehoshua counters with three good things: beard, wife, and children, blessing God for having spared the barber from them. The barber objects, and Rabbi Yehoshua insists that the retort is a reproof.

sub.desc_en: The barber asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha the distance from his place to Korchin, and Rabbi Yehoshua answers with a riddle.
The barber insults Rabbi Yehoshua, calling him a bald man fleeing at four.
Rabbi Yehoshua retorts that the barber, a rootless uprooted one, is at eight.

items.text: Rabbi's question to Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta about not greeting him
items.text_en: Rabbi's question to Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta about not greeting him
items.desc_en: Rabbi asks Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta why he did not greet him on the festival as his ancestors did. Rabbi Shimon answers with a riddle: rocks became high, close ones became far, two became three, and the peacemaker of the house ceased, alluding to the physical decline of old age.

sub.text: Rabbi's question to Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta
sub.text_en: Rabbi's question to Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta
sub.desc_en: Rabbi asks Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta why they did not greet him on the festival as his ancestors greeted his ancestors.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's poetic answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's poetic answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta answers with a poetic description of old age: rocks became high, near became far, two became three, and the peacemaker in the house ceased.

items.text: Further allegories of old age and Barzillai's testimony
items.text_en: Further allegories of old age and Barzillai's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues interpreting Kohelet 12: the doors in the street are the body's orifices, the sound of the grinding is low because the stomach doesn't grind, the voice of the bird wakes the old man, and the daughters of song are silenced. Barzillai the Gileadite's words to David are cited as proof that the elderly lose their senses of taste, speech, and hearing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the allegorical doors in the street as the body's orifices, the low grinding sound as the stomach's inability to digest, the rising at a bird's voice as the elderly's light sleep, and the silencing of singing daughters as the loss of appreciation for music.
Barzillai the Gileadite's words to David are cited as proof that the elderly lose their senses of taste, speech, and hearing.

items.text: Rav and Rava's critique of Barzillai, and Rabbi Yishmael's praise of Torah scholars
items.text_en: Rav and Rava's critique of Barzillai, and Rabbi Yishmael's praise of Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav says Barzillai was a liar, citing a 92-year-old maidservant who could still taste food. Rava says Barzillai was promiscuous, and promiscuity hastens old age. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei teaches that Torah scholars gain wisdom as they age, while ignoramuses become more foolish.

sub.desc_en: Rav says Barzillai was a liar, citing a 92-year-old maidservant in Rabbi's house who could still taste a dish.
Rava says Barzillai was steeped in lust, and lust causes old age to jump upon a person.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei: Torah scholars gain wisdom in old age, while ignoramuses gain foolishness, citing verses.

items.text: More allegories: fear of heights, the almond tree, and the desire for women
items.text_en: More allegories: fear of heights, the almond tree, and the desire for women
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the remaining verses: even a small mound seems like a mountain, the path is full of terrors, the almond tree is the tailbone, the grasshopper is the sexual organ, and the caperberry is desire. Rav Kahana's story about Rav's sigh at this verse indicates that Rav's desire had ceased. Rav Kahana then explains that 'He spoke and it was' refers to a wife, and 'He commanded and it stood' refers to children, and a Tanna teaches that a woman is a vessel full of filth and blood, yet everyone runs after her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'גַּם מִגָּבוֹהַּ יִירָאוּ' (even from a height they will fear) as referring to the elderly who see even a small mound as a great mountain, and continues explaining the rest of the verse allegorically.
Rav Kahana, while reciting the verse before Rav, sees Rav sigh and infers that Rav's desire (for women) had ceased.
Rav Kahana explains that 'He spoke and it was' refers to a wife, and 'He commanded and it stood' refers to children.
A Tanna teaches that a woman is a vessel full of filth and blood, yet everyone runs after her.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's parable of the righteous in the World to Come
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's parable of the righteous in the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that 'man goes to his eternal home' means each righteous person is given a dwelling according to his honor, like a king and his servants who enter through one gate but lodge according to their status.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation of 'going to his eternal home'
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation of 'going to his eternal home'
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that each righteous person is given a dwelling according to their honor, like a king and his servants entering the city through one gate but lodging according to honor.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak on youth and old age
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak on youth and old age
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak interprets the verse 'For youth and black hair are vanity' to mean that things a person does in youth blacken his face in old age.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation of youth and blackness
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's interpretation of youth and blackness
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that things a person does in youth blacken his face in old age.

items.text: The pain of worms for the dead and the soul's mourning
items.text_en: The pain of worms for the dead and the soul's mourning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says that worms are as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh, citing a verse. Rav Chisda adds that the soul mourns for the deceased for seven days, citing verses about mourning.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak on the pain of worms
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak on the pain of worms
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says that worms are as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rav Chisda on the soul's mourning
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda on the soul's mourning
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda says that a person's soul mourns for him for seven days, citing verses about mourning.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on comforting a mourner without comforters
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on comforting a mourner without comforters
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that if a deceased person has no comforters, ten people should go and sit in his place. The Gemara then begins a story about a neighbor of Rav Yehuda who died and had no comforters.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that for a deceased with no comforters, ten people go and sit in his place.

sub.text: Story of a neighbor of Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Story of a neighbor of Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: A story is told of a neighbor of Rav Yehuda who died and had no comforters.

items.text: Opening story about Rav Yehuda and the dead
items.text_en: Opening story about Rav Yehuda and the dead
items.desc_en: A story is told that Rav Yehuda would carry a dead person for ten days and sit in his place; after seven days, the dead appeared to him in a dream and thanked him for putting his mind at rest.

items.text: Debate about when the dead know what is said before them
items.text_en: Debate about when the dead know what is said before them
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that the dead know what is said before them until the grave is sealed. Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi debate whether this awareness lasts until the grave is sealed or until the flesh decays, each citing a verse.

items.text: Parable of the king and the garments, and its application to the righteous and wicked
items.text_en: Parable of the king and the garments, and its application to the righteous and wicked
items.desc_en: The Sages teach a parable about a king who gave garments to his servants; the wise folded them and the foolish soiled them. The king rewards the wise and punishes the foolish. This is applied to God: for the righteous, the body rests in peace and the soul is bound in the bundle of life; for the wicked, there is no peace and their souls are slung away.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer on the souls of the righteous and wicked
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer on the souls of the righteous and wicked
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that the souls of the righteous are stored under the Throne of Glory, while the souls of the wicked wander and are slung from one end of the world to the other by angels.

items.text: Discussion about the intermediate ones and the fate of the righteous
items.text_en: Discussion about the intermediate ones and the fate of the righteous
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks Rav Nachman about the souls of the intermediate ones. Rav Nachman reports Shmuel's teaching that both the righteous and wicked are handed over to Dumah, but the righteous have rest and the wicked do not. Rav Mari adds that the righteous will eventually become dust, citing a verse.

items.text: Story of Rav Achai bar Yoshiya and Rav Nachman about the resurrection of the righteous
items.text_en: Story of Rav Achai bar Yoshiya and Rav Nachman about the resurrection of the righteous
items.desc_en: Rav Achai bar Yoshiya snorts at some porters in Rav Nachman's land. Rav Nachman questions him, citing Rav Mari that the righteous become dust. Rav Achai responds that this applies only to those with jealousy in their hearts; otherwise, their bones do not decay. He then proves that the righteous will rise, citing a verse about opening graves, and explains that the verse 'for dust you are' refers to one hour before the resurrection.

items.text: Response to a heretic about the soul of Shmuel and the twelve-month period
items.text_en: Response to a heretic about the soul of Shmuel and the twelve-month period
items.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Avahu how Shmuel could be raised by the necromancer if his soul is under the Throne of Glory. Rabbi Avahu answers that this was within twelve months of death, during which the body remains and the soul ascends and descends; after twelve months, the body is nullified.

items.text: Opening statement on the soul's ascent
items.text_en: Opening statement on the soul's ascent
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that the soul ascends and does not descend, setting the stage for a discussion about the afterlife.

items.text: The eulogy as an indicator of one's status
items.text_en: The eulogy as an indicator of one's status
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat quotes Rav that a person's eulogy reveals whether they are a son of the World to Come. Abaye asks Rabba who would eulogize him if everyone hates him, and Rabba replies that Abaye and Rabba bar Rav Chanan suffice.

items.text: Who is a son of the World to Come?
items.text_en: Who is a son of the World to Come?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav who is a son of the World to Come, and Rav answers with a verse. Rabbi Chanina says it is one with whom the Sages are pleased. The Gemara then discusses regional customs regarding eulogies.

items.text: Repent one day before your death
items.text_en: Repent one day before your death
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches Rabbi Eliezer's statement to repent one day before death. His students ask how one knows the day of death, and he explains that one should repent today, lest they die tomorrow. Solomon's verse is cited.

items.text: The parable of the king's feast
items.text_en: The parable of the king's feast
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai tells a parable of a king who invited servants to a feast without a set time. The wise ones prepared and sat at the door, while the foolish went to work. When the king suddenly called, the wise entered adorned and the foolish entered dirty. The king rewarded the wise and punished the foolish. Rabbi Meir's son-in-law adds that both sit, but the wise eat and the foolish are hungry and thirsty, as per the verse.

items.text: Alternate interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Alternate interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Another interpretation: 'Your garments be white' refers to tzitzit, and 'oil on your head' refers to tefillin.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with 'Hadran alach Sho'el'.

items.text: Mishnah: One who is overtaken by darkness on the road
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who is overtaken by darkness on the road
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one is overtaken by darkness on the road, he may give his purse to a gentile. If no gentile is with him, he places it on the donkey. When he reaches the outer courtyard, he removes vessels that may be handled on Shabbat, and for those that may not, he unties the ropes and the sacks fall by themselves.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for giving to a gentile and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for giving to a gentile and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages permitted giving the purse to a gentile because one might otherwise carry it four cubits in the public domain. Rava specifies that this applies only to one's own purse, not to a found object. A dispute arises whether a found object that comes to hand is like one's own purse, and the question remains unresolved.

items.text: Comparison of gentile, donkey, and deaf-mute, imbecile, minor
items.text_en: Comparison of gentile, donkey, and deaf-mute, imbecile, minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if a gentile is available, one gives the purse to him rather than placing it on the donkey, because one is commanded regarding the donkey's rest but not the gentile's. For a donkey versus a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor, one places it on the donkey because the latter are human. Among the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, the imbecile takes precedence.

items.text: Inquiry about deaf-mute versus minor
items.text_en: Inquiry about deaf-mute versus minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry about the precedence between a deaf-mute and a minor, and cites a teaching from Rabbi Yitzchak in the name of Rabbi Eliezer regarding terumah of a deaf-mute, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not take an animal out to non-sacred use because of uncertainty.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not take an animal out to non-sacred use because of uncertainty.

items.text: Gemara's question about terumah and the deaf-mute vs. minor
items.text_en: Gemara's question about terumah and the deaf-mute vs. minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a Mishnah in Terumot regarding five who cannot separate terumah, and debates whether the Mishnah's ruling about a deaf-mute and a minor is because the deaf-mute is given to the minor or vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about the Mishnah in Terumot listing five who cannot separate תרומה (priestly portion), and asks whether the ruling about a deaf-mute and a minor is because the deaf-mute is given to the minor or vice versa.
The Gemara presents two possible interpretations: either the Mishnah gives the deaf-mute to the minor, or it gives the minor to the deaf-mute.
The Gemara records two versions of the answer: some say the Mishnah gives the deaf-mute to the minor, and some say it gives the minor to the deaf-mute.

items.text: The case with no gentile, donkey, deaf-mute, or minor
items.text_en: The case with no gentile, donkey, deaf-mute, or minor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak reveals that there was another case (carrying less than four cubits) that the Sages concealed due to 'The honor of God is to conceal a matter', to prevent one from coming to carry four cubits in the public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the Mishnah lists no gentile, donkey, deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor — what is the 'other' that was hidden?
Rabbi Yitzchak reveals that there was another case (carrying less than four cubits) that the Sages concealed.
The Gemara asks what that other case was, and answers that it was carrying less than four cubits at a time.
The Gemara asks why the Sages did not want to reveal this case, and answers that it is because of the principle 'The honor of God is to conceal a matter'.
The Gemara asks what honor of God is involved here, and answers that revealing this case might lead one to carry four cubits in the public domain.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about the se'ah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about the se'ah
items.desc_en: A baraita records that Rabbi Eliezer said 'on that day they filled a se'ah' and Rabbi Yehoshua said 'on that day they emptied a se'ah', and each gives a parable: Rabbi Eliezer compares to a basket full of cucumbers and gourds that can hold mustard, while Rabbi Yehoshua compares to a bowl full of honey that rejects pomegranates and nuts.

sub.desc_en: The baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says 'on that day they filled a se'ah' and Rabbi Yehoshua says 'on that day they emptied a se'ah'.
Rabbi Eliezer's parable: a basket full of cucumbers and gourds can still hold mustard.
Rabbi Yehoshua's parable: a bowl full of honey rejects pomegranates and nuts.

items.text: Placing a burden on a donkey and the distinction between a friend and a donkey
items.text_en: Placing a burden on a donkey and the distinction between a friend and a donkey
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can place a burden on a donkey if it causes the donkey to work. Rav Adda bar Ahavah answers that one places it on the donkey while it is walking, and removes it when it stands. Rav Pappa distinguishes: what is forbidden with a friend (but exempt from a sin-offering) is permitted with a donkey ab initio.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can place a burden on a donkey on Shabbat, since this causes the donkey to work, violating the prohibition of 'לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה כׇל מְלָאכָה' (you shall not do any work).
Rav Adda bar Ahavah answers that one places the burden on the donkey while it is walking and removes it when it stands, thus avoiding a prohibited act of placing a burden on a stationary animal.

Rav Pappa resolves the distinction: an action that would be חייב חטאת (liable for a sin-offering) if done by one's own body is, when done through a friend, פטור אבל אסור (exempt but forbidden), but when done through one's donkey, it is מותר לכתחילה (permitted ab initio).

items.text: Carrying a bundle on one's shoulder by running
items.text_en: Carrying a bundle on one's shoulder by running
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah teaches that if one's bundle is on his shoulder, he should run under it until he reaches his house, but not walk slowly. The reason is that running provides no recognition, preventing a proper lifting and placing. The Gemara resolves the concern about entering his house by saying he tosses it behind him.

items.text: Liability for causing one's animal to work on Shabbat
items.text_en: Liability for causing one's animal to work on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that one who causes his animal to work on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering if unintentional and stoning if intentional. Rava refutes this with two answers: first, all Torah prohibitions are equated to idolatry requiring a physical act by the person; second, a Mishnah implies there are cases (like techumim and kindling according to Rabbi Yossi) that are not capital offenses.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that one who causes his animal to work on Shabbat is liable for a sin-offering if unintentional and stoning if intentional.
Rava initially supports Rami bar Chama by citing the verse that equates the animal's work to the person's own work, implying the same liability.
Rava objects that all Torah prohibitions are equated to idolatry, which requires a physical act by the person, so one is not liable for causing an animal to work.

Rava further objects by citing a Mishnah that implies there are Shabbat violations (like techumim and kindling according to Rabbi Yossi) that are not capital offenses, contradicting Rami bar Chama's blanket rule.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's statement
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's statement
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that one who bestially copulates with an animal on Shabbat is exempt from a sin-offering if unwitting, but liable for stoning if intentional.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that one who bestially copulates with an animal on Shabbat is exempt from a sin-offering if unwitting, but liable for stoning if intentional.

items.text: Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a Mishnah that states only actions for which one is liable for a sin-offering when unwitting are liable for stoning when intentional, implying that bestiality, which lacks a sin-offering, should not incur stoning.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges: For a Shabbat desecration that carries a sin-offering for unwitting violation, intentional violation is punishable by stoning. But if no sin-offering applies, then stoning also does not apply — contradicting Rami's rule.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the objection
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah does not exclude other cases; rather, it states a general rule, and there are exceptions like bestiality where stoning applies despite no sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies: The statement actually means: For an act that carries a sin-offering for unwitting violation, intentional violation is stoning. But there is also an act that carries NO sin-offering for unwitting violation, yet intentional violation IS stoning — and that act is bestial copulation.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah states a general rule but does not exclude other cases; it then identifies bestiality (מחמר) as an exception where stoning applies despite no sin-offering.

items.text: Textual variant and identity of Rava
items.text_en: Textual variant and identity of Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a textual variant regarding the identity of Rava, and suggests that there may have been two people named Mari bar Rachel.

sub.desc_en: A digression about the identity of Rami bar Chama: Rava is his brother, and some say his father. The later language suggests Rav authorized Rami bar Rachel as a judge in Pumbedita, implying there were two different Rami bar Rachels.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and its rationale
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and its rationale
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who bestially copulates with his animal on Shabbat is exempt from any punishment. The Gemara explains: no sin-offering because all Torah prohibitions are equated to idolatry (which requires intent); no stoning because the Mishnah's rule excludes this case; and no lashes because the negative commandment is a warning for court-imposed death, and such prohibitions are not punishable by lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Yochanan taught a tradition ruling that one who bestially copulates with his animal on Shabbat is exempt from any punishment.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that one who acts unintentionally is exempt from a sin-offering because all Torah prohibitions are equated to idolatry, which requires intent.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that one who acts intentionally is exempt from stoning because the Mishnah's rule only applies to acts that incur a sin-offering when done unintentionally, and this act does not.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that one is also exempt from lashes because the negative commandment involved serves as a warning for court-imposed death, and such prohibitions are not punishable by lashes.

items.text: Clarifying the biblical prohibition
items.text_en: Clarifying the biblical prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote 'you' in the prohibition, implying that only the person is liable, not his animal, even according to the opinion that one is flogged for causing his animal to work.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote 'you' in the prohibition, implying that only the person is liable, not his animal, even according to the opinion that one is flogged for causing his animal to work.

items.text: Rav Huna's solution for glass vessels
items.text_en: Rav Huna's solution for glass vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says that if an animal is carrying glass vessels, one may place cushions under them and untie the ropes so the sacks fall. The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that one may only take vessels that are movable, and Rav Huna's case involves craftsmen's horns that are not fit for use. The Gemara answers that the ropes are small straps, so the cushions are not nullified from their intended use.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if an animal is carrying glass vessels, one may place cushions under them and untie the ropes so the sacks fall.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that one may only take vessels that are movable on Shabbat, implying Rav Huna's cushions are not movable.
The Gemara answers that Rav Huna's case involves craftsmen's horns that are not fit for use, and the ropes are small straps so the cushions are not nullified from their intended use.

items.text: Supporting baraita about glass and untithed produce
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about glass and untithed produce
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if an animal carries untithed produce (טבל) and glass vessels, one may untie the ropes and let the sacks fall even if they break. The Gemara explains that this refers to a coarse basket (כולסא) where the vessels are not fit for use, and the phrase 'even though they break' teaches that we do not worry about a small loss.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if an animal carries untithed produce (טבל) and glass vessels, one may untie the ropes and let the sacks fall even if they break.
The Gemara explains that the baraita refers to a coarse basket (כולסא) where the vessels are not fit for use, just like the untithed produce (טבל) is not fit for the animal.
The Gemara resolves that the phrase 'even though they break' teaches that we do not worry about a small loss.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's method for a load of grain
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's method for a load of grain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches: if an animal carries a sack of grain, one may place his head under it and shift it to the side so it falls by itself.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai permits placing one's head under a sack of grain on an animal and shifting it to the side so it falls by itself.

items.text: The incident with Rabban Gamliel's donkey
items.text_en: The incident with Rabban Gamliel's donkey
items.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel's donkey was loaded with honey and he refused to unload it until after Shabbat, but it died. The Gemara questions why he didn't take the vessels, and answers that the honey had crystallized (הדביש) and was only fit for camel fodder. Further questions about untying ropes or placing cushions are answered: the wineskins would tear, and cushions would become soiled and nullified from use. Rabban Gamliel held that the prohibition of causing pain to animals is only rabbinic, so he prioritized the loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the incident: Rabban Gamliel's donkey was loaded with honey, he refused to unload it until after Shabbat, and it died.
The Gemara asks: Why didn't Rabban Gamliel take the vessels (the honey containers) which are permitted to be moved on Shabbat?
The Gemara answers: The honey had crystallized (הדביש) and was only fit for camel fodder, so the vessels were not considered vessels of permitted use.
The Gemara asks: Why didn't Rabban Gamliel untie the ropes so the sacks would fall off?
The Gemara answers: The wineskins would tear, causing loss.
The Gemara asks: Why didn't Rabban Gamliel bring cushions and place them under the sacks to cushion the fall?
The Gemara answers: The cushions would become soiled and thereby nullified from their designated use (בטול כלי מהיכנו).
The Gemara asks: But there is the concern of causing pain to animals (צער בעלי חיים) — why didn't Rabban Gamliel act to alleviate the donkey's suffering?
The Gemara resolves: Rabban Gamliel held that the prohibition of causing pain to animals is only rabbinic (דרבנן), so he prioritized the financial loss over the rabbinic concern.

items.text: Abaye and Rabbah on using animals indirectly (צדדין)
items.text_en: Abaye and Rabbah on using animals indirectly (צדדין)
items.desc_en: Abaye found Rabbah rubbing his son against a donkey and objected that he was using an animal. Rabbah replied that this is indirect use (צדדין), which the Sages did not prohibit. He supports this from the Mishnah about untying ropes, which he interprets as involving a large saddle (חבר גוולקי) where the action is indirect. The Gemara rejects this, saying it refers to a limb (אבר גוולקי) or a small saddle (לכתא) where there is no indirectness.

sub.desc_en: Abaye found Rabbah rubbing his son against a donkey and objected that he was using an animal.
Rabbah replied that this is indirect use (צדדין), which the Sages did not prohibit.
Rabbah supports his position from the Mishnah about untying ropes, which he interprets as involving a large saddle (חבר גוולקי) where the action is indirect.
The Gemara rejects Rabbah's interpretation, saying the Mishnah refers to a limb (אבר גוולקי) or a small saddle (לכתא) where there is no indirectness.

items.text: Dispute about using a tree for a sukkah on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Dispute about using a tree for a sukkah on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a sukkah with two walls attached to a tree and one by human hands is valid but one may not ascend it on Yom Tov. The Gemara initially thinks this is because using the tree indirectly (צדדין) is forbidden. But it is refuted: if the tree is bent and the sukkah placed on top, one directly uses the tree. The Gemara concludes that the case is where the tree serves merely as a wall (גוואזא פרסיכנא), and the rule is that if removing the tree leaves the sukkah standing, one may ascend on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita: a sukkah with two walls by human hands and one by a tree is valid but one may not ascend it on Yom Tov, implying that indirect use of the tree (צדדין) is forbidden.

The Gemara initially rejects the objection by positing that the case involves a bent tree with the sukkah on top, where one directly uses the tree, but then refutes this by noting that the baraita's second clause permits ascending when three walls are by human hands.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the tree serves merely as a wall (גוואזא פרסיכנא), and the rule is that if removing the tree leaves the sukkah standing, one may ascend on Yom Tov.

items.text: Debate between Tanna'im and Amora'im on צדדין and צדי צדדין
items.text_en: Debate between Tanna'im and Amora'im on צדדין and צדי צדדין
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Meir (permitting ascent) and the first Tanna (prohibiting) is about whether indirect use (צדדין) is permitted. Abaye says all agree צדדין are forbidden, and they dispute about צדי צדדין (secondary indirectness). Rava says that whoever forbids צדדין also forbids צדי צדדין, and whoever permits צדי צדדין also permits צדדין. Rav Mesharshiya challenges Rava from a baraita about a nail, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Meir about ascending a sukkah on Yom Tov is about whether צדדין (indirect use) is permitted.
Abaye rejects the suggestion, arguing that all agree צדדין (indirect use) is forbidden, and the dispute is about צדי צדדין (secondary indirectness).
Rava offers a different analysis: whoever forbids צדדין also forbids צדי צדדין, and whoever permits צדי צדדין also permits צדדין.
Rav Mesharshiya challenges Rava's position by citing a baraita about a nail, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Eruv on a tree: the peg and the basket
items.text_en: Eruv on a tree: the peg and the basket
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one drives a peg into a tree and hangs a basket on it, the eruv is valid only if the basket is below ten handbreadths. The Gemara infers that without the peg, even below ten handbreadths it is invalid, implying that using the tree's sides (צדדין) is forbidden, but using the sides of the sides (צדדי צדדין) is permitted. Rav Pappa explains that the case involves a tight basket that moves the tree when the eruv is taken, thus using the tree itself.

sub.desc_en: Mishnah: If a peg is driven into a tree and a basket hung on it, the eruv is valid only if the basket is below ten handbreadths; if above ten, it is invalid.

Gemara infers: The reason the eruv is valid only below ten is because the peg is driven into the tree; if not driven, even below ten it is invalid — implying that using the tree's sides (צדדין) is forbidden, but using the sides of the sides (צדדי צדדין) is permitted.

Rav Pappa explains: The case involves a tight basket that moves the tree when the eruv is taken, thus using the tree itself; but if the basket is loose, using the tree's sides is forbidden, while using the sides of the sides is permitted.

items.text: Practical ruling: ladder on a palm tree
items.text_en: Practical ruling: ladder on a palm tree
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi applies the ruling that using the sides (צדדין) is forbidden: one should not place a ladder directly on a palm tree, but rather on beams outside the tree, and when climbing, one should not step on the beams but on the rungs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa clarifies: The case is a cramped basket; when taking the eruv, one leans on the tree itself, making the sides forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: preparing animal feed on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: preparing animal feed on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permitted and prohibited actions for preparing animal feed on Shabbat: one may untie bundles of grain and crumble palm branches, but not cedar branches; one may not crush pods or carobs for any animal, except Rabbi Yehuda permits carobs for small animals.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi gives a practical ruling: For a palm tree ladder, don't place it on the tree (sides forbidden), but on beams outside; when climbing, don't step on beams, but on the rungs.

items.text: Rav Huna's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Huna's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that 'פקיעין' and 'כיפין' are the same (two and three strands respectively), while 'זירין' are cedar branches. The Mishnah means one may untie bundles and also crumble, but for cedar branches neither is permitted. Rav Chisda explains Rav Huna's reasoning: we may exert effort with food (מיטרח באוכלא) but not create food (שוויי אוכלא).

sub.desc_en: Mishnah: Permitted to loosen sheaves before animals and to break up figs, but not the bundles. Not to crush carobs or dates before animals, whether thin or thick. Rabbi Yehuda permits carobs for thin animals.
Rav Chisda explains Rav Huna's reasoning: we may exert effort with food (מיטרח באוכלא) but not create food (שוויי אוכלא).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda argues that 'פקיעין' and 'זירין' are the same (two and three strands), while 'כיפין' are cedar branches. The Mishnah means one may untie bundles but not crumble them; for palm branches one may crumble, but for cedar branches only untie, not crumble. Rava explains Rav Yehuda's reasoning: we may create food (שוויי אוכלא) but not exert effort with food (מיטרח באוכלא).

sub.desc_en: Gemara asks: Rav Huna says peki'in (sheaves) and kipin (figs) are distinct; peki'in are two, kipin are three, zir'in are cedar. The Mishnah says: permit to loosen peki'in and to break up kipin, but not zir'in — not to break nor loosen.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's interpretation of the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's interpretation of the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains the Mishnah: for 'פקיעין' one may untie but not crumble; for 'כיפין' one may crumble; for 'זירין' one may neither crumble nor untie.

sub.text: Rava's explanation of Rav Yehuda's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rav Yehuda's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rava explains Rav Yehuda's reasoning: we may create food (שוויי אוכלא) but not exert effort with food (מיטרח באוכלא).

items.text: Challenge to Rav Huna from the Mishnah's ruling on carobs
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Huna from the Mishnah's ruling on carobs
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna: the Mishnah prohibits crushing both pods and carobs, implying carobs are soft like pods, so we do not exert effort with food. Rav Huna deflects by saying carobs are hard like pods, referring to small unripe ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna by citing the Mishnah that prohibits crushing both pods and carobs, inferring that carobs are soft like pods, which contradicts Rav Huna's view that we do not exert effort with food.
Rav Huna deflects the challenge by arguing that the comparison is reversed: carobs are hard like pods, and the Mishnah refers to small unripe carobs (עילי זוטרי).

items.text: Refutation of Rav Huna from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Huna from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that Rabbi Yehuda's permission for carobs for small animals (דקה) implies that for large animals it is forbidden, which fits Rav Huna's view that we may create food but not exert effort. However, if Rav Huna held the opposite, Rabbi Yehuda would permit even for large animals. The Gemara then questions whether 'דקה' means small or large, but a contradiction arises from the Mishnah's earlier clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that Rabbi Yehuda permits carobs for small animals (דקה) but not for large ones, as a challenge to Rav Huna's position.
The Gemara explains that if the first Tanna holds we may not exert effort (מיטרח) but may create food (שוויי), then Rabbi Yehuda's permission for small animals fits as creating food.

The Gemara objects that if the first Tanna holds we may not create food but may exert effort, then Rabbi Yehuda would permit carobs for large animals all the more so, contradicting the Mishnah's limitation.
The Gemara suggests that 'דקה' in Rabbi Yehuda's ruling might not mean small animals literally, but rather large animals that are 'particular' (דייקא) about their food.

The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's earlier clause explicitly distinguishes between 'דקה' and 'גסה', proving that Rabbi Yehuda's 'דקה' means small animals literally, leaving the contradiction unresolved.

items.text: Beginning of a new topic: cutting up animal feed
items.text_en: Beginning of a new topic: cutting up animal feed
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion about cutting up food for animals, but the segment is incomplete.

sub.desc_en: Gemara says: Come and hear: We may cut…
Gemara objects: The Mishnah's opening says 'between thin and thick', implying Rabbi Yehuda's 'daka' means thin literally — contradiction.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Yehuda from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Yehuda from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Yehuda's view that one may not exert effort in preparing animal food on Shabbat, citing the Mishnah that allows placing pumpkins before an animal and carrion before dogs. The Gemara infers that just as carrion is soft, so too pumpkins are soft, implying that effort is permitted.

items.text: Second challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Second challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another challenge from a baraita taught by Rav Chanan from Nehardea, which states that one may crumble straw and alfalfa and mix them. This seems to permit effort in food preparation. The Gemara deflects by saying the straw is old and the alfalfa is small shoots.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of feeding animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of feeding animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not force-feed a camel (אין אובסין) nor cram food (אין דורסין), but one may feed it by hand (מלעיטין). Similarly, one may not perform המראה on calves, but may feed them by hand. One may scatter food for chickens, give water to מורסן (bran mash), but not knead it. One may not give water to bees or dovecote doves, but may give water to geese, chickens, and Herod's doves.

items.text: Definition of אֵין אוֹבְסִין
items.text_en: Definition of אֵין אוֹבְסִין
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what אֵין אוֹבְסִין means. Rav Yehuda explains: one may not create an אֵבוּס (a feed trough) inside the animal's stomach. The Gemara questions whether such a thing exists, and Rav Yirmiya from Diftei testifies that he saw an Arab who fed a camel a kor and then loaded it with a kor.

items.text: Definitions of המראה and הלעטה
items.text_en: Definitions of המראה and הלעטה
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definitions of המראה and הלעטה. Rav Yehuda says: המראה is feeding in a place from which the animal cannot regurgitate, while הלעטה is feeding in a place from which it can. Rav Chisda says: both are in a place from which it cannot regurgitate, but המראה is done with a vessel and הלעטה is done by hand.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Yehuda from the Mishnah's terminology
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Yehuda from the Mishnah's terminology
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rav Yehuda from the Mishnah's use of מְהַלְקְטִין and מַלְקִיטִין. If מְהַלְקְטִין means feeding by hand and מַלְקִיטִין means throwing food before them, then for doves, even throwing is prohibited. The Gemara concludes that מְהַלְקְטִין must mean feeding in a place from which it cannot regurgitate, and מַלְקִיטִין in a place from which it can, implying that המראה is with a vessel, challenging Rav Yehuda.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's defense
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's defense
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda defends his position: מְהַלְקְטִין is feeding by hand, מַלְקִיטִין is throwing. The reason doves cannot be fed by throwing is that their food is not your responsibility, unlike chickens. This is supported by a baraita: one may give food to a dog but not to a pig, because the dog's food is your responsibility.

items.text: Support from the Mishnah's water rule
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah's water rule
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi supports Rav Yehuda from the Mishnah: water is given to geese and chickens but not to bees and doves, because the latter's food is not your responsibility. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifically mentions water, as even grain would be prohibited. The answer is that water is commonly found in swamps, so the prohibition is necessary.

items.text: Homily about the dog and practical advice
items.text_en: Homily about the dog and practical advice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona expounded at the Nasi's gate: God knows the dog's food is limited, so its food stays in its stomach for three days, as taught in a Mishnah about ritual impurity. Rav Hamnuna derives that it is proper to throw a piece of meat to a dog. Rav Mari specifies the amount: the weight of its ear, and a stick after it. This applies in the field, not in town, lest the dog become accustomed. Rav Pappa says: there is none poorer than a dog, and none richer than a pig.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Yehuda's definitions
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Yehuda's definitions
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught in accordance with Rav Yehuda: המראה is when one lays the animal down, opens its mouth, and feeds it carshinim and water at once. הלעטה is when one feeds it standing and gives it carshinim separately and water separately.

items.text: Attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
items.text_en: Attribution of the Mishnah to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
items.desc_en: Abaye reports that he asked his master (Rabbah) about the Mishnah's ruling on מוּרְסָן. His master said it follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that one is not liable for kneading until the final act of mixing. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda would agree regarding מוּרְסָן, which is not subject to kneading. But a baraita explicitly states that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda permits giving water to מוּרְסָן.

items.text: Dispute about kneading roasted grain
items.text_en: Dispute about kneading roasted grain
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: one may not knead roasted grain (קלי). And some say: one may knead. The Gemara asks who are 'some say'? Rav Chisda answers.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's view on mixing shatit
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's view on mixing shatit
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the earlier ruling as that of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, and notes that it applies only when one changes the usual order. Rav Chisda explains that the change is to add the ingredients 'hand by hand' (alternating).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the earlier ruling as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's, and Rav Chisda explains that the change is to add ingredients 'hand by hand' (alternating).

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with the prohibition of kneading
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with the prohibition of kneading
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah permits stirring shatit, but elsewhere it says one may not knead. The resolution is that the Mishnah refers to a thin mixture, while the prohibition is for a thick one. Again, this applies only when one changes the usual order.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah permits stirring shatit, but earlier it was said that one may not knead.
The Gemara resolves: the prohibition of kneading applies to thick mixtures, while stirring is permitted for thin ones, and this applies only when one changes the usual order.

items.text: Rav Yosef's explanation of the change and a story about feeding animals
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's explanation of the change and a story about feeding animals
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that on a weekday one puts vinegar first then shatit, but on Shabbat one puts shatit first then vinegar. A story is told about Levi who found a cattle-feed mixer kneading and feeding his ox; his father rebuked him, citing a ruling from Rav (via Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba) that one may knead but not feed, and if one does not gather with his tongue, they gather for him. This applies only when one changes the usual order.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one changes the order for shatit, and Rav Yosef answers: on a weekday put vinegar first then shatit, on Shabbat put shatit first then vinegar.

A story is told: Levi found a cattle-feed mixer kneading and feeding his ox, struck him, and his father reported Rav's ruling that one may knead but not feed, and if one does not collect with his tongue, they collect it for him.
The Gemara notes that this ruling applies only when one changes the usual order.
The Gemara concludes that this leniency applies only when one changes the usual order.

items.text: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya's explanation: warp and woof
items.text_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya's explanation: warp and woof
items.desc_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya in the name of Abaye explains that the change is to arrange the ingredients like warp and woof (crisscross). The Gemara objects that this does not mix well, and Rav Yehuda answers that one shakes the vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one changes the order for mixing shatit, and Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya in the name of Abaye answers: warp and woof (crisscross pattern).
The Gemara objects that this does not mix well, and Rav Yehuda answers: one shakes it in the vessel.
The Gemara objects that this arrangement does not mix well.
Rav Yehuda answers that one then shakes the vessel to mix the ingredients.

items.text: Ze'eiri's notebook: rulings on kneading and amounts
items.text_en: Ze'eiri's notebook: rulings on kneading and amounts
items.desc_en: Ze'eiri's notebook records that he asked Rabbi (Chiyya) about kneading and was told it is forbidden, but about crumbling (into a dish) it is permitted. Rav Menashya rules that one against one or two against two is fine, but three against two is forbidden. Rav Yosef says even a kav or two kavim is permitted, while Ulla says even a kor or two korim.

sub.desc_en: It is written in Ze'eiri's notebook: he asked Rabbi (Chiyya) about kneading and was told it is forbidden, and about crumbling and was told it is permitted.
Rav Menashya rules: one before one or two before two is permitted, but three before two is forbidden.
Rav Yosef says: a kav or even two kavim is permitted.
Ulla says: a kor or even two korim is permitted.

items.text: Levi's notebook: Rabbi's failed attempt to forbid kneading in Babylonia
items.text_en: Levi's notebook: Rabbi's failed attempt to forbid kneading in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Levi's notebook records that he asked Rabbi (Rabbeinu HaKadosh) about those who knead shatit in Babylonia, and Rabbi cried out against it but no one listened, and he lacked the authority to forbid it because of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's lenient view.

sub.desc_en: It is written in Levi's notebook: he asked before Rabbi (Rabbeinu HaKadosh) about those who knead shatit in Babylonia, and Rabbi cried out but no one listened, and he had no power to forbid based on Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

items.text: Astrological predictions based on day of birth
items.text_en: Astrological predictions based on day of birth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's notebook states that one born on Sunday will be a man with no 'one' in him. The Gemara clarifies this means either entirely good or entirely bad, because light and darkness were created on that day. Similar predictions are given for each day of the week: Monday (angry), Tuesday (rich and promiscuous), Wednesday (wise and bright), Thursday (benevolent), Friday (diligent in mitzvot), and Shabbat (will die on Shabbat, but will be called holy).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's notebook records that one born on Sunday will be a man with no 'one' in him.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'no one in him' and raises a difficulty from Rav Ashi's own birth on Sunday.
The Gemara resolves that 'no one in him' means either entirely good or entirely bad, because light and darkness were created on that day.
The notebook states that one born on Monday will be an angry man because the waters were divided on that day.
The notebook states that one born on Tuesday will be rich and promiscuous because vegetation was created on that day.
The notebook states that one born on Wednesday will be wise and bright because the luminaries were suspended on that day.
The notebook states that one born on Thursday will be benevolent because fish and birds were created on that day.
The notebook states that one born on Friday will be diligent, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies this means diligent in מצוות (commandments).
The notebook states that one born on Shabbat will die on Shabbat, and Rava bar Rav Sheila adds that he will be called holy.

items.text: Astrological predictions based on planetary hour of birth
items.text_en: Astrological predictions based on planetary hour of birth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina tells them to tell bar Levi that not the day's constellation but the hour's constellation determines character. He then lists traits for those born under each planet: Sun (radiant, eats his own, secrets revealed, unsuccessful thief), Venus (rich and promiscuous), Mercury (wise and bright), Moon (sickly, builds and destroys, eats others', successful thief), Saturn (plans fail), Jupiter (righteous), Mars (sheds blood). Rav Ashi adds that a Mars-born could be a surgeon, thief, butcher, or circumciser. Rabba says he was born under Mars, and Abaye notes that Rabba indeed punished and killed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says: not the constellation of the day causes, but the constellation of the hour causes.
One born under the sun will be radiant, eat from his own, his secrets are revealed, and if he steals he will not succeed.
One born under Venus will be rich and promiscuous, because fire was born in it.
One born under Mercury will be bright and wise, because it is the scribe of the sun.
One born under the moon will suffer illnesses, build and destroy, eat from others, his secrets are hidden, and if he steals he will succeed.
One born under Saturn will have his plans nullified, and some say: all who plot against him will have their plans nullified.
One born under Jupiter will be righteous, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: righteous in מצוות (commandments).
One born under Mars will be a shedder of blood, and Rav Ashi explains: either a surgeon, a thief, a butcher, or a circumciser.
Rabba says he was born under Mars, and Abaye comments that the Master also punishes and kills.

items.text: Dispute: Is Israel subject to astrological influence?
items.text_en: Dispute: Is Israel subject to astrological influence?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says that a constellation makes one wise, makes one rich, and Israel is subject to constellations. Rabbi Yochanan says Israel is not subject to constellations, citing the verse 'Do not learn the way of the nations... for the nations are dismayed, but not Israel.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says: a constellation makes one wise, a constellation makes one rich, and Israel has a constellation.
Rabbi Yochanan says: Israel has no constellation, citing the verse 'Do not learn the way of the nations... for the nations are dismayed by them, but Israel is not.'

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's consistency
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's consistency
sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan follows his own reasoning, citing the verse 'Do not learn the way of the nations... for the nations are dismayed, but not Israel' (ירמיהו י:ב) as proof that Israel is not subject to constellations.

items.text: Rav's proof that Israel is not subject to constellations
items.text_en: Rav's proof that Israel is not subject to constellations
items.desc_en: Rav also holds that Israel is not subject to constellations, citing the verse where God took Abraham outside and told him his heir would be his own son. Abraham argued that his astrological chart showed he would not have a son, but God told him to abandon his astrology, as Israel is not subject to constellations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav also holds Israel is not subject to constellations, citing the verse where God took Abraham outside and told him his heir would be his own son.
Abraham argues before God that his astrological chart shows he is not destined to have a son.
God tells Abraham to abandon his astrology, declaring that Israel is not subject to constellations.

items.text: Proof from Samuel that Israel has no mazal
items.text_en: Proof from Samuel that Israel has no mazal
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story of Samuel and Avlet to demonstrate that Israel is not subject to astrological fate. Avlet predicts a man will die from a snake, but Samuel says if he is a Jew he will return. The man returns safely, and a snake is found cut in two. The man explains he performed an act of charity to avoid embarrassing a poor man, and Samuel teaches that charity saves from death itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a proof from Samuel that Israel has no mazal, recounting how Samuel and Avlet sat together and Avlet predicted a man would die from a snake, but Samuel said if he is a Jew he will return.
Avlet finds the snake cut in two, the man explains he performed charity to avoid embarrassing a poor man, and Samuel teaches that charity saves from death itself.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Akiva that Israel has no mazal
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Akiva that Israel has no mazal
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story of Rabbi Akiva's daughter. Astrologers predicted she would die from a snake on her wedding night. She gave her portion of food to a poor man, and the snake was found dead. Rabbi Akiva taught that charity saves from death itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a proof from Rabbi Akiva that Israel has no mazal (astrological destiny), recounting that astrologers predicted his daughter would die from a snake on her wedding night.
The daughter was anxious about the prediction; on her wedding night she took a brooch and stuck it into the wall, which pierced the eye of a snake that had been following her.
Rabbi Akiva asked his daughter what she had done; she explained she gave her portion of food to a poor man, and he taught that charity (צדקה) saves from death itself, not just an unusual death.

items.text: Proof from Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak that Israel has no mazal
items.text_en: Proof from Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak that Israel has no mazal
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's mother. Astrologers said her son would be a thief. She made him cover his head and pray. One day his cloak fell off, he saw a date tree, his evil inclination overcame him, and he climbed and ate dates with his teeth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a proof from Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak that Israel has no mazal (astrological destiny).

sub.text: Story of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's mother
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's mother
sub.desc_en: Astrologers told Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's mother that her son would be a thief, so she never let him go bareheaded.
His mother instructed him to cover his head to instill fear of Heaven and to pray for mercy.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak did not understand why his mother gave him this instruction.
One day his cloak fell off while he was studying under a date palm, his evil inclination overcame him, and he climbed and ate dates with his teeth, fulfilling the astrologers' prediction.

items.text: Mishnah: Cutting animal feed on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cutting animal feed on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may cut gourds for an animal and a carcass for dogs. Rabbi Yehuda says if the carcass was not prepared before Shabbat, it is forbidden because it is not mukan.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that one may cut gourds for an animal and a carcass for dogs on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda adds a condition: if the carcass was not prepared before Shabbat, it is forbidden because it is not מוכן (set aside for use).

items.text: Gemara: Rulings on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Rulings on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara records that Ulla said the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, while Shmuel said it follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a mnemonic sign (עָרֵל שַׁחַז) and introduces the dispute about the halakhic ruling.
Ulla rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Shmuel rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yehuda from Rav and Levi
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yehuda from Rav and Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav also held like Rabbi Yehuda, based on his ruling about bundles of coins. Levi also held like Rabbi Yehuda, as he would only examine a tereifah on Yom Tov while sitting on a stool, lest it be unfit even for dogs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav also held like Rabbi Yehuda, based on his ruling forbidding bundles of coins on Shabbat.
The Gemara notes that Levi also held like Rabbi Yehuda, as he would only examine a tereifah on Yom Tov while sitting on a stool, lest it be unfit even for dogs.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Shimon from Shmuel, Ze'iri, and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Shimon from Shmuel, Ze'iri, and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel said the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, and Ze'iri also held like Rabbi Shimon, as he interpreted a Mishnah about a dead animal to refer to consecrated animals, but for unconsecrated animals it is permitted. Rabbi Yochanan also said the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, but the Gemara questions this because Rabbi Yochanan generally rules like a stam Mishnah, and the Mishnah here is stam.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon.
Ze'iri also holds like Rabbi Shimon, interpreting a Mishnah about a dead animal as referring only to consecrated animals, but for unconsecrated animals it is permitted.
Rabbi Yochanan also says the הלכה follows Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara objects: Does Rabbi Yochanan really say that? He generally rules like a stam Mishnah, and the Mishnah here is stam.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's initial discussion
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's initial discussion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not split wood from beams on Yom Tov. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan teaches this as following Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda. A baraita is brought about starting with a pile of straw but not with wood in the muktzeh, and the Gemara explains that this refers to expensive wood where even Rabbi Shimon agrees it is muktzeh due to financial loss.

sub.desc_en: Mishnah states: one may not split wood from beams on Yom Tov.

items.text: Second baraita and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Second baraita and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Another baraita is brought about watering and slaughtering desert animals versus domesticated ones. Rabbi Yochanan finds another anonymous teaching: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about removing bones and peels from the table on Shabbat. Rav Nachman explains that Beit Shammai follows Rabbi Yehuda and Beit Hillel follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that distinguishes between desert animals (which may not be watered or slaughtered on Shabbat) and domesticated animals (which may).

Rabbi Yochanan finds another anonymous teaching where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute removing bones and peels from the table on Shabbat, and Rav Nachman explains that Beit Shammai follows Rabbi Yehuda and Beit Hillel follows Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about muktzeh
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about muktzeh
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about the halakha regarding muktzeh. One says that throughout Shabbat the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon except for muktzeh due to disgust, like an old lamp. The other says even muktzeh due to disgust follows Rabbi Shimon, except for muktzeh due to prohibition, like a lamp lit that Shabbat, but muktzeh due to financial loss even Rabbi Shimon agrees, as taught in a Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Gemara clarifies: there it refers to expensive cedar/pine wood, which even Rabbi Shimon agrees is muktzeh due to financial loss.
The second opinion (Ravina) holds that even muktzeh due to disgust follows Rabbi Shimon's lenient view, and the exception is only muktzeh due to prohibition (איסור), like a lamp lit that Shabbat.

The Gemara adds that both opinions agree that muktzeh due to financial loss (חסרון כיס) is prohibited even according to Rabbi Shimon, citing a Mishnah that lists a large saw and a plowshare as items that may not be moved on Shabbat.

items.text: Mishnah: Annulling vows and measuring on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Annulling vows and measuring on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one may annul vows on Shabbat and ask about vows that are for the needs of Shabbat. One may also seal a skylight, measure a patch, and measure a mikveh. A story is told about Rabbi Tzadok's father and Abba Shaul ben Botnit who sealed a skylight with a jug and tied a bucket with a reed to check if a cistern had a handbreadth opening, from which we learn that sealing, measuring, and tying are permitted on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Mishnah: one may annul vows on Shabbat, and inquire about vows needed for Shabbat.
The Mishnah lists additional permitted actions: sealing a skylight, measuring a patch, and measuring a mikveh.
The Mishnah recounts a story about Rabbi Tzadok's father and Abba Shaul ben Botnit who sealed a skylight with a jug and tied a bucket with a reed to check if a cistern had a handbreadth opening.
The Mishnah concludes that from their actions we learn that sealing, measuring, and tying are permitted on Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's first inquiry about annulment and asking
items.text_en: Gemara's first inquiry about annulment and asking
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether annulment of vows is permitted only for needs of Shabbat, while asking about vows is permitted for needs but not without need, and that is why they are separated. Alternatively, perhaps annulment too is only for needs, and the separation is because annulment does not require a court while asking does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: perhaps annulment of vows is permitted both for needs and without need, while asking about vows is only for needs, and that is why they are separated in the Mishnah.
The Gemara offers an alternative: perhaps annulment too is only for needs, and the separation is because annulment does not require a court while asking does.

items.text: Resolution from Rav Zutei's baraita
items.text_en: Resolution from Rav Zutei's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from Rav Zutei of the house of Rav Papi that one may annul vows on Shabbat only for the needs of Shabbat, not without need. This supports the possibility that annulment is only for needs.

sub.desc_en: Gemara brings a baraita: one annuls vows on Shabbat only for Shabbat's need.

items.text: Alternative inquiry: annulment time limit
items.text_en: Alternative inquiry: annulment time limit
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version of the inquiry: whether 'for need' applies to both annulment and asking, implying annulment is only for the day (until nightfall), or perhaps 'for need' applies only to asking, but annulment is permitted even without need, implying annulment is all day. The baraita from Rav Zutei resolves that annulment is only for the day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version of the inquiry: whether the phrase 'for need' applies to both annulment and asking (implying annulment is only for the day, until nightfall), or perhaps it applies only to asking, but annulment is permitted even without need (implying annulment is all day).

The Gemara cites a baraita from Rav Zutei of the school of Rav Pappa, which states that annulment of vows on Shabbat is only for the purpose of Shabbat, resolving that annulment is only for the day (until nightfall).

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution and Tannaic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution and Tannaic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi notes that the Mishnah states annulment of vows is all day, with leniencies and stringencies. He explains that this is a dispute between Tannaim: one opinion holds all day, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon say only from time to time (24 hours).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi cites the Mishnah that annulment of vows is all day, with leniencies and stringencies, and explains the practical implications.

Rav Ashi resolves the apparent contradiction by noting that this is a dispute between Tannaim: the Tanna Kamma holds annulment is all day, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon hold it is only from time to time (24 hours).

items.text: Inquiry about asking vows when one had time
items.text_en: Inquiry about asking vows when one had time
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether asking about vows on Shabbat is only when one had no time before Shabbat, or even if he had time. It brings a proof from the rabbis who attended to Rav Zutra bar Rav Zeira and permitted his vow even though he had time.

sub.desc_en: Gemara resolves: annulment is only for Shabbat need, not for non-need.

The Gemara cites an incident where the rabbis attended to Rav Zutra and released his vow on Shabbat, even though he had opportunity before Shabbat, indicating it is permitted even with prior opportunity.

items.text: Story about sealing the skylight and Rav Yehuda's explanation
items.text_en: Story about sealing the skylight and Rav Yehuda's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story of sealing the skylight with a jug and tying the bucket with a reed. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that there was a small alley between two houses where there was impurity, and they needed to measure to see if the impurity could pass.

sub.desc_en: Mishnah: they plugged the light with a stopper and tied the kettle with a rope.
Rav Yehuda explains in the name of Rav that there was a small alley between two houses where there was impurity, and they needed to measure to see if the impurity could pass.

items.text: Baraita about the cracked tub
items.text_en: Baraita about the cracked tub
items.desc_en: The baraita describes a cracked tub placed over a skylight, and the actions of plugging the light with a cake and tying the lid with a reed to check if the tub has a handbreadth opening. This serves as the basis for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes a cracked tub placed over a skylight, and the actions of plugging the light with a cake and tying the lid with a reed to check if the tub has a handbreadth opening.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that from the baraita's actions we learn that one may plug, measure, and tie on Shabbat. This sets up the question about the permissibility of these actions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita's actions that one may plug, measure, and tie on Shabbat.

items.text: Incident with Ulla and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Incident with Ulla and Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Ulla visited the house of the Exilarch and saw Rabbah bar Rav Huna sitting in a water channel and measuring it. Ulla questioned him, arguing that the Sages only permitted measuring for a mitzva, not for non-mitzva purposes. Rabbah bar Rav Huna replied that he was merely occupying himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita's actions that one may plug, measure, and tie on Shabbat.
